en: The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume One.
Expounded by the Great Master Yisong of Tiantai.
Recorded by Ling, a disciple of the Wuyi Gate.
To explain this by means of the scripture, it is divided into two major sections: first, the title; second, the scriptural text. The first section is further divided into two parts:
first, the title of the Dharma, beginning with "Great Buddha"; second, the human title, beginning with "Tang Dynasty. Now, I shall first explain the title of the Dharma.
The twenty characters beginning with "Great Buddha" constitute the general name of this entire scripture. Within this single title, there are both general and specific aspects. The specific title...
The mention of "the Great Buddha" and so forth in the middle [of the text] is established on the basis of the sūtra; it is not without justification.
As stated later in the eighth fascicle, when Mañjuśrī requested the naming of the sūtra, the Tathāgata personally proclaimed it from his golden mouth: "This single sūtra has five aspects."
The first is titled: *The Supreme Jewel Seal of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa-Sitātapatra, the Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions*.
The second is titled: *Protecting Kinsmen and Causes: Delivering Ānanda and the Bhikṣuṇī of this Assembly from their Natures, Attaining the Bodhicitta, and Entering the Ocean of Universal Knowledge*.
The third is titled: *The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Cultivation and Realization*.
The definitive meaning [is as follows]: the fourth is titled *The Great Vaipulya Wondrous Lotus King, the Dhāraṇī-Mantra of the Mother of the Buddhas of the Ten Directions*;
the fifth is titled *The Consecrated Verses, the Śūraṅgama of the Myriad Practices of All Bodhisattvas*.
Thus it was personally proclaimed by the golden mouth of the Tathāgata; the compiler, from among these five titles, retained three and concealed two, thereby forming this single title.
Thus we know that the three characters "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Mahā-buddha-uṣṇīṣa*) are taken abridged from the first title; this is what is meant by "preserving one.

As for the second [title], it is hidden and not preserved. Furthermore, we know that the eight characters "The Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and the Definitive Meaning" (*Tathāgata-rahasya-hetu-bhāvanā-sākṣāt-kriyā-nītārtha*) preserve the entirety of the third title; this is what is meant by "preserving two. As for the fourth, it too is hidden and not preserved.

Furthermore, one should know that among the eight characters of the "Śūraṅgama" of the ten thousand practices of all bodhisattvas, the fifth title is taken as a summary, which means retaining its three essential elements.
Thus it may be seen that the Tathāgata expounded those five kinds through his wondrous wisdom, and the compiler, through his skillful intelligence, compiled this single title;
hence it is called "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (and so forth). This briefly narrates the provenance of the sutra.
Thus it is. To explain its meaning: regarding the three characters of "Great Buddha-Crown" (*Dà fó dǐng*), there have been many ancient interpretations; I shall now cite only one or two.
Some say that the character "Great" (*Dà*) is a praise for the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama, because it is most honored and supreme, just like the crown of a Buddha's head;
therefore, it is called the "Great Buddha-Crown. If explained in this manner, it clearly points to...
"Great" (*mahā*) is the essence of the Dharma, while "Buddha-uṣṇīṣa" (*buddhoṣṇīṣa*) is a metaphor.

If one explains this by means of the Dharma and its metaphor, these three characters—*Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa*—constitute the title of this sutra; the sutra is the sutra that possesses this title. On what explicit textual authority is this meaning based?
It is found only in the following passage, which states: "There is a samādhi named Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa," and does not say "like the Mahā-buddhoṣṇīṣa. Therefore...
This shows that it is incorrect to explain these three characters by means of a dharma-illustration (*dharmanidarśana*). Furthermore, some say:

"Great" (*mahā*) is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), "Buddha" (*buddha*) is Prajñā, and "Crown" (*mudrā*) is Liberation (*vimukti*). This is because they allocate the three characters to the three virtues (*triguṇa*).

If this were so, then in which sūtra are these three virtues not discussed, and in which title are they not expounded? Yet [the proponents] uniquely carve up and divide [the title] using only these three characters.
This arrangement is not only inappropriate in meaning; it is also stylistically unsteady.
From this, we know that interpreting these three characters as the "Three Virtues" is likewise untenable. Ultimately, why is it called the Great Buddha-Crown? There is no other reason:
it is precisely what is referred to below as the "eternally abiding true mind. This eternally abiding true mind is present before you and me right now.

Whether noble or ordinary, defiled or pure, there is none who does not possess [these qualities]. This is truly because, throughout vast kalpas, due to a single moment of non-awakening, one is moved and turned by that ignorance (*avidyā*).
One may, in every thought-moment, engage in conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena; or, in every state of mind, harbor greedy attachment toward all things.
Since it is called "conceptual discrimination," there is no transgression that will not be summoned. Furthermore, since it is called "greedy attachment," [it likewise brings about its retribution].

Consequently, there is no evil they do not commit. Because of this, they invite calamity and create further evil. The eternally abiding true mind, which is fundamentally neither born nor extinguished, is instead turned into something subject to birth and extinction.
The eternally abiding true mind, which is fundamentally without coming or going, is instead turned into something that comes and goes.
Thus, they transmigrate through the three realms and sink into the four modes of birth, like a ring without end or a wheel that never ceases. This is not only the case for sentient beings.
It is so. Although Ānanda is said to have left the household life, he conceived the aspiration for enlightenment upon seeing the marks of the Tathāgata’s thirty-two signs.
Although he is said to be of great learning, he listened to the Dharma conditioned by the sound of the Tathāgata’s eightfold voice and fourfold eloquence.
Consequently, when he encountered the lustful woman Caṇḍā, he was turned by her; when he heard the heterodox incantations of Brahmā, he was likewise captivated and ensnared. To investigate this...
The reason for this is entirely because Ānanda did not recognize the eternally abiding true mind, but instead took only sounds and forms as his concern.
Consequently, when he encountered the Tathāgata, he was transformed by the Tathāgata; when he saw Puṇḍarīka (Dengjia), he was ensnared by Puṇḍarīka.

This was because, while the Tathāgata wished to rescue and protect him, it was not that [the Tathāgata] lacked great supernatural powers; rather, [Ānanda’s] own hands did not provide him aid. It was not that [the Tathāgata] lacked great...

Although he was eloquent in his preaching, his mouth did not utter a single word; instead, light radiated from the crown of his head, and within that light were manifested Buddhas who alone recited the mantra.

Why was this so? It was to ensure that Ānanda would fully comprehend it. Since the Buddha had already stated that these were "manifested" (nirmāṇa), the various marks of the thirty-two marks of a Great Man are themselves non-marks. Furthermore, since the mantra was spoken by these manifested Buddhas, all its eight [lines]...
The fourfold eloquence of sound is sound that is not sound; yet even the marks of the Tathāgata are said to be non-marks—how then can the marks of Caṅkā be taken as marks?

Even the voice of the Tathāgata is said to be non-voice—how then can the voice of the Brahma-mantra be taken as voice? From this, one may understand that what is seen and heard internally is external.
Within these sounds and forms, the entirety of the True Principle (Zhenzong) is present, such that not a single thing can be grasped; yet the eternally abiding true mind manifests spontaneously.

This very eternally abiding true mind—vast, penetrating, perfectly interfused, and all-pervasive—is precisely the "Great" (Da) in the title of this scripture, referring to the Buddha’s Crown (Buddhōṣṇīṣa). This very eternally abiding true mind is luminous, clear, and illuminating...
It is not clearly understood. This is precisely the Buddha of the Great Uṣṇīṣa (Mahā-uṣṇīṣa) mentioned in the title of this present work.
In terms of this eternally abiding true mind, there is nothing that does not surpass it; it is the "uṣṇīṣa" (the crown) of the Great Buddha mentioned in the title.
Thus, the three characters "Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa" are entirely the ontological essence (*dharmatā*) of the eternally abiding true mind. All are due to the Tathāgata’s...

This is the manifestation of the incantation spoken by the Transformation Buddha who emits light from his crown. Specifically, it refers to using a concrete phenomenon to reveal a principle and employing a symbol to indicate a meaning.
What is the phenomenon? What is the symbol? It is the mark of the invisible crown and the Buddha of the unconditioned mind.

What is the meaning? What is the principle? It is precisely the eternally abiding true mind, the wondrously pure and luminous essence. Now that the principle has been revealed, phenomena are likewise the principle;
since the meaning has been made manifest, forms are likewise the meaning. For this reason, it is called the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
As for who can attain the essential principle of this Great Buddha-Usnīsa, it is none other than the Tathāgata; thus, he is called the "Tathāgata.

A Tathāgata is a title for one who has attained the fruit [of enlightenment]. Whereas sentient beings turn their backs on awakening and unite with the dust of the senses, they possess only the "as-it-is" (tathatā) but do not "come" (āgata).
Only the Tathāgata, through the wisdom of wondrous clarity, unites with the Tathāgatagarbha; being both "as-it-is" and "coming," he is therefore so named.
Regarding the Tathāgata, there are three types. First is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata, which refers to Vairocana pervading all places;
it is that wherein not a single form or scent is not the Middle Way. Second is the Sambhogakāya Tathāgata, which refers to the realization of the principle of suchness through the wisdom of suchness;
it is that wherein the principle is suchness and wisdom is suchness. Third is the... [Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata].
The *dharmakāya* Tathāgata is such that wisdom merges with principle (*li*), thereby giving rise to its function; it is like the moon in the sky, whose reflection descends upon the myriad waters.
These three are all those who have attained this. As for the *dharmakāya* Tathāgata, it is neither attained nor un-attained;
that which is attained is precisely the vastness of the Buddha’s crown—pervasive, transparent, and perfectly interfused. The *saṃbhogakāya* Tathāgata...
It is attained through non-attainment. That which is attained is the Buddha who is the Great Uṣṇīṣa, the numinous clarity that penetrates and illuminates.
The Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata’s attainment is itself non-attainment; that which is attained is the Great Buddha’s Most Revered, Supreme, and Exalted Uṣṇīṣa.
Thus, one knows that the Tathāgata is the one who has realized the principle-substance (*dharmatā*) of the Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa. Therefore, it is called the "Great Buddha-uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata. Now...
By what cause does this Tathāgata attain it? Therefore, it is called the "Secret Cause" (*guhyahetu*). As for the Secret Cause:
the Tathāgata takes the principle-substance of the Great Buddha-Crown (*mahā-uṣṇīṣa*) as his causal mind; this is that which is most subtle and secret.
As the subsequent text states: "There is a samādhi named Great Buddha-Crown.
Since it is called a *samādhi* and named "Great Buddha-Crown," one should know that *śamatha* is also named Great Buddha-Crown, and *dhyāna* is also named Great Buddha-Crown.

Regarding *śamatha*: it is the contemplation that all phenomena are empty; this refers to the state where "all is empty because of one emptiness. Regarding *samādhi*, it is the contemplation of one...
All phenomena possess [this nature]; this is what is meant by "in one there is all. In the contemplation of *dhyāna*, all phenomena are centered;
this is what is meant by "in one there is all centering. To raise one is to manifest three; to speak of three is to manifest one.
The perfect fusion of the one and the three is inconceivable; this is the wondrous *śamatha*. It is the Reward Body Tathāgata, by means of the Great Buddha-Crown...
The spiritual luminosity that clearly illuminates the essence of reality is that which serves as the cause for the *samaya* [body].
The *samādhi* is the Nirmāṇakāya Tathāgata, who takes the most supreme and exalted essence of reality of the Great Uṣṇīṣa as his cause. The *dhyāna* is the Dharmakāya Tathāgata.
This takes the vast, penetrating, and perfectly integrated principle-body of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa as its cause; hence it is called "The Secret Cause of the Tathāgata’s Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa.
However, this cultivation is cultivation of the nature (*dharmatā*), and this realization is realization of the nature.

Because it is cultivation of the nature, it is inherently different from the ordinary person who is biased toward the mundane, different from the followers of the Two Vehicles who are biased toward emptiness, and different from those of the partial gradual [approach] who are biased toward...
Among these, those such as the aforementioned people cannot all be said to have cultivated the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).

Only when the Tathāgata brings forth cultivation from the entirety of his nature (*prakṛti*), cultivating that which is inherent within the nature, can it be called the cultivation of the definitive meaning. Because they realize this nature, their realizations are naturally distinct:
some realize the states of celestial demons (*deva*) or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); some realize the states of *śrāvakas* or *pratyekabuddhas*; and some realize the [subsequent] stages.
Regarding the sequential distinctions: those people and others cannot all be said to have realized the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*).
Only the Tathāgata can obliterate cultivation within nature and realize that which is inherently present within nature; only then can it be called the realization of the definitive meaning.

Thus, one should know that by means of the three [practices] of the Great Buddha-Crown, one gives rise to the three [samādhis] such as *śamatha*, and thereby attains the three [bodies] such as the *dharmakāya*.

And thus the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is manifested. Therefore, speaking of them collectively, the "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Tathāgata’s Secret Cause, Cultivation, Realization, and Definitive Meaning" refers to what is possessed by those who have attained the fruit of a Tathāgata. As for those on the causal stage of Bodhisattvas, it is likewise not outside of this.
Hence it says, "all Bodhisattvas. Regarding all Bodhisattvas, speaking generally, there are distinctions of Great and Small, and of partiality.

Because they are not identical, they are called "various" (*zhū*). If we refer to what is specifically indicated in this present sutra, it begins with Dry Wisdom (*gāndhī-prajñā*) and culminates in Wondrous Enlightenment (*miao-jue*);
in between, there are the many stages of the Ten Faiths, the Ten Abidings, and so forth, totaling fifty-seven. Therefore, it says "various bodhisattvas.
Furthermore, these bodhisattvas also take the nature-endowed principle-body of the Great Buddha’s Uṣṇīṣa as the causal basis for their practice. Thus...

It is called the "ten thousand practices" (*sahasra-caryā*). "Practice" takes the sense of advancing toward and attaining as its meaning. Briefly stated, these are the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*); extensively stated, they are the eighty-four thousand dharma-gates.
Now, speaking from a middle standpoint, we simply speak of the ten thousand practices. If sentient beings possess the six obscurations, [the six perfections serve as their remedies].
One counteracts [these afflictions] by practicing the six perfections from the essential nature of the Great Buddha-Crown.
If sentient beings possess eighty-four thousand afflictions, one counteracts them by practicing eighty-four thousand Dharma-gates from the essential nature of the Great Buddha-Crown.

Now, regarding what is called the "ten thousand practices": if even a single moment of thought involves relinquishment, that is itself giving (*dāna*); if a single moment of thought is free from transgression, that is itself ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Even up to a single moment of thought being free from delusion, that is itself wisdom (*prajñā*). As it is with the six perfections (*ṣaṭ-pāramitā*), so it is with the ten perfections (*daśa-pāramitā*).
Since this is so for the ten perfections, it is likewise so for the ten thousand practices. Although there are ten thousand practices, there are none that do not arise from the Great [Vehicle].

One takes the fundamental principle of the Buddha-Usnīṣa as the object of cultivation; thus it is said that the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas are such that one knows the reason why Tathāgatas, as those who have attained the fruit, obtain their fruit is solely through this Great Buddha-Usnīṣa, and the reason why Bodhisattvas, as those who are on the path of cause, accomplish their cause is likewise solely through this Great Buddha-Usnīṣa.
In this way, whether in principle, in practice, or in realization, there is not a single thing that does not reach ultimate perfection.
Because it is firm and solid, it is called *Śūraṅgama*. *Śūraṅgama* is a Sanskrit term; in this [language], it means "the ultimate firmness of all matters.

How is it known that all things are ultimately firm? As explained in the following text, where the Tathāgata, in response to Ānanda, elucidates the destruction of the deluded mind to reveal the true seeing, as well as the individual manifestation of each of the three categories and seven elements.

There is no non-eternal, abiding true mind; it is the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, in response to Purna, that which clarifies the origin of delusion is the Great Nature, which is merely pervasive.
First, it is shown through the negation of all dharmas—from "neither mind nor emptiness" up to "neither permanence, bliss, self, nor purity.

Next, it is shown through the affirmation of all dharmas—from "mind itself is emptiness" up to "mind itself is permanence, bliss, self, and purity. Thus, all dharmas are simultaneously both negated and affirmed.
Third, from "the mind is empty" up to "permanence, bliss, self, and purity," all are detached; this detachment is neither identity nor non-identity.
It is solely the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind, and so forth. Through these two rounds [of teaching], is this not the ultimate and firm principle?
Furthermore, since Ānanda first requested instruction, he has suddenly been granted by the Heavenly King the metaphor of the magnificent mansion as the primary cause.

He entered through the gate and departed. The Tathāgata, for his sake, first broadly elucidated the two kinds of determination; next, he specifically pointed out the fundamental root of perfect penetration;
and thirdly, he further demonstrated the establishment of the *bodhimaṇḍa*. Are these three stages not indeed the ultimate and steadfast core of practice?
Furthermore, because Ānanda requested instruction on the "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) and the forty-four mental states...
Up to and including perfect enlightenment, the Tathāgata has elucidated each of these for them. Is this not the ultimate and firm realization?

In this way, whether it be the Tathāgatas who are the fruition, the Bodhisattvas who are the cause, the dharmas of fruition belonging to those in fruition, or the dharmas of the cause belonging to those on the path—regarding all three aspects of principle, practice, and realization, there is nowhere that they are not ultimately firm.
Therefore it is said: "The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" (and so forth). The separate title is thus concluded. The single character *jīng* (sūtra) is the general title.
In the Sanskrit language it is *sūtra*; here it is translated as *qìjīng* (scripture of accord). What is meant by "scripture of accord"?

It is because that which is expounded in this scripture accords with the principle of all Buddhas above and accords with the capacities of sentient beings below. Furthermore, "sūtra" means permanence and dharma; it is eternal.
Thus, the Three Periods do not change; the Dharma is equally observed by the ten realms. Furthermore, regarding the term "Sūtra":

in this land, what is composed by sages is called a *jing* (scripture), while what is composed by worthies is called a *zhuan* (biography). In the Western [Heaven], what is spoken by the Buddha is called a *jing*, whereas what is spoken by Bodhisattvas is called a *lun* (treatise).
Because it takes the place of those [treatises], it is called a *jing*. Moreover, within this general title, it also encompasses...

Regarding the two meanings—the general and the specific: if sentient beings in other directions possess particularly sharp and keen faculties, then all six sense objects may serve as the substance of the sūtra.

For example, as with the fragrant food of Vimalakīrti; that which is equal to the wheel of food is also equal to the wheel of Dharma, and that which is equal to the wheel of Dharma is also equal to the wheel of food.
Thus, even the sense object of taste can serve as the substance of the sūtra. This is like how certain lands may emit light or rain down flowers.
Those who behold this light and its radiance all attain enlightenment; thus, the sense-object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) may serve as the essence of the Sutra.

Just as there is a land where one uses celestial robes for touch, those whose bodies are touched by them also attain enlightenment; thus, the sense-object of touch (*spraṣṭavya-dhātu*) may serve as the essence of the Sutra.
As in the Land of Universal Fragrance (*Gandhavatī*), those who smell its fragrance also attain enlightenment; thus, the sense-object of odor (*gandha-dhātu*) may [serve as the essence of the Sutra].

This is the essence of the Sūtra. For instance, if there were a land where sentient beings could merely contemplate all dharmas and attain realization within a single thought-moment, then the mental object (*dharmāyatana*) itself could serve as the essence of the Sūtra.

However, because the sentient beings of this Sahā world are dull in all other faculties while only their faculty of hearing is sharp, the following passage states: "The true essence of the teaching in this region is pure and resides in sound."
Upon hearing this, one knows that in this land, only the sensory object of sound constitutes the essence of the sūtra. This is so when speaking specifically;
however, if speaking generally, even in this land the sensory object of form may constitute the essence of the sūtra.

For instance, those who attain awakening by hearing the sound of the Dharma while the Buddha is present take sound as the essence of the sūtra. But after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa, all the teachings consist solely of paper and ink.
Regarding the transmission and preservation [of the Dharma]: sentient beings can also attain awakening by contemplating these black characters on this white paper.

Thus, in this land, the sense-object of form (*rūpa-dhātu*) may also serve as the essence of the sūtra. However, from one perspective, sound exists only in the present, whereas form persists even after cessation.
If we further investigate, that which is obtained from a physical scroll after [the speaker] has ceased belongs to the category of form as the essence of the sūtra. Or, from...
When Dharma masters and spiritual friends hear [this teaching] and thereby gain entry, sound may also be considered the essence of the sūtra.
In this way, one knows that in this land, both the objects of sound and form pertain to both the present and the period after extinction.

Thus far, cause and effect have been discussed together, and the general and the specific have been presented in combination; hence it is said, "The Great Buddha-Crown," and so forth. If we analyze this according to the fivefold profound mystery...

Explaining the meaning: this title takes "person and dharma" as its name (*nāman*); the "ever-abiding true mind" as its essence (*śarīra*); "subtle and secret contemplation" as its primary principle (*mūla*);

"shattering the false to reveal the true" as its function (*kriyā*); and the "perfect and sudden *sarpis*" as its doctrinal characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). Furthermore, regarding both the general and specific aspects, each possesses three dimensions—teaching, practice, and principle—the meanings of which are all evident.
Having completed the explanation of the title concerning the Dharma, the details regarding the person are as found in the General Commentary (*Sūtra-śāstra-sāmānya*) and elsewhere.
[The various schools] no longer provide detailed records [on this matter].

The texts of the two sutras are divided into three parts: namely, the introduction, the main body, and the dissemination. From "Thus have I heard" up to "returned to the Buddha's presence" constitutes the introductory section (*nidāna*).
From "Ānanda saw the Buddha" up to near the end of the tenth fascicle, where he is no longer attached to the three realms, constitutes...
The Main Body (*śarīra-bhāga*). From "Ānanda, if again... up to the end of the sutra constitutes the Section on Dissemination (*pariṇāmana-bhāga*). The first part is further divided into two:

first, the Section of Testimony to Authenticity (*samyaktva-avadhāraṇa-parivarta*), namely "Thus have I heard," etc.; second, the Section of the Narrative Introduction (*nidāna-parivarta*), namely "At that time, the World-Honored One," etc.
The first of these is further divided into six, namely the six matters preceding the sutra. These shall be explained in their respective order.
The first two characters, "Thus" (evam), constitute the essence of the Dharma as heard; they are also terms that point toward the Dharma. Furthermore, they are words of faith and compliance.
As for pointing toward the Dharma: the former refers to the brevity of the title, while the latter refers to the extensiveness of the entire sutra.
This means that although the title and the text differ in their general and specific aspects, that which they expound is one and the same essence of the Dharma.
"Thus. Regarding "faithful compliance": it is like worldly matters where one who believes says, "This matter is thus," while one who does not believe says, "This matter is not thus.
Now, as for the essence of the Dharma in this sutra, because it is that which the sentient beings of the nine realms should faithfully comply with, it is said to be "thus.
This is from a general perspective. If one wishes to clarify its meaning deeply, what is called "not different" is named "thus" (tathā). There is no...

It is not that one says "this is it. What the present sutra teaches—that the mind perceives the five aggregates up to the seven elements—is all the eternally abiding true mind, the wondrously pure and luminous essence. Is this not "non-different" which is called "suchness"?

Only this eternally abiding true mind, the wondrously pure and luminous essence—is this not "not non-existent" which is called "is-ness"? It is precisely through such "thusness" that this constitutes the Dharma-body of the present sutra.

Next, the two characters "I hear" (*ahaṃ śṛṇomi*) refer to the person who hears. This means that the aforementioned nature of the Dharma was not heard by anyone else, but was heard specifically by me, Ānanda.
"I" (*ahaṃ*) has the meaning of a sovereign subject. There are three different types of "I": the conceptualized "I," the conceited "I," and the nominal "I.
When Ānanda heard this sutra, he had already realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), having eliminated the delusions of vision (*darśana-heya-kleśa*).

Since [the self] has been severed, there is no longer the conceptualization of a self. At the time of the compilation [of the scriptures], having already realized the four fruits of the path and exhausted the afflictions of the realm of thought (*dhyāna-kleśa*), there was likewise no conceited self.
Since these two types of self are absent, any mention of "I" is solely for the purpose of maintaining the teachings and propagating the scriptures;
thus, it does not hinder the establishment of a provisional "I" within the context of non-self. This is what is called the "nominal self" (*nāma-ātman*). It is also...
It is the True Self.
The two characters "one-time" (ekasmin samaye) indicate the temporal period during which the sutra was preached.

As for why it does not specify a particular time but simply says "at one time," it is because, just as the Western lands [India] refer to the three intervals (*trikāla*) while this land [China] divides the year into four seasons, the calendars and reckonings of these respective regions differ. Furthermore...

Fifty days and nights of humans constitute one day and night in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (Cāturmahārājika). Fifty days and nights in the Heaven of the Four Great Kings constitute one day and night in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven.
Thus, the durations of days and nights differ between the human realm and the heavens. This is why it is designated simply as "one period" (ekakāla).

If one were to further investigate this, it is because the capacity of the recipient and the teaching of the Buddha meet, and the paths of response and resonance intersect, that they are termed "one period."

The single character "Buddha" (佛) refers to the Teacher who expounds the sutras. Because he has perfectly realized the ten bodies (*daśakāya*), fulfilled the three types of awakening (*trividhabodhi*), and is like a blooming lotus or one awakened from a great dream—being most honored, most noble, and standing transcendentally alone—he is called a Buddha;
that is none other than Śākyamuni.
The "five" refers to Śrāvastī and other such locations; these are the places where the teaching was proclaimed. In the Sanskrit language, it is called Śrāvastī, which here means "Abundance of Virtue.
As for its things, there is an abundance of wealth and desires; as for its people, there is an abundance of liberation and extensive learning.
Therefore, it is called "Abundance of Virtue."
The sixth section concerns those who are equal to the Great [Bodhisattvas]. These are companions who have heard the Dharma together, and they are divided into three groups:

first, the Śrāvakas, who depart with the Great [Buddha]; second, the Pratyekabuddhas, who likewise depart; and third, the Bodhisattvas, who depart for the ten directions. The first group is further divided into five parts:
namely, citing examples, indicating numbers, revealing ranks, praising virtues, and listing names. These shall be explained in sequence. First, "with a great assembly of bhikṣus."

This is an illustration by category; its meaning is the same as that of the *Cāṅ* (Tasting) Sūtra. However, it refers specifically to "great bhikṣus" because this sūtra lists the assembly according to the Mahāyāna.
If it were not Mahāyāna, the principle of "inner secrecy and outer manifestation" would not be evident. For example, in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*, one should rely on the Hīnayāna perspective.

If it were not for the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), there would be no need to open up the provisional (*upāya*) to reveal the real (*bhūtārtha*). Therefore, from the self-elevating analogy through the enumeration of names, all belong to the Mahāyāna.

"Two thousand two hundred," etc., indicates the number; this is self-evident. "The three are all equal," etc., reveals the stages (*avasthā*). Regarding "outflow-free" (*anāsrava*), there are two meanings:
first, non-leakage (*asaṃsṛti*); second, non-falling-away (*aprapāta*). In each and every instance, they maintain the principle of the *dharmatā*.
Because it is not lost, there is no leakage (*āsrava*). Birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) do not cause one to fall into its midst; therefore, there is no falling into outflows.

If one explains "outflowlessness" (*anāsrava*) in terms of afflictions and birth-and-death, it means that one does not leak or fall into the two kinds of afflictions—the causes consisting of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-citta*) and ignorance (*avidyā*)—nor into the two kinds of birth-and-death—the results consisting of the fragmented (*paricchinna*) and the transformational (*parivṛtti*). The Arhat fully possesses this.

The term "Arhat" (羅漢) retains its original sound (*lǎohàn*) as a polysemous non-translation because it encompasses three meanings: being "unborn" (*wúshēng*), "slayer of thieves" (*shāzé*), and "worthy of offerings" (*yìnggòng*). Regarding "the unborn":

in the Hinayana, this refers to severing the fetters of the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*), whereby the bonds of the retributive fruit of the fragmented existence (*prādeśika-phala-bandhana*) will no longer give rise to further birth.

Now, in the Mahayana, upon entering the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), one partially severs ignorance (*avidyā*) and partially perceives the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*), thereby fully understanding the root of birth.
Because there is neither arising nor ceasing, and no cessation either, it is called "non-arising. As for "slaying the thief," "thief" takes the sense of plundering;
this is because the afflictions (*kleśa*) are able to plunder the wealth of merit and the life-force of wisdom of the *dharmakāya*.
In the Hīnayāna, one merely stops the eighty-eight proclivities (*anuśaya*) of the view-delusions and the eighty-one grades of the thought-delusions. Now, regarding the Mahāyāna:
It is not only that he slays *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa*, but he further slays *avidyā*; therefore, he is called a "slayer of thieves" (*arhat*).
As for "Worthy of Offerings" (*arhat*), in the Lesser Vehicle, one is merely worthy of receiving offerings from gods and humans as the master of the field of merit;

now, in the Mahāyāna, one is worthy of receiving offerings from the sentient beings of the nine realms as the master of the field of merit. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "We of this day are truly *arhats*."
The Han [Arhat] should receive offerings therein. He possesses the three meanings of the Mahāyāna, such as non-arising (*anutpāda*), and is thus not called an "Arhat" but rather a "Mahārhan.
Regarding the four types of Buddha-sons (*jinaputra*) and so forth, this is a praise of their virtues. This is divided into two parts: first, from "Buddha-son" onwards, there is the direct praise;
second, from "from the Buddha" onwards, there is the indirect praise. Although there are these two sections, they collectively clarify the stages (*bhūmi*).
The three [epithets] beginning with "unborn" (anutpāda) serve as a general praise. Within the specific praise: the two characters "abiding and maintaining" (sthiti-dhāraṇa) praise the unborn;

the phrase "excellently transcending" praises the slayer of thieves (arhan); the two characters "capable" praise the one worthy of offerings (arhat). The two characters "Son of the Buddha" (buddhaputra) run directly through all three phrases. To speak of the "Son of the Buddha":
the Tathāgata is the father within the Dharma, and the Śrāvaka is the son within the Dharma, just as in the world.
One who is capable of continuing the legacy of the *jīqiú* (the loom and leatherwork) and capable of transmitting the *shūlǐ* (books and rites) is a son who sustains the family.

Now, being within the Dharma, born from the Buddha’s own mouth and transformed by the Dharma, having attained a portion of the Buddha-Dharma, such a person is fit to succeed to the rank of the Dharma King and able to inherit the ancestral estate of the Dharma House;

thus, they are a son who transmits the Dharma and is called a "Son of the Buddha" (*buddhaputra*). As for the abbot, since that person has already realized non-arising (*anutpāda*), [they are established in this position].
This fully reveals the Middle Way, remaining unshaken by the two extremes of existence and emptiness.

Contemplative wisdom serves as that which abides and sustains, while the principle of truth serves as that which is abided in and sustained; it is for this reason that the virtue of non-arising is extolled in terms of abiding and sustaining.

"Skillfully transcending all realms of existence" (*bhava*): "existence" refers to that wherein cause and effect do not perish; it consists of the realm of desire, the realm of form, and the formless realm.
This is because the causes of views and afflictions inevitably summon the fruit of the segmented cycle of birth and death (*pariccheda-maraṇa*).

Since those of the Lesser Vehicle have already slain the enemy of the causes—views and afflictions—they no longer undergo the fruit of segmented death, thereby transcending the three realms of existence within the world. Now, as for the Mahayana...
He is the cause for slaying the thief of ignorance and the means for severing the fruit of death through transformation; he further transcends the three realms of existence beyond the boundaries.

Therefore, it is said that he "transcends all existences. Thus, by means of his virtuous transcendence, one praises his merit in slaying the thief. Regarding the phrase "able [to act] within the lands" and so forth:
since such a person is capable of being a field of offerings for the nine realms, there are no sentient beings who, upon seeing him, do not [submit] to his majesty.
Taking their ritual deportment as a standard out of fear [of falling away], there is not a single sentient being who does not achieve that deportment.
Therefore it is said, "One is able to... (and so forth). This is why the virtue of being a worthy recipient (*arhat*) is praised by means of ritual deportment. Such is the primary praise.
Within the second section of the praise, first, from the two lines beginning with "From the Buddha," the reason for abiding and maintaining [the Dharma] is praised; second, [the field is] purified.

Two phrases. These further praise the reason for his excellent transcendence. Three: the four phrases on the response-body (*nirmāṇakāya*). These further praise the reason for his majestic deportment (*īryāpatha*).

Regarding the first, the underlying intent is to explain what it means to dwell as a son of the Buddha and uphold the Dharma; thus, it shifts to say "following the Buddha," and so forth. The Buddha possesses inconceivable three wheels:

the body is the wheel of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-cakra*); the speech is the wheel of turning the Dharma (*dharma-cakra*); and the mind is the wheel of discerning capacities (*indriya-parīkṣā-cakra*). These are wheels.
It carries the meaning of crushing and grinding. Since the three—body, speech, and mind—are all capable of crushing the evil karma of sentient beings, it is likened to a wheel.

To enter the minds of others by means of what one has personally realized is called "turning. Because the sons of the Buddha assist the Buddha in proclaiming [the Dharma], it is said that they "turn the wheel following the Buddha.
Throughout the Tathāgata’s single period of teaching and guidance, there were such doctrines as these that could be spoken.

There are such sentient beings who may be saved. Once he has assisted in proclaiming [the Dharma], he entrusts those sentient beings who are to be saved with the teachings appropriate for their instruction;

hence, it is called "entrustment" (yizu). If, in the interim, the faculties and the teaching do not slightly accord with one another, or if the two aspects of preaching the Dharma and saving sentient beings have not yet ceased to exist, one is still not fit for entrustment—how much less could there be the "Sublime" (Miao)?
He is worthy of being entrusted with the final charge. Now, he is able to employ such a teaching to meet such a capacity;

as the capacity and the teaching harmonize, and the person and the Dharma are mutually appropriate, although it is said that in preaching the Dharma there is no dharma to be preached, it does not hinder his preaching the Dharma all day long;

and although it is said that in saving sentient beings there are no beings to be saved, it does not hinder his saving sentient beings all day long. Therefore, it is not merely that he is worthy of being entrusted with the final charge, but...
Furthermore, it is said that [the Buddha] was "wondrously worthy of entrustment. It is thus; were it not for the abbot’s practice of the Middle Way, how could he have been like this?

For this reason, the two phrases following "following the Buddha" turn to praise the reason why he serves as an abbot. In the middle section, the intention is to ask: by what means does one excellently transcend all states of existence (*bhava*)?

It is therefore turned to the description of "adorned and purified," and so forth. "Adorned" (*yan*) takes the sense of embellishment; that is to say, goodness— (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on a Buddhist scripture, likely concerning the role of a monastic leader (*sthavira* or *upādhyāya*). The translation reflects the philosophical and exegetical style of the original.)

"Not complete. "Pure" (*śuci*) takes cleanliness as its meaning; it signifies that no evil remains unremoved. *Vinaya* is translated here as "disciplinary law" (*lüfǎ*), which carries the sense of prohibition, much like the legal codes of the secular world.
Within the *vinaya*, every detail—whether major or minor, permitted or prohibited, what is to be done or avoided, and the maintenance of precepts or their violation—is clearly understood.
This is the sense of being adorned with the perfection of all that is good. Furthermore, regarding...
Regarding the categories of major and minor precepts, prohibitions and permissions, one does not merely restrain the body from acting upon them, but also restrains the mind so that they do not arise;

eventually, even the mental signs of such thoughts vanish. This is what is meant by the principle of purity, wherein no evil remains unremoved. Therefore, it is called "strictly purifying the *vinaya*."

Thus, there are no causes or effects within the three realms of existence that are not transcended. Since one has attained this for oneself, one further transforms sentient beings within the three realms of existence by purifying their *vinaya*.
One fulfills all that is honorable and complete, and eliminates all that is evil and absent.
Thus, one likewise transcends the causes and effects of the three realms of existence. Therefore, it is said: "To establish a grand model for the three [realms]."

The realm (*dhātu*). It is thus. If one has not transcended all that exists, how could one be capable of such a thing? Therefore, the two phrases "adorned" and "purified" further praise the reason for this transcendence.
Among these three, the intention is to explain what constitutes the accomplishment of majestic deportment; thus it is further stated as the "response body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth.
This enables one to manifest forms according to the species within the worlds of the ten directions, causing sentient beings to see [the Buddha].
There is not one who is not delivered from the cause of the accumulation of afflictions and the fruit of suffering in birth and death.
Therefore, it is called the *nirmāṇakāya* (Response Body) [and so forth]. It does not merely manifest its body throughout the ten directions;

it can further manifest its body throughout the three periods of time, such that for sentient beings who behold it, there is no suffering to be extracted that it does not extract, and no bliss to be bestowed that it does not provide, thereby transcending [all limitations].
Because afflictions are like dust and dirt that entangle one in the cycle of birth and death, it is said that they "rescue and deliver" (and so forth).

The former [passage] speaks of "delivering sentient beings," while the latter speaks of "transcending all dusty entanglements"; these texts mutually clarify one another. This is because by transcending all dusty entanglements, sentient beings are enabled to attain deliverance;

and because sentient beings attain deliverance, dusty entanglements are thereby transcended. The difference lies merely in whether the focus is on the person or the dharma, as in the following example:

It is so. Were it not for his awe-inspiring majesty and his exemplary deportment, how could he be thus? For this reason, the passage beginning with "The Response Body" (*nirmāṇakāya*) and so forth praises the reasons for his majestic deportment.
Thus far has been the primary praise and the subsequent praise; therein, the virtues of the Śrāvaka are revealed without exception.
Furthermore, the two lines beginning with "Moreover, O Son of the Buddha" may serve as a general praise for that which is attained while abiding in a single state of mind.
The three wisdoms uphold the three truths manifested within a single thought-moment; without transcending them, they transcend, surpassing the sentient beings of the nine realms.
Such is the sustaining power of the Buddha’s son and such is the skillful transcendence of the Buddha’s son. This can be further praised individually as follows:

the first two phrases represent *samādhi* (concentration); the second two phrases represent *prajñā* (wisdom); and the third two phrases represent *śīla* (precept), which is the unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskāra*) triple [discipline].

This is the section on "Learning. The four phrases beginning with "the response body" (nirmāṇakāya) conclude the discussion on universal benefit. It is called "immeasurable" because it does not stop at a single land;

it is called "future" because it extends throughout the three periods of time. This refers to how the path of transformation pervades the ten directions horizontally and exhausts the three temporal limits vertically.
Fifth, "their names," etc., lists their names. Śāriputra is translated as "Son of the Sparrow" (Qiuzi); he received this name from his mother.
Among the great assembly, he was foremost in wisdom; it is he who, in the *Śūraṅgama*, entered the perfect penetration by contemplating eye-consciousness.
Maudgalyāyana—here translated as "Great Mung Bean"—was foremost in supernatural powers among the great assembly;
it is he who, in the *Śūraṅgama*, entered the perfect penetration by contemplating mental consciousness. Kauṣṭhila—here translated as "Great Thigh"—was the maternal uncle of Śāriputra. Among the...
The Great Assembly regards him as the foremost in debate. He is now the one who entered the perfect penetration through the contemplation of nose-consciousness in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra: "Pūrṇa" is a Western name for a man; "Maitrāyaṇī" is a Western designation for a woman.
"Pūrṇa" means "Full," which is the name of his father. "Maitrāyaṇī" means "Compassion," which is the name of his mother.
He was even named after his parents; thus he is called Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra. Among the great assembly, he is foremost in preaching the Dharma.

He is the one who, in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, entered the perfect penetration (*pratyavekṣaṇā*) by means of the gustatory consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*). Subhūti is here translated as "Born of Emptiness" (*Kūṭaja*);
at his birth, the storehouses were all empty, and upon his renunciation of the world, he understood that the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) are empty. In the great...

Śāriputra was foremost among the assembly for his realization of emptiness; he is the one who, in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, entered the perfect penetration by contemplating the faculty of mind (*manas*).
Upānibandha means "the nature of sensory objects is empty"; he is the one who, in the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra*, entered the perfect penetration by contemplating the object of form (*rūpa*).
These six individuals are the leaders among the one thousand two hundred and fifty followers; therefore, they are called "foremost.

Regarding the two types of *pratyekabuddhas*, although the text is brief, they should also be explained according to the Mahāyāna perspective. Their initial mind is that of those still in training (*śaikṣa*).
In their investigation of reality and severance of delusions, they do not merely investigate the reality of partial emptiness, but also investigate the reality of the Middle Way. Not only...

One cuts off the delusions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and likewise cuts off the delusion of ignorance (*avidyā*). In the state of the *aśaikṣa*, the truth is fully realized and delusions are exhausted;

it is not merely the realization of the truth of partial emptiness, but rather the truth within the Perfect [Teaching] that is finally realized. It is not merely that the delusions of views and thoughts are exhausted.

Thus, the delusions of ignorance are about to be exhausted. In this way, one knows that through progressive contemplation (*anuloma*) there is arising, and through regressive contemplation (*pratiloma*) there is transition and cessation.

One contemplates not only the two kinds of causes and conditions—conceivable and inconceivable—within the realm of *dhātu*, but further contemplates the two kinds of causes and conditions, both conceivable and inconceivable, outside the realm of *dhātu*.
Furthermore, one understands that when referring to those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), it is not said to be the "final mind," and when referring to the initial mind, [it is not the final].

It is said that there are those in training (*śaikṣa*); this is merely a mutual clarification. This is because those beyond training (*aśaikṣa*) are the final mind, while those in training are the initial mind.
Although they differ in terms of having training or not, and in being initial or final minds, both those who are neither before nor after come together at the assembly of the Dharma.
Therefore it is said, "Furthermore... (and so forth). This passage is addressed to the bhikṣus and others; its purpose is to formally conclude the subject matter.

In meaning, it serves as a summary of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas. The intent is that the śrāvakas explained above are as numerous as those [previously mentioned], and the pratyekabuddhas are as numerous as these;
it was precisely on the day of the *pravāraṇā* ceremony that they encountered this.

This is why we have come together to the Buddha’s presence. Regarding "concluding the summer retreat" (*xiūxià*): the Sangha must enter the summer retreat (*jiéxià*), and it is now precisely at the time for its conclusion; hence it is called "concluding the summer.

It is appropriate for those who have left the household life to enter the summer retreat, for there are three reasons for this: first, if one wishes to settle the mind and enter the Way, one must enter the summer retreat;

second, if one wishes to protect and sustain living beings, it is likewise appropriate to enter the summer retreat; third, if one wishes to avoid various criticisms [from the laity], one must enter the summer retreat.

One should also observe the summer retreat (*varṣā*) because of public censure. Regarding "censure": worldly people may mock those who have left the household life, saying, "Even rats and magpies have nests and burrows, yet these wandering practitioners have no fixed dwelling place," and so forth.
Although the observance of the summer retreat is a single intention, it encompasses three aspects; thus, the Sangha's observance of the summer retreat must not be neglected.
Regarding the *pravāraṇā* (self-criticism): some say that after the exhaustion resulting from the ninety-day restriction of movement (*śīla-pada*), [the ceremony is held].

It would merely be a matter of unrestrained indulgence. If that were so, how could it be appropriate for one who has left the household life? One should know that "self-indulgence" (*pravāraṇā*) means:
if one has personally transgressed the Vinaya, whether there is someone who has seen it, heard of it, or suspects it without yet having full confidence, they may raise all such matters at will.
Thereafter, one should reverently face the Buddha and confess, laying everything bare. Therefore, it is called "self-indulgence."

Third, regarding the bodhisattvas: they begin with those from the ten directions up to the leaders. If bodhisattvas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are included, they belong to the general introduction (*sādhāraṇa-nidāna*);

those belonging to the bhikṣus and others belong to the specific introduction (*asādhāraṇa-nidāna*). The text and its meaning are intermingled, which I fear may not be convenient. As for "consulting to resolve doubts and eliminate uncertainty," this pertains to the domain of the bodhisattvas;

it does not go beyond the three stages of understanding (*adhimukti*), practice (*caryā*), and realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). It is like having an understanding that is not yet complete, or a practice that is not yet perfected.
It has not yet been practiced. It appears as though realized, yet it is not truly realized; there are obstacles in the mind, so how can the Way progress?
For this reason, after the ninety-day retreat (*varṣā*), you must consult and resolve each point one by one. Do not allow hesitation to remain in the mind, for it will hinder the Great Way.
Thus, such consultation belongs to the Bodhisattva, while such resolution belongs to the Tathāgata; both teacher and disciple [must act accordingly].

[The characters] are listed together because the subject and object are presented in conjunction; thus, it is said that [the Buddha] was consulted for a decision. Regarding "Compassion and Austerity" (*maitrī-vairambha*): compassion is lovable and can encompass all who are loved;
austerity is formidable and can subdue all. This is a preliminary explanation. However, if one discusses it according to reality:
To possess virtues without exception is called "compassion" (慈); to shatter delusions without exception is called "severity" (嚴). Regarding the phrase "one who will seek the profound meaning" (將求密義):

"will" (將) refers to that which is about to be so, yet not yet so. "Profound meaning" (密義) refers, in essence, to the three—wondrous *śamatha* and so forth—mentioned below, as well as the initial expedient means.
The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata spread his seat" (*如來敷座*) refers to entering meditative absorption (*samādhi*). This is the body of the Tathāgata, such as...
Because the Vajra is indestructible, it is called "tranquil" (*yan*). Because the Tathāgata’s mind is like space and cannot be moved or turned, it is called "peaceful" (*an*).

Regarding the pure assembly at the Dharma feast, from the perspective of the Bodhisattvas, this is because they have already shattered ignorance and severed the *pariṇāmika-vipariṇāma* (transformative death).
Discussing the entire great assembly, after the period for self-indulgence and the resolution of doubts has concluded, all transgressions and faults [are purified].
They all repent; all their doubts and perplexities are thereby resolved. Thus it is said that the pure assembly at the Dharma feast "attains what they have never attained before.

This means that whenever the Tathāgata enters meditative absorption for a session, he invariably expounds the Dharma. To hear what has never been heard before and to see what has never been seen before is what is meant by "attaining what they have never attained before.
Regarding the "kalaviṅka-like celestial voice" and so forth, these refer to the sounds as explained in the subsequent text.
Dust (the sensory object) is fundamentally neither produced by causes and conditions nor is it of spontaneous nature;
thus, the auditory dust is likewise pure and primordial, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. The Tathāgata has already realized this principle, such that all sounds pervade the ten directions.

While the Tathāgata has indeed realized the principle of the Dharma-realm, the Bodhisattvas have also long ago attained the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, no longer waiting for sound to arrive.
The ears reach toward the locus of sound; though [the Buddha] is in the ten directions, the ears naturally hear the Buddha’s voice and come to the site of enlightenment.
As for Mañjuśrī acting as the leader: first, he possesses a superior intention, being able to lead the assembly and receive offerings;

second, he is able to take the dharanis and go to provide protection; third, he is able to convey doubts and ask questions on their behalf; and fourth, he is able to select the perfect penetration that is appropriate for the occasion.
By means of the "Introduction" (Nidāna), there are five [purposes]: first, to request the compilation of the Sūtra’s title so that future generations may receive and uphold it;
second, to issue the "Exceeding the Sequence" (Sūtrāntara-avatāraṇa). This is divided into two parts: first, the timely falling into error by Śrīpāla and others who were the appropriate recipients;

second, the compassionate rescue by the Tathāgata and others. The first part is further divided into two: first, the causes for the falling into error, namely Śrīpāla and others at that time; second, the actual falling into error, namely "at that moment."

And so forth. The first [section] further has two parts: first, the reason why the *pātra* traveled a long distance; second, the reason why it traveled only a short distance. The first of these further has two parts:

first, the king and his ministers prepared the offerings (corresponding to the passage beginning with "At that time..."); second, the distribution of the portions to the noble ones (corresponding to the passage beginning with "The Buddha commanded..."). The first of these further has two parts.
At first, King Prasenajit [of Śrāvastī] descended into the city; then, the ministers and commoners of the two cities followed. Regarding King Prasenajit:
"Prasenajit" is translated here as "Victorious Army" (Shèngjūn) and also as "Moonlight" (Yuèguāng); he was the sovereign of the kingdom of Śrāvastī. As for the term "memorial day" (huìrì):
one name for it is "taboo day" (jìrì), which refers to the anniversary of the father's death. There is a saying: "If the day of the father’s death is ever brought up, the son..."
I am overcome with grief and conceal this matter, remaining silent; hence the term "the day of the taboo" (*huìrì*). It is also called "the day of remembrance" (*jìrì*).

If that were the case, a son would not wish to hear of his father’s death; how could such a person truly be a son? One should know that the terms "the day of the taboo" and "the day of remembrance" refer to this.
Whenever the anniversary of a father’s death occurs, all other matters are forbidden and not carried out; they are concealed and not spoken of.

This is why it is called the "day of the taboo" (*huìrì*) and also the "day of avoidance" (*jìrì*). As for those of equal status, King Bimbisāra prepared a vegetarian feast for his father to provide merit for the afterlife;
this may be called the height of filial piety. He did not visit other places but instead invited [the Buddha] to the inner palace; this may be called the height of...
The Emperor was solemn. That he did not dispatch his subordinates to go out and welcome the Buddha may be called the ultimate in sincerity.

That he prepared an extensive array of rare delicacies and unsurpassed flavors may be called the ultimate in abundance. Furthermore, that he personally invited the great Bodhisattvas may be called the ultimate in reverence.
Since this was so, it is no wonder that the Buddha’s own manifestation was unavoidable. The two ministers—
It can likely be seen that both the King and his ministers prepared offerings, as this was the day of the *svayaṃvāra* (the day of self-indulgence).
The two sages and saints responded accordingly: the Tathāgata himself responded to the King’s invitation, while he commanded Mañjuśrī to lead the assembly to respond to the ministers’ invitations.

This appears to be because the Buddha was restricted to responding to the King’s request, while the monks responded to the ministers’ feast; it seems somewhat unequal. How could the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas—?
"Is this not unequal? He replied, "The Buddha is the King of the Dharma; the king is the king among men. The minister is the minister of the king of men;

the Sangha is the minister of the king of Dharma. Since the King of Dharma corresponds to the king of men, and the ministers of Dharma correspond to the ministers of men, this is ultimate equality, not inequality."

The second [section], on the proximate causes, has three parts. First, "only [those who] go far" refers to those who travel a great distance and lack offerings. Second, "immediately" refers to practicing loving-kindness with equanimity.
Third, "passing through" refers to the proper practice of begging for alms. Regarding the first point, "going far and lacking offerings," as for those who first accept individual invitations:
some say that Ānanda, while serving as an attendant, had three personal vows, one of which was not to accept individual invitations.
First: Why is it that you now accept individual invitations? Answer: The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* clarifies that one does not accept individual invitations;

this refers to not following the Tathāgata in accepting such invitations, and not to oneself alone. Since there are already elders (*sthavira*) and others present, it is evident that on such a day there is not a single person who should not be invited.

As for the claim that one has previously accepted an individual invitation and thus lacks the leisure to attend the monastic sequence (*saṃghakrama*), this is merely a discussion regarding the order of the assembly.
Regarding the mind: because the mind has varying degrees of breadth and narrowness, one should specifically invite a worthy field of merit.

Because fields of merit have degrees of excellence, if one speaks in terms of the field, providing for many ordinary monks is not as meritorious as providing for a single person who practices the ten wholesome paths of action;

providing for many who practice the ten wholesome paths is not as meritorious as providing for a single person who has attained the first fruit [of the path]. From this point onward, the merit increases progressively through successive stages. If, however, one speaks in terms of the mind...
It is said that providing for many arhats is not as meritorious as providing for a single ordinary person (pṛthagjana) according to the sequence of the Saṃgha.

From this, one can know that inviting separately is based solely on the relative excellence or inferiority of the field of merit (*puṇyakṣetra*) being honored; thus, one selects [specific individuals] for a separate invitation.

In contrast, the sequence of the Saṃgha depends only on the breadth or narrowness of the donor’s own mental capacity; therefore, one should follow the sequence of the Saṃgha and it is not appropriate [to bypass it].
To distinguish these terms: the *sthavira* (Elder) is one’s peer; the *ācārya* (Preceptor) is one’s model of discipline.

The Buddha ordained that two bhikṣus travel together, so as to prevent transgressions and strictly regulate their conduct. To say "returning alone" means that he was seen without an Elder or a Preceptor.
"Without offerings" means that he was not present in the regular order of the Saṃgha. Now, Ānanda has already accepted a separate invitation.

Yet he does not participate in the ranks of the monastic community; furthermore, when begging for alms, he has neither companions nor offerings. Thus, he mistakenly falls into the first of the "nearby causes" (*upapatti-hetu*).

Regarding the second [point], the practice of impartial compassion, there are two parts: first, practicing alms-begging with immediate equanimity; second, the intention that arises is [immediate] *ārya* (noble).
This is difficult to reconcile. The passage beginning with "At that very moment" (*jishi*) describes the ritual procedure for begging for alms.

The passage beginning with "In his mind" (*xinzhong*) describes the mental aspiration for begging for alms. It seems confusing that the initial seeking is followed by what is called the "final" [offering].

However, the "initial seeking" refers to the time when Ānanda was first forming the intention to beg for alms, whereas the "final" refers to the point when the king and his ministers prepared the offering.
Although there are differences, they are all ranked as "foremost"; those who have not yet made offerings, excluding kings and ministers, are considered "last.
Regarding the term *dānapati* (donor): *dāna* is *dāna*, which is also "giving" (*boshu*). *Patī* means "to transcend.

Generally, to harbor thoughts from moment to moment that one's own possessions should not be given to others is stinginess (*mātsarya*). To harbor thoughts from moment to moment that one desires to obtain what belongs to others...

This is what constitutes greed. Because of this stinginess and greed, there is no karma that is not created and no suffering that is not invited. Thus, one knows that stinginess and greed are the very root of the ocean of suffering in birth and death.
Now, not only do you refrain from coveting the property of others, but you have even torn open the sack of stinginess to practice giving.
From this, you shall transcend the ocean of suffering in birth and death; therefore, you are called a *dānapati* (donor). Only then can you practice impartial compassion.
"Method" (*fang*) is precisely "Dharma. The Tathāgata possesses great compassion that is equal and impartial. Ānanda intended to practice this Dharma;

therefore, it is called "practicing equal compassion according to method. This is precisely the point where Ānanda formed his conception; hence it says, "he gave rise to the intention for equality," and so forth.

If there were internally a mind of purity and impurity, or nobility and meanness, and externally objects of purity and impurity, or nobility and meanness—[then such a state would not be true equality].
When the mind and its objects are separated and the subject and object stand in opposition, how can one achieve the perfection of equanimity?
This is because Ānanda aspired for the simultaneous extinction of both mind and object, so that subject and object would no longer be mutually dependent;

only then is it the Tathāgata’s practice of impartial compassion, whereby the immeasurable merit of sentient beings may be fully realized. Next, he clarifies his intention, stating that Ānanda wishes to practice the equality of the Tathāgata.
Compassion does not arise without cause; it truly looks up to and embodies the intent behind the Tathāgata’s admonitions. Therefore it is said, "He already knows...
(and so forth). This is truly because Subhūti and Kāśyapa—one wealthy and one poor—are unequal in two respects, and within them there exists a mind of discrimination.
Externally, there are the realms of poverty and wealth; that is to say, the mind and its objects are separated, and subject and object stand in opposition.
This is unevenness, not evenness; it is the presence of obstruction, not the absence of obstruction. Regarding those who "venerate and look up to" [the Buddha], they are like those two people:

having already abandoned wealth to follow poverty, they cannot avoid obstructing wealth with poverty; yet having abandoned poverty to follow wealth, they likewise cannot avoid obstructing [themselves] with wealth.
Yet, by obstructing the poor, this causes the poor not to fail to give rise to slander and the wealthy not to fail to give rise to doubt.

Now, wishing for equality—where the poor do not obstruct the wealthy, and the wealthy do not obstruct the poor; where the poor and the wealthy do not obstruct one another—doubt and slander can be kept far away.
This is the intention of the Tathāgata. Because Ānanda wished to put it into practice, he spoke of "reverent admiration" and "expounding and revealing."

Furthermore, regarding the third correct practice—begging for food with solemn reverence for the rules of purification—the *Piṇḍapāta Sūtra* states: "When entering a city, do not perceive the characteristics of the city;
when seeing people, do not perceive the characteristics of the people."
The second [point] concerns falling into error. Regarding the phrase "at that time," etc.: Ānanda was a sage who had attained the first fruit of the path (srotāpanna).

Why was he turned by a courtesan and seized by an evil spell? It is because he had only destroyed the delusions of conceptual views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), but had not yet destroyed the delusions of craving and attachment (*tṛṣṇā-kleśa*).
To speak from the ultimate perspective, although it is said that Ānanda had awakened the aspiration for enlightenment, he did so while still perceiving objective signs (*nimitta*).
It is the mind. Although it is said that one listens to the Dharma, one listens to the Dharma by taking sound as a condition.

Since the arousal of the mind occurs because of perceiving forms, although the marks of the Tathāgata’s thirty-two signs differ from the marks of the courtesan Gaṅgā, the mind capable of seeing them is one and the same.
Since one listens to the Dharma by taking sound as a condition, although the sounds of the Tathāgata’s eightfold voice and four analytical knowledges differ [from ordinary sounds]...

The voices of the Brahmā-deva’s heterodox incantations differ, yet the mind capable of hearing them is no different. For this reason, in the past you turned the ordinary toward the sacred for the sake of the Tathāgata;
today you turn the orthodox toward the heterodox for the sake of a courtesan. In all cases, it does not transcend the two characters of "sound" and "form.
The term *sā* (娑) below indicates the reason why [the mind] is able to encompass these. *Sāṃkhyāyana* is translated here as "Yellow-Haired One."
He was a non-Buddhist (tīrthika). In a previous life, he had obtained this evil spell from Brahmā.
Dhanagā also practiced this spell, and by means of it, she sought to entice Ānanda; hence the phrase "with *sa*," etc. Regarding "the lewd body" (*yin gōng*), etc.:
the lewd demeanor of Dhanagā’s entire person is called "the lewd body," while Ānanda’s exclusive adherence to the precepts is called "the essence of the precepts" (*jiè tǐ*). Since...
It is said that he personally caressed her, intending to destroy the essence of his precepts. This refers to the fact that Caṅkā was about to sexually violate Ānanda;
it does not mean that Ānanda intended to approach Caṅkā. As stated in the subsequent text: "The Tathāgata knew that she was employing her sexual arts upon him."
Furthermore, the later passage states: "Because the mind is pure, one has not yet discussed being submerged. This is truly verifiable. Question:
How is it that this sutra borrows the great transformative power of Ānanda to manifest falling into a brothel as the catalyst for the teaching?

Answer: When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas save the world, there is nothing they do that does not bring benefit or promote the sublime. At the critical juncture of adversity or favor, they exercise sovereign mastery whether moving against or with the current. Indeed...
Because a single attachment to lust is the very root of birth and death and constitutes the most profound harm, the subsequent text states:
"All sentient beings take lust as the basis for their nature and life; birth arises from this, and death arises from this.

They emerge and submerge like a head bobbing in water, yet remain entirely unaware. Thus, fearing that they would lose their Dharma-body and perish in their wisdom-life, the Tathāgata exhorted them with earnest urgency.
I have issued this admonition to protect you; yet those who are in a state of delusion ultimately fail to attain awakening. Consequently, on a small scale, they lose their bodies and their families;
on a large scale, they lose their states and the world. Even cases where they endanger their wives and children or bring shame upon their parents are beyond counting.
How, then, can their Dharma-body and wisdom-life be preserved? For this reason, this present sutra borrows the person of Ānanda as its great [example].

This is a provisional manifestation. Amidst the darkness of sleep, he suddenly let out a shout; it is like providing a single banner for those who are deaf and blind, serving as a vessel for the great ocean of birth and death in future generations.

The second section, "The Tathāgata’s Compassionate Rescue," is divided into three parts: first, the Tathāgata concludes the midday meal and returns; second, at that time, he emits light and recites a mantra;
third, he instructs Mañjuśrī to take the mantra and go forth to provide protection. Regarding the first part, "Concluding the Meal and Returning":

when the Tathāgata knows the character "know" (知) of the other [the recipient], this is the illumination of his transformative, expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*). The remainder may be understood accordingly.

In the second section, regarding the emission of light and the recitation of mantras: at that time, the World-Honored One and others, when considered in terms of their cultivated nature (*bhāvanā*) and innate nature (*prakṛti*), possess two kinds of threefold virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
The crown of the World-Honored One represents the *dharmakāya*, for the formless crown is most vast and great.
The light of the hundred jewels and fearlessness represents *prajñā*, for the radiance of the hundred jewels shines universally and brilliantly. From within this light, [the following] is produced:
The precious lotus symbolizes liberation, for the lotus flower represents the non-duality of defilement and purity. These three dharmas clarify the three virtues within the essence of nature.
As for the presence of the Buddha’s transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*), it symbolizes wisdom (*prajñā*), for the Buddha is awakening itself, free from all defilements.
His sitting in the full lotus posture (*paryaṅka*) symbolizes the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), for in this seated meditation he enters samādhi, wherein stillness and illumination are non-dual.
The proclamation of divine mantras (dhāraṇī) signifies liberation; for the power of mantra is inconceivable. By means of these three dharmas, one cultivates the three virtues within the Middle Way.
First, the World-Honored One and others all do so with respect to the Buddha-body, thereby signifying the three virtues within the nature (*prakṛti*).
Next, there are the Buddhas and so forth; since these all pertain to the transformation-buddhas (nirmāṇakāya), they symbolize the cultivation of the three virtues of the middle [stage].

This collectively reveals that the fundamental and the emergent are non-dual, and that cultivation and nature, as well as appearance and reality, are mutually identical. This is because, according to the principle expounded in this sutra, the principle-aspect is the Dharma-body, the practice-aspect is Prajñā, and the realization-aspect is Vimukti;
thus, two sets of the three virtues are employed merely to symbolize their manifestation.

Third, regarding the section on going to protect [the practitioner] with mantras: A question is raised that since the mantras are already divine and wondrous, why is it necessary to go and protect them so that they may attain liberation?
The answer is: although the mantras are divine and wondrous, they are like the emperors of the world; whenever there is an official proclamation, it is necessary to dispatch officials.

This is not because the edicts and mandates themselves lack power. However, this sutra takes Ānanda’s mistaken falling [into the hells] as its introductory occasion. Thus, the Tathāgata wishes to rescue him...
He himself recited the mantra, causing light to radiate from the crown of his head. This light further transformed into emanation-buddhas, and these emanation-buddhas also recited the mantra.
There is nothing else; this is entirely intended to initiate the purpose of the entire sutra. By citing an elephant, he indicates a meaning; by summoning a phenomenon, he reveals a principle.

One should know that when citing what kind of elephant to indicate what kind of meaning, or summoning what kind of phenomenon to reveal what kind of principle, the *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is signless (*animitta*).
Regarding the marks: throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-body. The Tathāgata’s prajñā is neither spoken nor unspoken;

throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not prajñā. The Tathāgata’s liberation is neither manifested nor unmanifested; throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not liberation.
It is simply because Ānanda is deluded and lacks awakening, obscured and lacking understanding, that he perceives [only] the thirty-two [marks].

One arouses the aspiration for enlightenment by perceiving the marks [of a Buddha]; one listens to the Dharma by taking as an object the sounds of the eightfold voice and the four analytical knowledges.
Thus, the faculties and their objects remain distinct, and the subject-object duality is not lost; it is merely birth-and-death, not non-birth-and-death.

For this reason, upon encountering the form of the courtesan Sundarī, although it was not identical to the marks of a Buddha, one was nonetheless turned by it; yet when hearing the mantra of Brahmā, although it was not...
It seems that even the Buddha’s voice is thus subsumed. From the beginning, the Buddha’s intention was to use the finger to point at the moon; now Ānanda has instead mistaken the finger for the moon.
From the beginning, the Buddha’s intention was to use the trap to catch the fish; he has caused Ānanda to instead cling to the trap as if it were the fish.
Reaching such a state, there is nothing that can be done; one must simply employ a great expedient means through non-...
From the crown of his head, he emitted light, and within that light were manifested transformation Buddhas who recited mantras.
[The Buddha’s intention was that] Ānanda might see the transformation Buddhas within the light and realize that the marks of the thirty-two characteristics cannot be taken as characteristics;

and that by hearing the transformation Buddhas recite the mantras, he might realize that the sounds of the eight qualities of voice and the four analytical knowledges cannot be taken as sounds. Thus, even the Tathāgata’s marks are not, in fact, marks. And...
How could the marks of the courtesan Ḍombī be considered true marks? Even the voice of the Tathāgata is not truly a voice;
