how then could the voice of Brahmā’s evil incantations be considered a voice? In this regard, it is not that I wait for Ḍombī to transform me—Ḍombī transforms herself for me;
why then would I be transformed by her? It is not that I wait to subdue Brahmā—Brahmā subdues himself for me.

That is further subsumed by it: not only is the mark of the Tathāgata realized as being neither mark nor non-mark, but even the marks of Gaṇikā are likewise neither mark nor non-mark, for there is nothing that is not the Dharma-body. Furthermore, not only is the sound of the Tathāgata realized as being neither sound nor non-sound.
Even the voice of Brahmā is both sound and non-sound; there is nothing that is not Prajñā. All of these are the great liberation manifested through the Tathāgata’s spiritual power.
Furthermore, know that whether the Tathāgata manifests or does not manifest, there is nothing that is not liberation.

There is not a single thing that is not the secret treasury of the three virtues—the Dharmakāya, Prajñā, and Liberation of the Tathāgata. If one can realize this, then upon seeing form, one sees [the nature of] self...
Not being stained by form; hearing sounds, one is not stained by sounds. Seeing forms does not stain one’s seeing of forms, so that one may continue to see forms all day long;

hearing sounds does not stain one’s hearing of sounds, so that one may continue to hear sounds all day long. Only then can it be called "hearing hearing," and only then can it be called "seeing seeing.
This is why what follows is clarified: from the point of destroying the deluded mind to reveal the true seeing, [one proceeds] beyond the five aggregates.

From the six sense bases up to the seven elements, there is not a single thing that is not the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā), the pure and original essence of the Tathāgata-garbha mind, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

From this, by raising the elephant to illustrate the meaning, there is nothing that does not manifest; by summoning the phenomenon to reveal the principle, there is nothing that does not penetrate it.
For this reason, light is emitted from the crown of the head, and within the light, transformation Buddhas appear, who preach the mantra. Thus it is.
Thus, one knows that the Prologue initiates [the teaching] by taking the three virtues within the nature as its starting point;

thereby, the ultimate, firm principle elucidated in the Main Exposition can be seen. Furthermore, the Prologue initiates [the teaching] by taking the three virtues within cultivation as its starting point;
thereby, the ultimate, firm practice and the ultimate, firm stage elucidated in the Main Exposition can also be seen. Moreover—
To explain: the introduction contains the virtue of the *dharmakāya*, while the main exposition contains the ultimate, firm principle;

the introduction contains the virtue of *prajñā*, while the main exposition contains the ultimate, firm practice; the introduction contains the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*), while the main exposition contains the ultimate, firm realization.
Thus, the introduction serves as the prologue to this main exposition, and the main exposition is the fulfillment of that prologue.

This is the formal exposition. If there are those of superior faculties and sharp intelligence who perceive the Way through direct observation, they will already have gained benefit from this single instance of the teaching of form.

However, as for those of middling or inferior capacities who have not yet clarified this principle, there is further the teaching of sound in the subsequent sections. The introductory section is concluded.

The second part, the Main Body (*śarīra*), is further divided into two sections. First, from "Ānanda saw the Buddha" up to "You should uphold this" in the middle of the eighth fascicle constitutes the Right Path (*mārga*).
Second, from "Having spoken these words" up to the end of the tenth fascicle, "not longing for the three realms," constitutes the Aids to the Path (*sambhāra-mārga*).
The first section is further divided into four parts. The first clarifies the ultimate, firm principle; it begins from "Ānanda saw the Buddha" and continues as follows:

1. Remaining in contemplation and listening within the first four fascicles. 2. Demonstrating the ultimate, steadfast practice, from "and the great assembly" up to the contents of the seventh fascicle, where it says "as wished.
3. Revealing the ultimate, steadfast stage, from "immediately rising from his seat" up to the eighth fascicle, where it says "named *mithyā-sakhā* (false friend).
4. Concluding with the name of the ultimate, steadfast state, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī... onwards.
"You should uphold this. The first part is further divided into two sections. The first extends from here until the end of the third fascicle;

it addresses Ānanda to clarify the destruction of the false and the manifestation of the true, thereby opening the way to perfect understanding. The second extends from the beginning of the fourth fascicle until the passage "yet still retains the capacity for observation and hearing";

it addresses Pūrṇa to clarify how delusion regarding the truth gives rise to the false, thereby opening the way to perfect understanding. The first of these [two] is further divided into three parts. The first begins with "Ānanda" and addresses those who are ready to receive the teaching.

The request for instruction; second, the assembly’s aspiration to hear it from the passage beginning "At that time"; third, the Tathāgata’s response and exposition from the passage beginning "The Buddha said.
Regarding the first, the request made by the appropriate recipient: *bodhi* (enlightenment) is the essence of the fruit to be realized;

*śamatha* and the other two [meditations] are the causal practices that realize it. If one wishes to proceed from cause to fruit, there must necessarily be an entrance gate—namely, the very first stage.
It is so. Regarding the three, śamatha and the others: the essence of śamatha is true cessation; the function of samādhi is cessation according with conditions;

and dhyāna is cessation that quiets the two extremes. Thus the three cessations are unified in this way. Śamatha is the contemplation of emptiness (śūnyatā-vipaśyanā); samādhi is the contemplation of the provisional (upāya-vipaśyanā);
and dhyāna is the contemplation of the middle (madhyama-vipaśyanā). Thus the three contemplations are likewise unified. Such is the establishment of the Dharma by the Sages.
It is not a matter of one-sidedness. "Cessation" (śamatha) means to still the scattering [of the mind]; "contemplation" (vipaśyanā) means to illuminate the darkness.

When discussed in terms of emotional states, darkness leads to scattering, and scattering leads to darkness. Therefore, when establishing methods for remedial treatment, how could one employ cessation alone without contemplation, or contemplation alone without cessation?
Thus, śamatha is cessation, samādhi is contemplation, and dhyāna is the non-duality of cessation and contemplation. Furthermore, cessation and contemplation are joined together.

Thus it is. Although there have been three successive sections of analysis and synthesis above, these three sections are all unified: to mention one is to mention all three, and to speak of three is to speak of one.
They are neither vertical nor horizontal, neither combined nor separate. Since the three meanings are identical, let us clarify them by means of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*).
In the śamatha contemplation of emptiness, if it is empty, then all is empty; even the provisional of the Middle Way is empty—this is what is meant by "when one is empty, all are empty.

In the samādhi contemplation of the provisional, if it is provisional, then all is provisional; even emptiness and the Middle Way are provisional—this is what is meant by "when one is provisional, all are provisional.

In the dhyāna contemplation of the Middle Way, if it is the Middle, then all is the Middle; even emptiness and the provisional are the Middle—this is what is meant by "when one is the Middle, all are the Middle."
This is the ultimate point. The three [practices] are perfectly interfused and inconceivable; therefore, they are called "wondrous śamatha," "wondrous samādhi," and "wondrous dhyāna.
Because there is no cause other than this, the essence of the fruit itself functions as the causal mind, and conversely, the causal mind realizes the essence of the fruit.
Thus it is said that the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain bodhi, and so forth. *Pūrvayoga* (Preceding Practice).
In the sections below, such as the "Śamatha" chapter, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the seven elements (*sapta-dhātu*) are examined;

this is also consistent with the "Pūrṇa" chapter’s comparative exposition of the three *tathāgatagarbhas*. Regarding the "initial skillful means," the question concerns where to apply oneself in the three types of practice.

This specifically points to the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*) as the initial skillful means. Therefore, in the subsequent section on selecting the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-avavāda*), it is said:
It is said: "The true essence of the teaching in this land resides in purity within hearing and sound; if one wishes to attain samādhi, one must truly enter through hearing.

Furthermore, Avalokiteśvara himself declared: "I entered through hearing" (and so forth). One can thus know with certainty that the faculty of the ear is the most expedient means of perfect penetration (*guanyong*).
Viewing these points together, because he inquired about the three—wonderful *śamatha* and so forth—the first three fascicles [of the *Mohe zhiguan*] are presented.
Everything elucidated in the first half of the sutra is nothing other than a response to the questions asked. This is because those questions concerned the initial expedient means (*upāya*).
From the point where Ānanda requested entry into the jeweled house onward, everything elucidated is likewise nothing other than a response to the questions asked.

This is because those questions concerned the attainment of *bodhi*. From the seventh fascicle through the eighth, it begins with the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) and culminates in the Subtle [Wisdom].
The fifty-five stages of the path to bodhi within the intermediate section are likewise nothing other than responses to the questions posed.

Third, within the Tathāgata’s response and instruction, there are two parts: first, from this point until the end of the third fascicle, the Tathāgata responds to the request; second...
At that time, Ānanda reached the end of the seven-word verse and attained realization according to his capacity. This section is further divided into three parts:

first, the response to *śamatha* (calm abiding), which extends from here until the middle of the second fascicle; second, the response to *samādhi* (concentration), which extends from "You have not yet clarified this" until the middle of the third fascicle;
third, the response to *dhyāna* (meditative cultivation), which extends from "He addressed the Buddha" until the end of the third fascicle. The first part is further divided into four sections.

First, from "The Buddha said" downward, there is the inquiry regarding the arousal of the resolve for enlightenment (*bodhicitta*). Second, from "The Buddha said" downward, both the true and the false are indicated together.

Third, from "You now" downward, there is the exhortation to advance with a straightforward mind (*ṛjukacitta*). Fourth, from "I now" downward, the false is directly refuted. The first [section] also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer.
Regarding the question concerning the phrase "suddenly renouncing the deep and heavy affection of the world": among the things in the world, nothing is more weighty than the grace of one's parents;

nothing is deeper than the love for one's wife and children. Unless one leaves the household life to study the supramundane Dharma in order to attain the life of wisdom and realize the Dharma-body, there is no way to transcend this. Therefore, one must suddenly renounce the deep and heavy [affections] of the world.
This is affection. Regarding the second answer, as for the passage "I see the Tathāgata," etc.: Ānanda’s great root of illness is precisely this.

For although he resolved his mind upon seeing the marks of the thirty-two signs, the internal faculty of sight, the external objects of form, and the intermediate consciousness that discriminates—all three of these:
faculty, object, and consciousness—belong entirely to the realm of arising and ceasing. This is...
Even though one may have attained the first fruit [of the path], one is still not yet free from being turned by the courtesan Caṇḍālī or being ensnared by the evil spells of the Brahmā-devas.

If one can thoroughly penetrate that the three—sense organs, sense objects, and consciousness—are in their very essence quiescent, yet without hindering the fact that these three—sense organs, sense objects, and consciousness—remain vividly present as they are;
and that within this state of vivid presence there is quiescence, and within quiescence there is vivid presence; where obstruction and illumination are of one suchness, and all is emptiness.
There is non-duality. This is what is called wondrous *śamatha*, wondrous *samādhi*, and wondrous *dhyāna*. What can that *ḍākinī* do to you?
For the reason that the three—*śamatha* and the others—clarified below do nothing more than eliminate the root of one's afflictions.
Question: Why is it necessary to examine the arousal of the bodhicitta? Answer: To cultivate *bodhi*.

The practice is no small matter; the essential point lies in ensuring that the arousal of the bodhicitta is upright and correct. If the arousal of the mind is not correct, how could the Way ever be attained?
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "If one takes birth-and-death as the cause while seeking the fruit of non-birth-and-death, such a thing is impossible."
This is precisely what is meant here.
Within the section that presents the two pairs of truth and falsehood, the words "Excellent, Ānanda," and so forth, must be understood properly. This means:

"That you have been able to give rise to this aspiration is indeed excellent"; thus, he exclaims "Excellent. However, the aspiration arising from the perceived appearances is not yet entirely perfect.

Therefore, it is further said: "You all... (and so forth). As for "all sentient beings," sentient beings are a conventional designation established by means of the real dharmas of the five aggregates; these are precisely the nine realms. Hence, it is called "all.
Whether as ordinary beings within the six paths or as sages within the three vehicles, both ignorance and the dharma-nature are beginningless. What is now referred to as "beginningless" is...

This is ignorance (*avidyā*). This is the cause of origination (*samudaya*). As for birth and death (*saṃsāra*): within the six destinies (*ṣaḍgati*), there is the birth-and-death of segmented existence;
within the Three Vehicles (*triyāna*), there is the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāmika*). Although these differ, they all collectively belong to birth and death.

Being born and dying, dying and being born—birth after birth, death after death, death after death, birth after birth—it is like a ring without end, a wheel that does not cease. Therefore, it is called "continuous succession" (*prabandha*). This is suffering (*duḥkha*).

Result. Thus, these afflictions and the cycle of birth and death all arise because of not knowing the Truth. Therefore it is said: "All [arise] because of not knowing the Permanently Abiding" (and so forth).

Furthermore, because one does not know the delusive, it is said: "Employing the various... (and so forth). These two phrases concerning the Permanently Abiding are explained by analyzing their constituent characters:
that which spans the three periods of time without arising or ceasing is called "Permanence. That which pervades the ten directions without coming or going...
Coming is abiding. To be forever detached from all that is false is truth. To be unattached to all defilements is purity. To contemplate and illuminate all phenomena is clarity.
That upon which all phenomena rely is the essence. As for the mind, its function is the nature, and its nature is the essence.
To explain this in summary: when the three thousand natures and characteristics are present within a single speck of dust...
To establish it as "empty void" (śūnyatā): not even a single atom is established, yet this does not obstruct the three thousand natures and characteristics.

To establish it as "wondrous existence" (prabhāsvara-sattā): within the three thousand natures and characteristics, not even a single atom is established; where not even a single atom is established, there are the three thousand natures and characteristics.

To establish it as "perfect middle" (madhyama): the three and the one are mutually identical; the three and the one are non-dual. A mind such as this is precisely the eternally abiding true mind (tathatā-citta). As...
The nature of this is precisely the essence of pure and luminous nature. Yet, because you do not know this reality, there is this beginningless cycle of birth and death.
Because you do not know the reality, that which you employ consists solely of various deluded thoughts; thus it is said, "employing various deluded thoughts.
If ordinary beings employ only that which is illusory existence, and those of the Two Vehicles employ only partial truth, [then how could they attain liberation?]

That which the Bodhisattva employs is exclusively the Middle Way alone. Thus, in contrast to such [views as] eternalism and so forth, or the wondrous existence of true emptiness and the perfect Middle, [the other views] are merely deluded thoughts.
Since they are deluded thoughts, they are not the true essence; therefore, there is the revolving of birth and death.
Thus, deluded thought is the cause and the revolving cycle is the fruit. Furthermore, you must not— (Note: The provided text ends abruptly with "汝又不" [you also not], leaving the sentence incomplete.)
[The Buddha] said: "I know. This is why there is this continuity of birth and death. Why is it that in this passage, having already indicated the truth, you again indicate the delusion?
Since Ānanda has already asked about the three—*śamatha*, [vipaśyanā], and [the third], the Tathāgata will answer and clarify them below.

Speaking in terms of destroying delusion, he destroys the deluded mind, destroys deluded views, and destroys the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing, as well as their spontaneous conjunction."
Since states such as disharmony are all without exception illusory, their illusoriness is pointed out to serve as a handle for subsequent refutation.
Speaking in terms of revealing the True [Mind], it reveals the True Mind and the True Seeing; even when the seeing of seeing occurs, that seeing is not [ordinary] seeing.
Furthermore, the five aggregates and the three categories are all nothing other than the Tathāgata-garbha mind, the wondrous nature of True Suchness. The seven elements, beginning with earth...

The Great Non-existence is fundamentally pure and pervades the entire Dharma-realm; these all manifest the True. Therefore, the True is designated as the underlying basis for what is to be manifested later.
Thus, the True is designated so that others may know the True, and the False is designated so that others may know the False.
If one knows the true, the true should be cultivated; if one knows the false, the false should be shattered. If one can cultivate the true, the false will naturally shatter;
if one can shatter the false, the true will naturally manifest. When this stage is reached, how could there be the continuity of birth and death?
It is for this reason that this is specifically pointed out for those who are ready to receive the teaching.

Third, the exhortation to advance with a direct mind has two parts. First, the actual exhortation: "You now," and so forth. Second, citing a parallel case: "The Ten Powers," and so forth; this is evident.

Fourth, the correct refutation of falsehood has two parts. First, from "Ānanda" downward, the interrogation and examination. Second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the refutation and revelation. Within the first [part], there is again...
Two. First, an examination of what it is that one cherishes: Ānanda and others. Second, an inquiry into the location of the mind and the eyes: the Buddha’s discourse and so forth.
Regarding the first, the examination of what it is that one cherishes, there are questions and answers, all of which can be seen [in the text].

Second, regarding the investigation of the location of the mind and its objects, there are two parts. First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he indicates the meaning. Second, from "I now" onwards, is the question and answer. The first part [of the second] also has three sections:
namely, the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis. The first, the principle, is easily understood. Regarding the second, the analogy: "For example, like a king," etc.

The "king" refers to the eternally abiding true mind, because it is able to reign over the land of the *dharmatā*. As for the "thief"— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly with "賊" (thief).*

This is precisely deluded imagination. It is what is called the six mediums that invite thieves to plunder the family’s own treasures. "The soldiers" refers to the dharmas such as *śamatha* and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "causing you to transmigrate within the threefold union": Ānanda, because of this, his mind and eyes followed sounds and pursued forms;
at the very beginning, these were the forms of the Tathāgata’s thirty-two marks and the sounds of his eightfold voice and fourfold analytical eloquence.
They subsequently transmigrate through the seductive forms of the demoness Dēnggā and the heterodox sounds of the Brahmā heavens;
all of this is due solely to the fault of the mind and the eyes.

The second section, consisting of questions and answers, has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the initial question, the inquiry focuses specifically on the mind and the eyes, as these pertain to the process of transmigration (*saṃsāra*).
In the subsequent answer, regarding the "ten kinds of ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*), there should be twelve according to the "twelve classes of beings" mentioned later in the text;
however, because those who are empty, distracted, or submerged do not abide within the mind or the eyes, only ten are mentioned here. These "ordinary beings" are...
Sentient beings. In the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*, they are all referred to as "ordinary beings" (*pṛthagjana*). This is because each of the ten [types] individually attracts its own respective fruit;

since their causes consist of both good and evil, the resulting fruits are either excellent or inferior. Regarding the "four objects of the floating root," this refers to the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).
The four great elements—earth, water, fire, and wind—act as its substantial basis, while the four subtle particles—form, sound, odor, and taste—act as [its objective support].
That which has been established is now presented comprehensively; thus, it is said: "the four dusts of floating roots.

Regarding the phrase "World-Honored One and others," it is because Ānanda had consistently identified the mind as being within the body and the eyes as being on the face, and did not dare speak directly.
Therefore, [the Buddha] first cited ten types [of cases] to clarify that his mind was inside, thereby making it known that his eyes were likewise on the face. Next, he cited...
The Tathāgata, by clarifying that the eyes are on the face, knows that the mind is likewise within. This is merely a matter of citing one aspect to mutually illustrate the other;
it is spoken with full detail from the perspective of the subsequent [analysis] regarding oneself. The meaning is this: just as the Tathāgata’s eyes are on the face, so too is it for me, Ānanda.
Furthermore, it means that the ten kinds of ordinary beings’ minds are within the body; this serves as an analogy.
I, Ānanda, am likewise so. Therefore it is said: "I now... (and so forth).

The second section, "Refuting the False to Reveal the True," is further divided into two parts. First, from "The Buddha told Ānanda" onwards, he refutes the false mind. Second, after [Ānanda] has heard this, he again proceeds to reveal the true seeing.
The first part is further divided into two. First, the "Seven Locations" refute that the false mind has no locus; this is what is meant by "The Buddha told Ānanda," etc.

Furthermore, there are two or three places where the false essence is interrogated and found to be non-existent; these are the passages beginning with "Ānanda was among the great assembly," and so forth. Within the first section, there are again seven parts:

first, from "The Buddha addressed Ānanda" downward, which refutes the calculation that [the self] is within the body; second, from "Ānanda bowed his head" downward, which refutes the calculation that [the self] is outside the body.

1. From "Ānanda said to the Buddha" below, the refutation of the calculation regarding the hidden root (*mūla*). 2. From "Ānanda said to the Buddha" below, the refutation of the calculation regarding the internal and external (*adhyātma-bahirdhā*).

3. From "I [say]" below, the refutation of the calculation regarding following and combining (*anugata-saṃyoga*). 4. From "Ānanda said to the Buddha" below, the refutation of the calculation regarding the intermediate (*antara*).

Seven: Ānanda addresses the Buddha; this section below refutes the calculation of non-attachment. It is further divided into three parts. First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he cites the facts to examine them in detail.

Second, from "At that time" onwards, he bestows a head-stroking, offers admonitions, and grants permission. Third, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he cites the facts by way of analogy to refute [the opponent's view].
The first of these is further divided into three: first, defining internal and external, starting from "The Buddha said"; second, defining priority and sequence, starting from "Ānanda"; third...
The sequence for establishing the causal basis begins with Ānanda’s departure. First, one establishes the internal, external, and intermediate.
When you are now seated here, etc., this is because Ānanda is used as an analogy for the mind, the lecture hall for the body, and the Jeta Grove for the mountains, rivers, and the great earth.
As for "light, darkness, obstruction, and emptiness," this is why Ānanda is inside the lecture hall while the Jeta Grove is outside the lecture hall; thus, one first establishes [the boundaries].

The internal and external are thus. Regarding the sequence of the two concentrations and the statement, "You are now in the hall," this is because Ānanda first saw the Tathāgata and others while inside the hall;
by analogy, one should recognize that if the mind were located within, it ought to have seen the heart and liver first.

In this way, when looking outward from afar, one sees the groves and gardens; by analogy, if you recognize that the mind is within, you should likewise first see the heart and liver, and only then see what is external.
Furthermore, the sequence of priority and posteriority is exactly like this.

Regarding the third point concerning the causal basis—namely, your belonging to the groves and gardens and so forth—since the lecture hall is analogous to your body and your mind is within, how could you possibly see what is outside?
Regarding the grove and garden: because the openings of the windows and doors are analogous to the apertures of the sense organs (*indriya*), we infer that the mind is within;
it is by means of the apertures of the sense organs that one is able to see the external. This is again a definitive cause based on reasoning.

Furthermore, just as in this case, one should know that in the three preceding sections, the matter was first established through investigation, and subsequently, in the following section, those very words were used as examples to overturn and refute [the opponent's position]. This is the method of the Tathāgata.
This is the subtle discernment [of the Tathāgata]. Were it not so, this passage would be useless; yet how could the teaching of the Tathāgata be useless?
All subsequent instances are to be understood in this manner.
Regarding the second part, the "Consecration by Touching the Crown and Granting Permission," there are two intentions for touching Ānanda’s crown:
first, to grant permission by touching his crown prior to opening his understanding of the eternally abiding true mind;

second, because the head is where the deluded mind is to be destroyed at seven locations, and since that deluded mind is what he has been calculating, he might suddenly become terrified when it is destroyed—therefore, he touches his crown to comfort him. There is...
Regarding "samādhi and so forth": samādhi is the cause; the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa is the fruit. Furthermore, samādhi is practice, while the Śūraṅgama King is the principle.
This is the state where cause and fruit are non-dual, and practice and principle share the same essence.
If the cause of samādhi is designated by the name of the fruit, the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, then one knows the reason why samādhi is called samādhi.
The entirety of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa is samādhi; furthermore, the fruit of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa is the name for the cause of samādhi.
Thus, one knows that the reason it is called the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa is that the entirety of samādhi constitutes the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa.

This refers to what is called the non-duality of cause and effect, and the identity of cultivation with nature and phenomena. The principle of the *Śūraṅgama-sūtra* is likewise clearly manifested in this manner. It concludes thus:
This refers to the practice of the non-duality of principle, wherein cultivation and nature are mutually identical. Regarding the phrase "endowed with the myriad practices":

since the name *samādhi* is the Great Buddha-Crown Śūraṅgama King, and it is further said to be "endowed with the myriad practices," this precisely reveals that the fruit-virtue of the Great Buddha-Crown and the ontological essence of the Śūraṅgama possess the myriad practices of *samādhi*. If expressed in terms of the six perfections, first—
To be mindful of non-attachment is called giving; even a single moment of non-delusion is called wisdom. As it is with the six perfections, so it is with the ten perfections;
as it is with the ten perfections, so it is with the myriad practices. Therefore, it is said that the myriad practices are fully perfected.
As for the phrase "the Tathāgatas of the ten directions," since Samādhi is named the Great Buddha-Crown and also the King of Śūraṅgama, it is the full perfection of the myriad practices.
This is precisely the gate through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions emerge from birth-and-death and the path leading to Nirvana.
Because they take the complete fruit to constitute the cause and the complete principle to constitute the practice, it is called "the one gate.

Because cause and effect are non-dual and practice and principle are as one—such that it cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words—it is called "the Path of Wondrous Adornment. As it is said:
This is to know that this samādhi is their gateway; this samādhi is also their path. It is not so for only one direction or one Buddha;
therefore, it is said to belong to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions. Ānanda previously asked about three types [of samādhi];
now, since this samādhi is named the Great Buddha[-samādhi] and also the King of Śūraṅgama, and is further endowed with the myriad practices, it belongs to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
The wondrously adorned path that transcends through a single gate is such for both *śamatha* and *dhyāna* as well.
Now, as this is the initial stage of elucidating it for them, I shall explain it in its entirety. However, I treat only *samādhi*, because this sutra emphasizes the manifestation of the truth.
Yet, when there is manifestation, all are manifested together; thus, within *śamatha*, when the true mind is manifested, it is described as "ever-abiding."
In the *Zhenshin* (True Mind), when revealing the truth of seeing, it says: "At the moment of seeing the seeing, that seeing is not [the ordinary] seeing.

In the *Samādhi*, when revealing the truth of the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the three categories (*dhātus*), it says: "The Tathāgatagarbha-mind, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).

In the *Cenana* (Dhyāna), when revealing the truth of the seven elements such as earth, it says: "Pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. This is what is meant by establishing one [truth] for each.
It stands firm in its entirety. It is not only samādhi that is the wondrous existence which manifests the truth;

furthermore, when the true and the deluded mind are manifested, they are simultaneously shattered—this is what is meant by "shattering one, all are shattered. It is not only śamatha that is the empty void which destroys the deluded;
furthermore, destroying and manifesting occur at the same time, such that truth and delusion mutually dissolve—this is what is meant by "unifying one, all are unified. It is not only dhyāna...
That is the perfect center wherein negation and establishment occur simultaneously. Therefore, it is called wondrous śamatha, wondrous samādhi, and wondrous dhyāna.
As for the term "samādhi" used here in its negating sense, it precisely reveals that the three dharmas are perfectly interfused and inconceivable.
The refutation of the three examples is further divided into three parts. First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the case is re-examined according to the precedent.
Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the opponent's position is restated and refuted through reasoning. Third, from "Therefore" onwards, it is concluded that [the mind] does not reside within.

Within the first section, the re-examination according to the precedent, there is a question and an answer; this constitutes another round of scrutiny. Although the preceding section cited the case in detail for examination, now, wishing to refute it, one fears that...
I do not know why this is so; therefore, I have re-examined it.

The second section, which restates the opponent's position and refutes it, is further divided into two parts. First, the restatement of the position, referring to Ānanda and others. Second, the refutation, beginning with "At that time," and so forth.
Within the first part, regarding the phrase "You are also like this," the intended meaning is: you claim that sentient beings are in the hall.
That one does not see the Tathāgata and that there are no groves or springs—such a thing is impossible. Thus it is as you have said.
However, from my perspective, this applies not only to sentient beings but to you, Ānanda, as well.
This is because I am citing your statement that sentient beings in the hall should see the Tathāgata and the groves and springs; thus, your mind is within.

The application of this principle can be understood by analogy. In the preceding section on "Examining and Determining Phenomena," the intention was to use Ānanda’s presence in the lecture hall as an analogy for the mind being within;
the Tathāgata and the great assembly as an analogy for the internal organs such as the heart and liver;

and the Jeta Grove as an analogy for external phenomena such as mountains, rivers, and the great earth. Therefore, it is restated: "You are also like this" (and so forth). Second, the refutation through reasoning is threefold.

First, the refutation by taking away [the premise]; second, the refutation by not allowing [the premise] to proceed; third, the refutation by reprimanding [the premise]. Regarding the first, the refutation by taking away:
as for the phrase "At that time," the meaning is this: you maintain that the conscious mind truly exists within the body.
If we apply this to your own case as an example, it is like your own Ānanda being in the lecture hall. You were previously in the hall...
Regarding the seeing of the Tathāgata and others, by analogy with your own mind being within the body, you should likewise first see everything that exists within the body. Therefore it is said:

"At that time... (and so forth). Although we grant your calculation for the sake of argument, could there ever be a sentient being who first sees all that is within the body—just as you might first see the Tathāgata and the great assembly while in the hall, and only later observe external objects? It would be just like your own case.

Next, does one see things such as forests and springs? Therefore it is said, "Is there [such seeing]? (and so forth). The two instances of the character *jiàn* (to see)—in "previously seen" and "the capacity to see"—have the same meaning as *zhī* (to know/cognize);
however, because they are treated according to the analogy of the sense-faculties (*neng*), they are termed "seeing. By this, the thesis that the mind resides within is not established.
Second, regarding the refutation of the concession: one should first supplement the following counter-argument: "Even though the mind is within, it does not..."
If one were able to first see within the body, the Tathāgata would immediately refute this, saying: "Even if you grant that the mind is inside, one does not see the heart, liver, and so forth;
this is just like granting that [a person] is inside a hall, yet one does not see the Tathāgata. Therefore it is said: "Even if... (and so forth).
As for the growth of the nails, the lengthening of the hair, the turning of the tendons, and the throbbing of the vessels—such things as these pertain to both the internal and the external.

One must certainly understand each point clearly and distinctly. To illustrate this: although one does not see the Tathāgata when inside the lecture hall, those among the great assembly who are present both inside and outside should indeed see him.
Therefore it is said, "The fingernails grow" (and so forth). In the same way, the mind is within the body, yet one does not see the heart, liver, and other organs.
By analogy, when you are inside the hall, how could it be that you do not see the Tathāgata? It is simply that you do not see him.

"It is simply that [the mind] does not see them. Furthermore, you do not see your own nails, hair, and so forth; yet while you are in the hall, the great assembly also does not see you—is this possible?
Therefore it is said: 'How could it not know? By this reasoning, the position that the mind is internal is also untenable.
Regarding the third refutation, "it would necessarily not be equal," the meaning is that what has been explained above concerns your assertion that the mind is internal.

"You do not know what is within. If you are indeed so ignorant, then since your mind is within yet does not even know what is inside, how can it possibly know all external things—such as mountains, rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, and the obstructed void—which have no connection whatsoever with the internal?
It would be like being inside a hall and not seeing the Tathāgata; how then could you see the groves and springs outside the hall?"
If you were inside a hall, you would necessarily see the Tathāgata and the great assembly within, and only afterwards see the groves and springs outside, because your body is situated inside.
If you reckon that the mind is inside, yet you do not see what is within, then it does not conform to the analogy of being inside a hall and seeing the Tathāgata and the great assembly.
If you do not even know what is inside, how could you know what is outside? Thus, it is not so.
This is the same principle as seeing the forest and springs from outside the hall. How could your calculation be "inside"? Therefore it is said, "It certainly is not... (and so forth).

By this, the calculation that the mind is inside is also refuted. The three preceding sections—refutation by subtraction, refutation by concession, and refutation by interrogation—all employ examples based on the established facts to dismantle them. Only then can one see that you are currently sitting right here before me.
The phrase "and so forth," as you have stated, has its basis and its resolution. It should be understood that the three fetters do not exist internally.

Second, the refutation of the notion that they exist outside the body consists of two parts: first, Ānanda and others state their position; second, the Buddha’s response thoroughly refutes it. First: [the statement of the position].

Furthermore, there are two parts. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, the actual presentation; second, from "The meaning is... onwards, the request for verification. Within the first part, there are again two sections. First, the establishment of a position;
[beginning with] "Ānanda and others. Second, the shifting of the position; [beginning with] "For this reason... Within the first section on the establishment of the position:

"Those who hear such a Dharma-sound of the Tathāgata" refers precisely to the aforementioned argument that [the mind] being internal is untenable. "To awaken to and know... is the position being established.

The second section, the rebuttal, is divided into two parts. First, from "For example" onwards, it introduces the preceding argument through an analogy. Second, from "All" onwards, it provides the actual analogy.
Within the first part, the analogy of the light of a lamp and so forth illustrates that the consciousness-mind, being within, does not perceive what is internal.

The second part, the formal analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), also has two sections. First, the presentation of the principle (*dharma*), beginning with "All... and so forth. Second, the application of the analogy (*upanaya*), beginning with "It is also like... and so forth; both are clearly visible.

Within the second section, the request for proof, the phrase "those who understand the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) as the Buddha does" does not refer to the "definitive meaning" mentioned in the title.
Ānanda’s intention was that what he had previously conceived was refuted by the Tathāgata because it was not of definitive meaning; he thought that the Tathāgata would certainly...
Because [the mind] is external, it is considered the definitive meaning (nītārtha). Now, I have awakened to the realization that the mind truly exists externally;

I wish to accord with the Tathāgata’s intent regarding the definitive meaning. Could it be that, by means of the definitive meaning, I am merely borrowing from the Tathāgata’s definitive meaning? Therefore, it is said:
"To accord with the Buddha" (and so forth).

The second [section], the examination through refutation, is divided into three parts: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the matter is examined and determined; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the opponent's position is restated and refuted through reasoning;

third, from "Therefore" onwards, it is concluded that [the self] does not exist externally. The first part [of the first section] is further divided into two: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the first [question]: [Text continues...]
Regarding the one who came to beg for alms, some have raised the doubt: "On the day the Sūtra was preached, it coincided with a vegetarian feast provided by the king and his ministers;
why then did he go begging for alms? The Tathāgata also accepted their offerings; why then did he say, 'I have already partaken of my meal'?

This is likely because they do not understand that the parable spoken by the Tathāgata is analogous to the Dharma and thus take it as a literal precedent, failing to realize that this was not actually a case of begging for alms while accepting an offering. As stated above:
Regarding the phrase "having just come": "just" (shì) means "immediately" or "as soon as. Regarding the phrase "having fasted overnight" (*sùzhāi*): "overnight" (*sù*) means "in advance.
This includes the sense of the time when even a single person has finished eating. It refers to the fact that once the bhikṣus have completed their alms-round, they return to take their meal.
Therefore it is said: "Observe this... (and so forth). The two lines concerning "one person" serve as an analogy for the mind being outside the body, such that the mind and the body do not interact.
Since there is one person and many people who are separated from one another, how could one person eating cause many people to be satiated?
Ānanda’s response likewise conveys this meaning; he uses the example of the mind being outside the body to show that there would also be a distinction between self and other.

How could it be that the mind has cognition while the body also experiences sensation? Therefore, in the subsequent section on the formal refutation, this very case is used as an analogy for the refutation.
Although there are three further rounds of inquiry concerning phenomena and principle, they all share this same intent. In the second response, regarding "the body and life being different":
although the Arhat has severed the fetters of the cause (hetu-bandhana), the fetters of the fruit (phala-bandhana) still remain; thus it is said that the body and life are different.

The second section, "Citing the Assertion and Refuting it through Reasoning," is divided into two parts. First, "Citing the Assertion," which begins with "Then the Buddha said... and so forth. Second, "Refuting through Reasoning," which begins with "Body and mind...

and so forth. This is further divided into three: first, refutation based on principle, beginning with "Body and mind..."; second, refutation based on facts, beginning with "I now..."; and third, further refutation through interrogation, beginning with "The Buddha said...".
The conclusion that [the self] does not exist externally can be seen throughout; I shall not record them again here.
The third section, "Refuting the Calculations Regarding the Latent Root," is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the presentation of the calculation;
second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the refutation. The first part is further divided into two: first, a general presentation; second, a specific indication.
Within the general presentation, the phrase "knowing it to be in one place" refers to Ānanda’s hidden intention, as he had previously calculated that [consciousness] resided within.
The internal is refuted; calculating it as being external, the external is refuted. For this reason, I do not dare to point specifically to any particular location here, but it is simply one place.
Second, the specific pointing is further divided into two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s inquiry, namely the words of the Buddha and so forth, which are evident.

Second, the response of the one suited to the occasion, namely Ānanda and others. The text has three sections: the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamā*), and their synthesis (*yoga*). First, the principle may be...
[The Buddha] said: "In the two similes, 'just as' and so forth, lapis lazuli is used to represent the sense organ (indriya) and the eye to represent the mind (citta).

Just as lapis lazuli does not obstruct the eye and the eye is thus able to see, so too consciousness (vijñāna) is latent within the sense organ; when the organ sees, the mind immediately performs discrimination.
Therefore it is said, 'just as' [and so forth]. However, although Ānanda relies upon this simile, he nonetheless commits a transgression against the Dharma."
This illustrates the fault of inconsistency; therefore, the Tathāgata refutes it immediately in the following passage, as can be seen in the third section of the main text.
Second, the analytical refutation is also divided into three parts. First, the examination and determination based on the analogy, beginning with "The Buddha said... and so forth.
Second, the citation of the thesis and its refutation through reasoning; this begins with "The Buddha said... Third, the conclusion that [the root] is not hidden;

this begins with "Therefore... The first [section] also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. Within the initial question, following the phrase "Just as lapis lazuli...", one should supplement it as follows:
"Your words are such as these, and your tenets are such as these; I shall therefore question you based on those very words and tenets of yours. Thus.
It says: "That person... (and so forth). In the second response, it can be seen that such scrutiny and verification establish that the dharma and the *dṛṣṭānta* are not equivalent;
this is merely setting the foundation for the refutation.

The second section, the citation of the opponent's position followed by its refutation, consists of two parts. First, the citation of the position, beginning with "The Buddha said... and so forth. Second, the formal refutation, beginning with "You should see... and so forth. This formal refutation further divides into two:
first, the general refutation beginning with "You should see..."; second, the specific refutation beginning with "If you see...
and so forth. Regarding the general refutation, it is as follows. Within the specific refutation, the eye is analyzed by means of the ear: if [the eye] sees [itself], then the eye... [is not seen].
This is the faculty that sees; that which possesses illumination and discernment. "Objects" are the realms that are seen. Regarding "immobility":
if one sees mountains and rivers and then sees one's own eye, the faculty that sees becomes identical to the realm that is seen. Therefore it is said, "the eye is identical to its object.
Now, if the faculty were identical to the object, and the object were immobile, then the faculty would likewise be immobile.
How can it be as you have stated above—that the faculty follows the seeing and immediately performs the discrimination? Therefore, it cannot be established that [the faculty] "follows" [the seeing].

First, it has been clarified that the refutation of "seeing" is established. Next, it is evident that there is no "not-seeing. Thus, the position regarding "seeing" is such that the dharma and the analogy are inconsistent.
How could it possibly be latent within the faculty, like a crystal placed over the eye and so forth? (Third Conclusion)
It can be understood that "it is not the case that the hidden root is itself" and so forth.

Fourth, the refutation of the calculation of the internal and external as two. First, from "Ānanda" downward, the calculation is set forth; second, from "The Buddha said" downward, it is refuted. The first [section] also has two parts:
first, the formal presentation, which is "Ānanda" and so forth; second, the request for verification, which is the passage on "meaning and words. Regarding the first, the formal presentation:
"In the middle: 'I now [think]... and so forth. This means that I initially reckoned the mind to be within, but was refuted by the Tathāgata’s definitive statement that it is not known internally.
Even when I reckoned the mind as being hidden within the sense organs, I was refuted by the Tathāgata through both scripture and analogy. Yet, how could my mind ultimately have no basis?
I must still contemplate until I attain it; thus it says, 'I now... and so forth. Below the passage beginning with 'opening the eyes,' [the text] should be supplemented."
It is said: because the cavities are located on the outside, there is light where there is an opening. Regarding the passage "closing the eyes," etc., one should also supplement it by saying:
because the viscera are located within, there is darkness where there is concealment.

Although Ānanda possesses the vision of light, the vision of the external, the vision of darkness, and the vision of the internal, what he emphasizes is primarily the internal. His intention is to rescue the first [position].
[The opponent claims that] it exists within the inner ear; therefore, the Tathāgata refutes this. The initial passage states:
"When you close your eyes and see darkness... (and so forth). Even in the concluding summary, it says: "As for your claim that seeing darkness is called 'seeing the internal,' this can be refuted.
Furthermore, the specific refutation focuses exclusively on the points of "seeing darkness" and "seeing the internal. The second [point], the request for proof, may be understood accordingly.

The refutation through reasoning is divided into three parts: first, the refutation regarding external vision based on the Buddha’s words; second, the refutation regarding internal vision based on the analysis of separation;

third, the summary and conclusion of the refutation. Some say that the section beginning with "If you... refutes the failure of seeing the external through the vision of light, while the section beginning with "If separated from...
refutes the failure of seeing the internal through the vision of darkness. However, these [interpretations] are all incorrect.

However, first, regarding external vision, we refute the claim that seeing darkness constitutes seeing the internal; second, regarding internal confrontation, we likewise refute the claim that seeing darkness constitutes seeing the internal.
Within the first section—refuting [the view] by means of external vision—it is further divided into two parts.
First, the initial determination: this is from "The Buddha said" onwards; it may be understood. Second, the refutation: this is from "If [it is] with" onwards. This is further divided into two parts:

first, the refutation by means of opposition, starting from "If [it is] with"; second, the non-oppositional refutation, starting from "If [it is] not. Within the first section on refutation by opposition, the text asks:
"How is it established as internal? One should supplement this with the following counter-argument: "Although the darkness spoken of by the Tathāgata is before one's eyes..."
This would not differ from the darkness within the internal organs; thus, they could form a pair. To refute this, it is said: "If [darkness] were formed... (and so forth). The meaning is as follows:

if you claim that the darkness before one's eyes is the same as the darkness within the body and therefore forms an internal pair, then the internal darkness of the burning viscera and the external darkness of a dark room would be one and the same darkness. Suppose, for instance, you were staying in a dark room...
In the middle [of the room], the entirety of the darkness within that dark chamber is all your own internal organs; how could the dark chamber itself become your internal organs?
The two lines of the second response can be understood accordingly. This is why it is impossible for you to see the darkness or see the interior.
The second section, the refutation by means of internal analysis, is divided into two parts. First, the direct refutation: "If [darkness] were separate... and so forth.

Second, the consequential refutation: "When seeing the face... and so forth. Regarding the first, the direct refutation: prior to the phrase "if it were separate," one should also supplement a further hypothetical argument, stating:
"That which I call 'darkness' is that which can be seen while closing one's eyes within the body; whereas what the Tathāgata calls a 'dark room' is [external]."
It exists within the body and is only seen when the eyes are opened. Therefore, my "seeing within" is distinct from external seeing.
Since it is distinct from external seeing, does it not constitute an internal counterpart? He immediately refutes this, saying, "If it were distinct," and so forth.

This means that you claim internal darkness is different from the darkness in a room; yet, if an internal counterpart could be established by being distinct from the room's darkness, he says, "If... [to refute it].
"Separated" (and so forth). This is the citation of the text; "closing the eyes and departing" refers to the actual refutation, which should be understood.

Within the second section, the "turning refutation," it is further divided into three parts: first, the refutation that [the eye] is in space and not within; second, the refutation of the confusion between self and other;
third, the refutation of the dual cognition of the body and the eye. Regarding the first of these, one should first raise the point that [the eye] is in space.
This is not the meaning of "not external. After the textual analysis, one further concludes and refutes the fault of [the self] being in emptiness rather than external.
The same applies to the following two cases. Subsequently, one should sequentially conclude by saying: "How could a single body become two Buddhas?
Since a single body cannot become two Buddhas, how can there be two awakenings within a single person? If a single person lacks two awakenings, how can there be a Tathāgata..."
"Seeing is your own substance. Since the Tathāgata’s seeing is not your substance, how could the faculty [of sight] reside in empty space to see your face?
Since the faculty in empty space does not see your face, how could it open its eyes to see light and thereby see your face?
Since opening the eyes does not reveal the face, how could closing the eyes to see darkness be called 'seeing within'? Thus one investigates."

[The refutation] is thus concluded. It is clear that the failure of the views of "seeing darkness" and "seeing within" is likewise established. The convergence of these three arguments can be understood.

Regarding the fifth refutation concerning the calculation of "conjunction," from this point onward, all three types [of arguments] cite the sutras to formulate counter-arguments. Ānanda’s intention was as follows: first he calculated it as being within;

next, he calculated it as being without; third, he calculated it as being hidden within the sense organ; and fourth, he calculated it as being both within and without—all of which arose from his own [perspective].

[Ananda] saw [the truth], which is why he was refuted point by point. Now, regarding the question established based on the meaning of the Dharma taught by the Tathāgata, it is truly impossible to refute it;
therefore, all that follows is established by citing the sūtras. This is merely because Ānanda’s words have failed and his logic has reached its limit.

Within the section on "Conformity," there are two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downward, he gives rise to attachments based on the sūtras; second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the Buddha restates those attachments and subjects them to analysis.
Refutation. This section also has two parts: first, citing the sūtra; second, erroneous calculations. Regarding the first, citing the sūtra: "By means of the mind," etc.
This implies that phenomena are fundamentally unborn; it is by means of the arising of a single thought of discrimination that various phenomena subsequently arise.
Furthermore, the mind itself is also unborn; it arises by means of the various phenomena that are discriminated.
The mind capable of discrimination likewise arises from phenomena; since phenomena arise from the mind, if the mind has not yet arisen, the nature of phenomena is utterly unobtainable.
Since the mind arises from phenomena, if phenomena have not yet arisen, the essence of the mind is likewise utterly unobtainable.
Thus, when neither phenomena nor the mind can be apprehended, this is what is meant by the "emptiness of both mind and phenomena."

Furthermore, the "dharmas" are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) and so forth, and the "mind" (*citta*) is the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) and so forth. It is precisely by means of the objects that cognition arises, and by means of cognition that the objects arise;
thus, one's entire self-nature is produced. Therefore it is said, "arising from the mind," and so forth. Such is the Tathāgata’s true intention. As for the second misconception:
Ānanda, not understanding the Buddha’s meaning, falsely conjectured: "From the perspective of what the Tathāgata has taught..."

The mind follows wherever it conjoins. Using the Tathāgata’s teaching to examine my own mind, Ānanda, I consider that the mind must also exist in accordance with the place where it conjoins. Therefore, I say: "I now... (and so forth).

Regarding the phrase "nor is it," the two characters "nor" (亦非) should be viewed in terms of both identity and separation. Since it is said to "follow wherever it conjoins," then where would it not [exist]?

It is pervasive; it cannot be definitively established as being identical to the three—internal, external, or intermediate—and it cannot be definitively established as being separate from the three—internal, external, or intermediate.
Therefore, it is said: "Nor is it... (and so forth). One should understand that although Ānanda has cited both the mind and the dharmas, he intends two meanings.
The calculation concerns only [the notion of] "conjunction.

This section, which cites the opponent's position and refutes it, is divided into three parts: first, citing the position (beginning with "The Buddha said," etc.); second, the refutation (beginning with "This mind," etc.);
and third, the conclusion of the refutation (beginning with "Therefore," etc.). Of these, the first part, citing the position, is clear. The second part, the refutation, is divided into two.
The first part is a general refutation of this mind; the second part, "If there were no... and so forth, is a specific refutation.

Within the initial general refutation, the phrase "this mind" and so on generally refutes their conjunction by means of their lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*). The intended meaning is that since the mind exists in accordance with whatever it conjoins with, [the conjunction itself lacks an independent reality].
Thus, since this mind of yours that is capable of joining lacks even its own substance, with what could it join? It is like a box and a lid meeting:
the box has substance and the lid also has substance, and only then can their union be established.

Now, being without substance, how can a union be formed? Therefore it is said, "This mind... (and so forth). Although you know that its union cannot be established, I shall nevertheless question you; thus [it says] below:

There are two refutations concerning the non-existence of an essence and the existence of an essence. These two specific refutations are divided into two parts: first, the refutation regarding the non-existence of an essence, beginning with "If it were non-existent," etc.;
second, the refutation regarding the existence of an essence, beginning with "If it were existent," etc. Within the first section on the non-existence of an essence:

the nineteen elements (*dhātus*) and so forth possess only their names but lack substantial reality; what, then, could be joined? It is like the eighteen elements and the six sense objects (*viṣayas*). As for the sense organs (*indriyas*)...

The objects (*viṣaya*), consciousnesses (*vijñāna*), and sense bases (*āyatana*) each have their respective points of conjunction. If there were nineteen bases and seven objects, what base would exist outside of the eighteen bases?
And what object would exist outside of the six objects to serve as a point of conjunction? Now, you claim that although they lack intrinsic substance, they can still undergo conjunction;
this is like the case of a nineteenth base or a seventh object, for which no logical sense of conjunction can be established. Therefore, it is said that this argument is untenable.

However, if it lacks an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then its "conforming to conjunction" cannot be established. Second, the refutation based on the existence of an intrinsic nature is divided into two parts:

first, the refutation regarding the internal and external, as well as entering and exiting, which begins with "If there were... and so forth; second, the refutation regarding the one and the many, and the pervasive and the localized, which begins with "Ānanda... and so forth.

The first section also has two parts. First, "If there were... and so forth, which constitutes the actual refutation; this may be understood. Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, it brings [the discussion] back to its essential point.
This also has two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, Ānanda shifts his argument according to the occasion; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata provides the correct synthesis.

Within the first part regarding the shifting of the argument, the text is clear. Within the second part regarding the Tathāgata’s correct synthesis, the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" means that although seeing is indeed the eye, the reason why...
Seeing does not reside in the eyes or ears; this is because one uses the room as an analogy for the body, Ānanda for the mind, and the door for the eyes.
Since Ānanda is inside the room and the door cannot see, it follows that seeing resides in Ānanda and not in the door.

By this analogy, one can know that seeing resides in the mind and not in the eyes. Therefore, it is said: "If the eye... (and so forth). "Those who have already died" refers to all [such individuals].

When a person has died, their eyes still remain. It is not possible for the other sense faculties (*indriya*) to have died while the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) still persists, because when the faculties die, the eyes also die.
This refutation through the categories of two, one, many, pervasive, and restricted is divided into two parts: first, the determination [of the opponent's position], such as Ānanda and others;
second, the refutation, such as "if one" and so forth. This is further divided into four: first, "if one," which refutes by means of a single entity; second, "if... [and so on].

1. "If it is manifold," it is refuted by means of its manifold nature. 2. "If it is one," it is refuted by means of its unitary nature. 3. "If it is pervasive," it is refuted by means of its pervasive nature. 4.
"If it is not pervasive," it is refuted by means of its non-pervasive nature. All of these can be understood accordingly.

The sixth section, "Refuting the Intermediate [Position]," is divided into two parts. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, there is the arising of attachments based on the sūtra. Second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, there is the restatement of those attachments followed by their refutation.
The first part is further divided into two: first, the citation of the sūtra, namely "Ānanda and others"; second, the erroneous calculation, namely "just as we [think]."

Regarding the initial citation from the sūtras, "I also heard that the Buddha [taught] with Mañjuśrī and others," this refers to the teaching of the *Laṅkāvatāra* and other sūtras within the Vaipulya (fangdeng) class.
As for "true reality" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*), it is called true reality because it is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks. "Being without marks" means there are no marks of saṃsāra;
"not being devoid of marks" means there are no marks of nirvāṇa. Since both nirvāṇa and saṃsāra are unobtainable, their very substance is the truth.
Because it is always so, it is called the "true mark" (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*). Regarding the statement that "the mind is not within," and so forth: the mind is the very substance of the true mark.
It is vast, penetrating, perfectly interfused, and pervades the entire dharma-realm; therefore, it is neither within nor without.

If there were any obtainable interior or exterior, how could that be the substance of the true mark? An interpretation such as this alone accords with the Tathāgata’s true intent. As for the passage beginning with "As I... [and so on].
This was merely Ānanda’s erroneous calculation. As we previously stated, it should also be supplemented by saying:

"According to what the Tathāgata has taught, it is evident that the mind is neither within nor without. Therefore, he says, "As I [have understood]... (and so forth). "There is nothing seen within," and so on, reverses what was previously refuted and what was conceptually constructed.
"Now, because they know one another," and so forth, refers to the middle of the state of meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Second, restating the position and refuting it through reasoning, which has three parts. First, the refutation based on the body and location, beginning with "The Buddha said," etc.

Second, the refutation based on the faculties and objects, beginning with "Ānanda," etc. Third, concluding that it is not in between, beginning with "Therefore," etc. The first part [the refutation based on the body] also has two sections.

First, the Buddha’s statement regarding going, which establishes the point; this is clear. Second, the refutation by examining the act of going itself, which also has two parts. First, regarding the body: "If [the person] is below," etc. Second...
Regarding the location: if it is situated below, all can be known. Second, the refutation based on the sense organs (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), which is divided into two parts.

First, from "Ānanda" downward, the disciple’s shifting calculations are presented; this can be understood. Second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the Tathāgata’s refutation; this is further divided into two. First, the determination, from "The Buddha said" downward;

this can be understood. Second, the refutation, from "If you detest... downward. This is further divided into two. First, the simultaneous refutation of both [the organ and the object], from "If you include... downward.

The second [category] involves both [the inclusion and the refutation], whereas the first does not involve both. Regarding the initial category that involves both, "involving both" refers to consciousness and mind involving the duality of the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and the objects (*viṣaya*).
The "thing" (*vastu*) consists of the faculties and objects, while the "essence" (*tattva*) consists of consciousness and mind. If the mind involves the faculties and objects—

The sense organs possess the capacity for illumination and thus further involve cognition; the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) are themselves devoid of cognition. If these were to be combined, they too would possess cognition.
Consequently, the entities of the organs and objects would become entangled with the essence of the mind. Therefore, it is said that "the entities and the essence are intermingled. Why is this?
Because the entities of the organs and objects are not the same as the essence of the mind. Thus, it is said that "the entities are not the essence."

"Know. Thus, both aspects are combined. One half resides in the objects (*viṣaya*); since objects are originally without cognition, they now possess cognition. The other half resides in the sense organs (*indriya*);

since the organs possess illumination and discernment, they likewise possess cognition. If both possess cognition, then the two parties—the organs and the objects—stand as adversaries against one another.
What is called "you and I knowing each other" results in merely two positions. How, then, can there be that which you call "the mind"?
This is the middle position. Therefore it is said, "it forms an opposition" (and so forth). Second, the two do not encompass the middle. Regarding "the two do not encompass":
this means that it neither encompasses the sense organ (*indriya*) nor the object (*viṣaya*). Therefore it is said, "the two do not encompass.

Since the sense organ does not encompass [the object], even though it illuminates and discerns, it is difficult to call it "knowing. Since the object does not encompass [the organ], even though it lacks cognition, it is difficult to call it "not knowing. It is thus.

It cannot be called knowledge, nor can it be called non-knowledge; therefore, it is said to be "neither knowing nor not-knowing. As for those sense-faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*), you are able to give rise to them.
Since it has already been stated that they are neither knowing nor not-knowing and are utterly devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), where does that which is produced by your mind abide?

What characteristics or forms does it possess in its intermediate state? Therefore, it is said: "it is precisely non-existent" (and so forth). The preceding [passage] combined both [aspects], while this refers specifically to the sense-faculties.

Dust is the object and consciousness is the substance; this is how it is explained. If the sense organ is the substance and dust is the object, then while the object is fundamentally without cognition, the substance is capable of illumination and discernment.
If the mind encompasses both, then that which possesses illumination and discernment inherently has cognition, and even that which lacks cognition would also have cognition.
Thus, whether it be the organ or the dust, there is no fixed determination; hence it is said that "objects and substance are confused. This is because of the dust’s...

Objects do not possess the nature of illumination and cognition as the substance of the sense organs does; therefore, it is said that "objects do not know by way of their own substance. The formation of opposition and so forth is the same as previously explained.
Thus, the conclusion at the end—that they are not the intermediate [consciousness]—can be understood.

The seventh section, "Refuting the Calculations of Non-attachment," is divided into two parts. First, from "Ānanda" downward, there is the arising of attachments based on the sutra. Second, from "The Buddha said" downward, there is the restatement of those attachments followed by their refutation.
The first part is further divided into two: first, citing the sutra, starting with "Ānanda"; second, the erroneous calculation, starting with "Then we, etc.

Within the citation of the sutra, although it says "neither within," and so forth, this merely reveals a partial emptiness. There are those who, upon seeing [the text] turn together [with the person], [erroneously conclude that the self exists].
These two characters refer to the *prajñā* (wisdom) turning the teaching. This is because they do not understand the characteristics of the teachings.
If it were within the *prajñā*, how could there be such a statement regarding the "combined turning" (*gòng zhuǎn*)?

That which is called "combined turning" refers to instances where [the teaching] serves as an inspiration or as an aid for those who are the primary audience (*dāngjī*), thereby assisting in the propagation of the Buddha’s transformation; thus one knows that this is the constant [truth].
The term "equal" (*sama*) refers to the fact that, when analyzed, the existence within the twenty-five realms of existence is equally non-existent;

this clearly reveals the emptiness of the principle of the partial truth (*ekāṃśa-satya*). Such is the Tathāgata’s true intent. As for the passage beginning with "Then I," this is Ānanda’s erroneous calculation.
The phrase "then we" (*vayam*) signifies that [the Tathāgata] used the Tathāgata’s teaching to determine the intention of myself, Ānanda. By "myself, Ānanda... [he means...]
My mind accords with what the Tathāgata has said. This sutra is free from attachment; I, too, am free from attachment. These two aspects are in perfect harmony.
However, I do not know whether the Tathāgata will grant his seal of approval or not; therefore, it says, "then we [are as one]."
Second, the citation of the opponent’s position followed by its refutation. This is divided into three parts: first, the citation and determination; second, the refutation; third, the conclusion.
Regarding the first, the "citation and determination," the phrase "whether it exists or does not exist" intends to mean that all objective phenomena are termed "all.

When you say "non-attachment to all," do you mean there is attachment because something exists, or rather [because it does not]? (Note: The provided text fragment ends mid-sentence regarding the second alternative.)
"Is non-abiding [the same as] non-attachment? This interpretation accords naturally with the intent of the subsequent refutation; there is no need to adopt other explanations.

Second, the refutation and critique, which is divided into two parts: first, the direct critique beginning with "If it does not exist," and second, the further refutation beginning with "The signless," along with the conclusion and summary, all of which are evident.
Question: How does one refute that deluded mind so that it does not exceed eight [instances]?
[Question: "Are there not fewer than six, but rather seven? [Answer: "The Dharma-medicine of the Tathāgata is administered according to the ailment.
Generally, the attachments and calculations held by the world do not exceed four types; yet these four types together comprise seven.

Since Ānanda was a manifestation of great expedient power (*mahopāya*), how could he not have provided for this in advance? Therefore, there are precisely these seven as antidotes for each [type of attachment]. One is one."
The first is that which is reckoned by all ordinary beings; it refers to the single instance within the body. The second is that which is reckoned by all non-Buddhists;

it refers to the three instances—the latent faculties outside the body, as well as those both inside and outside. The third is that which is reckoned by the initial resolve of the partial and gradual Bodhisattvas.
This corresponds to the two middle sections of the combined sequence. The fourth is what those at the initial stage of the Two Vehicles conceive;

it corresponds to the section on Non-attachment. This was established by both teacher and disciple to elucidate the resonance between capacity and response, serving as a medicinal remedy for future generations;
it is not that Ānanda actually experienced these events. Having thus refuted the deluded mind through the seven locations, there is no further end to it.
In two or three places, the essence of delusion is shown to be fundamentally non-existent. As for what are called the "three places":

first, pointing out and refuting that this is not your mind, namely the passage beginning with "If you now wish to know... Second, pointing out that this is the false appearance of conceptualization regarding external objects, namely the passage beginning with "Ānanda was startled...
Third, pointing out that this is merely a reflected image of the discrimination of external objects, namely the passage where Ānanda says...
The Buddha said they are equal. Now, this is divided preliminarily into two parts: first, from "At that time Ānanda departed" to "he reproached himself and made his request";

second, from "At that time the World-Honored One" to "the Tathāgata manifested auspicious signs to provide instruction. The first part is further divided into two: first, from "At that time" onwards, he reproaches himself;
