second, from "I only pray" onwards, he requests the Dharma. The first of these is further divided into two: first, the act of taking refuge and paying homage, from "At that time" onwards; second, the presentation of his words.
"I am the youngest. First, the expression of homage may be understood as before. Second, regarding the presentation of his words:
"I am the youngest," etc., means that Ānanda was the son of King Droṇodana, while the Tathāgata was the son of King Śuddhodana.
Since Ānanda was born at the very moment the Tathāgata attained enlightenment, it is known that Ānanda was the youngest among the brothers; therefore, he says, "I am the youngest."

Regarding the younger brother: from the very youngest stage up to the point of not yet knowing the true limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), it can be seen that there are two successive cycles of arising and responding.

There are three parts to the request for the Dharma: first, the formal request, beginning with "I only pray," etc.; second, the clarification of the benefit, beginning with "causing all," etc.; third, the instruction to listen attentively.

Regarding the phrase "to act thus" and below: within the initial section on the formal request, the passage "reveal to us the path of *śamatha*" means that the aforementioned Ultimate Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is the principle to be reached, whereas the present *śamatha* is the practice by which one reaches it. Therefore, what was previously called "reaching" is here termed the "path."
Regarding the second section on the benefits: "Causing all... and so forth. *Icchantika* is translated here as "lacking faith. *Mleccha* is translated as "evil views.

The meaning is that if they were to receive a single exposition of the Tathāgata’s path of *śamatha*, not only would we be benefited by the manifestation of the eternally abiding true mind, but even these types of beings should likewise shatter their evil views.
Faith has been produced. Previously, because you had not heard of the true nature, you did not believe and instead gave rise to wrong views.

Now, if you hear of this true nature, you will naturally transform your lack of faith into faith, and transform your wrong views into right views. This can be understood by listening attentively with the three types of attention.

The second section, "The Tathāgata Manifests Auspicious Omens and Provides Instruction," consists of two parts. First, from "At that time" onwards, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the provision of instruction.

The first part further has four sections: first, from "At that time" etc., the emission of light; second, from "Throughout all Buddhas... etc., the shaking of the earth; third, from "In this way" etc., the convergence of the world-systems;

fourth, from "In those worlds" etc., the distant hearing [of the sound]. Regarding the first, the emission of light, it symbolizes the inconceivable virtue of wisdom. Regarding the second, the shaking of the earth...

The first represents the inconceivable virtue of severance (*prahāṇa*). The third, the "convergence of the realms," represents the inconceivable essence of reality (*dharmatā*). The fourth, "famous afar," represents the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

Regarding the initial phrase "from his face-gate" (*mukha-dvāra*): the face-gate lies between the two ears, the two eyebrows, and the two eyes, symbolizing the secret treasury of the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*).
This is because the face-gate is the most honored part of the entire body, and the three virtues are likewise [the most honored].

It manifests the essence of the ultimate fruit; thus, it symbolizes this. The emission of various rays of light symbolizes that [wisdom] issues forth from the secret treasury of the three virtues as the wondrous *śamatha* and other forms of gnosis.
That is to say, it is entirely because the essence of the fruit issues forth as the true cause that it is symbolized by the emission of various rays of light from the mouth (the *mukha-dvāra*).
The brilliance of those rays symbolizes the perfection of this *śamatha* and other forms of gnosis.

Contemplate that perfect illumination is entirely empty, entirely provisional, and entirely middle. That which is called "obliterating all phenomena" means that when they are obliterated, they are all simultaneously obliterated;

thus, even the middle and the provisional are obliterated. Furthermore, "unifying all phenomena" means that when they are unified, they are all simultaneously unified; thus, even the empty and the provisional are unified.
Therefore, its radiance is used to represent this, like hundreds of thousands of suns, representing hundreds of thousands of samādhis. By means of these three...
Wisdom constitutes wondrous practice. One spontaneously achieves hundreds of thousands of samādhis; therefore, this is symbolized by hundreds of thousands of suns.

This symbolizes that the virtue of wisdom is such as this. Second, since the virtue of wisdom has not yet been perfected from the beginning, the inconceivable virtue of cessation could also not yet be realized.
Now that the virtue of wisdom is perfected, all ignorance within the six sense faculties is completely severed and exhausted.
Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The cycle of birth and death is these six sense organs; peace, bliss, wondrous permanence, and the sublime constant are also these six sense organs.
It further states: "Entering deeply through one gate, entering one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
From this, one knows that the cycle of birth and death is entirely contained within the six sense organs. For this reason, one should shatter the ignorance of the six sense organs. Ignorance...
Having shattered birth and death and severed [all defilements] to fully accomplish the virtue of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*), it is therefore symbolized by the six kinds of earth tremors.
Such is the manifestation of the virtue of cessation. Previously, the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and cessation had not yet been accomplished or realized;

consequently, this inconceivable essence of reality (*tattva*) could not be manifested. Now, regarding wisdom, the virtue of wisdom is accomplished; regarding cessation, the virtue of cessation is realized. This inconceivable...
The essence of principle (*tattva*) is manifested from this; all realms, from the hell realm up to the Buddha realm, are fully revealed.
Therefore, this is symbolized by the simultaneous opening and manifestation of the lands of the ten directions.

Since the ten realms are thus fully revealed—just as the hell realm becomes a single *dharmadhātu*—and since there is no *dharmadhātu* existing apart from the *dharmadhātu*, the other nine realms likewise cannot be found. As it is said:
The Buddha-realm becomes a single Dharma-realm. Outside of the Dharma-realm, there is no separate Dharma-realm; thus, even the nine realms cannot be apprehended as distinct.
Since there is nothing that is not the single great universal principle-body, it is represented by the synthesis of all worlds into one realm.

Furthermore, the essence of this principle is entirely derived from the two virtues of wisdom (*jñāna*) and abandonment (*prahāṇa*). For the Buddha is wisdom itself, and his majestic power (*anubhāva*) is abandonment.

Thus, by means of the Buddha’s majestic power and so forth, it is indicated that the essence of the principle is manifested through wisdom and abandonment. Such is the manifestation of the essence of the principle.
In these four ways—whether as wisdom, as abandonment, or as principle—all are fully accomplished, realized, attained, and manifested.
Thus, the practitioner should personally proceed from this to practice so as to obtain the wondrous gateway of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.

If there is a single awakening through the ear-faculty, then as for sound, sound is the Dharma-realm; as for the faculty, the faculty is the Dharma-realm. There is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm.

It must be that the sound-dust (*śabda-viṣaya*) of the Tathāgata comes to the ear-side of the Bodhisattva, while the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) of the Bodhisattva goes to the location of the Tathāgata’s sound.

Therefore, it is represented by "hearing from afar. Such is the representation of perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*). Why manifest such auspicious signs as a representation? There is no other reason;
they all consist of the Tathāgata’s transformative guidance, which does not go beyond the two teachings of form and sound. Thus ends this section.
The emission of light: the emission of light is fundamentally the inconceivable merit of wisdom (*jñāna-guṇa*) inherent from the beginning. The first shaking of the earth:

the shaking of the earth is fundamentally the inconceivable merit of cessation (*prahāṇa-guṇa*) inherent from the beginning. The merging with the realms: the merging with the realms is fundamentally the inconceivable essence of principle (*tattva-śarīra*) inherent from the beginning.
The far-reaching hearing: the far-reaching hearing is fundamentally the inconceivable perfect penetration (*pariśuddha-vyāpti*) inherent from the beginning. Now, this sutra...

What is elucidated here consists entirely of four types. Thus, within the manifestation of auspicious omens, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that provides this symbolic report; it is not a matter of forced contrivance.
From this point on, those with sharp faculties, whose capacities are suited to direct perception, will find the Way present before their eyes;

they are able, in that very moment, to accomplish this wisdom, realize this virtue, manifest this essential principle, and attain this perfect penetration. As for those of dull faculties who cannot yet transcend the benefit derived from verbal teachings, [the following applies].
Therefore, there is the passage where the Buddha instructs him to depart.
Second, the "Revelation," which is divided into two parts. First, the Buddha’s direct instruction to Ānanda and others regarding the two kinds of roots.

Second, the explicit demonstration that the locus of delusion has no substantial reality, beginning with "Ānanda, you now... The first part is further divided into two: first, the Buddha’s censure of delusion; second, [the refutation of the view that] both...
The first [section] further has two parts. First, regarding sentient beings: "The Buddha said," and so forth. Second, regarding practitioners: "All who cultivate," and so forth.
Regarding the first, those who do not practice are called "all sentient beings," and thus they are categorized as sentient beings.

Regarding the second, those who do practice are called "practitioners," and thus they are categorized as practitioners. Within the first of these, if stated generally, "all sentient beings" refers to...

The nine realms. Various forms of perversion (*viparyāsa*). To lose the truth is called "perversion" (*diān*); to mistake the delusive for reality is called "inversion" (*dǎo*). This refers to sentient beings in the nine realms:
just as those in the six paths perceive the four aspects of the body and sensations—such as impermanence—as permanent, or the impure as pure;

and just as those of the Two Vehicles perceive the four aspects of the body and sensations—such as permanence—as impermanent, or the pure as impure; and just as those of partial and gradual Bodhisattvas...

Regarding the body, sensations, and so forth—the four aggregates—these people constantly reckon them as impermanent, or as both permanent and impermanent, and so on, up to reckoning them as pure, or as both pure and impure.
This is because they do not know that their original nature is truly permanent, truly blissful, truly self, and truly pure. This constitutes the loss of the truth.
Consequently, they give rise to notions of permanence and impermanence, both permanence and impermanence, and so on, up to purity and impurity, both purity and impurity.
This is what is meant by "recognizing delusion. Therefore, it is said that there are various kinds of inversions (*viparyāsa*). To explain this in detail:

this passage specifically refutes all ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*) who do not practice, as they give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*), create karma (*karman*), and invite retribution (*vipāka*) regarding the four bases such as the body.

These constitute the three paths (*trivartman*). Regarding these three—affliction, karma, and suffering—whenever afflictions arise, one inevitably creates evil karma; once evil karma has been created...
Karma inevitably brings about the retribution of suffering; this is fixed and immutable, and is therefore called "natural.
Thus, one knows that all sentient beings are [the result of] the retribution of suffering, as well as various inverted evil karmas and afflictions (*kleśa*).

From beginningless time, because ignorance is beginningless, the karma and its fruits are likewise beginningless. This can be clearly seen through further analogies, such as the analogy of the "evil sentence. (2)
Among these practitioners, [the text] rebukes all practitioners who are unable to give rise to cultivation from within nature and must instead cultivate apart from nature;
who are unable to realize that delusion is itself truth and must instead discard delusion to seek truth. For this reason, they do not achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Following "Bodhi," one should supplement the text by asking: "If they do not achieve *bodhi*, what do they achieve? Therefore, it says "even unto" (*nai zhi*), summarizing [the various states].
This does not exclude what was previously explained regarding the various types of inversion, including the two vehicles and those who follow the partial or gradual path.

Thus, even up to the aforementioned point, there remains a category of those who become partial or gradual bodhisattvas; these are now omitted for brevity, which is why it says "up to" (乃至) [and so forth].
One must understand that the path of Māra is likewise formed through practice; therefore, the "Three Determinations" below states: "Even if one possesses wisdom..."

When meditative concentration manifests before one, if the mind of lust is not severed, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māras; if the minds of killing, stealing, and falsehood are not severed, one will inevitably fall into the path of ghosts;
and as for being possessed by demons or succumbing to the demon of attachment and views, one loses the seed of the Tathāgata.

The second [section] shows the causes, which is further divided into two parts. First, "all due to" and so forth indicates the general heading; second, "how so? and so forth provides the inquiry and explanation.
Within the first part, the phrase "all due to" and so forth means that for those who do not practice, they are bound by the three paths, while for those who do practice, they fail to achieve bodhi.
This is entirely because they do not know the two roots. Therefore, it says, "all due to" (and so forth). [This refers to] erroneous cultivation.

"Practicing erroneously" means that one does not realize that delusion is entirely identical to truth; thus, one abandons the substance of delusion and seeks truth elsewhere outside of it—this is error.

"Being distracted" means that one is confused by delusion and fails to recognize it as such; consequently, one gives rise to further deviant practices upon the very substance of delusion—this is distraction.
In this way, those who are superior practitioners certainly practice in a confused manner, and even those who are not practitioners practice in a confused manner.
This is because among ordinary people, there are those who extensively cultivate the precepts and goodness, while non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) also cultivate the threefold wrong training;
thus the analogy can be understood. Second, the interrogation and explanation, which also has two parts. First, the phrase "how so" is the interrogation, which is evident. Second, Ānanda...
This is an equal explanation. Furthermore, it is divided into three parts: first, showing the true; second, showing the deluded; and third, concluding with a reprimand.
Regarding the first part, "all sentient beings" and so forth, this also refers to the nine realms as "all sentient beings.

"Grasping" (*pāna*) refers to the subjective perceiver (*ālambaka*), and "condition" (*pratyaya*) refers to the objective object (*ālambana*). For example, among humans, there are the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*).

Taking objective conditions as their intrinsic nature: outsiders take the conditions of annihilationism and eternalism as their intrinsic nature; the gods take the conditions of sensual pleasure as their intrinsic nature;
those of the Two Vehicles take the condition of mere emptiness as their intrinsic nature; and partial or gradual Bodhisattvas take sequential conditions as their intrinsic nature.
Although these differ in depth and in being either heterodox or orthodox, when subsumed under principle, they are all... [total].
Because one does not know that the delusion of the affliction of ignorance (*avidyā*) is the very root of birth and death, yet regards it as one's own inherent nature (*svabhāva*), it is said:
"First... and so forth. Next, the passage beginning with "beginningless" refers to the true nature of Bodhi, which is the inherently pure Nirvana.
The "primordially pure essence" is what is called the eternally abiding true mind, the wondrously pure and luminous essence. That is to say:
True-nature Bodhi (*tathatā-bodhi*) is the essence of intrinsically pure Nirvana. "The original luminosity of the consciousness-essence" refers to the eight consciousnesses.

Because they exist through the conjunction of arising-and-ceasing with True Suchness (*tathatā*), one portion of arising-and-ceasing constitutes the "consciousness-essence," while one portion of True Suchness constitutes "original luminosity.
If one is deluded regarding this, even True Suchness becomes arising-and-ceasing; if one awakens to it, arising-and-ceasing is itself [True Suchness].

Regarding *tathatā* (Suchness): here, both the true and the false are indicated together; hence it is said that "the essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous. There are two meanings to "the essence of consciousness":
first, consciousness is the most subtle, referring to the distinct units and measures of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing; thus it is called the essence of consciousness.
Second, when this consciousness issues forth through the eye-faculty, it becomes the essence of seeing; when it issues forth through the ear-faculty, it becomes the essence of hearing.
Even when it is activated through the faculty of the mind, it is called the essence of cognition; therefore, it is named the "essence of consciousness" (*vijñāna-śukra*).

As for "original clarity" (*yuan-ming*), it means that its fundamental nature is originally pure and white. If one were to allocate the essence of consciousness and so forth among the various consciousnesses, this original clarity refers to the ninth consciousness (*navama-vijñāna*).

"Consciousness-essence" refers to the eight consciousnesses. "That which can produce" refers to the first seven consciousnesses. Some say it refers to the first six consciousnesses; however, here they are combined as seven.
While the six consciousnesses certainly take the six external objects as their conditions, the seventh consciousness likewise takes the eighth consciousness as its own internal self.
For this reason, it is assigned to the [first] seven consciousnesses. That which remains beyond these conditions is precisely the originally pure essence mentioned above.

Regarding the phrase "by means of all [delusions]" and so forth in the third section: this rebukes those who do not know the reality of truth and thus lose it, and who do not know the falsity of delusion and thus employ it.
"Worthlessly entering" refers to rebuking those who, failing to know the truth, do not seek to manifest it;
and failing to know delusion, do not seek to destroy it; thereby resulting in their wandering through the six realms of existence, which is not what ought to be. Therefore...
When it says "wrongly entered," one knows that the initial mention of "birth and death" (saṃsāra) is in contrast to the subsequent "nirvāṇa.

When it says "the root," this refers to the afflictions (kleśa) in contrast to the subsequent "bodhi. Thus, in the passage beginning with "That you now... and so forth, it precisely clarifies the afflictions that are the root of birth and death.

The character "zìxìng" (self-nature)—specifically the word "zì" (self)—is precisely the concluding pointer to the root of birth and death; there is nothing else. It refers to you and all sentient beings.
"That which takes the攀緣心 (the mind that clings to objects) as its own nature" refers to this very point; it clarifies that they do not understand their delusion.
Furthermore, the subsequent mention of "bodhi" and so forth is also spoken in contrast to the beginningless and endless life-and-death cycle and its fundamental source.

Thus, fearing that you might not know the true essence, I have pointed out that which is left behind by the false conditions of the *vijñāna*-essence and the like; this is precisely what you must know.
The term "that which is left behind" (yízhě) refers to the very essence of Bodhi and Nirvana, the fundamentally pure substance.

The upper passage speaks of "fundamental purity," while the lower passage speaks of "that which is left behind by conditions"; these texts mutually clarify one another. It should be understood that the afflictions which constitute the root of birth and death, such as prior攀緣 (pānyuán—clinging/conditions), have already been fully explained.
Now, the mention of "the essence of consciousness" (shí jīng) and so forth is intended to demonstrate that which has been left behind.
Because it is the true essence, it is elucidated once more. Thus, first its ignorance of the delusory is clarified, and next its ignorance of the true is clarified.

Second, the correct revelation that the locus of delusion has no substance is divided into three parts; the first is the refutation of the conditioned mind, beginning with "Ānanda, you... and so forth.

The second [point] concerns the substance of delusion; it begins with "Ānanda was startled," and so forth. The third [point] explains that the substance of clarity is non-existent; it begins with "Ānanda said to the Buddha," and so forth.

This constitutes the three sections refuting that the substance of delusion fundamentally does not exist. The first of these also has three parts: first, from "Ānanda" downward, he uses the raising of his fist to test his vision;
second, from "The Buddha said" downward, he relies on the vision to interrogate the mind; third, from "The Buddha said" downward, he directly rebukes it as not being the mind. First:

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the direct demonstration of the fist, beginning with "Ānanda and others"; second, the differentiation of the subject and object, beginning with the Buddha’s words, etc.

Regarding the first part, the direct demonstration of the fist: when the Tathāgata raised his fist, he had previously refuted the deluded mind by means of the seven locations of stillness, yet Ānanda did not know that this mind was ultimately illusory, nor did he know that this deluded mind ultimately lacks a substantial essence. Now...
Because one wishes to refute [the claim that they] lack substantiality, one first displays the fist to interrogate [the opponent]. Regarding the "five wheels" (*pañcamaṇḍala*):

some say that the Buddha’s five fingers represent the five great elements—earth, water, fire, wind, and space—and are therefore called the five wheels. Others say that because there are wheel-marks (*cakrāṅka*) upon the tips of the Tathāgata’s fingers, they are called the five wheels.
In the second section, "Discriminating the Subject and Object," the phrase "that which dazzles the eyes and mind" refers to...

According to the principle of *smṛtyupasthāna* (mindfulness), one should speak only of the eyes; yet, the inclusion of the mind here serves as a preliminary case for the inquiry into the mind that appears later in the text.
Were it not for the manifestation of great skillful means (*mahopāya-kauśalya*), how could such a thing be possible?

When [the Buddha] says, "I and the great assembly shall likewise take what is seen with the eyes," this is also a point where Ānanda attempts to evade the issue, fearing that the Tathāgata would refute him as he did previously; therefore, he includes...
The Great Assembly’s words: "Second, based on the observation [of the mind], the investigation of the mind is divided into two parts. First, the Buddha’s direct questioning;
second, Ānanda’s erroneous responses—both can be seen. Third, from the Buddha’s words below, the direct refutation that it is not the mind—this too can be seen."
The second finger belongs to the substance of delusion. This is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downwards, Ānanda asks with astonishment;
second, from "The Buddha said" downwards, the Tathāgata points out what belongs to delusion. Within the first section, regarding Ānanda’s astonished inquiry:

as for the phrase "startled," although Ānanda had previously presented his arguments repeatedly and was met with the Tathāgata’s successive refutations without showing even the slightest sign of fear, he still thought, "My mind is not [in that place]."

"It is right here. Who would have known it had come to this point? Not only is the locus upon which it relies unattainable, but even the mind that relies upon it is utterly shattered. For this reason, there arises great alarm and fear.
Second, "The Tathāgata points to what belongs to the middle" means that the various dharmas of the six sense-objects are designated as "the objects before one. These various...
Phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions and perish when those causes and conditions disperse;
they are fundamentally not real, and are thus called "illusory appearances. Now, your mind arises from this, and is therefore called "the perception of illusory appearances.
To mistake a thief for one's own son means that if his true nature could have assisted my Dharma-body, prolonged my life of wisdom, and given birth to my merit and dharmas.
One who is capable of inheriting the fruit-position of the Dharma King and the family estate of the Mahāyāna is truly my son.

If, however, one harbors false conceptualizations that seek to destroy my Dharma-body, lose my wisdom-life, and plunder my merit and Dharma-wealth, such a person cannot inherit the throne of the Dharma King nor uphold the family estate of the Mahāyāna;
they are a thief, not a son. If you, on the contrary, recognize this as the true nature, then...
This is like mistaking a thief for one’s own son; hence it is said, "Mistaking a thief for one’s son. "You have lost your original constancy":

"original" refers to primordial luminosity, and "constant" refers to true nature. This primordial luminosity and true nature are inherently possessed from the beginning, through which bodhi is attained and nirvana is realized.
Now, since you have instead identified with delusive appearances and thoughts that confuse your true nature, your original constancy has been lost. From this point on—
One wanders through the six realms of existence and transmigrates within the three worlds; hence it is said, "You have lost [your true nature]," and so forth.

Third, the detailed explanation that [the mind] has no intrinsic substance, which is divided into two parts: first, Ānanda’s request (from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" onwards); second, the World-Honored One’s response and explanation (from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards).
The first part is further divided into three: first, Ānanda’s enumeration of what was used (from "Ānanda" onwards); second, his detailed presentation [of the inquiry] (from "If this... onwards).
The Doubt. Third, "I Show" indicates the conclusion of the intent and the request for instruction.

Within the initial section that sequentially recounts what was employed, the passage beginning with "Ānanda said to the Buddha" and so forth—regarding its origin—it is generally because the Tathāgata rebuked him for [clinging to] what is not the mind, further stating, "This is but a false conceptualization of external objects," as the Tathāgata has thus taught; yet Ānanda still did not understand it.
This is not the mind; it is a mark of false conceptualization. It is for this reason that I have made this one request. Regarding "causing me to leave the home":
there are three kinds of leaving the home. First, leaving the secular home; second, leaving the home of the triple world; and third, leaving the home of ignorance.

If, upon hearing the names of the Honored Ones of the Triple Gem, one gives rise to a sincere heart, they abandon their fields and gardens and renounce their private household. They ascend to a distinct [state].

Leaving behind one's parents, and further departing from wife and children, shaving off beard and hair, and donning the robes and carrying the alms bowl—like a cloud amidst the sky, or like a wild crane—one becomes neither a subject for a Son of Heaven nor a friend for a feudal lord. This is what it means to leave the secular household.

Having thus gone forth, if one can know suffering, sever its accumulation, aspire toward its cessation, and cultivate the path, practicing in accordance with these principles, one will surely attain such [liberation].
Upon realization, the afflictions of view and thought are shattered once and for all; the birth-and-death of segmented existence is spontaneously severed.
One no longer transmigrates through the six destinies or the four modes of birth. From this point on, one transcends the triple world that is like a house on fire;

one transcends the triple world that is like a prison. This is what is meant by "leaving the home of the triple world. Whether heard from a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*) or from a Dharma teacher...
From within the sutra scrolls, one attains this eternally abiding true mind, the essence of purity and luminosity.
Thereupon, one gives rise to the three—subtle *śamatha* and so forth—which are perfect contemplation, perfect illumination, perfect realization, and perfect manifestation.

All ignorance and afflictions are completely severed and exhausted, such that there is forever no further entanglement. This is what it means to depart from the house of ignorance. As for the house from which Ānanda has departed...
It goes without saying regarding the householders of the mundane world. At that time, he had already realized the first fruit (*srotāpanna*). Furthermore, it says below:

"Having eliminated six categories through the path of cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*), he has realized the second fruit (*sakṛdāgāmin*); thus, he shall also depart from the household of the three realms (*tridhātu*). This is as stated in the subsequent passage.
It eliminates my inverted conceptions accumulated over billions of kalpas and severs the six grades of subtle afflictions cultivated within the mind.
Having already horizontally severed the delusions of thought that share the same substance as the realm beyond, the family of ignorance is likewise brought forth. Therefore, it is said:
"It causes me to leave the home life and [encounters] spiritual friends. Regarding spiritual friends, there are two kinds: first, those who know the Dharma; second, those who know...

Regarding their capacity for discernment: they have fully mastered and comprehended every teaching spoken by all Buddhas—whether partial or complete, sudden or gradual—and they point them out, saying, "What is partial?
What is complete? What is sudden? What is gradual? In this way, they may be said to be well-versed in knowing the Dharma.
Furthermore, regarding the capacities of all sentient beings—whether those of humans or devas, great or small—they [comprehend] them all.

Having clearly understood this, he pointed it out, saying: "Who possesses the capacity of a human? Who possesses the capacity of a deva? Who possesses a small capacity? Who possesses a great capacity?
In this way, one may be said to know capacities well. From this point forward, one can naturally adapt the teaching to suit the capacity."

Because he accords with the capacities [of beings] through his teaching and expounds the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, he is called a "good spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*). As the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sūtra) states:
"To hear his name is called 'knowing'; to see his form is called 'recognizing. Furthermore, these names are applied from the perspective of others.
After describing the cultivation of goodness, one should conclude by saying: "In terms of leaving the household life, this is my own mind; in terms of making offerings to the Buddhas and..."
Knowledge is also my mind; even the arousal of the resolve to practice is my mind—how could it not be my mind?
Therefore, it is said that "all employ this mind. Even in the preceding passage, one should supplement it by saying: "This is not the case for those who cultivate goodness alone."
Even if there were a lapse of a single thought-moment or a failure of a single glance that might lead to slandering the Dharma, it would be my own mind;
or if it were to cause the regression of one's roots of goodness, it would also be my own mind. Therefore it is said: "Even if... (and so forth). To further conclude:
Thus, when discussing the cultivation of goodness, it does not lie outside this mind; when discussing the commission of evil, it likewise does not lie outside this mind. How could it not be this?
"My mind. Yet the Tathāgata rebuked him, saying, "Is this not your mind? Second, he fully sets forth his doubts, which is divided into three parts:
first, the doubt that earth, wood, and so forth have no mind; second, the doubt regarding the difficulty of relinquishing what one clings to and begrudges;
third, the doubt arising from resentment at the Buddha’s censure. The intent of these is all evident. Question: How is it known that this passage contains [these meanings]?
Regarding these three doubts: the answer may be understood by correlating them with the text of the Tathāgata’s response that follows the word "提" (ti).
The concluding summary and request for instruction following "三我實" (sān wǒ shí) can likewise be understood.

The second part, the response and explanation, is divided into four sections: first, from "At that time" onwards, the narrator describes the context; second, from "The Tathāgata" onwards, the primary explanation of the doubts;
third, from "Immediately" onwards, the silent understanding of the great assembly; and fourth, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the Tathāgata’s concluding reprimand.

First, within the introductory narrative of the Sūtra’s author, there is the intention to cause the mind to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).

Regarding this *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*, if explained in its general sense: the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing. Its arising is an arising through conditions;

though it arises, it never truly arises. Its ceasing is a ceasing through conditions; though it ceases, it never truly ceases. It is merely an arising through conditions and a ceasing through conditions, yet the essence of the nature of phenomena remains utterly devoid [of such activity].
Because it is free from arising and ceasing, it is called the "Dharma of Non-arising. This is the principle of the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-satya*).

Because this principle is accepted and confirmed within the mind, yet cannot be fully articulated by ordinary people, it is called "Patience" (*kṣānti*). It is only at the first stage of the Perfect Teaching (*yuan*) or the first ground of the Distinct Teaching (*bie*) that this can be manifested.
As for the present sutra, it takes only the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure luminosity, as its basis.

Regarding the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*): that which causes the mind [to arise] is precisely what is to be destroyed. This is neither your mind nor the delusory appearances and conceptions of the external objects (*viṣaya*).
Although they belong to the delusory, the delusory has no self-nature; because it exists by virtue of the Real (*tathatā*), the delusory is entirely identical with the Real.
Therefore, the mind that has been refuted can enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* (the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena).

To "enter" means that by means of this very mind, one gives rise to the three wisdoms, such as wondrous *śamatha*, which serve as the manifest illumination. Thus, the principle of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*)—the eternally abiding true mind, the essence of pure and luminous nature—is spontaneously revealed.
Therefore, it is said collectively: "One desires to cause the mind to enter the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*."

This is so. The single character "entry" (ru) signifies wisdom (*jñāna*). The "dharma of non-arising" signifies principle (*li*). The character "patience" (ren) signifies the stage; it is one of the five patiences (*pañca-kṣānti*).
As for the "lion throne" (*siṃhāsana*): the lion is the king among beasts. If he does not emerge, that is one thing;

once he emerges, all other beasts hide their tracks. If he does not roar, that is one thing; once he roars, the brains of all other beasts split open. This serves as a metaphor for the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
If this King of Kings does not manifest his body, that is one thing; but once he manifests, the māras and heterodox teachers are obscured. If he does not preach the Dharma, that is one thing;

but once he preaches, the māras and heterodox teachers are struck with fear and submission. Therefore, his preaching of the Dharma is called the "Lion’s Roar," and his teaching is said to have the flavor of lion’s milk.
He named his dwelling the "Lion’s Cave" (Siṃhaguhā) and designated his seat the "Lion’s Throne" (Siṃhāsana).
One should understand that this throne is spoken of figuratively; it does not refer to a physical shape resembling a lion. As for his stroking Ānanda’s head:

prior to the destruction of the deluded mind in its seven locations and before there was anything [to be attained], that which he had calculated did not come about in a single morning or evening, but rather over many lifetimes and many kalpas.
[The Buddha] had brought [Ānanda] to this state. Fearing that he might be terrified if [the teachings] were suddenly shattered, [the Buddha] had previously rubbed his head to comfort him.
Now, as [the Buddha] was simultaneously shattering the mind that relies upon these [teachings], Ānanda became startled and fearful; therefore, [the Buddha] again rubbed his head to comfort him.

Second, the correct explanation of the doubts raised, which is divided into three parts: first, the explanation of the doubt regarding the lack of mind in earth and wood, beginning with "The Tathāgata, etc.";

second, the explanation of the doubt regarding the difficulty of relinquishing what is clung to and begrudged, beginning with "If you, etc."; and third, the explanation of the doubt regarding resentment toward the Buddha’s censure as being wrong, beginning with "I am not, etc."

The first section can further be divided into three parts. First, [the Buddha] refutes [the opponent's view] by stating generally that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone, using the passage beginning with "Tathāgata.

Second, he refutes it by specifically establishing the essence [of reality] based on the true causal mind, using the passage beginning with "All. Third, he refutes it by using the examples of material forms and empty space to illustrate the true mind, using the passage beginning with "Ānanda.
Regarding the first of these: the underlying intent is that you suspect that if there were no mind, you would be the same as earth and wood; yet your...
The doubt is as follows: look at what has been taught by our Tathāgata. He never said that the mind is like earth or wood;
therefore it is said, "The Tathāgata [says...]. Regarding "the Tathāgata and others": generally speaking, the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only.
However, when pointing directly at them, all phenomena do not transcend the two categories of form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*). This refers to the so-called five... [five aggregates].

The aggregates (*skandhas*), sentient beings, and the realm of the land are these various phenomena. All of them arise from True Suchness (*tathatā*) failing to maintain its own nature through a single moment of non-awakening.
Taking this non-awakening as the cause, there subsequently arises the condition of false conceptualization of appearances.

Thus, these various phenomena—the seeds, the sense objects, and the vessel-world—arise in a chaotic manner. One thereby knows that although these phenomena are called false appearances, they entirely proceed [from True Suchness].
The true substance exists; it is like a reflection in a mirror, where the entire reflection is the mirror itself, or like waves upon water, where the entire wave is water.
In this way, that which gives rise to all phenomena is possessed solely by the mind, and that which is possessed solely by the mind is what gives rise to all phenomena.
From this, one knows that all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind. Why is your mind not the same?
Regarding "earth and wood" and "the second pair": as for the phrase "all things are equal," the intended meaning is: what are the "dharmas" mentioned above?

They are precisely the causes and effects of the ten realms as the primary retribution (*pratyaya-phala*), and the objects of the ten realms as the environmental retribution (*bhājana-loka*). Therefore, it is said, "all things" (and so forth).

Although the primary retributions of the ten realms differ, they all possess their respective causes that evoke their respective fruits; since there are both good and evil causes, the fruits accordingly [follow].

There are the beautiful and the ugly; hence there are the paths of goodness and the paths of evil. There are ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), there are noble ones (*ārya*), there are those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), and there are bodhisattvas.
There are those who practice the causes and those who have attained the ultimate fruit. Their distinctions of superiority and inferiority, high and low, are clearly distinct.
This constitutes all cause and effect. Such cause and effect are entirely formed with this mind as their substance. Therefore, it is said: "One."
All causes and effects have their substance formed by the mind. Furthermore, the ten realms of beings and their environments—when spoken of collectively, they are the world;
when spoken of individually, they are atoms. Although the realms and atoms of the ten realms differ, they likewise have their substance formed by this mind.
Therefore it is said: "The substance of all worlds and atoms is formed by the mind. Such is the reason for the causes within the primary retribution (the sentient beings).
As for causes, there is no cause existing apart from the mind; rather, the entire mind constitutes the cause. As for effects, there is no effect existing apart from the mind;
rather, the entire mind constitutes the effect. This principle applies equally to the environment (the dependent retribution).
From this, one further knows that both the environment and the body (the primary and secondary) are constituted by the mind as their substance. Why, then, is your mind like soil or wood?

Third, using the appearance of form and empty space as an analogy to break through [delusion] by means of the true mind. This is further divided into two parts: first, Ānanda and the others cite the appearance of form and empty space;
second, "how much more so," etc., uses this to illustrate the wondrously luminous nature of the mind. Regarding the first, "How is it, Ānanda, etc.?
the meaning is that from the perspective of my, the Tathāgata’s, view, every phenomenon is a manifestation of the mind alone; every phenomenon is established because of the mind.

Regarding its substance: this refers to the two phenomena of form and emptiness existing within that world. For instance, the most minute among those possessing characteristics is like a blade of grass or a leaf;
the most subtle is like a single thread or knot. Even though a single blade of grass or a single leaf is the most minute, [it is composed of these].
If one investigates its cause, there must be the essential nature of a root-seed; even in the finest of a single thread or a single knot, there is the essential nature of its original source.

Not only is this true for those things that possess manifest characteristics, but even if one investigates empty space, it has the designation of "Great Clarity" (*taiqing*) and the appearance of a manifest form. As stated in the *Two Teachings*: "How much more so..."

The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) means that one should reason in this manner: even material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*) possess an essential nature, and even empty space (*ākāśa*) possesses a name and appearance;
how much more so, then, can your true nature (*tathatā*) lack its own intrinsic substance? Therefore it is said, "How much more so... (*prāg eva*), and so on.

This is used as an analogy for the essence of the mind (*citta-tattva*). Regarding the "pure essence": it is called "pure" because neither birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) nor afflictions (*kleśa*) can be found therein.

To enter into birth and death without being defiled is called "wondrous" (miao). To abide amidst afflictions without being stained is called "pure" (jing). To illuminate all phenomena perfectly is called "luminous" (ming).
To be able to manifest inconceivable power and function is called "mind" (xin). To be able to possess the inconceivable principle and essence is called "nature" (xing).
The phrase "the nature of all minds" (xing yiqie xin) is a textual error; it should read "all mind-natures" (yiqie xingxin). The above has been explained according to a single phrase.

When discussing all phenomena, it is taught that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone. When considering the ten realms in terms of the environment and its inhabitants (the dependent and the primary), both the environment and the inhabitants are established as the substance of the mind.
Finally, it is further stated that all physical forms possess an essential nature; even that which is empty has a name and appearance.
This serves as an analogy to show that your own mind must likewise possess a substance. If such [phenomena] lack inherent nature and yet are not "mind," how could your mind be the same?
Regarding earth and wood, you doubt, saying: "Am I then as insentient as earth and wood? Within the second section, "The Objection Regarding Attachment and Difficulty," it says:
"As for those like you," this means you suspect that apart from this mind of cognition, nothing else exists.
I now ask you: if you cling to this mind and maintain that it ultimately does not cease to exist, then set it aside for a moment.
If the activities of the six sense objects were to possess a complete nature in themselves, one could then say that apart from this cognitive awareness there exists a separate essence of mind.
However, even if you were now to extinguish seeing, hearing, and so forth, these would still be but shadows of mental objects (*dharmāyatana*).

How then can you say that apart from this cognitive awareness there is a separate mind? Therefore it is said: "If you... and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the activities of the various objects," the performance of the activity has not yet [ceased].

"Accomplishment" refers to activity (*kṛtya*). When an activity is once accomplished, it is called karma (*karman*). What is now termed "activity and karma" specifically points to the cause of the conjunction between the sense faculties and their objects.
"Internally maintaining a state of profound seclusion" refers precisely to a state that is deep and tranquil; it merely means that the conscious mind does not engage with external conditions.
However, this is truly not the state of being "tranquil and unmoving. "The reflected phenomena of the discrimination of mental objects" refers to *dharma*.
This is a metaphor for the intermingling of phenomena. The mind gives rise to discrimination because of the objects of the dharma-realm (*dharmāyatana*), just as a shadow exists because of a form.

Therefore, it is said that "the discrimination of the dharma-realm is a matter of shadows. Even if one extinguishes seeing, hearing, and so forth, these still remain matters of discriminating shadows.

Thus, you should know that this is fundamentally not your own mind-nature. How can you doubt that there is nothing else apart from this awareness, and why do you cling to it so tenaciously as to find it difficult to relinquish?
Third, regarding the section on dispelling the suspicion that the Buddha’s refutation is incorrect: as for the phrase "dust is not permanent," the intention is this:
you ask, "How is it that the Tathāgata says this is not the mind? This is because you resent the Tathāgata’s refutation of your claim that it is the mind.
This is your doubt, Ānanda. Such is your uncertainty. However, I, the Tathāgata, have never commanded you to negate the mind.
You should, for now, examine your own mind minutely: does your mind-nature possess an essence when separated from external objects?

If it were ultimately non-existent, your Dharma-body would likewise be subject to annihilation, leaving nothing to be cultivated or realized. Therefore it is said: "External objects are not... (as stated).
[He said: "It is simply that you take this mind of discrimination regarding conditioned objects to be the true mind.

If you say that the true mind is the Dharma-body, then since it is now the same as the hair and horns of a tortoise or a hare, would your Dharma-body also be like the hair and horns of a tortoise or a hare—without cultivation and without realization?
Since you yourself recognize this which is not the mind to be the mind, why do you doubt me?"
Did the Tathāgata reprove you for not having a mind? Previously, within Ānanda’s formal petition, he set forth three doubts;
the Tathāgata explained each one for him. This is why [Ānanda] remained silent and felt self-reproach. It can be understood that the great assembly likewise accepted this in silence.
Regarding the fourth section on the Tathāgata’s reprimand, concerning the phrase "all those in the world" and so forth:
some say that although one has already attained the state of an Arhat, one has not yet attained the status of a Great Arhat; thus, they fear that such a claim would be excessively boastful.

Others say that within the four dhyānas and the four formless absorptions there are two divergent paths; if one follows these divergent paths, one cannot attain the state of an Arhat. Thus it is said.

I fear that [the explanation] is too restrictive. Regarding those who have now accomplished the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*) but have not yet attained the exhaustion of outflows (*āsravakṣaya*):

although they have accomplished the ninth of these nine successive attainments—the attainment of the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodhasamāpatti*)—they have not yet exhausted the conceptualization of false marks (*abhūtalakṣaṇasaṃjñā*).

For this reason, they have not yet attained the fruit of an Arhat of the fourth stage. This is because the conceptualization of false marks is precisely the affliction of deliberation (*vicikitsā-kleśa*). As stated in the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi-śāstra*, fascicle 7.

The commentary on the *Madhyāntavibhāga* explains the cessation of sensation and perception (*nirodhasamāpatti*) as follows: "Those who have not yet gained faith and acceptance in the meaning of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*) will not give rise to this meditative attainment if they are born in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), for they fear that the mind of the formless realm would become subject to annihilation.

Based on this, although one may achieve the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), it is the same case as being unable to become an Arhat. That text states, "fearing that the mind of the formless realm would become subject to annihilation," because...

Since one is already in the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*) and furthermore extinguishes consciousness, both form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) would be absent; thus, there is the fear that this results in annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*).

If one were in the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*), such a concern would not arise. As for the nine successive attainments (*navānupūrvavihārasamāpatti*), they consist of the four dhyānas, the four formless attainments (*catasra ārūpyasamāpattayaḥ*), and the cessation of sensation and perception (*saṃjñāvedayitanirodha*), totaling nine.
One proceeds from the accomplishment of the first dhyāna to the second, advancing step by step and passing through each stage in succession.
Above. Therefore, it is named "Successive Order.
Second, revealing the true seeing is divided into three parts: first, from "After Ānanda had heard" to "the nature of seeing is quiescent and eternal";

second, from "Ānanda received the Buddha’s [instruction]" to "the nature of seeing has no place of return"; third, from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" to "the nature of seeing is free from characteristics. The first part is further divided into three; the first...

The first part directly reveals the nature of seeing; this corresponds to the passage beginning with "Then Ānanda heard the Buddha... (下). The second part doubly reveals the nature of seeing; this corresponds to the passage beginning with "Although Ānanda [was thus]...

(下). The third part further resolves remaining doubts; this corresponds to the passage beginning with "At that time, Ānanda... (下). The first of these [three parts] is further divided into two: first, Ānanda departs to present his request;

second, from "Immediately" (即時) onwards, the instruction is revealed. The first of these [two] is further divided into two: first, the simultaneous presentation of delusion and enlightenment; [this begins with] Ānanda... (阿難).
...and so forth. Second, both the mind and the eyes are requested; "only wish" and so forth. The first [section] also has two parts: first, from "Ānanda," below, the presentation of delusion;
second, from "today," onwards, the presentation of awakening. Within the first [part], "samādhi" is a Sanskrit term; in the Chinese language, it means "harmonized and upright concentration."

This means that all sentient beings are crooked and not straight; the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas use this [samādhi] to harmonize and straighten them. Hence it is called "the samādhi of harmonizing and straightening.
Regarding "body and mind do not substitute for one another," this refers to the fact that the body of the Tathāgata and my own mind, Ānanda, cannot substitute for each other.
To lose my fundamental mind means that the fundamental mind is no longer the originally luminous self-nature.
This is the original mind (*mūlacitta*). For its initial aspiration was that the Tathāgata might bestow upon it the samādhi;
having come to this state, it ultimately failed to realize its hope, and thus it is said to have "lost the original mind. Regarding the analogy of the impoverished son and so forth:

it need not be said that original enlightenment (*mūlajñāna*) is like the father and initial enlightenment (*ādyabodhi*) is like the son. Its meaning simply refers to the time before one has left the household life, when the Tathāgata—
He is my elder brother and I am his younger brother. Now that he has become a member of the Saṃgha, the Tathāgata is my father and I am his son.

As for the term "poor son," it refers to one who has not yet obtained the Dharma-wealth of the Tathāgata’s merit; though he is a son, he remains poor. Regarding "having abandoned his father and fled":
since one is a son of the Dharma, one ought to rely upon the Awakened Father and cultivate practice to open up sublime understanding. Yet, at present, one is unable to cultivate such practice.
They interpret the Tathāgata’s teachings as if they were a mere renunciation; thus it is said that they "abandon their father and flee.

Regarding the second [point], the phrase "entangled by the two obstacles" refers to the afflictive obstacle (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive obstacle (*jñeyāvaraṇa*). Where are they entangled by these two obstacles?
It is simply when one possesses much learning but does not practice; this is the entanglement of the cognitive obstacle. For them to ascend... [text ends]
It is turned by the courtesan-like [afflictions]. This is the entanglement of the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*). "Affliction" means being clouded and agitated.
Because of this clouding and agitation, one either engages in conceptual discrimination or in craving; consequently, all wholesome deeds and superior practices cannot be cultivated.
Therefore, it is called the "hindrance to phenomena" (*vastv-āvaraṇa*). As for "the knowable" (*jñeya*): that which is known is not itself the hindrance, but rather that which is hindered.

It obstructs the objects of knowledge (*jñeya-āvaraṇa*). Consequently, all rational principles (*tattva*) fail to become clear; therefore, it is called the "obstruction to principle" (*li-zhang*). Regarding the "quiescent and eternal nature of mind":
the fact that the characteristics of the mind are fundamentally empty is called "quiescence" (*śānti*); the fact that the essence of its nature remains manifest is called "eternal" (*nitya*).

Furthermore, this nature of mind does not exist as something separate from anything else; all phenomena (*dharma*) are precisely it. This is because all phenomena are, in their very substance, quiescent and extinguished.

Therefore it is called "quiescence. Although it is quiescent extinction, it is nonetheless vividly present; therefore it is called "permanence. In sum, quiescence and illumination are of one suchness;
quiescence and illumination are non-dual. This is precisely the eternally abiding true mind, the inherently pure and luminous essence; it is merely a variation in phrasing.

Second, both the mind and the eyes are invited into the center. Regarding those who are "poor and exposed": they are called "poor" because they lack the wealth of merit and Dharma to provide for themselves;
they are called "exposed" because they lack the parents of provisional and ultimate truth upon whom to rely. To give rise to the wondrously luminous mind is the true mind;
to open the eye of the Way is the true seeing. Someone has said: "Ānanda has already had his deluded mind refuted by the Tathāgata through the seven locations."
Regarding the three locations where delusion is bound, its substance has no origin. Even when pressed in this way, you still act as if your mind and eyes were asking questions;
this is not correct. You do not understand the depth or shallowness of the meaning of the question, but merely look at the tone of the answer.
When the Tathāgata answers in such a manner, how could Ānanda—without having left his old ways—ever have consented to it? Furthermore, there are others who...
It is said: "In this context, the interlocutor and the Tathāgata engage in one request and one teaching; this constitutes the convergence of views and the return to the fundamental nature.

This is also not correct. If it were taken as the convergence of views and the return to the fundamental nature, there would be an inconsistency between the two layers of fourfold question-and-answer sequences occurring before and after.
Previously, when investigating the mind, Ānanda said: "Seeing is the function of the eye; mental cognition is not the function of the eye, for it does not fulfill the definition of seeing."
The Buddha said: "If the eye were able to see, then when you are inside a room, would the door be able to see?
At this point, [Ānanda] had already realized the return to the fundamental nature; therefore, it does not correspond with what was stated previously. If the subsequent passage says:
"Although Ānanda and the great assembly heard these words, their mouths remained silent while their minds had not yet attained awakening," if this refers to the realization within this context—
Having seen the nature, why did Ānanda and the great assembly remain silent with their mouths while their minds remained unenlightened?
This is why it does not correspond with what follows. According to Ānanda’s request: "I do not know the nature of the mind which is quiescent and eternal;

I only pray that the Tathāgata, out of compassion for one who is destitute and exposed, will manifest the wondrously luminous nature and open my eye of the Way. Yet how is it that the Tathāgata suddenly [proceeds] with...?

This constitutes a response that fails to address the question. If one claims that Ānanda’s preceding inquiry—concerning the ignorance of the nature of the mind as quiescent and eternal—was indeed a question regarding the "returning to the nature," why would the Tathāgata suddenly answer by saying, "He has attained the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric" (and so forth)? Therefore, it does not correspond with the answer. As it is said:
In these preceding and succeeding exchanges of question and answer, the responses are for the most part inconsistent with the inquiries.

If one views them through the lens of "returning to nature" (huijian guixing), they appear internally incongruous. Now, by viewing them as a direct manifestation of the quiescent and eternal true nature, the questions and answers finally harmonize like a box and its lid;
from beginning to end, they will be as clear as the sun and stars.

The second part, the "Revelation," is divided into two. First, the manifestation of auspicious omens, beginning with "At that very moment... and so forth. Second, the teaching itself, beginning with "He addressed Ānanda... and so forth.

Regarding the first, the manifestation of omens, this also serves as a benefit through form. While the previous section was for the purpose of destroying deluded mind, this section is for the purpose of revealing true vision.
As for the phrase "from the *svastika* on his chest... and so forth: light symbolizes wisdom; this wisdom arises from the resultant essence of the myriad virtues.
And it emerges. The *svastika* (卍) is brought about by the auspiciousness of myriad virtues; therefore, this *svastika* is represented by the surging forth of precious light.
That light is brilliantly radiant, representing the possession of this wisdom that can perfectly illuminate and perfectly contemplate; thus, it is represented by the brilliant radiance of that light.
With a single instance of contemplative illumination, hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates are thereby accomplished; hence, there are one hundred... [marks].
The thousand colors represent this. In total, they represent the light of wisdom (*jñāna-āloka*) in this manner. The ten directions below represent the realm of principle (*tattva-viṣaya*).

If the light of wisdom were not yet perfected, the realm of principle would not manifest. Now that the light of wisdom has been perfected, this kind of realm of principle manifests spontaneously (*dharmatayā*).
Therefore, it is represented by the atoms of the ten directions and so forth. In this way, the entirety of wisdom is the realm, and the entirety of the realm is wisdom; realm and wisdom are one.
It is the state where the non-dual object and wisdom are one and the same. Regarding this light of wisdom and its underlying principle, who has realized it as a fruit?
Who is currently practicing it as a cause? Only the Buddhas of the ten directions have realized it for themselves; therefore, it is symbolized by "pervasive sprinkling" (*bianguan*) and so forth.
Only those such as Ānanda today are currently practicing it; therefore, it is symbolized by "revolving until" (*xuanzhi*) and so forth. As it says:
That which constitutes the fruit being a fruit has no other basis for being a fruit than the light of wisdom;
that which constitutes the cause being a cause likewise has no other basis for being a cause than the light of wisdom.
Although cause and fruit differ, their light of wisdom is one and the same.
There are two parts to the explanation, which are further divided into two. First, the announcement that he will speak; second, the actual exposition.

Within the first part, regarding the phrase "the great banner of the Dharma" (*mahā-dharmadhvaja*): a banner has the meaning of destroying the heterodox and erecting the orthodox. To call it the "great banner of the Dharma" means that there is no heterodoxy that is not destroyed and no orthodoxy that is not erected.
Destroying heterodoxy is as previously described in the refutation of the deluded mind in the seven locations.

The basis of that which depends has no location; in these three points, the false mind—the dependent—is refuted as being without substance. To establish the correct vertically is precisely to manifest true vision here and now.

If there is a vertical establishment within the subduing of the heterodox, it is like subduing its bases—whether internal, external, or even non-attachment—and thereby establishing the correct, which is neither internal nor external, nor even non-attachment. It is like subduing that...

It is able to subvert the heterodox views of the dependent mind’s false appearances, conceptualizations, and so forth; it establishes the correct state of the non-dependent mind, which is free from false appearances and conceptualizations.

Within this establishment of the correct, there is the destruction of the heterodox, as seen in subsequent sections concerning the transcendence of arising and ceasing, inversion, and the conditions of causality, spontaneity, conjunction, and disjunction. For this reason, it is called the Great Dharma.

Regarding the phrase "attaining the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric," etc.: this is a sentence of meaning as it is read today. If one were to compose it as a formal grammatical sentence, it should read:
"Attaining the wondrous, subtle, and esoteric nature—the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind. To explain the characters at first glance: that which is inconceivable is called "wondrous" (miao).

That which is profound, firm, obscure, and remote is called "subtle" (*wei*). That which cannot be measured or discerned is called "mysterious" (*mi*). That which is free from defilement is called "pure" (*jing*).

That which can illuminate and perceive is called "luminous" (*ming*). If one discusses this according to reality: the nature of subtlety and mystery is that the essence of the nature is empty and quiescent; this is the true within the conventional.
The mind of purity and luminosity is that the characteristics of the mind are vividly present; this is the conventional within the true. Thus it is said:
This is the non-duality of the ultimate and the conventional; it is the equality of negation and illumination. It cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed through speech;
therefore, it is called the "wondrous, subtle, and secret nature" and the "wondrously pure and luminous mind. This refers to the request to explain the arising of this wondrously luminous mind.

Regarding "attaining the pure eye": it is called "pure" (*qing*) because afflictions (*kleśa*) cannot defile it, and it is called "clear" (*jing*) because birth and death (*saṃsāra*) cannot pollute it.
Because it illuminates all things as being entirely true, the single eye must possess the five eyes (*pañca-cakṣus*) to constitute true vision.
This is said to be a request for the opening of one's own Dharma-eye.

The second part, the Section on the Correct Exposition, has two divisions. First, the verification based on the facts concerning Ānanda and others; second, the elucidation by way of analogy concerning the Buddha’s words, etc.
The first division also has two parts: first, the question; second, the answer. The question is easily understood. Regarding the second, the answer:
"Blazing like a mountain of jewels, born of purity" means that the Buddha’s golden body is entirely produced through the perfuming of unsurpassed morality, concentration, and wisdom.
Because it is attained through cultivation, it is said to be "born from purity.

Second, the section on "Illuminating by Way of Analogy" is divided into two parts: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the categorization is established; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the actual demonstration is provided.

Regarding the first category within the fixed [teachings], the statement "I now speak these words of truth to you" does not mean that what was said in the past was false and only what is being said now is true.
One must understand that all that was clarified previously served merely to shatter the deluded mind; from this point onward, the True Vision is revealed.

Since that which is revealed is the Truth, that which reveals it is likewise real; therefore, it is said, "I speak these words of truth to you. The meaning of the question therein may be understood as follows:
Regarding the statement in the response, "The matters and meanings are similar," this was Ānanda’s erroneous reply.
He took the eye’s capacity for seeing as an analogy for the hand’s capacity for clenching; while the phenomena appear similar, their underlying meanings are actually different.
Therefore, the Tathāgata rebuked him below, saying: "Your claim that they are similar is not correct."

The second part, the section on the correct demonstration, has two divisions. First, "the blind man sees darkness," which refers to the Buddha’s statement beginning with "The Buddha told... and so forth.

Second, "seeing does not depend on the eyes," which refers to Ānanda’s statement beginning with "Ānanda said... and so forth. The first of these [sections] further has three parts: first, the direct refutation of the erroneous meaning, beginning with "The Buddha told...";

second, the explanation of the reason for this, beginning with "Because..."; and third, the actual manifestation that [seeing] is not extinguished, beginning with "Therefore... By thus investigating through these three successive layers, then—

The blind man gazes into darkness to demonstrate that the nature of seeing is indestructible. That the nature of seeing is indestructible allows one to know that the very substance of the nature of seeing is truly eternal.
"Two visions are not related to the eyes" constitutes the second [point]. First, from the passage beginning with Ānanda, the objection is presented. This is self-evident.
The second part, "The Buddha told," etc., provides an explanation and clarification. It also has three sections: first, the determination;
second, the formal explanation; third, the concluding manifestation. The first is easily understood. The second, the formal explanation, also has three parts:

first, "Ānanda," etc., restates the matter; second, "That darkness," etc., provides the formal analogy; third, "If a lamp," etc., performs the analytical refutation. Furthermore, it is thus analyzed and revealed.
Thus, one sees that seeing does not depend on the eyes for its clarity; the nature of seeing is unborn.
That the nature of seeing is unborn allows us to further know that the very essence of the nature of seeing is truly quiescent. What is called "extinction" has never actually been extinguished;

rather, it is the conditions that are extinguished, not the nature of seeing that undergoes extinction. What is called "arising" has never actually arisen; rather, it is the conditions that arise, not the nature of seeing that arises.
This is the arising [of the nature]. In these two instances, both directly reveal the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*).

Regarding the second, the double revelation of the nature of seeing, there are also two parts: first, the silent request by the disciple, namely the passage beginning with "Although Ānanda... and so forth;

second, the explicit teaching by the Tathāgata, namely the passage beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One... and so forth. Within the first part, Ānanda and the great assembly have already [spoken] with their mouths...

As for his silence: Ānanda, having previously had his deluded mind refuted through the "Sevenfold Refutation of the Deluded Mind" and now being interrogated regarding the non-existence of the essence of delusion through the "Threefold Interrogation," realized that these two sequences could not overcome his fear.
Weeping with grief, he thus made his request to reveal the wondrously luminous mind and open his Dharma-eye. Although the Tathāgata was about to respond, he ultimately did not speak.
This is clear. It is only by using a blind person’s gazing into darkness that one reveals that the nature of seeing does not perish and is, in its very substance, truly eternal.

Furthermore, by showing that seeing is not dependent on the eyes, one reveals that the nature of seeing is unborn, its eternal substance being truly quiescent. Regarding this, there is nothing that the Tathāgata does not clearly understand.
Nevertheless, Ānanda and his peers had still not attained realization. If one has not yet asked oneself, one may ask again; however, what was previously asked has already been asked.
If the Tathāgata has not yet spoken, one may wait for him to speak; however, what he has already spoken has now been spoken. At this juncture, there is nothing further to offer as an oblation;
one can do nothing but remain silent with mouth and ears. As for those whose minds have not yet awakened, their delusions have already been shattered.
The mind has no locus; the essence of delusion is fundamentally non-existent. Yet, one has not yet understood the reason why it has no locus and no essence.

Now, although you have manifested the true permanence of the nature of seeing and perceived the true stillness of that nature, you still do not know the reason for its true permanence and true stillness.
Therefore, it is said that the mind has not yet attained awakening.
The second part, "The Tathāgata’s Manifest Explanation," is divided into two sections. First, from "At that time, the World-Honored One" onwards, Ānanda is awakened through the mediation of Cunda.

Second, from "Then the Tathāgata" onwards, the great assembly is rebuked through the mediation of Ānanda. The first section is further divided into two parts. First, from "At that time" etc., Cunda skillfully uses the metaphor of adventitious dust.
Second, from "Immediately" etc., Ānanda turns back his understanding regarding the host and space. The first of these is further divided into three parts. First...

The Tathāgata asks about the cause; this is the first section, "At that time, [Ananda] lowered [his hand]. Second, Śāriputra answers regarding the fruit; this is the second section, "At that time, Kauṇḍinya lowered [his hand].
Third, the Tathāgata confirms it; this is the section beginning with "The Buddha said. Regarding the first of these, as for "opening the five fingers of the wheel":

previously, when refuting the deluded mind, he clenched his five fingers; now, to reveal true vision, he opens his five fingers. If one discusses this from a general perspective, it is simply intended to have him concentrate his mind. If...

Extending this further: what is called "shattering delusion" means there is nothing to be shattered when shattering; what is manifested within this shattering means there is nothing to be manifested when manifesting the truth.
Manifesting that which was previously shattered is like a finger being bent—that which is extended is precisely that which was bent.
The instructions given to Ānanda are what the Tathāgata proclaims; it is not that there is some separate proclamation apart from this proclamation.
Because Ānanda made this request, it is called "instruction. When I say "I first attained the Way," it means that what the Tathāgata has attained is not something separate;
it is the realization of what is inherent within one's nature, and thus it is called "attaining the Way.
*Bodhi* is the fruit-wisdom of the Mahāyāna, whereas *Arhat* is the ultimate designation in the Hinayana teachings. "Adventitious afflictions" refers to the two delusions of views and thought.

Furthermore, there is a distinction between those [afflictions] within and outside the realms (*dhātu*). Those severed by the Mahāyāna are afflictions outside the realms and are also called "specific afflictions" (*viśeṣa-kleśa*).
Those severed by the Hīnayāna are afflictions within the realms and are also called "universal afflictions" (*sāmānya-kleśa*).

Some say that these adventitious afflictions (*āgantuka-kleśa*) should not belong to the Mahāyāna, because they were present at the Deer Park (*Mṛgadāva*). Nevertheless, there are indeed distinctions between the Great and the Small [Vehicles].

It is distinct. For example, while the five bhikṣus who attained the first fruit were indeed followers of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna), and what was severed by those who partially realized arhatship was limited to within the realms;
yet, when the eighty thousand devas and others awakened to the patience of non-arising (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti), was this not the true stage of the Great Vehicle (Mahāyāna)?

What is severed at bodhi should naturally pertain to beyond the realms. Thus, one knows that severing the views and afflictions (dṛṣṭi-kleśa) beyond the realms is precisely the realization of bodhi. Severing...

Regarding those within the realm who have eliminated both views and afflictions, they attain only arhatship. Furthermore, there are many varieties of both bodhi and arhatship. There are three types of bodhi:

first, expedient means; second, true nature; and third, ultimate wisdom. As for what is realized by the five [arhats], from the perspective of its manifest aspect, it may also be called bodhi according to the teaching;
however, regarding the three types [of bodhi], they have not yet seen even a dream of them. There are two types of arhat: first...
To sever the pervasive afflictions is the Small Vehicle; to sever the specific afflictions is the Great Vehicle.
As the Lotus Sūtra says: "We of today are true arhats; we should receive offerings therein. This is what that means.

The second part, Dharmakīrti’s response, is divided into two sections. First, from "At that time" (*tasmin samaye*) onwards, there is a general summary; second, from "The World-Honored One" (*bhagavān*) onwards, there is a detailed exposition.

Within the initial general summary, regarding the phrase "one who alone has attained the name 'understanding'": when the Tathāgata was at the Deer Park turning the Wheel of Dharma of the Four Truths for the five bhikṣus, he asked, "Do you know?
