Do you understand? They replied, "We have known; we have understood. Therefore, it is said that he alone attained [the name].
Explaining the names. This section has two parts: first, the analogy of the host and the guest; second, the analogy of empty space and dust.
Regarding the first, the analogy of the host and the guest: "For example" refers to the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*).
Since these are called delusions of view, they involve pervasive conceptualization across all phenomena, just as a traveler [wanders] through the four [directions].
Wandering and traveling throughout the various paths and doctrines, it is said: "It is like a traveler.
Because one follows erroneous interpretations to seek erroneous principles, it is like a traveler who, at the onset of dusk, must seek lodging. Thus it is said: "One casts oneself into a guest-house.
In seeking erroneous principles, one cannot avoid calculating permanence; this is no different from a traveler’s stay. Furthermore, calculating annihilation is like a traveler’s... [departure].

Their food does not differ; hence it is said that "sometimes they stay overnight and sometimes they eat. Having already entertained either the notion of permanence (*śāśvata*) or the notion of annihilation (*uccheda*), they use permanence to refute annihilation and annihilation to refute permanence.
As permanence and annihilation refute one another, neither is established. This is like a traveler who stays overnight and finishes his meal;
once permanence and annihilation have been refuted, there arises yet another calculation—that of both permanence and annihilation (*ubhayatva*). This is like a traveler who finds no restful dwelling.

The guest is used as a metaphor for the delusions of view in this manner. As for the principle of the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), it is naturally free from views such as annihilationism and eternalism;
it is like the host who has nowhere to go. Thus it is said: "If one is truly the host, there is nowhere to which one goes.
The true principle is thus metaphorized by the host. Thereupon, one reflects and deliberates upon the interval between these two—the delusions and the principle.
One can know that views such as those of annihilationism and eternalism are conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), like a guest who passes through without staying.

The principle of the partial truth (*tathyasatya*) which is free from these four views is like a host who dwells without going anywhere. Therefore it is said: "Reflecting in this way... (and so forth).
In this way, one knows that the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are guests and not the host. For this reason, I have set forth [this teaching].
At that time, regarding the discrimination of the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-heya*), one awakens to this meaning of non-abiding; thus it is called "guest.
Therefore it is said: "That which does not abide is termed the meaning of 'guest. Second, within the analogy of the empty dust, "dust" is a metaphor for the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-heya*).
The aforementioned delusions of view involve resolving false principles with false interpretations, which is like the overcast rain of heaven.
The delusions of view have already been shattered and the ultimate truth has been revealed, like the first clearing of the sky after rain; hence it is said, "it is like a newly cleared sky.

Although the delusions of view have been destroyed, the delusions of thought still remain; one therefore continues to observe the principle of partial truth by means of the wisdom that analyzes emptiness.
What is called "contemplating the ultimate truth through deep reflection" is like the sun rising over the valley after a fresh clearing, its light ascending into the heavens;

hence it is said, "the clear sunlight ascends to heaven. Although one uses contemplative wisdom to observe the realm of ultimate truth, this is merely the ability to observe through cessation (*śamatha*);

it is that which is revealed by the analytical emptiness (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*) and is solely the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*). It is like the light of the clear sun entering through a crack in a wall; hence it is said, "light enters a crack."
There is nothing else therein; it is simply because by departing from existence one reveals emptiness, and by departing from the conventional one reveals the ultimate.

Through this repeated and layered observation, the eighty-one grades of delusions of thought manifest in a chaotic flurry before one—moment after moment of greedy attachment, mind after mind of refusal to let go—just like the appearance of motes of dust in a beam of light.
Therefore, it is said: "The various appearances of dust within emptiness are revealed. Regarding these delusions of thought...
The characteristic of delusion is dark and turbulent, like fine dust that is light and swift; this is what is called "wild horses" (gandharva-nagara) and "dust and grime.
It flickers and is unstable; thus it is said that the substance of dust is in motion. In this way, dust is used as a metaphor for the afflictions of thought.
As for the principle of the partial truth of reality (*tathyatā*), its entire essence is empty and quiescent—what is called suffering being without oppression, and so on, up to the Path.
There is no capacity for penetration; it is as tranquil as empty space. Furthermore, using emptiness as a metaphor for ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is thus.

Thereupon, by reflecting and deliberating upon the interval between delusion and principle, one may know that the true principle of partial truth—which is free from craving and attachment—is limpid, profound, and silent, like the limpid stillness of space. As for those afflictions of thought...
The characteristics of craving and so forth are like a whirlwind, shifting and turning; they are like dust being stirred up. Therefore it is said:
"Reflecting in this way... (and so forth). From this, one knows that the afflictions of thought are like dust and not empty space.
For this reason, in the past, I, Dignāga, realized upon the craving of these afflictions of thought this meaning of "shifting and turning," which is named...

It is dust (*rajas*). Therefore it is said that that which causes agitation is defined by the meaning of "dust. Regarding the two meanings of "guest" (*āgantuka*) and "dust," while the Tathāgata merely posed the questions, Dignāga presented the explanations.

He did not only explain the views and afflictions (*darśana-heya* and *bhāvanā-heya*) as guest and dust; he also explained the principle of truth (*satya-dharma*) as the primary emptiness (*mukhya-śūnyatā*).
If this were not a joint performance by teacher and disciple, how could such an exposition have been possible?

Among the three instances where the Tathāgata granted his seal of approval, the phrase "it is thus" (evam) is used because Kāśyapa was able to employ the metaphor of adventitious dust for the afflictions (*kleśa*) and the metaphor of the host-like space for the truth of reality (*tattva*).
He compared the movement of adventitious dust to the afflictions, and he compared the non-migration and unchanging nature of the host-like space to the truth of reality. Thus, regarding the guest...

Dust is space; afflictions are the ultimate truth. By establishing metaphors through dharmas and applying dharmas through metaphors, the dharma and the metaphor are perfectly aligned with the Buddha’s intent;
therefore, he confirmed it by saying, "Thus it is" (*evam*). Question: The delusions of view consist of ten underlying tendencies (*anuśaya*);

why does he single out only the four views? Answer: While the ten underlying tendencies—both sharp and dull—apply universally to both worldlings and non-Buddhists, here he mentions only the sharp ones.
This is the first point. Since even non-Buddhists hold such views, theirs are indeed extreme. Question: This sutra reveals the nature of mind as quiescent and eternal;

it is entirely the Middle Way and pertains to the specific delusions (*viśeṣa-kleśa*). Why, then, does it rely on the universal delusions (*sāmānya-kleśa*) severed by Cūḍapanthaka and the limited principle he realized to serve as its illumination?

Answer: There is no "great" or "small" in the Dharma; greatness and smallness reside in the capacity of the practitioner. There is no "delusion" or "awakening" in the principle; delusion and awakening reside in the person.
Although Cunda recounted what was severed and realized at the Deer Park, once Ānanda’s great capacity for awakening had been stirred,
it was not hindered from leading him to realize the nature of quiescence and permanence.

Second, the Tathāgata immediately departs. Ānanda’s turning back to explain the "host" (the subject) as empty and awakening to the text on quiescent permanence is because the Tathāgata originally intended to use Cundabhadrī’s explanation of adventitious dust to awaken Ānanda; now that Cundabhadrī has finished her exposition, [the Tathāgata departs].

The Tathāgata thus leads Ānanda to awakening. One must understand that this intention originates from Ānanda’s previous request, expressed in the passage where he did not know the nature of the mind which is quiescent and eternal.
This is divided into two parts: first, "At that moment," etc., wherein the finger is bent to lead Ānanda to realize the distinction between subject and object;
second, "The Tathāgata," etc., wherein light is projected to lead Ānanda to understand the emptiness of sensory objects. Thus, one knows that the Tathāgata, at the outset—
First, by employing Cien’s explanation regarding the host and guest, he presses Ananda to realize that the nature of seeing is permanent.
Second, by employing Cien’s explanation regarding the emptiness of dust, he presses Ananda to realize that the nature of seeing is quiescent.

In this way, his previous request concerning quiescence and permanence is clearly answered. Within this single passage, there are two kinds of quiescence: the quiescence of the mind-nature and the quiescence of the nature of seeing.

It is always manifest without exception. The first section further has three parts. First, examining and determining by counting on the fingers; this corresponds to the passage beginning with "At that time. Second, verifying and understanding through analogy;

this corresponds to the passage beginning with "The Buddha said. Third, the Tathāgata’s approval; this corresponds to the passage beginning with "The Buddha said. The first part is self-evident. Regarding the verification through analogy, it is divided into two sections.

First, verifying through opening and closing, corresponding to the passage beginning with "The Buddha said. Second, verifying through movement and stillness, corresponding to the passage beginning with "The Buddha said."

Second, the emission of light to cause Ānanda to understand that both dust and space are empty also has three parts: first, from "The Tathāgata" downward, the emission of light serves to verify and determine;

second, from "Ānanda" downward, he relies on this precedent to verify and understand; third, from "The Buddha said" downward, the Tathāgata provides his seal of approval. All of these can be seen [in the text].
Second, [the Buddha] uses Ānanda as a pretext to reprove the great assembly. Some say that this is actually a formal reprimand of Ānanda; however, this is certainly not the case.
Since he opens his mouth by saying "the great assembly," how could this be a reprimand of Ānanda? Furthermore, it says, "You, observe Ānanda.
If he were reprimanding Ānanda, would he have Ānanda observe Ānanda? Thus, we know for certain that this is simply borrowing Ānanda’s realization [to instruct the assembly].
This section rebukes the faults of the great assembly. It is divided into four parts: first, the exhortation from "If, furthermore... onwards; second, the actual verification from "You observe...
onwards; third, the censure of errors from "How can... onwards; and fourth, the concluding rebuke from "The nature-mind... onwards. Regarding the first part:

as for the phrase "If, furthermore," the intention is that you all are together in this Dharma assembly of the *Śūraṅgama*, equally endowed with the tranquil and eternal nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). As for Ānanda...
Dignāga realized that the mind perceives within adventitious dust and understood the principle of the Truths within the primary emptiness. Having passed through this once, he attained awakening;

though his hand opens and closes, he saw that the seeing-nature itself neither opens nor closes. Since the Buddha’s hand does not abide, the seeing-nature is even more devoid of stillness—how could it be non-abiding?
This is how the meaning of the primary emptiness amidst adventitious dust reveals that the seeing-nature is eternal. Furthermore, he awakened to...
When my head moves, the seeing-nature itself does not cease; who then is it that causes the shaking?
This reveals the meaning of the guest-dust versus the host-space, whereby the stillness of the seeing-nature is made manifest.

Even if you wish to understand the stillness and permanence of the seeing-nature through the analogy of the guest-dust and the host-space, as Ānanda did, you should likewise regard the "shaking" and such as being the dust.
Therefore it is said, "If again... (and so forth). One should supplement the phrase "that which is subject to movement is called dust" with the two lines:

"that which is tranquil and still is called space. This means that by perceiving the arising and ceasing of the nature of seeing, one awakens to the permanence of the nature of seeing as non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, one should supplement the phrase "that which does not abide is called a guest" with the line: "that which has no fixed destination [is called the host]."

The two lines beginning with "In the past, it was called the master" immediately take the movement and shifting of the nature of seeing as the means to awaken to the stillness of the unmoving nature of seeing.
That the sutra does not explicitly state this is merely a matter of abbreviation; however, its meaning has never been absent.

Regarding the second point, "Observe, Ānanda," and so forth, this is precisely an occasion to borrow Ānanda’s realization of the stillness and reality of the nature of seeing through the medium of sensory objects and space, thereby providing a single instance of experiential verification.
Furthermore, as for "you all," you too shall rely upon Ānanda as a guest to realize the habitual nature of seeing; this shall serve as one authentic verification.

Regarding the phrase "among these three, how is it that you now... and so forth, this rebukes them by pointing out that since they are already in the same assembly as Ānanda and equally possess the quiescent and eternal [nature], and since Ānanda has already attained realization, why do you all still take this flickering body as [your true self]?
The True Body (*dharmakāya*). Are you unable to awaken to and perceive that which is unmoving as the True Body? You still take the realm of agitation to be the true realm;
are you unable to awaken to and perceive that which is without expansion or contraction as the true realm? The above rebukes their ignorance of the distinction between the real and the delusive.
From here on, it rebukes their pursuit of the delusive and loss of the real. Since you all [perceive] the realm of agitation...
Taking the body as the body, they further take the realm of movement as their object. Thus, beginning ends and endings begin; they pursue the delusive and lose the real.
To lose what is real is "upside-down" (*viparyāsa*); to be attached to what is delusive is "inverted. Thus they act with inverted conduct.
Regarding the phrase "the nature of the four minds," etc., this concludes the description of the state of such inversion. Nature...
The phrase "the mind" is a reprimand for losing the true nature. The phrase "recognizing objects" is a reprimand for pursuing delusion.

The phrase "samsara" reprimands you by stating that your inherently quiescent and eternal mind-nature has never been lacking; yet now, having lost the truth of this nature-mind, you instead recognize external objects as yourself.
This is precisely what it means to transmigrate within the very midst of perceiving a quiescent nature. If you can awaken to this, it will immediately be revealed.
Even while within saṃsāra, one constantly perceives its nature as quiescent.

To take upon oneself a single phrase and hold those who transmigrate through birth and death to be "saṃsāric beings"—this does not descend from heaven, nor does it emerge from the earth, nor is it bestowed by humans; rather, it is something you yourselves have taken up.
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama, Volume One;
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama, Volume Two.
Spoken by the Great Master Yisong of Tiantai.
Recorded by Lingshu, a disciple of Master Guyi.

From the beginning of this scroll up to the two passages concerning "those who are to be pitied," this constitutes the third section, which further explains remaining doubts. It is divided into two parts.
First, the resolution of doubts concerning the reality and falsity of body and mind; this corresponds to the first section. Second, the resolution of doubts concerning inverted conduct;

this corresponds to the second section. The first [of these two] is further divided into two parts: first, the request for instruction, beginning with "At that time..."; second, the exposition of the teaching, beginning with "The Buddha said...". The first [of these two] is further divided into two parts.

First is the secret request made by the appropriate recipient; this corresponds to the section beginning with "At that time" (*er shi*). Second is the manifest inquiry by King Anāthapiṇḍada; this corresponds to the section beginning with "Then he" (*shi bi*).
Within the first part, the secret request of the appropriate recipient, regarding the phrase "hearing the Buddha’s instruction," there are two meanings: the distant and the near.

As previously explained, [the Buddha] first used his bent finger to cause Ānanda to realize that the nature of seeing is constant, even as the hand itself opens and closes, while the act of seeing neither opens nor closes. Furthermore...
The emission of light caused Ānanda to realize that the nature of seeing is quiescent; even as his head moved, the nature of seeing remained without cessation.

This was an instruction given by means of the universal [manifestation], such as the emission of light from the crown of the Buddha’s head, the emission of light from the mouth, and the emission of light from the *svastika* on his chest, as well as the bending of the five fingers and the opening of the five fingers—thus, the emission of light from these three locations and at these two times.

Pointing with a finger is collectively termed "pointing. Whether it be the seven points where the deluded mind is shattered and found to have no location, or the three points where the essence of delusion is interrogated and found to be fundamentally non-existent;
or the case of the blind man seeing darkness, wherein the seeing-nature is shown never to have ceased, thereby manifesting the permanence of the seeing-nature;

or the case of seeing not being dependent on the eyes, wherein the seeing-nature is shown never to have arisen, thereby manifesting the quiescence of the seeing-nature—such is the shattering of the deluded mind. Such...
The manifestation of true vision all belongs to instruction (*śāsana*). This refers to "instruction" (*śāsana*) in terms of its remote significance.
One must understand the skill of the sūtra compiler in narrating events; the very two characters for "instruction" (*śāsana*) fully encompass the intent of this entire fascicle of the sūtra.

It is like a child who has lost its mother suddenly encountering a compassionate mother; those who have left the household life take the Tathāgata as their mother to rely upon, and those who study the Path [take him likewise].
Sustained by the flavor of the Dharma-milk, the Dharmakāya thus attains growth and the life of wisdom increases.
Although Ānanda has left the household life, he differs from those who lack a mother’s protection in that he has resolved his mind [on enlightenment] through the perception of marks;
yet, because his mind has not yet entered the Path and he listens to the Dharma by means of sounds, he is no different from one who lacks the sustenance of its flavor. Now, being here...

Within the assembly at the Śūraṅgama Sūtra, having received the repeated instructions and detailed exhortations of our Buddha, the Tathāgata, I have finally attained the realization that the deluded mind is subject to arising and ceasing, while the true vision is quiescent and eternal.
From this point on, I shall no longer suffer the premature loss of my life-force of wisdom (prajñā-jīvita) nor the ruin of my Dharma-body (dharma-kāya).
To illustrate this through a metaphor: it is like an infant who has lost its mother’s milk suddenly encountering the Dharma King.
This is the compassion of our mother. As for the request to hear how the Tathāgata manifested [the truth], it is because Ānanda has long taken a thief for his son;

this has penetrated deeply into his very marrow and is by no means a superficial matter. Now, on one hand, he was awakened by Cunda’s pointing out that both the host and guest are empty and that all sensory objects are void;
and on the other hand, he was repeatedly pressed by the Tathāgata’s snapping of fingers and flashing of light. Although...

One may be able to penetrate the seeing-nature such that when the hands themselves open and close, one perceives no opening or closing; or awaken to the stillness of the seeing-nature such that when the head itself moves, the nature has no cessation.
Yet, if one has not yet recognized true knowing and remains attached to the seeing, then what is called "forming an understanding based on others" will lead one back into delusion.
For this reason, today you have again raised this question; however, you do not yet know the distinction between the real and the false, or the substantial and the empty.

Arising and ceasing are non-arising and non-ceasing; from the beginning, the entirety of delusion is itself reality, and even the entirety of arising and ceasing is itself non-arising and non-ceasing.

This is because those who call themselves "enlightened" still do not know who is reality and who is delusion, or who is arising and ceasing and who is non-arising and non-ceasing. Therefore it is said: "I wish to hear the clarification."

[The text] emerges. By this, one knows that the two characters "manifest" (xian) and "emerge" (chu) are also spoken of from the perspective of the Tathāgata. The two characters "illuminate" (ming) and "reveal" (fa) have two meanings:
first, it refers to the distinction between the real and the false, and between arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing.

That which arises-and-ceases through the false and the illusory is one [aspect of] illumination and revelation; that which is non-arising-and-non-ceasing through the real and the true is another. Although there is the real...
The false and the arising-and-ceasing, as well as the non-arising-and-non-ceasing, each have their respective reasons for being elucidated; therefore, it is said that "both elucidate the nature.
This refers to the elucidation discussed within the section on what is explained by the True and the False, etc.
The first point means that the reasons why this kind of reality becomes true reality, and the reasons why the false, etc., becomes delusion, are all elucidated through the scriptural teachings.
This is further elucidated within the section concerning the capacity to express the distinction between the true and the false.

Furthermore, regarding the request to hear how the Tathāgata reveals [the truth], it was because previously the Tathāgata had refuted the deluded mind at seven points until it was rendered groundless, and interrogated the essence of delusion at three points until it was shown to be fundamentally non-existent.
Yet, the reason why delusion was thus refuted remained unknown; therefore, [the teaching] proceeds to the section on revealing the True Vision.
Although you have awakened to the fact that while your hands open and close, your vision neither opens nor closes, the Buddha’s hand does not abide;

yet as for my seeing-nature, it is even without stillness—so what could be called "non-abiding"? Furthermore, when my head moves, my seeing-nature is even without cessation—so what could be called "shaking"?
It is precisely by using this very deluded mind that has been thus refuted as the basis for awakening that you have come to this point. And...
I wonder how it can be that within the same body and mind, the former is empty and not real, false and not true—
whereas emptiness and falsity give rise to birth and extinction, yet reality and truth are without birth or extinction? Furthermore, how is it that now this is true and not false,
real and not empty— wherein truth and reality are without birth or extinction, while emptiness and falsity give rise to birth and extinction?

Therefore, this doubt arises; it is actually a manifestation of great skillful means. How could this be anything other than truly knowing that the entirely false is the true, and that the entirely subject to birth and death is itself non-arising and non-perishing?

Regarding the second section, the "Manifest Questions of King Prasenajit," such as when King Prasenajit rose and addressed the Buddha, and the first section, the "Manifested Inquiry of Ānanda’s Vow," at first glance these two appear to be contradictory. However, if one examines these two inquiries with precision:

One question concerns arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing; another concerns annihilation versus non-annihilation. Although their phrasing differs, their meaning is in fact the same.
For this reason, although the Tathāgata’s response appears to have been spoken specifically for King Aśoka, when examined through its underlying principle, it never fails to accord with the truth.
This is because the essential purport of his answer consists of only two points: first, that the body undergoes arising and ceasing; second, [that the mind does not].
Since the nature is without arising or ceasing, one knows that what the body has in terms of arising and ceasing is precisely that which Ānanda asked about:
the empty, the false, and the subject of arising and ceasing. That which is without arising or ceasing in its nature is precisely that which Ānanda asked about:
the true, the real, and that which does not arise or cease. Therefore, although there was one answer and one non-answer, in truth this answered both. Thus...

The "Subsequent Questions of King Ajātaśatru" following Ānanda’s inquiry. Furthermore, regarding the "Subsequent Questions of King Ajātaśatru" following Ānanda’s inquiry, there are two intentions [behind it].
First, King Ajātaśatru had previously heard the assertions of the non-Buddhists concerning annihilation (*uccheda*).

Since there is the conceptualization of annihilation, there must necessarily be its counterpart, permanence (*śāśvata*). It appears that by understanding annihilation and permanence, he understood arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*). Now, having again heard...

The Tathāgata is neither born nor extinguished; one should know that what the non-Buddhists say is incorrect. However, the reason for [the Buddha’s] following [Ānanda’s] inquiry is none other than this:
because they do not yet understand that the unborn and undying is fundamentally different from birth and extinction. This is why there is the question, "How can it be manifested?
and so forth. Second, as for what Ānanda asked: regarding the arising and ceasing of the true and the false, and the unborn and undying, as well as the self—
The doctrines of annihilationism heard from the non-Buddhists and the principle of neither-arising-nor-ceasing taught by the Tathāgata appear to be similar;
therefore, he subsequently poses his question. His intention is that the Tathāgata might answer both at once, so that he himself may hear both at once.
The Tathāgata, having already discerned this, answers both with a single phrase.
"Furthermore, regarding the phrase 'even now still harboring doubts' (*huxi*): as for the nature of the fox, it is characterized by the greatest degree of suspicion.
For example, even when it sees ice that is fit to tread upon, it still fears it might be water; only after listening to ensure there is no sound does it then step upon it.

By this, one can clearly see that the fox-nature is full of doubt. Hence, it is called 'fox-doubt' (*huxi*). As for the claim made by some that King Bimbisāra was the one who doubted: this refers to [the situation] if it were the Tathāgata..."

If what was said yesterday were not what is said today, it should be considered incorrect; if what the Tathāgata says today were the same as what was said yesterday, it should be considered incorrect.
Because of this lack of consistency, such a doubt arises. This, however, is not the case. If one views it in this way, although the words may sound pleasant, they do not accord with the true meaning.
One should rather say that in the past, Kātyāyana took annihilation to be *nirvāṇa*.
"Venerable Purna, today the Tathāgata defines *nirvāṇa* as neither arising nor ceasing.
When his words are compared with those of the former, my mind cannot help but harbor doubt.

Yet I do not know how the Tathāgata might elucidate this so that I may truly realize it—truly knowing this mind within the ground of reality where there is neither arising nor ceasing—and [how] Kātyāyana’s..."
To "sever and extinguish" means to suddenly destroy. It is only by interpreting it in this way that one captures the actual tone of King Nanda’s words.
As for the phrase "to verify and know": when this mind is firm and possesses a basis, it is called "verification" (zhèng); when it is clear and free from doubt, it is called "knowing" (zhī).

The second [section] on the exposition is divided into two parts: first, the Buddha’s instruction beginning with "If a Buddha... and second, the King’s realization beginning with "When the King heard...".

The first part is further divided into two: first, that the body has birth and cessation, as in "If a Buddha..."; second, that the nature is without birth or cessation, as in "If a Buddha...". The first of these is further divided into four:

first, the question regarding whether there is cessation or no cessation, beginning with "If a Buddha..."; second, knowing cessation despite not yet having ceased, beginning with "The Buddha said..."; third, the Buddha said...; [and so forth].
The first [section] discusses cessation in terms of form; the four Buddhas’ statement discusses cessation in terms of time. The first intention is easily understood.

Regarding the second, the phrase "I observe that what is present undergoes moment-by-moment transition and falls away" means that one minutely observes that as the preceding moment ceases, the succeeding moment arises;
as the succeeding moment ceases, yet another subsequent moment arises. In this way, one knows by means of each successive moment.
Yet they pass away and perish with each preceding thought-moment. Thus it is said that "thought-moments pass away and perish.
Furthermore, because the subsequent thought-moment is new and the preceding one is old, and since the subsequent is old, the following subsequent moments are again new.

In this way, one knows that by means of each subsequent thought-moment, one becomes ever-newer than each preceding thought-moment. Therefore it is said that "the ever-new does not abide. Such is the passing away of each thought-moment and the non-abiding of the ever-new.
Regarding "abiding": if one uses a metaphor to clarify this, it is like fire turning into ash. This is the gradual waning and gradual perishing of the fire;
it wanes further and further, and perishes further and further. Thus, its waning and perishing continue without rest.
Since the waning and perishing of the fire is like this, it is said, "like fire" (and so forth). Following "without rest," one should conclude by stating: "In terms of the Dharma..."
Moment by moment, things pass away; they are ever-new and never remain. To infer this through analogy: it is like fire turning to ash, gradually wasting away.
Furthermore, it is just like this. By observing the union of the phenomenon and the analogy, one knows with certainty that this body must perish.
Therefore it is said: one must decisively know that this body shall follow toward total extinction. Third, regarding the discussion of extinction in terms of form:
in the Tathāgata’s question, there were two points concerning youth and old age; King Nimi’s response contained three points, from youth to maturity and from maturity to old age.
Fourth, regarding the discussion of extinction in terms of time: "Your physical appearance should not wither all at once."
The Tathāgata’s words seem to suggest that although King Pāyāsi’s body has perished, as I observe it, its essence should not have suddenly decayed.
Because of this one question posed by the king, there follows a fivefold response concerning successive death and transformation.
"Subtle change and secret transition" refers to what is stated later in the text: "I see subtle transition" and "the changes of years and transformations of months. This...

This is a general indication. To transfer from this [state] to that is "transformation" (*bian*); for something to exist and then suddenly cease to exist is "metamorphosis" (*hua*). This precisely constitutes the meaning of "transformation and metamorphosis" (*bianhua*) in the present text.
As for "passing away" (*culuo*), it is not the same as what is stated in the *Book of Documents* (*Shangshu*), where the death of a person is called "passing away" (*culuo*).
I merely borrow its terminology without adopting its underlying meaning; that is to say, it refers to the fact that while vigor truly departs, senility gradually approaches.
A *kṣaṇa* is the shortest unit of time. As the *Ratnaketuparivarta Sūtra* states: "Within a single thought-moment (*cittakṣaṇa*), there are ninety *kṣaṇas*.
How small, then, is that duration! The rest may be understood accordingly.

The second section, on the non-arising and non-ceasing of the two natures, has three parts. First, from "The Buddha said" below, there is a brief inquiry regarding true nature. Second, from "The Persian" below, there is a direct answer stating that it is not known.
Third, from "The Buddha said" below, there is an extensive pointing-out and instruction. The first part, the brief inquiry regarding true nature, can be understood [as follows].
Regarding the second point, "directly answering 'I do not know'": when I say "I truly do not know," my intention is this:

the Tathāgata asked me whether, since I already know that transformation has cessation, I might also know that within cessation there is non-cessation. As I reflect upon it, I only know the cessation of that which ceases;
I do not know the non-cessation within cessation. Therefore, I say, "I truly do not know. Third, [the section on] explaining extensively...
The pointing-out consists of four parts: first, the granting of permission; second, the inquiry; third, the formal demonstration; and fourth, the clearing of objections.
First, the granting of permission is as stated in the Buddha’s words and so forth; this may be understood accordingly. Second, the inquiry has two parts:
first, from "Great King" onwards, the Ganges is discussed in terms of time; second, from the Buddha’s words onwards, the ability to see is examined in terms of its characteristics.

First, regarding time, according to what King Nimi said concerning the Ganges River, because it is never altered or changed, it is said to be "exactly as it was, without difference" and "also without any difference.
Nevertheless, as the preceding wave ceases, the succeeding wave arises; as the succeeding wave ceases, the next succeeding wave arises again.
In this way, that which ceases gradually ceases, and that which arises gradually arises. Thus, arising and ceasing continue without end.
It does not cease. Viewed from this perspective, there is a distinction. As the sages of the world have also said:

"That which passes away is like this [river], never ceasing day or night. Here too, there is a distinction: in the Buddha-dharma, if one speaks in terms of *lakṣaṇa* (phenomenal characteristics), there is cessation;

if one speaks in terms of *dharmatā* (essential nature), there is no cessation. This is what Master Sengzhao meant when he said: "The rivers and streams rush forth in competition, yet they do not flow."

...as well. Second, regarding the examination of the capacity to see based on its characteristics, it can be understood. Third, in the section providing the correct demonstration: "The nature of this seeing-essence has never been wrinkled.
Here, "seeing-essence" refers to the consciousness-essence; that is to say, when it is distinguished as being within the eye, it is called the seeing-essence and so forth.
The single character "nature" (xing) refers to the true nature (zhenxing). The reason for now mentioning the true nature together with the seeing-essence is truly because—
Because the true nature is without trace, it is difficult to awaken to; one merely relies for a moment on the seeing-essence of the "second moon" to clarify it.
After the passage concerning its original lack of arising and ceasing, the conclusion should be stated as follows:

"It should be known that what changes is empty and not substantial, false and not true, arising and ceasing yet not arising and ceasing. Therefore, when it undergoes cessation, that which does not change is..."
It is substantial rather than empty, real rather than false, and neither arising nor ceasing rather than subject to arising and ceasing.

Since there is no arising or ceasing, is it not the case that within the empty and the false there is inherently the substantial and the real, and within arising and ceasing there is inherently the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing?
This is why I previously asked: "Do you know that within the body there is that which neither arises nor ceases? (Section Four)
Regarding "beyond the middle": "What is meant by 'equal'? This brings out the fault of not knowing the real. "And yet they are equal" brings out the fault of not knowing the illusory.

Since it was stated above that "that which changes undergoes cessation, while that which does not change is fundamentally without arising or ceasing"—namely, that which is neither empty nor substantial, neither illusory nor real, and neither subject to arising and ceasing nor non-arising and non-ceasing—it is thus non-arising.
How can you speak of birth and death regarding this unextinguished true nature, and say, "This body of mine will ultimately perish"?
There is no other reason; it is entirely because you do not know that its true nature is neither born nor extinguished. Therefore it is said:
"How can... (and so forth). Before you encountered the Tathāgata, you asked about these words of annihilation, yet you did not understand their meaning.
It is permissible for those who act wrongly to do so. Yet, you have encountered the Tathāgata not for just a single day;
why then do you fail to understand that the non-arising and non-ceasing taught by the Tathāgata constitutes true nature?
Why do you still cite the words of annihilationism to raise doubts, asking, "Did Kātyāyana and Pūraṇa Kāśyapa both say that the cessation of this body after death is called Nirvāṇa? No.
This is because you do not understand that these are false and subject to arising and ceasing; therefore it is said, "and yet... (and so forth).

By this, one knows that if one studies the Way without following the correct path, or leaves the household life without meeting an enlightened teacher, it is unlikely that one's understanding and views will remain free from error.
Please consider King Nimi as a test case and observe him. He asked: "Will this body of mine eventually [end]?"
Regarding the phrase "from transformation and cessation," who among men would not be so? Why then did King Ajātaśatru alone know this and ask about it?
The answer is that there are two reasons why King Ajātaśatru was able to both know and ask: first, King Ajātaśatru was over sixty-two years of age and could be called old;
it was precisely because he was old that he could understand the nature of change and transformation, and thus he asked this question. By this, one may know the nature of change and transformation.
Even at sixty years of age, one cannot escape it. These two kings were lords among men and may be called noble;
yet, precisely because they were noble, they were more susceptible to being inspired to conversion, and thus they asked this question.

By this, we know that although one’s status may reach the pinnacle of nobility, even a king cannot escape transformation and change. Whether noble or old, they recognized transience and extinction, and so they raised their inquiry.
As for those who have practiced the path— those who were once young and lowly but later became strong and mature—

if they do not turn their backs on the bitter sea of birth and death to borrow a precious raft from the Great Awakened One, how lamentable! Thus, it can be seen that King Bimbisāra was also a manifestation of great power who assisted in propagating the Buddha’s transformation and supported the transmission of the Dharma Vehicle.
Regarding the second section on realization, the passage beginning with "The King heard these words" refers to what was asked by King Prasenajit:

the nirvāṇa of cessation and the nirvāṇa of non-arising and non-extinction. What Ānanda doubted was whether [the state] is truly real as non-arising and non-extinction, or falsely illusory as arising and extinction.
The Tathāgata’s response follows: from the perspective of the physical body, there is arising and extinction.

If discussed in terms of its fundamental nature (*dharmatā*), it is neither arising nor ceasing. Since the answer regarding non-arising and non-ceasing was given by way of its nature, one may further infer that although the body undergoes arising and ceasing, no such arising or ceasing can ultimately be found. This is the case within the portion concerning Ānanda.
If one knows that reality is itself non-arising and non-ceasing, then even the arising and ceasing of the illusory is, in its entirety, the reality of non-arising and non-ceasing.

In this way, it not only answers King Aṅgulimāla’s question regarding cessation and non-cessation, but also resolves Ānanda’s doubt concerning arising and ceasing versus non-arising and non-ceasing. Although it is said that the Tathāgata gave but a single answer, [it addresses both].

Thus they replied together. Although it was said that Ānanda and King Bimbisāra heard it at the same time, this is because what had never been seen before has now been seen, and what had never been heard before has now been heard;
therefore, the king and the great assembly leaped for joy in their bodies and rejoiced in their hearts.
Ānanda immediately rose from his seat and departed. This is the second section, the passage concerning Śakra’s inverted actions and Ānanda’s doubt. It is divided into two parts:

first, the arising of doubt following the [Buddha’s] footsteps (the section beginning with "Ānanda"); second, the lowering of the arm to provide instruction (the section beginning with "At that moment"). The first part is further divided into two: first, the description of the ritual protocol by the scribe (the section beginning with "Ānanda");
second, the presentation of words by the World-Honored One according to the occasion (the section beginning with "The World-Honored One"). The first of these may be summarized as follows:

"Understood. Regarding the phrase "if among these two there is such seeing, hearing, and so forth," this refers back to the preceding passage where the Tathāgata demonstrated to King Prasenajit that the essence of seeing (*jijing*) is neither born nor extinguished, thereby giving rise to doubt.

Regarding the phrase "we and our like," this refers back to the end of the previous fascicle where the assembly was rebuked for having lost the true nature (*zhensheng xing*), thereby giving rise to doubt.
The intended meaning is that the Tathāgata has shattered my deluded mind and revealed my [true nature].
True seeing is also seeing and hearing. To show King Aśoka the essence of seeing is also seeing and hearing.
Why, then, would it be that for King Aśoka it is subject to arising and ceasing, while for us it is not subject to arising and ceasing?
If for us it were to lose its true nature and result in deluded activity, why would it not be so for King Aśoka? If King Aśoka’s [seeing] were subject to arising and ceasing...
This is precisely non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is it that we are not so? There is no difference in our station, yet there is a distinction in what is shown to us;

it is as if [the Dharma] were intimate to King Bimbisāra and distant to us. However, intimacy and distance are entirely matters of emotional perception; how could the Dharma King have such partiality?
Therefore, we harbor delusion that has not yet been dispelled, remaining like those still covered in dust and grime. We only pray that you will arouse great compassion.
Compassion washes away my defilements. Part Two:
The Section on Extending the Arm to Reveal [the Truth] has two parts. First, immediately removing [the afflictions] by citing an event to clarify perversion.

Second, knowing how to remove them by distinguishing delusion and awakening through the Dharma. The first part also has two sections. First, the actual explanation, beginning with "Immediately... and so forth. Second, the summary and reprimand. The Buddha immediately...
This is the latter part. The first section also has two parts: first, [the passage] beginning with "At that very moment" etc., which takes the correct as inverted;
second, [the passage] beginning with "The Buddha said" etc., which takes the inverted as correct. Regarding the general meaning of these two passages:

when the Tathāgata displays his golden arm and so forth, it is precisely to manifest that true nature is free from conceptual discrimination. Since a golden arm possesses no [intrinsic] inversion or correctness, why speak of inversion and correctness?
It is merely a matter of reversing the beginning and the end. Take true nature as an example: what true and false could there be?
To speak of "true and false" is simply to describe the turning over of delusion and awakening. This is because sentient beings, conversely, take the true to be inverted and the false to be correct;

consequently, they cause them to revolve within the sea of birth and death, never having a day of reaching the shore. The Tathāgata, wishing to shatter this inversion, therefore provisionally uses gold.
The physical arm was examined and determined beforehand. Regarding the beginning: *mudrā* is translated here as "Seal-Hand.

When the Tathāgata’s hand desires to accomplish merit and virtue, there is nothing that his turning hand does not achieve; when he desires to destroy Māra and externalists, there is nothing that his fingers do not shatter.
Therefore, it is called the "Seal-Hand. As for Ānanda’s words, etc.: because the Tathāgata lowered his hand and pointed downward, Ānanda [spoke].
The mind is likewise inverted; yet I have not yet dared to speak thus directly. Instead, I rely on the statement that "the sentient beings of the world" are inverted.
However, Ānanda, I do not know who among them is correct and who is inverted; therefore, I say, "the sentient beings of the world," and so forth.
This, too, is merely a point where Ānanda’s own [hidden] mind is revealed. Next, as for the passage beginning with "Ānanda and others," although—
What the people of the world consider correct is actually merely what Ānanda himself maintains as correct.

If one follows the correct principle, then—as previously indicated by pointing downward—it should be considered correct; subsequently pointing upward would then be inverted. This is according to what Ānanda has answered.
This is to take the upright as inverted and the inverted as upright. That pointing downward with the hand is considered upright while pointing upward is considered inverted is due to nothing else:
human beings are born between heaven and earth; above they emulate heaven, and below they resemble earth.
As the vital energy (*qi*) of heaven and earth naturally descends, so too the human arm should follow this order, taking the downward direction as natural and the upward direction as contrary.
These are merely words spoken by those who move and shift their positions. As for the Great Images of Heaven and Earth, they are naturally fixed and immutable;
likewise, the human body is also fixed and undergoes no transition or alteration.
This is why pointing downward with the arm is correct, while pointing upward is inverted. Within the second section on reprimand, such cases refer to taking what is correct to be inverted.
This inversion takes what is inverted as correct; such an inversion is merely a matter of exchanging the head and tail of the arm.
Regarding "head and tail": the shoulder of the arm is the tail, and the hand of the arm is the head.
Thus, one knows that taking the downward orientation as inverted is the head being exchanged for the tail, while taking the upward orientation as correct is the tail being exchanged for the head.
This is the primary point; hence it is said, "If it is like this... (and so forth). Regarding the phrase "those worldly people who view things with a twofold [bias]," there are two interpretations.
One interpretation is that "twofold" (*bei*) refers to a category (*lei*). This means that worldly people take what is inverted for what is correct and take what is correct for what is inverted;

those who view things in such a manner all belong to the same category. The second interpretation is that "twofold" refers to the sense of "doubling" (*beishi*), as in the expression "twofold or tenfold. Since they take what is correct...
This constitutes one instance of inversion; to further take that which is inverted as correct is another instance of inversion. Hence it is said: "The first is a doubling of perspective.

Second, distinguishing delusion and awakening by means of the Dharma has four parts: first, "Then you shall know" and below provide the analogy; second, "According to your... and below constitute the detailed examination.
Third, "at that time" refers to being deluded and distressed below; fourth, "the Buddha's arising" refers to the revelation and instruction below.

Regarding the first [of these], the phrase "then one knows," etc., means that if one clarifies the Dharma by way of analogy, the Tathāgata takes what is correct as correct and what is inverted as inverted;
thus it can be known that the body of the Tathāgata is inherently pure. If you, Ānanda, take what is correct as inverted and what is inverted as correct...

Thus, you can know that your own bodies are not inherently pure; their nature is fundamentally different from this [purity]. If one were to compare your body with the body of the Tathāgata to clarify the distinction:

since the Tathāgata regards what is correct as correct and what is inverted as inverted, his body may indeed be called "Right Universal Knowledge" (Samyaksaṃbuddha). However, if you regard what is correct as inverted and what is inverted as correct, then...
Their bodies may then be designated as having "inverted natures. "Inverted nature" is a reversal of the characters; it should rather be called "inverted nature.
Their names differ in this manner. Thus, it is not only that their bodies differ, but even the names for their bodies differ.
There is no other reason than that the Tathāgata has awakened to this true nature, whereas Ānanda and others are deluded regarding this truth.
This is because of their intrinsic nature (*dharmatā*). The reason for instructing you to "contemplate them according to [your own experience]" is for the purpose of thorough investigation.

Regarding the two cases, the phrase "according to you" carries the sense of following one's own inclination. Some say this refers to the inversion of your own body versus the inversion of the Buddha’s body (and so forth).
This, however, is not the case. Since the preceding text states that the Buddha’s body is called "Perfectly All-Knowing" (*samyaksambuddha*), how could it be otherwise?
It is said that the Buddha’s body is inverted; although the phrasing is obscure and brief, the meaning is self-evident. The intent is this:

even if you examine it with the utmost sincerity, your own body is designated as being "inverted by nature," whereas the Buddha’s body is named "Perfectly All-Knowing. Thus, it goes without saying that the Buddha’s body is called "Perfectly All-Knowing.
However, since your body is already designated as being "inverted by nature," it follows that whatever designation exists in the world must have a corresponding reality.
"Now, where does your name reside? Therefore it is said, 'according to you' (and so forth). To investigate the reason for this:
it all stems from not knowing the Real and thus abandoning the Real, and not knowing the False and thus clinging to the False; these are merely names. Among the three [categories],...
One does not know where the inversion of body and mind resides. This very ignorance of leaving the True behind while identifying with the false is the locus of the name "inversion of nature.
The fourth section, "The Exposition," is divided into two parts: first, the narration by the scribe, beginning with "The Buddha arose," etc.;

second, the words of the Tathāgata, beginning with "All you good [sons]," etc. Within the first part, the narration by the scribe, the phrase "The Buddha arose," etc., refers to what Ānanda previously presented.

In the section on "Doubt," it says: "I pray that you will arouse compassion to wash away my defilements. Therefore, it is now said that the Buddha arouses compassion and emits the sound of the ocean tide.

Just as the sound of the ocean tide in the world does not miss its appointed time and arises whenever the moment arrives, so too the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma necessarily accords with the capacities of sentient beings;
when there is a capacity, he speaks. This is like the sound of the ocean tide, which never fails its timing.

The second section, "The Tathāgata’s Teaching," is divided into two parts. First, from "All wholesome [dharmas]" onwards, it correctly clarifies the inversions. Second, from "Obscured darkness" onwards, it further explains the recognition of delusion.

The first part is further divided into three. First, citing the past, namely "all wholesome [dharmas]," etc. Second, clarifying the present, namely "your body," etc. Third, refuting the false, namely "what kind of... and so forth.
Within the first of these, regarding "I am permanent," etc.: "permanent" refers to the period prior to the Vaipulya (fangdeng) teachings.
This is not merely a statement made for the present time. Regarding "form and mind" (*rūpa-citta*) and so forth, they should be explained by means of the hundred dharmas (*śata-dharma*).

"Form" (*rūpa*) has the meaning of "obstructive matter"; this refers to the eleven form-dharmas (*rūpa-dharma*). "Mind" (*citta*) has the meaning of "discernment" (*vijñapti*); this refers to the eight mind-dharmas (*citta-dharma*).
"The various conditions" (*pratyaya*) refer to the twenty-four dissociated factors (*viprayukta-saṃskāra*). Although these do not [inherently] exist among the various dharmas...
It is so. Furthermore, because it is provisionally established based on the states (*avasthā*) of matter and mind, it is called "all conditions" (*pratyaya*).

Speaking specifically of one type among the twenty-four—namely, acquisition (*prāpti*) and non-acquisition (*aprāpti*)—it is like the case where it rained yesterday but is sunny today: if there was acquisition yesterday but non-acquisition today, then there is acquisition today but non-acquisition yesterday.
Once this one case is thus understood, the others may be known by analogy. As for that which directs the mental factors (*caitta*), it is the sovereign mind (*cittarāja*).

They are that which are "driven" (citta-samprayukta). Just as a king has ministers or a master has companions, they are thus called the "mental concomitants" (*caitasika*), which are fifty-one in number.

As for the "objects of cognition" (*ālambana*), these are the six unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*). Because they are the objects of the noble mind (*ārya-citta*), they are called the "dharmas that serve as objects.

The former [the mental concomitants] all belong to the delusory, while the unconditioned are the true. Though there are one hundred dharmas when the true and the delusory are combined, [the essence remains as such].
All arise from what is manifested by the eternally abiding true mind; therefore, they are said to be "manifested solely by the mind.

To speak according to our own school, this is what is meant by "principle as the basis" (*lǐjù*) and "phenomena as the manifestation" (*shìzào*). In terms of principle as the basis, it is "solely the mind";

in terms of phenomena as the manifestation, it is "that which is manifested. Within the basis, there is nothing to be based upon, for the entirety of manifestation constitutes the basis; within manifestation, there is nothing to be manifested.
All is created through the faculty of discernment (*vikalpa*). This passage cites the reason why it was so in the past. Regarding the second point, "your body," and so forth:

the meaning is that just as the aforementioned superior forms, mind, and all phenomena are manifested from the sole manifestation of Mind-only, so too your six-foot body subject to birth and death, and your mind that discriminates sensory objects, are nothing other than manifestations of the eternally abiding True Mind.

Therefore, it is said: "your body, your mind," and so forth. That the three thousand natures and characteristics and the ten realms and thousand suchnesses are spontaneously and perfectly manifested within a single thought-moment is called "wondrous clarity.
The state in which they are spontaneously and perfectly manifested is the totality of emptiness and stillness; this is called "true essence.
At the very moment of spontaneous and perfect manifestation, there is the totality of emptiness and stillness; and that which is the totality of emptiness and stillness is precisely...
The Dharma-nature is perfectly manifested; thus, the equality of cessation and illumination, and the non-duality of emptiness and existence, constitute the wondrous mind (*miao-xin*).

Since the mind capable of manifestation is called both "wondrously luminous" and "true essence," and since this wondrous mind is none other than the wondrous principle of the three truths (*san-di*), how could the body and mind manifested by it exist apart from this? Regarding these three [truths], what is meant by "equality"? As stated above...
It clarifies that your body and your mind are not a single thing that is not an object manifested within the wondrously luminous mind.

Since the manifesting mind is the wondrously luminous true essence—the wondrous mind of the Three Truths—then the manifested body and mind are both identical to the fundamental wondrousness, the perfect wondrousness, and so forth.
"Fundamental wondrousness" means it does not depend on artificial contrivance, but has been possessed from the very beginning.

"Perfection" (yuan) refers to that which is vast, penetrating, and perfectly interfused, such that there is nothing it does not pervade. "Clarity" (ming) refers to the numinous clarity that penetrates through all things, illuminating everything.
"Precious Clarity" (baoming) refers to the wondrous nature that inherently possesses all myriad virtues within the *tathāgatagarbha*.

To speak of these "wondrous" qualities one by one is precisely to reveal the three aspects of the inconceivable: the perfect within the perfect, the provisional within the perfect, and the empty within the perfect.

Because they are all truths, they are all termed "wondrous. These are collectively alternative names for the eternally abiding true mind. Above, in reference to that which can manifest, it was called the "wondrously luminous true essence" and the "wondrous mind";
here, clarifying that which is manifested, it is likewise termed the "fundamentally wondrous, perfectly wondrous, and luminous mind," and so forth.

Thus you know that what is manifested has nothing manifested; it is entirely the manifestation of what is possessed by the wondrous mind. Furthermore, you know that what is possessed has nothing possessed;

it is entirely the possession of the body and mind that are manifested. Since your own body and mind are fundamentally wondrous, perfect, and luminous, why do you all lose this fundamental wondrous perfection and luminosity, instead recognizing this delusion within awakening? Therefore it is said: "How can one..."

Furthermore, regarding those who recognize delusion within enlightenment: if one can thoroughly comprehend that both body and mind are objects manifested within the wondrous mind—what is called "no phenomena outside the mind" and "no mind outside phenomena"—such that mind and phenomena are mutually identical and subject and object are non-dual.
The unique, perfectly wondrous, luminous mind—the precious, brilliant, and sublime nature—is unobtainable in delusion;
it is unobtainable in awakening; it is unobtainable as real; and it is unobtainable as false.
Since even taking the real to be real and taking awakening to be awakening is ultimately unattainable, how could one take delusion for awakening or take the false for the real? Now, it is said:
"Awakening" is merely a term used out of necessity for those deluded sentient beings; it is not that there is actually anything to be awakened to.
Yet, at the end of the first fascicle, when the Tathāgata snapped his fingers and flashed a light, Ānanda said: "The hand opens and closes, yet the seeing has no opening or closing;
the head shakes, yet the nature has no cessation. This seemed as though he had already realized the quiescent and eternal true nature. However—
This refers to awakening within delusion. Having arrived at this state, one then says:
"If these faculties of seeing and hearing are neither arising nor ceasing, why does the World-Honored One say that we have lost our true nature and act in a state of inversion?

Thus, one again suspects that the discrimination of sensory objects constitutes the quiescent, eternal, and true nature; this is yet another instance of delusion within awakening. Therefore, the Tathāgata took him...
Whether of body or mind, all phenomena are pointed out as being none other than objects appearing within the luminous mind.

It is directly rebuked, saying: "Why do you all lose sight of the wondrously luminous nature of the mind, instead taking the delusion within awakening to be the perfectly luminous nature of the mind? Therefore, it is said: "To mistake delusion for awakening."

The second part, the explanation of the recognition of delusion, is divided into three sections: first, the explanation of delusion through "the darkening and obscurity" and so forth; second, the explanation of recognition through "one delusion" and so forth;

third, the concluding reprimand through "you" and so forth. Regarding the first section: as for "the darkening and obscurity becoming space," the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*) is originally quiescent and eternal.
Due to a single moment of non-awakening, ignorance (*avidyā*) arises. Taking ignorance as a condition, it causes the original true emptiness to become...
It is instead transformed into "stubborn emptiness" (wankong). Thus, the Great Awakening, through the movement of a single thought, is transformed into ignorance (avidyā);
it is consequently termed "obscuration. With ignorance acting as the condition, true emptiness (zhenkong) is transformed into stubborn emptiness; it is consequently termed "emptiness" (ākāśa).
Therefore, it is summarized as: "Obscurity becomes emptiness. This refers to what is stated in the subsequent text: "Due to delusive ignorance, there is empty space.

Thus, insentient emptiness becomes the object of perception (*ālambana*), and ignorance becomes the perceiving subject (*ālambaka*). As subject and object become intertwined and neither abandons the other, they eventually coalesce to form the dark matter of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
Hence it is said: "Within the obscurity of emptiness, darkness coalesces to become form. This refers to the subsequent text.

This refers to how, based upon emptiness, the perception of worlds is established and clarified into a realm. Together with what precedes it, this constitutes the arising of the *adhiṣṭhānika-niśraya* (the environment as dependent retribution).
Because these dark and turbid colors of the four great elements are mixed within the midst of false perceptions and conceptions, they form my body of the four great elements.
Therefore, it is said: "The various colors and false conceptions take their own marks as the body. This is precisely what is meant by "cognition" in the passage below.

This refers to sentient beings. This is the arising of the primary retribution (*vipāka*). Because objects come forth to draw the mind toward them, it is said that "the gathering of conditions causes internal agitation.
Because the mind goes out to grasp at objects, it is said that "it rushes outward in pursuit. Furthermore, regarding "gathering conditions" and so forth:

this means the six sense-objects gather at the inner mind, ultimately resulting in every thought-moment of greedy attachment and the mind’s conceptual discrimination; thus, one cannot withstand the agitation.
It moves. Furthermore, with the inner mind directed toward external objects, it rushes when it should pursue and wanders when it should flow. As stated below:

"Beginning with the four objects of the floating roots, it flows away and rushes toward form," continuing until, "the sixth [root], with its four objects of the floating roots, flows away and rushes toward dharmas.
Because of this, form and mind mutually enter one another, gathering and converging within and without; thus, the mind passes through one cycle.
The inherently luminous has been turned into darkness; the inherently tranquil mind has been turned into agitation.
Taking this very state of darkness and agitation as the characteristic of the nature of mind, it is said: "One takes the state of dark agitation as the nature of mind.
One must understand that the originally abiding true mind, its primordial luminosity and self-nature, is the essence of Great Enlightenment and True Suchness (*tathatā*). Because...
That a single thought-stirring [of delusion] subsequently pursues the void through confusion and reaches such a state—is this not indeed delusion?
Regarding the second [section], "one is deluded regarding the equal" refers to the recognition of the false. The essence of the mind is fundamentally all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm;
yet because one recognizes this through delusion, one consequently clings to it as being within the physical body. This is the calculation [of the view] that it exists within.
This is because you do not know how to depart from falsehood. You fail to realize that beyond this physical body, even the great earth is but an object within my wondrously luminous mind.
Why, then, do you further cling to your own mind as being instead within the physical body?
For this reason, it is further elucidated through a parable; the text of the parable is clear.

Among the three [categories], those who are "twice as deluded among the deluded" are so called because they are first deluded by losing the truth through ignorance, and then deluded again by mistaking the false for the true.
This refers to the Dharma. We shall now restate the previous example to clarify this point. Previously, with...
To take the correct as inverted is one delusion; to take the inverted as correct is another delusion.

However, the previous inversion of the correct and the inverted was established in advance for the purpose of addressing the current delusion regarding the true and the false. Therefore, arriving at this point, we reiterate those points to clarify them together.
Furthermore, regarding the passage beginning with "the darkening becomes space," if it is said that ignorance arises because of a single moment of non-awakening, [it follows that]...
It appears as if sentient beings existed first. Again, it is said that the various colors and deluded perceptions, through their mutual conceptualization, constitute the body;

this appears as if the world existed first. Now, when we speak of the world and sentient beings together, though one might say there is a sequence of priority and posteriority, in reality there is no such sequence.
Why is this? The world is formed collectively through the karmic power of sentient beings, and sentient beings arise by virtue of the world.
Thus, one knows that prior to the existence of the world, these sentient beings had accumulated karmic power in other worlds;
once that karmic power was established, the world came into being. In this way, it is clear that sentient beings existed first. Worldly...
Sentient beings are born after the realms have been formed; thus, it appears that the world existed first.
Therefore, it is said that although there is a sequence of before and after, in reality there is no such sequence, because they mutually constitute one another. Question:

Since the world is formed by the collective karmic power of sentient beings, the text below states that when a single person awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space of the ten directions completely vanishes. How is this so?
Many Buddhas have already come forth, having awakened to the truth and returned to the source. Why, then, does empty space still remain as it was? The answer is:
although worlds are collectively formed by the karmic power of sentient beings, the attainment of Buddhahood by a single person can only destroy that person’s own karma;
it cannot yet destroy the karma of others who have not attained Buddhahood. For this reason, empty space remains intact. If one considers this from the perspective of...
To clarify this through analogy: the karmic power of sentient beings collectively creates the world, just as a thousand lamps gathered in a single room.

Although there are a thousand lamps, their light is but one. If one person among them attains Buddhahood and causes the void to vanish, yet the void remains intact, it is like removing a single lamp while the light does not diminish. As can be seen from this, when one person attains Buddhahood...
It merely destroys the karmic power of a single person. Even if one were to destroy empty space itself, empty space would still remain as it is.

However, for one who attains Buddhahood, once ignorance is destroyed, the Dharmakāya naturally manifests; thus, while empty space is not destroyed, it is destroyed, and being destroyed, it is not destroyed.
Therefore, the one who attains Buddhahood perceives no empty space. As for us here and now, we are entirely a mass of ignorance. Regarding that which [the Buddha] perceives...
Once it is destroyed, empty space cannot be perceived or seen. Likewise, although many Buddhas have attained enlightenment, empty space remains fully present;

there is no room for doubt. Question: The world is formed by the karmic power of sentient beings. However, as long as non-awakening (*abodhi*) has not yet arisen within the essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*), sentient beings do not yet exist. How, then, can there be the karmic power to form a world? Answer: Regarding this statement—
Thus there is a sequence. Yet, regarding actual phenomena, there is no priority or posteriority. The world of sentient beings has existed from the very beginning as a single whole;
it is only that we speak of the power of karma in terms of its results. This is because, upon the essence of True Suchness (tathatā), if ignorance does not stir, all remains as it is;
but once it stirs, one spontaneously creates karma. Karma inevitably brings about the retribution of its fruits. Therefore, it is in terms of these results that we speak of the power of karma.

Furthermore, if you wish to understand how the power of karma summons and brings about its retributive fruits, it is because one fails to realize that there is nothing capable of illuminating [reality].

Consequently, the distinction between subject and object arises, immediately forming an obstruction. That is to say: because of the subject, the object is established; once the object has been falsely established, your false subject comes into being.
Within this, there naturally arises the sentient beings who are the agents of creation and the world-system which is the object of creation, as well as the world-ages that bring these into existence.
These are sentient beings composed of the elements (*dhātu*). Thus, is it not the case that the world of sentient beings exists simultaneously?
From "Ānanda received the Buddha’s [instruction] and departed" onwards is the second section, the passage on the nature of seeing being without anything to return.

It is divided into two parts: first, "Ānanda received... and so forth, which directly reveals that there is nothing to return; second, "Ānanda said... and so forth, which further explains remaining doubts. The first part is further divided into two, the first of which is...
Ānanda’s request below; the two Buddhas’ response and instruction below. The first [section] also has two parts: first, the narrator’s account of the doubt (the passage beginning with "Ānanda");
second, the disciple’s formal address (the passage beginning with "Although I..."). Regarding the first of these, "Ānanda received the Buddha... and so forth:

previously, because the Tathāgata had extended his hand for him to manifest the distinction between the inverted and the upright, it was called "compassionate rescue"; furthermore, as for the pointing...
Since both body and mind are objects within the wondrous mind, it is called a "profound instruction.

Because one regrets that the true mind was lost since beginningless time and has only now come to know it, one sheds tears. One joins the palms before the Tathāgata because there is still something to inquire about;

this constitutes the second part, where the practitioner presents their words. Furthermore, there are three [sections]: first, from "Although I... downwards, which indicates what has already been realized; second, from "But I... downwards...
[The author] has not yet attained realization. Regarding the three vows for the Buddha to descend and grant instruction:
first, as for the phrase "such a wondrous sound," this refers to how both the provisional and the real are none other than what manifests within the wondrously luminous mind.

The intent of the passage "realizing the wondrously luminous mind" and so forth is that, having heard such a wondrous sound, [the author] realized that the nature of the wondrously luminous mind is fundamentally vast, penetrating, perfectly interfused, and neither arising nor ceasing.
Cessation is without going and without coming; it is the eternally abiding true mind, the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*). The commentary states:
"Those who have already awakened" refers to those who have awakened to the wondrously luminous mind as their awakening.

In the subsequent section, the phrase "we and others" implies that since we have heard the wondrous sound and awakened to the wondrously luminous mind, we ought to listen to the Dharma with that wondrous mind, yet at present we still employ the conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*).
I gaze upon and look up to [the Master] with reverence; yet it is as they say: "To merely obtain [it] without being able to employ it. Therefore, he says, "And so I... (etc.).
However, this is not that I do not wish to recognize it as the wondrous mind; rather, it is simply that I truly have not yet dared to do so. Hence, he says, "I have not yet dared... (etc.).
The commentary states that "one who has not yet awakened" refers to one who listens to the Dharma with a conditioned mind (*pratyaya-citta*). The three requests may be understood accordingly.

The second part, the response, also has two sections. First, the Buddha states that the mind which takes objects has a point of return; second, Ānanda and others demonstrate that the nature of seeing has no point of return. The first section also has two parts:
first, from "It is like a person" onwards, it clarifies the dharmas that serve as objects; second, from "If... onwards, it clarifies the mind that serves as the subject.

Each [section] consists of three parts: the principle (*dharma*), the illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*), and the application (*upanaya*). Regarding the first [section]: "The Buddha said" constitutes the principle;

"It is like a person" constitutes the illustration; and "You too" constitutes one sentence of the application. There are those who take the passage beginning with "If, within the mind that acts as the perceiver...
and apply it to the principle of the object (*ālambana-dharma*)—this is incorrect. Within the initial principle, the phrase "You too" and so forth refers back to Ānanda.
What is presented here is by means of the mind that takes [the teaching] as its object. This "mind that takes as its object" is precisely the mind that discriminates sensory objects;
it is subject to arising and ceasing, not free from arising and ceasing. "Dharma" refers to the realized, eternally abiding principle of nature;

it is free from arising and ceasing, not subject to arising and ceasing. It also refers to the linguistic expressions that convey it. If you listen to the Dharma with a discriminating mind, [you will fail to grasp it].
Thus, both the expressive language and the essence of the principle expressed thereby also belong to the objective conditions for the listener.

This is because one perceives arising and ceasing through the lens of arising and ceasing. However, since the expressive language itself is fundamentally subject to arising and ceasing, the nature-body of the dharma—which is neither born nor extinguished—is inherently not something you can attain. Therefore, it is said: "You all... (and so forth). View it in this way.
This aligns with the analogies. Among the two sets of analogies: the person represents the Tathāgata’s capacity to teach; the finger represents the verbal teachings;
