the moon represents the dharmatā—the reality characterized by non-arising and non-ceasing—which is what is expressed; and the people represent Ānanda and others who heard it together.
The brightness of the bright moon is an analogy for the essential nature of the dharmatā that is expressed, because it is neither born nor extinguished.
Therefore, "darkness" refers to the darkness [of ignorance]. This is a metaphor for the linguistic teachings that serve as the means of expression (*vyañjana*).

Because these are subject to arising and ceasing, the intended meaning is that the listener of the Dharma should, through the finger of the expressive language, apprehend the moon of the expressed reality (*artha*).
If one mistakes the finger of the expressive language for the moon of the expressed reality, not only will one fail...
Having realized the moon of the principle that is signified, one must also let go of the finger of the language that signifies it.

It is not merely that one does not know the moon signified nor the finger signifying; furthermore, one fails to recognize that the moon signified is the luminosity of non-arising and non-ceasing, while the finger signifying is the darkness of arising and ceasing.
There is no other reason for this than that it all stems from the discrimination of objects through conditions.

Thinking that one can hear [the sound], one lacks clear understanding of how the signifier (*vācaka*) and the signified (*vācya*) are subject to arising and ceasing, while [the nature of reality] is neither arising nor ceasing.
Therefore it is said: "It is like a person... (and so forth). This is an explanation based on the literal text.

If we consider the underlying meaning, it is not only that one fails to understand that the arising and ceasing of darkness constitutes arising and ceasing, while the non-arising and non-ceasing of light constitutes non-arising and non-ceasing; one also fails to understand the signifier itself.
One takes the finger for the moon it points to and the moon for the finger itself.
Not only is one lost to the finger’s capacity as a signifier of the moon, but one is also lost to the reason why one listens to the Tathāgata and the reason why the Tathāgata speaks.
Not only is one lost to listening and speaking, but one is also lost to the reason why one is oneself and the reason why the Tathāgata is the Tathāgata.
"Tathāgata. It is explained in this manner; both the phrasing and the meaning are perfectly clear. The threefold correspondence can be seen:

first, "As for the following" explains the principle (*dharma*); second, "The analogy follows below" provides the illustration (*upamāna*); third, "This also... provides the application (*upanaya*). First, the principle is evident.
Within the subsequent analogy, the "guest" represents the mind that conditions (*ālambana-citta*), and "staying overnight at a roadside inn" represents the conditioning.
The mind listens to the Dharma. The two preceding lines briefly illustrate the mind that conditions itself to listen to the Dharma: once the sound heard ceases, the listening mind likewise vanishes.
This is what is meant by having discrimination when encountering sensory objects and being without discrimination when separated from them.

However, the "palms" and "pavilion" serve as metaphors for the true nature (*tathatā*), which differs from the discriminating mind conditioned by sensory objects; it neither undergoes transmigration nor departs.

It comes. Its meaning is twofold: first, it may be used as a metaphor for the quiescent and eternal true nature; second, it may be used as a metaphor for the primordial luminosity of the seeing-essence.

Taken together, there are again two parts. The first directly reveals the true mind; this is also the section beginning with "This too... and so forth, which can be understood. The second turns to reprimand the deluded mind;

this is the section beginning with "How could... and so forth. This, in turn, has three parts: first, the direct reprimand, beginning with "How could it be..."; second, the analogical reprimand, beginning with "In this way..."; and third...
Rebuttal. Regarding the passage beginning with "Free from all [objects]," etc.: What does "free" mean?

It means that when your mind, which takes objects as its condition, listens to the Dharma, it is entirely devoid of any capacity for discrimination regarding those conditioned sounds. How can you recognize this as the true mind?
Therefore it is said: "How so? (and so forth). It is not only that there is no mind capable of discrimination in the absence of sound;

if one were separated from form, separated from fragrance, and even separated from mental phenomena (*dharma*), there would likewise be nothing capable of discriminating. Therefore it is said: "This then... (and so forth). This constitutes the formal censure.
These two phrases may be treated as a conclusion belonging to the formal censure, or they may be treated as an introduction serving as an example for the censure. Thus, the formal...
The "Text on Resolving Doubts" concludes here. Regarding the second point, "such as these," there are two intended meanings.

First, it means that since he has already detached from the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), the discriminating mind that takes them as conditions cannot be apprehended; hence it says, "thus... and so forth.

Since the sense faculties do not take the objects as conditions, nor do they encounter them, it says, "not form" (*arūpa*). Although it is said that the faculties and objects do not connect, this merely results in the internal mind.
It is a profound stillness; therefore, it is not empty. As for "internally maintaining the juncture of profound stillness" such that external paths cannot know it:
one simply observes that prior to eighty thousand kalpas, its arising is not seen, and after eighty thousand kalpas, its cessation is not seen.
Within this interval, it is dark and indistinguishable; this is called the "Dark Truth" (*tattva*). Thus it is said, "Kusha... and so forth. Second, "that which is thus":
This refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). As for the phrase "even to the point where discrimination is entirely absent," this means that the six consciousnesses do not function.

"Neither form nor emptiness" refers to the seventh consciousness (*manas-vijñāna*). It is called "not form" because it does not, like the six consciousnesses, take the six sense objects as its conditions.
However, because it conceives of the eighth consciousness moment by moment as an internal self, it is said to be "not empty. "Kuśa and so forth" refers to the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).

Furthermore, because the eighth ālayavijñāna exists as a synthesis of the perishable and the imperishable, it contains within it a portion that is white, which is the so-called "True" (tathatā), namely the imperishable; and a portion that is black, which is the so-called "False" (mṛṣā), namely the perishable.
The non-Buddhists do not understand the reason for this; they merely observe the two characteristics of black and white, perceiving them as entirely devoid of movement or stillness. From themselves—
This means being obscured regarding the true reality; thus it is said, "Kusha" (and so forth). Consequently, although there is but one phrase, there are two meanings.

When your conditioned mind listens to the Dharma, even if it is separated from external objects, although the six consciousnesses may initially cease to function, in the end it remains identical to what is grasped by the non-Buddhists.
Can you take such a mind to be real? Such is the reprimand by analogy. Among these three, [the first] is "separation."
Regarding the phrase "the conditions and so forth of all dharmas": this refers to the discussion based on the preceding six, seven, and eight consciousnesses.

Apart from the six sense objects, there is no discriminative nature of the six consciousnesses; apart from the self within the eight consciousnesses, there is no discriminative nature of the seventh consciousness;
and apart from the root-body, the vessel-world, and the seeds, there is no discriminative nature of the eighth consciousness. Therefore, it is said: "apart from."
"Regarding 'As for you all' (and so forth): that which you take to be the true nature is merely the conditioned mind; it is not the true nature.
Since it is devoid of the non-discriminative nature apart from all phenomena, you should know that the natures of your minds each have their own place of return.
Therefore it is said: 'As for you all' (and so forth). As for 'What is the master?', this is the formal conclusion of the reprimand. Since it is the conditioned mind..."
Each has its own place of return, like a traveler who stops briefly before departing.
How can one regard these as the masters of true nature, when the master of true nature is, in turn, lost? Therefore it is said: "How can there be a master?"
Second, from Ānanda’s words, it follows that the nature of seeing has no point of return. This is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downward, the repeated request;

second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the further explanation. Regarding the first part: "If we... refers to the preceding passage of refutation beginning with "separated from all dharmas and conditions.
When the Tathāgata speaks of the wondrously luminous primordial mind, this is precisely the essence of seeing. However, Ānanda...
He has not yet realized that the essence of clarity and the nature of seeing are distinct; therefore, in the following passage, the Tathāgata selects and clarifies them for him.

This section further consists of four parts: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he selects and clarifies; second, from "You should" onwards, he admonishes and grants permission; third, this great...

The following provides the actual demonstration. The four [sections] below constitute the conclusion and the reprimand. Regarding the first [of these], the phrase "Now, you all" refers to Ānanda’s prior request, which asked:
"The Tathāgata speaks of the wondrous, luminous, primordial mind; why does it have no place to return? Therefore, the Tathāgata restates this for him, saying: "Now, you all... (and so forth).
"The essence of seeing, the luminous source" is precisely what was previously called "the consciousness-essence, the original luminosity. This belongs to...
The eighth ālaya-vijñāna exists as a synthesis of the arising-and-ceasing and the non-arising-and-non-ceasing aspects of the ālaya-vijñāna.

With respect to its arising-and-ceasing aspect, it is the "seeing-essence" (jiejing); with respect to its non-arising-and-non-ceasing aspect, it is the "original luminosity" (yuanyang). This "seeing," and so forth...
This precisely distinguishes that the seeing-essence (*darśana-bindu*) is not the wondrously luminous true seeing-essence; yet, it is nonetheless not separate from the truth.
To clarify this by means of an analogy, it is like a second moon. Although the second moon is not the true moon, it is produced by the pressing of the eyes and is thus closely proximate to the truth;
furthermore, it is not a reflection of the moon. Likewise, although the present seeing-essence is not the true substance, it arises entirely from the true nature (*dharmatā*).
Furthermore, this existence is also close to the truth; moreover, it is not a conceptualization based on sensory objects. Thus, it is like a second moon.

A "moon-reflection" refers to the moon in water, used as a metaphor for the mind that conceptually discriminates based on sensory objects. This moon-reflection exists when there is water and does not exist when there is no water;
likewise, that conceptualizing mind exists when it encounters sensory objects and does not exist when separated from them. Therefore, it is compared to this.
Regarding the moon’s reflection: the true nature should be likened to the real moon. Thus, this wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind—the true nature—is like the real moon;
the seeing-essence—the eighth consciousness—is like the second moon; and the discrimination of objects—the first six consciousnesses—is like the moon’s reflection.
Both the phenomena and their metaphors can be clearly seen. Yet, by employing this seeing...
To clarify and manifest the true nature is nothing other than this: it stems entirely from Ānanda’s previous request to bring forth the wondrously luminous mind and open my Dharma-eye.

Yet, as this wondrous mind leaves no trace, its awakening is truly difficult to achieve. Therefore, [the Buddha] skillfully relies upon the visual essence (*darśana-śuddhi*) to push toward its manifestation through successive layers.
When one reaches the point of "seeing the seeing," even the visual essence is shattered. This is specifically to distinguish what is not the true nature.
The true moon and the moon-reflection distinguished by the conditions of the sensory objects are revealed to be merely the second moon of the essence of vision (*darśana-śuddhi*).
This can be understood through two admonitions and one permission. Third, the actual demonstration has two parts: first, the objects have a point of return;

this refers to "this great [element]" and so forth. Second, the vision has no point of return; this refers to "your vision" and so forth. The first part also has two sections: first, these great elements definitely depart from their objects; second, you all depart.

Regarding the return to clarity: first, concerning the section on "discrimination," as for the phrase "furthermore, that which sees conditions," the preceding four and the subsequent three are all objects of cognition (*ālambana*), whereas only this [consciousness] is the subject of cognition (*ālambaka*). This is because it exists when there are sense-objects and does not exist when separated from them;
thus, it is also listed among them. Second, regarding the return to clarity, there are three parts: first, from "You all... onwards, the introduction is established; second, from "How... onwards...
Explanation: Thirdly, the various subsequent sections provide a detailed expansion. Regarding the first [of these], as for the "various manifestations" (*nirmāṇa-lakṣaṇa*):

taking what is non-existent to be existent is the meaning of "transformation" (*pariṇāma*), while taking what is existent to be non-existent is the meaning of "manifestation" (*nirmāṇa*). This refers specifically to the eight types mentioned above.

For example, a lecture hall originally lacks the characteristic of luminosity; yet, due to the sun’s orb, it suddenly comes to possess it—this is what is called "transforming non-existence into existence.
Once luminosity exists, it may again suddenly vanish during the middle of the night—this is what is called "transforming existence into non-existence.
The other two cases can be understood by analogy. Regarding the second point, "the seeing has no place to return," this is divided into three parts. First: "As for your seeing... [and so forth].

The heading [is given]. Second, from "What is it that... below is the explanation. Third, from "All those things that can... below is the conclusion. The meaning of the text for the heading and the explanation is clear.
Only regarding the conclusion, the phrase "all those things that can be returned" and so forth should be compared with the passage in Ānanda’s request above:

"I have realized the Buddha's [teaching], yet I have not yet dared to recognize it as my own fundamental ground of mind. The intention is to say: "What you claim to have realized is the wondrous mind."
What you are employing is the conditioned mind. It is not that you do not wish to recognize the wondrous mind; it is simply that you have not yet dared to recognize it (and so forth).
Your doubt should be addressed in this way: let us examine each point together with me, the Tathāgata. All those things that can be returned belong to what is seen; they are not your seeing-nature.
That which now cannot be returned must, by its very nature, be your seeing-nature. Why then do you say you have not [yet recognized it]?
"How dare you presume that your mind is wondrous? For this reason, he immediately rebukes him, saying: "Thus you know that your mind is fundamentally wondrous, bright, and pure," and so forth.
It is only in this way that the preceding inquiry and request find their conclusion, and this response finds its definitive point.

Within the fourth section, the "Summary of the Rebuke," the phrase "Thus you know" and so on refers to the fact that after each successive point had been examined and refuted as previously detailed, nothing remained that could be returned [to the opponent].

"Your true nature. That which does not return is your true nature. If this true nature is your mind-nature, you should know that from time immemorial your mind has never been anything other than wondrous, luminous, and pure.
Thus it is said: "Then you shall know... (and so forth). This refers to the literal phrasing of the text. However, if one reads it according to its underlying meaning:
One should say: "Your mind is fundamentally wondrous; your mind is fundamentally luminous; your mind is fundamentally pure.
Because you have realized that all phenomena are, in their very substance, quiescent—not obtained from without but inherently complete—you say: "Your mind is fundamentally pure."
Furthermore, one can contemplate and illumine that all dharmas are spontaneously and perfectly manifest by their very nature (*dharmatā*), not obtained from without, but rather intrinsically endowed.

Therefore it is said: "Your mind is fundamentally luminous. Moreover, although it is said that all dharmas are quiescent in their own essence, this state of quiescence is precisely where they are spontaneously and perfectly manifest.
Although it is said that all dharmas are spontaneously and perfectly manifest, this state of perfect manifestation is precisely where they are [quiescent].

The essence is quiescent; it is neither emptiness nor existence, for both emptiness and existence have vanished together. It is neither negation nor illumination, for negation and illumination are equal.
There is nothing that is not the Middle Way, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Furthermore, this is not something acquired from without, but is rather inherently possessed by nature.

Therefore, it is said: "Your mind is fundamentally wondrous. Thus, three are one and one is three; the triad and the unity are without obstruction, and the one and the three are perfectly interfused. Hence, they are collectively termed [the One Mind].

It was said that [the mind] is fundamentally wondrous, luminous, and pure. Later, however, he rebuked him, saying: "The wondrous, luminous, and pure mind is not something that exists from the beginning.
It may be that your lack of awakening is excusable; it may be that what is entirely delusive is itself the truth.
Since it is fundamentally complete, and the entirely delusive is itself the truth, why do you yourself remain deluded and unawakened? Why are you muddled and ignorant, having lost [it]?"

That the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind, which is primordially present, undergoes transmigration within the ocean of birth and death and is thus drifted and drowned by it—this is truly what is to be pitied. Therefore, it is said: "Then one knows... (and so forth).
The second part, "Dispelling Remaining Doubts," is divided into two sections. First, Ānanda expresses doubt regarding the seeing of objects after the person has departed.

Second, Ānanda addresses the Buddha regarding the doubt concerning the expansion and contraction of the great and small. The first section is further divided into two: first, Ānanda’s request for clarification based on his doubt;

second, the Buddha’s response and explanation. Within the first of these, the two lines beginning with "Although I... cite the previous statement: "That which you do not return to is not you; then who is it?"

This passage serves merely as a point of doubt. Regarding this single doubtful passage, it is said that what Ānanda identified as the nature of seeing that does not revert is merely the "seeing-essence" (jiàn-jīng).
However, because his true nature had not yet been realized, he asked this question. If this were so, it would be entirely inconsistent with the Buddha’s answer.
If one infers the intent of the question from the answer, [it is clear that] at the beginning, [the nature] was listed...
The five eyes differ distinctly in their scope of vision. One’s own vision does not become confused with another’s. Based on this, one should understand that which was questioned:

"If the nature of my seeing is said to be non-returning and thus pervasive of all people's natures of seeing, then the natures of seeing of all other people are likewise non-returning and pervasive of all.
Thus, each person's vision would mutually pervade the others'—this would be more than enough [to cause confusion]."
Chaos. How is it known that this is my faculty of vision and not the faculty of vision belonging to another person?
Therefore, it is said: "How so? (and so forth). Next, Ānanda is led through the realms from the Four Heavenly Kings down to the human world, and is thus made to discern what he sees:
"Which is my substance? Which is the objective phenomenon? It is further stated: "This is the object; it is not you. Furthermore...
It is said that clouds are objects and not you; it is further said that all things are objects and not you.
Since the nature of seeing is fundamentally distinct from material phenomena, the nature of seeing and material phenomena do not intermingle. Based on this, one should understand the doubt:
if the nature of seeing pervades all things and all things are thoroughly contained within my seeing, then how can the images of objects and my seeing-nature [be distinguished]?
They are mutually pervasive and cannot be distinguished from one another. How can it be known that this is my own nature of seeing and not the appearance of external objects?
Therefore, it is said: "How so? (and so forth). Only by viewing the matter in this way can it be said that the question lies within the answer and the answer lies within the question;
thus, it is known that a single doubt contains two meanings.

The second part, the "Explanatory Response," is divided into two sections. First, the actual explanation, beginning with "The Buddha said... Second, the summary and reprimand, beginning with "If you... The first section is further divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the person, beginning with "The Buddha said..."; second, the explanation of the objects of perception, beginning with "Now, as for us...

Within the first of these, the five eyes are listed in full because their respective degrees of excellence differ, thereby demonstrating that the person’s vision and one's own vision do not become confused.
Among the five eyes, Ānanda possesses the wisdom eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*); Nanda possesses the divine eye (*divya-cakṣus*); all bodhisattvas possess the dharma eye (*dharma-cakṣus*);

the Tathāgata possesses the buddha eye (*buddha-cakṣus*); and sentient beings possess the fleshly eye (*māṃsa-cakṣus*). For instance, although Ānanda perceives up to the first dhyāna, he still requires the power of the Buddha;
this is because he remains at the stage of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*) and possesses only a partial realization of the wisdom eye. Yet, even this partially realized wisdom eye—
Since the first dhyāna has not yet been attained, one must still rely on the Buddha’s power.
Thus, although the five eyes differ in their levels of excellence, Ānanda’s confusion regarding the nature of his own vision can be resolved at once.

The second section, "Dispelling Doubts Regarding the Perception of Objects," is divided into two parts. First, from "Now, let me... onwards, there is the exhortation to perform discrimination. Second, from "Let me...

onwards, there is the actual performance of that discrimination. Within the first part: regarding the phrase "Now, let me [discriminate] with you," the preceding section already resolved the doubt concerning the confusion between the view of a person and the view of a self;
now, this section shall resolve the doubt concerning the confusion between the nature of seeing and external objects and phenomena. Therefore, he proceeds by observing them together.
This is an exhortation to analyze [the matter].

It can be seen that the second section, which provides a further explanation of the analysis, is divided into two parts: first, "Now we [all]" as a general statement; second, "Especially you" as a specific address.
Within the initial general statement, the phrase "Now we" refers to how the Tathāgata previously came from the Four Heavenly Kings together with Ānanda to observe the scene from above.
He exhorted him to distinguish between what is his own nature of seeing and what are the external objects. Ānanda was ultimately unable to make this distinction.

Now, the Tathāgata leads Ānanda to select from among these perceived objects which is the essence of his own nature of seeing, Ānanda, and which are the images of the perceived objects. Therefore it is said: "Now I... and so forth.
The second section has four further parts. First, from "Exhausting your vision" (*jì rǔ jiàn yuán*) downward, it explains that the object is not the seeing.

Second, from "As for these various... downward, it explains that the seeing is not the object. Third, from "If the seeing... downward, it explains that the seeing itself is the object. Fourth, from "Furthermore, then...
downward, it explains that the object itself is the seeing. Regarding the first part: "Exhausting your vision's source" means, in other words, exhausting the power of the eye. The sun...

The moon palace and so forth represent what is seen above; the seven golden mountains and so forth represent what is seen in the middle; and the gradual [stages] and so forth represent what is seen below.

The meaning is that from the four heavens above down to the human realm, and including all that is seen in between—though there is the sun that illuminates the day and the moon that illuminates the night, as well as rising clouds, flying birds, and the wind—[all these are perceived].
The swaying of things, the rising and falling of dust, the bending and withering of trees, the flowing and standing of mountains and rivers—these are but fine hairs and blades of grass.
The spiritual movements are those of humans and animals. Thus you have experienced all that surrounds you.
As for what you see above you, the palaces of the sun and moon, these are material phenomena; they are not your seeing-nature. As for what you see within you...
The seven golden mountains are also material phenomena and not your seeing-nature.
Furthermore, as for what you see below—though there be clouds, birds, wind, dust, and even humans, animals, and so forth—all these are likewise material phenomena and not your seeing-nature.
Thus, by inferring according to objects, all are objective phenomena and not your seeing-nature.
Why then do you doubt that the seeing-nature and objective phenomena are confused? Of these two [points], Ānanda, "these various... and so forth, restates what was previously seen.
Whether superior, middling, or inferior—from the sun and moon down to humans and animals—there are two meanings regarding that which is beheld with purity.
First, it refers to Ānanda’s capacity to see; this is the wisdom-eye (*prajñā-cakṣus*). Because the wisdom-eye clearly perceives emptiness, it is said to "behold with purity.
Second, it refers to what is seen by those [beings]: although there are mountains, rivers, the great earth, light, darkness, and obstructions...
The distinctions between space and so forth are all manifested within the wondrously luminous mind; therefore, they too are pure.

Since it is stated therein that these are "identical to your seeing-essence" and that "the nature of seeing has no difference," and further concludes by saying, "truly, this is your seeing-nature," one knows that while the objects seen naturally possess distinctions, your seeing-nature is everywhere pervasive. Why, then, do you doubt the seeing-nature?
Objects and forms constitute a state of confusion. Regarding the three [points], as for the phrase "if you see," etc., the meaning is this:

you suspect that the nature of seeing and objects and forms are confused with one another. Previously, I have already explained this twice for you by showing, based on the fact that objects are not the seeing, that the seeing is not the object;
thus, it is clear that the nature of seeing and objects and forms do not confuse one another. If you further investigate this, since...
If you suspect that the nature of seeing and the forms of objects are intermingled and confused, then your seeing would be the same as the objects themselves.
Therefore, it is restated: "If seeing were an object, then since your seeing is an object, my seeing would also be an object.
In that case, Ānanda, you could also see the seeing of me, the Tathāgata. Thus it is said: "Then you... (and so forth). Ānanda then—
He calculated and said: "How could I possibly see the vision of the Tathāgata? However, the very place where one views an object together with him is precisely the vision of seeing the Buddha.
He then recorded this, saying: "If one views an object together [with him], it is called seeing my, the Tathāgata’s, vision.
When I am not seeing, one should also see the place where I do not see. Why is this now..."

"Do you not see the place where I do not see? Therefore it is said, "If they were the same... (and so forth). This is the general refutation. As for the subsequent detailed analysis: "If you see my non-seeing," then my non-seeing would be like a physical object or image.
How could my non-seeing be something visible like a physical object or image? Thus, that which you perceive as "non-seeing" is naturally not [non-seeing].
"I do not see that which is seen. Therefore it is said: "If you were to see... (and so forth). Suppose one does not see;
even the ground of my non-seeing would not see the place where I see. Since the place where I see is not seen, my seeing is naturally not an object.
Thus it is said: "Naturally it is not an object. Since my seeing is not an object, your seeing is likewise not an object. Since it is not an object...
How could objects not be the nature of seeing? Since this nature of your seeing is clearly visible, why do you doubt that the nature of seeing and the objects and forms are a confused mixture?
Therefore it is said: "How could they not be yours? Regarding the phrase "Furthermore, then... and so forth:
three previous rounds of explanation have already been made; [thereby] your doubt concerning the confusion of the nature of your seeing with objects and forms should [be resolved].
This has already been refuted. If you ultimately maintain that the nature of seeing and material objects mutually see one another, then when you see an object, that object should also see you.
Therefore it is said: "Furthermore, [if this were so]... (and so forth). However, your nature of seeing possesses cognition, whereas those material objects lack cognition.
Since they are already posited as mutually seeing one another, that which possesses cognition must indeed cognize.

If that which is ignorant were also to know, then the substance of objects and the nature of seeing would become confused and disordered. Therefore, it is said that their substance and nature are intermingled.
However, the reason the world is established as it is lies in the fact that the nature of the seer and the objects seen do not become confused with one another.
If, as you suspect, the nature of seeing and the substance of objective forms were intermingled, then the world itself—
It should not be established [as such]. Therefore it is said: "Then you... (and so forth). Yet, the world still remains established as it is;
thus we know that the substance of the nature of seeing and material objects are inherently not intermingled.

Why then do you harbor doubts based on the mutual confusion of the nature of seeing and material phenomena? The preceding discussion—ranging from "matter is not seeing" to "matter is itself seeing"—is like the fourfold analysis.
This dispels [the doubt]. Thus, Ānanda’s suspicion regarding the confusion between the nature and material phenomena will be clarified at once.
Therefore, the subsequent "If you all... is a reprimand.

Regarding the second point of refutation: if your two propositions conclude that there is a hierarchy among the five eyes, this means that when you perceive something, it is naturally your own perception and not my perception;
how, then, could there be any confusion between your perception and my perception?
Therefore it is said: "If you... and so forth. The two phrases concerning the nature of seeing conclude that this nature of seeing is all-pervasive;
it means that while the objects of perception appear as distinct and unmixed phenomena, your nature of seeing is naturally and universally pervasive.
Since it is all-pervasive, if it is not your own nature of seeing, whose seeing could it be?
"Is it your nature? Therefore it is said, 'you have seen your nature' (and so forth). What does 'how can you' mean? It is a direct reprimand. The meaning is this:
such seeing of your nature must certainly belong to you; why do you doubt it yourself and refuse to acknowledge it, instead taking my words as proof of its reality?
Therefore it is said, 'How can you... (and so forth).

The second [section] explains the doubt regarding the expansion and contraction of the large and small [mandalas]. It is divided into two parts: first, Ānanda’s request based on his doubt; second, the Buddha’s response and explanation. The first part is further divided into three:

first, the description of the large and small [mandalas] starting from "Ānanda"; second, the description of the expansion and contraction starting from "World-Honored One"; third, the formal request starting from "I now.
Within the first description of the large and small, the mention of the Four Heavenly Kings and others describes the large, namely:
The further one goes, the larger it becomes; returning to the original state and so forth describes the small, meaning that the closer one is, the smaller it becomes.

Thus, the expansion and contraction of these two can be understood. Third, regarding the request for instruction: those who do not know where this principle resides are said to be "unaware" (and so forth).

This means they do not know whether to contract the large into the small to fit it between [the gaps] until it is severed, or which of the two [methods] is correct. Hence, it is said: "They do not know," and so on.

The second part, the "Explanatory Response," is divided into three sections. First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, is the formal explanation. Second, "If it were so... presents a counter-objection. Third, "All... concludes with a demonstration.
The first section [the formal explanation] is further divided into three parts: the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*dṛṣṭānta*), and their synthesis.

Within the first [the principle], the phrase "all the worlds" refers to the Four Heavenly Kings up to the eaves and porches, distinguishing between the large and small [realms]. Within the second [the analogy], if one says "it is fixed... [the following applies].
The space within it ought not to be circular. That it is now circular shows that the square shape is not fixed.
If you say it is not fixed, then there should be no square space within a square vessel; yet there is still square space within the square vessel, which means it is not fixed as being non-square.
In total, there is neither square nor circle; the squareness and roundness reside in the vessel. If this is applied to the Dharma, the square vessel...

If one were to combine the single realm of the object seen with the empty space, and combine that with the seeing-nature of the subject who sees, would the fixed direction necessarily result in a fixed "greatness" of seeing?
Or, if the direction were not fixed, would it necessarily result in a "greatness" of non-seeing? If it were fixed as great, then upon entering a single room, one should not see what is small;
yet now one sees what is small, so we know it is not fixed as great. If it is not fixed as great, then when seeing a single...

The element (*dhātu*) should not be seen as large; yet now it is seen as large, and it is fixedly [perceived] as large. From this, one knows that there is no largeness or smallness in the seeing itself; rather, largeness and smallness reside in the objects (*viṣaya*).

Thus, you proceed to apply the principle of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), as you have stated (etc.). Regarding the threefold conjunction, there are two parts: first, the actual application of the principle;
second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the exhortation to eliminate [the error]. Within the first part, the actual application, when you say "etc.," the intended meaning is that the present space...
As for their squareness or roundness, these are not fixed within the squareness or roundness [of the objects].

Since squareness and roundness reside in the vessels, you must admit that the size of the nature of seeing is likewise not fixed in its own size; rather, the size resides in the objects. Therefore it is said: "The principle of the nature is thus.
Since space itself has no size, and size resides in the vessels, this serves as a metaphor for how seeing has no size, and size resides in the objects. How could there be...?
To contract the large into the small and to pinch it until it is severed—how can one say that what is perceived still exists? Therefore, it is asked: "How can it be said to exist?

The second [section] encourages the removal of the middle. Regarding the phrase "If again," etc., it generally instructs that one should not determine the size of the perceiving faculty based on the size of what is seen.
The character "入" (ru) refers to entering that which is neither square nor round.
This refers to the meaning of awakening and entering into realization; that is to say, one wishes to awaken to and enter into the emptiness that has neither squareness nor roundness.

Regarding the second counter-objection, concerning "entering the room" and so forth: if, upon entering emptiness, one could contract the large into the small, then when looking up at the sun, one should likewise be able to pull it down from its height.
Yet in this world, how could one possibly pull the perceived nature [of the sun] down until it is level with the surface of the sun?
Therefore it is said, "If it were like this... (and so forth). As for things such as building a wall: when a wall is being built, one can insert a break;
yet when a hole is pierced, the traces should still be made to continue. Is it possible in the world today to perceive the continuity of the nature of seeing through a pierced hole?
This principle is not so; since one cannot pull back the seeing to align with the day [of its origin], how could it enter the room and contract?
To view it as small is the first incorrect point. Furthermore, one cannot continue the traces by piercing through a hole; how could one build so as to cause it to be severed in the middle?
This is the second incorrect point. Therefore, it is said that this interpretation is not correct.
Within the demonstration of the three fetters, this may also be divided into two parts. First, the demonstration of delusion, beginning with "All things," etc.

Second, the demonstration of awakening, beginning with "If one can," etc. Regarding the first part: "All things," etc., correctly demonstrates why Ānanda perceives the large as large and the small as small;
it is entirely because he has lost his own true nature of seeing and has instead been turned by external objects and sensory dust. Therefore...
One contemplates the great and the small; yet, within one’s own seeing-nature (jìngxìng), there has never been anything large or small.
Therefore it is said: "All things... and so forth. Second, regarding the section on awakening: "If one can turn back objects," etc., this refers to a real matter and is not empty talk.
Why? Because the body of the Tathāgata takes the Dharma-realm as its body. As for the Tathāgata’s...
When one possesses this mind, the mind likewise takes the dharma-realm as its substance.

Since the dharma-realm constitutes the body, which is fundamentally perfect, harmonious, vast, and transparent, there is nothing within the greatness of the dharma-realm that does not manifest. Because such is the body, it is called "perfect" (*yuan*).

Since the dharma-realm constitutes the mind, which is fundamentally numinous, luminous, and penetratingly clear, there is nothing within the greatness of the dharma-realm that is not illuminated. Such is [the nature of the mind].

Because it possesses this mind, it is called "luminous. Being endowed with such a body and mind, why labor over one's own site of practice (*bodhimaṇḍa*) before one can universally contain the vastness of the lands of the ten directions within the small space of a single hair-tip? There is no other reason;

it is entirely due to the fact that his body is the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and his mind is the Dharma-realm. Although it is said to be as small as a single hair-tip, it is nonetheless the Dharma-realm. Even if [it were] ten...
The vastness of the lands is itself the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Since the Dharma-realm manifests as the Dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm;
thus, the lands of the ten directions are all contained within the manifestation of my own body.

Furthermore, since the Dharma-realm illuminates the Dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm; thus, the lands of the ten directions are all contained within the illumination of my own mind.
Once one reaches this state, what "smallness" is there in a single hair-tip, and what "greatness" is there in the ten directions?
This is the perfect interfusion of the large and the small. What "multiplicity" is there in the ten directions, and what "oneness" is there in a single hair-tip?

This is the unimpeded nature of the one and the many. This is the inconceivable, wondrous function of the Tathāgata. But how can this be so? It is solely because one is able to master objects. To master objects means nothing other than...

It is simply a matter of awakening to the nature of one's own vision. Thus, it is known that Ānanda, being deluded regarding his own nature of vision, was turned by external objects—perceiving the large as small and the small as large. The Tathāgata, having awakened to his own nature of vision, is able to turn objects to his own purpose.
One can achieve the perfect interfusion of the large and small, where the one and the many are without obstruction. A single delusion or a single awakening results in such gains or losses as these.
Should those like Ānanda not exert themselves?

From the passage where Ānanda addresses the Buddha until the end, this is the third section concerning the nature of vision being free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*). It is divided into three parts:

first, the freedom from the characteristics of right and wrong, namely the passage beginning with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha"; second, the freedom from the characteristics of causality and spontaneity, namely the passage beginning with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha";
and third, although it concerns the characteristics of inverted conjunctions, it likewise begins with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha."
The first section also has two parts. First, from "Ānanda departed" onwards, it clearly elucidates the departure from marks.
Second, from "At that time, Mañjuśrī" onwards, it further explains remaining doubts. The first of these also has three parts.
First, from "Ānanda" onwards, he raises a doubt based on what preceded. Second, from "Seeing that... onwards, doubts arise in succession. Third, "I only pray that... [and so forth].
The following requests clarification regarding what has not yet been understood. First, within the section on "arising doubt based on the preceding," [the text says]:
"If such as these... Ānanda here restates the previous point that the nature of seeing cannot be contracted to become small or expanded to become large.

Now, with "If such as these," Ānanda restates the previous point that if one can transform objects, then one is identical to the Tathāgata, and so forth. His intention is to say: "Since my nature of seeing is already small, it is not because of contraction."
The Great does not depend on expansion; this is my wondrous nature. Therefore, it is restated as "if such" (and so forth).

Furthermore, previously it was clarified that being able to transform objects is identical to the Tathāgata’s perfectly luminous body and mind, and so on; this refers to the Tathāgata’s clarity in awakening to and perceiving the nature.
Ānanda did not understand this, and consequently doubted that the perception of the nature should be located before him. Therefore, it is restated.

He said: "If this wondrous nature should now be before me, then among these two successive arguments, the meaning is that since the wondrous nature is before me, the perception of what is outside the body must certainly be my true nature. Therefore, he says: 'The seeing must be my true self.
If the perception of what is outside the body is necessarily my true self, then what is this mind within my own body? Thus [he spoke].
He said: "I now [say this]... If the view of what is outside the body were necessarily my true self, how could the mind within my body have the capacity for discrimination?
Does that view outside the body not also discriminate my body? Therefore he said: "And now [I say this]...
If it cannot discriminate my body, then it must truly be my mind that enables me to perceive it.
[He] sees. Therefore it is said: "If [it were] real... (and so forth). If my seeing were such that the nature of seeing were myself, then my own body would conversely not be myself.
Therefore it is said: "The nature of seeing... (and so forth). If this were so, how would it differ from what the Tathāgata previously challenged me with, namely the statement:
"Since you see objects, objects also see you"? Therefore it is said: "How is it different? (and so forth).
If we examine closely the difficulties within Ānanda’s successive arguments, that which he values most is the single phrase "right before my eyes.
Since it is right before me, it must be visible upon all objective phenomena.

This is why, in the subsequent text, the Tathāgata singles out this very phrase and refutes it through two rounds—first as "seeing" and then as "non-seeing"—yet it cannot be found in either case. (Third Request)
It may be understood that this indicates the state of those who have not yet awakened.

The second section, "The Exposition," is divided into four parts: first, from "The Buddha said" downward, a general negation based on the underlying intent; second, from "If it were real" downward, a specific refutation by establishing reasoning;
third, from "Thereupon" downward, the assembly being at a loss; fourth, from "The Tathāgata" downward, the Tathāgata’s consolation. Regarding the first of these:

Regarding the statement that "this meaning is not real," it means that if one were to say [the Buddha] is currently present before you, this would not only be improper according to what the Tathāgata has taught, but it would also fail to accord with the significance explained in any single sūtra. Second, the refutation through establishing distinct principles is twofold.

First, the reasoning established by Śrīta and others can be understood. Second, the specific refutation beginning with "Furthermore, now... has two parts: first, the section beginning with "Furthermore, now... clarifies the departure from this view;

second, the section beginning with "The Buddha again... clarifies the departure from non-view. The first of these [the departure from this view] further has three parts: first, the investigation and examination beginning with "Furthermore, now...";

second, the response beginning with "Ānanda..."; third, the confirmation beginning with "The Buddha said...". The first of these [the investigation] further has two parts: first, pointing to the object; "Furthermore... [and so on].

Now, this is equal; it may be understood. Second, the examination of the two fingers. If they must indeed be equal, there are again two parts: first, "If they must go," which is a general statement that may be understood;
second, "Ānanda goes," which is a specific demonstration. This, too, has two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downward, one examines by means of the object; second, from "You may...

downward, one examines apart from the object. Both may be understood. Second, the response, which also has two parts: first, Ānanda’s reply beginning with "I say... is a response by means of the object.
Inference. Regarding the two [types of] World-Honored Ones who are equal: the answer concerning the inference regarding the object is as follows. The first answer is evident.

Within the second answer, there are those among the initial learners of the Śrāvakas who have suppressed and severed the *dṛṣṭi* (views) but have not yet severed the *kleśa* (afflictions); and there are Bodhisattvas who have suppressed and severed both *dṛṣṭi* and *kleśa* but have not yet severed *avidyā* (ignorance).
For these reasons, none of them are able to analyze out and extract the subtle vision (*sūkṣma-darśana*). Second, it clarifies the separation from that which is not the aspect of vision.
Four points: First, "The Buddha again" and so forth reiterates the statement. Second, "Now again" and so forth further examines it. Third, "Ānanda" and so forth provides the response.

Fourth, "The Buddha said" and so forth grants approval. The rest may be understood accordingly. Regarding the statement that "apart from this seeing, there is no non-seeing," and that the Buddha approved both by saying "It is so, it is so":
some say that Ānanda stated that apart from objects there is no such seeing, and the Tathāgata approved [this].
One might say, "So it is, so it is. Furthermore, Ānanda said that apart from objects there is no non-seeing, and the Tathāgata likewise confirmed this, saying, "So it is, so it is.
Since he has already confirmed it previously, he should not confirm it again later; or since he has confirmed it later, he should not have confirmed it previously.
How can he provide confirmation for both the former and the latter? Is it not as if the Tathāgata were acting inconsistently?

Is this like the heterodox views of both-affirmation-and-negation or both-negation-and-affirmation regarding permanence and annihilation? Answer: This is not so. Originally, there are two aspects: the real and the false.
If one considers the essence of reality (*tattva*), it is entirely free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*) and forever transcends the hundred practices.

It is like the clarity of the fundamental seeing; since there is no such seeing, there is likewise no non-seeing. Therefore, as the Tathāgata says below: "This seeing and its objects are originally bodhi."

How could there be "is" or "is not" within this wondrous, pure, and luminous essence? If one considers it from the perspective of its delusory nature, since that essence is delusory, it is ultimately unattainable;
thus, there is neither the vision of "is" nor the vision of "is not. Therefore, as the Tathāgata says below:
"This vision and its objects are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. How could there be 'is' or 'is not' within them? It is merely a matter of skillful [expedient means].
This is speech that accords with the conditions of things and follows the inclinations of others. When the other says, "There is no such view," he responds, "There is no such view.
When the other says, "There is no non-view," he responds, "There is no non-view. For this reason, within Ānanda’s two layers of inquiry, [the Buddha] both confirmed them, saying, "So it is, so it is.
Within the realm of the Tathāgata, there is not a single thing that is not permissible.

How could this be the same as the heterodox calculations of the non-Buddhists? While the three great assemblies were bewildered, [the text] states that "one who is not a non-learner" (aśaikṣa) is indeed a learner (śaikṣa).
This is merely a negation by exclusion (paryudāsa-pratiṣedha). To investigate the truth and sever delusions is called being a learner;

when delusions are exhausted and truth is fully realized, one is called a non-learner. Now, the statement "not a non-learner" is made because their delusions have not yet been exhausted and their realization of truth has not yet reached its limit. From here...
The "three fruits" is a general term for those who have returned [to the world]. Regarding the phrase "vaguely not knowing," etc.:
at the beginning, there is no such view as to grant approval in this way or that; at the end, there is no such non-view as to grant approval in this way or that.
If one merely confirms that there is no view of "is" while not confirming that there is no view of "is-not," it is still a case of knowing [the truth] and remaining composed.
Furthermore, if one merely confirms that there is no view of "is-not" while not confirming that there is no view of "is," this too is a case of knowing [the truth] and remaining composed.
Now, since you have both confirmed that there is no view of "is" and confirmed that there is no view of "is-not," why is it that you do not simply...

I am left utterly bewildered and ignorant. Since all [the Buddhas] have granted their seal of approval, if one clings to the "rightness" of the view that there is no rightness, one loses the "rightness" of the view that there is no wrongness;
if one clings to the "rightness" of the view that there is no wrongness, one again loses the "rightness" of the view that there is no rightness.
This is why I am filled with trepidation and lose my composure. Among the four ways the Tathāgatas offer consolation, the Tathāgata knows...

Regarding the phrase "those who are equal": since the great assembly was both bewildered and ignorant, and further filled with trepidation and loss of composure, there was concern that they might harbor doubts similar to the externalist views of Makkhali Gosāla and others. Therefore, this statement was made to comfort them. As for the expression "as it truly is" (*yathābhūtam*):

the upper character "ru" (如) refers to *tathatājñāna* (the wisdom of suchness), while the lower character "ru" refers to *yathārtha* (suchness as it is). It is by means of the wisdom of suchness that...
To speak according to the principle is to be free from doubt oneself. Regarding the "four kinds of immortality," these are as described in the ten fascicles below:
being both changing and constant, both arising and ceasing, both increasing and decreasing, both existent and non-existent, and so forth.
"Do not disgrace my sorrowful longing" is a word of encouragement. "Sorrowful compassion" refers to the Tathāgata’s compassionate pity for Ānanda; it means to long for [him].

Admiration. Indeed, those who admire Ānanda are sentient beings. Because Ānanda practices the bodhisattva path, bearing the responsibility of seeking the supreme above and transforming others below, it is for this reason that he is used as an incentive for progress.

The second part, the section explaining remaining doubts, is divided into two. First, at that time, Mañjuśrī and others made their request; second, the Buddha told Mañjuśrī and others, providing the answer. The first of these is further divided into two:
first, from "At that time" onwards, the scribe records the ritual proceedings; second, from "The World-Honored One" onwards, Mañjuśrī presents his words. Regarding the first of these:
as for Mañjuśrī rising from within the great assembly and addressing the Buddha, this is inferred according to the underlying meaning.
This has two meanings. First, the great assembly previously heard that regarding Ānanda’s statement "there is no such seeing," the Tathāgata confirmed it by saying, "So it is, so it is.
Furthermore, regarding Ānanda’s statement "there is no non-seeing," the Tathāgata likewise confirmed it by saying, "So it is, so it is.
Because of these two points, they were not without shock and doubt; thus, they were at a loss, not knowing what to do, and filled with trepidation.

Regarding [the disciples] who were terrified and lost their composure: although they had received the Tathāgata’s single round of compassionate consolation, they merely managed to avoid a collapse of their spirits;
yet, they were unable to pose another question. For this reason, Mañjuśrī made a formal request on their behalf.

Second, within the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi* assembly, he proclaimed and expounded that which is solely the nature of mind—quiescent and eternal. This is the very essence of the fruit of unsurpassed Bodhi; it is not something that...
Profound wisdom cannot be easily comprehended. Yet, since Buddhas and Bodhisattvas gather and transform sentient beings, how could they fail to awaken them and simply abandon them?
For this reason, the Tathāgata offers consolation at the outset, while Mañjuśrī poses his questions thereafter.

The second section, Mañjuśrī’s Presentation of His Words, is divided into three parts: first, the World-Honored One and others recount what they previously did not understand; second, the World-Honored One and others voice their doubts on his behalf;
third, the phrase "I only pray," etc., expresses the wish for him to grant an exposition. Regarding the first part: as for the phrase "this great assembly," etc.

The meaning is this: when the Tathāgata taught the nature of the view of tranquility and permanence, he could not accept the view of existence as being "seeing," nor could he reject the view of non-existence as being "non-seeing.

Therefore, when Ānanda spoke of the absence of such seeing, the Buddha immediately confirmed it, saying, "So it is, so it is. Furthermore, when Ānanda spoke of the absence of non-seeing, [the Buddha likewise responded].
The seal of approval was given, saying: "So it is, so it is. Yet, there is also approval for the absence of such views, and approval for the absence of non-views.
Although there is no lack of profound intent within the realm of the Tathāgata, it is exceptionally difficult for the minds of the great assembly to comprehend.

For this reason, some remain utterly bewildered and ignorant, while others are struck with terror and lose their composure. This has merely been a brief mention of the state of not yet awakening. Therefore, it is said:

Regarding these various [passages] (and so forth): within the two [sections], the phrase "if it is such as this" directly cites the preceding text to raise a doubt and pose a request on behalf of another.
The underlying meaning is that since Ānanda has identified the nature of seeing as something visible, there ought to be a specific object pointed out.
Furthermore, when the Tathāgata commanded each of them to point out the seeing that had come from outside, they were able to find only these objects and no such seeing.
Since they initially admitted there was seeing, yet upon further investigation claimed there was no seeing, they ought not to have been granted approval by the Tathāgata;
yet the Tathāgata did grant them his approval. This is the first reason for which this great assembly harbors doubt. Moreover—
Ānanda knew that no vision could be found; thus, there should have been nothing for him to gaze upon.
Yet, when the Tathāgata commanded him to point out each instance of his past movements, everything he identified was merely material objects, with nothing that could be established as "vision.

Since he had previously argued that there was no such thing as vision, yet later stated that there was nothing that was not vision, his position should not have been accepted. Thereupon, the Tathāgata further...
He then confirmed this for them. This was the second reason why the great assembly harbored doubts. Thus it is said: "If such were the case... (and so forth).
Yet that great assembly did not understand where the meaning of this teaching was leading; they were thus struck with a sense of total bewilderment and trepidation.
However, this was not caused by the lightness or meagerness of their past roots of goodness. Therefore, it is said:
Now (as explained at length). Among these three [sections], two responses can be understood as being divided into three parts:
first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, there is a direct clarification based on the Dharma; second, from "Mañjuśrī" onwards, there is an illustration by citing persons as examples;

third, from "This is" onwards, there is a concluding demonstration of delusion and awakening. Within the first part: the Tathāgatas of the ten directions are the realized ones (*phala-pudgala*). Bodhi...

"Sā" refers to the person. "Samādhi" refers to the Great Samādhi of the Śūraṅgama. "The seeing and the objects of seeing are equal" means that "seeing" is the sense organ (the root), and "objects of seeing" are the sensory objects (the dust).
"Conceptual appearances" refer to the discriminating mind; these are what are known as the triad of organ, object, and consciousness.
These three dharmas encompass all phenomena. In their entirety they are illusory, like flowers in the sky that fundamentally do not exist;
hence it is said, "As for seeing... (and so forth). However, delusion does not establish itself independently; it exists because of the True. Hence it is said, "This seeing... (and so forth).
As for the mention of the "ten directions" and so on, the intended meaning is that such distinctions as right and wrong are entirely removed from the wondrous, luminous, and pure mind. If...
To bring this forth, one must infer and elucidate it based on what has been realized by the Tathāgata as a fruit-realizer and what has been cultivated by the Bodhisattva as a path-practitioner.
Therefore, it says: "In the ten directions... (and so forth). Regarding "abiding in samādhi" oneself:
it is by means of this that the Tathāgata becomes a Tathāgata through realization, and it is by means of this that the Bodhisattva is a Bodhisattva through cultivation.
Although the cultivation and realization of cause and effect differ, none do so without relying on this; therefore, it is called "abiding in samādhi.

This is because samādhi is to contemplate by means of the very nature itself, to illuminate through absolute transcendence, and to realize that emptiness and existence are non-dual, where cessation and illumination are equal.
If one speaks of "obscuring" (遮), it is a state of profound stillness and true quiescence, where all phenomena are present before one yet not a single speck of dust is established.
If one speaks of "illuminating" (炤), it is a state of vast clarity and perfect manifestation, where the myriad phenomena are naturally and perfectly arrayed.

Therefore, when one says that "seeing is equal [to the object]," this refers to the very point of obscuration—where all phenomena are present before one yet not a single speck of dust is established. This "seeing is equal... is the state of vast clarity...
However, this is the very point where the myriad phenomena of the universe are perfectly manifested, shining forth in accordance with the natural law (*dharmatā*).

Thus, one knows that seeing and so forth are the substance of delusion itself. Since they are like flowers in the sky and fundamentally non-existent, how could there be any "seeing" or "non-seeing" to be found therein?
Furthermore, one knows that this seeing and so forth is the true essence itself; since it is originally wondrous purity, [how could it be otherwise?]
The essence of clarity. How is it that within this there is that which is "seeing" and that which is not "seeing"?

For this reason, Ānanda, at the very beginning, when you turned toward all objective phenomena and investigated them one by one, saying, "There is no such seeing," I immediately confirmed it, saying, "So it is, so it is."
Furthermore, he again examined all phenomena and objects, concluding that they were nothing other than seeing.
I also confirmed this, saying, "So it is, so it is. Yet, in this matter, I, the Tathāgata, have no hidden meaning; what cause for doubt could there be?
One must know that the nature of arising and ceasing is fundamentally illusory, like flowers in the sky which have no inherent existence.
Thus, the very nature of arising and ceasing is fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence. This is not something that Buddhas and Bodhisattvas alone cultivate or realize;

rather, it is what all Buddhas have realized—realizing that there is nothing to be realized—and what sentient beings inherently possess. It is what Bodhisattvas cultivate—a cultivation that is itself non-existent.

That which is cultivated is what sentient beings inherently possess. If one can employ the three wisdoms inherent in nature to give rise to the three contemplations within cultivation, then one may manifest the three truths—ultimate, conventional, and middle—precisely through the dharmas of the sense organs, objects, consciousness, and their arising and ceasing.
Furthermore, both seeing and non-seeing can be known. Therefore, the Tathāgata specifically [taught] by means of the Buddha...
The *samādhi* cultivated and realized by Bodhisattvas serves as the illumination of the Dharma. To clarify this directly according to the Dharma, it is as follows.

Next, the text provides an illustration by citing a person, which is divided into two parts: first, the citation of the person starting with "Mañjuśrī"; second, the illustrative explanation starting with "The Buddha said.

The first part [the citation of the person] is further divided into two: first, the question; second, the answer. Regarding the first [the question], the phrase "I now," etc., intends to mean that within the essence of wondrously pure luminosity...
There is nothing to be obtained in terms of seeing this or not seeing that. If one wishes to provide an illustration for clarification, there is no need to borrow from afar;
it can be understood by taking Mañjuśrī, the questioner himself, as the immediate example. Therefore, it is said: "I now ask you. To interpret the text, it should be stated:
"Apart from this Mañjuśrī of yours, is there another Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī? By this, one knows that the initial phrase "like this Mañjuśrī of yours" [is the point].

This is the true Mañjuśrī. By analogy with the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence, there is further the phrase "this is Mañjuśrī," which refers to that which is Mañjuśrī outside of the true Mañjuśrī;

this is analogous to the existence of "this seeing" within the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence. Third is the phrase "non-Mañjuśrī," which refers to that which is non-Mañjuśrī outside of the true Mañjuśrī;
this is analogous to the existence of "non-[seeing]" within the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence.
"I see it. Regarding the phrase "among these two" and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows:
the Tathāgata asked me whether there is another Mañjuśrī besides this Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī, or whether it is this very Mañjuśrī who is Mañjuśrī; hence he said, "It is thus.
Although the Tathāgata posed this question, when I, Mañjuśrī, observe it, I, Mañjuśrī, am the true Mañjuśrī. Apart from this true Mañjuśrī...

There is no separate entity that is Mañjuśrī; he is Mañjuśrī himself. Therefore it is said, "World-Honored One" (and so forth). Regarding the section beginning with "For what reason," this explains that there is no such thing as Mañjuśrī, yet there is nothing that is not Mañjuśrī.
For what reason? Apart from Mañjuśrī, there is no other Mañjuśrī who constitutes Mañjuśrī. It is because there is nothing else.
This is not because the world functions through such dualistic oppositions as "is" and "is not. If there were even one [such entity], [it would be so].
Mañjuśrī must necessarily have a counterpart who is not Mañjuśrī; therefore it is said, "If there were... (and so forth).
However, speaking from the perspective of my own Mañjuśrī today, it is not that Mañjuśrī does not exist; there is simply only the one True Mañjuśrī.
Apart from this True Mañjuśrī, there is certainly neither such a Mañjuśrī nor a non-Mañjuśrī; therefore it is said, "But I... (and so forth). Thus it may be understood.
"Seeing my true Mañjuśrī" answers "the true Mañjuśrī. "Truly there are no two aspects of right and wrong" answers "Mañjuśrī without the two aspects of right and wrong.

Thus, one should know that the intent of Mañjuśrī’s response may be understood by analogy with the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence (miāo jìng míng tǐ), which possesses neither the seeing nor the non-seeing.
There are two further illustrations of these two points: first, from "The Buddha said" below, it illustrates the preceding; second, "This is originally... [illustrates the latter].
The following is an example of the second part of the first section. Regarding the passage beginning with "The Buddha said," etc., the intended meaning is as follows:

I asked you whether, apart from Mañjuśrī, there exists a Mañjuśrī or a non-Mañjuśrī. My purpose was precisely to illustrate by analogy that upon the wondrously pure and luminous essence, neither "this seeing" nor "non-seeing" can be apprehended.
Now you say that there is only the single true Mañjuśrī, devoid of the two characteristics of "is" and "is not."
One should know that the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence is like your true Mañjuśrī.
That neither "seeing" nor "not seeing" can be apprehended is like having no dual characteristics of "is" and "is not" outside your true Mañjuśrī. Therefore it is said: "This seeing... (and so forth).
The double analogy is again twofold. First is the analogy for the fundamental [principle], namely "the fundamental is... and so forth. Second is the formal analogy, namely "just as the third...

and so forth. Regarding the first, the passage beginning with "the fundamental is... intends to convey this meaning: how is it that the wondrously pure and luminous essence (*prakṛti*) allows no room for the two views of "is" and "is not"?
This is because the nature of the seeing and its objects of seeing is fundamentally the wondrously pure and luminous essence, which from the outset is devoid of the duality of "is" and "is not."

Because it is seen, it is said: "This is fundamentally... (and so forth). However, because sentient beings are deluded regarding seeing and the objects of seeing—namely form and emptiness—they take form and emptiness as the "seen" and seeing and hearing as the "seer. Thus, when they approach them, there is "seeing"; when they distance themselves from them, there is "non-seeing.
Therefore, it is said: "Delusion constitutes... (and so forth). Within the second section, the "Correct Simile," the text is divided into two parts.
The first part, from "As in the second moon," below, illustrates the delusory; the second part, from "Mañjuśrī," below, illustrates the real. Regarding the first:

the phrase "as in the second moon" and so forth means that although the seeing and its conditions are delusory and empty, they closely approximate the real; thus, it is clarified by means of this analogy.
It is like a second moon produced by pressing upon the eye; it is closely approximated to the true moon. Therefore, it is said to be "like a second moon.
Since the true essence itself lacks the two views of affirmation and negation, how could false appearances possess any attainable affirmation or negation? This is further clarified through analogy:
the true moon certainly possesses no dual characteristics of affirmation and negation, yet a second moon is produced by pressing upon the eye—how could that [second moon] possibly [exist]?
Is there such a duality of "this moon" and "not-this moon"? Therefore it is said: "Who is it that... (and so forth).
Regarding the passage concerning Mañjuśrī and others, the intended meaning is: Why is it that ultimately there is no such duality of "is" and "is-not"?

Because the wondrously pure and luminous essence of true nature (*tathatā*) fundamentally lacks any obtainable distinction between the view of "is" and the view of "is-not. This is clarified by means of an analogy, which is as follows:
In the world there is but one moon; there is no such thing as a second moon that is real, nor is there a moon-reflection that is unreal.
Thus it is said of Mañjuśrī [and so forth]. What has preceded is an exposition based directly upon the Dharma, now illustrated by citing an example of a person.
If one explains this in detail, it becomes clear that when Ānanda first said, "There is no such seeing," I immediately confirmed it, saying, "So it is, so it is.
When he later said, "There is no non-seeing," I likewise confirmed it, saying, "So it is, so it is.
Since the meaning of these points is perfectly lucid, what cause for doubt or alarm could there have been for that great assembly?

Yes. Among these three, they are equal. Thus, they fail to realize that the seer, the object of seeing, and the sense-faculties, objects, and consciousness—these three—are in their entirety wondrously pure.
Instead, they give rise to deluded thoughts and various discriminations, and are unable to transcend this state of "seeing" and "not-seeing."
It is because of these things that I, the Tathāgata, demonstrate that I have realized the entire substance of all phenomena as the universal void; hence they are called "true essence" (*zhenjing*).
Furthermore, because they are spontaneously and perfectly manifested, they are called the "wondrously enlightened nature of clarity" (*miaojue mingxing*).

Therefore, today I am able to cause you, Ānanda, and the great assembly to transcend both the pointing finger and what is not the pointing finger. There is no need to further elaborate on the distinction between the finger and what is not the finger.
The *Nanhua* [Zhuangzi] uses it for practical application; this is like what was previously stated regarding "not being without indication" and the pointing finger used for demonstration.
It is simply the aforementioned "is" and "is not. Regarding that which is pointed at, we call it "no view of is" and "no view of is not.
Regarding that which points, we call it "no pointing finger" and "no non-pointing finger. This merely changes the characters; the meaning does not differ. Furthermore, you—

The current instruction to "you two" originally refers to Ānanda and the assembly. If Mañjuśrī were merely acting as a petitioner on their behalf, then the subsequent demonstration regarding delusion and enlightenment would not concern them.

Second, the characteristic of being naturally devoid of causes and conditions. This is divided into two parts: first, Ānanda’s address to the Buddha and so forth, which correctly clarifies this absence; second, Ānanda’s address to the Buddha and so forth, which further resolves doubts.

The first part is further divided into two: first, Ānanda’s removal of his own doubts and his request for instruction; second, the Buddha’s response to remove his doubts and provide an exposition. The first of these is further divided into three:

first, Ānanda’s removal of his doubt that [the teaching] is identical to that of the non-Buddhists; second, the World-Honored One’s removal of his doubt regarding its contradiction with previous teachings.
Sūtra. Third, how to dispel doubts by requesting an exposition. This section may further be divided into three parts: first, "Truly as you have said," etc., which recounts the Buddha’s teaching;
second, "As for those who previously," etc., which addresses the non-Buddhists; and third, "What phrases are there? which formally establishes the doubt. Within the first part:

The fourteen characters beginning with "Awakening to conditions" (*jue yuan*) fully encompass both the phrasing and the meaning from the point where the nature of seeing (*jianxing*) is revealed as quiescent and eternal.
How is this known? "Awakening" (*jue*) refers to the nature of awakening (*jue-xing*); "conditions" (*yuan*) refers to the sense organs (*gen*) and their objects (*chen*).

"Pervading the ten directions" means that this nature of awakening, along with the organs and objects, is nowhere not pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is what is meant by "there is nothing outside the mind."

"Dharma. Outside of dharmas, there is no mind; this refers back to the preceding passage stating that the seeing and the objects of seeing are fundamentally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi.
"Serene" (zhanran) refers to the state of spiritual clarity and penetrating transparency; this refers back to the preceding passage stating that all dharmas can be returned to their source.
It refers solely to the nature of seeing which has no place of return, and to the nature of seeing which lacks such characteristics as shrinking from large to small or being constricted and severed.

"Permanently abiding" (changzhu) means that which is neither born nor extinguished. "Constant" (chang) specifically points to the preceding passage where the hand opens and closes while the seeing itself neither opens nor closes, thereby manifesting the constancy of the nature of seeing.
"Abiding" (zhu) means that which neither goes nor comes; this specifically points to the preceding passage.

The head moves of its own accord without cessation, thereby manifesting the stillness of the nature of seeing. "The nature is neither arising nor ceasing" means that it does not cease, and thus is not subject to extinction.
This refers back to the previous passage where the blind man’s perception of darkness demonstrated that the nature of seeing does not cease, thereby revealing the permanence of the nature of seeing.
"It is neither arising" means it is not subject to birth; this also refers back to the previous passage concerning how the seeing of the nature is independent of [external objects].
The statement that "the nature of seeing is unborn" reveals the quiescence of the nature of seeing.

Furthermore, by reading this in conjunction with the fact that "the nature is neither arising nor ceasing," it refers back to the previous passage in response to King Aśoka, wherein it was stated that arising and ceasing are themselves non-arising and non-ceasing.

One must understand that the Tathāgata, wishing to shatter the false and reveal the true, at times manifests the permanence of the nature of seeing through its non-extinction, and at other times manifests...

The stillness of the nature of seeing is revealed through non-arising. At times, the stillness of the nature of seeing is manifested as being eternally neither arising nor ceasing, even amidst arising and ceasing.

Furthermore, the stillness of the nature of seeing is manifested as being eternally free from the marks of self and other, object and subject, large and small, expansion and contraction, right and wrong, and so forth.
