Thus, through these layered instructions and successive deconstructions, Ānanda—now [is addressed].

Within these fourteen characters, both the phrasing and the meaning are so comprehensive that nothing is left unencompassed; this is what is meant by "skillfully expounding the essential points of the Dharma.

Regarding the second [of the two points]: as for the *tattva* (ultimate reality) discussed therein, one first contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and finds no beginning, and subsequently contemplates eighty thousand kalpas and finds no end.
In the interval between them, the two marks of motion and stillness clearly do not arise. This appears to be the true reality; therefore—

What is called "Primal Essence" (mūlaprakṛti), as well as the practice of smearing oneself with ashes and so forth, refers to the ascetic non-Buddhists (tīrthika). Their notion of a "True Self" is similar to the "Divine Self" (puruṣa);
they claim this True Self pervades the ten directions, but these are all merely false speculations. Regarding the three [categories], it is asked: what is the difference between them?
The meaning is this: the Tathāgata, the Dharma King, is not at all comparable to those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

Nevertheless, when one compares what the World-Honored One has taught—that awakening, its conditions, and the pervasive realm of the ten directions are quiescently and eternally abiding, without arising or ceasing—and what the non-Buddhists conceive of as the Primal Essence (*prakṛti*) and the Self (*ātman*), which they also claim pervade the ten directions, the two appear to be neither identical nor different. Yet, the Dharma King...
How could this teaching be the same as external doctrines? Ultimately, what is the nature of the middle way? One will naturally attain clear discernment;
the heterodox and the orthodox are not comparable. Regarding the second doubt concerning contradictions with previous sūtras, it may also be divided into three parts:

first, "The World-Honored One," etc., which restates the meaning of the sūtra; second, "Those outsiders," etc., which sets forth the intent of the sūtra; and third, "I now," etc., which establishes the doubt.
These are the words [of the Buddha]. This meaning refers to "those outsiders" and so forth mentioned below. "Those" refers to the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas). "I" refers to the Tathāgata himself.
"Spontaneously" (zìrán) means that Heaven is naturally so. As it is said: "Who opened the rivers and seas and piled up the mountains and peaks?
Who cleared away the thorns and brambles and exhausted the phoenixes? And so on, regarding the straightness of the pine and the curvature of the thorn, the crane’s...

The whiteness of a white crow and its blackness are equal. Regarding "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*): that which initiates [a process] is called the cause (*hetu*); that which brings it to completion is called the condition (*pratyaya*).

The cause is like a grain seed; the conditions are like the soil, water, and human labor. I now establish this equality within the midst of doubt, and its meaning is identical to that [of the previous passage].

The intention is this: the nature of awakening (*bodhi-dhātu*) as taught by the Tathāgata is neither arising nor ceasing, and so forth; it appears not to be the same as the causes and conditions of the past.
It is the same. Furthermore, it resembles the "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Therefore, it is said: "I now... and so forth.
However, the nature of awakening clarified by the Tathāgata is the principle of the Great Vehicle’s Perfect and Sudden teaching;

it is inherently different from the causes and conditions used previously to refute heterodoxy, and it does not even match the causes and conditions of the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), let alone the spontaneity of the false outsiders. Ānanda clearly understands this.

The same applies here; it is simply that no one is able to comprehend this principle, and thus they harbor such doubts. Regarding the third request for instruction, which asks, "How [is it]?"—the intent is this:

the Tathāgata’s teaching is inherently different from that of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), yet we ourselves are unable to understand it clearly and thus give rise to doubt within our minds. Therefore, he asks, "How do you reveal and instruct [us]? and so forth.

The second section, "Revelation," is divided into three parts. First, the departure from spontaneity (*svabhāva*), beginning with the Buddha’s words, etc. Second, the departure from causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), beginning with Ānanda’s words, etc.
Third, the summary and demonstration, beginning with "You should know," etc. The first part is further divided into two: first, a direct refutation, beginning with the Buddha’s words;

second, a reductio ad absurdum, beginning with "You should for now," etc. Within the first of these, the phrase "I now," etc., follows the previous text’s method of citing phenomena to reveal the principle.
To harmonize phenomena through principle so that phenomena and principle are perfectly interfused is called "revealing and showing" (*āviṣkaraṇa*).

As in the preceding text, whenever a metaphor is established based on the Dharma to illustrate the Dharma, such that the Dharma and the metaphor are clearly conjoined, this is called "expedient means" (*upāya*).

As in the preceding text, whether it be body or mind, or even mountains, rivers, and the great earth—all are objects within the wondrous mind; thus, there is no phenomenon outside of the mind. And as for seeing...
To see that conditions are fundamentally the wondrous essence of bodhi is for the deluded to be entirely identical with the true.

When such mental phenomena vanish and the true and the deluded share a single substance, this is called the "True and Real Instruction. Having already used dharmas and parables as skillful means and matters and principles as revelations, I further declare to you the "True and Real":
there are no dharmas outside the mind, and the deluded are entirely identical with the true. Not only do you fail to awaken to this, but...

Because [Vasubandhu] perceived that [Ānanda’s] delusion was identical to that of the non-Buddhists who advocate spontaneity (*svabhāva*), he proceeded to enumerate their views in detail and thoroughly rebuke them; hence he says, "You still... (*yū ryou*, etc.).
From "Ānanda" downwards, he formally restates the opponent's calculation. This section on refuting through reasoning is divided into two parts: first, "You, moreover... establishes the premise;

second, from "Ānanda" onwards is the refutation itself—both of which are easily understood. Second, the section on being apart from causes and conditions is divided into two parts; first, Ānanda says:

The equal transformation and calculation can be understood. Second, the Buddha says, "You all should investigate and refute [this]. This also has two parts: first, from "The Buddha says" below, he refutes the cause;

second, from "Furthermore" below, he refutes the conditions. The first part also has two sections: first, the determination; second, the refutation. The second part also has two sections: first, the determination; second, the refutation.
These can all be understood as well. The third section provides a summary and indication, namely: "One should know," and so forth. This is divided into two parts:

first, the actual demonstration; second, the concluding reprimand. Regarding the first part: prior to "one should know," one should first state that previously you maintained [the self] to be either spontaneous (*svabhāva*) or produced by causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), and I have refuted each of these one by one.
Since neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity are tenable, there is nothing else remaining. In total—
Because this wondrously luminous essence is fundamentally free from both spontaneity (*svabhāva*) and causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*), it says, "One should know that...
and so forth. It is also not spontaneous; there should be a phrase "it must exist because it is not [merely] non-causal," which exists according to the meaning, though the text is abbreviated.
The two phrases beginning with "not caused by" are the primary negation; the two phrases beginning with "not non-caused by" are the secondary negation. There is no...
It is not that a single phrase merely negates and then negates again. For the "negation" of that which is neither caused nor spontaneous must itself be negated;
likewise, the "negation" of that which is neither uncaused nor non-spontaneous must also be negated. This absence of a single phrase further negates the negation of negations;
it is the affirmation of that which is neither affirmation nor negation. All these are successive negations, for they are based on the wondrous clarity.
When the substance is negated, it is negated in its entirety; therefore, it is said that "one is free from all marks. Yet, this does not preclude their simultaneous establishment;
therefore, it is also said that "one is identical with all dharmas. Thus, one should know that "being free from all marks" is the simultaneous negation of both [identity and difference].
This is precisely all phenomena (*sarvadharma*), and it is also the illumination of both [phenomena and their emptiness] while remaining detached from them.

However, the first phrase serves to dispel deluded attachments; thus it refers to "characteristics" (*lakṣaṇa*). The second phrase establishes the dharma; thus it refers to "dharma" (*dharma*). This means that when one is negated, all are negated;

when all are negated, one is negated—this negates attachment but does not negate the dharma. When one is established, all are established; when all are established, one is established—this establishes the dharma but... [does not establish attachment].
This establishes the underlying principle. One should understand that "detaching from all marks" refers to the true emptiness described in the preceding passage:

that the seeing, the objects of seeing, and the marks of what is conceived are like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent. "That is all dharmas" refers to the wondrous existence described in the preceding passage:
that this seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of Bodhi. By resolving it in this way alone—
This is so. It is not necessary to repeatedly apply the medicine of the Dharma to it. Regarding the phrase "Now you [etc.]":

the meaning is that within the essence of wondrous clarity, if one thing is negated, all are negated, and not even a single speck of dust can be established; if one thing is established, all are established, and the reality naturally manifests in its entirety.
Since such is the wondrous essence, why do you all harbor doubts regarding it as being either caused by conditions or produced spontaneously? Therefore, it says: "Now you... (and so forth).
"Among the middling [categories], there is the 'middling-of-the-middling,' which is the essence of wondrous luminosity (*prabhāsvara*). To 'apply the mind' is merely to raise an intention.

'Proliferating conceptualization' (*prapañca*) refers to the suspected causes and conditions as well as spontaneity (*svabhāva*). The following section employs analogies: the palm of the hand represents the conceptual proliferation of causes and conditions and spontaneity;
empty space represents the essence of wondrous luminosity; and 'grasping and rubbing' represent applying the mind and suspecting that the essence is caused by external conditions."
This is naturally so. How could there be anyone in the world capable of grasping or rubbing empty space? Therefore it is said: "It only serves to increase [the confusion]," and so forth.

The second section, beginning with Ānanda’s address to the Buddha, is a further clarification to resolve doubts. It is divided into two parts: first, the inquiry arising from doubt; second, the revelation.
Within the first part, the two phrases beginning with "Necessarily subtle" cite the preceding passage on the refutation of causes and conditions. Previously, Ānanda...

The difficulty of doubting that the seeing of nature belongs to causes and conditions is as follows: when the Tathāgata examines it in terms of causes—whether from light to darkness, or from emptiness to obstruction—it cannot be found.
Furthermore, examining it in terms of conditions—from emptiness to obstruction, or from light to darkness—it likewise cannot be found.
Proceeding further to what is neither cause nor condition, even to that which is free from all marks and is itself all dharmas, he thereby reveals the wondrous.
The essence of illumination is why the text states, "It must be wondrous," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "neither cause nor condition," one should supplement it as follows:

"Yet, regarding what the Tathāgata has said today, if we infer the past by means of the present, and verify the present by means of the past, for what reason did the World-Honored One always say that the seeing-nature possesses four kinds of conditions? (etc.). As for the "four kinds of conditions" and so on: the eye [perceives] by way of separation.

Because it is known through cognition, it is conditioned by emptiness (*ākāśa*). Because the sun, moon, or lamp cannot produce seeing, it is conditioned by light (*āloka*). Because discernment necessarily relies upon the mind, it is conditioned by the mind (*citta*).

Because the eye serves as the predominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), it is conditioned by the eye (*cakṣus*). Within this context, there are only these four. As for the *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), there are nine types.
Among these nine, "emptiness" refers to being conditioned by emptiness; "light" refers to being conditioned by light; "eye" refers to being conditioned by the eye; and the remainder...
The mental formations (*manasikāra*) that differentiate between defilement and purity, along with their fundamental seeds, are all subsumed under the causal mind (*hetu-citta*).

Since there is a mind capable of cognition, the objects of cognition are likewise subsumed within the mind. However, when discussing the aspects (*lakṣaṇa*) in the context of Consciousness-Only (*Vijñaptimātra*), four categories are expanded into nine.
Since this sutra discusses the nature (dhātu), it merely combines the nine into four. Although the methods of opening and closing differ, their meaning is no different.

Following the passage on "caused by the mind" and "caused by the eyes," one should further conclude: "What was taught in the past is likewise so. Thus, there is one for the present and one for the past.
The difference between heaven and earth is something for which the Tathāgata certainly has a definitive teaching; yet, as I, Ānanda, observe it, they are one and the same in the nature of seeing.
Why it was previously endowed with causes and conditions, and why it is now free from causes and conditions, can neither of us know.
Therefore, he asks: "What is the meaning of this?"

The second section, "Revelation," is divided into four parts. First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he restates what was previously taught. Second, from "I further... onwards, he addresses the current doubts. Third, from "Therefore...
onwards, he directly refutes the essence of seeing. Fourth, from "You all... onwards, he concludes the instruction and exhorts them to diligence.

The meaning of the first part is clear. The second part is further divided into four: first, from "I further... onwards, the subtle concentration; second, from "Ānanda... onwards, the response; third, from "If... onwards...

The refutation by means of the peerless [reasoning] can all be understood. Fourth, regarding the demonstration through the reprimand of the "if-equal" [position], it is divided into two parts: first, the counter-reprimand, namely "If they are equal...";
second, the actual demonstration, namely "If, moreover..."; these may also be understood. Third, the direct refutation of the essence of vision (*dṛṣṭi-śuddhi*), which is divided into two parts.

The first [section] refutes external objects; this refers to the passage beginning with "Therefore" (*yī gù*). The second refutes internal views; this refers to the passage beginning with "You again" (*rǔ fù*).

Regarding the first [of these], from the phrase "seeing light" up to "accomplishment," these are the actual words of the text. If one were to express it according to the meaning of the phrases, it should be stated as follows:
"At the time of seeing light, the object seen is not accomplished as light," and so on, up to: "At the time of seeing obstruction, the object seen is not accomplished as obstruction."
Thus, the preceding passage mentions "seeing light and so forth," while the subsequent passage contains the phrase "the four meanings are accomplished.
This is certainly due to the skillful compilation of the sūtra’s redactor, as well as the refined phrasing of the scribe.

Since it speaks of "seeing light, darkness, and so forth," yet the reason for seeing light and darkness is not the light and darkness themselves—which are what is accomplished—then these must be the objects perceived as external dust (*bāhyarajaḥ*).
This is refuted. Regarding the four phrases beginning with "At the time of seeing the seeing" within the second section, there have been many ancient interpretations.
The most prominent one merely states: "The upper character 'seeing' (jiàn) is true seeing (zhēnjiàn); the lower character 'seeing' is the essence of seeing (jiànjīng).
When true seeing sees the essence of seeing, that is true seeing; it is not the same as the essence of seeing," and so forth. However, this does not understand how true seeing sees the seeing.
The essence of seeing. What is that which is able to see? What is that which is seen? And what is the time when that which is able to see sees that which is seen?
According to the discourse of our school, the two characters "seeing-seeing" (*jian-jian*) are explained as the contemplative wisdom (*guan-zhi*) observing the principle of truth (*di-li*).

The former refers to the ability to see possessed by contemplative wisdom; the latter refers to the object seen, which is the principle of truth. This principle of truth is precisely the essence of seeing.

The "seeing-essence" (*jing*) is precisely the eighth consciousness, the essence of consciousness. It exists through the conjunction of the conditioned arising-and-ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*) with True Suchness (*tathatā*).

Therefore, it was previously stated that "the essence of consciousness is fundamentally luminous. Here, "essence of consciousness" refers to its aspect of arising-and-ceasing, while "fundamentally luminous" refers to its aspect of True Suchness.
Since the delusion of arising-and-ceasing exists by virtue of True Suchness, this entire body of arising-and-ceasing is in its totality True Suchness—a single, wondrously pure and luminous substance.
Therefore, the character "view" (jiàn) below refers to that which is seen by the principle of truth (*tattva*); since wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*) issues forth from this wondrous essence.

The character "view" above refers to the capacity of contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) to see; it is precisely by means of the wondrous wisdom thus produced that one illuminates the wondrous realm from which it issues.
This is what is called the inconceivable three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) illuminating the perfectly interfused three truths (*tri-satya*).

In this way, wisdom illuminates the object, and the object gives rise to wisdom. When object and wisdom are as one and subject and object are non-dual, at that moment, contemplative wisdom is perfected and the principle of the Truths is fully revealed.
Therefore it is said: "At the time of seeing the seer, the seeing is not seeing. The upper character "seeing" (jiàn) refers to true seeing;
the lower character "seeing" (jiàn) refers to the essence of seeing. This is because true seeing is already the inconceivable wonder.
When one contemplates that which is revealed, it is seen that the entire body is the inconceivable, wondrous realm; it is fundamentally different from the essence of seeing (*darśana-viśuddhi*).
Furthermore, since this essence of seeing is itself the wondrous, pure, and luminous substance—the inconceivable realm—it is no longer the essence of seeing.
Therefore, it is said: "seeing is not seeing. "Seeing is already free from seeing" means that true seeing is free from the essence of seeing. Since it is the entire body...
Yet it is manifested; thus, what is called "detachment" is actually detachment while not being detached. Therefore, it says, "Even seeing is detached from seeing.
As for the phrase "seeing cannot reach it," this means that once true seeing has detached from the essence of seeing, it is no longer within the reach of the essence of seeing;
hence, it says "seeing cannot reach it. Thus, having previously refuted external objects and now having revealed true seeing, it says that seeing is not [the essence].
If even the seeing of seeing is detached from seeing and cannot be reached by it, then the internal seeing is likewise destroyed. Therefore, it says, "You again... (and so forth).

Below the phrase "cannot be reached," one should say: "Previously, it was clarified that the nature of seeing has no place of return, and thus the deluded seeing that discriminates based on sense-objects was destroyed.
Reaching this point, the seeing-essence of the second moon is also destroyed; there is nothing that is not the single wondrous, pure, and luminous substance."
He then continued, saying: "Why do you again take the causes and conditions and so forth to be a source of doubt? Thus he said, "Why... and so on.

From this, one knows that the case of refuting the seeing-essence had already been foreshadowed in the preceding passage where it was stated, "Although this seeing is not the place of the wondrous, bright, and pure mind.
However, this particular passage arises entirely because Ānanda mistakes delusion for reality; the locus of that delusion lies entirely therein.
Regarding "the mind and the seeing": this is for the purpose of shattering the deluded mind. It does not merely shatter the seven locations that lack a supporting basis;
it also shatters the three locations that lack a supporting essence. This leads to the manifestation of true seeing.

Since the deluded seeing that discriminates conditioned objects has been shattered, there is nothing left to serve as a handle for manifesting true seeing. Therefore, the text skillfully relies upon the essence of seeing to bring it forth.

This is what is meant by "using a thief to attack a thief" and "using poison to cure poison. When the true seeing (*bhūtadarśana*) is thus revealed, even the essence of the second-moon vision is shattered.
Yet, it is precisely through this essence of vision that true seeing is manifested; as it is said, there is nothing to be destroyed, yet the essence of vision is spontaneously destroyed;
there is nothing to be revealed, yet true seeing is spontaneously revealed. Therefore, it is not merely the conditions (*pratyaya*) that are destroyed.
This is the deluded vision that discriminates between dust-like phenomena; it is also the breaking of the seeing-essence of the "second moon.
The fourth section concludes with an exhortation to progress, which is divided into two parts. First, from "You all... onwards, is the conclusion and demonstration.
Second, from "I now... onwards, is the exhortation to progress. Within the first part: regarding "You all," Ānanda is merely a śrāvaka, and his wisdom is the most shallow.
Narrow. Their vision is exceedingly base and inferior. Because it is shallow and narrow, they know only the Hīnayāna and do not know the Mahāyāna.

Furthermore, because it is base and inferior, they see only pervasive emptiness and do not see true emptiness. Thus, although they possess knowledge and views, they are the same as those without understanding.
As for the pure reality (*viśuddha-tattva*), it is neither characterized by marks nor devoid of marks; that is to say, it is without the marks of birth-and-death or nirvāṇa.
Furthermore, because every characteristic is truly real and every phenomenon is substantially authentic, this true reality is in fact empty quiescence (*śūnyatā*).
That afflictions cannot defile it is its purity; that birth and death cannot pollute it is its clarity.
Since you are śrāvakas, your knowledge and vision are narrow and inferior; like those who lack discernment, you are unable to penetrate this pure and true reality on your own.
It is not that there is no penetration, but rather that there is no obstruction. The true mark of purity is precisely the wondrously pure and luminous essence.
Because one cannot penetrate it, one is deluded into regarding [phenomena] as being caused by conditions or as being spontaneous. Therefore, it is said: "You all... (and so forth).

Regarding these two, why is it that contemplating [the first] is called "good"? If one merely ceases the deluded views that differentiate objects and conditions, it can simply be termed "contemplation.
Now, however, one further breaks through the perception of the second moon within the essence of clarity;
this is not merely contemplation, but rather "excellent contemplation" (*sādhu-manasikāra*). The wondrous path to Bodhi is *śamatha*; Bodhi is the fruit.

This is that which is penetrated. Śamatha is the cause and that which enables penetration. Since the entire essence of the fruit is taken as the causal practice, it is called the "wondrous path to Bodhi.

Now, the term "path to Bodhi" is used in contrast to śamatha because Ānanda initially requested, saying, "The Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the wondrous śamatha that constitutes the realization of Bodhi," and so forth. Furthermore, this was said by the Tathāgata when he was about to provide the answer.
At the beginning, it was stated that there is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown, the Single Path for the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions to Transcend to the Sublime Adorned Way.
Thus, now, as the answer regarding śamatha is nearing its conclusion, it is called the "Sublime Path to Bodhi. The intent is this:
although you are narrow-minded, inferior, and ignorant, unable to penetrate the pure true reality (*dharmatā*), how could I ever abandon you? Now...
I shall instruct you: you must contemplate well within the place of contemplation;
do not give rise to weariness or indolence regarding the sublime path to Bodhi, and you will naturally attain realization of the pure true reality.

This is why it was said previously that one cannot attain realization, whereas now it is said that one must not give rise to weariness—this is the profound intent of the Tathāgata. Ānanda and the others themselves did not [understand this].

This gives rise to despondency. Third, the section on the characteristic of the union free from inversion, which is divided into two parts: first, the request through doubt; second, the revelation. The first part is further divided into three: first, Ānanda and others expressing their doubts;

second, the formal request for an answer beginning with "I humbly pray"; third, the acceptance of the command beginning with "Having done this. The first of these is further divided into three: first, [the initial expression of doubt].

The first "Cen ji wu" (I have already awakened) refers to the section beginning with "Ānanda descended. The second "Cen wei wu" (I have not yet awakened) refers to the section beginning with "The various subordinates descended.
The third "Cen geng wen" (I ask again) refers to the section beginning with "Now. Regarding the first two:

the intention is that we have received the Buddha’s teaching on this nature of seeing, and it is clear that we have all abandoned the notions of causality and spontaneity; hence it says, "For our sake... and so forth. However, we do not yet know this nature of seeing.
Regarding all things that are in combination and those that are not, one cannot help but have doubts concerning their separation and non-separation;

hence it is said, "All combinations... (and so forth). Not only has one failed to attain awakening through this, but having further heard the Buddha’s teaching that "when seeing sees, that seeing is not seeing," since the former was already unclear and now this is heard as well, one is not merely perplexed, but utterly bewildered.

The bewilderment increases all the more. Therefore it is said, "At this moment... (and so forth). Regarding "bewildered": to say one is "bewildered" (mi) means that the principle has not yet been clarified;
to say one is "confused" (mon) means that the mind has not yet opened. Thus, within the single passage expressing doubt, there are three meanings.
However, to regard "causality" (in-en) and "spontaneity" (jinen) as already enlightened, and to regard "harmony" (wa-gō) and "non-harmony" (fu-wa-gō) as not yet enlightened—this is the first [point].
The first point relies on what has already been stated in the preceding refutation of the spontaneity (*svabhāva*) of causes and conditions;

the second relies on what has not yet been stated in the subsequent refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) and non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*). Furthermore, while these various [notions of] conjunction and so forth have not yet been opened up here, the section below contains the refutation of conjunction and non-conjunction.
Herein, regarding "seeing seeing" and "non-seeing," the following text clarifies these two kinds of false views.

Furthermore, because his request stated that "the awakened mind is luminously pure," the subsequent text likewise interrogates him regarding the "pure fundamental mind" and so forth, as well as the phrase "both being awakened clarity.
Within the second request and its response, the term "Great Wisdom Eye" (*mahā-prajñā-cakṣus*) refers, in a general sense, to the eye of wisdom that clearly perceives emptiness;
this is explained from the perspective of the Hīnayāna. However, what is meant here in the present text is...
The seeing and its conditions are equal in appearance, like flowers in the sky, fundamentally non-existent; hence it is called the "Great Wisdom Eye.
Furthermore, this does not merely refute the deluded seeing that discriminates conditioned objects; it further refutes the second moon and the essence of seeing.
Moreover, having previously refuted the deluded mind, it does not merely refute the locus upon which it has no support, but further refutes the substance that has no capacity to depend. Therefore...

It is not called the "eye of wisdom," but rather the "great eye of wisdom. As for the phrase "the awakened mind is luminous and pure," this is because within the wondrously awakened, luminous mind there is neither darkness nor defilement.
If we were to discuss this by combining the points of inquiry, there are also three meanings:
"seeing the seeing is not seeing," "the awakened mind is luminous and pure," and "conjunction and non-conjunction. Although there are three textual passages, [they form a single thematic unit].
The primary intent lies in two points: the "seeing of seeing" and "clarity and purity" constitute the direct request, while "harmony and disharmony" constitute the secondary request.
This can be seen by cross-referencing with the subsequent text of the response. The threefold reception of the mandate can likewise be observed.
The second part, the "Revelation," is divided into two. First, from "At that time, the Bhagavān... onwards, [the section on] being free from inversion. Second, from "Ānanda, although you...

onwards, [the section on] being free from conjunction. The first [of these two] is further divided into two: first, the introduction by the scribe, beginning with "At that time..."; second, the teaching spoken by the Tathāgata, beginning with "He addressed Ānanda... and so forth.

Regarding the beginning and middle [of the passage], "compassion" (*anukampā*) and so forth: the World-Honored One, seeing that Ānanda and the others had already said their minds were still not awakened and further said they were increasingly bewildered and distressed, thereupon exercised his unconditioned great compassion (*nirālamba-mahākaruṇā*) out of pity and sympathy for them.
Regarding "about to" and so forth: it is a vast, perfect illumination in which all are equally provisional; therefore, it is called "all *samādhis* and *dhāraṇīs*. This...
It is called "Dhāraṇī" because it can universally encompass all dharmas without dispersing them, and it can maintain all meanings without losing them.

What is now termed the "Great Dhāraṇī" encompasses all phenomena within the state of samādhi without exception, and maintains all their meanings without exception. Taken together, it is therefore called the Great Dhāraṇī of all samādhis.

The "wonderful path of cultivation" refers to that within *samādhi*, wherein the three thousand natures and marks, the ten realms and their thousand suchnesses, and the single provisional and simultaneous provisionality—all arise from the nature as cultivation.
Taking this as the path by which one penetrates, one spontaneously arrives at the great ocean of bodhi and nirvāṇa.
"Expounding" means to unfold, open, and explain. Although this first fascicle concludes here with what is called "refutation,"...
The deluded mind reveals true seeing; "seeing" here refers to the faculty of sight. This is entirely comprised of the two dharmas of form and mind, as explained within the context of *śamatha*.

When one reaches *samādhi*, however, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and the three categories [of six sense organs, six objects, and six consciousnesses] are none other than the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
This is precisely what is meant by the detailed exposition that form and mind together constitute the five aggregates—namely, "integrating form and opening up the mind. Furthermore,
To "expound and explain" means to analyze and elaborate upon form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*) so as to constitute the twelve bases (*āyatana*). This refers to analyzing form while subsuming mind.
Furthermore, to "expound and explain" form and mind so as to constitute the eighteen elements (*dhātu*) refers to analyzing both form and mind together. Hence, it is called "expounding.
"About to" (*jiang yu*) refers to the juncture between what has already occurred and what has not yet occurred. If one proceeds from this point, it belongs to the *samādhi* [section]; I fear...
This is also not yet the case. As it says below, "Regarding *śamatha*, the mind has still not been fully understood.

The Tathāgata’s intention was that he originally wished to explain the wondrous *samādhi*; however, because you have still not fully understood the mind of *śamatha*, he therefore spoke of the combination of inverted states to complete the matter of *śamatha*. This leads to the passage below: "Ānanda, you have still not..."
The section on "Clarifying the Departure" explains *samādhi*.
This is divided into three parts by the Tathāgata: first, the instruction to Ānanda and others to resolve their delusions; second, the admonition and permission beginning with "You now...";

and third, the correct exposition beginning with "All...". Regarding the first part: although you possess strong memory—*qiáng* (strong) should be pronounced in the level tone (*píngshēng*)—if one follows the text as it stands [it would be read differently].

The sound is also acceptable. Since you possess a powerful memory, you ought to generate understanding in accordance with what you hear, initiate practice based on that understanding, and enter through realization by means of practice;
only then will your extensive learning become effective. You do not act in this way, but merely increase your learning. Therefore it is said: "Although you... and so forth.
Because of your extensive learning, your mind has still not yet fully comprehended the subtle illumination of *śamatha*.

Furthermore, regarding "subtle and secret contemplation and observation": it is like the aforementioned destruction of the deluded vision that discriminates conditioned objects, as well as the destruction of the visual essence that perceives a second moon.
It is the state of perfect contemplation and perfect illumination, where all is stilled in true quiescence.

That which is destroyed is destroyed without being destroyed; that which is revealed is revealed without being revealed. Therefore, it is called "subtle and secret contemplation and observation. Within the section on the "Warning and Granting of Permission,"...

Regarding "all that is with outflows" (*sāsrava*): it is as Ānanda does today—reckoning the mind to be within and reckoning the seeing to be in the eye—and further reckoning such characteristics as being caused by conditions, being uncaused, or being natural.
All these are called "with outflows. This is also because one has not yet shattered the discrimination that relies on sense-objects, nor the "seeing-essence" (the second moon).

Because one has not shattered the reliance on sense-objects, one causes the cause to fall into the outflow of view-delusions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), and consequently causes the fruit to fall into the outflow of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the "fragmentary" [birth], as long as the essence of vision has not been shattered, one causes the cause to leak into ignorance and the fruit to leak into the transformation-death (vaiparītya-nirvāṇa).
As for the phrase "also causing them to be equal," it refers to the single clarity of *śamatha*, which causes sentient beings with outflows in future lives to rely upon this for cultivation.
Without falling into the conceptualizations of internal or external, nor into the characteristics of causes and conditions or spontaneity,
nor into the discrimination of objects or the vision of a second moon, the essence of the fruit of Bodhi is spontaneously realized.
The third section, "The Exposition of Correctness," is divided into three parts. First, from "All sentient beings... onwards, two types of deluded views are listed. Second, from "What are called...
onwards, the two types of deluded views are interrogated and explained. Third, from "Ānanda, I cause you to... onwards, the two types of deluded views are clarified together.
Regarding the first part, the listing, there are two types: individual karma and commonality; ancient commentators' interpretations of these also differ. Some say:

To claim that individual karma (*pratyeka-karma*) refers to the delusive seeing created by a single person, Ānanda, while collective karma (*sabhāga-karma*) refers to the delusive seeing created by many sentient beings—this explanation is incorrect.
The Sūtra merely speaks of "all sentient beings" and never makes a distinction between one and many.
Furthermore, to say that individual karma is spoken of from the perspective of the creator, while collective karma is spoken of from the perspective of the created—this too is incorrect.
The Sūtra simply states that it is due to two inversions; it never makes a distinction between subject and object.

Furthermore, some claim that "distinct karma" (*bipākakarma*) is spoken of in relation to the objective realm (*ālambana-viṣaya*), while "common lot" (*sabhāgatā*) is spoken of in relation to the essence of seeing (*darśana-śuddhi*). This is also incorrect.
From the first fascicle, where Ānanda requested, "Please bring forth the wondrous, luminous mind and open my path-eye," up until this fascicle, it says: "Thus, your mind-nature each has..."
That which is returned and that which is destroyed are the conceptualizations based on sense objects; these are the first six consciousnesses, namely the "branch-final" ignorance (*mūlamoha*).

From the passage in the *Treatise on the Origin of Humanity* where the Tathāgata says, "Although this vision is not the wondrous, brilliant, and pure mind," down to "when one sees the seeing, the seeing is not seeing," that which is destroyed is the "second moon"—the seeing-essence (*darśana-viśuddhi*), which is the eighth consciousness, namely the "root."
This is fundamentally ignorance. How could one reach this point and then again take the discrimination of objective conditions and the second moon as counterparts to the seeing-essence?
Now, "distinct karma" pertains to the time of creating karma and belongs to the cause; "common karma" pertains to the time of summoning retribution and belongs to the fruit.
This is because, within the cause, one creates the karma of deluded seeing, and upon the fruit, one experiences the retribution of deluded seeing.

Therefore, the text on common karma (*sabhāga-karma*) states: "Observing various inauspicious signs, such as two suns or two moons, one knows that while the causes created differ—this is called 'distinctive karma' (*bhinnakarma*)—the retribution received is not different; this is called 'commonality' (*sabhāgatā*). It is like when people commit wrongs;

although their specific acts differ, when they reach the place of punishment, the sentencing and imprisonment are invariably the same. Although what was discussed previously was for the sake of [the *ālaya-vijñāna*]...
When that which is difficult to see is seen, the essence of seeing (*darśana-śakti*) is likewise shattered. Yet, because it remains as yet unclarified, this is further elucidated.

If this essence of seeing were not shattered, then the commissioning of karma, the reaping of its retribution, and the coming and going within birth and death would all be nothing other than that [deluded mind];
for this reason, there is this single passage. Such is deluded seeing. As for the phrase "inverted discrimination" (*viparyāsa-vikalpa*), etc., it means that to lose the truth is called "inversion."
"Upside-down" (*viparyāsa*) refers to the recognition of the delusory as real; this is precisely affliction (*kleśa*). Since afflictions exist, one will inevitably create evil karma;
hence it is said, "arising in its own place. If evil karma is created, it will inevitably result in retribution; hence it is said, "revolving according to that karma.

Thus, the three—delusion, karma, and suffering—follow one another like a shadow follows a form, or like an echo accords with a sound. This is what was previously referred to as the seeds of karma arising spontaneously, like an evil... [text fragment].
This is a collective grouping. That [text] speaks of "spontaneity" (*svayambhū*); here it is stated as "the respective locations" and "their respective karmas.

This collectively clarifies that there has never been any deviation or discrepancy, nor any moment of abandonment or separation. The above constitutes the introductory heading; what follows, beginning with "What are they?", is the detailed enumeration, which is self-evident.

Next, the section on interrogation and explanation is divided into two parts: first, individual karma; second, common karma. Both include the posing of the inquiry and the subsequent explanation. Regarding the first:
as for what constitutes the posing of the inquiry, Ānanda departs from the explanation to pose it; thus the inquiry may be seen.

The second section, "Explanation of the Section on Manifestation," is divided into four parts: First, from "Ānanda" onwards, citing events to establish certainty; second, from "In your mind" onwards, analyzing and refuting based on meaning;
third, from "Therefore" onwards, concluding and demonstrating their falsity; fourth, from "As in the [previous] chapter" onwards, further clarifying through analogies.

Regarding the first part, the phrase "Just as in the world" and so forth is a citation of actual events rather than a metaphorical illustration. Although the word "just as" (yathā) is present, it should be interpreted as "as if" (tadyathā).
This is like looking [at something]. "Worldly people" is a metaphor for all sentient beings. "The eyes" is a metaphor for true wisdom (*tattvajñāna*).

"Red cataracts" is a metaphor for when true wisdom, in a single moment of non-awakening, turns into ignorance (*avidyā*); hence it is said, "the eyes have red cataracts. Once ignorance has been stirred, one enters the long night of birth and death;
therefore, "night" is used as a metaphor for this. "The lamp" is a metaphor for ultimate truth (*paramārthasatya*). Seeing the light of the lamp at night—

To illustrate: although that which is heard and seen throughout the long night of birth and death is nothing but ultimate truth, it is compared to the sight of a lamp’s light at night, wherein a separate circular shadow appears.

To illustrate that although what is heard and seen is entirely ultimate truth, not only is one unaware of this, but there is furthermore something else—namely, delusion—it is compared to the appearance of a separate circular shadow. This is further illustrated by the overlapping of the five colors. As for its...
Within the midst of falsehood, these arising and ceasing five aggregates are formed; therefore, they are illustrated by the analogy of the layering of the five colors.

This section on "Distinguishing Based on Meaning" also has two parts: first, "the seeing that is inseparable from the lamp," which refers to the passage beginning with "In your mind... and so forth; second, "the seeing that is separate from the lamp," which refers to the passage beginning with "Furthermore...
and so forth. Regarding the first part, the phrase "What do you think? is the Tathāgata’s word of inquiry and examination directed at Ānanda.
The meaning is this: within the long night of birth and death, you perceive upon the ground of ultimate reality a separate, illusory shadow—the form of the five aggregates arising and ceasing.
What is your intention regarding this? Therefore, it is asked: "What do you think? I shall now question you:
within the night of birth and death, as for that illusory light and color of the five aggregates perceived separately upon the ground of ultimate reality—is it not precisely [that very same thing]?
If there is this form within truth itself, or if there is this form within true vision itself, it is therefore said: "This night... (and so forth).
These are definitive statements. Ānanda subsequently refutes them: first he refutes that it is the lamp, and next he refutes that it is the vision.
Regarding the phrase "At the beginning and middle, if this... and so forth, the intended meaning is as follows: The form of the five aggregates of false delusion is itself the true principle.
However, since there is no person devoid of ignorance who can perceive this true principle, why is it that those who do not currently possess the red cataracts of ignorance do not see it?
It is only those with the red cataracts of ignorance who perceive these circular shadows of the false five aggregates. Since they have become...
The red cataract seen by one with ignorance is not something that can be known within the true principle of the lamp. Regarding these two [cases]:

if they were identical, the meaning would be this: if these five aggregates, which are illusory forms, were themselves the true seeing, then since that true seeing has already become the illusory forms of the five aggregates, there should no longer exist the false vision of the red cataract of ignorance.
Since that which is delusory has no self-substance and depends entirely upon the True, if there were no ignorance or deluded vision,
then what else could be called that "red cataract" capable of seeing the circular, illusory shadows of the five aggregates?
If it is indeed seen by the red cataract of ignorance, then it can be known that the illusory forms of the five aggregates exist not through true vision.

In this way, when one investigates using the lamp as the basis for seeing, nothing can be established. Next, regarding the investigation of seeing apart from the lamp, there should likewise be two definitive propositions:
"that which is conditioned but not the lamp is color" and "that which is not seeing is color. Their absence here is due to brevity.
First, one refutes [the view that the truth] is separate from the lamp; next, one refutes [the view that it is] separate from seeing. Regarding the first: "If these... and so forth.

Here, the lamp serves as the analogy for the True Principle (tattva), while the curtains, screens, and other items serve as the analogies for phenomena such as mountains and rivers. The intended meaning is that the five aggregates are illusory reflections;

if they were to exist apart from the lamp-like True Principle, they would not be the True Principle. Since they constitute the True Principle, then upon all phenomena such as curtains, tables, and couches, [it should likewise be present].

The five aggregates emerge as empty, false, and circular reflections. Now that the screens, curtains, and ritual tables have vanished, it can be known that these five eliminations of empty, false, and circular reflections do not exist apart from the ultimate truth. Regarding the subsequent section, "apart from seeing," and so forth:
The meaning is this: since they do not exist apart from true reality (*tattva*), they must likewise not exist apart from true seeing.
If there were five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as false, illusory reflections existing separately from true seeing, then they should not be illuminated by the deluded vision of ignorance (*avidyā*).
Because these delusions lack inherent substance and depend entirely upon true reality, the deluded eye of the present is originally identical to true seeing; thus, the five aggregates are illusory...
If illusory form exists apart from true seeing, it likewise should not be beheld by the illusory eye.
If it should not be beheld by the illusory eye, how is it that today the illusory shadow of the five aggregates is seen by those with the red cataract of ignorance?
Since it is seen by those with the red cataract of ignorance, the circular shadow of the illusory five aggregates is not [real].
It can be known that apart from the seeing of reality, there is nothing else; likewise, even when one seeks it apart from the lamp and the seeing, it is entirely unobtainable.
Within the section concluding the demonstration of falsity, the phrase "therefore, etc. concludes the preceding point that the false form of the five aggregates is identical to the lamp.
When one examines the seeing [of the lamp], it cannot be found apart from the lamp; when one further examines the seeing [of the lamp] itself, it likewise cannot be found.

Therefore, the phrase "For this reason, one should know" correctly demonstrates the reason why the false form of the five aggregates is like the seeing of the lamp—that is, that the seeing of the lamp cannot be found apart from the lamp, nor can the seeing of the lamp itself be found.
Although the form of the five aggregates is false, falsehood does not establish itself independently; it exists by virtue of the True.
There is. As it is said below, the five aggregates (pañca-skandha) are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous true nature of suchness (tathatā).

Therefore, it is said that "form truly exists within the lamp. However, these shadows of the false and illusory five aggregates, though said to truly exist within the ultimate truth, are nonetheless produced by the disease of vision caused by ignorance (avidyā).
Thus, one should know that the "disease of vision" constitutes the shadow; the capacity to see is deluded vision, and that which is seen...
Seeing these five aggregates: both the shadow that is seen and the seeing that perceives it are all illnesses caused by ignorance (*avidyā*).

Therefore, it is said that "the shadow and the seeing are both defects. Speaking in terms of the false delusions of ignorance, if one were to see clearly, then the shadow that is seen and the seeing that perceives it would both be illnesses and defects.
That such things are all illnesses and defects means that the person [who sees them as such] possesses true vision.
It is not that the disease itself is the optical aberration. Therefore, it is said that seeing the aberration is not the disease.

Thus, since it has been stated that while the forms truly reside in the lamp, the seeing of the disease constitutes the shadow, one should not say that the shadows of the five aggregates are identical to the true principle.

Nevertheless, although the seeing of the disease as a shadow occurs while the forms truly reside in the lamp, one likewise should not say that the shadows of the five aggregates exist apart from the true principle.
Since it has already been stated that what is seen is a visual defect and not a disease, one should not say that the shadow of the five aggregates is identical to true seeing.
Yet, because it is seen by one who is not diseased, one should likewise not say that the shadow of the five aggregates is distinct from true seeing.
Therefore, it is said: "In the end, one should never say... (and so forth). If this is the case, then all previous attempts to equate seeing with the lamp have proven untenable.
It is obtained. Yet, if one sets aside the lamp and seeks it through inference, it likewise cannot be obtained. Thus, the reason why the two [lamp and darkness] do not exist is not unclear.

This is further elucidated through four layers of analogy, divided into two parts: first, the establishment [of the analogy] such as "as the first," etc.; second, the application [to the subject] such as "this also," etc.
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the text], as for the phrase "like the second moon" and so forth:

it means that since the false form of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) cannot be identified with ultimate truth or true seeing and thus inferred to be "a lamp" or "seeing," nor can it be separated from ultimate truth or true seeing and thus inferred to be "not a lamp" or "not seeing"—
if one were to use a metaphor to illustrate this principle, it would be like the second moon, which is not the [actual] moon.

Its substance is not the reflection of the moon; therefore it is said to be "like a second moon," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "For what reason," this explains the grounds for why it is neither the substance nor the reflection.
The two phrases "this form" and "not this form" correspond to the aforementioned "it is the lamp" and "it is the seeing," and "not the lamp" and "not the seeing.
This is the literal phrasing; however, according to the sense of the passage, one should say: "it is the moon" and "it is the seeing."
It is apart from the moon and apart from seeing. Now, "form" (xing) replaces "moon," and "apartness" (li) replaces "non-being" (fei). These characters correspond to one another.
Since the second moon is produced by pressing upon the eye, a person of wisdom should not say that this is the form of the true moon or that it is seeing.
Although it is not the true moon, because it arises from pressing the eye while looking at the true moon, it closely approximates the true; thus, a person of wisdom [recognizes its nature].
Furthermore, one should not say that this is not the reflection of the true moon and thus is not seeing. In this way, it is known that one should not say "this is the moon" or "this is seeing.
Therefore, it is said to be "not the substance. Moreover, it is known that one should not say "it is not the moon" or "it is not seeing."
Therefore, it is said that it is not a reflection. Regarding the phrase "the same applies here" in the middle section:

this means that since the second moon is produced because of pressing on the eyes, one cannot say it is either the moon or the vision. Likewise, these five aggregates are entirely false and produced because of the red cataract of ignorance;
how then can one designate them, asking who is the lamp and who is the vision? Furthermore, regarding the second...
Although the moon is produced by the pressing of the eyes, it remains extremely close to the true moon; thus, one cannot say that it is separate from the moon or separate from the seeing.
Likewise, although the present five aggregates are false and illusory, being produced by the cataract of ignorance, they entirely depend upon the true substance.

How then could one further claim that "this is not the lamp" or "this is not the seeing"? Therefore, it is said: "This also... (and so forth). This is why it was stated previously that one should ultimately not say, "This is the lamp."
In this vision, there is that which is neither lamp nor vision. One can know that the five aggregates (pañcaskandha) and their delusory forms exist entirely due to the false vision of ignorance;
one perceives these five aggregates and their delusory forms precisely through the false vision of ignorance.
Thus, they cannot be said to be true principle or true vision, yet they also cannot be said to be not true principle or not true vision. As previously stated in the [Āgama]...
Ānanda said, "There is no such seeing," and the Tathāgata confirmed, "So it is, so it is.
Ānanda said, "There is no non-seeing," and the Tathāgata likewise confirmed, "So it is, so it is. Previously, he refuted the vision of the second moon;
now, he further clarifies the karmic causes of deluded vision by analogy. Therefore, the meaning of these two cases is identical.
The second explanation, the "Section on Shared Karma," is divided into four parts. First, the phrase "How so? poses the inquiry, which is self-evident.

Second, the section beginning with "Ānanda" provides the explanation, which is further divided into two. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, there is a general explanation of the land. Second, from "If again... onwards, there is a specific indication of adverse conditions. Within the first part:
the "Great Continent of Jambudvīpa" is one among the three thousandfold world systems. Its east-west extent and so forth are measured by the Great [Cakravāḍa].
This is discussed in terms of the [four] continents. As for "the rest" and so forth, this refers to everything within the trichiliocosm other than the great continents.

Regarding the second type, there are only two countries where the people of a single nation collectively experience adverse conditions; this precisely means that deluded views as causes invite deluded views as effects.
Details regarding the "halo," "fittingness," and so forth are fully explained in the *Yuan-tong-shu* (Commentary on Perfect Penetration).

The third section, "The Two Kinds of Deluded Vision Combined with the Brightness," is divided into two parts: first, the general heading beginning with "Ānanda" and below; second, the specific exposition beginning with "As it was...

and below. Regarding the first part, as for the phrase "I now," etc.: what has been investigated and explained thus far concerning the two kinds [of vision] has been discussed only by way of illustration.

The analogy of the dharma should be explained in combination. However, within the process of inquiry and explanation, one first treats the distinct cases and then the common ones. Now, in this combined explanation, it should likewise be so.
It is precisely when the inquiry and explanation of the common factors (*sabhāga*) are concluded that one should retreat from the common factors and advance to the distinct karma (*asabhāga*).

Thus, the analogy of the dharma should be explained in combination; hence it is said: "I now... (and so forth). From this, it is known that "advancing" means to bring forward, and "retreating" means to set aside.

The second part, the specific demonstration, also has two sections. First, "the departure and retreat of those [others] are the same while the advance is distinct. Second, "the departure and retreat of those [others] are distinct while the advance is the same.
The first of these also has two parts. First, the analogy of the advance, which refers to "those [others]" and so forth. Second, the combined explanation, which refers to "you" and so forth.

Regarding the first of these (the analogy of the advance), "those [others]" and so forth is the passage that restates the previous examples, establishes the certainty [of the argument], and provides the refutation by means of the dharma. Although it appears...
"Such as... [etc.]—this restates the previous point to conclude that within the illusory, the "form" (rūpa) actually resides in the lamp and other such objects.
However, "the vision," etc.—this restates the previous point to conclude the phrase regarding how, within the illusory, the vision is a cataract (*taimira*) rather than a disease.

The previous statement that "form actually resides in the lamp and other such objects" demonstrates that the illusory form of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is such that the vision cannot be found within the lamp, nor can it be found apart from the lamp. Furthermore, the previous "vision"...
The phrase "the cataract is not the disease" indicates that the illusory and empty colors of the five aggregates are, in their very nature, the true seeing, which cannot be apprehended;

yet apart from this true seeing, they likewise cannot be apprehended. Therefore, the text here restates this by saying, "Although it appears... (and so forth). The meaning is the same as that [previous passage], which can be seen by examining it.
However, while the colors previously mentioned actually exist within the lamp, the present statement says they are not produced by color. The former pointed to the entirety of delusion.
This is true; it is simply that the false cannot be apprehended at present. If one correlates this with what follows below, "those" (彼等) serves as the example for "you all" (汝等).
"Though manifest" (雖現) and so forth serves as the example for "seeing with" (見與). "The eye-disease" (眚) and so forth serves as the example for "awakened seeing" (覺見).
Furthermore, "seeing" (見) and so forth serves as the example for "that which is awakened to" (覺所). Within these two combined clarifications, there are again two parts.
First is the formal application (*upanaya*), which is the analogy: "It is like your going. Second is the conclusion (*nigamana*), which is:

"This is indeed going. Regarding the first [the formal application]: the analogy "it is like your... corresponds to the preceding "it is like that..."; thus, the meaning of both the four sections concerning "this" and "that" is fully revealed.

The phrase "it is like your... below applies the analogy to the preceding "it is like that...". The phrase "seeing and... corresponds to the preceding "although manifest...". The phrase "perceiving seeing... corresponds to the preceding "the cataract... and so forth.
...is equal. "The awakening of what is below corresponds to what is above; thus 'seeing' and so forth are equal. Such divisions and correspondences—whether by analogy or by synthesis—are not unclear.

Regarding the first point: "All are produced by the disease of seeing since beginningless time" means that although what was seen above differs in terms of the environment (*bhājanaloka*) and its inhabitants (*sattvaloka*), it is entirely produced by your Ānanda’s own deluded seeing of ignorance since beginningless time.
[This is] the Ear. Thus, it is as described above. Next, regarding the middle section:

"Originally, my enlightened awareness perceived the cataract upon the object" means that although the aforementioned seeing and its conditions—the seer and the seen—appear to be actual objects, when investigated thoroughly, [they are not].
All these are the pathological defects of the visual essence (*dṛṣṭi-śuddhi*) as it perceives objects within the true nature of the wondrously enlightened, luminous mind.
This is because the deluded perception of the visual essence is, in its entirety, the wondrously luminous true substance itself.

Thus, one should know that the "seeing" mentioned above—the seeing that discriminates conditioned objects—is also the visual essence; the "seeing" mentioned below—the seeing of that which is seen—is likewise only the visual essence. Therefore...

This corresponds to the "manifestation" [in the previous summary]. Among the three [categories], "awareness and vision are the cataract" means that the essence of vision within the mind of wondrous, enlightened clarity is itself the cataract.
"Fundamental awareness," etc., refers to the substance of fundamental awareness. "Awareness of conditions" refers to the conditions perceived by the essence of vision;
it is the entire substance of wondrous clarity and is not the cataract. Therefore, this corresponds to the "cataract" [in the previous summary].

[The text continues: "...and so forth. Regarding the four [points], as for "that which is equalized by awakening" (*jue-suo-deng*): the character "awakening" (*jue*) in the first phrase refers to true awakening (*zhen-jue*), while the "awakening" in "that which is awakened to" (*suo-jue*) refers to the essence of seeing (*jian-jing*).
Because the essence of seeing is afflicted by the disease of delusion, yet true awakening itself does not fall into that disease or delusion;
this is why it corresponds to the preceding phrase, "yet the seeing... and so forth. In the second section, the summary and response, regarding the phrase "this is indeed... and so forth: because...
Ānanda had previously raised a doubt, saying: "Now, hearing again that 'the seeing of seeing is not seeing' increases my confusion and distress; this is why I have come to this point.
Since he sought to clarify the deluded vision of individual karma through this analogy of the Dharma, [the Buddha] replied:
"This is indeed... (and so forth). The meaning is: regarding your previous doubt that "the seeing of seeing is not seeing," now, through this analogy of the Dharma, it has been clarified; not only...

When one truly perceives that which is real, the essence of seeing (*darśana-śakti*) is also entirely real. Furthermore, it is not only the deluded perception conditioned by objects that must be eliminated;

the essence of seeing that perceives the "second moon" is likewise eliminated. How, then, could there still be any discerning awareness—such as hearing or other senses—conditioned by objects that could be obtained?
Therefore, it says, "This is indeed," and so forth. The following section is the formal conclusion. The meaning is: for this reason...

Therefore, you should know that although what you perceive, Ānanda, contains various distinctions between the holy and the ordinary, as well as between the primary and secondary bodies, the capacity for such seeing is entirely the cataract of deluded vision caused by ignorance.
Yet, this is not the true seeing of one who is free from the disease of vision and its cataracts.
Therefore it is said: "For this reason" (and so forth). The passage beginning with "That seeing" below explains why it is not the case that one sees the optical aberration (*taimirika*).

Because that true seeing—the wondrous, subtle, and brilliant nature—is in reality not the seeing-essence of a diseased aberration, I, the Tathāgata, do not designate the seeing-essence as true seeing.
Therefore it is said: "That seeing" (and so forth). Thus, one should know what is clarified by the "distinctive karma" (*bhedakarma*).
This is the karmic cause produced by deluded vision.

Second, the distinction between retreating and advancing, and the commonality of their shared portion (*sabhāgatā*). First, the analogy for advancing; second, the combined explanation. Within the first section on the analogy for advancing:

"As with those" uses the commonality to illustrate individual karma. "First, illness and so forth" refers to one who possesses the specific defect of red cataracts (*taimirika*) by way of individual karma.

Human beings are like a single nation that collectively experiences adverse conditions due to their shared *sabhāgatā* (homogeneity). The analogy between the individual and the nation is thus established.

Furthermore, that which is seen by one person’s deluded error and that which is seen as an inauspicious omen by an entire nation are both created by the karma of the visual essence (*darśana-śakti*). It is from this that pestilence and evil arise. To further investigate this...
This arises entirely from the false perceptions produced by ignorance since beginningless time; therefore it says, "That perception... (and so forth).
Within the second section, "Combining the Illumination," there are two parts: first, the formal application of the analogy of Yama and below, which is the actual correlation;

second, "If one can... and below, which is the concluding response. Regarding the first part, the analogy of Yama and so forth: first, the single country is used as an analogy for Jambudvīpa in the south, and next, it is analogized to [Sahā]...

"Vā. Once again, the ten directions are exemplified, proceeding from the narrow to the broad. Whether this direction or the ten directions, whether the primary retribution or the secondary environment, all are seen as being summoned and evoked by karma.

"The same is below" means that the aforementioned lands—the secondary environment—and sentient beings—the primary retribution—are all produced from the fundamentally enlightened, originally luminous, and non-outflowing wondrous mind. This is what is seen.
"Listening and so forth" correctly clarifies the characteristics of that which is produced. There is nothing else;

it arises because from within the wondrous mind of enlightened clarity (*jue-ming*), the stillness becomes adhered to and vision is emitted, continuing until the stillness becomes adhered to and cognition is emitted—this is how the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) are produced.

Furthermore, the essence of vision reflects forms, continuing until the essence of cognition reflects phenomena—this is how the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*) are produced. "Harmonious conjunction" and so forth refers to enlightened clarity... [text continues].
That which is equal is true; seeing and hearing and so forth are false. This is one perspective. However, if we discuss it further:

the clarity of awareness may also be viewed as the essence of seeing. Thus, this essence of seeing is the delusion of arising and ceasing, whereas the untainted, wondrous mind is the truth of original clarity.
Through the mutual conjunction of these two—the one true and the one false—the retributions of birth and death are consequently formed. This is...
The union of the true and the false brings about the birth and death of transformation (*pariṇāma-vaśitā-maraṇa*).

If one considers the faculties of the six sense organs and the objects of the six sense fields—whether it be the faculties or the objects—the mutual conjunction of these two results in the retribution of birth and death;

this is the birth and death of fragmentation (*bheda-maraṇa*) brought about by the conjunction of faculties and objects. Therefore, whether in this world or in the worlds of the ten directions, whether regarding the lands of the environment (*niśraya-vipāka*), [the same principle applies].

If sentient beings who are the primary retribution are likewise identical in their awakened clarity (and so forth), then it can be known that such commonality of perception is not something that does not arise from being summoned and elicited by the karma of seeing.

One should know that this sentence may also serve as a direct answer to Ānanda’s request for instruction on the purity and clarity of the awakened mind. Therefore, it says: "Awakened clarity is without outflows" (and so forth). 2.
In the concluding response, the phrase "if one can," etc., is the direct answer to Ānanda’s prior request to "reveal to us the clarity and purity of the awakened mind.
Thus, after arriving at this point and following the established pattern of the teaching, he finally replies: "If one can... (and so forth).
However, prior to these words "if one can," it should have been stated: "Since birth and death have already been formed, if one wishes to sever them, one should..."
First, the causes are eliminated; hence it says, "If one can... (and so forth). This is merely an explanatory statement based on the preceding passage.
The phrase "all harmonious conditions" refers to the two instances of harmony: that between the true and the false, and that between the sense organs and their objects.

Conditions involving the true and the false pertain to the eight consciousnesses, while conditions involving the sense organs and their objects pertain to the six consciousnesses. If the eight consciousnesses of the true and the false are separated, then transformation occurs.

The causes of death are eliminated. When the six consciousnesses are separated from their faculties and objects, the causes of birth-and-death within the realm of segmented existence (*paricchinna-saṃsāra*) are eliminated.
Thus, the earlier statement "if one can" and the later statement "then again" further demonstrate that the cause of birth-and-death is precisely this conjunction and so forth.
The conjunction [of conditions] and so forth is the very root of the perception of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). When the cause of birth and death is extinguished, that is the perfection of *bodhi*.
When the fruit of birth and death is severed, that is the profound entry into *nirvāṇa*. Therefore, it is said below: "perfection" (and so forth).

Following "perfection," the text answers the question regarding the clarity and purity of the awakened mind (*bodhicitta*). The meaning is: if you wish for the Tathāgata to reveal the clarity and purity of the awakened mind, there is no other way.
One should, in all cases, distance oneself from all conditions of conjunction. By eliminating the causes of birth and death, one attains the realization of nirvana through bodhi.
The awakening of the mind to its luminous purity is fully realized herein. Because bodhi is self-attained, it is called "perfectly fulfilled bodhi.
Because nirvana is self-realized, it is called "neither arising nor ceasing. Since bodhi is attained, it is inherently undefiled by afflictions. Therefore—
It is said that the fundamentally pure mind is the realization of *nirvāṇa*; it does not itself undergo the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, it is called "fundamental enlightenment is eternally abiding. Is this not precisely the clarity and purity of the awakened mind?

Within the request for instruction, seeing the seer as not being a seer and the clarity and purity of the awakened mind are primary; all combinations and non-combinations are secondary. Thus, regarding—
The two kinds of false views answer the primary request concerning the seeing of seeing and non-seeing—the inquiry into the pure and luminous nature of the awakened mind.

What follows below answers the secondary request concerning their conjunction and non-conjunction. Thus, there is indeed a sequential order between the question and the answer, and between the primary and the secondary.

The second [section], "Ānanda, although you have departed," concerns the text on departing from the combination. It is divided into two parts: first, the restatement of what was previously asked, namely "although you...
and so forth; second, the actual refutation, namely "I now... and so forth. Regarding the first part, as for "although you... and so forth:
This refers to what was stated earlier in the section on the inquiry arising from doubt:

"As the Buddha, the World-Honored One, has proclaimed for our sakes the nature of causes and conditions as well as spontaneity (*svabhāva*)," and so forth. This refers to that which he had already realized; now, specifically citing what he had realized, it says, "Although you... and so on.
The "originally enlightened essence" (*jueyuan*) is precisely the "essence of seeing" (*jianjing*). As it is said: "The essence of seeing is originally luminous."

The second part, the actual refutation, is divided into two sections. First, from "I shall now go" onwards, the refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*) is presented. Second, from "O White One" onwards, the refutation of non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*) is presented.

The first section is further divided into two parts. First, the dismissal of doubt, which is self-evident. Second, the actual refutation, which begins with "If that were so, you... This is further divided into two parts.

First, the refutation of conjunction (*saṃyoga*); second, the subsequent refutation of union (*saṃghāta*). Regarding the analytical refutation of conjunction: because the meanings of conjunction and union are distinct, they are differentiated.
For example, when water and soil are mixed together, this constitutes conjunction; when a box and its lid fit perfectly, this constitutes union. Therefore, they are analyzed and refuted separately.
The intent of the analysis of causes and conditions is the same as before. The initial refutation of "harmony" is twofold: first, the determination [of the subject], which refers to you all;
second, the refutation [of the object], which refers to light and so forth. Regarding the first: the term "wondrously pure seeing-essence" (*jijing*) refers precisely to the seeing-essence.

Previously, when analyzing the act of seeing itself, it was once revealed through refutation that this is indeed the true seeing; therefore, it is called the "wondrously pure seeing-essence. Second...

The refutation consists of two parts: first, the refutation of the conjunction of light and so forth; second, the application of that [refutation] to darkness and other objects below. The first part [the refutation of conjunction] further has four sections:

first, the refutation of intermixture; second, the refutation of identity through separation; third, the refutation of partiality and totality; and fourth, the refutation of the loss of intrinsic nature.
Regarding the first section, "intermixture," the phrase "if light and so forth" means that light does not illuminate itself.

It is through seeing that clarity is revealed; therefore, it is said that "observing clarity, clarity manifests. Now, seeing and clarity may seem to possess a sense of blending, yet seeing has no physical substance—how could they intermingle?

Furthermore, seeing and clarity can be clearly distinguished; it is simply because one uses the faculty of seeing to perceive the clarity of the object that their distinct characteristics can be discerned.
If one were to claim they blend or intermingle, what kind of form or image would result? What form...
Since an elephant cannot be obtained [in this manner], it follows that there is no such thing as the union of seeing and light. Second, if they were separate, then seeing would be possible;
third, regarding the point that "seeing must occur within the midst of the half-full and half-empty," the intended meaning is this:

just as clay and water can only be considered a mixture when each constitutes exactly half, how could seeing—the seer and the seen—and light all being perfectly complete (full) ever constitute a mixture?

Regarding the four losses of their essential nature (*prakṛti*), "the seeing and the equal" refers to the fact that the seeing which is capable of perceiving and the clarity which is the object perceived are not identical.
