If these two become intermingled, they lose their respective natures as the perceiver and the clarity of the perceived; this is what is meant by "name" and "letter."
If that which can see is mixed with that which is seen, then the names of "seer" and "seen" are lost.
If that which is seen is mixed with that which can see, then the names of the "seen" and its "designation" are likewise lost. Therefore, it is said that seeing must be equal [to what is seen].

Since the designations of subject and object are lost through this mixture, to claim that "seeing and clarity are in harmony" is not correct. Thus it is said: "Mixture leads to loss," and so forth. This principle may be applied to other objects as well.

[This] is known. Second, the refutation of the combination [of light and darkness] also has two parts. First, the refutation of that which is determinately visible; second, the refutation of the other cases. Furthermore, there are two [sub-sections]: first, the refutation of the conjunction of light and so forth;
second, the application of this to other objects, such as darkness and so forth. Regarding the first of these: "Since one does not see light and so forth" refers to its—
It is simply that one cannot discern that light is not darkness; the other two cases may be understood by analogy with this.
Second, the refutation of non-conjunction is divided into two parts: first, the inquiry and request; second, the refutation through reasoning, beginning with the Buddha’s words. Regarding the first:

the "source of cognition" (*jue-yuan*) is the visual essence, which is the sense organ (*indriya*); the various external conditions are the objects (*viṣaya*); and mental reflections and deliberations are consciousness (*vijñāna*).—Ānanda.

Having been refuted regarding the notion of conjunction (*saṃyoga*), he further resorts to the calculation of non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*); thus, he raises a doubt by asking whether the triad of sense organ, object, and consciousness is not in conjunction.
This section on the refutation through reasoning has two parts: first, "The Buddha said," etc., which restates the doubt; second, "I further," etc., which is the actual refutation.
The restatement of the doubt is clear. The actual refutation is divided into two: first, the refutation of non-conjunction; second, "Furthermore, wondrous... [the refutation of conjunction].

The refutation of non-conjunction has two parts. The first [part] also has two: first, the determination that it is visible; second, the refutation, which also has two: first, the refutation of non-aggregation;

second, the refutation of other objects by analogy with the preceding darkness—all of which can be understood. The refutation of non-conjunction also has two: first, the determination; second, the refutation. The refutation also has two:
first, the formal refutation of non-conjunction with light; second, the refutation of other cases by analogy with the preceding darkness.
The objects are all visible. This concludes the response regarding *śamatha*. From "Ānanda, you still...
onwards is the second part, the text responding to *samādhi*. It is divided into two sections: first, a general summary; second, a detailed exposition.
The first section is further divided into two: first, a brief clarification, which refers to "Ānanda and others"; second, an extensive manifestation, which refers to "In this way... and so forth.

Furthermore, regarding the initial brief clarification: "You have not yet understood," etc., means that what you have heard thus far has only elucidated *śamatha* (calm abiding) with respect to the two phenomena of mind and vision;
the five aggregates (*skandha*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) have not yet been fully expounded.
Therefore, it is said, "You have not yet understood. As for "all floating dust" [phenomena], all dharmas arise and perish, and as they perish and arise, they are utterly devoid of fixed stability.

It is merely like the fluttering and swaying of motes of dust. Regarding "all illusory and transformative appearances": in the Western Land (India), there were great illusionists who used illusory drugs to conjure men, women, oxen, horses, and the like.
As for "transformations," beings such as devas and ṛṣis, having attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), can likewise manifest various wondrous and extraordinary forms.
Other sūtras explain the ten similes in detail; the first is said to be "like... [the reflection of the moon in water].
"Illusion. Later it is said to be "like a transformation. In between there are further examples such as reflections in a mirror, the moon in water, and flowers in the sky;
here, the first and last are cited, hence the term "illusion-transformation" (māyā-nirmāṇa).

Regarding such characteristics of illusion and transformation, the wise recognize them as being illusory and transformative, whereas the foolish take them to be true and real. Thus, there are no phenomena that do not resemble illusion and transformation. Therefore—

The term "all" (*zhù*) refers to illusory transformations (*huàn huà*). In the preceding passage, it says "floating dust is called 'all,'" whereas here it says "illusory transformations are called 'all phenomena' (*zhū xiàng*)," which serves as a corresponding response.

The two phrases "arising in their own place" (*dāng chù chū shēng*) mean "in that very moment" (*dāng niàn*); "immediately" (*suí jí*) implies "at that very time. The character "transform" (*biàn*) is merely a stylistic device;
it means that while deluded thoughts may not arise, should they do so, they arise in that very moment. This is as described below regarding "causes and conditions" (*yīn yuán*).

This refers to their conjunction and so forth. As long as deluded thoughts do not depart, they persist; once they depart, they are extinguished wherever they go, as in what follows regarding the separation of causes and conditions.
Regarding the phrase "illusory falsehoods are called characteristics": this refers to the aforementioned arising in one place and perishing in another.

Such arising and ceasing are merely illusory transformations and false fabrications that possess these appearances; hence it is said, "in this very place" and "following along with every place. As the preceding text states:
"The seer, the conditions for seeing, and the perceived appearances are like flowers in the sky—they have never existed from the beginning. As the subsequent text states:
"Observing these appearances, they are fundamentally false and cannot be pointed out or described; it would be like attempting to gather the flowers of the empty sky to tie them into a garland."
The fruit is empty; therefore, it is said that illusory falsehood is designated as "phenomena. Regarding all dharmas, such is the nature of their false appearances.
As for the true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, although it is said to arise, within it there is that which does not arise—namely, True Emptiness.
Although it is said that they are extinguished, there is within them something that is inherently not extinguished; this is what is called "wondrous existence" (*miaoyou*).
It does not exist apart from these illusory and delusive appearances, but is precisely these very illusory and delusive appearances themselves.

Therefore, it is said that "their nature is such. As the preceding passage states: "This seeing and its objects are originally the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of bodhi. As the subsequent passage [states]:

It says: "Contemplate that the fundamental nature is originally true, being solely the wondrous, truly luminous, wondrously enlightened, and luminous mind. Therefore it is said: 'Its nature is truly the essence of wondrous enlightenment and luminosity.
Regarding this passage, it may be divided into the extensive and the concise; though the texts differ, their meaning is in fact no different.
This [passage] stating "all floating dust" (and so forth) is precisely what is stated below as "in this manner, even unto... and so on. This refers to its "nature."
(As stated above). This refers to the subsequent passage beginning with "Not realizing," etc.

Part Two: Extensively Revealing [the Meaning] has two sections. First, the forward deduction starting with "In this way," etc. Second, the reverse deduction starting with "Unequally," etc. Within the first section:
the phrase "In this way" below designates the names of all superficial objects; the phrase "causes and conditions" below sets forth the characteristics of all superficial objects.

The harmony of causes and conditions constitutes all phenomena (*dharmas*). To speak briefly of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), they all arise because sentient beings, since beginningless time, have grasped the matter of the four great elements and stored it within the field of the eight consciousnesses as their direct cause (*upādāna-hetu*).

Furthermore, they rely upon the two drops of red and white fluids from the union of parents as their remote condition (*pratyaya*). From this, the matter of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) is formed.
As for the body: because its causes and conditions come together, it is called "conjunction. Because birth occurs therein, it is called "birth.
Although it is said that there is birth, it arises entirely from delusion; therefore, it is called "delusive. This birth is as previously stated: "arising in its own place.
As for the separation of causes and conditions: since this body exists, one cannot avoid having a lifespan of varying length.
If a cause or condition undergoes even a single moment of separation, it is termed "extinction. Because it arises from delusion, it is said that "delusion is termed extinction.
This is as described above regarding "extinction according to circumstances. Viewing these together, they correspond to what was stated above:
"illusory falsehoods are called phenomena. Regarding the phrase "next, [they] are by no means equal," this refers to the fact that the illusory marks of arising and ceasing are fundamentally...

This is fundamentally the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. It is only because sentient beings are deluded that it remains unopened, and because they are obscured that they do not awaken.
They fail to realize at all that within the Tathāgatagarbha there is no arising and ceasing, nor any coming and going.

Although it is said that "arising conditions arising," within the Tathāgatagarbha, arising has never actually arisen. Although it is said that "ceasing conditions ceasing," within the Tathāgatagarbha...
Extinction has never been extinguished. Although it is called the "aspect of departure," as for the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, there is nowhere to which it departs.
Although it is called the "aspect of arrival," as for the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, there is no source from which it comes. Therefore it is said: "By no means... (and so forth).
The Tathāgatagarbha possesses both innate virtues (*prakṛti-guṇa*) and cultivated virtues (*bhāvanā-guṇa*); if one were to speak further, there are also realized virtues (*sākṣāt-kriyā-guṇa*).
Although these three are not identical, they equally possess the general name "Tathāgatagarbha" (Buddha-nature) as it accords with reality. This is inherently possessed and not obtained from without;
therefore, it is called the "original suchness Tathāgatagarbha. The section beginning with "permanently abiding" (changzhu) correctly reveals the essence of the Tathāgatagarbha.
That which is without arising or ceasing is called "constant. That which has no coming or going is called "abiding. That which is free from darkness and obscurity is called "wondrously luminous.
That which does not shift or change is called "immovable. If it is without even the slightest defect, it is called "perfectly round.

From its lack of arising and ceasing up to its lack of defect—all such states are ultimately empty and false; that which is called "true" is beyond them. Furthermore, that which is neither one nor different is called "suchness" (*tathatā*).
Furthermore, it is neither separate from arising and ceasing, coming and going, nor even from defects and the like;

yet, its very essence is eternally abiding, pervasive, and perfect. This is called the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Such is the analysis according to the literal meaning of the characters.

If explained according to the intended meaning, it is as clarified in the following passage: "All dharmas are both identical and non-identical, and both non-identical and non-non-identical, being neither identical nor non-identical. Now...
The phrase "eternally abiding wondrous clarity" (*nitya-sthita-prabhāsvara*) signifies that all phenomena are simultaneously identical [to it]. This is what is meant by the statement:
"The Tathāgatagarbha is originally luminous; the mind is wondrous. It is simultaneously identical with all phenomena.

The myriad phenomena of the universe are naturally and perfectly manifested, none of which fail to abide eternally, thereby constituting "wondrous existence" (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*). Thus, the three titles and four virtues of the Buddhas are simultaneously identical and constitute this wondrous existence.

The bodhisattva’s practices from giving up to wisdom are likewise simultaneously and wondrously present. The two vehicles’ Four Noble Truths and Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are likewise simultaneously and wondrously present.
Even the mundane heavens’ five aggregates, three categories, and dharmas of arising and ceasing are likewise simultaneously and wondrously present.
This is what is meant by: "When one is established, all are established; the ten realms are all established together. Thus...

This is the inconceivable, perfectly interfused conventional truth; it is the provisional contemplation (*parikalpita-śamatha*) of inconceivable, perfect interfusion. Therefore, it is said to be "eternally abiding, wondrously luminous.
Furthermore, the phrase "now immovable and all-pervading" means that with respect to all phenomena, there is neither identity nor separation.

This is precisely what is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrously luminous source of the mind. Regarding all phenomena, it is neither identical nor separate—this is the simultaneous negation and illumination (*samvṛti-satya* and *paramārtha-satya*).
Equanimity is free from both identity and difference; it is non-dual and immovable. Thus one achieves the Middle Way.

Therefore, among all things—from the Buddhas' three titles and four virtues down to the ordinary person's five aggregates and three categories of phenomena, including their arising and ceasing—there is not a single thing that does not simultaneously embody both identity and difference within this Middle Way.
This is what is meant by "one encompassing all" and "the ten realms being encompassed together," which is inconceivable.
This deliberates upon the Middle Truth of Perfect Interfusion; it is the inconceivable Middle Contemplation of perfect interfusion. Therefore, it is said that "it is immovable yet all-pervading.
Furthermore, the single phrase "the wondrous True Suchness-nature" is entirely non-affirmative. This is what is called the Tathāgatagarbha, the fundamentally wondrous, original mind.
Regarding all phenomena, it is entirely non-affirmative; before one's very eyes, not a single speck of dust among the myriad dharmas can be established. It is not otherwise.

Suchness (tathatā) constitutes its ultimate emptiness (śūnyatā). Therefore, from the Three Titles and Four Virtues of the Buddhas down to the five aggregates (skandha), three categories (dhātu-āyatana-vijñāna), and the phenomena of arising and ceasing of ordinary beings—there is not a single one that is not both "neither-is-nor-is-not" and is ultimate emptiness. This is what is meant by: when one is extinguished, all are extinguished;
when the ten realms are simultaneously extinguished, this is the inconceivable, perfectly interfused True Truth (paramārtha-satya). It is inconceivable and perfect.
This is the contemplation of emptiness by Tánrǒng. Therefore, it is called the "wondrous nature of True Suchness" (*tathatā*). Is this not, indeed, the ontological essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*?
Hence, it is said: "The fundamental *tathāgatagarbha*" (and so forth). The first phrase under the heading "the nature is truly" is likewise another name for the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Since all phenomena are the *tathāgatagarbha*, if one discusses them horizontally, they pervade the ten directions.
Regarding the realms (*dhātu*): what coming or going can be found? If one discusses this vertically, penetrating to the profound source of the Three Truths, what birth and death can be found?
Furthermore, the suchness of sentient beings and the suchness of the Tathāgata are a single suchness without a second;
what further delusion or awakening could there be? Thus it is said, "The nature is true" (and so forth). One should know that this passage may also be clarified in this manner.
[This is] false. [The phrase] "truly" below does not manifest the true nature;

"truly" below serves as a concluding indication. Second, the detailed exposition is divided into four parts, namely: the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), the twelve bases (*āyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*dhātu*).

Regarding the first, the five aggregates, there are two sections: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. Within the first section: "The five aggregates" are also called the five *skandhas*. As for *skandha*, it means—

"Accumulation" (*skandha*) is its meaning; "aggregate" (*skandha*) takes "covering" as its meaning. If one distinguishes them by way of merit and fault, they are like the three paths and the three obstructions.
For instance: that which is solid and obstructive is form (*rūpa*); that which experiences is sensation (*vedanā*); that which perceives characteristics is perception (*saṃjñā*);

that which flows and shifts is formations (*saṃskāra*); and that which discerns is consciousness (*vijñāna*). These are called the five aggregates (*pañca-skandhāḥ*). If one refers back to the general heading mentioned above, these are what is clarified by the two characters "five aggregates."
This refers to all floating dust-like phenomena and such illusory appearances as those mentioned above.

The two phrases beginning with "Fundamentally [it is] thus" refer to the true nature of these things—whether they are equal or unequal—and their ultimate reality. Now, the text raises a general inquiry;
although the wording is brief, its meaning is comprehensive and leaves nothing out. Subsequent sections should be understood by this same principle.

The second section, the detailed explanation, consists of five parts, which explain form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). First, the explanation of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is divided into three parts:

first, citing examples to illustrate the principle, as in "For example" and so forth; second, refuting [the notion] by means of those examples, as in "These various" and so forth; third, concluding by showing their falsity, as in "Therefore" and so forth.

The second [section on the remaining aggregates] also has two parts: first, establishing the reasoning; second, the actual refutation. Within the first [of these], there is the following passage: "There is a person... and so forth.
The same applies to all subsequent sections; they will not be fully set forth here. It is said that citing examples is merely to distinguish them from metaphors.

Taking the pure eyes of sentient beings as an example illustrates the capable-observing true wisdom (*tathatājñāna*). Taking the observation of a clear and bright sky as an example illustrates the true principle (*tattva*) being observed—namely, observing the principle of suchness (*tathatā*) with the wisdom of suchness.
The single, vast empty sky illustrates the non-duality of wisdom and principle. It is utterly devoid of...
There is an analogy for the absence of the characteristics of the nine realms. The above illustrates the True [Nature]. "That person" below illustrates the arising of delusion from the True.

"Because there is nothing" means because there is no cause. "Not moving the pupils" refers to gazing straight ahead. This illustrates the absence of a cause and the failure to take True Wisdom as one's object of contemplation.
"Staring until weariness arises" means that because of this straight gaze, weariness is produced; "weariness" is synonymous with illness.
For example, a single moment of non-awakening is inverted into ignorance (*avidyā*). Because one does not illuminate the principle with true wisdom, ignorance is able to arise.

The separate perception of flowers in the empty sky serves as an analogy for how, when there is ignorance regarding the true principle, one perceives the false flowers of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) within it.
Furthermore, all manner of delusory and chaotic non-characteristics serve as an analogy for the aggregate of form.

When there is no arising, the characteristics of the nine realms immediately manifest. The above serves as an illustration; the two phrases concerning the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) merely clarify the principle.
As for the statement "the aggregate of form is likewise," its meaning is explained by applying the principle to the illustration provided.

Thus, one knows that the aggregate of form is fundamentally the true reality (*tattva*), yet it arises due to the single thought-moment of ignorance (*avidyā*) of sentient beings. The same applies to the [remaining] four aggregates below.

However, there are two parts to the refutation by means of analogy. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, the principle is established; second, from "In this way" onwards, the actual refutation. Regarding the first:
as for these various illusory flowers and so forth, according to correct reasoning, they are fundamentally neither the sky nor the eyes.
Therefore, it is said below: "How could they be a clear sky? They exist only because of ignorance; they truly do not belong to the clear and bright eye."

The middle section may also be divided into two parts: first, refuting that it is space; second, refuting that it is the eyes. Regarding the first part, it is already clear. As for the latter, one should argue in reverse:
"Ānanda, you do not allow another Ānanda to exist within you; how then could empty space allow the arising and ceasing of the flower-appearance?"
Since the characteristics of the flower cannot arise or cease, how could there be any coming or going of the flower?
As there is no coming or going, how can it be said that the flower comes from space? Thus, one knows that the principle of the flower coming from space is untenable.

Next, regarding the passage "the eyes should be without cataracts," one should supplement it by saying: "If the eyes were without cataracts, the flowers would have to obscure space. Then, he continues: "How then [could they appear] in clear weather?"
"Empty and termed 'pure eye'": this is an illustration based on using a pure eye to observe a clear, bright sky; that is to say, using *tathatājñāna* (such-wisdom) to illuminate *tathatā* (suchness).

Originally, there were no color-aggregates (*rūpaskandha*) or the delusory flowers [of cataracts]. Now, wishing to break through them, one uses wisdom and principle to manifest them. One should also argue in reverse:
"Since the clear, bright sky is termed the 'clear and pure eye,' how could there be flower-like cataracts in the eye? Furthermore—
It obscures space; yet, since it does not obscure space, how could it obscure the eye? If it obscures the eye, how can there be seeing?
Since the eye cannot be seen, how can [the flowers] enter or exit from the eyes? Since they do not enter or exit, how can the flowers emerge from the eyes?
Thus one knows that the principle of the flowers emerging from the eyes is untenable. Because they neither come from space nor emerge from the eyes, therefore, as before—
He said, "These various floating flowers do not come from the void, nor do they emerge from the eyes. Regarding the threefold demonstration:
as for the phrase "therefore," since they have neither come from the void nor emerged from the eyes, these flowers are illusory.
For this reason, one should know that the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is likewise illusory. Why? Because it was originally non-existent.
Regarding causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*): they are not only fundamentally neither causes nor conditions, but also fundamentally neither spontaneous (*svabhāva*).
Since they are neither causes nor conditions and yet not spontaneous, they are solely the wondrous true suchness-nature (*tathatā-svabhāva*) of the Tathāgata-garbha.

All instances of analytical refutation (*bhaṅga*), inverse characteristics (*pratīpa-lakṣaṇa*), and the demonstration of the meaning of falsity (*mṛṣā-artha*) throughout the subsequent sections on the sense bases (*āyatana*) and elements (*dhātu*) should be understood by this same principle; they need not be detailed further.

[The text] proceeds to explain the second part, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Within the first section, which cites examples to clarify the doctrine, there is a person who likewise represents sentient beings;

hands and feet represent seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. Since hands and feet each come in pairs, they constitute four. "Tranquil abiding" represents the sense faculties (*indriya*), as these do not themselves take objects (*viṣaya*) as their conditions.
Nor is there any accidental meeting. When the hundred limbs are harmoniously encountered, it is analogous to the mind not arising with respect to any phenomena and remaining non-discriminative.

When things suddenly seem to arise as delusions, it is analogous to the sense organs and their objects not meeting, such that even neutral sensation (*upekṣā-vedanā*) cannot be apprehended. In its nature, there is neither opposition nor compliance;

this is analogous to being detached from the three sensations of suffering, pleasure, and neutrality. The above examples illustrate the reality of the Tathāgatagarbha. As for the person below [this level]:

The first example illustrates how delusion arises from the Truth (*tathatā*). Because there is no [external cause], it is like the single thought-moment of non-awakening giving rise to ignorance (*avidyā*).
The two hands illustrate that once ignorance has taken root, the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) confront one another.

Rubbing them together in the air illustrates how, within the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) where no connection exists, a knot of connection is produced through the confrontation of the sense organs and their objects. Below the two hands, it illustrates the sense organs...
Dust and its counterpart give rise to the three feelings of suffering, pleasure, and equanimity. Roughness and smoothness serve as examples for the feeling of suffering;
cold and heat serve as examples for the feeling of pleasure; and various other characteristics serve as examples for the feeling of equanimity. Second, regarding the refutation through analogy:

[the touch] does not come from space to produce the contact that gives rise to the feeling; nor does it emerge from the palm. This specifically refutes the feeling that is produced, rather than the contact that produces it.
Therefore, when there is conjunction, it is the faculty of touch (*kāya-vijñāna*) that cognizes [the object], and so forth.

Third, the explanation of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*). Within the initial section that cites examples to clarify the dharma, although there are two instances—the mention of "sourness" and the perception of a "precipice"—both are actual entities of the aggregate of perception;
thus, these are used as examples. Consequently, all five aggregates are treated as examples rather than metaphors. However, above...

Regarding the nature of sensation (*vedanā*), both the true and the delusory are first clarified, followed by the delusory. This establishes that it is solely like the delusory, thereby demonstrating that the delusory arises from the true and that the entirety of the delusory is itself the true;
once one knows the delusory, one naturally knows the true. Second, [the analysis] proceeds by analogy to refute [the notion of a separate self].

This also consists of two parts. The first, the establishment of the reasoning, is easily understood. The second, the actual refutation, also has two parts: first, the refutation of the theory regarding sourness; second, the analogy with the perception of a precipice.
Indeed, within the section establishing the reasoning, there should also have been a passage concerning the analogy of the perception of a precipice; it is simply omitted here.
However, while this refutes the theory of sourness and the perception of a precipice, it does not refute the water flowing from the mouth or the tingling numbness in the feet.

The four aggregates of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). First, among the examples cited to illustrate the dharma: "torrents" refers to swift, rushing currents; this illustrates the arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of the aggregates of formations as they proceed in succession.

"Waves" refers to the continuous succession of the aggregates of formations, wherein there is the moment-to-moment transition of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. Regarding "the prior limit" and so forth:

the cessation of the preceding moment gives rise to the succeeding moment, and the cessation of that succeeding moment gives rise to the next subsequent moment, all of which follow a sequential order.

It is not inconsistent. Second, [the text] refutes [the opponent's position] by applying it to the established examples. First, within the formulation of the principle, four rules are fully established; these are the four natures, namely: self, other, and so forth.

It can be seen that throughout the entire scripture, the analytical examination does not exceed these four natures. Although there are only two meanings in the preceding and following sections, they should likewise be fourfold.
Therefore, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*), and the seven... [are subsequently established].
All [of these] generally possess four [aspects]. Regarding the refutation of the "middle" [position]: as for the phrase "if it exists because of water," the intended meaning is this:

if the torrent were produced by water, then while the nature of that which produces it (the water) is inherently still and tranquil, that which is produced—the torrent—should not have a nature identical to that of its producer.
Furthermore, if the torrent exists because of water, then the stream that is produced...
The nature [of the sprout] should not be identical to the water that produces it. It is like a tree having flowers: the nature of the flower is inherently different from the tree itself.
Therefore, it is said: "If [the sprout] were caused by... (and so forth). The meaning of the two phrases "there is" and "has" is that one must say it exists because of the water.
Water is the producer; the flow is the produced. If there is that which is produced, it must possess characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
since these characteristics exist, they ought to manifest. If they do not manifest, then what is it that constitutes water? Therefore it is said, "there is something" (and so forth).
As for the phrase "if they are identical," the meaning is that water is the producer whose nature is clarity, while purity is the produced whose nature is movement.
If the nature of that which is produced were itself mobile, it would be identical to the nature of that which produces.
Consequently, when the producer becomes clear and still, it would paradoxically no longer be the substance of water. Therefore, it is said: "If they were identical... and so forth.

Regarding the five aggregates of consciousness: taking the example to illustrate the dharma, there is a person who likewise represents sentient beings. Taking the *piṅgala* bird as an example illustrates the grasping of the four great elements to form a body.
Blocking both nostrils illustrates the arising of the two attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma-grāha*) to obstruct the two emptinesses of person and phenomena (*pudgala-dharma-śūnyatā*).

Filling the space within, the vase serves as an analogy for the body, and the emptiness serves as an analogy for consciousness. This refers to what is called "one delusion becoming the mind, which is certainly confused as the interior of the physical body.

The phrase "a thousand li" and so forth serves as an analogy for the consciousness-mind that shifts and flows from moment to moment. "Using it to provide for another country" serves as an analogy for receiving retribution according to one's karma.
Within the section on "using analogies to investigate and dismantle [delusions]," there are two passages: "if it comes from that direction" and "if it enters from this direction."
There may be a textual error here. It should read: "If it comes from that direction, when the hole is opened and the bottle is inverted, one should see emptiness emerge.

If it enters from this direction, then since the emptiness already stored within the original bottle has departed, there should be a deficiency of empty space on the ground where the original bottle stood.

Reading the text in this manner, the logic regarding "that" and "this," and regarding "emerging" and "entering," is entirely consistent. If one follows the original text as it stands, [it states: "Since it has been stored..."

The "going away" in the phrase "emptying away" should be understood as "going there from here. Furthermore, beneath "entering this direction," there should be the four characters "reaching that direction and going.
Viewed in this way, both the exiting and entering of this and that [direction] will be consistent.
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama, Volume Two;
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama, Volume Three.
Spoken by the Great Master Yisong of Tiantai.
Recorded by Lingshu, a disciple of the Guoxi lineage.

This passage clarifies the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), the twelve bases (*dvādaśāyatana*), and the eighteen elements (*aṣṭādaśadhātu*). These are simply the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses.

When discussed from the perspective of sentient beings, they are nothing other than illusory and false designations. When analyzed from the perspective of the Buddhas, they are all the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Now, because sentient beings do not understand that these various things are illusory transformations and false attachments, [the text] refutes them one by one by means of the four natures (*caturvidha-svabhāva*), thereby revealing the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Question:
Since the three—sense organs, objects, and consciousness—are all, in every dharma, the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness, what then constitutes their actual reality?
"Is it seen that all are the Tathāgatagarbha? Answer: "The three—sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—do not transcend form (*rūpa*) and mind (*citta*).

As stated previously: 'Form, mind, and all conditions are manifested solely by the mind. Furthermore, it is said: 'Your body and your mind are both things manifested within the wondrous mind. And again:

'When one is deluded, one takes this as the mind and fails to realize that from the physical body outward, including the mountains, rivers, empty space, and the great earth [are all such manifestations].'"

All these are things within the wondrously luminous true mind. Since it is said that the mind is the wondrous mind, this refers to what is called the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
That which can produce and manifest is already entirely wondrous; therefore, that which is produced and manifested must also be wondrous.
This means that while the principle (*li*) is fundamentally wondrous, its coarseness arises from the perceptions of sentient beings. Thus, the various [appearances] of sentient beings...
When one discriminates among various attachments, one does not even know that they are illusory, let alone know them to be real.

As for the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who have attained full realization, although there are three thousand distinctions and ten thousand variations among the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses, when investigated to the ultimate, which of these is not a manifestation of the wondrous mind of the Tathāgatagarbha? Therefore, every faculty is the Dharma-realm, and every object is likewise so.
The Dharma-realm is that which is cognized by consciousness. As for its arising, it arises through conditions; yet in its arising, there is never any arising.
As for its ceasing, it ceases through conditions; yet in its ceasing, there is never any ceasing. Thus, when the sense faculties blaze forth, their very substance is not seen;
when objects blaze forth, their very substance does not arise; and when consciousness blazes forth as discernment, its very substance is not [apprehended].

Regarding discernment (*vijñapti*): how could there be that which produces and that which is produced, as well as the grasper and the grasped, such that one would cling to them through the fourfold analysis of self and other?
Since each of these four—self, other, both, and neither—has been individually refuted, it is concluded in each case:
"Fundamentally, they are neither caused by conditions nor are they spontaneous. Since they are neither caused by conditions nor spontaneous, are they not, indeed, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha?

Indeed, this very point is the actual reality; there is no other actual reality apart from it. Now, the analysis of the bases (*āyatana*), elements (*dhātu*), and aggregates (*skandha*) each has its specific purpose.

In the analysis of the bases, one primarily refutes the sense organs (*indriya*) while concurrently refuting the objects (*viṣaya*). In the analysis of the elements, one primarily refutes the objects while concurrently refuting the sense organs.

As for the aggregates, one primarily refutes consciousness (*vijñāna*) while concurrently refuting both the sense organs and the objects. This constitutes the essential principle; it must not remain unknown.

Now, first, the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*) are explained. If one follows the preceding five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*), this is the second [section]. It is divided into two parts: a general inquiry and a specific explanation.

Within the general inquiry, regarding the "six sense bases," the *Fajie Cidi* (The Sequential Order of the Dharma Realm) states: "The term 'base' (*āyatana*) has the meaning of 'entering' (*praveśa*)."

In essence, the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) mutually act as gateways for one another. As it is said: "When an object enters a faculty, the faculty is activated; when a faculty enters an object, the object is activated.
This is because faculties and objects originally lack self-nature and exist only through mutual dependence. To discuss this according to the present text:

for instance, when the two kinds of delusory objects—light and darkness—act as conditions, the faculty of sight arises in their midst. This is an instance of an object entering a faculty, like inhalation.

These objective phenomena (dharmas) are called the nature of seeing; they are also the sense organs (indriya) encountering their objects (viṣaya). However, what is being refuted here primarily concerns the sense organs themselves.

As for the six sense bases (āyatana) and the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, when discussed in relation to the preceding [analysis], their meaning is analogous to that of the five aggregates (skandha); this can be understood by applying the same principle.
The same applies to the sense fields (āyatana) and the elements (dhātu).
The second part, the detailed explanation, consists of six sections, which explain the eyes, ears, and so forth. Each section contains three sub-divisions:
citing an instance to illustrate the principle, analyzing the instance to refute it, and concluding by demonstrating its falsity. For the first and last [sections], there are no further subdivisions.

Only the second section, which analyzes the instance to refute it, is further divided into two: first, establishing the reasoning; second, the actual refutation. The subsequent sections do not repeat these again; one may infer this by analogy.

[Answer: It is seen. As for the initial presentation of examples (*udāharaṇa*) to illustrate the Dharma, it need not be divided. If one wishes to divide them, the example for the eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*) is as follows;
the subsequent examples for the ear-base up to the mind-base (*mano-āyatana*) are all analogous to this. Furthermore, the eye-base encompasses the section on the eye;

the ear-base encompasses the section on the ear; the nose-base encompasses the section on the nose; and so on, up to the mind-base encompassing the section on the mind. This is the presentation of examples.

This reveals the dharma. Within the sense-base of the eye (*cakṣur-āyatana*), the specific instance cited—"namely, that very pupil"—borrows the example of how the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) can manifest [the dharma] to serve as the phenomenon manifested here. When these two are compared, there are three points of difference.

The former is the general category of the preceding examples; this is the specific instance that manifests it. This is the first difference. The former is real; this is false. This is the second difference.
The former discusses what is encompassed by color-form (*rūpa-dharma*) in its broadest sense;

here, the discussion is restricted solely to what is subsumed within the faculty of the eye (*cakṣur-indriya*), making it narrow in scope. This is the third difference. This also contains a profound meaning that must not remain unknown.

In the "Manifesting Dharmas" section, the statement that both the eyes and their labor are "the appearance of fatigue arising from the staring of Bodhi" refers to the total emergence of delusion from the True.

As for the other five sense-bases (*āyatanas*) also being called "the appearance of fatigue arising from the staring," this is because the example of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) was already applied to the eye-base;
the remaining five are treated accordingly. It is because of light and darkness and so forth that form arises and the eye perceives it.
The "inner agitation" [of the preceding aggregate] is like the former; the "adhesive clarity giving rise to vision" [of the following] is like the latter.

From "inhaling this" onwards refers to the eye producing the appearance of form. The "external rushing forth" [of the preceding] is like the former; the "essence of vision reflecting form" [of the following] is like the latter. The same applies to what follows below.

Regarding the "vision residing in the center that gives rise to seeing," some say it is the essence of vision (*darśana-śuddhi*), while others say it is the discernment of objects (*viṣaya-vikalpa*). This...

None of these are correct. The essence of seeing that conditions sensory objects is mostly a matter of the consciousness-element. Herein, we clarify only the eye-entrance (*cakṣur-āyatana*), which is exclusively the pure material faculty (*rūpa-indriya*);
it is also called the ultimate faculty (*paramārtha-indriya*). Yet, it does not exist apart from the ephemeral faculty (*tuccha-indriya*);

rather, the ultimate faculty manifests by residing within the ephemeral faculty. As for the "ultimate," it is what is seen by the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*), which is superior to the ephemeral faculty. Regarding this—
Regarding the objective aspect (*nimitta-bhāga*) of the eighth *ālaya-vijñāna*: first, it serves as the object-condition (*ālambana*), and second, it can give rise to consciousness;
thus, while being a single entity, it possesses two functions. This is much like the two horns of a snail, which necessarily grow together.

As for the claim that all six sense organs possess both [aspects], if one were to say that the "ultimate" (*paramārtha*) and the "dust-like" (*tuccha*) refer to the two horns of a snail, that would be incorrect. Absorb this.

The way the sense-objects (viṣaya) attract [the faculties] is like a magnet attracting iron. Whether it be that the substance of the stone and the iron have similar natures, or that their inherent qualities (dharmatā) are interrelated, they do not attract unless they meet;
yet once they meet, they attract. The principle regarding the relationship between the faculties (indriya) and the objects is exactly the same.
This "seeing" is distinct from those [objects], meaning that it exists by virtue of the objects; apart from the objects, it has no essence. This applies to all five [faculties] below as well.
Regarding the establishment of the principle, the phrase "not arising from the sense organ" refers to the fact that the ultimate nature of seeing does not emerge from the physical, ephemeral organ;

this applies equally to the sense base of the mind (*manāyatana*). In the section on the direct refutation, the passage beginning with "if it comes from light" means that if the nature of seeing were to come from the light that is seen, it would have no connection to darkness. When it is dark...
When the appearance of light manifests before you, the light itself has already ceased; thus, the seeing-nature that came along with it must also have ceased.
Although darkness is now present before you, you should not be able to see it. Yet, since you can still see the darkness, it does not cease along with the light.

If it does not cease with the light, how could it come from the light? Thus, one knows that there is no logical principle for it to come from the light. Below, whenever a conclusion is reached... [text ends]

The refutations should all be applied accordingly. As for the phrase "if it arises from the faculty," this refers to the faculty of sight, which originally takes the two—light and darkness—as its essential nature (*svabhāva*).
Now, if the faculty were to arise independently, it would have no connection with light and darkness.
Since there would be no such connection, its essential nature could not be established, as stated above: "this seeing is separate from that," and so forth. This is all due to [the nature of] seeing.

If the nature [of the sense] depends upon an object, it exists when there is an object and does not exist when there is no object; the same applies to the refutation of the other five senses arising from their respective organs.

Furthermore, regarding the statement "if the emptiness itself sees," etc.: if one is in empty space and sees an elephant returning yet cannot see the organ [of sight], then one knows that the seeing of the elephant in the empty space is the empty space itself seeing.
What concern is this for your eye-base (*cakṣur-āyatana*)? The subsequent cases are all like this. However, both the brightness and darkness of the eye...
Seeing, and so forth, up to the arising and ceasing of the mind—all are known. This correctly demonstrates the functional power of the six sense faculties.

If sentient beings were to rely solely on their own calculations, they would see only light and not darkness, and so forth, knowing only arising and not cessation. The three entrances of ear, nose, and tongue can all be understood in this way.
Regarding the entrance of the body, as for the sensation of contact perceived when in conjunction, its manifestation is known through separation; some say that there is no contact [when separated].
[The object] knows itself. One perceives its contact only through conjunction; conjunction does not know itself, for one perceives its conjunction only through separation.

If this is so, although the text clarifies the principle, it is not yet appropriate. Now I say that separation can also know [the object]. Question: Regarding the four characteristics of separation and conjunction, opposition and compliance (*viśleṣa-saṃyoga-virodha-anukūla*), why do you speak of only two objects (*viṣaya*)?
Answer: Because opposition and compliance are subsumed within separation and conjunction. For example, in the case of smoothness (*ślakṣṇatva*), it is [perceived] through conjunction.

That which is "separation" (viyoga) is favorable [to it], while that which is "conjunction" (saṃyoga) is unfavorable. That which is "roughness" (khara) is unfavorable to separation, while it is favorable to conjunction. Therefore, although there are four [factors], they are spoken of as only two.

Within the sense-base of the mind (manāyatana), the two phrases "fatigue" (klama) and "exhaustion" (pariśrama) refer to the two faculties—the ultimate (paramārtha) and the phenomenal (tūla)—which, by depending upon one another, constitute sleepiness and drowsiness.
The ultimate faculty takes the phenomenal as its support; this phenomenal fatigue is that which depends [upon the former].
If the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*) does not function as an active manifestation, it constitutes sleep;

however, when one has sufficiently satisfied the superficial sleep, the ultimate reality—which serves as its support—is able to manifest again. The two lines concerning "perceiving objects" refer to the contrast between waking and sleeping.
"Surveying the objects" (*lǎn chén*) refers to the fact that the mental faculty (*manas*) and its mental objects (*dharmas*) are merely the fading shadows of the five sensory objects.

"Inversion" (*viparyāsa*) refers to the aforementioned characteristics of sleep, waking, recollection, and forgetfulness; when considered from the perspective of the true essence, these all belong to the category of inversion. Furthermore, for recollection to suddenly turn into forgetfulness, or for forgetfulness to suddenly turn into recollection, is likewise an inversion.
Regarding arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing (*utpāda-sthiti-anyathātva-vināśa*), as stated at the beginning of the second fascicle of the *Vijñaptimātratāsiddhi*: "Arising indicates..."
This dharma did not previously exist; "abiding" indicates that this dharma possesses functional activity; "change" indicates that this dharma is not static;
and "cessation" indicates that there is no time after this dharma. Now, it is likely that recollection is taken as arising and abiding, while forgetting is taken as change and cessation.

Furthermore, as stated below regarding "inhaling and practicing," etc., inhaling is simply taking this arising and so forth as what is practiced. Thus, one knows that both recollection and forgetting are present.

The four characteristics are arising, abiding, changing after having abided, and ceasing after having changed. "Practicing within absorption" refers to the practice of returning [to the object]; it is like the practice of "studying and practicing at the proper times.
One takes these very characteristics—arising and so forth—as the practice at the proper times. Therefore, they are established without mutual transgression.
As for "conjoining the mind with effort," "effort" refers to the aforementioned characteristics such as drowsiness, recollection, forgetfulness, and so on. This is the collection of knowledge.
The former [state] corresponds to what is external, taking "arousing" as its function; thus it is said, "arousing seeing and arousing hearing," and so forth.

The present [state] corresponds to what is internal, taking "gathering" as its function; thus it is said, "gathering knowledge and absorbing. Here, "internal objects" (inner *viṣayas*) refers to the shadows of the five external objects (*pañca-viṣayas*) that have fallen away and been discarded, which are absorbed as internal objects.
Regarding "seeing, hearing, and flowing against the current": "flowing" (*liú*) refers to conditions (*pratyaya*). One borrows the five sense organs (*pañcendriya*) for this purpose.
This shows that the mental faculty (*manas*) is able to take objects retrogressively, for seeing, hearing, and so forth can only take objects in a forward direction.
The first five sense-objects, being external, cannot take internal *dharmas* as objects retrogressively; even if they were able to take them retrogressively, [they would still be unable to do so].

That which cannot itself take internal mental objects as its condition is the stage where it does not grasp them; this is precisely what is called the nature of the faculty of mind (*manas-indriya*) that cognizes.

Regarding the two states of waking and sleeping corresponding to the opening and closing of the body: when the physical form opens, it is called waking, because when a person is awake, the six sense faculties are all open.
When the physical form closes, it is called sleeping, because when a person is asleep, the six sense faculties are all closed. It is just like this.
The *Liezi* says: "When one awakens, the forms open; when one sleeps, the forms conjoin"—this is what is meant.

The thirty-two locations are divided into two parts: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. Within the general inquiry, it says "the twelve locations" (*dvādaśāyatana*), which refers to the six sense organs (*indriya*) and six sense objects (*viṣaya*) together making twelve.
A "location" (*āyatana*) is that which serves as a basis; specifically, it takes the sense objects as the basis for the sense organs.
The basis: because the sense-faculties take the objects as their basis, they are called the twelve *āyatanas* (bases) by virtue of being mutual bases for one another.

However, what is currently being refuted pertains specifically to the objects (*viṣaya*). As for other sūtras also calling them the twelve *āyatanas*, it is simply because they are designated as "bases" (*āyatana*) here due to the preceding mention of the six [internal] bases (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*).
Generally, "entrance" (*āyatana*) is spoken of in terms of that which enters, while "base" (*āyatana*) is established as a name for that which is entered. If, by this...
The general inquiry corresponds to the preceding general enumeration, such as the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), which are visible.

Second, the detailed explanation is divided into six parts, namely the explanations of the sense bases from the eye and form (*cakṣur-āyatana*) up to the mind and mental objects (*mano-dharmāyatana*).

Each of these contains three sections: citing an instance, examining and determining, and refuting through logical analysis to demonstrate that it is empty and false. The first of these always begins with Ānanda. Second...
They all likewise depart following Ānanda; only the point of physical contact departs as it was when present. All three depart for this reason;

this is the general heading here, which will be evident from the text itself. First, regarding the sense-base of the eye and visible forms: the section beginning with "Ānanda" below cites an actual instance to establish the point, while the section beginning with "In your mind" establishes the principle.
The same applies to all subsequent sections; however, within the section on the sense-base of the mind and mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), this...
The following section serves to establish the definitive conclusion. The initial statement, "You should first [examine]... and so forth, refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) as the locus;

Śrīgupta and others refer to the sense objects (*viṣaya*) as the locus. All subsequent passages follow this pattern. Within the refutation that analyzes and deconstructs the opponent's thesis, the phrase "If, moreover, the eye-organ...
and so forth means that since form arises from the organ, the organ must possess the nature of producing form. If, at the time one perceives empty space—which is not form—the organ does not merely...
If the form that is produced should be dissolved, then the nature that produces it must also be dissolved. Therefore, it is said, "seeing emptiness," and so forth.
This is because the manifestation [of consciousness] is established through the existence of the seer and the seen.
If both the produced form and the producing nature are dissolved, then manifestation can no longer be apprehended. Therefore, it is said, "if dissolved," and so forth. Because there is...

The characteristics of form can manifest emptiness. If one says that manifestation means that everything is utterly non-existent, then since the characteristics of form are already non-existent, by what means will the substance of its emptiness be manifested? Furthermore, it may be said that the characteristics of form are produced by the eye-faculty;
if the form that is produced is non-existent, then the nature that produces it is also non-existent. Who, then, would act as the seeing-nature?
This is to distinguish the substance of emptiness; hence it says, "the characteristics of form and so forth.

"Emptiness is also like this" means that what manifests emptiness is solely the characteristic of form, and what manifests the characteristic of form is solely the substance of emptiness. Now, since the substance of emptiness is absent, who is there to distinguish the characteristic of form?
Therefore, it says, "emptiness is also like this. Second, regarding the sense bases of the ear and sound, among the matters [of daily life], when food is prepared...
The one who beats the drum intends to assemble the multitude. Once the multitude has assembled, the one who strikes the bell intends to have them come to the meal.
Within the logical analysis of the refutation, if the two lines "neither coming nor going" were absent, it would prevent the opponent from shifting their argument.
Fearing that once their position is refuted, the opponent might shift their argument by saying, "Sound does not come, and the ear does not go," these lines are established first.
He said: "If sound and the ear do not come and go, then there is likewise no hearing.
It is untenable to claim that sound comes to the ear or that the ear goes to the place of the sound, because sound has no fixed substance; a single sound can enter all ears simultaneously.

To say that sound 'comes' is a mere conceptual fabrication. Furthermore, the ear also has no fixed substance; a single ear can hear all sounds simultaneously. If one says [the ear goes], it is likewise a conceptual fabrication.
The "going" [of the ear toward sound] is likewise a false conceptualization. In total, whether it be the ear or the sound, there is not one that does not pervade the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Therefore, both the coming of the sound and the going of the ear are false conceptualizations that can be refuted. Third, regarding the locus of the nose and fragrance:

within the section on "reiterating the conceptualization and refuting it through reasoning," the phrase "meeting with smoke, vapor, and so forth" refers to the Buddha’s teaching that the nose perceives through contact. How so?
If the smoke has not yet risen into the air, how is it that everyone within forty *li* knows of it? Therefore, it is said, "as with the nose and so forth.

Some say that although the nose perceives only what is in contact with it, once one attains the pure and sovereign spiritual power (*ṛddhi*) of the six sense organs, one can smell the incense smoke even before it has reached a great distance.
To harmonize these views: while it seems possible to hear [the sound], there is nevertheless a flaw; such is the case for the six sense organs.
To what stage of purification does this refer? It is the completion of the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā*). How could an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*) currently possess such a state?
If an ordinary person were able to hear from afar, it would further contradict the Buddha’s intent as understood through the *Zhonghe* (Compendium).
This is entirely due to the extraordinary power of the incense. The *Bowuzhi* states: "Under the Han system, incense weighing less than one jin was not permitted to be offered as tribute."
There was a foreigner who came to present tribute. Because his offering had not yet reached one *jin* (a unit of weight), it was not formally accepted.

That envoy stopped at the Wumen Gate and burned a single *zhu* (a minute measure); the entire city smelled it. Thus we know that even before reaching a great distance, the power of the incense is such that it is heard [sensed] across forty *li*.
Regarding the section on the "Tongue as the Seat of Taste" in the *Jushi zhong*: if one encounters items such as *sū* (butter) or *lao* (curd) therein, they are [to be consumed] nearby.
Among the śramaṇas today, there are some who, based on this [text], claim that butter and curd are permissible to eat. This is not so.
The Buddha established three conditions under which these may be consumed: first, when one is ill; do the śramaṇas today eat them because they are actually ill?
Second, when grasses and vegetables do not grow; do the śramaṇas today eat them because grasses and vegetables do not grow? Third...
This is a manifestation of great spiritual power. Can a śramaṇa now truly eat as the "contrary-practice" (nigūḍha-caryā) bodhisattvas of antiquity did?
If one wishes to eat this without the three causes [for breaking the precept], it would greatly contradict the holy teachings. Therefore, it is said that such instances may occasionally occur;
it should be understood that these are not fixed occurrences during the two designated times. As for the "two times," the Buddha prohibited eating other than at the single time of midday.
By employing skillful means, he further permits the early meal; thus it is said there are "two times. Regarding the refutation through logical analysis:
as for the claim that [taste] arises from space and so forth, since space is void and possesses nothing at all, how could there be any taste that can arise?
If there must be such an arising, then space itself would be the producer. What kind of taste, then, do you consume when you eat that very space? Therefore...

It says, "If one is born... (and so forth). Regarding the five types of bodily contact, when citing matters of practice, the instruction that you must always [wash] at dawn and so on—specifically the act of rubbing the head—is a regulation established by the Buddha.
However, with what intention was it necessary to rub the head? Generally, the body, hair, and skin are received from one's parents;
not daring to damage or injure them is a great classic of the Confucian tradition. Now, those who leave the household life shave their beards and hair...
As for the hair: one desires to relinquish that which is cherished though small in order to accomplish that which is sought though great. What kind of greatness is this?
It is the desire to transcend birth and death, to attain Bodhi, to expound the Dharma, and to transform and deliver sentient beings.

In this way, the kindness of the king and parents can be repaid, and the virtue of donors and teachers can also be requited. One should know that what is being sacrificed is but a single physical body.
This is one kind [of smallness]. Therefore, it is considered small. That which is accomplished is not merely that one gains the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom for oneself;
rather, it ensures that all sentient beings who see or hear [the teaching] receive benefit and do not fail to attain the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
Thus, what is accomplished is not only great, but great beyond greatness. For this reason, it is considered great. Consequently, shaving the head does not constitute an obstacle.

If even Taibo, who cut his hair and tattooed his body, was still praised by Nishan as possessing "supreme virtue," then how could the śramaṇa’s shaving of his beard and hair possibly harm supreme virtue?
It is feared that although these śramaṇas have shaved their hair and beards, they do not diligently seek what is to be accomplished;
therefore, the rule was established to rub their heads at dawn. This is not only to urge them toward progress in cultivation, but also to assist them in [overcoming] indolence.

This forgets the initial thought. It is a definitive determination within the midst [of reality]. "The locus of 'that which is rubbed' (mo-so) is not the same as the conventional discussion of subject and object.

The hand is the subject that touches; the head is the object touched. Now, within this single body, there is fundamentally no subject or object. This is what is meant by refuting [the notion of] subject and object.

This is merely to refute the erroneous conceptions of sentient beings and thereby reveal the *tathāgatagarbha*. Within the refutation through the examination of these conceptions, there are four points:
first, "If [the head] were in [the body]," etc., which refutes [the notion] by means of mutual presence; second, "If [they] were each," etc., which refutes [the notion] by means of dual existence;

third, "If [it were] the head," etc., which refutes [the notion] by means of a single entity; fourth, "If [it were] two," etc., which refutes [the notion] by means of two entities. Within the refutation by means of two entities, it concerns the capacity...
Regarding "neither the object nor the subject": if [the faculty] resides in the hand, then the head is without cognition; if it resides in the head, then the hand is without cognition.
Since both the capable [subject] and the object cannot be established, how could there be empty space that comes into contact with you?

Therefore, it is said, "if the two," and so forth. Regarding the sixth sense-base, the mental objects (*dharmāyatana*), among the examples used to ascertain the nature of the object of perception (*ālambana*) and so on:
"Good" does not transcend the three of precept, concentration, and wisdom; "evil" does not transcend the three of greed, hatred, and delusion.
"Dharma" refers to the dharma-objects (dharmāyatana), meaning the objects of the mental faculty (manas). If they are unwholesome, they are evil; if they are not evil, they are good;

if they are neither wholesome nor evil, they are indeterminate (avyākṛta). These are fixed principles; therefore, it is said that they "generate and constitute the Dharma-principles. This Dharma is also the Dharma.
It is an object (*dharmāyatana*). The two minds—namely, the mind that is identical to the mind and the mind that is distinct from the mind—are what is called the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
To cite [your] calculation and refute it within the context of "the mind being identical": the mind is the mental faculty, and the phenomena (*dharma*) are the objects of the mind (*dharmāyatana*).

"Not an object" means that which is not an object of the mind is, in fact, the mind itself; this is what is meant by "negation through exclusion" (*paryudāsa-pratiṣedha*). That is to say, if your "object of the mind" arises simultaneously with the mind, then since that which produces [it] is already the mind, the produced...
That which arises must also be the mind; thus, according to your [position], the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*) would be the mind rather than a dharma-object.
Therefore, it is said, "If it were identical," and so forth. If it were a dharma-object, it would then constitute an object of cognition (*ālambana*).

Now, since it is the mind and not a dharma-object, how can the mind take itself as its own object? Hence, it is said that it is "not an object of the mind. This is because the sense-faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*)...

If they were to correspond, they would constitute a sense-base (*āyatana*). Since they are not the objective dharmas that serve as objects of perception (*ālambana*), how could they constitute a sense-base?

Therefore, it is asked: "How can they constitute a sense-base? Apart from the mind, what is called "mind" is the measure of the mind; that is, your mind is precisely the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).

Thus, the "dharma of dharmas" is precisely the dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*). Regarding the statement, "That which knows is called mind," the intended meaning is that while the dharma-object is devoid of cognition, the mental faculty (*manas*) possesses cognition.
If the dharma-object were to possess cognition, it would be identical to the mental faculty; therefore, it is said that that which knows is designated as "mind."
Your mental objects (*dharmāyatana*) are objects and not the mind. If they were identical to the mind, they would differ from your mental objects;
therefore, it is said they are "different from you," meaning they are not your mental objects. Thus, it is said they are "not objects. Since they are not mental objects, they must be the mind.
Although they are indeed the mind, they are the same as the minds of others, because your mental objects are separate from [your own] mind.
Therefore, it is said that they are identical to the measure of another’s mind (*paracittamātra*). One should supplement this by adding a further objection:

"Though it is said not to be an external object (*viṣaya*), it is nevertheless my own mind and not the mind of another. He then refutes this, saying: "According to your view, the faculty of mind (*manas*) is the mind; yet the mental object (*dharmaviṣaya*) is also your mind."
"How is it that your mind has become divided into two? Therefore, it is said: 'It is precisely you yourselves. If it were not 'knowing' and so forth, then 'not-knowing' would simply be ignorance.
If one says it is ignorance, there is nothing in the world that can be called ignorance apart from forms, sounds, and the like, as well as illusory appearances.
Your 'dharma-dust' (mental objects) are merely the fading shadows of these things; though it is called 'ignorance,' [it is nothing more than this]."
It is inherently different from these. If one asks where such [a thing] might reside apart from these, it is said, "If it is not... and so forth.
Now, regarding the form of the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and the emptiness of space, I do not perceive your "dharma-object" (*dharma-viṣaya*) at all as something that can be represented;
therefore, it is said, "Now, within... and so forth. However, beyond the five sense-objects of the human realm, there may yet be further five sense-objects.
Furthermore, is there yet another void beyond this void that serves as the representation for your mental object (dharmāyatana)?

Therefore, it is said that "it should not be so," and so forth. This means that the mental object is what is perceived by the mind-faculty (manas), while the mind-faculty is that which perceives the mental object.
Now, since there is no representation, the mind has nothing to perceive; yet this does not mean that [the mind] itself is non-existent. Therefore, it is said: "The mind is not..."
Regarding the sense bases (*āyatana*): they are established as such through the mutual interaction of the object-field (*dharmāyatana*) and the mental faculty (*manas*).
Since there is no longer any object of perception (*ālambana*), how can they be established as bases? Therefore, it is said: "From whom are the bases established?"
The forty-eight elements (*dhātu*) are also twofold: first, a general inquiry; second, a detailed explanation. Regarding the eighteen elements mentioned therein:

the three categories of faculty (*indriya*), object (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) each have six types, thus constituting eighteen. As for the term "element" (*dhātu*), it takes the meaning of a boundary or limit.
Since the faculties, objects, and consciousnesses each have their own distinct limits, they are called "elements. Furthermore, "element" carries the meaning of a cause. Therefore—

The text below states: "That which arises from the eye, having the eye as its constituent element (*dhātu*), and so forth. Furthermore, *dhātu* carries the meaning of "seed" (*bīja*). The three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—each possess their own specific seed-nature and generic category.
If one were to correlate this with the previous general enumeration, it would be as explained in the section on the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*).
The second part, the detailed explanation, consists of six sections, which explain the elements of the eye, form, and consciousness, up to the elements of the mind, phenomena, and consciousness.
The first section, explaining the elements of the eye, form, and consciousness, is divided into three parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, pointing to the teaching to establish the matter;

second, from "Ānanda" onwards, restating the opponent's position to analyze and refute it; third, from "Therefore" onwards, concluding by demonstrating its falsity. The same applies to the remaining five sections. Within the first of these, there is first the pointing to the teaching.

This consciousness is definitively established below. Regarding the initial reference to what was explained therein, such as "as you have clarified," this is what is taught within the sūtras of the Hīnayāna by the Tathāgata.
This is because the Hīnayāna maintains that only the sense organ (*indriya*) and the object (*viṣaya*) together can produce consciousness.
However, it is not so in the Mahāyāna; even a single sense organ or a single object can produce consciousness. To investigate this according to reality:
Thus, consciousness is also capable of giving rise to both the sense organs and their objects.

However, since these two statements were spoken by the Buddha, yet he says, "as you have explained," this is entirely because Ānanda, during the "Investigation of the Seven Locations" (*saptasthāna-paryeṣaṇā*), had already been repeatedly refuted by the Tathāgata regarding both the internal and the external.
Unable to withstand this, his words were exhausted and his reasoning was defeated; therefore, he established this conceptualization in the sixth section.

Later, he further cited what the Tathāgata had said as a counter-argument, stating: "As the World-Honored One has said, 'With the eye and forms as conditions, eye-consciousness arises' (and so forth).
Herein, the intent was to refute Ānanda’s attachment to the realm of sentient beings' consciousness;
thus, [the Buddha] took the words Ānanda had cited and rendered them a definitive conclusion, saying: 'As you have clarified. This is why he spoke only of 'clarity' and did not speak of..."
This is merely stated as an example; for the following five cases, it is likewise said, "it is just as you have explained.

Second, within the refutation that examines and dismantles the opponent's thesis, there are three parts: first, the refutation of production from the sense organ; second, the refutation of production from the object; and third, the refutation of the impossibility of production from both the sense organ and the object together.

Regarding the impossibility of their co-production, this applies only to the consciousness of mind and mental objects (*manodharmavijñāna*), as there is no ear [involved therein]. Furthermore, within each of these refutations:

In all cases, one first refutes that consciousness arises [from them] as being unestablished; next, one refutes that they constitute a "constituent" (*dhātu*) as being unestablished. The same applies to what follows below. Within this section:
first, based on the subsequent passage, one refutes that the eye arises as a constituent; second, based on the subsequent passage, one refutes that form arises as a constituent;
third, based on the subsequent passage, one refutes that they arise together as a constituent.
Regarding the beginning: "If consciousness arises dependent on the eye," etc., this refutes the claim that the cause of consciousness arises from the eye.
To say that consciousness arises from the eye implies that the eye is the producer and consciousness is the produced; thus, the eye would have no connection to form or emptiness.
Since it has no connection to form or emptiness, it would lack the capacity to discern them; hence, the phrase "if dependent on [the eye]," and so forth. However, as for consciousness...
Its meaning is "discernment" (*vijñapti*). Since there is no discrimination (*vikalpa*), what use would one have for that consciousness? Therefore, it says, "Even if there were," and so forth.

The passage beginning with "Your seeing" refutes the claim that the eye constitutes a constituent element (*dhātu*), as it is not established. "Your seeing" refers to the visual faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*).

This means that while consciousness arises with the eye as its cause, it is the eye that has the capacity to produce it. Thus, your faculty of seeing that can produce [consciousness] is not the same as objective colors such as blue or yellow.
If that which produces [consciousness] is already not blue or yellow, then the consciousness produced by you is entirely false and lacks any representation.
Therefore, it is said, "your seeing," and so forth. It is because there is representation that boundaries can be established; since there is no representation here, [no boundary can be set].

How then can boundaries be established? Therefore it is asked: "From what are the boundaries established? If [it is argued that] consciousness arises because of form (*rūpa*), this refutes the claim that consciousness arises from form as its cause.
That is to say, if visual consciousness (*cakṣurvijñāna*) arises because of form, with form acting as the productive cause, then it could only be associated with form.
If it were to encounter empty space, your visual consciousness ought to cease, because its productive cause—[namely, form]—is absent.
Since that which is produced has no basis for being produced, how could it possibly exist? Therefore, it says, "if [it were] due to causes, etc.

Since your consciousness has already ceased, how can you know it as empty space? Therefore, it says, "what kind of thing, etc. The section beginning with "If [it were] form," etc., refutes the claim that form constitutes the boundary [of space].
The intention is that since your visual consciousness arises from form, it would be identical to form.
It is so. Suppose form were subject to change and transformation; your consciousness should likewise perceive that change and transformation. Therefore, it is said, "if form, etc.
If form were to change while your consciousness did not change, you would not even know the characteristics and appearance of that form;

how then could you establish the sense-spheres (*dhātu*)? Therefore, it is said, "your consciousness, etc. If it is claimed that when form changes, your consciousness also changes, then since the consciousness...
It follows the transformation. How could there be any characteristic of a realm to be apprehended? Therefore, it is said that "it follows transformation," and so forth.
If you say that while form itself migrates and changes, your consciousness does not change, then your consciousness would be eternal.
