Hence, it is said that "if it does not change, it must be eternal. Your consciousness originally arises from form; since you claim it does not change, it should not recognize the location of empty space. This is because it is not...
Since it has already been produced, one does not even know its location; how, then, could it establish a boundary (*dhātu*)?

Thus, it is known that whether [the sense organs] are considered to change or remain unchanged, the establishment of a boundary based on form (*rūpa*) is entirely untenable. If one were to combine both types [of factors], the refutation of their co-arising as a boundary remains unestablished.
One should supplement this with an alternative calculation, stating: "My consciousness arises from the faculty of the eye and the object of form."
Regarding "arising together": this is then recorded as "if it is simultaneous," and so forth. "Combining" refers to the formal refutation below. "Combining" is synonymous with "together.
The "li" (separation) at the top should be read as "wu" (non-); the "li" at the bottom should be read as "kai" (open). The meaning is:
if your consciousness were to arise from the sense organ and the object together, then they must combine within a single location to act as the producer; only then would it be possible.
If visual consciousness arises with a single location serving as its place of origination, then the producer and the produced would stand in opposition to one another;
yet within your consciousness, there is no such intermediate position. Therefore, it is said: "If they unite, the center is lost.

If you say that although they arise together, they do not originally occupy the same location, then if they arise together without being in the same location, you must open up the two—the sense organ and the object—into separate entities.

It is capable of producing [consciousness]. Since two locations have already been opened, the resulting eye-consciousness would then be half-conjoined with the faculty and half-conjoined with the object;
thus it is said that "if separated, they must both conjoin. If they are indeed conjoined in both ways, then that which possesses the illumination of the faculty should certainly possess cognition.

If you claim that the objects of cognition are non-discriminative, they must still possess the quality of being known. If this were so, then the substance of the objects and the nature of the faculties would become intermingled and confused;
thus it is said that their substance and nature are in disarray. In this way, if one considers them in conjunction, the center is lost;
yet since your consciousness lacks even a central position, how could the boundaries of your consciousness be established? Furthermore, if one considers them in separation...
If the two were combined, then the faculties and their objects would become intermingled and confused; from where, then, would the boundaries of your consciousness arise? Therefore it is asked:

"How are the realms established? If one observes them in combination, one cannot establish the realm as the eye because consciousness arises from the eye, nor can one establish the realm as form because consciousness does not arise from form.
Furthermore, if they were to co-arise, and the realm were established based on this co-arising, then—
Furthermore, it is not possible; how then can visual consciousness be established as a constituent element (*dhātu*)? The subsequent cases are to be treated analogously.

Regarding the second [set], the elements of the ear, sound, and auditory consciousness: within the refutation of the proposed thesis, [it is argued] that if [consciousness] arises because of the ear, and so forth, the claim that its cause is the ear is untenable.
That is to say, if your consciousness arises because of the ear, then the ear would be the producer and the consciousness the produced. However...
That the ear functions as an ear depends entirely upon the two objects of motion and stillness. If these two objects do not appear, your faculty would have no object of cognition whatsoever;
thus it is said, "motion, stillness, and so forth. Since the two objects do not appear, the hearing-faculty must likewise have nothing to cognize.
If the faculty that produces [cognition] cannot even be established, how could the consciousness produced by it take on any form?

Is it their appearance? Therefore, it is said that "there certainly is none," and so forth. If one takes "hearing" and so on as the basis, this refutes the claim that the ear constitutes a distinct element (*dhātu*), which would be untenable. The meaning is:
if one takes the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) as the element, the function of the ear is entirely established through the presence of movement and stillness.

If these two objects do not exist, then the hearing-faculty of the ear cannot be established either; for even this faculty— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the interdependence of the sense organ and its object.*
If it cannot be obtained, then it can be understood that the *dhātu* (element) is not established. Therefore, it says, "if one takes [the object] as equal," and so forth.

This refutes the *paramārtha-indriya* (ultimate sense organ) as being an unestablished *dhātu*. What follows below refutes the *bhrānta-indriya* (phenomenal sense organ) as being an unestablished *dhātu*.
The meaning is that since the aforementioned movement and stillness do not arise, the hearing faculty is not established; thus, as a *dhātu*, it is also not established. How then can you...

The shape of the ear is like that of a curled lotus leaf. Since the four great elements and the derived material phenomena are things with form that can be touched, could these be your auditory consciousness-element?

Furthermore, it may be said: since there is no sound-object to trigger your faculty of hearing, how could the physical form of your ear—composed of the eight factors of subject and object—trigger your faculty of hearing through such objects as the tactile sensations of the eye’s physical body?
Does it arise with your ear-consciousness as its constituent element (*dhātu*)? Therefore, it is said: "What kind of thing would that be?

In this way, since even the ear-consciousness cannot be apprehended, upon what could one further rely to establish it as a boundary or constituent element? Therefore, it is said: "Then [it would be] the ear, etc.
If it were produced from sounds and so forth, the argument that consciousness is not produced from sound would be undermined. If your consciousness were to depend upon sound...
If sound were the producer and consciousness the produced, then it would have no relation to the faculty of hearing. Therefore, it is said that "if [consciousness] were produced," and so forth.
Since it would not relate to hearing, there would be no hearing at all. If there were no hearing, then the characteristics of the sense-object of sound would all be unknown as to their location.
In such a case, even the sound that acts as the producer would not exist, let alone that which is produced by it.
From what does consciousness arise? If you say it arises from sound, then it is said that there is no hearing and so forth.

By stating that "consciousness arises from sound," one refutes the claim that sound constitutes a constituent element (*dhātu*), which is untenable. The phrase "initially, consciousness arises from... is a concessive statement. The underlying intent is:

although I previously refuted your position and shown that the characteristic of sound (*śabda-lakṣaṇa*) does not even exist, since you assert that consciousness arises from sound, I shall likewise grant this for the sake of argument.
"Your sound-objects exist because of the nature of hearing; thus, there is the appearance of sound. Therefore, it is said that "consciousness arises from [sound]," and so forth.

"Hearing should... and so on is the refuting argument. The meaning is that although you may concede the existence of the sound that produces [consciousness], since consciousness arises because of that sound...
Then it would be no different from sound. If consciousness were to hear when sound is heard, one would say that "hearing should also hear consciousness.

If you say that one hears only sound and does not hear consciousness, then since consciousness itself would not be heard, its very substance would not even exist; how then could it be established as a constituent element (*dhātu*)?
Therefore, it is said that "not hearing is not a constituent element. If you say that when sound is heard, consciousness also hears, then the substance of consciousness is identical [to sound].
It is thus with sound. Therefore it is said that upon hearing, the sounds are identical. Once the sound is heard, consciousness is also heard; hence it is said that "consciousness has been heard.
Since consciousness has been heard, there is no one who makes a distinction; who knows the consciousness within the hearing? Thus it is said, "Who knows the consciousness of hearing?
Viewed from this perspective, consciousness is not a thing that possesses cognition. If consciousness...
Without knowledge, one would ultimately be the same as grass and trees. If one were like grass and trees, how could one establish boundaries?

Therefore, it is said that "if there were no [conditions], etc. It should not be that the Śrāvakas and others refute the co-arising [of consciousness], for if they did, the establishment of boundaries would be untenable.

The meaning is that, as stated above, if consciousness arises from the ear, the ear is taken as its boundary; if consciousness arises from sound, sound is taken as its boundary—and in neither case is this tenable.
This is established. How could the sense-object of sound and the sense-organ of hearing arise together with your consciousness to constitute a middle realm?

Therefore, it is said that "it should not be so," and so forth. Since they would be co-arising, half would reside in the organ and half in the object; thus, the two aspects of organ and object—the subject and the object—would stand as equals.
How, then, could there be a middle position for your consciousness? Therefore, it is said that "the realm has no middle position. If this were the case...

It is not only that the middle position within your consciousness is untenable as a boundary; rather, since both the internal sense-faculties and the external objects are non-existent, from what could your consciousness know them to be "faculties" or "objects"?

Therefore, it says, "then the internal," and so forth. Regarding the "boundary between the nose, fragrance, and consciousness," this refers to the refutation through the examination of the proposed [position].
The phrase "if it arises because of the nose" and so on refutes the idea that the cause of that consciousness is its arising from the nose.

This is not established. If one takes the lower [definition] to generally indicate the two types of nose, the "mark of the twin claws" refers to the physical sense organ (*bhautika-indriya*), while the "nature of smelling and knowing" refers to the ultimate sense organ (*paramārtha-indriya*).
If one takes the lower [definition] to specifically refute the two types of nose: first, one refutes the physical sense organ; this refers to the fleshy form and so forth.
Second, one refutes the ultimate sense organ; this refers to the smelling and knowing and so forth. Within the initial refutation of the physical sense organ, the cause is first refuted.

"Birth. This refers to breaking down the "body" (*kāya*) into its constituent elements (*dhātu*). Within the analysis of ultimate reality (*paramārtha*), there are two parts: first, the refutation of birth from causes; second, the breakdown of the two substances into elements.

Within the first section, the refutation of birth from causes, there is first a general inquiry, followed by a specific refutation starting with "flesh" and so forth. This specific refutation has three parts: namely, flesh, space, and fragrance.
First, regarding flesh, it is known through visibility. Second, regarding the knowledge of space: within this, "space" refers specifically to the space at the tip of the nose.

Furthermore, although emptiness resides in the nose, it is truly no different from the great void. Third, regarding the point that "knowing fragrance belongs to the middle [realm]," the text below asks, "How does this concern you?
One should supplement this by saying: "Although it belongs to the cognition of fragrance, it is still the cognition of my nose. He then refutes this, saying:
"If the cognition of fragrance were your nasal cognition, then the fragrances and odors that are known would necessarily arise within your own nose. Therefore...

It refers to things such as fragrance. To break them down into their constituent elements (*dhātu*): in the first two cases, the objects and so forth are analyzed by subsuming the sense organ under the object; this can be understood accordingly.

Second, regarding "if the nose [perceives] the foul," etc., the objects are analyzed by subsuming them under the sense organ. The two phrases "if it is foul, it is not fragrance" mean that if the nose perceives what is foul, it should not perceive fragrance;
if the nose perceives what is fragrant, it should not perceive what is foul. It is not merely a matter of saying "this is... [as previously stated].
"Perfume is not stench, and stench is not perfume. [The opponent] argues that "perfume should not be stench," and so forth. One should supplement this by adding the following counter-argument:
"My nose does not merely smell fragrance and not smell stench, nor smell stench and not smell fragrance; rather, it smells both fragrance and stench. Therefore, he proceeds to refute this, saying:
"If the objects you smell were two distinct things, then the smelling nose would likewise have to be two. Thus...

"Such as fragrance and so forth. Regarding "if the nose were one," this means that if the nose capable of smelling were only one, then even though there are fragrant and foul objects to be smelled, they would likewise be limited to only one.
Therefore, it says "if the nose [were one]" and so forth. "The two natures" refers to the formal conclusion that the [olfactory] element cannot be established;

that is, since the two natures of fragrance and foulness cannot be definitively determined, your consciousness— ...[is not established]. (Note: The source text appears to be a commentary on the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* regarding the analysis of the sense bases.)
From what can the function [of consciousness] be perceived so as to establish the elements (*dhātu*)? Therefore, it says, "the two natures, etc.

If [it is argued that consciousness] arises because of fragrance and so forth, the claim that consciousness arises because of fragrance is refuted. Regarding the phrase "if because of [fragrance], etc.":
if your consciousness arises because of fragrance, then fragrance is the producer and consciousness is the produced. Thus it says, "if because of [fragrance], etc. With respect to this:

This consists of two points. Since you claim that fragrance is capable of producing [consciousness], I fear that the consciousness produced by you may not necessarily be able to know the nature of your own fragrance.

Therefore, I cite an analogy: "like the eyes and so forth. Just as that which arises from the eye cannot, in turn, observe the eye itself, so too it follows that your consciousness, existing because of fragrance, should not be able to know the fragrance. Thus it is said:

This refers to [the cognition of] fragrance and so forth. If consciousness were necessarily able to know fragrance, then since fragrance is inherently without cognition while your consciousness possesses cognition, it would not be produced by fragrance.

Therefore, it is said that "knowing is not arising. If one says it does not know, then since consciousness is defined by its capacity for discernment (*vijñapti*), if it does not know fragrance, it is not consciousness. Therefore, it is said that "not knowing is not consciousness. Thus, knowing and not knowing are two...
All these are untenable. [The opponent asks: "Does consciousness then arise because of fragrance? [The author replies: "Fragrance does not know that it exists," and so forth;
this refutes the claim that fragrance constitutes a distinct realm (*dhātu*), as it is not established. This means that fragrance does not know itself to be fragrance;

it entirely depends upon the discrimination of consciousness to be known. Since the consciousness that arises is itself devoid of cognition, there is ultimately no basis for fragrance to be what it is.
It would then be manifest. Since the fragrance is not manifest, it cannot constitute a realm; thus it is said that "fragrance is not equal.
That "consciousness is not equal" directly refutes its failure to constitute a realm. The meaning is that it is not only the fragrance that fails to constitute [a realm]:
since your consciousness arises because of the fragrance yet does not know the fragrance, the establishment of the consciousness-realm has no source. Therefore...
It is said that consciousness is not equal [to its conditions]. Since there is no intermediate space between them, the refutation of co-arising as a constituent element (dhātu) remains unestablished.
If consciousness were to arise from the co-arising of the ear-faculty and the sound-object, then there would necessarily be an intermediate space where the consciousness is produced.

Once it is revealed that the internal faculties and external objects have the capacity to produce [consciousness], yet there is no consciousness produced in between, then the producing faculties and objects—both internal and external—cannot be established either. Thus it is said, "Since there is none," and so forth.
Since neither the middle nor the internal and external can be found, how could that nature of the auditory consciousness possibly exist? In this way, the three...
All are false and illusory; how could they together constitute a birth and together constitute a realm? Therefore, it says "those various [factors]," etc.

Regarding the tongue, taste, and consciousness realms: within the section on refuting the conceptualization by citing and analyzing them, the phrase "if [consciousness] arises from the tongue," etc., refutes the claim that the cause of consciousness arises from the tongue as unestablished.

This means that if consciousness were to arise from the tongue, the tongue would be the producer and the consciousness would be the produced. Since consciousness is [already... the tongue... [the argument follows].
If [the tongue] were merely produced, one could only perceive the flavors produced by the tongue itself;
one would not be able to perceive the sweet, sour, bitter, or pungent flavors produced by worldly things such as sugarcane. Therefore, it is said that "if it were due to causes," and so forth.

Now, since your consciousness still perceives the flavors of worldly things such as sugarcane, it cannot be known to be produced by the tongue. You should taste your own tongue yourself to refute this.
This would result in the failure of the constituent elements (dhātu). Since your consciousness arises from the tongue, it must be able to taste the tongue itself.
Please taste your own tongue: is it sweet or is it bitter? In either case, that which tastes is the same as that which is tasted.

Therefore, it is said, "You yourself," and so forth. This is a certainty. If you were to break the underside of your tongue and taste it, if it were bitter, then ultimately what [would be the subject]?
"Does the tongue taste itself? Since the tongue cannot logically taste itself, it is said that 'the tongue is not [equal].
Furthermore, there is no principle by which the tongue could taste itself; ultimately, which one among them would perceive and distinguish whether that flavor is bitter?
Therefore, it is said that 'the tongue is not equal. If you were to taste the tongue and it were not bitter, then there would be no flavor at all. As for flavor..."
It is not produced. Since the realm is established by means of taste, how could it be otherwise? Therefore, it says "the nature of the tongue," and so forth.
If [you claim] it is produced because of taste, this refutes the position that the consciousness is produced from taste; such production is not established.

If your consciousness were produced from taste, then taste would be the producer and consciousness the produced. Since your taste can produce consciousness, your consciousness would, in turn, be identical to taste. Therefore, it says "if... and so forth.
This refers to the "equality" [of the case]. It is refuted by the same logic as the following example.

That is to say, since your consciousness is identical to taste, it should not be able to taste various flavors; it would be like the tongue not being able to taste itself. Therefore, it is said to be "equal" to that [case].
Since your consciousness cannot taste flavor itself, how can you know whether that flavor is "flavorable" or "not flavorable"? Thus it is said:
What does "equal" mean? Since you do not know what this flavor is, it can be understood that consciousness is not the flavor itself, nor is it produced by the flavor.
Furthermore, "all things are equal" means that the attempt to establish the flavor as a distinct realm is untenable. First, consciousness is refuted by means of the flavor;
subsequently, the essence of consciousness is refuted by means of the flavor. If your consciousness is produced because of the flavor, then as for the power of that flavor—
Since all that arises is produced by consciousness, it is not singular; thus it is said, "Furthermore, [it is] one," and so forth.

If your consciousness were produced from multiple flavors, then since the producer is manifold, the produced would also be manifold, and your consciousness would consequently possess multiple entities.
Thus it is said, "Since the flavors are equal," and so on. In this way, could your consciousness possess multiple entities? If you say it can...
Although that which produces is manifold, that which is produced is but one. Therefore it is said:

"If the substance of consciousness is one, and if that which is produced is but one, then even though the producers are many, they must likewise be of a single flavor as the producer. Thus it is said:
"The substance must be born of flavor. If all flavors together constitute a single flavor to become the producer, then your produced consciousness—regarding its producer—is it salty or bland?
"Equal" (sama) and so forth refer to the flavors of what is appropriate and inappropriate, what is a combination, what is co-nascent, and what is subject to transformation;
thus it says "salty, bland," and so on. As for "transformation" (vipariṇāma), this refers to such things as roasting and baking, as well as fermentation and the like.

However, the reason consciousness (vijñāna) is called "consciousness" is solely because of its function of discernment (vikalpa). Since there would be nothing capable of discerning if that function were absent, it should not be called "consciousness."
Therefore, it is said that they are equally differentiated. In this way, can your consciousness be established as a single entity?
Since the flavor is the object of cognition and the consciousness is the subject of cognition, only then is the "tongue-flavor-consciousness element" (jihvā-rasa-vijñāna-dhātu) constituted.
Now, since both the flavor that produces the consciousness and the consciousness that is produced are indeterminate, how can the tongue-flavor-consciousness element be established? Thus it is said:
"What does 'what is it' mean? It ultimately means that one should not, by means of empty space, conceptualize that which gives rise to your consciousness as being "that which gives birth.
Therefore, it is said, "What is it? In this way, it is untenable for consciousness to arise because of flavors or for flavors to constitute its realm (*dhātu*).

If one attempts to establish a general connection as a realm, it will not succeed. One should rather say: "In the beginning, when tracing back the cause, it arises from the tongue; the tongue [is the cause]."
It cannot arise from the tongue. Furthermore, it cannot arise from the flavor; nor can it arise from both the tongue and the flavor together.
If this is so, how can you claim that the realm of your consciousness arises from the faculty of the tongue and the object of flavor?

Indeed, it is ultimately impossible for the mind of consciousness to arise from empty space and then differentiate itself to form a realm. Therefore, it is said: "How could it be...? [The text continues: "The tongue..."
Regarding the combination of flavors and so forth, [this argument] refutes their co-arising as a constituent element (*dhātu*), for such a state is not established.
If you claim that consciousness arises through the co-arising of the tongue-faculty and flavor-objects, this is likewise incorrect. To discuss it further:
your consciousness exists between the faculty and the object which are in opposition; yet, once those faculty and object have already combined, what further use is there for [consciousness]?
Your consciousness performs the discrimination; thus, your consciousness has no self-nature. Therefore, it is said that this applies to the tongue, flavors, and so forth.

If there were roots and objects divided into internal and external, with your consciousness situated in between to form their boundaries, then since your consciousness itself lacks self-nature, how could those boundaries arise? Hence it is asked: "How can a boundary be produced? In this way, consciousness—
Because they arise together and share a common boundary, none of them are established.

Regarding the body, touch, and consciousness elements: in the analysis and refutation of your thesis, if you claim that consciousness arises from the body and so forth, we refute the notion that its cause is the body;
such an arising is not established. If your consciousness were to arise from the body, then there would be no dual objects of touch—namely, contact through conjunction or separation. As for touch...
If dust were non-existent, then even your faculty of the body would not exist; how then could it give rise to your consciousness for the purpose of discrimination?
Thus, it is illogical that consciousness arises from the body; hence it is said, "if [consciousness] is caused by [the body]," and so forth. "If it arises from contact," and so forth.

This refutes the claim that consciousness arises from contact, which would be untenable. If your consciousness were said to arise from the sense-object of contact, it would have no connection with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*).

Therefore, it says "if [it were] due to [contact]," and so forth. If there were a body-faculty that perceives the union or separation of the sense-object of contact, it could give rise to your consciousness for the sake of discrimination.
Since you have already stated that your body certainly does not exist, who then possesses this void [consciousness]?

One who knows that emptiness is not the body and understands its conjunction and separation—such a person cannot even find the production of the object-field of touch (*spraṣṭavya-viṣaya*), so from where could the consciousness produced thereby arise? Thus, it is illogical for consciousness to arise because of contact;
hence it is said, "Who possesses [it]? and so forth. The passage beginning with "Objects do not touch cognition" refutes the impossibility of their co-arising. The intended meaning is as follows:
If you claim that consciousness and the tactile object arise together with the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*), yet the tactile object is simply a physical thing;

a physical thing does not constitute "touch," for it is manifested through the body. Therefore, it is said that "the thing does not touch, but is known. Furthermore, the body itself does not know by itself; it is triggered by touch.
Therefore, it is said that "the body knows there is touch. Since it is said that the body's knowing arises because of touch, the body is then identical to touch. Thus, it is said:

To know the body is itself touch. Furthermore, it is said that the object of touch (spraṣṭavya) is manifested through the body; thus, touch is the body itself. Therefore, it is said that knowing touch is the body.
If one knows by means of touch, then that which knows touch is not the knowledge of the body. Hence, it is said that touch itself is not the body.
Furthermore, contact has the body as its cause; thus, the body is both contact and non-contact. Therefore, it is said that the body itself is non-contact.
If this were so, then that which constitutes the body could not be considered the body, and that which constitutes contact could not be considered contact.
Consequently, the faculties of the body and the objects of contact would become mutually confused and disordered, leaving no original ground for them to exist.
It is determined that these refer to the body and touch; hence it says "body, touch," and so forth.

Discussing it from this perspective, one knows that the phrase "the object is not two" means that the two—knowledge and touch—cannot exist independently. One knows that the phrase "knowing the body" means that touch is established through mutual dependence.

The two phrases concerning "contact" (sparśa) immediately show that contact and cognition mutually negate one another. The two phrases concerning "body-contact" together conclude that neither is established.
By joining the body [to the object], he refutes their shifting argument. Their shifting argument states: "It need not be discussed whether there is cognition or contact;
at the very moment of separation and union, cognition and contact exist of themselves. He then refutes this, saying: "If you say that at the moment of separation and union..."
There is that which is called "knowing. When it is in contact with the body, if one seeks that contact, it is found to be entirely the nature of the body;
how then could there be anything to be contacted? When it is separated from the body, if one seeks the body, the cognition is found to be entirely the characteristic of empty space;

how then could there be anything to be known? Therefore, it is said that when in contact with the body, and so forth. Although you may shift your argument regarding the moment of separation and contact...

There is that which knows contact; yet, when one investigates it through the perspective of conjunction and separation, it cannot be found. Thus, even the sense organ of your body and the object of contact cannot be established as arising together;
how much less can the consciousness produced by them? The above refutes the view that consciousness arises from both [organ and object] together.

Having moved beyond the internal and external, this refutes the impossibility of their being established as distinct elements (*dhātu*). For now, we have merely refuted the impossibility of a shared element.

If, in the preceding [analysis], the body as a cause and contact as a cause were refuted only insofar as they produce [consciousness] but not insofar as they constitute its constituent elements (*dhātu*), then now they must be refuted comprehensively.
Whether the body alone constitutes the element, contact alone constitutes the element, or the body and contact together constitute the element—in all cases, they are not established.

This means that when it was previously investigated whether consciousness arises from the body as its cause, the body itself could not be found; when it was investigated whether consciousness arises from contact as its cause, contact likewise could not be found.
Furthermore, one investigates that consciousness arises dependent upon the body and contact. Yet, this body and contact cannot be apprehended.
Thus, one knows that the body cannot be established as internal, nor can it be established as external.

Since the body and contact arising together cannot be established as either internal or external, and even the body and contact that are capable of producing [consciousness] cannot be established, how could there be a middle wherein consciousness is produced?

[The middle] position does not exist. Not only are the internal and external not established, but the middle also cannot be posited. Furthermore, because the middle cannot be posited, the internal and external are also empty.

Therefore, it is said that "the internal and external are equal. One can see from these two phrases regarding the internal and external that because the internal and external are not established, the middle is also not established.

As for the two phrases regarding the non-duality of the middle, this is likewise because the position of the middle is not posited, and thus the nature of the internal and external is also empty. Its...
Even if there were such a thing as a conscious being at that time, from what basis would it establish its realm? Therefore, it is said: "It is you yourselves.
In this way, not only is birth not established by causes, but the realm itself is likewise not established.

Regarding the mental faculty, the phenomena, and the consciousness element (*manodhātu*, *dharmadhātu*, *manovijñānadhātu*): in the section on citing the entities, "mental faculty" refers to the mental organ (*manas*), and "phenomena" refers to the objects of the mind (*dharmaviṣaya*).

In the section on definitive determination, "due to the mental faculty and due to phenomena" means due to the mental organ and the objects of the mind. In the section on restating, calculating, and refuting through analysis:
If you claim that consciousness arises from the mind (*manas*) and so forth, this refutes your position that the cause of consciousness arises from the mind;

for it would mean that consciousness is produced from the mental faculty (*manendriya*), wherein the mind is the producer and consciousness is the product. I now ask you: by what cause does this producing mind itself exist?
If one investigates its origin, it must necessarily depend upon the mental objects (dharmas) that are contemplated; only then can your faculty of mind (manas-indriya) be manifested.

Thus it is said, "if [it] depends on [them]," and so forth. Therefore, we know that because there are mental objects, your faculty of mind capable of producing cognition arises as soon as they are present.
If there were no mental objects currently confronting you, your faculty of mind capable of producing cognition would have no basis for arising. Thus it is said, "if there were none," and so forth.

If one is separated from the objective dust of dharmas, the subjective faculty of the mind can never be found to possess any form or characteristic; therefore, it is said that "apart from conditions, there is no form.
If there were objective dharmas as conditions and the subjective faculty of the mind, your consciousness would arise from between them to perform discrimination.
Now, since apart from conditions there is no form, even if your consciousness were to arise, what would it have to employ as its function?
Therefore, it is asked: "What use would consciousness have? Thus, it is established that there is no logical basis for the claim that consciousness arises dependent upon the mind (*manas*).
Furthermore, your assertion regarding the mind and consciousness and so forth is refuted as being unable to constitute distinct realms (*dhātu*), as clarified in the *Abhidharmakośa*:

the cognizing mind is itself the mind (*citta*); the various acts of deliberation are the mind (*manas*); and the nature of discernment is consciousness (*vijñāna*). Moreover, some say that the cognizing mind is the eighth [consciousness].
"Consciousness (*vijñāna*). "The various deliberations" refers to the seventh consciousness; "the nature of discernment" refers to the preceding six consciousnesses. Furthermore, a sutra states:

"That which accumulates and gives rise [to phenomena] is the mind (*citta*); that which deliberates is the intellect (*manas*); that which discerns is consciousness (*vijñāna*). These names are established based on their respective functions.
However, although these three appear at first glance to be distinct aspects of consciousness, upon further investigation, this is not the case.

This is because this section discusses only the sixth consciousness (*ṣaṣṭha-vijñāna*) and the mind-faculty (*manas*). If one were to view these as three types of consciousness, there would be two inconsistencies:
first, since this is among the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), it should clarify only the six consciousnesses; if one posits three consciousnesses, it would be inconsistent with the eighteen elements.
Second, within this section it states that "sameness and difference are only of two kinds"; if one posits three consciousnesses, this would likewise be inconsistent.

It is not associated with either identity or difference. By this, it is understood that the "knowing mind" (*jñānacitta*) is precisely the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), while the "various deliberations" (*vicāraṇā*) are simply the mental faculty (*manas*).
This is because [the latter] can take as its objects the shadows of the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) that have already passed away.

Regarding the nature of "discernment" (*vijñaptitva*), it refers collectively to both the mental consciousness and the mental faculty, as both are capable of discernment; thus, the term "inclusive" (*sādhāraṇa*) is used. One must not, on account of this inclusion, [conclude that there are] two [distinct entities].
This phrase refers to the three kinds of consciousness. It means that you claim the conscious mind arises from the faculty of the intellect (*manas*);
thus, both the arising consciousness—the mind—and the various deliberations of the faculty of the intellect which produces it, possess a nature of discrimination.
Let me ask you this: as for the discerning nature (*vijñapti*) of these two, are they identical or are they distinct?
Therefore, it says, "Furthermore, you all... This is intended to lead you to investigate and refute [the opposing view].

If the consciousness-mind and the mental faculty (*manas*) were identical, then since the mental faculty possesses discrimination, the consciousness-mind would likewise be able to discriminate. How then could consciousness be said to be produced by the mental faculty? Since it has already been stated:
That which is produced would then not be identical [to its cause]; therefore, it is said that "the mind is the same as the mental faculty" (*manas*).

If the consciousness-mind were different from the mental faculty, then while the mental faculty possesses discrimination, the consciousness-mind would have nothing to cognize; therefore, it is said that "it is different from the mental faculty.

That which constitutes consciousness as consciousness is precisely its capacity to cognize. If it were different from the mental faculty and had nothing to cognize, how could one call it consciousness?

[The opponent asks: "Is this produced by the mind? [The Master] should supplement the counter-argument, saying: "Although it differs from the mental faculty (*manas*), it must originally have something to cognize. He then refutes [the position], saying:

"If consciousness has the capacity for discrimination, it should discriminate the objects of cognition (*dharmāyatana*). Since you claim it is produced by the mental faculty, by what means does it discriminate?
Could it possibly discriminate back upon the very mental faculty that produced it? Therefore, he says, "If there were... and so forth.

If they are identical in this way, then the nature of being produced is not established. If they are different, then the natures of having consciousness and lacking consciousness are likewise not established.
Therefore, it is said that they must be identical. Since identity and difference cannot even be established, from what could the element of consciousness (vijñānadhātu) be established?

Therefore, it is asked: "How are the elements (dhātus) established? By stating, "If consciousness arises dependent on dharmas," etc., one refutes the claim that consciousness arises dependent on dharmas as being unestablished.
If your consciousness were to arise dependent on the dharma-object (dharmāyatana), then the dharma would be the producer and consciousness would be the produced.

However, among all worldly phenomena, none transcend the five sense-objects such as form; and these five objects are, moreover, the respective domains of the five physical faculties (indriyas), none of which belong to the mental faculty (manas).
Regarding the "dharma-object" (dharmāyatana) that is subsumed [within the eighteen elements]: there is simply no such thing as a dharma-object capable of producing [consciousness].

Therefore, it says, "if it were due to causes and so forth," and so on. The [opponent] argues collectively: "Although all objects are what the five sense-faculties confront and are not subsumed under the mental faculty (manas), consciousness must nevertheless arise dependent upon the dharma-object.
He then refutes this, saying: "If your consciousness is definitively produced from a dharma-object, you should examine this with earnest sincerity."
Observe: what kind of characteristics do the phenomena of the mental object (dharmadhātu) possess? Therefore, it is said, "your consciousness," and so forth.

Yet, when each is examined one by one, they are merely the arising and ceasing of color and space perceived by the eye-faculty, and the arising and ceasing of movement and stillness perceived by the ear-faculty.

Even down to the conjunctions and separations, and the arising and ceasing, encountered by the body-faculty—these are all the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) and not mental objects (*dharma-viṣaya*).
Beyond the various marks of arising and ceasing of these five sense-objects, no mental object can ever be found. Therefore, it is said: "If one is separated from [them]," and so forth.

Then it would follow that the production of *dharmāyatana* (mental objects) is non-existent. Furthermore, they further argue: "The arising and ceasing within form, emptiness, and so forth, are precisely what constitutes *dharmāyatana*.

He then refutes this, saying: "If you insist that the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of these five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) constitute *dharmāyatana*, then at the moment of their arising, they are fundamentally the arising of the five sense-objects themselves and have no bearing on *dharmāyatana*. As for their ceasing, it is likewise..."
The cessation of the five sensory objects has no bearing upon the mental object (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, it is said that "when [the objects] arise, they are equal.
Thus, the mental object that can produce [consciousness] is also absent. How, then, could your consciousness arise dependent upon a mental object?
Since the cause is thus absent and so forth, its status as a distinct realm (*dhātu*) is refuted as being unestablished. In this way, since the mental object—the productive cause—is absent, and...
What kind of form, appearance, or characteristic does the consciousness produced by these causal conditions possess? Therefore, it is said, "As for what is called... and so forth.
Since even its characteristics cannot be apprehended, how could the boundaries of consciousness arise? Thus, it is asked, "How do the elements arise?
Beginning from the five aggregates and continuing until this point, each has been analyzed and exposed; not a single one remains.

Phenomena do not possess inherent attributes, for they are the illusory transformations of space; yet, there is not a single phenomenon that is not the wondrous true suchness of the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha.
If it were not for the inconceivable and wondrous provisional contemplation of samādhi, how could one perceive the truth of inconceivable and wondrous existence?
Therefore, in its refutation, it refutes that which has nothing to be refuted, and thus there is nothing [to be refuted].
It is not destroyed; where it is destroyed, it is immediately established. Its manifestation manifests nothing manifested, yet there is nothing that is not manifested.

Where it manifests, it is immediately destroyed. Therefore, in the previous general summary, it was said: "The five aggregates, the six sense bases, and so forth, all arise falsely through the conjunction of causes and conditions;
they are called 'extinction' falsely when causes and conditions disperse. It further says: "One does not realize that arising and extinction..."
The past and future are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—the eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, and all-pervading nature of wondrous True Suchness (Tathatā).
From the point where Ānanda addressed the Buddha, "From... onwards, it is a response to his request regarding the third *dhyāna*.

All of this arises because Ānanda previously petitioned the Tathāgatas of the ten directions concerning the attainment of Bodhi through the wondrous *śamatha*, the wondrous *samādhi*, and the wondrous *dhyāna*.

These three dharmas were each elucidated for the sake of others. From the time of the initial inquiry into the arousal of the bodhicitta, seven locations were used to shatter delusion, revealing that there is no object upon which it can rely;
three locations were used to interrogate the essence of delusion, revealing that there is no subject that can serve as its basis.

Following the example of a blind man seeing darkness, this demonstrates that the nature of seeing is indestructible; by showing that seeing is not contingent upon the eyes, it reveals the nature of seeing.
It is unarisen. Furthermore, by employing the analogy of Cunda as host and guest, he caused Ānanda to realize that the nature of seeing is constant:

though his own hand opens and closes, the seeing neither expands nor contracts. Again, by employing the analogy of Cunda as empty space and the dust, he caused Ānanda to realize that the nature of seeing is quiescent:
though his own head shakes and moves, the seeing has no cessation. He further demonstrated that while the body undergoes birth and death, the nature is without birth or death.

This explains the doubt regarding the distinction between the real and the false. Furthermore, by observing that while the arm has no "upside-down" or "right-side-up," the perception of it does have "upside-down" and "right-side-up," this explains the doubt regarding inversion.
From this, one clearly perceives that the nature of seeing has no point of return; within the phenomena of light, darkness, form, and emptiness, there is nowhere for the nature of seeing to return.

Thus, one clearly perceives that the nature of seeing is detached from these phenomena, and it remains far removed from all characteristics such as cause, image, and so forth. It is not merely that it negates the objects of the senses.
The deluded vision of discrimination, as well as the deluded vision of the essence of sight that perceives a second moon, is now refuted.
When one views the single seeing, that seeing is not "seeing"; even seeing is detached from seeing, for the true nature of seeing cannot itself be seen.
This explains the empty truth of *śamatha* through the two characters "mind" and "sight. Thereupon, he further addressed Ānanda: "From you..."
Not yet understanding the five aggregates (*skandha*), the six sense bases (*āyatana*), and even the eighteen elements (*dhātu*), one discusses their characteristics:

that there is no arising that is not a false manifestation through the conjunction of causes and conditions, and no cessation other than a false designation resulting from the separation of causes and conditions.

Yet when discussing their nature, it is fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha—eternally abiding, wondrously luminous, immovable, all-pervading, and the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Therefore, beginning with the five aggregates and ending with the ten...

The eight elements are each analyzed and deconstructed according to the four natures. Since they are neither produced by causes and conditions nor are they spontaneous, there is only the single, fundamental Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness (tathatā).
That which is called "destruction" has nothing to be destroyed; when the false is destroyed, its truth is revealed. That which is called "revelation" has nothing to be revealed;
when the truth is revealed, the false is destroyed. This is explained by opening the mind and its perceptions into five categories.
From the aggregates (*skandhas*) up to their expansion into the eighteen realms (*dhātus*), the subtle existence of *samādhi* is elucidated.
Reaching this point, the seven great elements are further elucidated; each is analyzed and deconstructed according to the four natures.

All of these are the conceptual constructions and calculations of the conscious mind, which mistakenly take them to be causes and conditions or spontaneous natures, in order to manifest the Truth. There is nothing that is not fundamentally pure and all-pervading.
Pervading the entire dharma-realm, this clarifies the perfect center of *dhyāna*. First, its origins and significance are set forth. If this text is divided into two parts:
the first is the inquiry and request, beginning with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha"; the second is the revelation and instruction, beginning with "At that time, the World-Honored One..."
The first section is further divided into three parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, he recounts what he previously heard; second, from "How so? onwards, he sets forth his current doubts;
third, from "I only pray that... onwards, he presents his request. The first two sections are explained together. Regarding "Ānanda and others":
Ānanda’s intention was that the Tathāgata had revealed within the state of samādhi that all phenomena are fundamentally the wondrous, true *tathāgatagarbha*.
"The nature of reality (tathatā), I have already awakened to. Yet it is fundamentally neither caused by conditions nor is it spontaneous;
it is neither of these two—conditioned causality nor spontaneity. It is not that I have no doubts, for this is what the Tathāgata has taught today.
When one examines this against what the Tathāgata previously taught, there are points of both agreement and difference. Therefore, it is said, 'The Tathāgata is equal,' and so forth. This...

This is what the Tathāgata spoke in the past. Thus, by using the present to verify the past and the past to verify the present, it appears that the principle of dependent origination cannot be set aside.
Why is it that until this very day, you have not merely set aside its natural course?
Furthermore, you have rejected both causes and conditions. Such [a view of] spontaneity (*svabhāva*) is what non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) conceive; its rejection may still be permissible.

However, causes and conditions are what the Tathāgata has taught. Why, then, do you reject them as well? In the case of the Tathāgata, rejecting both of these does not mean he lacks a definitive point of reference (*nirdeśa*).
For me, Ānanda, this meaning is not yet clear; thus I ask: "What is meant by 'eternally teaching'? As for the statement that he "constantly teaches":
Since ancient times, this has not occurred but once; therefore, it is said that he "constantly preaches. Regarding "all worlds," there are three types of worlds: first, sentient beings;

second, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); and third, the land. Taken together, these do not exceed the two categories of retribution—the primary and the secondary—nor the distinction between the animate and the inanimate.
As for "various transformations," in the case of sentient beings, they die and are born, and are born and die. Birth...
Birth and death, dying and being born, living and dying—these occur within the insentient. They transform the raw into the cooked and change existence into non-existence.
Although it is said that the various transformations of all worlds do not arise suddenly without cause, they are entirely manifested through the four great elements;

therefore, it is said, "all are due to [causes and conditions]," and so forth. Among these three, "revealing" and so forth refers to the refutation [of inherent existence] by means of causes and conditions.
"Spontaneity" (svabhāva) uses spontaneity to refute dependent origination (pratītyasamutpāda); both are merely conceptual proliferations (prapañca).

If one takes dependent origination as dependent origination, sentient beings will not yet escape attachment to existence. If one takes spontaneity as spontaneity, sentient beings will not yet cease their indulgence in emptiness.
Thus, failing to transcend these two extremes, neither constitutes the definitive meaning of the Middle Way. Now, since both dependent origination and spontaneity have been refuted..."

"Expulsion" (*pāṇa*) appears not to be a teaching of the two extremes. If one can explain the reason for this expulsion, then by clearly understanding the conditions through which one should expel and exclude, one will naturally not cling to existence (*bhava*);
by clearly understanding the spontaneity through which one should expel and exclude, one will naturally not indulge in emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This alone is the Middle Way, the definitive meaning, and the dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*). Therefore it is said: "To reveal and show... (etc.).
[It says: "This text specifically belongs to the elucidation of *dhyāna*. Therefore, when the disciple made his request, he spoke directly of the 'Middle Way.
If this were not a manifestation of great skillful means (*mahopāya*) wherein both teacher and disciple expound together, how could such a thing exist?"
The second part, the "Revelation," is divided into four sections. First, from "At that time" onwards, the censure; second, from "You now" onwards, the admonition and permission;

third, from "Ānanda" onwards, the reception of the mandate; fourth, from "Ānanda" onwards, the actual revelation. Regarding the first: "You previously felt weary of and detached from the Śrāvakas, etc. refers to this.
The "Preface" refers to the perfect fulfillment of the resolve through impartial and universal compassion.
Regarding the phrase "arousing the mind to seek diligently," it refers to the initial earnest entreaty addressed to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions to attain the realization of Bodhi.

Regarding the phrase "revealing the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya)," it refers to the preceding section on *śamatha*, wherein the deluded mind is shattered to manifest true insight; and wherein that which is to be shattered is itself non-existent, thereby revealing non-substantiality.
Regarding the "that which is manifested" and so forth: within the state of samādhi, the five aggregates and the three categories are all fundamentally the wondrous true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
This is the principle elucidated by the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao). As for the term "Middle Way" (Zhongdao):

it is called "Middle" because it negates both emptiness and existence; this principle is void and pervasive, without obstruction, and is thus termed a "Way. Being supreme and unsurpassed, it is called the "First."

First, there is a profound reason for designating this as "meaning" (*artha*). That which has been cultivated and realized by all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, being certain and not false, is designated as "truth" (*satya*).
Regarding the "true medicine," it refers naturally to the causes and conditions of worldly conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) and so forth, which were precisely the basis of Ānanda’s doubt;
it merely abbreviates the term "natural. As previously requested, it is said that there is a dharma free from conceptual proliferation. This is why—
To enumerate its objects of perception is conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). "Entanglement" (*paryavasthāna*) refers to doubt.
Speaking in terms of the metaphor, that which can give rise to a life-threatening ailment like a chronic malady is the secret art of the immortal; it serves as the true medicine.
Discussing this in terms of the Dharma, it is like the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It acts as the antidote to the diseases of afflictions (*kleśa*) and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*).
It is the medicine for death. There are no afflictions that it cannot shatter, and there is no cycle of birth and death that it cannot sever.
The Dharma-body is thereby attained and the life of wisdom is increased; this is the true medicine. Of these two [sections], the first sentence is a warning.
"I grant it at once. As for the phrase "I shall," etc., this refers to formally granting his request to elucidate *dhyāna*.

To expound the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) so as to complete the seven elements is called "differentiation" (*vibhāga*). To realize that within each and every place there is nothing that is not the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) is called "revealing and instructing" (*uddeśa*).

If we follow the previous explanation: as in the *śamatha* section, refuting the deluded mind and deluded vision is called "differentiation," while revealing the true mind and true vision is called "instruction.

In the *samādhi* section, expanding upon mind and matter as the five aggregates and three categories is called "differentiation," while showing that their very essence is the Tathāgata-garbha is called "instruction. This shall also be applied to future generations.
This means that Chan-na (Dhyāna) is the correct contemplation of the non-dual Dharma. It is not intended solely for you, Ānanda, and the assembly present here to practice;

it is also intended so that all future practitioners of the Mahāyāna in later generations may rely upon it to penetrate the true nature (*tathatā*). This true nature is the essence of the fruit of Bodhi. Chan-na...
That is the practice that enables one to penetrate the cause. Therefore, within the *Śamatha* [section], after revealing the seeing of seeing, it concludes by showing:
"You all are narrow-minded, inferior, and ignorant, unable to penetrate the pure reality (*dharmatā*). I now instruct you: you should contemplate this well;
do not grow weary or indolent on the wondrous path to Bodhi. This is because Ānanda initially requested [this teaching] regarding the ten directions.
The Tathāgata has attained the sublime śamatha of bodhi. Furthermore, at the beginning of his response, he first indicated:
"There is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown, the path of wondrous adornment through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend in a single gate.
For this reason, he permits its exposition. Dhyāna is also said to cause those who practice the Mahāyāna to penetrate the true reality (bhūtalakṣaṇa). Third.

Seeing. The section on the fourfold correct demonstration is divided into two parts. First, from "Ānanda, as you go" onwards, the meaning is explained in general. Second, from "Observe the nature of earth" onwards, the elements are demonstrated individually.
The first part [of the first division] is further divided into three. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, the doubt is restated. Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, it is addressed...
This is the analysis. The three sections following Ānanda’s question use metaphors to clarify the point; the first is easily understood.

In the second, the phrases "neither a combination nor that which is combined" mean that because Ānanda was about to take what the Tathāgata previously taught regarding the causes and conditions of combination and doubt the present causes and conditions of spontaneity—both of which are now being set aside—it is because he took combination to be the cause and condition that there is [the need to negate] that which is not a combination.
This is the natural sense of the matter. Now, wishing to clarify that both [positions] are to be rejected, I shall proceed by contrasting non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*) and conjunction (*saṃyoga*).
This is divided into two parts: first, "If that... and below refutes non-conjunction; second, "If conjunction... and below refutes conjunction.
Each [of these] possesses both the thesis (*dharma*) and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*). First, regarding "not within conjunction":
if those factors are like the examples such as "like that," the phrase "if those" in the thesis serves to cite their conjunction in order to demonstrate what is not conjunction.
The example is evident. At the end, one should conclude by saying: "This has been clarified by means of both the thesis and the example; it is not a conjunction in this way. This is non-conjunction.
Their characteristics are precisely the natural state (*svabhāva*), yet none are not false and illusory; how could one not reject them? Next, regarding the section on "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*):

the phrase "if [it were] conjunctive phenomena" uses analogies such as "whirling" and so forth. Within these phenomena, the first two phrases of the "conjunction" section restate what is being doubted.

The two phrases concerning "beginning and end" clarify the *niśrita-vipāka* (the environment or dependent retribution). The two phrases concerning "birth and death" clarify the *sambhava-vipāka* (the primary retribution or the sentient beings themselves).

Regarding "arising" (*utpāda*): among the four phases of formation and so forth, the lands do not exist outside of them. Formation and abiding constitute the beginning; destruction and emptiness constitute the end.

Since formation and abiding bring about destruction and emptiness, and destruction and emptiness bring about formation and abiding, they mutually constitute one another; hence it is said that "the beginning and the end constitute each other.
Furthermore, formation and abiding are "arising," while destruction and emptiness are "cessation. Because the arising of formation and abiding continues [into the subsequent phase]...

The cessation of the destruction-emptiness continues back into the arising of formation and subsistence; these mutually sustain one another, and thus it is said that "arising and cessation continue in succession.
Such is the nature of the dependent retribution lands, which are formed through such harmonious conjunction and transformation.
Next, regarding the middle [category]: sentient beings do not transcend the two characteristics of birth and death. Because there is birth, there is death; because there is death, there is birth.
As they mutually constitute one another's birth and death, it is said that "birth and death, death and birth.
From this, they are born again and again, born repeatedly without end; they die again and again, dying repeatedly without exhaustion. Birth and death have no limit.

Therefore, it is said that there is "birth and death within birth and death. If we discuss this in terms of the realm (*dhātu*), beginning with generation and ending with death, and ending with death while returning to the generation of the beginning—this is the mutual completion of the beginning and the end.

By means of the generation of the present, one continues the death and extinction of the past; by means of the death and extinction of the future, one continues the generation of the present. This is birth...
This is the continuity of cessation. Such is the nature of the sentient beings of the primary retribution, who are said to be produced through combination and transformation.
In this way, the arising and ceasing of lands and the birth and death of sentient beings all mutually sustain one another in a continuous succession that is utterly inexhaustible.
If explained by means of a metaphor, it is like the circle of a whirling firebrand that never ceases.

Furthermore, the harmony [of causes and conditions] is clarified through both the Dharma and metaphors in this manner. This characteristic of harmony is precisely dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).
Since it is not at all unreal, how could it be rejected? Among the three metaphors used to reveal this, the example of water and so forth serves as a general metaphor for harmony.
Union is not true harmony. True harmony is like water forming ice; non-union is like ice returning to water.
Thus, both this water-as-ice and ice-as-water are not the clear, translucent essence of water.
Likewise, that which is natural non-union and the conditions of union are not the fundamental nature of reality.
This is its essence. Because it is not a fundamentally pure essence, both "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) are excluded.
Formerly, those who spoke of causes and conditions did so to refute the spontaneity of the non-Buddhists; this pertained to the Hīnayāna, not the Mahāyāna.
Now, that both causes and conditions and spontaneity are excluded pertains to the Mahāyāna, not the Hīnayāna. You, Ānanda, have long...
This should already be understood. Why then do you cite past doubts regarding the present and claim that you do not understand this meaning?

Some say that the metaphor of the fire-wheel represents conjunction (*saṃyoga*), while the metaphor of ice and water represents non-conjunction (*asaṃyoga*). This is not so. Non-conjunction is illustrated by the metaphor of empty space, while conjunction is illustrated by the metaphor of the fire-wheel;
thus, each has its own distinct dharma and metaphor made clear. Yet, fearing that Ānanda might still not be enlightened, [the Buddha spoke further].
The principle of excluding both "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) is again summarized and clarified by means of the analogy of ice and water.

How could the analogy of the fire-wheel (*alāta-cakra*) possibly serve as a metaphor for both "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) and "non-conjunction"? It may be appropriate to use the analogy of ice and water to conclude the preceding section and introduce the subsequent one;
however, the intent behind concluding the former and introducing the latter differs in each case. Concluding the former is as explained above. As for introducing the latter:
In the latter case, the seven [realms] manifest according to karma within the Great Vehicle, like water forming ice. Their original purity is like the ice returning to water.
Speaking in terms of the Dharma, although there is a distinction between the true and the false, they are one in the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Speaking in terms of the analogy, although there is a division between ice and water, they are one in their moist nature. Thus, the defiled seven [realms] manifest according to karma.
It is "Great. Therefore, it is likened to water forming ice. Being fundamentally pure and still refers to the purity of the seven elements; therefore, it is likened to ice returning to water.

Within the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), there is originally neither defilement nor purity; it is only through delusion and enlightenment that defilement and purity are distinguished.
Therefore, when there is delusion, the purity of the Buddha-realm becomes the defilement of the nine realms, just as water turns into ice due to cold and congealing.
When there is awakening, the defilement of the nine realms becomes the purity of the Buddha-realm, just as ice returns to water through the harmony of warmth.
The Tathāgata intends precisely to clarify that the characteristics of the seven elements are all in accordance with karma.
[The text] reveals that the nature of the seven elements is, without exception, fundamentally pure; therefore, this is clarified in advance by means of analogies.

Second, the detailed exposition of each of the seven elements. Prior to the seven elements, one should first present the general meaning, as is fully set forth in the *Yuan-tong-shu* (Commentary on Perfect Penetration).

The seven great elements are not recorded again here after the preceding text. Some have said that while the mind and the three samādhis of *śamatha*, as well as the five aggregates of *samādhi*, all take what is near—the body—as their object, only the present *dhyāna* takes what is distant—external objects—as its object; this is why the seven great elements are explained.
This is not correct. For instance, when the mind and dharmas of *śamatha* perceive what is near, that very thing is both form (*rūpa*) and yet also distant. Just so...
"Samādhi. There is no need to discuss the rest. Among the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), how could the first five not be "near"?

Now, regarding *dhyāna*, there is likewise no need to discuss the five great elements (*pañcamahābhūta*). How could the consciousness of seeing (*cakṣurvijñāna*) be "far"? Therefore, it is absolutely impermissible to make such a statement.
The major sections are divided into seven, namely from the earth element (*pṛthivīdhātu*) up to the consciousness element (*vijñānadhātu*).
The first stage [of the analysis] is divided into four parts. First, the initial presentation: "Observe, etc. Second, the refutation through reasoning: "Ānanda, etc. Third, the pointing out:

"You, from the beginning, etc. Fourth, the censure: "The world, etc. Within the first part, the presentation, the nature of the nature of the stages (*bhūmi*)—which, in the case of Ānanda, is precisely the nature of the distinction between self and other—is therefore characterized by coarseness and subtlety; whereas in the Tathāgata...
This is precisely the true nature that is fundamentally pure and quiescent. This nature is inherently non-dual; it is only in respect to what Ānanda perceives that there appear to be differences.
This is because he has used the great element of earth to infer [the nature] through delusion. As for the following six sections, they all distinguish [the truth] based on the Real.
"Analyzing those" refers to what is called "analytical emptiness" (*vibhajya-śūnyatā*). However, analytical emptiness applies generally to practitioners of the Three Piṭakas and...
"O non-Buddhists, you should know that when the Three Piṭakas analyze emptiness, they refute all that the non-Buddhists possess.
The non-Buddhists only know how to analyze and further analyze—breaking the great earth down into subtle particles until reaching the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal) to constitute emptiness.
Yet they do not understand the reason why emptiness is empty. If practitioners of the Three Piṭakas observe it with contemplation, they see that everything is a harmony of causes and conditions."
When combined, they exist; yet upon thorough investigation, they are utterly unfindable. Just as the four great elements each return to their source, who is my body?

By investigating and exhausting the ultimate truth in this manner, one naturally differs from the "emptiness through analysis" of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), though the analytical emptiness of the non-Buddhists will naturally be refuted.
For now, however, I shall speak by way of their own position; thus it is said that [the elements] coarsely constitute the great earth and so forth.

The second section, "Refutation through Reasoning," is divided into two parts. First, from "If this... onwards, is the demonstration by analogy. Second, from "You now... onwards, is the refutation by analogy. Regarding the first part:
"If this" and so forth refers back to the previous analysis of those [atoms], namely, the color-form of the *paramāṇu* (infinitesimal atom).
Since it can be analyzed into emptiness, by analogy, emptiness can likewise give rise to the color-form of the *paramāṇu*. Therefore, it is said:
If it is such as this, then taking this as an example, one intends precisely to refute the opponent’s scheme of manifesting through conjunction.

Therefore, one proceeds to cite their doubt, saying: "As for what you have now asked," and so forth. This refutation by way of analogy is divided into four parts: first, citing the question, "As for what you have now...

and so forth; second, the counter-objection, "You should first... and so forth; third, the actual demonstration, "If form... and so forth; fourth, the conclusion of the refutation, "Form... and so forth.

"Is it still the same? This first section restates the question from the initial inquiry, specifically restating the question regarding the various transformations resulting from the causes and conditions of their conjunction;
hence, it says, "Are you now still the same? The second section, the refutation by way of counter-argument, is further divided into two parts:

first, from "You should for a moment... onwards, the refutation that space conjoins with form to become form; second, from "Furthermore, [space] adjacent to... onwards, the refutation that form conjoins with space to become space. Within the first of these, "You should for a moment... [is explained as follows].

The preceding [argument] should have been stated as follows: "Just as one analyzes the *paramāṇu* (atom) to constitute empty space, it would seem possible to combine empty space to constitute a *paramāṇu*.
Since you have asked, 'Is it by means of combination that the various transformed phenomena of the world arise?', I now ask you in return:
Can empty space be combined to form a *paramāṇu*? If you say it can, then observe for a moment: how many..."
Space combines to form a single *paramāṇu* (ultimate atom). Therefore, it is said, "You should consider them equal.

If one were to say this is impossible—since *paramāṇus* exist in the present—how could *paramāṇus* combine with *paramāṇus* to form a *paramāṇu*? However, in the end, it is not logical that *paramāṇus* should combine to constitute a *paramāṇu*.
Therefore, it is said, "It should not be so," and so forth. Furthermore, in the middle section, prior to the *paramāṇu*, it should also be...
The Buddha said: "I shall now question you in return. Since empty space cannot be synthesized from atoms (*paramāṇu*), then atoms likewise cannot be analyzed away to form empty space.
Ānanda, can you analyze atoms to produce empty space? If you say that you can,"
You should further observe how many infinitesimal particles (*paramāṇu*) of form must aggregate to constitute empty space. Therefore, it says "furthermore, the infinitesimal particles," and so forth.
There should likewise be a passage stating that if [space] were not [composed of such], it would be illogical for empty space to be composed of empty space.
This is merely a brief summary. Within the section on the "Threefold Correct Demonstration," regarding the period prior to [the formation of] form, it should be said:
"Ānanda, as for how you have understood this, from the perspective of my Tathāgata-view, there is no principle by which emptiness could combine with anything to form a *paramāṇu* (subtle atom)."
Furthermore, there is no principle by which the aggregation of atoms (*paramāṇu*) could constitute empty space. Why is this?

If one intends for the color of aggregated atoms to become empty space, it is originally an aggregation of color and not an aggregation of emptiness. Since color is being joined with color, how could the aggregation of atoms result in empty space?
Therefore, it is said: "If [it were] like color, etc. If, on the other hand, it were an aggregation of the emptiness of empty space...

When one seeks to form a *paramāṇu* (subtle atom), it must originally be a conjunction of space rather than a conjunction of matter. Since space is conjoined with space, how could it be that by conjoining with empty space one forms a *paramāṇu*?
Therefore, it is said, "If [space were] equal [to matter]," and so forth. You claim that through combination, the various transformed phenomena of the world are produced;
yet although these transformations are many, they do not transcend matter and space. Since space cannot be formed into matter, [the formation of atoms is impossible].
Furthermore, form cannot be established as emptiness; thus, one knows that your claim that the various transformed characteristics are produced through combination is entirely false and illusory.
Regarding the fourth point, the refutation by means of conjunction: the phrase "form, etc.

intends to show that when analyzed in this manner, it is certainly impossible for empty space to be established as the color of an atom (*paramāṇu*), and likewise, it is impossible for the color of an atom to be established as the emptiness of space. This makes it clear.

[It is so. According to your [position], it may still be possible to analyze the color of a *paramāṇu* (neighboring atom) into empty space; however, how could that empty space be synthesized back into a *paramāṇu*?
Therefore, it is said: "it is still [the same] as before," and so forth.

Regarding the three indications, the phrase "you originally did not know," etc., refers to Ānanda’s doubt concerning all the various manifested phenomena that arise from the conjunction of worldly conditions;
this lack of knowledge is delusion. This delusion of not knowing has no other cause than the failure to understand the true nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
It is specifically for the purpose of pointing this out that it is said, "you originally [did not know]," and so forth. There are three aspects to the *tathāgatagarbha*.

There are three kinds: namely, the virtue of nature (*prakṛti-guṇa*), the virtue of cultivation (*bhāvanā-guṇa*), and that which is realized. As for the virtue of nature, it refers to the principle of this Tathāgatagarbha-nature:
the suchness of the Tathāgata and the suchness of sentient beings are one suchness, not two suchnesses; whether there is a Buddha or no Buddha, its substance eternally abides.
When the Buddhas attain it, it does not become superior; when sentient beings lose it, it does not become inferior. Among the sages, it is not pure; among the ordinary, it is not defiled.
Thus, defilement and purity share the same source; high and low are equal; the sage and the ordinary are non-dual; and sentient beings and Buddhas are as one.
This is naturally and inherently present, not requiring artificial construction, for it is endowed with the merit of this nature. This is called "inherent virtue" (*xingde*).
It is the Tathāgatagarbha. Regarding the cultivation of virtue: although it is said that the nature-virtue is inherently possessed by all sentient beings, they remain entirely immersed in delusion.
However, when they hear this wondrous principle of nature-virtue from a Dharma Master or a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra), they give rise to inconceivable and wondrous contemplation.

Thus, the entire nature gives rise to cultivation, and the entire principle becomes practice. Through this, the Three Truths are manifested in distinct clarity, and the three delusions are [gradually eliminated] from this point on.

Yet they are divided and broken apart. However, in breaking, there is nothing to be broken; the very act of total breaking is itself manifestation. In manifesting, there is nothing to be manifested; total manifestation is itself breaking.
