Since it is wondrously luminous, although it is said to arise, in its very essence it does not arise; although it is said to cease, in its very essence it does not cease. Therefore, it is said: "Wondrously luminous, it does not..."
Cessation does not arise. In all cases, it takes the wondrous clarity of the awakened nature and the luminous subtlety of fundamental awakening as its wisdom.
This is precisely the wondrous wisdom of the Tathāgata’s non-arising and non-ceasing. The Tathāgatagarbha is that which can give birth to all phenomena.
That which is called "arising" is utterly unattainable, because it is the totality of true emptiness; yet it is able to fully embody all phenomena.
That which is called "endowment" is likewise unattainable, because it is the totality of true emptiness.

Therefore, the Tathāgatagarbha takes the wondrous clarity of intrinsic awareness and the clarity-wonder of fundamental awareness as its principle. This is precisely the Tathāgata’s non-arising and non-ceasing.
This is the wondrous realm. One uses the wondrous wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing to illumine the wondrous realm of non-arising and non-ceasing;
one further gives rise to the wondrous wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing by means of the wondrous realm of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, this wisdom has nothing to know; it takes the entire realm as wisdom. This realm has nothing to be a realm; it takes the entire wisdom as realm.

Object and wisdom are of one suchness; subject and object are non-dual. Thus it is said, "and such as... The phrase "perfectly illuminating the dharma-realm" precisely clarifies that the object of wisdom is fully manifest.
Since it was stated above that "entire wisdom is the realm," although there is an illuminator and an illuminated, it is simply wisdom illuminating wisdom.
Since it was stated above that "the entire realm is wisdom," although there is an illuminated, it is simply the realm [illuminating itself].
This refers to the illumination of the objective realm. Thus, in stillness, the three truths are simultaneously still; in illumination, the three truths are simultaneously illuminated.
Throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not the wondrous wisdom of non-arising and non-ceasing, as well as the wondrous realm of non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, it is said that "it perfectly illuminates the dharma-realm. Consequently, the following section correctly clarifies how, within the state where realm and wisdom are of one suchness, the great function arises.

Furthermore, there are four phrases beginning with "One is immeasurable," which are introduced. These are then elucidated through four sections beginning with "The place of enlightenment is immovable.
At first glance, it appears that these four sections merely explain two phrases; yet upon further investigation, since there are four introductory headings, there must likewise be four explanations.

However, the first and last sections concern the *niśraya-vipāka* (the environment), while the second and third concern the *sambhoga-kāya* (the primary retribution). Thus, the small and the large are mutually contained.

The section beginning with "Many are unimpeded" (多無礙) is as usual not recorded [in the main text]. The section beginning with "Extinguishing dust" (滅塵下) concludes the reason for the convergence of the *tathāgatagarbha*; this may be understood.
Second, within the "Manifestation of the Intention" (出意中), it extensively clarifies the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna*) of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

The passage beginning with "Neither mind nor emptiness" (非心非空等) fully elucidates the phenomena of the ten realms (*daśadhātu*). "Mind" refers to the element of consciousness (*vijñānadhātu*); "emptiness" and so forth refer to the six elements (*ṣaḍdhātu*), which subsume the five [other] elements.

The "aggregates" (skandhas) refer to the sense bases (āyatana) and elements (dhātu), such as the eyes and ears; these collectively comprise the dharmas of the six realms of existence. "Knowledge" and "ignorance" refer to the dharmas of the truths and conditions of the Two Vehicles.

"Generosity" (dāna), "precept-keeping" (śīla), and so forth, refer to the dharmas of the Bodhisattvas' Six Perfections (ṣaṭpāramitā). Such categories as these constitute the dharmas of the Buddha, who possesses the three titles and four virtues.

First, they are neither [identical nor different]; second, they are both identical and different; third, they are both neither identical nor different, and both identical and different, transcending both identity and difference.
This is not a sentence consisting of two phrases. According to its meaning, the phrasing should be: "separate from both 'is' and 'is-not,' yet identical to both 'is' and 'is-not.
When it is empty, it is the emptiness of all things; thus, even that which is "within" is empty. Therefore, it is said: "neither mind nor emptiness," and so on, up to "neither self nor purity.
What is meant by "neither" is that all ten realms are simultaneously negated. When it is existent, it is the existence of all things.
All that exists is precisely within emptiness; therefore, it is said that "mind is precisely emptiness," and so on, up to "self is precisely purity.
What is meant by "precisely" (ji) is that all ten realms are simultaneously "precisely" [empty]. What is meant by "middle" (zhong) is that within the one, all are middle.
Thus, one knows that at the beginning, mind and emptiness are both negated and both illuminated; and at the end, self and purity are likewise both negated and both illuminated.
Illumination. This refers to the equality of negation and illumination, where emptiness and existence are non-dual.

It is what is called the simultaneous departure from both the ten realms and their negation—where departing is not simultaneous with being, and being is not simultaneous with departing. This is what is meant by the dual negation and dual illumination. Thus, it may be called True Emptiness;

it may be called Wondrous Existence; it may be called the Middle Way. Therefore, speaking in terms of the "simultaneous negation of both," [the text] proclaims and reveals: "And yet, the Tathāgata..."
The "Treasury Edition" [reads]: "The wondrous, perfect mind. "Wondrous" refers to the existence of wondrous existence;

"perfect" refers to the center of the Middle Way; and "mind" refers to the emptiness of true emptiness. Because emptiness is primary, it is placed last, precisely to manifest that when emptiness is realized, all things are empty together.
Wondrous existence is then set forth as: "The original luminosity of the Tathāgata-garbha, the wondrousness of the mind. "Original" refers to the Middle Way.
Within this, "clarity" refers to the emptiness of true emptiness, and "wondrous" refers to the existence of wondrous existence. Since existence is primary, it is placed last;
this also reveals that where there is existence, both [emptiness and existence] are present. The Middle Way is then revealed and proclaimed as:

"the wondrously luminous mind-source of the Tathāgatagarbha. "Wondrous" refers to the existence of wondrous existence, "clarity" refers to the emptiness of true emptiness, and "source" (yuan) refers to the Middle.
Within the Middle Way, the Middle is taken as primary; therefore, it is placed last. This also demonstrates that when the Middle is revealed, all three are simultaneously the Middle.
In this way, one sees that raising one immediately implies the three, and speaking of the three immediately implies the one—this is the inconceivable, perfectly interfused Three Truths.
The threefold summary and reprimand consists of three parts: first, the teaching, which begins with "How could it be..."; second, the analogy, which begins with "It is like...";
and third, the conclusion, which begins with "As for you and... Regarding the first part, the phrase "How could it be... directly rebukes Pūrṇa and the great assembly.
The underlying meaning is that the Tathāgata unites the mind of non-arising and non-extinction with the *tathāgatagarbha*, and thus the *tathāgatagarbha* is such as this.
This is the wondrous essence. How could there be mutual encroachment, mutual extinction, or a lack of mutual accommodation? Therefore it is said: "How can it be... (and so forth).

The three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) refer to ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), who know only existence. Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas know only emptiness. Existence and emptiness cannot know themselves;
thus, when they are empty, both are empty, and even when they reach the Middle Way, both are the Middle Way. This is expressed through worldly language.
Regarding "this," if explained in terms of what is proximate, it refers to what Pūrṇa doubted: that things mutually oppress and extinguish one another rather than being mutually inclusive.
If explained in terms of what is remote, it refers to Ānanda’s calculations of the internal and external, up to the views of causality and spontaneity (*hetu-pratyaya* and *svabhāva*).

As for "the Buddha's knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*), there is a distinction between the subject and the object. That which is known and seen is the *tathāgatagarbha*; that which knows and sees is [the Buddha's wisdom].
The three wisdoms are known within a single moment of mind, and the five eyes are seen within a single eye. Regarding the two metaphors:
the lute, the harp, and so forth represent the Buddha and sentient beings; the exquisite sound represents the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

The fact that the lute and harp possess exquisite sound is a metaphor for the presence of the Tathāgatagarbha within both the Buddha and sentient beings. The exquisite fingers represent wondrous wisdom. If the Tathāgata possesses such exquisite fingers...
He is one who possesses the wisdom of the wondrous finger. Those sentient beings do not possess the wisdom of the wondrous finger. Therefore, it says below:

"As I press my finger, the Sea-Seal emits light. Regarding the three knots, as for the phrase "as I press my finger," there is nothing within the sea that is not fully present and nothing that does not emerge from it.
Yet, it is called "the Sea-Seal emitting light" because, as mentioned above, by means of [the finger], it...

When the wisdom of non-arising and non-extinction merges with the Tathāgatagarbha, and at the moment the Tathāgatagarbha—being solely wondrously enlightened clarity—perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm, the infinite manifests within the one, and the one manifests within the infinite; the various wondrous functions of its entire substance are fully revealed.

Therefore it is said, "as we are. Such is the case for the Tathāgata who possesses the wondrous finger. As for sentient beings, because they lack this wondrous finger, it is said, "You should for a moment...
(and so forth). This means that when one turns one's back on the *tathāgatagarbha* with a mind of arising and ceasing, the *tathāgatagarbha* accordingly manifests as form, emptiness, and so on.
That one does not obtain the wondrous finger is due to nothing other than a general lack of diligent application.

Because it is the supreme path, it is said that they arise from inequality. The preceding section first answered where delusion originates; next, the explanation of how the nature of greatness is universally pervasive was completed.
From the words of Pūrṇa onwards, the text serves to further resolve remaining doubts. This is divided into two parts. First, the explanation of "what."
The phrase "due to having delusory doubts" refers to Pūrṇa’s words and the like. The second explanation concerns the doubt regarding causes and conditions versus spontaneity;
this refers to Ānanda and others at that moment. The first explanation—asking "for what reason are there delusory doubts?"—may also serve as a summary of Pūrṇa’s inquiry.
Thus, the statement "if the deranged mind within ceases, its cessation is itself Bodhi" is made because the inherent nature (xing) supersedes cultivated practice (xiu).
[The term] "ear" [is used]. As explained below regarding the doubt concerning causes and conditions arising spontaneously (*svabhāva*), this may also serve as a summary of Ānanda’s question.

Therefore, although it is said that [Mahāmati] possesses great learning within the intermediate state, it merely increases the talk of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). This is because cultivation supplants the innate nature.
The first section is divided into two parts: first, from "Pūrṇa" downward, Pūrṇa’s inquiry; second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction. First, Pūrṇa...
Within that question, it says: "As for 'I and others,' the wondrous clarity of the nature-awakening inherently possesses sands-of-Ganges worths of inherent merits;
this is called the Jewel-Awakening. Because it is without defect, it is termed the Perfect Mind of Jewel-Awakening; because it is without darkness, it is termed the Luminous Mind of Jewel-Awakening;
because it is free from delusion, it is termed the True Mind of Jewel-Awakening; because it transcends thought and deliberation—"
It is called the wondrous mind of jewel-like awakening. Because it is free from defilement, it is called the pure mind of jewel-like awakening.
This essence of the jewel-like awakening mind is that which the Buddhas have realized and that which sentient beings possess.

The Buddhas realize nothing that was not already realized; they realize precisely what sentient beings possess. Sentient beings possess nothing that was not already possessed; they possess precisely what the Buddhas have realized.
"Equal and equal, non-dual and non-dual. Thus it is said, "I am equal [to them].

Although it is called the perfect non-duality, when discussed in terms of cultivation and realization, there is no lack of distinction; therefore, the following section clearly elucidates these differences.
"In the past, encountering beginningless delusive thoughts" means that because of delusion, what was originally luminous awareness became the world, sentient beings, karma, and its fruits.
This refers to arising. "Long remaining in saṃsāra" refers to the continuity of the karmic fruits of worldlings.
"Now having attained the Noble Vehicle" refers to the teaching of the Four Truths as expounded by the Tathāgata.

"Still not yet ultimate" means that because what they have accomplished is merely the wisdom of analytical emptiness, they remain far removed from the Bodhi of the Buddha; because what they have realized is merely partial.
"Ultimate truth. This is because one has not yet drawn near to Great Nirvana; this is still spoken from the perspective of the Hinayana.

If we consider the internal esoteric state versus the external manifestation, even those who have attained the *bhūmis* or the *vihāras* have not exhausted their afflictions nor fully realized the principle, and thus they have not reached the ultimate.
"All are completely extinguished" refers to the Tathāgata, for whom the five stages of dwelling are utterly exhausted and the two types of death are forever extinguished. That is to say:

To shatter all through one shattering, and to sever all through one severing. That which is uniquely wondrous, true, and eternal is such because the five stages of dwelling [in ignorance] have been exhausted;
thus, there are certainly no afflictions of falsehood, nor is there the death and rebirth of defilement. This is what is meant by:
"that which is non-existent cannot be shattered, and that which is non-existent cannot be severed. Ultimately, it is beyond thought, mind, speech, and deliberation—the tranquil Suchness.

This is the constant nature of things. Thus, although it is said that "I" and the Tathāgata are non-dual in their perfect fulfillment—sharing the same cause and the same fruit, the same cultivation and the same realization—there is nonetheless a vast difference between them, like that between heaven and earth. Therefore, it is said: "And yet I... (and so forth).

As for the phrase "May I venture to ask," the intention is to inquire how, based on the previous explanation of manifestations arising in accordance with karma, there is the emergence of the three types of birth, namely the world and so forth.
"How is it that the continuity of the three—such as the world and so forth—is manifested?

I have already received the Tathāgata’s instruction that all this arises because one falsely takes delusion to be the cause of awakening and clarity, thereby establishing an object within that clarity.
Consequently, there is the arising of these three, such as the world and so forth, as well as their continuity. I now clearly understand this and shall not [doubt] further."
This is indeed a point of doubt. However, one does not know what cause gives rise to this delusion that constitutes the false "clarity of awareness.

Therefore, it says, "I venture to ask," and so forth. One should thus understand that this question is entirely different from the previous one; they must not be viewed as having a single meaning, lest they become confused with one another.
The phrase "self-obscuration" refers to the arising of the world and its sentient beings through that which is falsely taken to be the clarity of awareness. It is the reception [of experience].
These refer to the continuous succession of worlds characterized by the awakening of clarity, emptiness, and darkness, and so forth.

The second section, "The Tathāgata’s Response and Instruction," is divided into two parts. First, "The False has No Fundamental Cause," which begins with "The Buddha said... and so forth. Second, "The True is Fundamentally Unattainable," which begins with "Pūrṇa...

and so forth. The first part is further divided into three sections. First, from "The Buddha said... onwards, he cites examples to distinguish and examine the matter. Second, from "The Buddha said... onwards...

The principles are summarized and explained in detail. The three points are as previously stated, appearing together with the matters raised below. Within the first section, which presents the matter to examine and discern, there are two parts:

first, the reprimand; second, the formal presentation. Regarding the first part, "Although you have removed your doubts," etc., refers to his previous sudden arising of doubts regarding the various conditioned characteristics (saṃskṛta-lakṣaṇa) such as mountains and rivers, as well as doubts concerning the four great elements (mahābhūta), such as earth and the rest, and how their characteristics might overcome or destroy one another rather than being mutually compatible.
I have already explained this for you; yet there remains further doubt that has not been entirely cleared away, as you pose this question based on a false cause.

From the words "I [say] below" onwards, I shall properly cite an actual event to provide a detailed examination. Śrāvastī is the City of Abundant Virtue (*Puṇyavatī*), cited here as an illustration of a world of the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*).
*Yajñadatta* is translated here as "Sacrificial Bestowal" (*Cishou*); he was so named because he was obtained through prayers and offerings at a shrine.
[This is] like [the case of] all sentient beings. Suddenly, in the early morning, one uses a mirror to look at one's face;
this is analogous to how, within the wondrously luminous nature-awareness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*), a single thought of non-awakening gives rise to a deluded mind due to delusive objects.

Loving the head seen in the mirror is analogous to following after delusive objects because of the deluded mind. That the eyebrows and eyes are visible is analogous to the fact that the dust-like images of delusive objects can be perceived.
To be so immersed as not to return is like this. To resent and blame one’s own head while failing to see its face or features: the "head" serves as an analogy for the true nature (*tathatā*);
"resenting and blaming" serves as an analogy for turning one's back on awakening. To regard it as a *chimei* (a mountain-demon) serves as an analogy for mistaking the true for the delusory.

To run about wildly and without cause serves as an analogy for the single thought of non-awakening giving rise to ignorance (*avidyā*). Because it belongs entirely to the realm of the empty and false, it is called "running wildly. Yet, with respect to the wondrous nature...

Originally there is no falsehood; therefore it is said to be "without form" (*wúzhuàng*). Furthermore, although the sentient beings of the nine realms differ from one another, what they cling to does not exceed the three types of biased views:
conventional existence, partial emptiness, and the "Middle Way. None of these arise from cultivation based on the complete nature; hence it is said to be "without form.

Nor do they involve the dissolution of cultivation to return to the nature; hence it is said they are "running wildly. Regarding the phrase "this person’s mind is deranged," this refers to Pūrṇa’s attainment of realization. Correct.

This is indeed highly consistent with the false cause you have asked about. Since it is said that his mind was deranged and there was no other reason, if mental derangement were the cause of his frantic running, why did he not run frantically before looking into the mirror?
If looking into the mirror were the cause of his frantic running, who among the people of the entire city does not look into a mirror? Why was it only Yañjadatta who ran frantically?
Since the cause for such frantic running cannot be found, how could that false cause possibly exist? Therefore, the answer provided is precisely and perfectly consistent with the question.
Second, the detailed clarification according to the Dharma is divided into four parts: first, according to principle, beginning with "The Buddha said," etc.;
second, according to teaching, beginning with "From all," etc.; third, according to practice, beginning with "In this way," etc.; fourth, according to fruition.

This is equivalent to attaining Bodhi. First, it says "in terms of principle" (*li*), because the state of wondrous enlightenment and so forth are principle. Second, it says "in terms of teaching" (*jiao*);
since [the Buddha] has clarified that deluded thoughts and so forth are themselves the Buddha, how could these not be the teaching? Third, it says "in terms of practice" (*xing*);

since it is said that the delusion of consciousness has no cause, the consciousness that recognizes this delusion is surely wondrous wisdom; therefore, it constitutes practice. Fourth, it says "in terms of... [text continues].
Regarding the "fruit" (*phala*): since it is called *bodhi*, it should naturally be the fruit. Following those four [sections], each should conclude by stating:
"How could there be any delusive cause to be found that might give rise to doubt? Such is the division of the text according to its meaning.

In the first section, the two phrases on "wondrous enlightenment" (*miaojue*) are identical to the two phrases on "intrinsic enlightened nature" (*xingjue*) above; they differ only in the substitution of characters. From "To clarify the wondrous... onwards, one should restate the question posed.
The commentary on this states: "As for the phrase 'already called' (and so forth), the next section begins with the two lines starting from 'From these [two]...
which refers to the arising of the world-systems as described above in the passage beginning with 'delusively taking [the mind] to be luminous awareness.

The two lines beginning with 'successively' refer to the continuity of the world-systems as described above in the passage beginning with 'awareness-luminosity and emptiness-obscuration. The two lines beginning with 'though the Buddhas' specifically point to the answer shown above regarding the world."

This refers to the arising and continuity of the three, such as the realms (*dhātu*). It may also be understood as a general response to the two questions concerning the origin of delusion and the universal pervasiveness of the Great Nature (*mahātva*).
The meaning is that although I have thus clearly revealed this to you, you are still unable to turn back from delusion to return to the True.
Therefore, you continue to question regarding the causes of delusion; this is merely a restatement of the thorough reprimands issued previously. Thus...

Although the text says "the cloud is equal to the Buddha" and so forth, among these three [points], "delusion as the cause" means that delusion itself is the cause; it is like a person giving an ear to themselves.
Delusion serves as the basis for the false. If one uses the wisdom of contemplation to realize that delusion fundamentally has no cause, then the false will have no place to rely.
Therefore, it is said that "consciousness is equal to delusion. If there is no basis, how can the false arise?

Since even arising cannot be found, how much less can there be cessation? Thus it is said, "there is not even [arising]," and so forth, as detailed in the *Yuan-tong shu* (Commentary on Perfect Penetration).
Among these four points, he further clarifies them by means of an analogy. The meaning is that sentient beings are not only without a pointable false cause while in delusion;
even if a Tathāgata were in a state of awakening, there would likewise be no false cause to point out. Therefore, he illustrates this with an analogy, saying:
The attainment of Bodhi is like a dream; as it is said, "that which exists during a dream is not non-existent.
Yet, as it is further said, "once one has awakened, it cannot be found. The above constitutes the analogy. As for the subsequent application to the Dharma, one should first state:
It is not that there are no objects within a dream; yet even when one has awakened, they cannot be grasped.

How much more so for that which is fundamentally non-existent due to delusion—how could it be pointed out by me, the Tathāgata who has attained Bodhi? Therefore, it is said, "How much more so," and so forth.

Thus, regarding these four sets of arguments based on principle, teaching, cause, and effect, not a single false cause can be found; it is therefore clear that there is no such thing as a false cause.
Should this still not be clear, one must further bring forth specific instances to demonstrate it collectively. Hence, it is said: "As with those [cases]," and so forth.

Within the section on bringing forth three instances to demonstrate collectively, the two lines beginning with "suddenly" correspond to the analogy; if applied to the dharma, they refer to the single cessation of the deranged mind.

This is the realization of what is originally possessed. Regarding the two lines beginning with "Even if": if applied to the Dharma, although one was previously in a state of delusion, following conditions without changing;
if one understands this, even while running about in madness, the head is not lost, and when the madness ceases, the head is naturally not something acquired from without.
Thus you should know that regarding the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, its delusion cannot be lost, and its cessation cannot be attained.
Since it is neither lost nor attained, how could there be a cause for delusion? This concludes the clarification that delusion is fundamentally without cause.

Second, the two truths are fundamentally indivisible. First, the Dharma [teaching], such as "Pūrṇa" and so forth. Second, the analogy, such as "for example" and so forth. The first [section] also has two parts:
first, Pūrṇa departs and is exhorted to cease from delusive conditions; second, by ceasing [delusion], he departs and allows the true nature to manifest. Regarding the first part:
"The nature of delusion," etc., reiterates what was previously explained—that delusion fundamentally has no cause—serving merely as an introductory inquiry. "You simply," etc.
This explains "clarity. To speak in general terms, it means that the eye is not turned by forms, the ear is not turned by sounds, and so forth;
thus the six sense organs do not engage with the six sense objects—what is called the non-encountering of organ and object.

However, if we discuss the reality of things, this applies to the conventional existence of ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), the biased emptiness of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and the mere "Middle" (*zhong*) of the Bodhisattvas. As for...
Although there are distinctions among these three, they are all collectively categorized as conceptual discrimination within the wondrous nature.

If one can thoroughly understand these three—emptiness, existence, and the middle—there is nowhere that is not the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is simply a matter of not following them by engaging in further conceptualization.

Regarding the phrase "the worldly and so forth," some claim that lust, killing, and theft constitute the three conditions; however, this is not the case. It should rather be understood as "the worldly... [and so on].
Regarding the three types of continuity within the realms of sentient beings, the present text speaks of "the world" and so forth. That [previous] passage states:
"By these causes and conditions, the world continues; ... up to: by these causes and conditions, the fruit of karma continues.
From this, one knows that it does not refer to the three [vices] of lust, killing, and theft, because it refers only to the single continuity of karmic fruition. As stated below regarding Ānanda:

As for the statement, "Because the three conditions of the karma of killing, stealing, and lust are severed, the three causes do not arise," this citation is incomplete and cannot be relied upon to establish that lust, killing, and stealing constitute the three conditions. Rather, the three causes are the discriminative mind that acts as the perceiving subject.
To speak of the ultimate reality, they are merely false perceptions masquerading as clear awareness. It is precisely because these false objects do not arise [in the absence of such perception]...
Because deluded thoughts do not arise, it is said: "When the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise.

Regarding the second point, "manifesting the true nature," concerning the phrase "resting is [itself]" (*xiē jí*): someone may doubt, asking, "How can a mad mind come to rest? How is it that resting is itself Bodhi?
One must understand that "is itself" (*jí*) means it is right here and now. This "is itself" should be clarified by way of six aspects.
"Resting" (*xie*) refers precisely to what was previously described as not following after discursive thought; thus, one should know that "resting" likewise possesses six aspects.
However, when clarifying "immediacy" (*ji*) through the lens of "resting," all [six aspects] may be attained, with the sole exception of the single principle (*li yi*).

Although the two characters *ken* (tendon) and *qǐng* (sinew) originate from the *Nanhua Jing* (Zhuangzi), here their terminology is employed while their original meaning is set aside. For while that treatise concerns the mastery of subtle skills, this discourse concerns the subtle nuances of practice.
This is precisely because the nature (*prakṛti*) supersedes the cultivation (*bhāvanā*); therefore, this statement is made. Question:

Why is it that in the section concerning Pūrṇa’s knots, the nature supersedes the cultivation, whereas in the subsequent section concerning Ānanda’s knots, the cultivation supersedes the nature? Answer:
Because everything previously explained to Pūrṇa pertained to the nature; as for Ānanda, it was not only his request regarding the three [practices] such as *śamatha*.

Practice. Furthermore, since practice is about to arise in the text below, it is for this reason that cultivation supersedes nature. This distinction is made provisionally according to the capacities of sentient beings;

however, cultivation has never been separate from nature, nor has nature ever been separate from cultivation. That cultivation and nature are mutually identical is precisely what constitutes the Perfect Teaching (*yuanzong*).
Regarding the two metaphors, the phrase "for example" and so forth serves as the primary metaphor for the principle that "resting is itself Bodhi."

The "person" is a metaphor for sentient beings. The "clothing" is a metaphor for the five aggregates (*skandhas*). Since the meaning of an aggregate is "to cover and conceal," it is compared to clothing.

The "wish-fulfilling jewel" is a metaphor for the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Just as the jewel can contain all treasures and rain down all treasures, so too can the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha fully contain all inherent qualities and give rise to all virtuous attributes; therefore, it is compared to this jewel.
The jewel represents the total absence of the wealth of merit and dharma. The dew represents the lack of the protective covering of compassion.
"Other regions" represents following after the nine realms. "Wandering for alms" refers to those within the nine realms who cling to existence, such as ordinary beings;
those who cling to emptiness, such as the followers of the Two Vehicles; and those who cling to the Middle Way, such as Bodhisattvas. Therefore, it is likened to wandering for alms in emptiness.

Because there are three kinds of existence yet no fixed certainty, it is likened to running about. Although there are actually two phrases, they serve as a metaphor for how, despite the nine realms of existence following after one, the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha* remains intact and unharmed.
"The wise person" is a metaphor for the *Tathāgata*. "Pointing out the pearl" is a metaphor for revealing the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
"Fulfilling one's wishes according to the mind" is a metaphor for generating wisdom from the nature of the *garbha* and then returning to contemplate that very nature.
This refers to the aforementioned "I" uniting with the Tathāgata-garbha through wondrous clarity that is neither extinguished nor born;
it signifies great abundance, serving as a metaphor for the non-duality of principle and wisdom (*prajñā*), and the non-duality of subject and object.

This also corresponds to the aforementioned statement that the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, such that the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one. Only then does one realize that these two phrases serve as metaphors for delusion.
At that time, there is no loss in awakening and no gain in realization; this is what is meant by "resting is itself bodhi.

Thus far, two rounds of responses have been provided based on the fact that delusion is fundamentally without cause and that the truth is originally without attainment. Since the truth is without attainment, how could delusion have a cause?
One should thus know that the doubt regarding the cause of delusion is resolved with clarity.
"Second, Ānanda departed immediately. This is the text concerning the natural arising of doubt regarding the causal conditions (*nidāna*).

These causal conditions are not the same as those previously analyzed and refuted within the demonstration of the nature of seeing (*darśana-svabhāva*). Those [previously discussed] were while still entangled in defilements (*saṃkliṣṭa*); these are beyond such entanglement (*niḥsṛta*). The former merely clarified the principle (*tattva*);
hereafter, one intends to clarify practice (*caryā*), wherein there is cultivation and realization. Fearing that sentient beings might suspect this to be a cause, [the text addresses it].

This inquiry is made for a specific reason; it is not like a drunken man who stumbles eastward and then westward, or westward and then eastward. This section is divided into two parts: first, Ānanda’s inquiry out of doubt, which begins with "Ānanda and others";

second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction, which begins with "The Buddha said. The first part [of the inquiry] is further divided into four sections: first, Ānanda’s citation of the previous argument to raise a counter-objection; second, his own realization and the realization of others;

third, the present teaching; [and fourth, the conclusion]. (The fourth is implied by the structure. First, Ānanda cites the preceding [argument] to raise a counter-objection. Second, from "I followed... onwards, he describes his own and others' attainment of awakening. Third, "Now I shall explain... [marks the transition to the teaching].

The following objection is identical to that regarding "naturalness. Fourth, [the section on] "Contemplating the Descent" requests the opening of the teaching; although the text is divided into four parts, the meaning is visible throughout.

Second, the Tathāgata’s response and instruction is divided into two: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the refutation is established; second, from "Bodhi" onwards, the admonition and exhortation.
The first section has three parts. First is the general refutation, beginning with the Buddha’s address to Ānanda. Second is the specific refutation, beginning with Ānanda’s departure.

Third is the concluding refutation, beginning with the burning wood. Regarding the initial general refutation, from the passage "The Buddha addressed Ānanda" onwards, it should be supplemented as follows:
"If you wish to employ metaphors to clarify your doubts regarding the nature of causes and conditions, there is no need to seek them elsewhere or cite distant examples."
"Cloud" refers to "suchness" (*tathatā*) and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the conditions for the nature of madness":

the nature of madness belongs to causes and conditions, whereas the nature of non-madness belongs to spontaneity (*svabhāva*). If the causes and conditions of the nature of madness are destroyed, then the spontaneity of the nature of non-madness will emerge.
This emergence is precisely cessation. One cessation and one emergence—this is the full extent of the principle of causes and conditions versus spontaneity.
Therefore, it is said that "the nature of madness" and so forth. This term "principle" (li) does not refer to the "wondrous principle";

it merely means that there is no such principle. The second part, the specific refutation, has three sections: first, Ānanda and others rely on phenomena; second, "therefore" and so forth concern the Dharma;

third, "just as" and so forth cite examples. The first of these [three] also has three parts: first, the refutation of causes and conditions and spontaneity; this begins with "Ānanda... and so forth. Second, the refutation of transformation...

"Calculating 'nature' is fundamentally the departure from delusion. These three points collectively summarize the formation of frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). If one awakens to this, one departs [from it]. The first section further has two parts:
first, from "Ānanda" onwards, using causes and conditions to refute nature; second, from "If [it were] self-" onwards, using nature to refute causes and conditions."
In the first part: "There is nothing that is not of itself" means that there is nowhere that is not natural (*svabhāva*). "For what reason? refers to the two lines [of the verse];
it asks by what causes and conditions one fears one's head and runs about madly. If there were even a single cause and condition, then the thesis of naturalness (*svabhāvavāda*) would be destroyed;
therefore, it says "for what reason," and so forth. In the middle section: "If it were of itself," etc., means that you—
If your natural head has madness due to causes and conditions, why do you not likewise lose your natural head because of those same causes and conditions?
Therefore, it says "if [it were] natural," and so forth. However, your natural head is fundamentally never lost;
it is merely produced by your own madness. As soon as it is produced, you perceive it as being lost. Thus, it says "fundamentally..."
This is the first point. Furthermore, when you were running about in a frenzy, your head may have undergone some change, which would necessarily have required causes and conditions to occur.
Since your head remains exactly as it was, what need is there for causes and conditions? Therefore, it is said that "it has never been so," and so forth.
Second, regarding the refutation of the counter-argument concerning spontaneity (*svabhāva*), one should supplement the counter-argument as follows: "That frantic running was simply spontaneous."
This is because it does not arise by depending on causes and conditions. Thus, he refutes [the opponent's position] through two cycles: the "insane" and the "non-insane.
The previous passage was explained from the perspective of the head; here, one should see it from the perspective of insanity.

Third, in the summary that establishes [this as] conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), the phrase "if one realizes," etc., means that since the head has never been lost, one is merely running about in vain due to madness; therefore, this certainly cannot serve as a cause.

Conditions (*pratyaya*) likewise cannot be considered spontaneous (*svabhāva*). Thus, one knows that both conditions and spontaneity belong to the world’s frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), for they are all false and illusory.

Ānanda’s doubts regarding conditions and spontaneity were thoroughly refuted by the Tathāgata through the account of Eya-jue’s fear of his head and frantic flight; it is evident that neither [view] can be maintained. However, I fear...
Still not fully satisfied, the subsequent passage refutes [the opponent's position] by means of the Dharma. This section on refuting through the Dharma is divided into two parts:

first, the refutation of causes and conditions (beginning with "Therefore," etc.); second, the refutation of spontaneity (beginning with "If there were," etc.). Within the first part, the refutation of causes and conditions:

The initial passage beginning with "For this reason" (*tasmāt*) refers to the matter entrusted to the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa-viṣaya*) as that which is to be destroyed. Furthermore, it restates what was previously said:
because the three conditions are severed, the three causes do not arise; thus, the madness-nature of your *Rāvaṇa* (Evil-Eye) within the mind naturally subsides, and this subsiding is itself *bodhi*.
This is because Ānanda’s doubts arose from this point onward; hence, terms such as *bodhi* are brought forth.
This is doubt. The meaning is that when your doubt ceases, it is itself Bodhi. When the mind of Bodhi arises, the three causes do not arise;
when the non-arising mind ceases, it follows this calculation of one arising and one ceasing, which are merely arising and ceasing existing through causes and conditions.
Therefore, it says "Bodhi, etc. [The phrase] "ceasing" leads to the following refutation. The meaning is that although your doubt is thus, you do not realize its...

In arising, there is never any arising; in ceasing, there is never any ceasing. This is precisely what destroys [the notion of] duality and reveals the identity of cultivation and nature, and of appearance and essence.
Without relying on artificial effort, one flows in spontaneously. How could there be any obtainable causes and conditions for a single arising or a single ceasing?
Therefore, it is said that "ceasing and arising, etc."—thus, causes and conditions are destroyed. Second, the refutation of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).

This is divided into two parts. First, the formal refutation starting from "If there were... and so on; second, the conclusion of the refutation starting from "If there were no... and so on. Regarding the first part, it should be supplemented as follows:
"I shall use the path of non-effort (*anābhoga*), in which both arising and ceasing are exhausted, to refute your doubts regarding the causes and conditions of arising and ceasing.
Will you not, Ānanda, consequently reckon this path of non-effort, in which both arising and ceasing are exhausted, to be spontaneous (*svabhāva*)? Thus, he restates [the opponent's position].
Regarding the statement, "If there were such a thing as spontaneity (*svabhāva*)," the following section provides the correct refutation. The intent is this:
you previously saw that the three causes do not arise and that cessation is itself enlightenment, and you consequently reckoned this to be "causality" (*hetu-pratyaya*).

Furthermore, seeing that both arising and ceasing are exhausted and that the path of non-effort (*anābhoga-mārga*) prevails, you reckoned this to be "spontaneity. Such is your doubt. Based on what you doubt, it follows that the mind would likewise be spontaneous.
The mind perishes due to causes and conditions. Since it arises and perishes one by one, it continues to arise and perish in this manner;

how could it be spontaneous? Therefore, it is said, "in such a way," and so forth. Regarding the second point, the summary refutation, the phrase "non-arising" and so on means that the aforementioned spontaneity of arising and the perishing due to causes and conditions both involve arising and perishing; they are not spontaneous. How then could they be considered spontaneous? Thus, he again summarizes the refutation, saying:
Only that which is without arising and without cessation can be considered "spontaneous" (*svabhāva*); hence the phrase "without arising," and so forth.

However, one does not realize that there must first be arising and cessation for there to be non-arising and non-cessation. Since arising and cessation do not exist, how could there be non-arising and non-cessation that could constitute spontaneity?

Thus, it should be understood that these two phrases are words used to refute [the opponent's position] by means of a conclusion. The third [phrase], "just as... (*tadyathā*), serves as an illustration.

Furthermore, there are two [points]: first, the primary analogy; second, the double negation. The intent is to speak of both "causes and conditions" (*hetu-pratyaya*) and "spontaneity" (*svabhāva*) simultaneously.

At its inception, seeing that the three causes do not arise and so forth, one then reckons them as "causes and conditions. At its conclusion, seeing cessation, arising, and so forth, one then reckons them as "spontaneous.
To clarify this by means of an illustration: your reckoning of causes and conditions is like the conjunction of various phenomena in the world.

To form a single entity means there is no difference. Your conception of "spontaneity" (svabhāva) is like the various phenomena in the world which, not being formed through combination, do not constitute a single entity;

thus they share the same characteristic. Therefore, it is said, "just as," and so forth. In the section on the "double negation," "original spontaneity" (*benran*) and so on negate both while simultaneously revealing both.
"Original spontaneity" is precisely "spontaneity"; "not-spontaneous" refers to "causality. This clarifies the analogy of combination.
The first phrase is the unification of both the conditioned and the unconditioned. The subsequent two phrases restate the aforementioned principles;

following this pattern, the latter part simultaneously negates and simultaneously reveals them. The first phrase, "the conditioned is precisely the unconditioned," refers to causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*);

this is explained by way of analogy. The phrase "the unconditioned is precisely the natural" refers to non-conditioning (*asāṃskṛta*); this is explained by way of the principle itself. Both causes and conditions and the natural are neither... [text ends].

It can be attained; therefore, it is said that "the state of being both together and separate is transcended. The next phrase, "transcendence," refers to the capacity to transcend the aforementioned state of being both together and separate.
"Union" refers to the object of transcendence within that aforementioned state of being both together and separate. Therefore, it is said that "both transcendence and union are neither."
Discard it again and again; reveal it again and again. Upon reaching this phrase where both separation and union are negated, even the "discarding" that performs the discarding cannot be found;

how then could the causes and conditions of that which is discarded possibly be found? Therefore, it is said that only this phrase is called the Dharma free from conceptual proliferation (*niṣprapañca*).
Although it is both in harmony and not in harmony, this principle was likewise previously calculated by Ānanda and his peers.
Therefore, both are refuted to reveal the truth. Above, the conclusion was reached by means of phenomena, stating that "causality and spontaneity are both conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*).

Here, the conclusion states that "only then is it called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation. Although the underlying meaning is the same, here both are simultaneously negated and simultaneously revealed;
thus it is said, "only then is it called the dharma free from conceptual proliferation. Since Ānanda is now in doubt regarding both causality and spontaneity...

The Tathāgata first refutes [the opponent] by analyzing their specific propositions; next, he refutes them by summarizing the general principles of the Dharma; and finally, he refutes them by citing illustrative examples.
Thus, one can understand that both causal conditions (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and spontaneity (*svabhāva*) are immediately resolved and clarified.
The second section, on exhortation and admonition, is divided into two parts. First, the general presentation: "Bodhi," etc. Second, the specific demonstration: "Although," etc.
Within the first part, the general presentation, one should initially state: "If you wish to cultivate Bodhi, you should do so by means of the dharmas within Bodhi itself.
Since you harbor doubts regarding causes and conditions and spontaneity (*svabhāva*), Bodhi and Nirvana remain far distant."
Therefore, it is said that "bodhi" and so forth are equal. This section below is precisely the passage where cultivation is used to subvert the innate nature (*xing*).
The second part, which specifically demonstrates [the meaning], has two sections: first, the admonition from "Although... onwards; second, the exhortation from "For this reason... onwards.

The first of these [the admonition] also has two parts: first, the direct admonition from "Although... onwards; second, the experimental verification from "You, although... onwards. Within the first of these, [it says] "merely increases frivolous proliferation," which refers to...
This is a doubt concerning the spontaneity of causes and conditions. Why must one wait for me? One should also have said previously:
"Your extensive learning is beneficial; it does not belong to frivolous debate. Not only will you not encounter Dhanagā, but even if you were to encounter her, you would be able to liberate yourself.
Why must you wait for my Buddha-Usnīṣa divine mantra to attain liberation? Therefore, it says, "Why must [one wait]? etc. (2)

The exhortation to share [the Dharma] has two parts. First, the formal exhortation, beginning with "Therefore," and so forth. Second, the experimental proof, beginning with "As in the case of Māra," and so forth. Regarding the first part:
"Secret and Subtly Adorned" refers to how, among the Tathāgata’s eight teachings, he may preach the gradual for one person and the sudden for another, such that they do not know of each other;
this is "secret. Furthermore, being able to produce the unconditioned from a single voice...
Regarding "measuring sounds": being able to produce immeasurable meanings from a single meaning is what constitutes "wondrous adornment.

As for "cultivating untainted karma," this refers to the cultivation of the three dharmas, such as *śamatha* and so forth. When cultivating *śamatha*, this inconceivable method of the contemplation of emptiness naturally manifests before one:
all phenomena are inherently empty, and not even a single speck of dust can be established. This is true emptiness; it is self-evident.
Falling into the mundane, being biased toward emptiness, or adhering merely to the Middle Way—even the cultivation of *dhyāna* is likewise [subject to these].

Regarding "distancing oneself from the two sufferings of hatred and attachment," to speak briefly, these refer to the two types of objects: the adverse and the favorable. With these instances of hatred and attachment as their cause, [the cycle of suffering continues].
One will inevitably receive groundless retribution of suffering. To elaborate further: beings within the nine realms of existence all possess hatred and attachment.

For example, ordinary worldlings hate emptiness and love existence; those of the Two Vehicles hate existence and love emptiness; and Bodhisattvas hate both emptiness and existence while loving the Middle Way.
Now, if one cultivates the untainted karma of *śamatha* and other practices, one will naturally distance oneself from the emptiness and existence of ordinary worldlings and others.
Regarding their hatred and love, it is therefore said that they are "far removed," and so forth. Next, concerning those who "together awaken to their past causes":
this refers to awakening to the cause of lustful desire in previous lives. Regarding the phrase "or receive a prediction [of enlightenment]":

one asks, since this sutra belongs to the Vaipulya (Vaipulya/ Fangdeng) class, and the prediction for Yaśodharā by the Tathāgata *Sahasraraśmivimalaprabha* is a matter belonging to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, how can she possibly receive such an empowerment here?
Is this a record? Answer: A sūtra has both a preceding and a subsequent part. The preceding part is the main sūtra itself;

the subsequent part consists of those similar passages found in other sūtras that are collected and subsumed into one. Now, by means of the *Lotus Sūtra*, they are subsumed into this very sūtra because they are of the same class.
How could it not also be said above: "That Gaṅgā was merely a single courtesan, yet she was still able to do such a thing"?
"You, Ānanda, are a man with a beard and eyebrows. How can you still linger in the realm of sights and sounds, deceiving yourself to such an extent?
Thus it is said, 'How can you...? To say 'still lingering in viewing and listening' is to censure his seeing of marks and his arousal of the mind by taking sound as an object;
it means he is unable to transcend the seeing and hearing of forms and sounds. It also censures his cause."

This is due to the natural arising of doubt. From the beginning of the first fascicle until the conclusion of the explanation of the ultimate, unshakable principle, the text proceeds from Ānanda and the great assembly onward;
this second section is the passage that demonstrates the ultimate, unshakable practice. It is divided into two parts: first, the request for instruction, which refers to Ānanda and the others;
second, the revelation of the teaching, which begins with "At that time" and so forth. The first part is further divided into two: first, Ānanda... [text continues].

It is difficult for the scribes to describe the characteristics [of the teaching]. Regarding the two points—“no superior” and “no inferior”—the words are spoken according to the needs of the audience.
First, concerning the phrase “hearing the Buddha’s instructions,” this refers to what the Tathāgata has taught since addressing Pūrṇa. As for the phrase “doubts and delusions eliminated,” etc.:
Although Ānanda had attained realization before the great assembly, since Pūrṇa began his questioning, his mind has not yet been entirely free from doubt.
Having received repeated and layered instructions, his doubts have been dispelled once more; thus it is said that "doubt and confusion are eliminated.

Not only were his doubts removed, but he also heard that the essence of delusion is fundamentally causeless and that the source of truth is originally unattainable. Thus, he thoroughly comprehended the Middle Way, the primary meaning.
Because it is the principle of the true mark of reality (*tattva-lakṣaṇa*), it is said that "the mind awakens to the true mark. Question:
Previously, Ānanda himself stated that his inverted thoughts of billions of kalpas had already been eliminated and that he had already attained the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

How is it that here he must again eliminate doubt and awaken to the true mark? Answer: That which was eliminated previously were the afflictions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*); that which is removed now are the afflictions of thought (*vicikitsā*).

Delusion! As for the fact that ignorance is precisely what must be severed: furthermore, what was previously realized pertained to the stage of the semblance cause (*sādharmya-hetu*) following the first stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*);

what is now realized is indeed the true causal stage (*bhūta-hetu*) of the first dwelling (*prathama-vihāra*). Thus, one knows that regarding the time of its dissolution, there is a sequence of priority;
regarding that which is dissolved, there is also a distinction between the coarse and the subtle; and regarding the time of realization, there is a difference between the distant and the near.
That which is realized also has degrees of depth and shallowness. Therefore, in the past, one eliminated inversions and attained the Dharma-body;
today, one removes doubts and realizes the true mark (*dharmatā*). This is the case for Ānanda alone;

if we consider the multitude of people, some may have destroyed the afflictions within the realm of desire (*dhātu*), some may have destroyed the afflictions outside that realm, and some may have attained a stage of semblance and thereby realized [the truth].
Regarding the true aspect (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*): there are those who realize the true aspect upon attaining the true stages (*bhūmi*).
As for the coarseness or subtlety of their delusions and the shallowness or depth of their stages, these cannot yet be described in a single way.

Therefore, in the Perfect Teaching (*vaipulya-yāna*), there are forty-two instances of shattering ignorance and forty-two instances of perceiving true reality. Second, the presentation of words by the audience is divided into four parts; first—

The praise is revealed through four sections: first, the praise of being unsurpassed; second, the description of the two World-Honored Ones; third, the formal petition; and fourth, the waiting for the imperial decree.

Regarding the first section, "unsurpassed great compassion" (*anuttara-mahākaruṇā*) means that there is nothing in the mundane or supramundane realms more venerable or supreme that could be added above it;
hence, it is called "unsurpassed. It possesses objectless compassion (*nirālambana-karuṇā*), which universally uproots [suffering].

Because it [relieves] the suffering of sentient beings, it is called "Great Compassion" (mahākaruṇā). The wisdom and merit of the bodhi thus attained are like gold extracted from ore, no longer mixed with dross.
The cessation-merit of the realized nirvāṇa is like wood that has been reduced to ash, never again becoming wood.
Because wisdom and cessation are raised together, it is called "Pure. It possesses all the wealth of the qualities of nature and gives birth to all the great [powers].
Merit is that which is most sovereign within both the mundane and supramundane realms; hence it is called the "Jewel King.

Because that which sentient beings possess is used to instruct those very sentient beings, it is said, "skillfully opening my mind," just as at the beginning of the fascicle it was said, "skillfully expounding the Dharma.
The passage beginning with "is able to" correctly expresses the meaning of "skillfully opening. It may directly state the characteristics of dharmas (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), or it may employ metaphors.

This clarifies the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*). Sometimes it directly reveals the essence of reality (*tattva*), and sometimes it relies upon phenomena to reveal the essence of reality;
because there are such differences, it is said to be "various" and so forth. To be submerged in the ocean of birth and death (*saṃsāra*) and never emerge from it is called "sinking."
To be deluded within the ocean of afflictions and never emerge from it is called "darkness.

Because [the Tathāgata] can cause sentient beings to shatter afflictions and sever birth-and-death, it is said that he "leads forth all [beings]," and so on. Regarding the second [section], "knowing the Tathāgata," etc., this describes the preceding point:
that the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrously enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm, wherein the one becomes the infinite and the infinite becomes the one.
First: To speak of it in terms of encompassing, it is called "containing" (hana); to speak of it in terms of giving birth, it is called "nurturing" (yoku).

The absence of cesspools, latrines, pits, ditches, thorns, and the like constitutes "purity. The presence of jeweled grounds, jeweled trees, golden cords, and demarcated paths constitutes "jewel-adornment.
Regarding the phrase "The Tathāgata is likewise," this recounts what you previously stated concerning the discourse on causes and conditions.

"Spontaneously," etc., refers to the passage admonishing and exhorting that the extensive learning accumulated over many kalpas is not equal to cultivating untainted karma (*anāsrava-karman*) for a single day.
Regarding the phrase "failing to reach cultivation," one should supplement it as follows: "Those who know according to what the Tathāgata knows are like that;
those who have been rebuked by the Tathāgata are like this. This present state of mine today, if illustrated through a metaphor, is just like..."
Regarding the phrase "one who is journeying and lodging": this refers to "I now," and so forth.
To speak of "journeying and lodging," before Ānanda left the household life, his mind was constantly discriminating toward existence (*bhava*), like a traveler staying overnight on land.

After he had left the household life, every thought became attached to emptiness (*śūnyatā*), like one who has moored for the night upon the water. Although he has understood the principle today, he has not yet [attained it].

Arising and acting is merely like a traveler lodging for the night. "Suddenly receiving [this]" refers to the Heavenly King, who is a metaphor for the Tathāgata—meaning he is the God among Gods and the Sage among Sages.
The "magnificent mansion" is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha* (the nature of the treasury).

The Tathāgata provides various instructions to cause one to awaken to this *tathāgatagarbha*, which is like bestowing a magnificent mansion. It is said: "Though one obtains a great residence, it must be entered through a gate."
Regarding "entering": the meaning is that if one wishes to enter a magnificent mansion, one must find its gate;

likewise, if one wishes to enter the nature of the treasury (*garbha*), one must also proceed by way of entry. To speak in terms of the analogy: the mansion is the place to be entered, and the person is the one who enters.
However, it is through the gate that one enters. To discuss this in terms of the Dharma: the nature of the treasury is the principle to be entered, while *śamatha* and so forth are the means.
This is the practice for entering [the Way]. However, that by which one enters is solely the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

Therefore, it is said in the selection: "If you wish to attain *samādhi*, truly enter through hearing. Here, the character "enter" (*ru*) precisely corresponds to the "enter" in that previous passage.
Among the three [options], turning from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle is called "abandoning the Lesser Vehicle without remainder."

Nirvana is, indeed, the supreme Great Parinirvāṇa. Regarding the path of the original arousal of the mind (*cittotpāda*): it is from this path that the Tathāgata aroused his mind and attained this Nirvana.
It is intended to enable those who would otherwise turn toward the Lesser Vehicle to also attain this path and advance toward the cultivation of the Tathāgata’s Great Nirvana.
Thus, one knows that Nirvana without remainder is the state of non-arising and non-ceasing toward which one proceeds.
This is the fruit. The path of the original aspiration is precisely that which leads toward the cause of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Therefore, in the subsequent text, the Tathāgata provides the first definitive answer. As for "by what means are past objects of attachment subdued?

this refers exactly to the selection of the afflictions of the six sense faculties to find the fundamental point of perfect penetration. Therefore, in the subsequent text, the Tathāgata provides the [second]...
This is the second definitive answer. Thus, one knows that this is the Tathāgata’s correct teaching in response to Ānanda’s request.

It is intended for those in training (*śaikṣa*), specifically those who have turned from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle; although they now face the Great Vehicle, they have not yet attained perfection, and are therefore called "those in training.
From the words "From what... onwards, there is a general desire to sever delusions and realize the Truth. However, it is not known by what cause [this occurs].
One attains entry. Therefore, it is asked: "From what [does one enter]? There are many kinds of objective conditions (*ālambana*).
When practicing *śamatha*, the contemplation of emptiness naturally manifests, whereby the objective conditions of conventional existence are spontaneously subdued.

When practicing *samādhi*, the contemplation of the provisional (*prajñapti*) naturally manifests, whereby the objective conditions of biased emptiness are spontaneously subdued. When practicing *dhyāna*...
The Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) naturally manifests, whereby the grasping at the two extremes of existence and emptiness is spontaneously subdued.
This is explained in this manner for the time being; however, when the three contemplations are cultivated in their totality, all forms of grasping will naturally and perfectly be subdued.
*Dhāraṇī* means "total retention" (*saṃgraha*). It is also called "obstructive retention" (*vighna-dhāraṇa*). It is termed "total retention" because...
It encompasses all phenomena without dispersing them; it upholds all meanings without losing them.
It is "obstructive-retention" (*saṃvara*), because it obstructs all evil so that they do not arise, and it retains all good so that they are not lost.

Entering the Buddha’s knowledge and vision means that knowing is the act of knowing through the three wisdoms within a single moment of mind, and seeing is the act of seeing through the five eyes within a single eye. The analysis is thus. If...

In brief, the meaning is this: it is intended to show from what the seeker of realization (*śaikṣa*) should restrain and subdue their mental objects (*ālambana*), from what they should obtain the *dhāraṇī*, and from what they should enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*buddhajñānadarśana*).
The Buddha’s knowledge and vision have not yet been entered because the *dhāraṇī* has not yet been obtained.

Because the dhāraṇī has not yet been attained due to the failure to subdue the objects of perception (ālambana), one should know that once the objects of perception are subdued, the dhāraṇī is spontaneously realized;
and when knowledge and vision enter [into realization], the objects of perception are spontaneously subdued and the dhāraṇī is spontaneously attained.
Although these are explained as being sequential, in reality they occur simultaneously. Among the four [aspects], it is said to be present in the assembly.

Regarding the word "etcetera" (*ādi*): since the description of the assembly already mentions "the great multitude," and the formal request further states "those of us in this assembly who are shrouded in darkness," it follows that everyone present was standing with single-minded attention, awaiting the Buddha’s compassionate voice and its wondrous purport.

The second part, the Exposition, is divided into two. First, the account by the sūtra compiler, beginning with "At that time," and so forth. Second, the words spoken by the Tathāgata, beginning with "You," and so forth.

Within the first section, the account by the sūtra compiler, the phrase "out of compassion for the pratyekabuddhas, śrāvakas, and others in the assembly" refers precisely to those who, during Ānanda’s request, renounced the Hīnayāna and turned toward the Mahāyāna, yet whose bodhicitta was not yet [fully] realized within themselves.

Regarding "those who abide": this refers to followers of the Two Vehicles who, although they have turned from the Small toward the Great, have not yet attained the path of their original aspiration nor realized *nirvāṇa* without remainder;
thus it is said, "regarding the bodhicitta," and so forth. As for "opening the Unsurpassed Vehicle" (*anuttarayāna*): "vehicle" (*yāna*) has the meaning of "transporting.
However, the transport provided by the Great and Small Vehicles differs. If one possesses the precepts and wholesome roots of humans and devas, these can only transport [one]...
Emerging from the three miserable realms (*tridurgati*), if one relies on the truths and conditions of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*), one can only be transported out of the triple world (*triloka*).

The gates of the partial and gradual teachings can only transport one out of the three voids (*trishūnya*). Only the inconceivable and subtle vehicle of the Tathāgata not only transports one out of the three miserable realms, the triple world, and the three voids, but also transports one into the secret treasury of the three virtues (*triguṇa-guhya-kośa*); therefore, it is named "Non-" [emptiness].

This is the Supreme Vehicle (*agrayāna*). Regarding the "wondrous path of cultivation": this refers to the three practices, such as *śamatha* and so forth, which are inherently possessed (*prakṛti-saṃvidyamāna*) within one's nature.

To mention one is to include all three; to speak of the three is to identify them with the one. Cultivation arises entirely from nature, and cultivation returns entirely to nature. It does not depend upon artificial fabrication or conceptual contrivance;
it is inconceivable. Second, the Tathāgata’s discourse is divided into three parts. First, from "You all must resolve... [the text continues].
He is certainly departing. Generally, there are two kinds of determination. First, from the beginning of the fifth fascicle, Ānanda and the great assembly depart;
this specifically points to the fundamental root of perfect penetration. Second, from the middle of the sixth fascicle, Ānanda adjusts his robes and departs;

this further demonstrates the rules for establishing [the practice]. The first of these also has two parts: first, the direct clarification of the two meanings, namely "You all must be determined... and so forth; second, the successive [explanations].
Dispelling Doubts: This refers to Ānanda’s address to the Buddha and so forth. The first section [of this] further has two parts: first, from "You all" onwards, is the formal presentation;

second, from "How so? onwards, is the inquiry and explanation. Within the initial presentation, the phrase "you all" and so forth refers back to the "wonderful śamatha" and other qualities that Ānanda first requested, as well as the "path of the original arousal of the mind" that he now requests. Some people, seeing these three wonderful [qualities]...
Regarding the term "samādhi": from this point onward, it is the formal response to the request for *samādhi*. It is clearly established by the single phrase "wondrous *samādhi*.

If one were to judge that what precedes is *śamatha* and what follows is *samādhi*, then since the first fascicle contains the title "Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Samādhi," would everything from the beginning of the "Seven Investigations" onwards belong to *samādhi*? Within this context, [the text] provides such admonitions as "you all... and so forth.
It is as stated previously in the *Śamatha-vyākhyā*: "Do not become weary on the sublime path to Bodhi; it is the same for all. One should accordingly encourage [the practitioner] below.
As for the phrase "arousing the initial mind of awakening" (*prathama-cittotpāda*): "awakening" (*bodha*) is precisely *bodhi*; thus, it refers to arousing the initial mind directed toward *bodhi*.

Second, the meaning of determination. First, one examines a single instance among the five aggregates (skandhas) and determines that the practitioner is the subject of observation and the five aggregates are the object of observation.
If one can select away the arising and ceasing that constitute the root of birth and death, one will practice in reliance upon the non-arising and non-ceasing.

Thus, even arising and ceasing become non-arising and non-ceasing. Therefore, the text says: "By means of stillness, one turns back that which is false and illusory—the extinction and birth—to subdue them and return to original enlightenment," and so forth.
Second, one must thoroughly examine the six sense faculties; this examination is definitively the capacity for discernment.

The six sense organs are what is to be examined. If one can discern and eliminate that which is not perfectly penetrating—the very root of afflictions—and instead cultivate according to that which is perfectly penetrating, then even that which was not perfectly penetrating will become perfectly penetrating. Therefore, the text says:

"If you enter deeply through a single door, entering that one state where there is no delusion, then those six faculties of cognition will simultaneously become pure. However, as for what is called "definitive," there is...
There are two meanings for "decision" (niyata). First, it is called "decision" because the Tathāgata, as a Sage, makes a definitive determination.

Second, it is called "decision" because the recipient receives a prediction from the Tathāgata that is fixed and unalterable. They share the same name "decision," yet these two meanings exist only in terms of the distinction between the capacity of the recipient and the response of the bestower.

The second section, consisting of the inquiry and the explanation, is further divided into two parts. First, the general inquiry: "What is meant by 'going'? Second, the specific explanation: "Ānanda and so forth. The first part, the general inquiry, is self-evident.
The second part, the specific explanation, is further divided into two. First, the primary meaning, beginning with "Firstly, going. Second, the secondary meaning, beginning with "Secondly, [staying].

The first of these [the primary meaning] is further divided into three. First, the exhortation to contemplate, beginning with "First, going. Second, the statement of the underlying intention, beginning with "If, regarding going..."
Third, the Correct Investigation. This is how one proceeds. Regarding the initial exhortation to contemplate: the phrase "if you wish," etc., restates the words previously requested by Ānanda.

The phrase "you should," etc., is the actual exhortation to contemplate. As for the question of whether the ground of practice (*hetu-bhūmi*) and the ground of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*) are the same or different:
ultimately, how can they be the same and not different? According to what follows in the section on the underlying intent, it says that birth and cessation are not...
Regarding arising and ceasing: when one correctly examines the initial state, it is said that it undergoes transformation and decay rather than being extinguished.

Thus, one knows that the cause of the Mahāyāna has nothing else as its cause, but is solely the eternally abiding true mind; and the fruit of the Mahāyāna has nothing else as its fruit, but is solely the eternally abiding true mind.
One takes the essence of the eternally abiding true mind as the causal mind; with this causal mind, one in turn realizes the essence of the eternally abiding true mind.

This is what is meant by "the cause encompassing the ocean of the fruit" and "the fruit reaching the source of the cause. Here, phenomena and principle are non-dual, and cultivation and nature are mutually identical.
One spontaneously attains sameness without difference. It is precisely because he wishes to exhort him to give rise to the mind through the eternally abiding true mind that [he says this].
It says, "They should be equal. Second, regarding the intention behind this: if they are equal, it is appropriate that their emergence be the same and not different;
therefore, it concludes by stating, "There is no such possibility. Third, the actual examination has two parts: first, pointing to specific phenomena with the phrase "these [are] equal";
second, defining what is meant by "equal" in terms of dharmas. Regarding the first part, pointing to specific phenomena: "the various receptacle worlds"—the world is...

These arise from the environment and its inhabitants (*bhajana-sattva*). Both possess limited dimensions, like a vessel that has boundaries; therefore, it is called the "receptacle world" (*bhājana-loka*). Regarding the phrase "the non-decaying void":
this refers to the void as being indestructible in contrast to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). However, if one were to discuss it in terms of ultimate reality:
Even empty space would perish. This is because, through a single moment of non-awakening, one turns true emptiness into stubborn emptiness.
If one reverses this non-awakening and returns to awakening, then stubborn emptiness should likewise be transformed back into true emptiness.

Therefore, the subsequent text states: "The empty spaces of the ten directions will all vanish away. Second, regarding the analysis of phenomena, there are two parts. First, the elimination of delusion: "Then you depart."

Second, the reliance on the True [Nature]. You are now departing. This first section also has two parts: first, the general indication from "Then you" onwards; second, the specific explanation from "How so" onwards.
Within the initial general indication, the phrase "then you all" correctly points out the characteristics of that which is subject to destruction.

From the words "Consequently," it states that the essence of the luminous awareness of nature divides into the six faculties of sight, hearing, and so forth, all of which arise from the entanglements of the four elements and so on. From the beginning...

Regarding "entering the end": this is because the six sense faculties of seeing and hearing are themselves the five aggregates (*skandhas*) such as form; it is merely a difference in whether they are opened or closed.
In terms of the five aggregates, if one considers the sequence from beginning to end according to their arising, consciousness (*vijñāna*) is the beginning and form (*rūpa*) is the end.

If one relies on their destruction, form is the beginning and consciousness is the end. Therefore, it is said below: "The cause of arising exists through consciousness; cessation follows from the removal of form."

The second part, the detailed explanation, also has two sections. First is the explanation of turbidity, which asks, "What is it? Second is the explanation of the five layers, which begins with, "That which you perceive," and so forth.
