Within the first explanation of turbidity, "for example" (*tadyathā*) serves as the analogy, while "your turbidity" and so forth represent the phenomena (*dharma*). In the analogy, clear water represents the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-consciousness);
because it is fundamentally wondrously luminous, it is described as "pure and inherently so. Dust and soil represent the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), which give rise to...
Because they have become solidified and obstructed, it is said that their "substance remains as an impediment. Regarding the phrase "the two natures are equal":

this metaphor illustrates how the original purity and wondrous clarity of the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature) and the solidified obstructions produced by the four great elements are fundamentally distinct—one true and one delusory—and are not the same.
The phrase "there are people in the world" and so forth is a metaphor for sentient beings who, pursuing the four great elements, delusively lose the truth of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
The two phrases concerning "earth" mean that earth is inherently obstructive; yet once it is cast into water, that which was obstructive becomes non-obstructive.
This refers to what is described in the subsequent text as earth, water, fire, and wind being made to revolve so as to be perceived. Water is inherently pure and clear;

yet once it receives earth, that which was pure becomes impure. This refers to what is described in the subsequent text as sight, hearing, awareness, and cognition being constricted and rendered obstructed.

It is that which obstructs. Features such as facial appearance serve as a metaphor for the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), wherein the four great elements—one true and one false—are blended and intermingled such that they cannot be distinguished.
This principle may be understood.
The second explanation concerns the five layers, which are the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*). It should be understood that the five turbidities herein differ from those explained in other sutras.

In other sutras, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*) has the five sharp afflictions (*kleśa*) as its essence; the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*) has the five dull afflictions as its essence;

and the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) is the provisional designation for the retribution induced by these ten afflictions, thus having these two turbidities as its essence. Since the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*) already involves sentient beings...

Living for a morning and dying at dusk, their lifespans are indeterminate; thus, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*) constitutes its essence. The turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*) likewise has no separate essence of its own.
Because these four turbidities converge in a single period, and because all three types of calamities—small, medium, and great—are invariably present, this is termed the turbidity of the eon.
Within this, it takes only the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its essence. Specifically, the turbidity of the eon takes the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as its essence. Form is...

Because of the meaning of substantial obstruction, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*) takes the aggregate of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) as its essence; for "feeling" has the meaning of experiencing.

Because of the meaning of conceptualization, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kāṣāya*) takes the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) as its essence; for "perception" has the meaning of grasping signs. Because of the meaning of movement and flux, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kāṣāya*) takes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as its essence;

for "formations" have the meaning of shifting and flowing. Because of the meaning of discernment, the turbidity of lifespan (*āyuṣ-kāṣāya*) takes the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as its essence; for "consciousness" has the meaning of differentiation. Thus, these [five aggregates] are...
Therefore, reflect upon this and it will become clear. Yet, how can one see that these five turbidities and the five aggregates constitute its essence?

It is not necessary to cite other scriptures from afar; even within the subsequent refutation of the demon of the aggregates (*skandha-māra*), when first refuting the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), it says:

"This person is then able to transcend the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). And so on, until the fifth refutation of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), where it says: "This person is then able to transcend..."

Regarding the defilement of the lifespan (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*): it is therefore certain that this sutra takes the five turbidities (*pañca-kaṣāya*) and the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as its substance.
These shall now be treated in sequence, beginning with the turbidity of the eon (*kalpa-kaṣāya*). As for the passage, "You see empty space," "seeing" refers to one of the five sense faculties;

by citing one, the remaining four are subsumed. "Space" refers to one of the five sense objects (*pañca-viṣaya*); likewise, by citing one, the remaining four are subsumed. [Thus] the five faculties and the five...

Dust and the sense organs are both material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*), and they take the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) as their essence; therefore, one cites each of them individually to clarify this point.
The seeing that is capable of perceiving and the emptiness that is perceived are both omnipresent; thus it is said, "Your seeing," and so forth.
Since both are omnipresent, there is no distinction between the emptiness that is seen and the seeing that perceives it; hence it is said that "emptiness and seeing are not... [dual].

[The text] says: "If you claim that space and seeing can be divided, then since space originally has no substance or form, if there were a space that could be divided, it would instead lack the very substance of space;
therefore it is said, 'space exists but has no substance. Your seeing is merely capable of discernment;

if there were a seeing that could be divided, it would instead lack the awareness of seeing; therefore it is said, 'seeing exists but has no awareness. 'Woven together, they falsely form [reality]'—this refers to weaving."
This sutra’s warp and woof take emptiness devoid of substance as the warp to weave the vision devoid of awareness;
taking the vision devoid of awareness as the warp, it in turn weaves emptiness devoid of substance. As this mutual process continues without end, delusive appearances are thereby established.
Thus, the forms of the sense organs and their objects are all empty and false, woven together into existence; consequently, the kalpas thus formed are inherently not pure.
"Pure. Thus it is said that they "interweave with one another," and so forth. The meaning of the subsequent four phrases regarding their interweaving should all be understood by this analogy.

Regarding the second, the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*): "Grasping" (*bó*) means to seize; it carries the sense of receiving and taking in the aggregates (*skandha*). Seeing, hearing, smelling, tasting, touching, and cognizing are originally the wondrously luminous nature of the treasury (*tathatā-garbha*).
However, because of once grasping at the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), the wondrous luminosity is divided into six. Therefore, it says "seeing, hearing," and so forth.

Furthermore, water, fire, wind, and earth are fundamentally without cognition. When a portion of the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature) manifests as the faculty of sight and so forth, that which was without cognition comes to possess cognition;

thus, it is said to be "water, fire, and so on. One should understand that the four great elements, which are without cognition, and the six sense-faculties, which possess cognition, correspond to one another to form a weave.
All of these involve reception and thereby constitute the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kaṣāya*). Within the third, the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*)—

"Recollection, cognition, recitation, and practice" refers to the mental states of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) regarding its characteristics. "Recollection" means remembering the objective marks (*nimitta*) of past objects;
"cognition" means cognizing the objective marks of present objects; "recitation and practice" means rehearsing the objective marks of future objects.

Because the deluded nature arises as internal knowledge and vision due to this recollection, cognition, recitation, and practice, it is said that "the nature gives rise to knowledge and vision. "Container" (*rong*) means reflection (*pratibimba*).
Because the shadows of all phenomena throughout the three periods of time manifest as external objective forms, it is said that "appearances manifest as the six sense objects.

Thus, these external appearances take the six sense objects entirely as their characteristics; therefore, it is said that "apart from the sense objects, there are no characteristics. The internal nature takes knowing and seeing entirely as its awakening;
therefore, it is said that "apart from awakening, there is no nature. One should, by means of this nature-less capacity, know that which is characteristic-less.
To know that relativity constitutes weaving—these are all manifestations of conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) that result in the turbidity of afflictions (*kleśa-kaṣāya*).

Within the fourth, the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*), birth and extinction ceaselessly continue; this is precisely the meaning of the shifting and flowing of the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Regarding "knowledge and vision" (*jñāna-darśana*) and so forth:
it means that while the knowledge and vision of sentient beings always desire to remain long in this world, alas, the fruits of karma inevitably undergo transformation in other realms. Therefore...
This refers to knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). One should understand that the desire to abide in knowledge and vision necessarily corresponds to the shifting operations of karma;
these all flow and transform to constitute the turbidity of sentient beings (*sattva-kaṣāya*). Within the fifth, the turbidity of life (*āyuḥ-kaṣāya*), there is fundamentally no distinct nature;

this is also the meaning of the discernment of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). It is simply by way of the non-discriminative nature that the discernment of consciousness is clarified. Thus it is said.

"Originally there is no differentiation" refers to what is called the original single essence of luminous intelligence (*ekābhijñāna*). "The various objects are separated" refers to what is called the division into the six harmonious aggregates (*ṣaḍ-saṃnipāta*).
The phrase regarding "nature" explains the preceding phrase on "originally non-existent"; the phrase regarding "function" explains the preceding phrase on "the various objects.
Because it is originally a single essence of luminous intelligence, they recognize one another; because it is divided into the six harmonious aggregates, they turn away from one another.

If one discusses their nature (*svabhāva*), no difference in function can be found; if one discusses their function, no identity in nature can be found. Therefore, it is said that "identity and difference lose their standard.
One should take the natures that know each other and the functions that oppose each other as the warp and woof.

All of these are established through discrimination and constitute the turbidity of life (*jīva-kaṣāya*). The preceding section concludes the elimination of the false. Second, the classification according to the True [Nature] has three parts. First, the Dharma.
"Your departure," etc., is the second [section], the analogy, such as "as clear," etc. The third is the conclusion, clarifying the characteristics, etc.
Within the first [of these], it may again be divided into two: first, from "You now," etc., is the heading; second, from "With the profound stillness," etc., is the explanation.

Within the initial heading, "seeing, hearing," etc., refers to arising and ceasing; "permanence, bliss," etc., refers to non-arising and non-ceasing. Thus, one seeks to cultivate non-arising and non-ceasing by means of arising and ceasing. Therefore—

It is said that one wishes to achieve a distant resonance with the ultimate; that is, since these are the arising and ceasing of seeing and so forth, and one wishes to resonate with the non-arising and non-ceasing of the eternal and so forth, one should select and eliminate the root of this arising and ceasing—the cycle of birth and death—and instead rely upon the nature of the perfectly湛 (zhan) and luminous clarity that is non-arising and non-ceasing.

Therefore, it says "one should," and so on. Regarding "relying on the non-arising" and so forth, it means that since the previously mentioned perfectly湛 and luminous clarity has already been distinguished...

The nature [of the faculties] forms the basis for seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing. To accord with the fruit that is neither born nor extinguished, one should reverse the characteristics of birth-and-death—such as seeing, hearing, and so forth—and return them to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. If these deluded appearances are reversed, the true nature will spontaneously become perfect.

Therefore, the following passage speaks of "the profound stillness" (*zhan*), and so on. Within the second interpretation, "the profound stillness of the profound stillness" refers to the perfectly profound nature at the crown of the head.

"Attaining restoration" (*chengkan*): "prostrate" (*fu*) here means "to restore. When the perfectly profound true nature revolves back from false and fluctuating birth-and-death, the original luminosity of the nature-awakening naturally attains restoration.
Therefore, it says, "by means of the profound," and so forth. Once the originally luminous nature of awakening has been attained, this is taken as the causal mind.
Therefore, it says, "attaining the origin," and so forth. This is precisely to establish the foundation for practice for those at the initial stage of the path.
Without yet discussing entry into the stages, this is explained provisionally by way of its efficacy; thus it says, "Only after [the cause] exists... (and so forth).

Since the cause is fundamentally the nature of enlightened awareness, which is neither born nor extinguished, the fruit should likewise be the nature of enlightened awareness, which is neither born nor extinguished.

The cause that is cultivated is cultivation of the nature (*xing-xiu*); the fruit that is realized is realization of the nature (*xing-zheng*). This is what is meant by the mutual identity of cultivation and nature, and of cause and effect.
Because they are non-dual, it is said that "thereafter, etc. Within the second analogy, it says, "like clarifying turbid water.

Previously, clear water was used as a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature). Because those four elements divided their stillness into seeing, hearing, and so forth, one now wishes to revolve that stillness back from its false state;
therefore, it is likened to clarifying turbid water by placing it in a still vessel. This metaphor implies that once the sense organs [are stilled], they no longer...

The conditions and objects do not coincide either. The two phrases "still" and "deep" metaphorically indicate that consciousness also does not function. In this way, both arising and ceasing are neither arising nor ceasing.

The passage beginning with "clear water" clarifies both the dharma and the metaphor together. This means that although the earth has settled and the water has appeared, they have merely subsided; the earth has not yet been entirely removed.
On the level of the dharma, this precisely refers to the initial subduing of the adventitious views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within and without the *dhātu*.

"Sediment" refers to the five stages of dwelling [the five abodes], which are completely subdued; hence the phrase "clear water" and so forth. "Removing the mud from below" is a direct metaphor for complete severance.

In the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*), one removes the mud of the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*). From the second stage of faith up to the seventh, one removes the mud of the delusions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*).

From the eighth to the tenth stage of faith, one removes the mud of "dust and sand. From the first *abhisamaya* (dwelling) up to the Equal and Wondrous [Enlightenment], one removes the mud of ignorance (*avidyā*). Such is the process of severance.

There is nothing that is not severed; hence it is said, "removing the mud," and so forth. Among the three knots, the phrase "the appearance of light" is like the aforementioned "only the wondrous enlightened clarity, perfectly illuminating the Dharma-realm.
The two phrases "all things" and so forth are like the aforementioned "one is the immeasurable, and the immeasurable is one," and so on.
All these correspond to the principle of equality. This correctly clarifies that the causal mind, which is neither born nor extinguished, accords with non-arising.

This is the stage of the fruit that is non-extinguished. Because at the summit of the mountain of Nirvana, the five abodes are fully exhausted, the two deaths are forever forgotten, and because Prajñā does not arise and all dharmas do not arise—non-arising, non-arising—it is so called.
"Second, the departure according to the second meaning" is the passage clarifying the second definitive meaning.

In the first definitive meaning mentioned previously, the fundamental root of the five aggregates and birth-and-death was determined: one takes the nature of perfect stillness as the mind for the causal stage (*nidāna-citta*).
In this second definitive meaning, the fundamental root of the six sense faculties and afflictions is determined; therefore, one must carefully examine the six [faculties].
The faculty of sensation (*vedanendriya*) flows contrary to the current of birth and death; by it, one attains the profound penetration of a single gateway through universal circulation.

This section is divided into two parts: first, the formal exhortation to examine with care (beginning with "Now you..."); second, the specific exhortation to deliberate and select (beginning with "You now...").

The first part is further divided into three: first, the exhortation to examine (beginning with "Secondly..."); second, the statement of the underlying intent (beginning with "In your cultivation..."); third, the actual examination (beginning with "Observe...").
Regarding the "initial exhortation to examine" within the section on "determination" (*niścaya*) and so forth:

this means that when one intends to resolve upon the bodhicitta and cultivate Mahāyāna practices, one must not only abandon the mundane sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses, but should also discard the emptiness (*śūnyatā*), wishlessness (*apranihita*), and other [aspects] of the Hīnayāna.
In brief, all forms of biased emptiness and the "partial middle way" (*buton chū*) should be relinquished; hence it is said, "determination," and so forth. This initiates the karmic activity.

"Karma" refers to evil karma; that which "arouses" it is affliction (*kleśa*). "Moistening birth" means that "birth" is the retribution (*vipāka*), and that which "moistens" it is likewise affliction.
The two instances of the word "who" in the phrase "Who acts and who receives? are intended precisely to prompt careful and thorough examination.

However, those who act and those who receive [the results] are all the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*). Some take the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*) as the masters of the agent and the eight consciousnesses as the masters of the recipient.
While this may be acceptable as a general discussion, it seems unlikely in the present text, because it focuses exclusively on selecting the six sense organs.
This is why it says below: "In what place could the false roots and objects be inverted? and further: "The six are..."
The thief-like mediator plunders one's own family treasures. Furthermore, by tracing back to the ultimate source of the flowing roots, one arrives at that which is neither arising nor ceasing.
One should verify these six faculties of experience (*ṣaḍ-upabhoga-indriya*). The conclusion states: "Entering into one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.

Thus, it is known that this refers specifically to the discernment of the six faculties. Although the six faculties are emphasized in terms of their activity and reception, one should also apply this to the eight consciousnesses.

Refined and explained: it is simply that the six faculties are fundamentally the eight consciousnesses. What is meant is that if one distinguishes them in relation to the eye, they become the nature of seeing;
and so on, up to distinguishing them in relation to the mind (manas), they become the nature of cognition.

"The second emerges from within the mind" refers to your practice, etc., which precisely brings forth the reason for the definitive resolution regarding the root of afflictions. "Abiding in the high," etc., is an analogy.
It is like a king suppressing rebels: he must first know the location of the rebels before he can dispatch troops to punish them.

This section on "Correctly Examining and Distinguishing" has two parts: first, "Observe this... and below, which points to the actual object; second, "Then you... and below, which applies the analogy to the dharma. Regarding the first part, pointing to the actual object:
the person who unties the knot does not merely wish to see the knotted thing itself, but specifically wishes to know [the nature of the knots].

The origin from which a knot is formed must be followed in order for it to be untied. Therefore, below [the text] states: "If one does not know the source of the knot's formation," and "if one wishes to remove a knot, one must first focus the mind upon the knot," and so forth.
Here, "knot" is a metaphor for the root of afflictions (*kleśa*); "untying the knot" is a metaphor for the definitive discernment (*viniścaya*) of the root of afflictions;
and "empty space" is a metaphor for the nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*). These two points—[the metaphor of the knot and the metaphor of empty space]—are applied...
The Dharma is further twofold. First is the general enumeration, which refers to "you all. Second is the specific explanation, which asks, "What is meant by 'equal'?

Within the initial general enumeration, the phrase "the eyes, ears, and so forth act as intermediaries for thieves to plunder the family treasure" is as follows: the "thieves" are a metaphor for the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*); the "intermediaries" are a metaphor for the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*);

and the "family treasure" is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*. This refers to that which is intrinsically possessed within nature; this constitutes the family treasure. It is because of these [faculties] that... [the thieves act].
This refers to the six sense faculties being bound by the six sense objects. That is to say, "the gathering of conditions causes internal agitation, while they rush outward in flight.
Regarding the phrase "like a vessel," etc.: it means that once the six sense faculties have been bound by the six sense objects, they are consequently unable to transcend those six objects.

This is as previously stated: "seeing does not transcend form; hearing does not go beyond sound," and so forth. The second part, the detailed explanation, is further divided into three sections. First:
First, it clarifies the world. Second, it clarifies how all [phenomena] interpenetrate. Third, it clarifies the determination of superiority and inferiority.
Regarding the clarification of the world and the demonstration of interpenetration, it is intended that one may know the root of afflictions (*kleśa*).

Regarding the determination of superiority and inferiority, it is intended that one may know the root of perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭābhijñā*). Once the root of perfect penetration enters one's grasp, the root of afflictions shall [be severed].
This is the downward transformation. Thus it is said that upon entering the One, there is no delusion, and those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
First, regarding the clarification of the world: what is meant by "equality"? It is because the world fundamentally does not exist at a distance;

it resides solely within the single thought-moment and the single kṣaṇa of sentient beings. From the seeing of the eye, the hearing of the ear, up to the knowing of the mind—these very things constitute it.
Such is the world and its realms. This refers to the so-called "ten periods of time," wherein past and present do not depart from constant mindfulness, and so forth.

Second, regarding the manifestation of characteristics as interpenetrating the center: "above and below have no fixed positions" does not mean that there is an above within the above or a below within the below such that they constitute fixed positions of above and below.
Rather, because there are four directions and each direction possesses its own above and below, it is said thus.
Regarding the statement that "above and below have no fixed positions, and in the middle there is no determinate direction":

this does not mean that when one designates the center, looking east it becomes west and looking south it becomes north, thereby making the center indeterminate. Rather, the intention is that the four intermediate directions (the *vidiśas*) all exist in dependence upon the four cardinal directions.

For instance, if there were neither east nor south, from what could the southeast intermediate direction be established? Therefore, it is said that in the middle there is no determinate direction. Above...

Having already enumerated ten, one now wishes to sweep away the zenith and nadir as well as the four intermediate directions (*vidiś*), so that only the four cardinal directions—east, west, south, and north—remain.
Thus one knows that the zenith and nadir have no fixed position and that there is no determinate direction in the center; it should be viewed in this manner.
As for "three times four" and "four times three": when the world traverses the directions, it is "three times four"; when the directions traverse the world, it is "four times three."
These constitute the four sets of three. To summarize from beginning to end: the first repetition is called the beginning, and so on until the third repetition, which is called the end.

As for "merit," this refers specifically to the power of karmic action; it is not like the merit of the *Lotus Sūtra*’s purification of the six sense faculties through the recitation of the scripture.

The third section, "Distinguishing the Superiority and Inferiority of the Three Samādhis," is divided into two parts. First, the heading: "You again... and so forth. Second, the explanation: "...like the eyes... and so forth.
Within the first part, the heading, the initial determination of superiority and inferiority is intended precisely as a prologue for the subsequent selection of the Perfect Penetration (*yuan-tong*).
There are six explanations for the two [senses], namely the eye, ear, and so forth. Regarding the first, the eye faculty:

as for "the eyes and so forth," taking those twelve hundred [beings] and dividing them into two parts across the ten directions, there are two hundred in the direction of true south, as previously seen.
Furthermore, seeing one hundred [leagues] each in the two intermediate directions of southeast and southwest, it is said that "the front is entirely clear.
Also, seeing two hundred [leagues] each in the two directions of east and west, it is said that "one looks to the left and right sides.

Since the two hundred [leagues] directly to the north behind, as well as the one hundred [leagues] each in the two intermediate directions of northwest and northeast, are all not seen, it is said that "the rear is entirely dark."
"Dark. Taken together, those who do not see are four hundred, while those who see are eight hundred; thus it is said that "two-thirds [see]. The following cases may be inferred accordingly.
Regarding the second, the faculty of hearing: "As with the ear, etc. This precisely reveals that the faculty of hearing excels the other faculties.
That is to say, while the object of sound has boundaries, the nature of hearing is boundless. As it is said: "If drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions..."

Regarding the first, it is heard simultaneously. Regarding the third, among the faculties of the nose: as for "the middle intersection is missing," exhaling is called "out" and inhaling is called "in.
Between the two pillars [of exhalation and inhalation], there is not a lack of a gap; therefore, it is said that "the middle intersection is missing. Regarding the fourth, the faculty of the tongue:
Regarding the phrase "such as the tongue," it takes up its capacity for expression as its functional activity (*kāritra*).

Since all mundane and supramundane knowledge is exhausted within expression—because knowledge resides in speech—there are spatial divisions (*pradeśa*) when considered from the perspective of verbal designation (*abhilāpa*); yet, from the perspective of the essential nature (*tattva*) of principle, there is fundamentally no limit.

Therefore, it is said that "speech has [limits]," and so forth. The five body-faculties (*kāyendriya*) may be understood accordingly. Regarding the sixth, the mind-faculty (*manendriya*), it is like the mind itself.

Regarding "silent acceptance" (*mo-rong*) and so forth: it means that while the phenomena of the ten directions and three periods—both mundane and supramundane, ordinary and sagely—are unequal, the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*) silently comprehends them;
hence, it is called "according to one's will" (*yìrúì*). The character "silent" (*mò*) is contrasted with the tongue’s vocal proclamation; these two are distinct.

The detailed analysis of the second [section], "Exhortation to Examine Thoroughly," has four parts: first, "Now you... and below, which provides actual verification; second, "If you can... and below, which involves comparison; third... [text continues].
I shall now explain this as requested. Regarding the intent behind the phrase "In the four directions": First, concerning the passage beginning with "You now," etc.:

the six sense faculties taking the six sense objects as their conditions constitute the "flowing with the current" (*anuloma-srotas*), which is the very root of birth and death; this is termed the "desire-flow of birth and death.

If one can reverse that flowing with the current, one immediately achieves the "flow of the Dharma-nature" (*dharmatā-srotas*). This is because the flow of the faculties is entirely derived from the essence of profound, tranquil awareness (*prabodha-tattva*).

As for the division into six parts: first, the scripture returns to the ultimate source to investigate the dharma of non-arising and non-extinction within its own essence; hence it says, "You now," and so forth.

Regarding "one should verify below": this instructs that one should immediately take what was previously established regarding superiority and inferiority and verify it—asking who is in accord with true nature, who is separated from true nature, who is in accord with true nature and thus profound, and who is... [separated].
If one is separated from the nature and thus shallow, who is it that merges with the true nature and becomes profound, thereby attaining perfect penetration?

If one is separated from the true nature and thus shallow, not attaining perfect penetration, who is it? Therefore, it is said, "constantly verified," and so forth. Next, regarding the phrase "if one can," etc.:
if one obtains the faculty of perfect penetration, one is then able to go against the deluded current of birth and death; naturally, [the marks...]
Because they accord with reality and do not contradict it, it is said that they are "able to be equal.
If one were to compare this with those who practice through faculties that lack perfect penetration, even a single day spent in such perfect penetration is superior to a kalpa of long duration.

For one who practices without attaining perfect penetration, even a kalpa as long as that would not equal a single day as short as this. Thus we know that a day and a kalpa are fundamentally multiples of one another. That which is as short as a day is still superior to a kalpa; that which is as long as a kalpa is, conversely, inferior to a day. If they are thus multiplied by such factors, how much more so? To compare them in this way—[one who desires... to practice... [would find... the kalpa far inferior to the day. How could it be otherwise? By weighing them in this manner, one who wishes to... [attain... the Way... [should] first understand the measure of time. If one does not understand the measure of time, how can one speak of the Way? Therefore, the Buddha spoke of the kalpa to clarify the measure of time. If one understands the measure of time, one will naturally understand the Way. If one understands the Way, one will naturally attain liberation. If one attains liberation, one will naturally transcend birth and death. How could a practitioner abandon the fundamental source of perfect penetration? Regarding the phrase "Among these three, I now... and so forth:

this refers back to the eight hundred, one thousand, and two hundred merits mentioned above as the basis for cultivation and manifestation; thus it says, "I now," and so on. As for "the six sense-faculties are profoundly still and perfectly luminous":

this indicates that although the six faculties belong to the realm of delusion, they originally branch out from the true nature of profound stillness and perfect luminosity. This is explained in terms of the True [Nature].
This is to clarify the delusion. Below, "comparing and weighing" means to cause them to discern in detail: who is one whose count of eight hundred merits is deficient;
who is one whose count of twelve hundred merits is full; and who is one whose count is full and thus capable of entering.
"Who is it that contracts [the mind] such that it cannot enter?"—this is why it says "number, quantity, and so forth. "I shall now... is a formal grant to explain.
"If you carefully discern and settle your mind, it shall become enlightened; let it cause you to give rise to practice based upon it, and through that practice, to realize entry.
This is why it says "I shall now," and so on. Among the four [sections], regarding "the ten directions," the intent is as follows: if one...

As for the Tathāgatas, those with superior faculties—namely, the eighteen realms consisting of the sense organs, objects, and consciousnesses—all may cultivate perfect penetration to achieve unsurpassed Bodhi;

hence it is said, "In the ten directions," and so forth. However, because your faculties are inferior, you are unable to exercise the perfect fusion and sovereign mastery of the eighteen realms such that they mutually encompass one another; hence it is said, "But you," and so forth. This is because your faculties are inferior.

For this reason, among the triad of sense organs (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), you are to select and set aside the six objects and the six consciousnesses, retaining only the six sense organs.
Within the six sense organs, further eliminate the other five and retain only the ear organ. This is identical to Master Zhiyi’s method of selecting the object of meditation:
just as one cuts down a tree to reach its root, cauterizes a disease to find its source, or reduces the measure from a *zhang* to a *chi*, and from a *chi* to an *cun*. Thus, one should know that...
Although the methods employed by the Tathāgatas and the patriarchs differ, their underlying principle is one and the same. Regarding the passage "entering the One without delusion" and so forth:
if one enters through a single gate against the current of birth and death and attains the truth through a single faculty (*indriya*), then all other faculties will likewise become pure.

Extending this further, it is not limited to the six faculties alone; rather, the six objects (*viṣaya*) and the six consciousnesses (*vijñāna*) can all be purified. Although it is said to be "one gate," it is [in fact] with...
That which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions enter is non-dual; this refers to the statement: "The nature of returning to the source is non-dual, though the expedient means have many gates.
Second, the successive resolution of doubts is divided into three parts. First, resolving the doubt regarding the "one entry" and the "six purities," as Ānanda said:
The Buddha departed. Second, resolving the doubt that cause and effect are not aligned; this refers to Ānanda’s request to the Buddha. Third, resolving the doubt as to how knots are tied and untied;

this also refers to Ānanda’s request to the Buddha. This first section is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downward, the request based on doubt; second, from "The Buddha said" downward, the response and explanation.
Within the initial request based on doubt, there are two points: first, it was previously stated that one must go against the flow of birth and death, and furthermore...
"Sixth, 'the six are profoundly still, perfect, and luminous. This means that since the six are already profoundly still, perfect, and luminous, what need is there to flow against the current?

Therefore, he asks: 'How does one flow against the current? Second, it was previously stated: 'Entering deeply through one gate, entering the one without delusion, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
This implies that since one has entered deeply through one gate and entered the one without delusion, this pertains solely to a single faculty."
Their roots and branches are fundamentally different; how then can they be pure at one and the same time? Therefore, he asks: "How does one enter deeply... (and so forth).
This refers to the arising of doubt regarding the "restraint of the tracks. The second part, the section on the explanation of the answer, is divided into two.
First, the explanation of the first doubt: "The Buddha said, 'Go. Second, the explanation of the second doubt: "Now you, go. Within the first explanation of the first doubt, the Buddha...
The passage beginning with "He told Ānanda" should be supplemented as follows: "You say that the six sense-bases are profoundly still and perfectly luminous;

why then must you flow against the current? Your doubt is such as this. However, as I observe it, when speaking from the perspective of true nature (*tathatā*), the six sense-bases are profoundly still and perfectly luminous;

yet when discussed in terms of deluded appearances (*mṛṣā-lakṣaṇa*), these are precisely what you, Ānanda, have not yet severed. Therefore, he says: 'You now... This refers to the first fruit (*prathamaphala*).

Because the delusions of view within the three realms have been ceased and eliminated, it says, "You now," and so forth. Yet, because the delusions of thought within the three realms remain unceased, it says, "However, you still," and so forth.

Since the delusions of thought have not yet been severed, how much less could there be the phase of arising—which is non-existent prior [to existence], the phase of abiding—which has a temporary function, the phase of change—which is not static, or the phase of cessation—which is non-existent subsequent [to existence]?

Furthermore, as long as various categories of ignorance and delusion have not been severed, how could one attain the sixfold profound, perfect clarity? Thus it is said, "How much more so," and so forth.
If one does not flow against the current in this manner, how can one obtain the sixfold profound, perfect clarity? Ānanda, what doubt do you have regarding this?

The second part, the explanation that resolves the second doubt, is divided into two sections. First, from "Now you... onwards, there is a general inquiry. Second, from "Ānanda... onwards, there is a detailed explanation.
Within the initial general inquiry, the phrase "Now you [and others] previously" should also be supplied.

Your doubt concerns how the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*), which are distinct and different from one another, can enter into a single state of non-delusion such that those six cognitive faculties (*ṣaḍvijñānendriya*) become pure simultaneously. This is what you have doubted.
It is as follows. Let me ask you this: are those six sense organs one, or are they six?
Therefore, it is said, "I now ask you. This second section, the Separate Explanation, has three parts: first, the Dharma [the teaching], referring to Ānanda and others;

second, the analogy, referring to the great [mirror] and so forth; third, the application, referring to "then you" and so forth. The first part [the Dharma] further has two sections. First, from "Ānanda" downwards, it is explained in relation to...

In principle, there is fundamentally neither one nor six. The two [sections] beginning with "Ānanda" arise from the delusion regarding the meaning of one and six. The first [section] further has three parts: first, the refutation of "one," which begins with "Ānanda, go...";
second, the refutation of "six," which begins with "If this..."; third, the concluding demonstration, which begins with "Therefore... (or "For this reason...").
In the first part, since it is stated that the ear does not see and so forth up to the feet having no speech, it can be seen that these are not one.
In the second part, since it says the ear hears, yet the mouth asks questions and the body respectfully receives them, it can be seen that these are not six either.
In the third part, it correctly demonstrates that those six faculties of cognition are neither located in a single place, nor are they ultimately six, nor are they six locations.
Yet in the end, they are not one. However, one can ultimately not say that your six faculties originally possessed one, nor that they originally possessed six.
Thus, it is known that both "one" and "six" are unattainable; hence the words "Therefore, etc. Next, regarding the arising of the meaning of delusion concerning "one" and "six," it says:
"Although the six have been dissolved, one has still not yet forgotten. This means that while the [delusion of] six has already been suppressed through reflection...

Because the delusive faculties and their objects do not coincide, it is said that although the six [faculties] have been dissolved, as stated below: "Originally, based on one brilliant spirit, the six harmonious combinations were formed.
Now that the six harmonious combinations have been dissolved, the one brilliant spirit still remains. Therefore, it is said that "the one has not yet perished."

This refers to designating the consciousness-essence as "one. There are two metaphors for this, each with two parts. First, the passage beginning with "Just as in the world" uses metaphors to illustrate the arising of the meanings of "one" and "six.

Second, the passage beginning with "In that world" uses metaphors to illustrate that fundamentally there is neither "one" nor "six. Regarding the first part: the metaphor of "the great empty space" and so forth illustrates the arising of the six;
the metaphor of "excluding vessels" and so forth illustrates the arising of the one. Regarding the second part: "same" and "different" mean that it is impossible for there to be a single [entity].
They share the same sixfold nature yet differ in their characteristics. Not only is there no characteristic of "one" or "six," but furthermore, there is no name for "one" or "six.
The phrase "how much more so" (*kaihe*) indicates this. The three combinations are divided into two parts: first, the general combination from "you" (*ni*) onwards;

second, the specific combination from "due to clarity" (*yōmyō*) onwards, which is self-evident. The specific combination is further divided into two: first, the actual combination, because delusion possesses the one and the six; due to... [text fragment].
This refers to "illumination" and so forth. Second, the formal summary: the principles do not allow for one or six; you merely equate them. The first section has two parts:
first, the emergence of the six kinds of appearances through illumination; second, Ānanda’s departure from his attachments, which collectively belong to the realm of delusion.

Regarding the first, the emergence of the six kinds of appearances, there are six stages in succession. Among these six, it says: "Adhering to the profound stillness, vision is produced," and so on, up to "adhering to the profound stillness, cognition is produced."

This should be read in contrast with the following passage, "Adhering to delusion, it gives rise to light. The former describes how delusion arises from the True; the latter describes how one becomes lost in delusion and loses the True. This is what is meant by:

"The solitary True cannot stand alone, and the isolated delusion cannot be established. The phrase "adhering to the profound stillness" refers to the sense-faculty being triggered by the two objects of brightness and darkness;
this is what is called "the object entering the faculty. The two lines beginning with "the essence of seeing" describe the faculty departing toward the objects.
This refers to the sense organs (*indriya*) entering their objects. "Forming the organs" means forming both the ultimate (*paramārtha*) and the superficial (*tuccha*) organs.

Although the explanation follows a sequential order, the actual events occur simultaneously. "The source of the organ," etc., refers to the ultimate organ that is formed; "the name of the cause," etc., refers to the superficial organ that is formed.
The two phrases concerning the superficial organ properly conclude that the ultimate organ relies upon the superficial organ to function.

This can be understood. Both faculties are composed of eight factors consisting of both the efficient cause (*kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna*). In the above discussion of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), only the efficient cause was mentioned;

therefore, it says "pure four great elements" (*mahābhūta*). As for why the four great elements are called "pure," they originally emerge from the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, just as the six sense organs are profoundly still, perfect, and luminous.
Within the discussion of the physical organs (*rajas-mūla*), only the material cause is mentioned; therefore, it says "floating roots and four sensory objects. For this reason...
Both [types] of sense organs should each possess eight factors. As it is with one text, so it is for the other five by analogy. Regarding only the tongue organ that is shaped like a crescent moon:
from the first, third, and fourth [factors] onward, it is an upward-facing moon; from the seventeenth and eighteenth [factors] onward, it is a downward-facing moon.
What is now called the "sloping moon" refers to that which occurs from the age of seventeen or eighteen onwards.

As for the statement that the floating dust within the mental faculty (manas-indriya) is like what is seen in a dark chamber, this is because the mental faculty possesses a form distinct from the other faculties.
Regarding the second section, "The Two Bonds Belonging Generally to Delusion," there are two parts. First, showing the cause, which refers to Ānanda and others.

Second, discerning the lack of substantiality, which begins with "Thus, etc. Within the first part, the phrase "Thus, etc. means that if one seeks the root and traces the source of these six faculties, they all arise from within the wondrous clarity of fundamental awareness (*prakṛti-vijñāna*);
therein exists a false luminosity capable of illuminating and a single object of illumination...
This clarifies that deluded cognition arises from this [delusion], whereby one loses its true nature and gives rise to false appearances; thus it says "in this way," and so forth.
Within the second [section], there is a formal analysis of how the six sense organs exist when encountering objects and do not exist when separated from them.
This second part further divides into two: first, from "But you... onwards, which concludes by answering the question; second, from "Not by... onwards.

This turns back and explains away the underlying objections. The first section has two parts. First, the external does not rely on objects; this refers to the passage beginning with "You merely," and so forth. Second, the internal does not rely on the faculties;
this refers to the passage beginning with "Following the extraction," and so forth. Regarding the first of these: you have stated above that one should first say, "Your question is:
how can one enter the single state of non-delusion so that those six sense-faculties become pure simultaneously? However, as I see it, there is no other method; it simply requires...
It is simply not following after external objects (*viṣaya*). Therefore, it says, "You should merely... (and so forth); this refers to the external non-reliance on objects.

Furthermore, one must internally not rely on the sense organs (*indriya*). Thus, it next says, "Following and uprooting... (and so forth). "Uprooting" (*ba*) means to oppose; "subduing" (*fu*) means to restore.
Now, the sense organs are that which is to be uprooted, while that which uproots them is the sublime practice of *śamatha* and so forth. One realizes that although the organs arise and perish...
The essence itself is neither arising nor ceasing. Through the object, wisdom is elicited; through wisdom, the object is illumined.

That which was formerly stuck to as a state of profound stillness now attains liberation of its own accord. The original truth of the internal nature is likewise restored. Thus it is said, "following the extraction," and so forth.
Having liberated oneself from false attachments and restored the original truth, one returns to the wondrously pure, luminous essence—the originally enlightened true nature.

It returns to its entirety; thus it is said that one "returns to the original truth. Taking these three wisdoms as the cause, one attains the restoration of the wondrous principle of the original truth.
Furthermore, within this restored wondrous principle, one gives rise once more to the originally inherent wondrous wisdom; hence it is said that "the original luminous radiance is manifested.

Upon reaching this state, object and wisdom are of one suchness, and subject and object are non-dual. It is not merely a matter of extracting a single sense organ; the same applies to the remaining five.
The faculties (*indriya*) should likewise be uprooted completely and liberated completely; thus it says, "all the others," and so forth.

In this way, one can see that upon entering a state of non-delusion, those six organs of cognition (*ṣaḍ-vijñānendriya*) are simultaneously purified. Second, the explanation of the underlying doubts has two parts:

first, the explanation of the faculties, beginning with "not by means of... and so forth; second, the explanation of the objects (*viṣaya*), beginning with "now you... and so forth. The first part [the explanation of the faculties] also has two sections; the first is... [text fragment].

Regarding the "correct explanation" (*samyak-vyākhyāna*), there are two parts: the citation of examples by Ānanda and others, and the initial correct explanation itself. Within the initial correct explanation, one must first present the following anticipated objection:
"Since the six sense organs have been uprooted and detached, and [consciousness] no longer manifests in dependence upon the internal organs, by what means will hearing and seeing occur?
To resolve this, it is explained: "At that time, seeing and hearing no longer employ these former sense organs; therefore, it is said that they do not depend on them."
It is equal [to the preceding]. Because it takes its own true illumination as the master and does not turn according to the six sense organs, it is said that "illumination does not follow the roots.

Although seeing and hearing are present before one, they merely rely upon the six organs to manifest their clarity; thus it is said that "the organs serve as the locus for the manifestation of illumination.
From this, although one speaks of "seeing forms," it is not concerned with the forms themselves; this is what is called the "true seeing that sees seeing."
Although it is said that hearing sound does not concern the sound itself, this is what is meant by the "true hearing" of hearing.

Thus, within a single faculty, there are the functions of all faculties; therefore, it is said, "By means of these... In the second citation of examples, the passage beginning with "Ānanda, how could you... [is as follows].

Fearing that Ānanda might not be fully convinced, [the Buddha] further cites the affairs of ordinary and lesser beings as an analogy to clarify the point—this being the method of using the shallow to illustrate the profound.
Thus, it says "Ānanda and others. In the passage beginning with "Śūnyatā" (舜若) and continuing with "Tathāgata," [the text] explains that the empty deity is capable of perceiving touch.
The two phrases concerning the Tathāgata mean that although he has no body, he is able to manifest a body. Since he is...
Two lines: although it is said that they manifest only briefly, they are nonetheless capable of perceiving and touching. The final conclusion states:

"Nanda, Kātyāyana, and others who have attained the *nirodhasamāpatti*—who, according to the Hīnayāna, are able to see, taste, and cognize without relying on the three faculties of eye, tongue, and mind;
and Śūnyatā, Gaṅgā, and Nanda—who, among ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), are able [to perceive] without the three faculties of body, nose, and ear..."
As for the statement that "the faculty of touch can smell and hear," even ordinary people of limited capacity are capable of this;

how much more so, then, could one whose sense organs and objects have been completely uprooted fail to be able to employ the six faculties interchangeably? This second section, the explanation of the differentiation of objects, has three parts:

first, the direct explanation starting from "Now you..."; second, the illustrative clarification starting from "Just as that..."; and third, the combined elucidation starting from "The conditions for seeing...". First, the direct explanation:

In the explanation: Now, you above should first present the anticipated objection: "If it is said that one does not follow internal objects and does not rely on external objects, how is it that various objective appearances still manifest before us? He then resolves this, saying: "Your six sense organs have not been uprooted;
if you can completely uproot them so that the internal nature shines forth with clarity, then all objective appearances will be like ice melting in hot water."
When ice melts, it returns to being water; if the characteristics of dust-like phenomena (dust-marks) were to dissolve, they would immediately become cognition and vision.
How could there be any further dust-marks to serve as a basis for doubt? Therefore, it says "Ānanda and others. As for the analogy of hot water melting ice:
those dust-marks originally manifest from the wondrous clarity, just as water becomes ice. Since the dust-marks have dissolved, one should reflect upon this.
It transforms into cognition, just as ice returns to water. These two examples clarify the Middle Way. As for the passage "Ānanda, those people...
and so forth, it is because Ānanda might still not have fully understood; therefore, the matter of worldly people is further cited as an example to clarify it, hence the words "Ānanda, etc.
Each point is made clear by applying the example to the Dharma, just as in those two sentences; however, the application has not yet been fully realized.
This refers to the uprooting [of the faculties]. If one takes the two phrases regarding the [six] faculties as an example, they illustrate the complete uprooting of the six faculties.

The two phrases regarding the six faculties illustrate the various changing appearances of the *pudgala* (dust-like objects). The two phrases regarding "that person" illustrate the inner luminosity that radiates light.

Although there are three phrases regarding "that," they illustrate how the power of inner light causes the appearances of dust to vanish and transform into cognitive awareness. Through this true nature, Fa Shang...
It is light that forms a circular illumination; it does not employ the faculty of the eye. Herein, one merely circles the hand externally, yet even this does not employ the eye.
Since the nature of these two cases is similar, this example is cited to illustrate the point. If one were merely to explain the literal text, one should say that the eye presides over seeing;
now, because the objects being gathered have come before the eyes, it is said that "seeing is gathered at the eye. This being so, in relation to them—
An object should be viewed with the eyes; yet, instead, one suddenly closes those very eyes capable of seeing.

At that time, only the appearance of darkness manifests before one, and one can no longer see the object in front. Therefore, it is said, "If one were to... and so forth. Among those gathered in another place, there are also people;
these people are not devoid of the six sense faculties. However, because they have already closed their eyes, they see only darkness.

Regarding their physical characteristics: because their heads and feet are so similar that they cannot be distinguished, it is said that "the six sense organs are equal. As for that person with closed eyes:
because he does not see with his eyes, he follows the other person's body with his hands, tracing it as he moves around them;
thus it is said, "that person," and so forth. Although that person cannot see with his eyes, he uses his hands to feel about, saying, "This is the head; this is the foot."
From head to foot, there is nothing that is not clearly understood; hence it is said, "Although they [the objects] are such... and so forth.
Nevertheless, although the characteristics of the hands and eyes differ, the nature of their cognition does not vary; hence it is said, "Cognition is the same. One should conclude by clarifying:

If even those who are inferior can achieve this, how much more so for the most excellent ones whose dust has been shed from the objects and whose faculties have been uprooted—yet they still possess the appearance of dust?
Could you possibly still harbor doubts? The third section, "The Conjunction of the Three," is divided into two parts: first, the conjunction of the object and the seeing;

second, the conclusion regarding the sense organ and the object. Regarding the first part: as for "the seeing and the object," this refers to how, due to past causes, one falsely perceives external objects through the light of consciousness.
If the clear illumination does not manifest before one, one is further unable to see; this is because one cannot give rise to true illumination.
Therefore, it is said that "the seeing depends on conditions" and so forth. If one can see without relying on delusion, true illumination will spontaneously arise as the contemplative light.
Thus, it is said that "the non-illumination arises of itself. At that time, all existing marks of darkness belong to my own true illumination; they no longer exist.
It becomes even more obscured; thus it is said, "then all [the faculties] are likewise. The interpretation of the text is as follows. If one applies this to the two textual passages as an analogy:
the two phrases concerning "conditions" and "views" correspond to the analogy of those two phrases regarding the Dharma that has not yet uprooted its roots.
The phrase "not clear" corresponds to the urgency of the analogy—forcing the eyes shut until the six faculties become perfected through the method of circling around the substance.
"Extracting the internal to manifest radiance" means that one should know these two phrases correspond to the three-phrase method of the former [text]:

all delusory phenomenal appearances (*bu-chén xiàng*) dissolve like ice melting in hot water, transforming into awareness at the very moment of thought. Only in this way does one see how the dharma-examples correspond;
the three are but a single breath. Next, regarding "the faculties and objects having already dissolved": this refers to the extraction of those faculties and objects.
Furthermore, let us consider the question previously raised by Ānanda: "How is it that by entering deeply through one gate, all six faculties can be purified simultaneously?

The Tathāgata has repeatedly elucidated this through both Dharma-explanations and parables. While the delusion regarding the distinction between "one" and "six" arises, from the perspective of ultimate principle, there is fundamentally neither "one" nor "six.
Consequently, when one faculty is uprooted, the other five are completely liberated; thus, all six [faculties]...
If all the sense organs were to function interchangeably, such that all objective phenomena were transformed into cognitive awareness, then Ānanda’s doubts would have been resolved on the spot.
This is why [the Buddha] rebuked him, saying that the sense organs and their objects are equal.

The second section, from "Ānanda addressed the Buddha" onwards, is the passage that resolves doubts regarding the inconsistency between cause and effect. It is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the inquiry and request;
second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the response and explanation. The first part is further divided into two: first, confirming the Buddha’s words, namely "Ānanda and others";
second, stating one's own doubts, namely "World-Honored One and others. Within the section confirming the Buddha’s words, it says: "As..."

Regarding the phrase "the Buddha and others": this refers to the first definitive meaning of the Tathāgata, which states that one should carefully examine whether the mind generated at the stage of the causal ground is identical to or different from the awakening of the resultant stage;

and within the second definitive meaning, it provides a detailed selection of one among the six sense faculties as the entry point into non-delusion, whereby those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified—this is the point of doubt.
Therefore, it is said that they are "equal to the Buddhas. Second, the presentation of one's own doubts is further divided into four parts:

first, from "The World-Honored One" downward, the presentation that the fruit is eternally abiding; second, from "If this" downward, the description that the cause is impermanent; third, from "How can" downward, the formal statement of the doubt and objection;

and fourth, from "How can" downward, the conclusion requesting instruction. Regarding the first [part], there are seven eternally abiding fruits, all of which belong to the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Regarding "realization" (*prāpti*): it refers to the fact that both *tathatā* and *buddhadhātu* have already been realized;
it is not merely a matter of possessing specific characteristics. The rest is as can be seen [in the text]; this is precisely what the Tathāgata calls the stage of fruition (*phala-bhūmi*).

Next, in the middle section, the phrase "if these [beings]" refers to the passage that elaborately analyzes how the six sense faculties enter into the single state of non-delusion (*aviparyāsa*), and so forth. This is because of the six sense faculties as causes...
"Because dust [objects] exist," it is said, "if such as these [were the case]," and so forth. The phrase "just as... serves to cite an analogy.

Specifically, it refers to the three instances in the first fascicle where the fundamental non-existence of the essence of delusion is established; therein it is stated that if there were a nature of discrimination apart from external objects, it would be your true mind.
Since [the mind] has no substance apart from objects, these are examples of how objects are but reflected shadows of discrimination. This is precisely what the Tathāgata... [taught].
This is what is meant by the "true causal mind. Regarding these three [categories], what is their significance? It is to establish a formal designation.

The meaning is that since the Tathāgata has stated that the "mind of the causal stage" and the "awakening of the fruition stage" correspond in name and designation, one knows that the ever-abiding causal mind, which is neither arising nor ceasing, is precisely matched with the fruition stage, which is likewise neither arising nor ceasing; thus, their names and designations are brought into accord.

[Objection: How can these six roots of delusion, which are ultimately subject to cessation, serve as the mind of the causal ground (*hetu-bhūmi-citta*) while one seeks to attain the Tathāgata’s awakening of the fruition ground (*phala-bhūmi*), which is neither born nor extinguished?
Thus [the text] asks, "How could this be so? The passage beginning with "World-Honored One" below provides the explanation.
"If separated from... and so forth means that the six sense organs exist because of their objects. "As if there were none... and so forth continues to cite the non-existence of the deluded mind.

The phrase "advancing and retreating according to the substance" and so forth does not mean that the faculty of sight is designated as "advancing" and so on up to the faculty of mind being designated as "retreating.

What is meant is this: if one advances and traces it back to the mind, then [the mind] ceases to exist when separated from its objects; thus, it is certainly not something that can be grasped as "my mind.

If one retreats and traces it back to the faculties, then [the mind] exists only because of the objects; likewise, it is not something that can be grasped as "my mind. Therefore, it is said "advancing."

[This refers to] "receding" and so forth. Since both mind and mental factors are ultimately ungraspable, with what could one establish a "mind of the causal stage" to seek the awakening of the "fruition stage"?
Therefore, it says, "With whom... and so on. The passage beginning with "The Tathāgata" concludes the argument.

Its meaning is that the Tathāgata previously taught that among the six faculties, the six states of profound stillness are perfectly luminous and can be selected as the fundamental basis for perfect penetration, thereby entering into the state of non-delusion.
"These six faculties of knowledge are simultaneously purified; this is the Tathāgata’s truthful word.
Now, when I minutely investigate the past, all six faculties are entirely subject to cessation. Thus, it would contradict and transgress the Tathāgata’s truthful word;
therefore, it is said that he "contradicts and transgresses his truthful word. If one were to say they cease in this manner, then the Tathāgata has already—
To speak of this as being neither arising nor ceasing—if one claims it is neither arising nor ceasing, then I have already refuted that as a doctrine of annihilationism.

Since there would be no fixed principle regarding this or that, before or after, it ultimately becomes mere frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*). Thus it is said: "In the end, it results in frivolous proliferation.

Since that which expresses [the concept] is frivolous proliferation, it goes without saying that the expressed—arising and ceasing—is likewise so. How, then, can such a mind be taken as the causal ground to seek the awakening of the fruition stage?
Among the four [types of speech], what is meant by "discursive proliferation" (*prapañca*)? The intention is this:
although it may be considered discursive proliferation, the Tathāgata has always said, "That which I have spoken is true and not false, real and not empty.
Thus, one knows that the Tathāgata’s own words should not be discursive proliferation. However, for the time being, I do not know what constitutes the Tathāgata’s truly authentic speech; therefore—
"What does 'and so forth' mean? Whether it be with the Tathāgata or with me, Ānanda, there is no lack of delusion or parsimony.
I pray that you will bestow your unconditioned great compassion to lift away my delusion and parsimony;

thus he says, 'I only pray you, etc. The second part, the "Answer and Explanation," is divided into three sections: 1. Reprimanding the delusion and granting the teaching: "The Buddha told him, etc. 2. Striking the bell to verify permanence: "At that moment, etc."

Furthermore, the three sections bring together delusion and enlightenment through various points of equality. Regarding the first section: "You have studied... and so forth, this is a reprimand for his delusion.

Because he has only severed the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) but has not yet destroyed the afflictions of thought (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) and ignorance (*avidyā*), it is said that he has "not exhausted all outflows" (*āsrava*).
Ānanda only knew that the clinging to stillness to produce seeing, hearing, and so forth was the cause of perversion; therefore, it is said, "Within his mind... and so forth. However...

Not realizing that total delusion is itself reality and that total arising-and-ceasing is itself non-arising-and-non-ceasing, you continue to be confused by taking it to be delusion and arising-and-ceasing;
this is true perversion. That you cannot recognize such perversion is entirely due to the fact that your various outflows (*āsrava*) have not yet been exhausted.
Therefore, it is called "true perversion. [The Master] says, "I fear for you," and so forth, granting him permission to speak. His intention is that since you have already asked, [I shall explain].

First: If I were to explain this directly according to the ultimate principle, I fear that although your mind may be sincere and respectful, as your outflows (*āsrava*) are not yet exhausted, you would still be unable to give rise to faith and submission.
For now, let me attempt to explain it for you by borrowing from shallow and mundane matters that are easy to understand.

Therefore, it says, "I fear for you all. Second, the examination of the permanence [of hearing] by striking the bell is divided into three parts: first, immediately below, the definitive determination of existence or non-existence;
second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the pointing out of the nature of hearing; third, from "You now" onwards, the conclusion, exhortation, and citation of examples.

Within the first part, there are two further sections: first, concerning the sense organ (the passage beginning with "Immediately"); second, concerning the object (the passage beginning with "The Tathāgata"). Within the first section concerning the sense organ:

Regarding "sound and resonance": the initial, direct roar is called resonance; subsequent sounds that are intermittent are called tones. Ānanda and the great assembly replied, "When there is sound, we hear;

when there is no sound, we do not hear. This is not the correct explanation. Although the sensory object of sound may exist or not exist, how could the nature of hearing itself exist or not exist based on its existence or non-existence? It is as in the following response concerning the presence or absence of sound.
This is what constitutes correctness. Second, the visible aspect is discussed in relation to objects. Third, the pointing-out of the nature of hearing also has two parts.

First, from "The Buddha said" onwards, he rebukes the deceptive confusion. Second, from "Ānanda" onwards, he correctly points it out. Within the first section on rebuking deceptive confusion, regarding the phrase "The Buddha said":
since the previous sections had already used the faculties and objects to guide him toward a definitive answer, he now rebukes his deceptive confusion. This is because...
To claim that sound and the report of hearing are indeterminate is merely evasive equivocation. The Buddha’s words are equal [in intent]. My intention was this:

when the subsequent sound has dissolved and there is no resonance, I asked whether there is sound; you said there is no sound—this is correct. When the preceding bell has ceased and there is no sound, I asked whether there is hearing;
you said there is no hearing—this is inverted. If, following the former state where there is neither sound nor hearing, the bell were struck again...

One should hear further: if one answers from the perspective of the subsequent sound whether there is hearing or no hearing, or whether there is non-hearing or no non-hearing, such a response lacks certainty;
is this not merely evasive speech? Therefore, it says, "The Buddha said," and so forth. Second, the actual pointing out [of the error] can be understood.
Third, the section on concluding the exhortation and citing examples is divided into two parts. First, the conclusion and exhortation: "Even you... and so forth. Second, the citation [of examples].

For example, it is like [the case of] heaviness and so forth. In the initial exhortation, the passage beginning with "You still... rebukes [the interlocutor] for not yet knowing that sound has coming and going while hearing is without arising or ceasing;
yet now, you are deluded by taking the sound-object, which has coming and going, to be the nature of hearing, which is without arising or ceasing.
How can you fail to wonder why you do not suspect the true and eternal cause to be subject to annihilation? Therefore, it says:

"You are still the same," and so forth. Second, the section on citing examples is divided into two parts. First, the example that the nature of hearing is not obscured within a dream, as in "even when heavy...
and so forth. Second, the example that the nature of hearing does not perish after death, as in "even if you... and so forth. The first part is easily understood. Regarding the second:
As for what was said regarding "even though you have such forms and such lives": the form is composed of the four great elements and is subject to decay; this is called the "dissolution of the form.

Although the life-force is maintained by the continuous connection of consciousness and mind, if consciousness departs even once, the life-force likewise dissolves along with it; this is called the "passing away of the radiance of life.
Even if these forms and lives of yours undergo dissolution and passing away, the nature of hearing remains inherently distinct from them.
Form and life are subject to dissolution and transition; therefore, it is said, "I grant you [this].

In this way, since the nature of hearing is truly constant and never severed or extinguished, one knows that seeing and the other faculties are likewise all truly constant and never severed or extinguished.
