The passage beginning with "Then Ānanda addressed the Buddha... is the section that resolves doubts regarding the nature of bondage and liberation. It is divided into two parts:

first, the doubt concerning the lack of intrinsic substance in bondage and liberation (corresponding to the section beginning with "Then Ānanda..."); second, the doubt concerning the dissolution of the six when the one is extinguished (corresponding to the section beginning with "At that time..."). The first part is as follows:
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the request based on doubt, which refers to Ānanda and others; second, the response and explanation, which begins with "At that time" and so forth.

The first part [the request] also has four sections: first, "Ānanda" and below, recounting what was previously taught; second, "The World-Honored One" and below, stating the present doubts; third, "I only pray" and below, formally requesting the resolution of the knots;
fourth, "Having made this" and below, waiting expectantly for the revelation. Regarding the first of these, the phrase "The Tathāgata" and so forth recounts the preceding [teachings].
In the second section on the definitive meaning, the Tathāgata said: "Observe how one who unties a knot does not see the knot itself;

how then can one know its untying? Thereupon, after clarifying the world and demonstrating the signs of the relative superiority and inferiority of the various meditative absorptions (*samādhi*), he instructed him to carefully discern which of these could serve as a fundamental basis for perfect penetration (*ekāyanamārga*) and to attain profound mastery in one gate.
"Entering. Upon entering into one [state] without delusion, those six faculties of cognition become pure all at once.
Although the Tathāgata has already made this statement and Ānanda already understands it, he fears that others may not yet know the origin from which the knots arise and how they are to be untied;
therefore, he restates what was said as a question, saying "The Tathāgata," etc. This is because of the root from which the knots were tied.
Regarding the questioner: this is Ānanda’s point of profound intent. Were it not for such profound intent, how could he have investigated the origin of his knots?

When discussing the origin of the knots, there are naturally two perspectives—distant and near. The distant refers to "delusion acting as the cause for luminous awareness, establishing objects based on that luminosity," and so forth.
The near refers to "within the wondrous perfection, the stillness becoming sticky, giving rise to vision," and so forth. Next, from within...
Regarding the phrase "from the beginningless limit," etc.: the death of a person is ignorance, and the birth of a person is also ignorance;
therefore, it is said that they both perish together and arise together. Regarding the phrase "even though one attains [recovery]," etc.:

just as a worldly case of malaria is well for one day and recurs again the next, Ānanda used this as a metaphor for how ignorance has, since time without beginning, both perished and arisen together. Even though one attains...
The much-hearing renunciant attains only a minor subduing [of defilements], which is like the days when a malarial fever is in remission.
Because the Dharma merely suppresses them while they still manifest, it is like the day the malarial fever recurs; thus it is said to be "like a tertian ague.
Regarding the three [periods] among these, the phrase "on this day" and so forth is a direct inquiry into the reason for their bondage and the method for their liberation. If...
To discuss the reason for bondage, it is as stated in the following passage: "When knowledge and vision establish knowledge, this is precisely the root of ignorance.
To discuss the method of liberation, it is as stated in the following passage: "When knowledge and vision are without seeing, this is precisely nirvana. These four points can be seen therein.

The second part, the section on the response and explanation, is divided into two. First, from "At that time" onwards, the manifestation of auspicious omens; second, from "Thereupon" onwards, the actual exposition.

Within the first section (the manifestation of omens), it may further be divided into three: first, from "At that time" downwards, the statement of the intent; second, from "With the Jambū" onwards, the display of the signs;

third, from "These various" onwards, the summary of the benefits. Regarding the first of these: it says, "For the sake of becoming a cause for transcending the world... [and so forth]. This serves as the introduction for what is to come.

Regarding the eye: since Ānanda has already inquired about the origin of the knots, as well as the simultaneous arising and ceasing of ignorance and so forth, along with the method for untying the knots, I now wish to elucidate this matter for him. If this matter were not clarified, it would remain so;
but once clarified, it will not only serve as an excellent cause for transcending the world, but can also act as the eye for all sentient beings. Next, he demonstrates:
Among these signs, the hand stroking Ānanda’s head is like the stroking of the crown of the head within *śamatha*, intended to shatter his attachments;
fearing he might be terrified, [the Buddha] comforts him. Now, by demonstrating this supreme and wondrous practice, he strokes his head again in order to urge him forward.
As for the sixfold earthquake, it symbolizes the shattering of the ignorance and afflictions of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) through the binding of them with correct understanding.

This is merely a textual point. As for the light from the *uṣṇīṣa* of the Buddhas of other directions returning to drench the Buddhas of this land, it serves to symbolize that they have equally realized the eternally abiding true mind and together manifested the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*.
Among the three benefits of the conclusion, these great assemblies attained what they had never experienced before;
for these great assemblies were about to practice this path—that which is yet unrealized by those who possess the eternally abiding true mind.
It should be realized. That which has never been manifested within the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha should now be manifested; therefore, it is said that "something unprecedented has been attained.
Part Two: The Section on the Formal Exposition. This is divided into two: first, the simultaneous proclamation by all Buddhas, beginning with "At that time...

and so forth; second, the personal teaching of Śākyamuni, beginning with "Ānanda... and so forth. Within the first section, regarding the address to Ānanda as "Excellent," this is because in the world...
Sentient beings do not yet know that there is birth and death; how could they know that there is ignorance? They do not yet know that the six sense faculties have knots;

how could they know that the six sense faculties have liberation? They do not yet know that their present body and mind are transmigrating through the three realms of existence and desire to escape them;
how could they know that future sentient beings will fall into the six paths and desire to deliver them? Now, A...
The question does not merely concern knowing the fruit of suffering in birth and death; it further concerns knowing the cause of suffering, which is ignorance.
It does not merely concern knowing that the six sense faculties possess knots; it further concerns knowing that the six sense faculties are themselves the resolution [of those knots].

It does not merely concern knowing the present body and mind transmigrating through the three realms of existence; it further concerns knowing the fullness and decline of sentient beings in the future.
The six realms of existence constitute the question. For this reason, the Tathāgatas of the ten directions raised their voices in unison and exclaimed, "Excellent!
Regarding the phrase "If you wish to know," although there are many underlying meanings within Ānanda’s inquiry, generally speaking, they concern only transmigration and non-transmigration;
thus it says, "If you wish to know," and so forth. The meaning is that that which causes you to transmigrate through birth and death is nothing other than [the mind itself].
It is precisely these six sense faculties. Because they grasp at the six objects through these six faculties, they give rise to both discrimination and craving;
consequently, they shift and flow from moment to moment, such that there is never a time for liberation, leading ultimately to sinking into the cycle of birth and death.
Furthermore, as for that which enables you to swiftly realize wondrous permanence, there is no other thing than these very six sense faculties.
If one can thoroughly understand that the six sense organs arise as inherently false and illusory, one will certainly not engage in discrimination toward them, nor will one harbor craving for them.
When the "adhesion" can be detached and the "roots" can be uprooted, the interaction between the faculties and their objects will vanish, and one will swiftly attain purity;
thus, the four virtues of Nirvana will spontaneously manifest before one. Therefore, it is said: "If you desire... and so forth.

The second part, "Śākyamuni’s Personal Explanation," also has two sections. First, from "Ānanda asked again" downward, is the restatement of the inquiry. Second, from "The Buddha said" downward, is the formal explanation of the answer.

Within the first section, regarding the phrase "Although he heard... and so forth: because he heard that the root of the fetters of birth and death is these six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), and that blissful, wondrous permanence is also these six sense organs, his intention was that the root of the fetters of birth and death is exclusively these six sense organs. Thus...

This can be understood. As for the claim that "blissful, wondrous, and eternal" refers to the six sense organs, I do not know it to be so; therefore, it is said that the mind has not yet attained clarity.

Regarding the phrase "I bow my head," the intention is this: I have often heard the Tathāgata say that it is impossible to seek the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction by means of the causes of arising and extinction.
Now, the six sense organs are the causes of arising and extinction, whereas the wondrous eternity is the fruit of non-arising and non-extinction.
It is so. Yet it is clear that it is precisely these six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), and nothing else, that cause me to wander through birth and death (*saṃsāra*).

If it is these same six sense faculties, and nothing else, that allow for the swift realization of blissful, wondrous, and eternal [nirvāṇa], then why do they likewise cause me to wander through birth and death?
How is it that these six sense faculties can swiftly lead to the realization of bliss, yet also cause me to wander through birth and death? Thus it is.
"My mind is truly difficult to clarify. Although the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have spoken thus, I only pray that our Buddha will provide an exposition for me.
Thus, he prostrated himself and addressed the Buddha (and so forth).

The second part, the response and explanation, is divided into two sections: the prose and the verse. The prose section is further divided into three parts: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the subject is introduced;
second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the meaning is established through explanation; third, from "Therefore" onwards, the conclusion is presented.

Within the first section, the introduction, although there are the three factors of sense organ, object, and consciousness, since Ānanda has already heard the Buddhas of the ten directions state that birth-and-death and wondrous permanence are both equally the six [sense bases],...
Taking the "roots" (*indriya*) as the point of inquiry, one knows that although there are three answers, the emphasis lies solely on the roots.

For this reason, while the presentation lists three explanations, there are only two conclusions and a single summary. If one were to view these three types in contrast with the question, they would likely not correspond;
for although the characteristics of the roots and objects (*viṣaya*) exist, they are all falsely conceived as perceptions from within the wondrously pure, luminous essence.

Because they are manifested by clarity, they are said to share a common source. Although there is bondage and liberation, because they are fundamentally manifestations of the *tathāgatagarbha* nature, they are said to be non-dual.
If one follows along with the sense organs and their objects, one undergoes transmigration, which constitutes bondage—this is what is meant by "chasing delusion with further delusion.
If one can thoroughly comprehend this and flow against the current, that constitutes liberation.
This is what is meant by returning the delusive to the true. In this state, what roots are there? What objects are there?

Roots and objects are, in their entirety, the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence. What bondage is there? What liberation is there? Bondage and liberation are nothing other than the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Therefore, they are said to share the same source and are non-dual. Since the root that is capable of perceiving and the object that is perceived share the same source, they are not...
Second: Thus, that which causes consciousness to arise does so by means of the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*).

Since the capacity of these faculties and objects to produce [consciousness] is fundamentally illusory, the nature of consciousness that arises from them is likewise illusory. To clarify this through a metaphor: it is like flowers appearing in the sky.
How could there be flowers in the sky? They are produced by staring with fixed eyes; yet, in the originally clear and bright sky, what flowers are there at all?

It is so. The capacity of the faculties (*indriya*) and objects (*viṣaya*) to produce [consciousness] is like staring fixedly with one's eyes; the nature of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*) that arises from them is like flowers in the sky (*ākāśa-puṣpa*).

Since the faculties and objects of one who stares fixedly cannot even be found, how could the nature of consciousness, which is like flowers in the sky, be real? Therefore, it is said that "the nature of consciousness is such.
Thus, not only is the nature of consciousness false and illusory, but the faculties and objects are likewise false and illusory. This is the second explanation.
In the section on "Formation," the text correctly explains that both the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are equally illusory.

That which causes them to be illusory is none other than this: external objects adhere to the profound stillness (*zhan*) and thereby activate the sense organs; this corresponds to what was previously described as "the gathering of conditions causing internal agitation.

Furthermore, the internal organs pursue delusion and reflect upon the objects; this corresponds to what was previously described as "rushing outward toward external things. This is what is meant by the so-called "delusive objects leading [the mind]."
The deluded mind. Because the deluded mind pursues deluded objects, it is said that "it arises from the dust," and so forth.
Thus, the characteristics of the dust as they are perceived cannot be taken as true characteristics; for they exist entirely through delusion and fundamentally lack inherent nature.

Likewise, the faculty of seeing which perceives them cannot be taken as true seeing; for it exists entirely through delusion and fundamentally lacks inherent nature. Therefore, it is said: "characteristics and seeing."

There is no intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If one were to clarify this through a metaphor, it is like two bundles of reeds leaning against each other; both lack self-nature. Therefore, it is said they are "like two bundles of reeds.
Since they are just like two bundles of reeds, how could they possess an intrinsic nature? Thus, both the sense faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are empty and false.

Regarding the third section, which summarizes the middle [truth], the two characters "you now" (*rǔ jīn*) should be construed with the following phrase "cognition and vision" (*zhì jiàn*), and should first...
He said: "Since both the faculties (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are devoid of intrinsic nature and are like intertwined reeds,
when one investigates on this basis, one knows that if you now employ the six faculties— such as cognition and vision— to cognize and see the six objects— such as forms and sounds—
and are thus led astray by them moment after moment, with mind following upon mind, this is entirely the manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*)."

Therefore, it is said: "You now," and so forth. Furthermore, it is known that if you do not take the six faculties—such as cognition and vision—as the agents of knowing and seeing, they will naturally not pursue the six objects—such as form and sound. Hence it is said: "Cognition and vision have no seeing.

Thus, the faculties fundamentally do not intersect with the objects, and the objects likewise do not contact the faculties. Subject and object are not established; faculty and object are beyond mutual dependence. It is solely this...
The true essence of Nirvana is neither born nor extinguished; therefore, it is said that "this is precisely [so]," and so forth. Thus one should know:
the reason ignorance is called ignorance is not because it is some distinct entity other than this; it is simply that within a single cognition and vision, the act of establishing cognition occurs.

Likewise, the reason Nirvana is called Nirvana is not because it is some entity other than this; it is simply that within a single cognition and vision, the absence of such vision occurs. This is why...
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions spoke to you in unison, saying: "The root of birth and death is none other than your six sense faculties; it is not any other thing.

Peaceful bliss, wondrous permanence, is likewise none other than your six sense faculties; it is not any other thing. I also say that these are all equally your six sense faculties and are fundamentally not any other thing.
That which is called the 'wild mind,' if it comes to rest—that rest is itself Bodhi. How could there be any other thing permitted to exist?"

And yet, why does he harbor doubt? Thus, it is said: "What is this? In this way, not only are the doubts of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions dispelled, but Ānanda’s own doubt regarding the binding and untying of the knots becomes even clearer.

There are two types of verse (gāthā). There are four reasons for the existence of verse: first, the literary form of the treatise; second, suitability for the capacities of the audience; third, to accommodate those who delight in poetry;

and fourth, because [the meaning] has not yet been heard. Regarding the literary form of the treatise: the literary convention of this land is to first narrate the facts through prose and subsequently inscribe their significance through verse.
The Tathāgata’s preaching of the sūtras follows the same pattern; therefore, there is first the long prose exposition (vṛttaka) and subsequently the repeated verse (geya).

Regarding "according to the capacities and circumstances": sentient beings of sharp faculties can comprehend even that which is elaborate and extensive, whereas sentient beings of dull faculties can only understand that which is concise and brief.
Since there are two types of faculties for those who are the objects of the teaching, there are likewise two modes of exposition for those who provide the teaching;
therefore, the prose section comes first, followed by the repeated verses. Regarding "to suit their inclinations," this refers to the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma.
There are prose passages and verses, like flowers that are either strung together or scattered. Some prefer scattered flowers, while others delight in strung flowers;
therefore, both prose and verse are provided to accommodate these various inclinations.
As for those who have not yet heard [the teachings], the audience at the Tathāgata’s Dharma assemblies is vast. As for those who have already gathered...

I have heard this in the prose section. If there are those who arrive later, it shall be explained for them again in verse. Although there may be a sequence of before and after regarding their arrival at the assembly, there is no one who is not reached by the Dharma.
These four types have been briefly stated as such. As for a detailed explanation, it is fully contained in the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra).
The text can be divided into two parts: from "At that time" onwards, the scribe records the introductory narrative; from "True nature" onwards, the Tathāgata’s formal teaching begins.

The Verses (*gāthā*). There are two types of verses: the first is called *geya* (corresponding verses), which are spoken in correspondence with the prose (*prose-verse*); these include [the sections on] True Nature (*tathatā*) and so forth.

The second is called *udāna* (independent verses), which are composed to provide specific illumination; these include [the sections on] Untying the Knots (*granthi-vimocana*) and so forth. This, too, is a general classification.

If one examines this in detail, it all amounts to a single point. The section on Verses (Geya) is divided into three parts: the verses that introduce the prose, those that provide the explanation, and those that conclude by revealing the meaning.
Regarding the first part, the single line beginning with "The True Nature" introduces the topic. The second part, the half-line beginning with "Words are false," provides the explanation.
The third part, the half-line beginning with "Concluding the explanation," concludes by revealing the meaning. Within the first of these, the term "True Nature" refers to the Tathāgatagarbha.

The "Mind" refers to the wondrous nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*). "Conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta*) refers to the mind, its perceptions, and the dharmas such as the five aggregates (*skandha*), the three categories (*dhātu*), and the seven elements (*mahābhūta*), because they exist through volitional construction.
"Empty" means that although these dharmas exist due to volitional construction, they are nonetheless entirely false and illusory in relation to the True Nature;
therefore, it is said: "The True Nature is empty of conditioned phenomena. Regarding the single [verse on] dependent origination:
This passage explains the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-śūnyatā*). Why are conditioned phenomena ultimately empty?

It is because they arise in total dependence upon the false conjunction of causes and conditions, and they perish in false separation from those causes and conditions. Since they are born of conditions, they are likewise extinguished by conditions.
It is just as a great master of illusion, using illusory arts and magical elixirs, conjures forth all manner of men, women, oxen, and horses.
Therefore, it is said that because they arise through conditions, they are like illusions. Because they are like illusions, it is said that conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) are empty.
Regarding "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*) below: this turns to reveal the unconditioned. Having clarified that within true nature (*tathatā*), conditioned phenomena are empty, as for the unconditioned—
How so? If one investigates it from the perspective of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), it does not arise or cease in the same manner as the arising and ceasing of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*).
Therefore, it is said that the unconditioned has no arising or ceasing. Yet, although it has no arising or ceasing, it is established entirely in dependence upon the conditioned as its counterpart.
Since the conditioned is illusory and false, the unconditioned is likewise illusory and false; hence, it is said to be "not real. To clarify this by means of a metaphor:
They are alike to empty flowers. Space is fundamentally without flowers; flowers exist because of cataracts in the eye.

Now, the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is fundamentally non-existent, yet it exists only through its opposition to the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*), just like flowers in space. Therefore, the dharma and the metaphor coincide in saying that they are unreal, like flowers in space.

If this is so, the two characters "true nature" (*tathatā*) should be read as connecting with the phrase concerning the unconditioned. Thus, one understands the three categories of mind, views, and phenomena.
The seven elements all reside within true nature. Therefore, the Extended Discourse states that the sense organs and their objects share the same source.
Furthermore, knowing that the conditioned is bondage and the unconditioned is liberation also pertains to true nature; thus, the Extended Discourse says that bondage and liberation are non-dual.
Moreover, since the mind, the views, the three aggregates, and the seven elements are all empty and like illusions, then the conscious mind itself must naturally be false and illusory.

Therefore, the long discourse states that the nature of consciousness is false and illusory. Furthermore, since even the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is unreal—like flowers in the sky—it is clearly understood that the roots, objects, and consciousnesses of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) must likewise be like flowers in the sky. Thus, the long discourse says they are "just like flowers in the sky.
The summary in verse has been completed. Next, regarding the middle section, the phrase "words are false" and so forth intends to mean that the conditioned is false, while the unconditioned is true.
Furthermore, that conditioned phenomena are like illusions and unconditioned phenomena are like flowers in the sky is for no other reason than this:

the true essence of the unconditioned is fundamentally non-existent and is manifested through the delusion of the conditioned. Since the conditioned delusion that manifests it is inherently false, the unconditioned truth that is manifested is likewise false.
Although there is a distinction between the conditioned and the unconditioned, their falsity is identical. Therefore, it is said that "delusion is equal [to the truth]," and so forth. As for...
This means that if a phenomenon is established through dependence, that phenomenon itself becomes dependent.

In this way, even the false cannot be considered false, and the true cannot be considered true. How, then, could there be a faculty of sight or an object seen? Therefore, it is said: "It is still not... and so forth.
The nature of consciousness arises from the faculties and their objects; now that both the faculties and their objects are absent, how [could consciousness exist]?
If you were to obtain a middle point from which your consciousness-mind arises, then the nature of consciousness would likewise be unobtainable;
therefore, it is said that the middle has no real nature. Thus, the three—sense organ, object, and consciousness—are all illusory, and are therefore likened to entwined reeds.

There are two meanings to "entwined reeds": first, they exist in mutual dependence; second, their interiors are empty and lack substance. Now, because of the object there is the sense organ, and because of...
The faculties (*indriya*), objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) are like the mutual dependence of two reeds in a sheaf;

these three are entirely illusory, like the hollow space within those reeds. Herein, if even the first line—which speaks of "reality"—is still illusory, then the nature of the faculties and objects goes without saying.
The second line of the verse corresponds to the two lines of the prose commentary concerning the objects; the following two lines correspond to the prose commentary on the mutual perception of forms.
These are two lines. Thus we know that although the prose section mentions only the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*), it also implicitly includes consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Regarding the third point, "binding and liberation," etc., this verse formally summarizes the manifestation of binding while also answering Ānanda’s question regarding the meaning of how there is binding and from what it is called liberation.
The intent is as follows: when you ask, "What is binding? in my view, it is simply a single thought-moment of non-awakening that arises.

If one understands that [the cycle of] birth and death enters into every thought-moment through cognition and vision, then one knows that the cause is not far off; it is simply the six sense faculties.

These constitute the fetters. As for your question regarding what is meant by "liberation," from my perspective, if one attains thorough realization in a single thought-moment, one then turns against the current of birth and death to achieve unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. One also knows that the cause is not far off; it is simply the six sense faculties. This is it.
I shall explain this for you. Thus, there is no separate entity that constitutes bondage; it is simply the six sense faculties. There is no separate entity that constitutes liberation;
it is also simply the six sense faculties. Although bondage and liberation differ, the six sense faculties are the same. Therefore, it is said that "bondage and liberation share the same cause.
From the perspective of liberation, one is called a sage; from the perspective of bondage, one is called an ordinary person.

Since the binding and the unbinding are identical, that which makes an ordinary person ordinary arises from the six sense organs, and that which makes a sage a sage likewise arises from the six sense organs.
Thus it is said: "There are no two paths for sages and ordinary people. Yet, how exactly are they identical? How is it that there are no two paths?
Observe the nature within the intersection, and you will know. Therefore it is said: "Observe this... [and so forth]. This refers to consciousness.
This refers to the nature of consciousness; that is, the eighth consciousness. "Interacting" (*jiao*) carries the meaning of reeds leaning against one another.

The phrase regarding emptiness and existence precisely clarifies the reason for this interactive nature: if it were devoid of objects, it would be non-existent, which constitutes emptiness; if it conditions objects, it exists, which constitutes existence.

All of these are merely superficial. To point directly at it: as mentioned above, the truth of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) cannot be taken as the ultimate truth, nor can the delusion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) be taken as not being the truth.
Both the emptiness of the unconditioned and the existence of the conditioned are discarded;
therefore, it is said that both emptiness and existence are neither. Although this nature of their intersection is the entire substance of the eight consciousnesses, it is the Tathāgata.
Regarding the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, both existence and non-existence are equally unattainable.

Furthermore, since the "mutually supporting reeds" represent the eighth consciousness—specifically the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-ghana*) which exists through the conjunction of the fundamental luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*) and ignorance—then both the emptiness of true ignorance and the existence of the deluded essence of consciousness are unattainable within the wondrously pure and luminous substance. Within the second [section], the two lines beginning with "this root" first empty the faculties and their objects; therefore...

It is said that there is emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā*). "Emptiness of persons" is synonymous with "emptiness of self" (*ātma-śūnyatā*). "Person" refers to a conventional designation (*prajñapti*), while "self" is a term for a sovereign controller.
If one can dissolve the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), such that no conventional designation can be found, how could there be a self as a sovereign controller?

Therefore, the emptiness of persons is the emptiness of self. The two phrases concerning "emptiness" refer to the contemplative wisdom that is able to empty—that is, the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

The two phrases concerning "liberation" refer to the truth-principle revealed by that emptiness. Furthermore, since that which is emptied by emptiness is further negated, it is said that "both are empty and non-arising.
The following section concludes with the name [of the samādhi]. This *samādhi* is capable of attaining...
This is the practice of [the Bodhisattva’s] conduct. It is the principle attained through the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
As for the characteristics of emptiness realized by those such as Aṅgulimāla and Ājñātakauṇḍinya prior to this, they are already clearly distinguished herein.

If one were to cite the passage from the "Perfect Penetration of the Ear Organ" regarding "that which enters having already become still," and so forth, to harmonize it with this, it is fully explained therein; by examining it according to that, it becomes evident. The above concludes the discussion on the binding of the cloth.

By demonstrating the delusion through the loosening of the headcloth and revealing the awakening through successive clarifications, Ānanda’s doubt regarding "the six being resolved and the one perishing" should naturally be dispelled.
Second, from the passage beginning with "Ānanda and the great assembly," [the Buddha] specifically points to the fundamental basis of perfect penetration to answer the initial inquiry.
This is the literary style [of the text]. Thus, when the Tathāgata questioned the assembly of sages, they all replied in general terms:

"From what expedient means did you first resolve to attain enlightenment and enter samādhi? This is divided into five parts. First is the inquiry and request based on the occasion, namely from "Ānanda and the others" up to that point.
Second is the universal proclamation by the Tathāgata, namely from "At that time, the World-Honored One" up to that point. Third is the individual accounts of the sages, namely...
1. Kauṇḍinya departs; 2. The four [disciples] manifest the seal of approval; 3. At that moment, the World-Honored One departs; 4. Mañjuśrī selects and chooses; 5. At that time, the Tathāgata departs.
(The two texts, numbers four and five, are found in Volume Six. Furthermore, there are three parts at the beginning: First, from "Ānanda" downward, both delusion and awakening are presented together;
Second, from "the World-Honored One" downward, the monastic and the lay request [instruction] together; Third, from "I only pray" downward, the request for the profound mystery is concluded.
Regarding the phrase "Bestowing. At the beginning. Wisdom-awakening is perfectly penetrating": some point to the three methods previously mentioned, such as *śamatha* and so forth;
others point to the passage in the old text concerning the "six dissolutions and the single disappearance.

If one examines this text according to its true meaning, pointing to the three methods such as *śamatha* is vague and inappropriate, superficial and irrelevant. Pointing to the "six dissolutions and the single disappearance" is likewise narrow...
"Not extensive" means it is restricted and not universal. There are necessarily two intended meanings for [the desire to be] "perfectly fitting and secure.

First, it refers to the passage in the "First Determination" concerning whether the mind of the causal stage and the awakening of the fruition stage are the same or different; hence, it says "wisdom-awakening" (*hui-jue*).
Second, it refers to the "Second Determination," which asks who possesses perfect penetration and who does not, as well as the attainment of following... [the text continues].

Regarding the passage on "perfect penetration" (*yuantong*) and "non-perfect penetration" (*buyuantong*), which states that they differ by factors of ten and hundred million, it is therefore called "perfect penetration.
Because the preceding two meanings were explained in a general sense, whereas from this point onward is the specific indication, he presents it at the very beginning of his inquiry and request.
In this way, it is not only fitting but also secure and appropriate; those who attain freedom from doubt will, in the [first]...
Within the first meaning of the awakening to wisdom, one examines the five aggregates to discern the root of birth and death;

based on the nature that is unborn, undying, perfect, and profound, one takes the awakening to ignorance as the fundamental mind of the stage of perfection. Thereafter, the cultivation and realization of the stage of perfection are fully accomplished—all of which has already been clarified.
Within the second meaning of perfect penetration, one examines the six sense faculties to scrutinize the root of afflictions and select one.

Regarding the six sense faculties that can be entered, one enters deeply through a single gate. Once one has entered without delusion, those six organs of cognition are simultaneously purified and all become clearly understood.
This also resolves the doubt concerning how entering one leads to the purification of all six, as well as the doubt regarding the apparent lack of correspondence between cause and effect.
Regarding the doubt as to how the fetters are untied, there is nothing that is not repeatedly resolved and explained; thus it is said, "wisdom-awakening and so forth.

As for "I and others," this means that by attaining the perfect penetration of wisdom-awakening, one becomes free from doubt. Speaking of the body, by distancing oneself from the root of birth and death, the Dharma-body may increase;
speaking of the mind, by distancing oneself from the root of affliction, the life of wisdom may be prolonged. Therefore...

This refers to the equality of body and mind. These all describe awakening. Although the following section describes delusion, the subsequent middle portion uses the phrase "our kind" as a conventional request.

Ānanda speaks for himself, saying that because the wind of objective realms blows upon and stirs the waves of consciousness, he has drifted like a tumbleweed through the five paths and withered away within the three realms of existence;
from this point on, he has had no Greatly Awakened parents to rely upon as his refuge.
One cannot avoid being alone. Without the compassionate protection of those with whom one shares a karmic affinity, one cannot avoid being exposed.
Not only have we been adrift for many kalpas, but we have also been solitary and exposed for many kalpas; thus it is said, "We, this generation. Such a state is utterly base and inferior.
Within this condition, one cannot conceive of it in the mind, nor can one find any way to deliberate upon it. Little do we realize what [this truly is].
By virtue of these causes and conditions, I have been humbled by the honor of being included among the celestial kin of the Tathāgata. Thus it is said: "How is the mind equal?
As for "celestial kin" (*tiantun*): such as sovereign and subject, husband and wife, and so forth, all arise from human union and are thus called "human relations" (*renlun*).

The order of siblings, however, is formed spontaneously by nature and is thus called "celestial kin. Yet, having drifted through accumulated kalpas, I am like an infant who has lost its mother's milk.

There is no difference. Furthermore, since the Buddha is of the same class as the heavenly beings, if he were suddenly to encounter his compassionate mother, it would be no different [from ordinary affection].

Thus, having already attained the Great Enlightenment, his parents have likewise received his unconditional compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*). He shall no longer undergo further wandering or experience being orphaned and destitute;

his Dharma-body attains longevity and his life-force is sustained. Therefore, it is said that it is "like losing one's milk," and so forth. The passage beginning with "If again... requests the Dharma below.

Compared with the past, the present is truly a time of profound favor. If, furthermore, one can achieve the fruit of unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment through this opportune meeting, the gratitude felt in one's heart will be no small matter. Thus it is said, "Furthermore, by means of... and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the secret mantras and so forth that have been attained": "secret mantras" refers to the two certainties because they appear later; "original awakening" refers to *śamatha* and so forth because they appear earlier.
Ānanda’s intention was this: "The Tathāgata has answered me regarding the dharmas of *śamatha* and so forth, revealing them repeatedly and instructing me one by one.
I have already awakened to this nature of the treasury (*tathāgatagarbha*), yet the method for its cultivation has not [yet been explained]."
[He replied: "I have attained it. However, there is no way to enter into its realization. Therefore, I request that you grant me a magnificent mansion, for one must enter through a gate.

Thereupon, the Tathāgata first showed him the First Determination: to carefully discern the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) as the root of birth-and-death, and to realize the ground of the fruit of non-arising-extinction by relying on the cause-mind of non-arising-extinction. Next, he showed him the Second Determination: to carefully observe the six [sense bases].

The faculties (*indriya*) and afflictions (*kleśa*) are the root of birth and death (*saṃsāra*). By selecting one [faculty] through which entry is possible, one makes it a single gate and enters deeply, attaining purification all at once.
One should contemplate this deeply with the mind: that it is no different and no distinct from the *tathāgatagarbha* realized within my own *śamatha* and other [practices].
Therefore, it is said that "that which is attained is equal," and so forth. Thus, the two phrases reiterate that "that which is attained is equal," and so forth. [This is what is meant by] "hearing."
Although awakenings differ, the nature of the *dharmadhātu* (the treasury-nature) is one and the same. Only in this way can one see the intent behind Ānanda’s request.
Regarding the three [aspects], the phrase "only grant [me] equality" means that although the Tathāgata has demonstrated the two definitive meanings, I, Ānanda, have only understood their principles;
I have still not yet attained the methods for cultivation. I pray that you will extend your unconditional great compassion and further instruct me.
"Secret and Sublime Adornment": this causes me not only to understand the principle, but to further advance in practice; only then is it the final teaching of the *Śūraṅgama*.
Thus, he says "please grant," and so forth. It is called "final" because it first clarifies the principle of *śamatha* and the rest as the foundation.

Next, regarding the sequence of his own request, it follows the others. Furthermore, within the request itself, it first provides a general clarification of the two definitive meanings, and secondly, it specifically points to the fundamental basis of perfect penetration as the conclusion.
Thus, one knows that the fundamental basis of perfect penetration is the "final of the finals" within the latter section.
Since he now makes this specific request, it is called the "last. Moreover, it is not merely the last part of a single sutra; there are those who rely on this point [to argue for its significance].

To claim that this sutra follows after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is truly laughable. Regarding the phrase "retreating to conceal his secret capacity" and so forth, the meaning is that this practice can certainly not be entered through a distracted mind, nor can it be received through explicit teaching;
therefore, one quiets the faculties and withdraws the thoughts, hoping for the Tathāgata’s silent transmission of the Dharma.

Regarding the second section, "The Tathāgatas’ Universal Announcement," the phrase "universal announcement" means that the Tathāgata already knew Ānanda’s intention to transmit the teaching through silent inspiration.

He then reflected that this practice was by no means a minor matter; rather, it is what has been taught by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and what has been cultivated by the Bodhisattvas of the three periods of time.
In the Tathāgata’s teaching, there is nothing to be taught, yet he speaks of what the Bodhisattvas cultivate; as for the Bodhisattvas’ cultivation, there is... [nothing].
That which is practiced is what has been taught by the Tathāgata; it is precisely for each person to hear and for each individual to comprehend.
How could one receive transmission in the darkness? It is seen that this is proclaimed universally to the great assembly.

As for why a Bodhisattva is called "Great," it is because they are able to understand the ultimate, steadfast principle, initiate ultimate, steadfast practice, and realize the ultimate, steadfast fruit. [Leakage]

Regarding those who have attained the state of a Great Arhat: speaking in general terms, because they do not fall into the outflows of views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) as a cause, they do not fall into the *paricchinna-bhava* (segmented existence) as a result.

However, according to the inner secret and outer manifestation of turning from the Small toward the Great, as a cause they will not fall into ignorance (*avidyā*), and as a result they will not fall into the *parināma-vaśika-bhava* (transformative existence). As for the Arhats and others mentioned below, and concerning their initial attainment:
This is the reason for the term "no-more-learning" (aśaikṣa). Furthermore, it need not be discussed solely in terms of the hidden and the manifest.

Thus, we know that an Arhat is considered "one beyond learning" because their afflictions of views and thoughts are exhausted and they have fully realized the principle of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).

As for Bodhisattvas from the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward, who partially shatter ignorance and partially realize the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), they may also be said to have partially attained no-more-learning. To be born within my Dharma is what is meant by—

"Born from the Buddha’s mouth, born through transformation by the Dharma. Question: Since there are twenty-five sages mentioned in the subsequent text, why does this section speak of only the eighteen *dhātus*?
Answer: Because the eighteen *dhātus* encompass the seven great elements. The five great elements, such as earth and so forth, are subsumed within the six objects (*viṣaya*).
The "great element of seeing" is the faculty (*indriya*) and is thus subsumed within the six faculties. The "great element of consciousness" is consciousness itself.
They are subsumed within the six consciousnesses; therefore, they are called "elements" (*dhātu*) and not "great elements.
Third, from the time of Kauṇḍinya onwards, there are the various texts in which the sages each set forth their experiences.

Some maintain that this sutra was already revealed and clarified after the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, and thus the twenty-five sages' realizations of perfect penetration are directly explained as the Perfect and Sudden teaching. Furthermore...

Some claim that since the Tathāgata previously stated that the three categories and seven elements are all the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, and the twenty-five sages relied upon this to cultivate and realize the nature of the garbha, then once the nature of the garbha is realized, it must also be explained according to the Perfect and Sudden teaching. This is not the case.

One fails to realize that this sutra is definitively situated within the Vaipulya (Vaipulya) period; it discusses all four teachings simultaneously and universally benefits all capacities. Originally...
There is only a difference in the meanings of "great" versus "small," and "partial" versus "complete. That [teaching] is not this one; this does not see that one.
To weigh them against each other, they are as far apart as heaven and earth. How could one simply explain them away by categorizing them as "sudden and complete"?

Furthermore, regarding the twenty-five sages, when the Tathāgata questioned them, asking, "Who was the first to resolve their mind? Who attained perfect penetration? By what means did you succeed? they each presented their own accounts.
What was previously cultivated and realized is as follows. This is, for example, like Vimalakīrti’s recounting of his past reprimands of Mañjuśrī;

although the teaching is given in the present, the events occurred in the past. How could he, because of this, be made to explain the *tathāgatagarbha* (storehouse nature) based on it as a practice and realization?
Now, I shall provide an explanation according to the great through the great, according to the small through the small, and according to the partial or gradual through the partial and gradual.

Commentary: Following the approach of the Perfect and Sudden (yuantun), this is explained according to the Perfect and Sudden. In this way, we ensure that the dialogue between teacher and disciple is not lost, nor do we deviate from the sequential order of the periods and flavors (shiwwei).
It is divided into five major sections: first, the six objects (liuchen); second, the five faculties (wugen); third, the six consciousnesses (liushi).
The four [elements] and the seven [bases] constitute the Great [Elements].
The fifth is the faculty of hearing. The first six are the objects; these six each have their own causes and conditions for being established as categories for awakening and for answering questions.

These are pointed out according to the text, so their sequence and limits can be seen. Regarding the order of the six objects, *niṣadyā* (seated posture) should come first; yet here, *śabda* (sound), as in the case of Cunda, is placed first.
There are three reasons why the faculty of mind (*manas*) is placed first. First, it is because in the Sahā world, the Buddha’s work is carried out through sound.
Second, it is because when the Wheel of Dharma was first turned, Ājñātakauṇḍinya was the very first to attain realization.

As for the third, the faculty of hearing (*śrotra*) is the perfect penetration (*vibhūti-saṃpanna*) for this region and serves as the primary expedient means here. Hearing does not arise spontaneously; names exist because of sound. Therefore, sound is placed at the beginning.
This is intended precisely to clarify that what is cultivated in the Universal Gate is indeed appropriate. First, regarding Kāśyapa’s contemplation within the sensory object of sound:
"Kāśyapa" refers to the causal basis; "at the Buddha's [feet]" refers to the moment of awakening; and "the Buddha asked... concludes with the response.

Regarding the first section, the two lines beginning with "I was" indicate the place where the Tathāgata preached the Dharma, as well as the location where Kāśyapa practiced the Path. Regarding the second section:

"Regarding 'the Buddha and so forth,' this refers to the turning of the Wheel of the Four Noble Truths. 'The Buddha’s questioning and so forth' means that after the Buddha had turned the wheel three times, he asked, 'Do you understand?
Do you know? Cunda replied, 'I have known; I have understood. Thus it is said, 'the Buddha’s questioning and so forth.
'Sealing my name as Ājñāta' means 'the first to understand'; this is to assign a name according to its actual reality. Below...
To understand this by way of analogy: "The wondrous sound is secretly perfect" (*miao-yin mi-yuan*) cannot be explained merely as the emptiness of the nature of sound.

Rather, it refers to when Cūḍapanthaka had already awakened to the Four Truths and realized the limited truth (*pratyekabuddha-satya*); he thoroughly understood that the sensory object of sound, when analyzed through the fourfold logical examination (*catuskoṭi*), could not be apprehended, and thus it was called "the wondrous sound is secretly perfect.
Regarding the phrase "Among the three, the Buddha asks," etc.: the Tathāgata asked me, "Who is perfect? (referring to the perfect penetration).
"Through what expedient means did you attain penetration? I observed sound as the perfect penetration; thus, I took sound as my expedient means.

This refers to the passage beginning with "The Buddha asked," and so forth. Below, the conclusion of the answer follows the pattern of identifying what was observed as either the perfect penetration or the expedient means, which can be understood by analogy.

Second, among the observation of the sense-object of form (*rūpa*), within the section on Upāli... [the character] *yin* (因) denotes the cause or reason. "Observing... [the character] *xia* (下) indicates the opening of the section.

This is the realization. The section beginning with "The Buddha asked" provides the concluding answer. Regarding the first point: "I also" is stated in response to what was previously said by Cūḍapanthaka.

Regarding the second point: "Contemplating impurity" generally refers to instructing those with lustful desires to contemplate impurity; this is what is known as the "impurity contemplation" for sentient beings with excessive greed.
There are five types of impurity: namely, the place of birth, the seed, the characteristic, the nature, and the ultimate.

The meaning is fully elucidated in the *Jizhu* (Collected Commentaries) and the *Fuxing* (Supplementary Practice). Here, "impurity" (*aśubha*) is the object of contemplation, namely the seeds and so forth.
"Contemplation" (*vipaśyanā*) is the subject of contemplation. It is not only the five [aspects] such as the place of birth that are impure;

one contemplates the internal body, the external body, and the internal-external body, all of which arise from impure karma. Thus, one gives rise to great revulsion and detachment. One awakens to all...
"Et cetera" (*ādi*): First, one realizes that this body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) is originally formed from the semen and blood of one's parents;
all its seeds of birth, up to its ultimate end, are impure. This is stated with respect to that which is produced.
As for the four great elements such as earth and so forth, they are the producers themselves; when one investigates them further, they too are impure. Therefore, it says "realizes."

These are the various stages of equality. The "white bones" and "subtle dust" constitute the six gates of contemplation. First, one contemplates impurity; second, one contemplates white bones; third, one contemplates subtle dust.

Although there are three names, they collectively belong to the contemplation of impurity (*aśubha-bhāvanā*). Subtle dust returns to empty space; this is the contemplation that analyzes form (*rūpa*) to its limit.
When both emptiness and form are non-existent, and both emptiness and form have perished, neither can be apprehended. This is the third, the Contemplation of Fragrance-Adornment (*Gandharva-vyūha*).

Regarding the observation of the fragrance-object (*gandha-viṣaya*): "The Rigor of Fragrance" (*Gandharva*) refers to the causal basis; "At that time" and following explain his awakening; "The Buddha asked" and following concludes the response.

In the first part, regarding the address "Fragrance-Rigor Youth" (*Gandharva-kumāra*): this does not mean he was actually a youth, but rather that he was adorned by wondrous fragrances and dwelt in the stage of true youth (*kumārabhūmi*).
"All conditioned phenomena" (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) refers to the objects of observation; that is to say, the three...
The phenomena of the twenty-five realms of existence all arise from the false conjunction of causes and conditions; when causes and conditions disperse, this falsehood is termed "cessation.

Therefore, they are called the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Among these two, "serene seclusion" (*yànhuì*) refers to what is appropriate for the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*);
"serene and silent" (*yànrán huìjì*) refers to dwelling in leisure and a quiet place. Thus, one knows that "seclusion" (*huì*) signifies concealment.
"Obscurity" does not refer merely to the obscurity of light and dark. I observe that when this qi descends, it is precisely the four natures (cāturmahābhūta) pushing and simplifying one another.
If fragrance were inherent in wood, once it has become smoke and fire, how could there still be wood? Therefore, it is said to be "not wood. If fragrance were produced from empty space...
If fragrance were eternal within emptiness, it should be constantly present; why then would it only exist when incense is burned? Therefore, it is said that fragrance does not reside in emptiness.
If fragrance were produced by smoke and fire, then all smoke and fire should possess fragrance; why would it be found only in this particular smoke and fire?
Therefore, it is said that they are neither smoke nor fire. One should know that "not from wood" means they do not arise spontaneously;

"not from smoke or fire" means they do not arise from another; and "not from space" means they do not arise without a cause. Since they do not arise from wood, nor do they arise from smoke or fire, it can also be understood that they do not arise from a combination of causes.
When examined and analyzed in this manner, none of these possibilities can be established. Therefore, it is said: "Departing from [the views of] non-existence and so forth."

Furthermore, since it is not wood and so forth, the sense object (*viṣaya*) cannot be apprehended. Since the sense object cannot be apprehended, the sense faculty (*indriya*) likewise cannot be apprehended.

Since both the sense faculty and the sense object cannot be apprehended, the discriminating consciousness (*vijñāna*) also cannot be apprehended. Therefore, it is said that "by this, the mental intention is dissolved.

Reaching this point, one is no longer driven by the faculties, objects, and consciousness; hence, it is said that "one manifests the outflow-free (*anāsrava*). Regarding the two—sense objects and sensory vapors—...

This phrase means that since it is neither wood nor other such things, its entire substance is empty and quiescent; it is the fragrance of the single, true, ultimate principle—secret, wondrous, and perfect.

Nevertheless, this analytical examination of the four natures exists within all four teachings: the "analytical emptiness" (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the *Āgama* (Tripitaka) teaching, the "essential emptiness" (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) of the *Vaipulya* (Shared) teaching, the "successive three contemplations" of the *Pratyekabuddha* (Distinct) teaching, and the "one mind and three contemplations" of the *Mahāyāna* (Perfect) teaching. These are distinguished according to the stages of the Arhat and the Bodhisattva.
This may be seen. Regarding the four sections: "The King of Medicine" (*Bhaiṣajyarāja*) refers to the causal basis; "Serving" (*upasthāna*) refers to the awakening;
"The Buddha asked" and so forth is the concluding answer. In the first [section], "transformation" (*vikāra*) refers to such things as roasting or baking, as well as fermentation and the like.
In the second, "serving the Tathāgata" and so forth means that throughout many kalpas, one has merely known the taste of medicine.
Thus it is said. Today, having served my Buddha and heard the Dharma for practice, one investigates through the four natures and finds that no flavor can be apprehended;

hence the phrase "having served," and so forth. Regarding the thorough knowledge of the nature of flavor: if flavor were produced from emptiness, then what flavor would be produced by tasting empty space?
Therefore, it is said to be "not from emptiness. "Existence" refers to the idea that flavor exists inherently. If flavor were produced from flavor itself...

Who knows that it is flavor? Therefore, it is said to be "not existent. If flavor were produced by the body-consciousness and the mind of the tongue, who would be the one capable of tasting, and who would be the one capable of knowing your flavor? Therefore, it is said to be "not identical with the body and mind.
If flavor were produced apart from the body, the tongue-consciousness, and the mind, then flavor would be something tasted and known by the tongue.
This one who can taste is the one who knows. If it were to arise apart from the body-consciousness of the tongue and the mind, who would taste and who would know your flavor?

Therefore, it is said that it does not exist apart from the body and mind. From "it is not empty" up to "it is not apart from the body and mind," none of these four modes of existence (*catuskoṭi*) can be found. Thus, it is said that one attains awakening by discerning the cause of flavor. (5)

Bhadra contemplates the sense-object of touch. "Bhadra" (跋陀) means the causal basis; "at the bath" (於浴下) refers to the point of awakening. "The Buddha asked" (佛問下) refers to the concluding answer. Regarding the first part:
a *bodhisattva* (*kai-shi*) is so named because they are themselves able to awaken to the wondrous principle, and cause those they transform to likewise awaken to the wondrous principle.
Since both their own practice and their transformation of others are capable of bringing about awakening, they are called a *bodhisattva*. We previously, at the [time of] the majestic...
Regarding the phrase "Ghoṣadatta and others": according to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*, there were twenty-two thousand billion Buddhas named Ghoṣadharāja.

It is imagined that Bhadra was in the world during the time of the first of these Buddhas when he slandered Maitreya (Aśoka), yet it was during the time of the last Buddha that he left the household life. The present reference to him as being "first" [is based on this].

This refers to the present time. Regarding the middle section: "Suddenly awakening to the cause of water" does not mean that one awakens to the cause of water without ever having practiced contemplation;

rather, it means "suddenly" in the sense that although one has always previously used the fourfold nature (catuskoṭi) to investigate and analyze [the nature of things] without yet attaining awakening, one now happens to attain awakening while entering the bath.
Therefore, it is called "suddenly awakening to the cause of water. Since this is not a [fixed] phrase, awakening to the sensory objects (viṣaya) is not...

It can be attained, yet it is not a fixed phrase. One awakens to the fact that the faculties (*indriya*) cannot be apprehended; in the interim, one remains serene. One awakens to the fact that consciousness (*vijñāna*) cannot be apprehended.
Thus, the triad of faculties, objects (*viṣaya*), and consciousness is entirely unapprehendable; therefore, it is said that "one attains non-existence.

It is not necessary to discuss this by distinguishing between the "external dust" and the "dharma-dust" regarding objects, nor by differentiating between the "floating dust" and the "ultimate meaning" regarding the faculties. This may be explained in such a manner.

That which cannot be washed away is the residual habit-energy that has not yet been forgotten. Even during the time of the former Buddha, although they had attained this awakening, their habitual afflictions (*kleśa*) were not yet entirely eliminated, and they had not yet attained the stage of No-More-Learning (*aśaikṣa*).
It was only upon meeting the present Buddha and hearing the Dharma that their afflictions were finally exhausted and they achieved the state of No-More-Learning.
This may also serve as a refutation of those who slander Namo-fujō (Namu Asaṅga), for even though they have attained awakening and clarity, their residual habits have not yet been forgotten.

Having passed through many kalpas, one must again encounter a Tathāgata before finally attaining the state of No-more-learning (aśaikṣa). Regarding "the marvelous touch is proclaimed and made manifest":

this means that touch does not touch itself; rather, it is through the knowledge of the existence of touch that one now realizes that within touch, the entire substance of touch is empty and quiescent, being solely the True Principle.
This is identical to the previously mentioned "the marvelous sound is secretly perfect" and "the marvelous fragrance is secretly perfect. 6. Kāśyapa’s Contemplation of Dharmas.
"Among the sense objects (*dharmas*)": "Mahā" [in *Mahākāśyapa*] refers to the causal origin. "I observe" indicates awakening. "The Buddha asks" concludes the response.

The first [section] is understandable. Regarding the second, as for "I observe" and so forth: since that which Kāśyapa observes is already the *dharma*-object (*dharmaviṣaya*), why speak of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*)?
One should know that the six sense objects are fundamentally not something else; they are merely the residual shadows of the five sense objects (*pañcaviṣaya*). Furthermore...
One may say they are the "six objects" (*ṣad-viṣaya*). Now, since they are called the six objects, the object of mental phenomena (*dharma-viṣaya*) is included therein.

Thus we know that when one mentions the object of mental phenomena while speaking of the six objects, it is because one sees that the object of mental phenomena is not separate from the five objects. As for the phrase "only by means of":

it is by means of the principle of universal emptiness and quiescence that one extinguishes the two aggregates of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*); once the object of mental phenomena has vanished, there is no further apprehension.

Because he has withdrawn from the objects before him, the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is extinguished. Furthermore, because he does not conceptualize the characteristics of those objects, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is extinguished.

From this point on, it is not only the aggregates of sensation and perception that are destroyed, but the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is also destroyed. When the aggregate of consciousness is destroyed, the afflictions of thought (*kleśa*) are spontaneously exhausted;

therefore, in the space of a finger-snap, he attains the state of an Arhat. Regarding "body and mind being equal": it is because he is able to act in this manner that his sensations are as [described].
His coming was entrusted with the instruction to enter the *nirodhasamāpatti* at Mount Kukkutapāda to await Maitreya’s descent, so that he might transmit the robe and the Dharma to him.
The clarification of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* is likewise identical in meaning to the prior "wondrous sound, subtle, and perfect" [of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*].

The second section, from "From Anuruddha... onwards, concerns the text on these five faculties (*pañcendriya*). Each also contains three parts: the causal occasion, the awakening, and the formal conclusion.
First, within the observation of the eye-faculty by Anuruddha: "Anuruddha" below refers to the causal occasion; "World-Honored One" below refers to the awakening. The Buddha...

This question provides the answer to the preceding section; the first part is clear. Regarding the middle section, "delighting in seeing" (*yaksan*) and so forth, according to the *Fahua shu* (Commentary on the Lotus Sutra), this refers to fixing the mind upon its object.
Since that objective focus has been lost, one deeply endures and delights in this kind of "ability to see"; hence it is called the "Samādhi of Delighting in Seeing the Radiance.
Speaking from the perspective of its own level, it is simply the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*); speaking across the stages, it is inherently possessed by nature.
Sublime Wisdom is able to manifest the unsurpassed wisdom and virtue of all sentient beings. Among these three, regarding "revolving the vision to follow its source," there are two meanings:
first, revolving the discrimination of objective conditions to follow the essence of vision; second, revolving the essence of vision to follow the original luminosity of true vision.
Second, regarding Cūḍapanthaka’s contemplation of the nose-faculty (*ghrāṇendriya*): "Cūḍa" refers to his former name; "the Buddha took pity on him" refers to his awakening;

"the Buddha asked... refers to the concluding answer. Regarding the first part, concerning "recollection and retention": even with the minimal effort of reciting a single verse for a hundred days, how could his faculty be so dull?
It was for no other reason than that, in the past, when he served as a Dharma master, he was stingy with the Dharma.

I shall report this. Regarding the second [of the two], "instructing us," according to the contemplation of visualization (*saṃjñā-vipaśyanā*) as discussed in our school, there are six methods for gathering distraction into stillness and illuminating darkness with clarity.
The first is called "counting": repeatedly counting the breaths of the nose from one to ten, and again from one to ten.
The second is "following": following the inhalation and exhalation of the breath, knowing why it goes out and why it comes in.
Third is "stopping" (*zhi*): this means binding the mind that observes to the breath that is observed. Fourth is "contemplation" (*guan*):

using this observing mind to clearly and distinctly illumine the object of observation. Fifth is "returning" (*huan*): withdrawing the object of observation back into the observing mind. Sixth is "purity" (*jing*):
reaching the point where subject and object no longer stand, and the whole body is empty and still. It is like...

This constitutes the sixth [point]. Whether one contemplates according to the magnitude of the teaching—whether it be partial or complete—there is nothing that cannot serve as an entry point for realization.

This is precisely what is referred to in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* as the "Six Wondrous Gates" (*ṣaḍ-ārya-mukha*). Because Cūḍapanthaka was able to cultivate contemplation in accordance with the instruction, it is said, "He taught us.
Regarding the phrase "all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are momentary," this refers to contemplating the breath; if such formations as arising and so forth are so swift...
Furthermore, his mind transforms ignorance into wisdom.
Third, regarding the observation of the tongue faculty by Kauṇḍinya: "Kauṇḍinya" refers to the cause; "the Tathāgata" refers to the awakening;
"the Buddha asked" refers to the concluding answer. The first [section] is clear. Regarding the second: "The Tathāgata," etc., is because he possesses the habit of ruminating like a cow.

When one is slandered by others, the Tathāgata shows the Dharma-gate of Buddha-remembrance (*buddhānusmṛti*). This not only brings about the accomplishment of *samādhi*, but also quells public slander.
Regarding "contemplating taste" and so forth: one contemplates that the cognition which tastes does not reside in the substance of the tongue nor in the substance of the flavor.
If the tongue itself were to taste it, how could it know the flavor? Furthermore, the tasting occurs upon the tongue.

What relevance does this have? Therefore, it is said that they are neither substance nor entity. Regarding the phrase "one should contemplate" (*ying nian*) and below: it is not merely that the nature of the sense organ cannot be tasted;

rather, the nature of the consciousness of the flavor-object (*rasa-viṣaya*) and its cognitive nature are both completely transcended at the moment of such contemplation. Hence, it is said, "one should contemplate," and so forth.

Consequently, there is nothing—from the internal retribution of body and mind to the external environmental retribution of the world—that is not liberated and cast off, thereby emerging from the three realms (*tridhātu*).
It is like a bird that has escaped from its cage, no longer subject to any bonds or constraints; thus it is said, "far removed from all such things.
Regarding "free from defilement" (*vimalā*): as previously stated, conceptual appearances are the dust and the nature of consciousness is the defilement;
when both are far removed, your Dharma-eye will immediately become clear and bright. Thus it is said, "free from defilement," though the difference lies merely in the scale [of the realization].
Regarding the fourth section, "Observing the Body-faculty" (*kāyendriya*): "Because of the cause of *pi-ling*" refers to the reason; "I recollect... and so forth refers to the realization;
"The Buddha asked... and so forth refers to the concluding answer. In the first part, "Frequently hearing that the Tathāgata...

and so forth means that within the three realms, the eight sufferings such as birth and old age, as well as all phenomena (*dharma*), are none other than causes of suffering. In the second part, "Although one perceives... and so forth means that one is able to...
It is the awakening that awakens and the pain that is awakened to. Although there is a subject and an object, they are both, in total, the single faculty of the body.
Regarding "the awakening is pure," etc., it means that within the pure mind, one cannot find either a body that awakens or a pain that is awakened.
"Furthermore, I... is another turn of expression; it means that within my own single body, there exists a clear and pure awakening.

"Mind, is there still the capacity of the body-faculty to perceive? Although the sense-object of touch and the body-faculty have been eliminated as described above, the mind that is capable of cognition still remains.
Thus, after he had maintained this mindfulness for a short while, the triad of faculty, object, and consciousness was entirely unapprehendable."

Therefore, it is said that "he collects his mindfulness" and so forth. Among these three [stages], "pure awakening with the body left behind" means that there is only the wisdom of the contemplation of exclusive emptiness, such that the triad of body—root, object, and consciousness—is entirely unapprehendable.
The "Five Emptinesses" appear within the contemplation of the mental faculty (*manas*). "Subhūti" below indicates the causal basis; "initially" below indicates the opening of awakening;

"the Buddha asked" below indicates the concluding answer. Regarding the first section: "I am vast," etc., means that when one realizes that all phenomena arise through conditions and cease through conditions, their entire substance is empty and quiescent, and thus the mind that knows them is also empty; hence it says, "I am vast," and so forth. Since one has realized all phenomena...

When the mind attains non-obstruction through the arising and ceasing of conditions, then although one’s births may be as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are merely the arising of conditions;
since the conditions themselves cannot be apprehended, the text immediately below states, "First, while in the mother's womb," and so forth. Regarding the second point, the phrase "first, while in...
indicates that because he had already long ago, throughout many kalpas, realized that all phenomena arise and cease through conditions, his mind attained [non-obstruction].
There is no obstruction; therefore, from the moment of birth in the womb, he already knows this. Whether it be body or mind, they arise through conditions and cease through conditions.
Yet both body and mind are in their entirety empty and quiescent, and thus ungraspable. This is why it says, "At first [in the womb]," and so forth.

Such instances refer to the emptiness of the circumstantial retribution (*pratyaya-vipāka*). By inferring from the body and mind, even reaching as far as the ten directions, there is nothing that does not arise through conditions and cease through conditions.

The entire body [of reality] is empty and quiescent; therefore, it is said, "Thus, etc. The above discussion on the emptiness and quiescence of the environment and its inhabitants belongs generally to one's own practice (*svayam-caryā*).

Furthermore, regarding "also causing, etc.": it means causing sentient beings to be converted and guided so that they all may realize that the environment and its inhabitants arise through conditions and perish through conditions, their entire substance being empty and quiescent;

hence, it is said, "Also causing, etc. Regarding "not having met a Buddha such as this" and "receiving, etc.": it refers to not having encountered a Buddha who thus awakens and develops [one's understanding].
Furthermore, the emptiness previously realized was merely the analytical emptiness (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) of the Tripitaka Teaching.

Now that I have received this instruction and awakening, I have advanced to the emptiness of the body of phenomena (*dharmatā-śūnyatā*) in the Shared Teaching, which does not require analysis; moreover, it is understood that the entirety of form is itself empty and quiescent.

Thus it is said: "The nature of awareness is true emptiness. Since one has already realized that the substance of form is itself emptiness, one no longer regards it as becoming empty only through prior analysis. Therefore it is said:
Emptiness is perfectly luminous; since the principle has been manifested, the fruit is self-realized, and thus it is said that one "attains arhatship.

Although called an arhat, this refers to the stage of "having already accomplished" common to all vehicles. One must not interpret this passage by borrowing the "middle nature of the seven elements" and the "true emptiness of awakened awareness.

If one speaks of "suddenly entering the Tathāgata’s [state]," that refers to the meaning of the Separate and Perfect Teachings. The "jewel-luminous ocean of emptiness" is what the Tathāgata has realized.

This is the essence of the principle. It is because both the phenomenon and the metaphor are presented together. That is to say, within this essential nature of the principle, all meritorious qualities and the wealth of the Dharma are produced;
this constitutes "treasure" (ratna). Furthermore, there is wondrous wisdom capable of illuminating and comprehending; this constitutes "clarity" (prabhāsvara).

Although it produces merit and provides illumination, it remains in the Tathāgata’s own essence as true quiescence; this constitutes "emptiness" (śūnyatā). Thus, it possesses both treasure and clarity.
Space is like the great ocean, capable of giving birth to all things and illuminating all things.
Although it gives birth to and illuminates them, while within the great ocean it has no thought of giving birth or illuminating; therefore, it is called the "Ocean of Space of Jewel-Brightness.
This is the principle realized by the Tathāgata. That which the Buddha knows is the knowledge of the three wisdoms within a single mind. Of the Buddha’s...
The seer is the seeing within the five eyes and the one eye. Where the Tathāgata possesses this principle-body (li-ti), there is this knowledge and vision;

where there is this knowledge and vision, there is this principle-body. Now that Śūnyatā-utpanna (Subhūti) has already attained the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness, he is non-dual with the Tathāgata’s principle-body.
Therefore, it is said that he has suddenly entered the Tathāgata’s ocean of the clarity of emptiness. Furthermore, with...
