The Tathāgata’s knowledge is without distinction; therefore, it is said that they share the same Buddha-knowledge and vision. Regarding the realization attained by Śūnyatā-utpanna:

according to the preceding passage, he attained arhatship through the perfect clarity of the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*); according to the subsequent passage, he was certified as having realized the liberation-nature of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).
Speaking of it profoundly, it does not exceed the seventh stage of the Shared Teaching; speaking of it superficially, it stops at the four fruits of the One Vehicle’s Tripitaka.

Its underlying principle is merely the partial truth (*ekāntika-satya*). As for the Tathāgata’s precious, luminous ocean of emptiness—the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—if considered from a proximate perspective, it corresponds to the first stage of the Distinct Teaching;
if considered from a remote perspective, it accords with the first abode of the Perfect Teaching. If it were merely emptiness...

How can those who have already attained the stage of "those who have completed their task" (*kṛtādhikāra*) and dwell in the limited truth (*pratyekasatya*) suddenly enter [the Mahayana], such that they are said to be "identical"? Answer: There are two meanings.

First, although this refers generally to those who have completed their task and the limited truth, it specifically refers to the "truth containing the Middle" (*madhyamāntargata-satya*). Regarding what is "contained":

if it is merely the "Middle," then these are those from the Separate Teaching (*prthaktva-yāna*) who come to be grafted onto the path. Regarding what is "spoken of": if it is the "Perfect Middle," then they are those who are directly addressed by the Perfect Teaching (*samyak-yāna*).
The teaching comes to receive [the practitioner]. Thus, the previous Tathāgatas extensively instructed the Great Arhats and those beyond training (aśaikṣa), all with this very intent.
Regarding the emptiness of liberation: although it was previously empty and quiescent, the subject that observes and the object observed had not yet merged.
Now that one has entered realization, there is no duality with the Buddha; principle and wisdom are equal, and the subject and object are of one suchness. Therefore, it is said:
"Emancipation is emptiness. Among these three, "all characteristics enter into non-existence" refers to what the *Vajra* calls the emptiness of all four characteristics.

"That which is not [existent] is exhausted" also refers to what the *Vajra* calls the emptiness of the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) rather than the emptiness of non-characteristics (*adharma-lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).
This is merely the shared *prajñā*.

The third section, from "Then Śāriputra departed" onwards, concerns the text on the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). In expounding upon the six consciousnesses, one must examine them with clarity;

do not allow them to involve the two extremes of the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*). Furthermore, the division into six is each accompanied by its own rationale for awakening and for providing the final resolution regarding the three categories.
First, regarding Śāriputra’s contemplation within eye-consciousness: "Śāri" refers to the causal basis; "I [attained]" refers to the realization;
"The Buddha asked... refers to the concluding response. Regarding the first part: as for "the mind sees," it means that eye-consciousness acts as the seer.
Since it is the mind that sees, one does not engage in conceptual discrimination regarding phenomena, nor does one harbor craving; thus, seeing by means of the mind naturally attains purity.

Regarding the phrase "mundane and supramundane" (*lokottara*): "mundane" refers to the two truths of suffering (*duḥkha*) and its origin (*samudaya*); "supramundane" refers to the two truths of the path (*mārga*) and cessation (*nirodha*).
Because within the Four Noble Truths, afflictions and awakening, birth-and-death and nirvana, mutually displace and supersede one another, it is called "mundane and supramundane."
By means of this purified visual consciousness, there is nothing among these Four Noble Truths that is not clearly understood; hence it is said, "seen once," and so forth.

Regarding the second [verse], as for the proclamation of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*): these various causes and conditions refer to the verse which my Buddha, the Great Śramaṇa, constantly spoke: "All phenomena arise from conditions and likewise cease from conditions. This is not the *Mūlamadhyamakakārikā*’s treatment of dependent origination.

The verse stating, "The dharmas that arise, I declare to be empty; they are also called provisional names, and are also called the meaning of the Middle Way," was spoken by the Tathāgata while he was still present in the world.
The *Śāstra* (Treatise) was composed by Nāgārjuna after his passing. How could one take what was written after his death as having been spoken in his presence, or treat Nāgārjuna as the Tathāgata?
If one relies on the four teachings within the vows of *śamatha-vipaśyanā*:
The four propositions beginning with "all phenomena are produced by causes and conditions" constitute the four propositions of the *Kāraṇaprajñapti* (the *Śarīra-sūtra*).
Just as one enters into the realization of emptiness as previously described, so too may all four teachings and their respective four propositions be applied.

For one who awakens to the boundlessness of the mind, having heard that all dharmas of the Tathāgata arise through conditions and cease through conditions, being in their entirety empty and quiescent, then the mind is likewise [empty].

The Dharma is, in its entirety, nothing but emptiness and stillness. Regarding the three phrases of "seeing" and "awakening": when one's mind sees and awakens to this, it subsequently attains clarity, purity, and perfection.
The afflictions of views and thoughts are spontaneously destroyed, and birth-and-death in discrete segments is spontaneously transcended.
One realizes that there is no ground for fear whatsoever, and thus enters the stage of the four fruits of the path. As for being the "eldest son of the Buddha," [the interlocutor] asks:
Question: Why is an Arhat of the Hīnayāna called the "eldest son" of the Buddha? Answer:
Although the Tathāgata possesses unsurpassed wisdom, Śāriputra, though belonging to the Hīnayāna, is foremost in wisdom. Because he is foremost, he may also be called the eldest son.
He was asked again: "Since you attained awakening by hearing the causes and conditions from the brothers Kāśyapa, how can it be said that you were born from the Buddha’s own mouth?
He replied: "Although I heard the Dharma from Kāśyapa and attained the first fruit of realization, it was only upon meeting the Buddha later that I perfected the subsequent stages of fruition."
Furthermore, the causes and conditions spoken by Kāśyapa were originally taught by the Buddha; thus, he too was born from the Buddha’s own mouth.
Regarding the two phrases "the three minds perceive the center": this means that his visual consciousness realizes the principle of dependent origination and dependent cessation.
When the essence of the faculties and objects is seen to be empty and quiescent, the discriminating mind finds nothing to discriminate; the light of partial true wisdom naturally arises.

It arises. Once this light is emitted, it is exceedingly bright and far-reaching; that is to say, the visual consciousness is purified, the auditory consciousness is purified, and even the mental consciousness is purified.
Therefore, it is said, "by means of seeing," and so forth. It is not necessary to cite the subsequent passage on "the ultimate stillness reaching through to the light" to explain this.

Second, regarding the Universal Worthy Contemplation within the auditory consciousness: "Universal Worthy" refers to his name; "his practice pervades the Dharma-realm" means he is called "Universal" (Pu); "his rank is adjacent to the ultimate Sage" means he is called "Worthy" (Xian).

In sum, he relies upon the principle of the Dharma-realm to give rise to the practice of the Dharma-realm and realize the fruit of the Dharma-realm. "World-Honored One" and below introduce the awakening; "the Buddha asked" and below provide the concluding answer. "Universal Worthy" is his specific name.

His conduct extends throughout the entire Dharma-realm, hence he is termed "Universal. His station is proximate to the ultimate Sagehood, hence he is termed "Worthy. Altogether, he takes the principle of the Dharma-realm as his basis to initiate the practice of the Dharma-realm and realize the fruition of the Dharma-realm.
The practitioner of Samantabhadra takes the dharma-realm itself as their practice; apart from the dharma-realm, no practice can be found, and apart from practice, no dharma-realm can be found.
Next, regarding "hearing with the mind," this refers precisely to the auditory consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*). As for "discriminating" and so forth...
Sentient beings consist of the nine dharma-realms. To discern who possesses the conduct of Samantabhadra and who does not is what is meant by "discrimination.
If one abides in equality, this clearly demonstrates the ability to accomplish the conduct of Samantabhadra for the sake of sentient beings.

To manifest the conduct of Samantabhadra means to be able to give rise to the practice of the Dharma-realm in accordance with the principle of the Dharma-realm. The six-tusked elephant and so forth should [be understood accordingly].
Supplementary note: It is not that only a single sentient being who practices the conduct of Samantabhadra reaches that place;
rather, among those hundreds of thousands of sentient beings who practice the conduct of Samantabhadra, there are none who do not reach that place by means of the six-tusked elephant.

Therefore, it is said that he manifests "divided bodies" and so forth. Regarding "that place," one should also supplement the text as follows: "Since I have manifested my body, if a person’s obstructions are shallow, they will naturally see me."
Even if their delusions and hindrances are deep such that they do not see me, I shall certainly place my hand upon their heads and protect them.

I shall cause their demonic activities to be expelled and provide them with consolation. Now, because the practices cultivated through the diligence of their body and mind will naturally achieve fulfillment, it is said, "even if those [beings]... How distant is the Ganges-sand of other directions! There is one...
"How few sentient beings there are! If it is thus for those who are distant and so few, one can know that for those who are near and so numerous, it is even more so.

Regarding the three [types of faculties], "the mind hears" and so forth collectively reveal that the ear-consciousness universally illumines and universally responds, such that there is nothing that does not exist and nothing that does not reach.
This means that by unifying the dharma-realm with the dharma-realm, there is not a single thing that is not the dharma-realm.

Regarding "Third, Sūndara contemplates within nose-consciousness": "Sūndara" refers to the cause and conditions; "World-Honored One" introduces the awakening; "The Buddha asked" concludes the response.
At the beginning, regarding "Entering the Path," one should raise the point by saying: "If one wishes to enter the Path, one must first..."

Regarding the observance of precepts: from the precepts arises meditative concentration (*samādhi*), which in turn gives rise to wisdom (*prajñā*). Although I possess the monastic discipline (*vinaya*), my mind is frequently distracted by lustful thoughts, and thus concentration cannot arise;
hence it is said, "although I possess [the precepts]," and so forth. Since concentration does not arise, from what could wisdom emerge?
Hence it is said, "I have not yet attained the outflow-free state (*anāsrava*). Next, regarding the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One," etc.: while I, Nanda, was constantly...
Since the mind of lust is distracted and agitated, one should certainly contemplate the white; yet because Kauṣṭhila previously possessed mundane wisdom, he too should contemplate the white.
Thus it says, "The World-Honored One, etc. As for contemplating the whiteness at the tip of the nose, this does not mean that the eye-faculty contemplates the nose-faculty;

rather, it is by means of the nose-consciousness that one contemplates the nasal breath. When the contemplation is perfected, the breath itself becomes white. "At first, etc. [refers to my initial state].

This is because their contemplation has not yet been perfected and the mind is not yet settled. As for "body and mind becoming equal," as contemplation gradually achieves completion, the smoke gradually dissipates;
thus, both the internal body and mind and the external world become perfectly luminous, transparently white and empty, like crystal.
Consequently, the white breath-nose naturally forms itself. As for "the mind opening," this refers to the aforementioned capacity...
When observing that which is observed, one has not yet reached the state where both subject and object are simultaneously extinguished; there is merely the white breath of the nose.
Now, as subject and object are both fused, the mind immediately opens and outflows are completely eliminated. All breaths become radiant light, illuminating the ten directions.
Thus it is said, "the mind opens," and so forth. To speak briefly: the phrase "the mind opens" signifies that principle is revealed and delusion is shattered.
The various "exiting" phrases (*shuchi*) signify that wisdom arises from the object. The "illuminating ten" phrases signify that wisdom illuminates the object.

The attainment of the "A" phrase signifies that, through the identity of object and wisdom and the non-duality of subject and object, the fruit-stage is spontaneously realized. Regarding the phrase "World-Honored One," etc.:

Regarding the predictions (vyākaraṇa), there are differences between the Exoteric and Esoteric. The fact that all the śrāvakas receive predictions within the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* constitutes an exoteric prediction.

In the assemblies of the Vaipulya [sūtras], those who, upon being rebuked by a single sūtra, immediately desire to turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle, should be understood as receiving predictions esoterically;

thus it says, "O World-Honored One," and so forth. Among these three, as for "I, by means of... and so on: once the inhalation and exhalation have ceased, the light of wisdom naturally arises. This light of wisdom...
All afflictions and karmic actions originating from that source are completely exhausted; hence it is said, "I, by means of [the power of]... and so forth.

Fourth, when Pūrṇa contemplates the tongue-consciousness, he thinks: "There was one called 'I' who went to assist the Buddha in preaching the Small Vehicle," and likewise, "there was one who went to assist the Buddha in preaching the Great Vehicle.
He fails to realize that "immeasurable kalpas" refers to the past, whereas "the World-Honored One" and so forth refer to the present Buddha. How could this be?
Can the ancient and the modern, though separated, be unified as one in terms of "great" and "small"? The section beginning with "Now, Pūrṇa" provides the causal basis;

the section beginning with "The World-Honored One" provides the awakening; the section beginning with "The Buddha asked" provides the concluding answer. Regarding the first part, concerning the phrase "proclaiming and teaching," this does not mean that the true reality (*dharmatā*) of the Mahāyāna is considered a profound realization;
rather, it refers solely to the realization of the impurity of the body by means of proclaiming and teaching the four [objects], such as the body and so forth.
They take the principle of the partial truth of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) as the true mark (*lakṣaṇa*).
That which is called the true mark of all phenomena is not termed "Buddha" by those of the Three Vehicles; therefore, it says "proclaiming," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "and so on":

this refers to the fact that the Buddhas of antiquity possess the three inconceivable wheels of body, speech, and mind, and may preach the sudden [teaching] for some individuals, or [the gradual teaching] for others.
It is taught as gradual; for some persons it is taught as Great, and for others it is taught as Small, so that they do not know of one another.
This is the Dharma-gate of Secrecy, also called the Three Mysteries and the Three Non-protections.
Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra then understood that according to the Dharma-gate of Secrecy taught by the Tathāgata, that which should be Small is taught as Small within the Great.
To teach the Great within the Small is to explain the Great; the same applies to the sudden and the gradual.
Causing both parties to be mutually unaware [of their own state] so that they are no different from the Buddha—this is the subtle and wondrous revelation.
Being able to provide such subtle and wondrous revelation, one possesses no fear even amidst a great assembly of majestic power; this is the attainment of fearlessness. Thus, one knows it is full.
The subtle and wondrous exposition by Maitreya is not something separate that constitutes the subtle and wondrous exposition;

rather, it is precisely the Tathāgata’s secret dharma-gate that constitutes the subtle and wondrous exposition. Furthermore, the Tathāgata’s secret dharma-gate is not something separate that constitutes the secret dharma-gate;
rather, it is precisely the subtle and wondrous exposition by Pūrṇa-maitrāyaṇīputra that constitutes the secret dharma-gate. Regarding this...
In the context of the Tathāgata, it is called a "Dharma-gate"; in the context of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, it is called "expounding and revealing.
Taken together, it is said to be "thus and so forth" (*evam-ādi*). Next, regarding the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One," this refers precisely to the present assembly.

Some claim that this is solely the time for the transmission of the *Prajñāpāramitā*, but I fear this is not the case; for how could the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* not clearly demonstrate that the flavors of the teachings across the five periods are without distinction?

It is not that [the Buddha] assists in proclaiming [the Dharma] solely at the time of the *Prajñāpāramitā*. Thus, one should know that when it is said here, "He instructs me," this refers to the occasion where he was foremost in preaching the Dharma;
therein lies the meaning of his instructing me. As for the "wheel of sound" (*śabdacakra*): the Tathāgata’s mouth is the wheel of the Dharma-turning.
Because this sound of the Dharma can crush and grind away the afflictions and karma of sentient beings, it is called the wheel of sound.
Furthermore, "because of the lion's roar" refers precisely to the aforementioned fearlessness. Whenever a Buddha preaches the Dharma, it is called the lion’s roar.

Since Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra assists the Buddha in turning the wheel of Dharma, he is naturally non-dual from the Buddha. Thus we know that although the World-Honored One speaks, there is nothing spoken;
he speaks of what Pūrṇa assists. Pūrṇa assists, yet there is no assistance; he assists in what the World-Honored One has spoken.
Therefore, in reference to the Buddha, it is called the "wheel of sound," whereas in reference to Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra, it is called the "lion’s roar.

Question: This clarifies the tongue-consciousness (*jihvāvijñāna*). Previously, it was stated that his eloquence is unimpeded; eloquence pertains to the sense faculty (*indriya*). Subsequently, it was stated that his Dharma-sound subdues others;
the Dharma-sound pertains to the sense object (*viṣaya*). Since these are the faculty and the object respectively, where is the tongue-consciousness manifested?

Answer: The consciousness that discriminates has fundamentally no other source. Now, wishing to reveal this consciousness, one considers from what it could be perceived apart from both the sense organs and their objects;
thus, the sense organs and objects are borrowed merely to illuminate it. Therefore, that by which one observes and that by which one awakens is solely the gustatory consciousness.

Regarding the five sections: "Upāli contemplates within body-consciousness" (*upāli*); *upā* means "to rely upon" or "to be caused by. "Receives the Buddha’s [teaching]" (*chêng fo*) refers to being enlightened.

"The Buddha asks... and so forth is the concluding answer. First, regarding the beginning: "Upāli" is here called the "Foremost" (*shang-shou*), because he was capable of serving as the leader and discipline among the assembly due to his rigorous mastery of the precepts.
He is also called the "Attendant" (*jin-chih-shih*), because he attended closely upon the Tathāgata.

Because it is capable of being upheld as a gateway to the Dharma (*dharmamukha*), "intimately following," "intimately seeing," and "intimately observing" clearly manifest that bodily consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*) serves as the functional instrument.
Regarding "liberation" and so forth, this refers to the attainment of the Way by the Tathāgata;

in total, the thirty-four moments of mind manifest simultaneously, whereby the afflictions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and thought (*saṃjñā-kleśa*), along with their residual habits (*vāsanā*), are severed and exhausted all at once. In the subsequent section, regarding "the three thousandfold world" and so forth, there is majesty...
That which is awe-inspiring is called *wei* (dignity). That which possesses ritual decorum to be followed as a model is called *yi* (propriety).
A bhikṣu possesses the two hundred and fifty precepts for each of the four postures—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—which totals one thousand.

When these one thousand are further distinguished according to whether they are fixed (*niyata*), shared with the Path (*mārga-sādhāraṇa*), or comprised within the restraint of discipline (*saṃvara-saṃgraha*), each being threefold, they total three thousand. These are the three thousand aspects of dignified deportment. By means of these three thousand...

The seven branches of body and speech, when taken as antidotes, constitute twenty-one thousand. When further categorized according to the four divisions of greed and so forth, they become eighty-four thousand.

This present figure represents the general count; these are the eighty thousand subtle [non-virtues] and so on. Regarding "innate actions" (*prakṛti-karman*): "nature" (*prakṛti*) has the meaning of being unalterable.
This refers to killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and so forth, which are not transgressed regardless of whether one has received the precepts or not.

That is all. To commit [a transgression] is invariably to incur guilt; this constitutes a natural offense (*prakṛti-sāvadya*). As for a prohibitive offense (*pratikṣepaṇa-sāvadya*), "prohibition" refers to the act of restraint.
Other precepts were established by the Tathāgata according to those who committed them, in order to restrain future conduct and prevent further transgressions;

this is called a prohibitive offense. Regarding the tranquility of body and mind: when one has long maintained the precepts with strict observance, one is able to uphold both that which is to be upheld and that which upholds it.

Yet both have perished. As for those like us, we provide instruction for the community regarding what is grave or light, what is permitted or prohibited, what constitutes an offense, and what is to be practiced or ceased;

this is to serve as the guiding principle within the assembly. Regarding "governing the body and governing the mind," some say that governing the body so as not to act refers to the perspective of the Hīnayāna, while governing the mind so that it does not arise refers to the perspective of the Mahāyāna. This, however, is merely a superficial interpretation.
How could it be that in the Hīnayāna there are only those who restrain the body but do not practice, while there are none who restrain the mind and do not give rise [to afflictions]?
Or how could it be that in the Mahāyāna there are only those who do not give rise [to afflictions] by restraining the mind, while there are none who restrain the body and do not practice?

Judging solely from this passage, how could they be partial to one side rather than being harmonized? Thus we know that at their inception, both the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna involved restraining the body and not practicing [unwholesome acts].
In their succession, all maintain a mind that does not arise. Later, even the maintenance of this state cannot be apprehended.
Therefore it is said: "I am equal.
(6) Maudgalyāyana contemplates within the mental consciousness. "The Great Eye" refers to the causal basis; "I suddenly" refers to awakening. The Buddha...

This is the question followed by the answer at the end. Regarding the first part, "proclaiming" and so forth refers to the causes and conditions previously explained in the section concerning Śāriputra.

As for why these causes and conditions are called "profound meaning": it is because various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to these phenomena, asserting that they arise from time, or arise from space, or further arise from atoms (paramāṇu), or even arise from Brahmā; all of these are erroneous.
Yet it is not correct. To refute such erroneous views, the Tathāgata declared that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions, and likewise cease from causes and conditions.
How could they possibly arise at a specific time or arise only under certain circumstances?
In this way, he not only refutes the errors of others, but does so for profound reasons; thus, it is said, "He proclaims," and so forth. Next, regarding "I [teach] instantaneously," etc.:

As for this, my intention is that upon hearing Kāśyapa explain this profound meaning of causes and conditions, he immediately attained a thorough realization of dependent origination and dependent cessation, and understood that no phenomena whatsoever can be apprehended;
hence it is said, "I suddenly [attained it]," and so forth. Regarding "the beard and hair fell off of their own accord" and so on:

if one speaks in terms of the Buddha’s supernatural power, what difficulty would there be in causing his beard and hair to fall off? Nevertheless, although such a thing occurred, [it was not by that power].
One need not view it in this way. Whenever the Tathāgata bestows his *kāṣāya* robe upon someone, their hair and beard fall away from that moment;
hence it is said they "fall off of themselves. As for the phrase "the supernormal powers manifest," this refers to the manifestation of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It means being able to penetrate how the arising and ceasing of all phenomena proceed entirely from causes and conditions; thus, rather than turning along with external objects, the supernormal powers will naturally unfold.
"Clearly so. As for "not merely," it means that his preeminence in supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) was praised not only by Śākyamuni Buddha alone, but by all Buddhas of the ten directions;
hence the phrase "not merely," and so forth. Regarding the three [sections], "I, by means of...
and so on, the intended meaning is that before encountering the Buddha, this mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) was, moment after moment, clinging to delusive objects, mind after mind...
Chasing after delusive conditions, one may, by receiving the Buddhist teachings and practicing them, immediately attain the return from delusion to truth.
From this point on, this originally inherent light of wisdom is able to be manifested and proclaimed; hence it is said, "I [attain] equality," and so forth.

This refers to turning back from the deluded mind that discriminates sensory objects and returning to the profound stillness of the essence of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*). If we speak in terms of the inner secret and the outer manifestation:
One may also recognize the essence of consciousness as returning to the clarity of ignorance; this can be seen in the illustrative text.
Fourth, the passage from "As for Ucchuṣma" up to the section on the "Seven Great Elements. Question: Since the seven elements follow a sequential order, the Earth element should come first.
Why, then, does it begin with Ucchuṣma? Answer: In this sutra, Ānanda is a manifestation of great spiritual authority (mahā-upāya). Because he has fallen...

The chamber of lust serves as a warning for sentient beings of future generations who commit sexual misconduct; thus, it is simply that Ucchuṣma, the subduer of the fire of lust, is placed at the beginning.
Furthermore, it was asked: "It is clear that Ucchuṣma’s role as a later admonition is placed first.

As for Maitreya of the future, whose 'Great Awareness' is it that causes him to abide before Avalokiteśvara’s 'Great Vision'? The answer is given in the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra*: "Sentient beings are unable..."
They enter into *nirvāṇa*. Because their conscious mind has not yet been shattered, one knows that this unshattered conscious mind is what obstructs the wondrous principle.

For this reason, Maitreya—who is able to penetrate *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only)—is placed at the forefront here, so that when sentient beings shatter their conscious mind, they may, upon hearing the *Amitāyus-buddhānusmṛti-samādhi*, realize the state of non-arising and non-extinction.

The wondrous principle of *nirvāṇa* is such that being born in the Pure Land is to be born in the pure land of *vijñaptimātra* (consciousness-only), and seeing Amitābha is to see the Amitābha of one's own nature (*svabhāva*).
Furthermore, since Śrī-vidyut-jvāla and Avalokiteśvara together serve as the two attendants of Amitābha, they should not be treated as belonging to two separate places;
for this reason, Śrī-vidyut-jvāla is placed last, so that he may follow immediately after Avalokiteśvara. This constitutes seven major sections in sequence.

This may be seen. The first section, "Ucchuṣma Contemplates the Fire-Element," is divided into two parts: first, the introductory narrative concerning Ucchuṣma and others; second, the formal response, beginning with the Buddha’s question.
The first part is further divided into three sections: first, Ucchuṣma and the others meeting the Buddha and receiving his instruction; second, relying on that instruction... [and so forth].
Cultivating the contemplation: Third, from this point downward, the contemplation is perfected and one enters realization. Regarding the first part, concerning "the Tathāgata and others":
while all the previous sages had risen from their seats, why is it that he alone did not? It is because Ucchuṣma belongs to the ranks of the Dharma-protectors and has never before sat down;
therefore, it is not said that he rose from his seat. His nature is predominantly characterized by desire; this is his habitual disposition.
[This is] the Ear. As for the name "Empty King" (Śūnyarāja) given to the ancient Buddha:

because he realized the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) and attained mastery over all phenomena (*dharma*), these terms are combined to refer to him as the "Empty King. Regarding the statement that "desire and so forth are originally substantially existent and not merely provisional metaphors":
at the very moment the mind of lust first stirs, the fire of affliction (*kleśa*) arises; at the time of the actual act of lust...
At the moment of right practice, there is the fire of evil karma; at the time one subsequently undergoes the retribution of sexual desire, there is the fire of karmic fruition.
Because these three fires of obstruction arise, it is said that "many [fires] are taught," and so forth. "Teaching us" refers to the initial moment when the object is perceived.
Some assign the character *leng* (cold) to the three great elements such as earth, and the character *nuan* (warmth) to...
The element of fire (*tejas-mahābhūta*). Such combinations as these are not [to be understood] in that way. This merely refers to observing the element of fire while speaking of "cold and warmth.
This is because when one's lustful mind stirs even slightly, all the cold energy becomes the appearance of warmth;

hence the statement regarding "observing everywhere" and so forth. Next, regarding "divine light" and so on: this precisely clarifies that the wisdom of contemplation is gradually perfected. When this kind of gnosis (*jñāna*) coalesces—
It does not flow. All lustful minds become the fire of wisdom; therefore, it is said that "divine light" and so forth.
One should know that at the time of sexual desire, since it has become a mass of fierce flames, there is no forest of meritorious qualities that is not incinerated.
At the time of contemplative practice, since it has become the fire of wisdom, all rivers of affection and attachment are completely dried up. Although there are these two fires—lust and wisdom—...

It is entirely due to the inherent nature (*prakṛti*) that there exists what is called "the true emptiness of the nature-fire" and "the true fire of the nature-emptiness," which is pure and fundamental yet manifests according to karma.
Thus, sexual desire becomes a mass of fierce flames, while contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*) becomes the fire of wisdom;
it is natural that this should bear the name "Fire-head. This is because the Samādhi of the Fire-light is designated as the "Fire-head," and [it corresponds] with what follows below.
The arising of the great jewel-flame is identical to that [of the previous case]. Regarding the second part, the summary and response:

"all outflows" (*āsrava*) and so forth refers to the arising of the fire of wisdom through right view. Because he protects the Buddha-dharma by means of his vow, the many flames upon his head manifest the form and momentum of subduing Māra.
Second, regarding the contemplation of the earth-element within the fire-element, there are also two parts. First, the causal origination, which includes "holding the earth" and so forth.

Second, the concluding answer, which begins with "The Buddha asked... and so forth. The first part also has three sub-sections. First, "holding the earth," where he encounters the Buddha and receives instruction. Second, from "I immediately...

onwards, following the instruction to practice the contemplation. Third, from "I, at... onwards, the realization of the contemplation and entry into the fruit of realization. The first of these may be divided into two: from "I thought... onwards, the encounter [with the Buddha].
There are many Buddhas. Meeting one Buddha is "Vīśākha. Among those who meet many Buddhas, the first is the practice of the primary path, namely "my mindfulness" and so forth;

the second is the practice of the auxiliary path, namely "or perhaps" and so forth. Regarding the first, as for the name of the Buddha being "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabhā*) and so on, it is because the three wisdoms within a single mind shine universally and are perfectly luminous.
If that radiance were directed toward principle, it would only illuminate existence and not illuminate emptiness, and so on.

It merely illuminates the middle and does not illuminate the two extremes; it discerns capacities, but discerns only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) and does not discern those of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*).

Even further, it discerns only Bodhisattvas and does not discern ordinary or small-vehicle practitioners; thus it is not called "Universal Radiance" (*Samantaprabhā*). Now, it illuminates principle such that there is no principle it does not illuminate, and it discerns capacities such that there is no capacity it does not discern;
therefore, it is named "Universal Radiance. "I act for... and so forth, correctly sets forth the primary practice of the Earth-Holding Samādhi (*Dharanimdhara-samādhi*).
Regarding "at major thoroughfares and the like," this refers to places where one might obstruct the passage of carts and horses;
as for "I shall treat them all equally," it means that where the fields are rugged or obstructed, I shall level and lower them; where they are narrow, I shall expand and widen them;
at river crossings where people cannot ford them, I shall construct bridges to facilitate their passage; and where travelers cannot proceed on the main roads, I shall carry sand [to fill the gaps].

The earth is used to fill it; thus it is said that [the land] is always equal, and so forth. The auxiliary practices (sahakāri-pratipatti) can be understood accordingly. Within the encounter with a single Buddha, there are also two types of practice:

the primary (maula) and the auxiliary. First, the auxiliary practice refers to the *Vaiśramaṇa* [Samādhi] and others. Second, the primary practice refers to the "Land of Peace and Bliss" (*Sukhāvatī*) and others.
Among the auxiliary practices, the name of the Buddha is *Vaiśramaṇa*, which in the language of China means "Pervasive Sovereignty over All. "All" refers here to all phenomena (*dharma*).
"Vasavartin" (the Sovereign) is the meaning of "King. Because his Dharma-body pervades all phenomena, he is like a king who possesses great sovereignty.
He is the final Buddha of the past *Kṣemadhara* (Adorned) eon.
"I am a person carrying a burden" means that I am a person carrying goods, like a porter today. "Taking only one *kākaṇī*" refers to a single coin. This...

It is said that he took only a single coin. Previously, it was stated that he did not take its value; this was because in times of plenty, food and drink were easily obtained, so he did not take the value.
This [instance] concerns a year of famine when grain and rice were extremely expensive, so he took one coin.

Regarding the passage in the *Zhengxing* (Correct Practice) chapter about Viśvabhū Tathāgata rubbing his head and so forth, the meaning is: "If you practice in this manner, why should the mind of your practice suffer?"—this refers to the world.
"Are there not many great beings? Can they all be leveled everywhere so that every person may carry their burden?
I shall now show you a single method: specifically, level the mind-ground. If the mind-ground is level, the world will naturally be level. There is nothing else;
mountains, rivers, and the great earth are none other than things within the wondrous mind. As it is said, 'Outside the mind there are no dharmas; outside dharmas there is no mind. Thus one knows."
The fields at the essential crossroads and ferry landings are none other than the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

Since this is the wondrous, pure, and luminous essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*-nature, why laboriously exhaust oneself in such ways? If the mind is made uniformly level, there will be nothing that is not level.
Therefore, it is said: "The Vaiśyas, etc. Second, practicing contemplation according to the teachings: "I am... and so forth, clarifies the leveling of the mind-ground.
This is wondrous contemplation. Thus one sees that the subtle particles of the body-faculty (*kāyendriya*) are produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

One sees that the subtle particles of the world are capable of producing the body-faculty. Although there are these two kinds of subtle particles—the producer and the produced—they are, in essence, the same wondrously pure and luminous substance of the Tathāgatagarbha. What distinction can be found between them? That is to say:
The nature of form is true emptiness, and the nature of emptiness is true form; it is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
Thus it is said, "I am," and so forth. In this way, the internal faculty of the body and the external world are one with a single minute particle and one with the hidden nature (tathāgatagarbha).
There is no such thing as a "toucher" or "touched" that can be apprehended; it is like empty space meeting empty space, or light meeting light.

Therefore, it is said that they are like "micro-dusts" (*paramāṇu*) and so forth. Thus, not only are the body-faculty and the micro-dusts both by their very nature (*svabhāva*) without mutual contact or friction, but even the body-faculty and weapons are likewise by their very nature without mutual contact or friction. Since all are the hidden nature (*tathatā-garbha*), how could there be [any contact]?
The body-faculty that can be touched by weapons and blades is what Master Zhaoming referred to as "holding one's head before a white blade is like cutting the spring breeze.
Thus it says, "even unto," and so forth. With such contemplation, the entire great earth becomes level of itself.

Within the section on entering realization through the accomplishment of the three contemplations, the phrase "I, at... precisely clarifies the entry into realization. Question: Since... [the text continues].

They attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Why is it that they only attain arhatship? The answer is: there are differences between awakening through understanding (*prativedha*) and awakening through realization (*sākṣātkriyā*).
This [attainment] consists primarily of merit for one's own benefit with little merit for the benefit of others; thus, one merely becomes an arhat. Although they are indeed arhats...

By means of the power of non-arising (*anutpāda*), one immediately turns from the small toward the great. If discussed in terms of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjiao*), this is the stage of "semblance identity" (*xiangsi ji*).
Therefore, one now enters the rank of a Bodhisattva. If discussed in terms of the Perfect Teaching, it is the stage of "partial realization" (*fenzheng wei*).
Some say that becoming an Arhat constitutes a Mahāyāna Arhat; this is not so. If they were already Mahāyāna, why would they need to turn their minds [toward the Great Vehicle]?

This marks the very moment of entering the stage of a Bodhisattva. Regarding the various accounts heard by others: some say this concerns events within the assemblies of all Buddhas; that is acceptable.

Others say it concerns the universal gate of persons and dharmas being certified within the current Lotus Assembly of the Buddha’s Dharma; that is also acceptable. If we consider it in relation to the present Buddha:

This is because the compilers of the scriptures collected that *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* and brought it back here; hence the phrase "I have heard from various [sources]," and so forth. Regarding the fact that Dharaṇīdhara attests to the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*:

the Buddha’s knowledge and vision and the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena as taught in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* have now been realized by Dharaṇīdhara, such that the subtle atoms of both the environment and its inhabitants are seen as being of one identical *tathāgatagarbha*. In this state of realization, they are precisely the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.
That which is realized is the true mark of all phenomena (*dharmatā*); it is non-dual and without distinction. This is why it is said, "I have previously clarified this.
Regarding the second part, the conclusion and response: "I, by means of... and so forth, refers back to the previous statement, "I am the mind that opens [to awakening]," and so on.

Although the body, the sense organs, and the world are the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, they manifest as the appearances of dust due entirely to a single thought of non-awakening. Therefore, it says, "originally such," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the phrase "when dust is eliminated, wisdom is perfected": this does not mean that wisdom is perfected only after dust has been eliminated.

Rather, it means that when the three wisdoms are perfected and the perfect contemplation shines universally, every single atom of the great earth is none other than wondrous wisdom; and every aspect of the wondrous wisdom of the three contemplations is none other than the great earth.

Object and wisdom are of one suchness; subject and object are non-dual. If explained from the perspective of the limits of negation and manifestation, it is like the arising of light and the simultaneous extinction of darkness:

as darkness is extinguished, light arises. Thus it is said that when the sensory objects (dust) dissolve, wisdom becomes perfect. However, in reality, wisdom does not only become perfect upon waiting for the dissolution of the objects.
The section "Observing Water as the Great Element of Light" in the third month is divided into two parts. First, the origin (nidāna), namely "Moonlight," etc.

Second, the summary and response, namely "The Buddha asked," etc. The first part is further divided into three. First, the youth named Moonlight meets the Buddha and receives his instruction. Second, "Observing," etc., following the instruction to practice the contemplation.
Third, "In this way," etc., the contemplation is perfected and one enters realization. Within the first section, "Meeting the Buddha and Receiving Instruction," the youth is named Moonlight.

Regarding "light": this Bodhisattva contemplates that water is composed of the Great [Element]. He realizes the Tathāgatagarbha-nature, which is fundamentally pure, all-pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm, and is the singular light of wisdom.
The moon is the essence of the Yin, and water is the offspring of the Yin.
Since he had already achieved success through the contemplation of water, he was given a name by combining that with his mother’s; thus he became known as the Youth Candraprabha (Moonlight).

He, too, was at the stage of the "Abiding in Boyhood" (*kumārabhūta*). As for the ancient Buddha named Jalamdhara (Water-Sky), he also attained the first principle of the heavens (*paramārtha-deva*) through the perfection of the contemplation of water—namely, the true emptiness of the nature of water and the true water of the nature of emptiness—and was therefore called Water-Sky. Thus, one should know that this was an ancient Tathāgata who had realized the fruit of Buddhahood.
Now, as for the Bodhisattva’s reliance on causes: by practicing the contemplation of water (*āp-kṛtsna*), he and [the Buddha] together realized this principle.
Past and present are not two; teacher and disciple are in perfect accord. This is why one is named Water Heaven (*Jaladeva*) and the other is named Moonlight (*Candraprabha*).

Regarding the instruction for all Bodhisattvas to practice the contemplation of water, the water-contemplation in this sutra differs from that in the *Sukhāvatīvyūha-sūtra* (Contemplation Sutra). There are two points regarding these differences. First:

These are the differences between the environment and the physical body (*niśraya-vipāka* and *sambhoga-vipāka*). Second, the difference between the ultimate reality and the skillful means. Regarding the first difference:
that sutra contemplates only the water within the environment, but does not contemplate the water within the body;

it is not like this [text], where there is nothing—whether internal or external—that is not contemplated. Regarding the second difference: in that [sutra], the contemplation of the lapis lazuli ground is not easily accomplished, whereas the water...

It is similar to [the analogy of] lapis lazuli. It employs water as a skillful means for cultivation; it is not like this present method, which directly uses the contemplation of water to reveal the nature of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
Second, regarding the cultivation of contemplation according to the teachings, the text may be divided into three parts. First is the contemplation for beginners.
Regarding the observation of "going": first, one observes within the mind; second, one observes within the mind that "I am going"; third, one observes the subsequent mind encountering "no-going.

As for the statement that the first and middle [moments] observe "equality," some claim that the various elements such as water and earth are all identical within the single *tathāgatagarbha*, and thus there is no mutual exclusion.
This is not so; it refers specifically to water, and does not concern all the great elements. It refers to its primary retribution (*vipāka*).
The nature of water and its dependent retribution (niśraya-vipāka) are both of the same single *tathatā-garbha* (storehouse nature), and thus they do not mutually exclude one another;

hence it is said, "contemplating the equality [of these]. From the beginning of the passage "From the first... onwards, this correctly contemplates that the two waters—the primary (the body) and the dependent—do not exclude one another.

From "From the first... to "...semen and blood," one contemplates from the outside toward the inside. From "Saliva and fluids" to "...excrement and urine," one contemplates from the inside toward the outside. Within the body... [etc.]

This is a general manifestation. From the internal to the external, and from the external to the internal, as one circulates, scrutinizes, and repeatedly observes, there is nothing that is not the same single *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Once one has personally seen the water, it is argued that both the primary (the environment) and the secondary (the beings therein) waters share this same single *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
In this context, it should be stated that [the medium] is fragrant water. The term "Mount Floating Banner King" (*Sudharmādhvaja-rāja*) is used figuratively, as it is situated within fragrant water.
Within the ocean of fragrant water, there is a great lotus flower, and within that flower are contained countless Flower-Treasury World-Systems (*kusumagarbha-lokadhātu*).
Within a single Flower Treasury (Padmagarbha) there are twenty tiers of worlds. As they rest upon fragrant water, their form is like that of floating objects;
thus they are called "floating. Each tier is piled high above the others, their form resembling a banner; thus they are called "banners. "King" refers to their being the highest and peerless.
Although the fragrant water is vast, it shares the same nature as the water of the primary retribution (vipāka), and there is no distinction between them.
Because there is a distinction, it says "seeing water" and so forth. Next, regarding the passage "I [perceive]... and so on:

the intention is that although the contemplation of the water of the environment and its inhabitants (*bhājanaloka* and *sattvaloka*) has been accomplished, one has not yet forgotten the internal body. The phrase "should depart" clarifies the reason why the internal body has not yet been eliminated.
Regarding "I emerged... and so on: after emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he suddenly felt pain in his body; this was because he recalled how Śāriputra had once practiced meditation.
He was settled on the banks of the Ganges. A one-night karma-ghost struck him on the head with its palm. After emerging from meditative absorption (*samādhi*), he felt a headache.
He said, "My past bodily pain was just like Śāriputra’s headache"; thus it is said, "like a house," and so forth.

Regarding "long since departed from the conditions of illness," someone asked: "An Arhat only severs the fetters of the cause (*hetu-bandhana*); do the fetters of the fruit (*phala-bandhana*) still remain?"
One may attain freedom from illness; for instance, there was Śāriputra’s headache and Pīṅgala’s bodily pain—all of these were Arhats, which serves as clear proof.
If this present Moonlight is also an Arhat, how can it be said that he has long been free from the conditions of illness?

Answer: The state of an Arhat cannot be discussed in general terms. If those such as Śāriputra had merely severed the fetters of the "seeds" (kleśa-bandhana) but had not yet departed from the conditions of illness, it would naturally follow that he still possessed doubt.
However, as for the Arhat Candraprabha, he should have already severed the fetters of the "fruits" (phala-bandhana).

It was for the sake of saving sentient beings that he intentionally took birth within the triple world; thus, he described himself as having been "long free from the conditions of illness. As for the possibility of regression, it is because... [text ends].
His heart pained him with doubt, thinking: "Could it be that I have regressed from the stage of Arhatship, which has caused this pain?

As for the phrase "his physical body was as it was before," if one examines the preceding text, there should be two meanings. The first is that previously he had not yet attained the dissolution of the body.
The second point refers to how, previously, when he emerged from meditative absorption, he suddenly experienced heart pain because a young boy had thrown a clod of earth or a pebble at him.
Now that [the obstruction] has been removed, even though his husband has passed away, his body no longer experiences pain; thus it is said that "the substance of his body is as it was before.

Among the three [categories], the King of Sovereign Power over Mountains and Seas is not a Buddha who received a prediction in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*; rather, he is an ancient being from a past life.
The Buddha’s ears! His merit is as high and piled up as a mountain; his wisdom is as deep and vast as the ocean.
All his supernatural powers are beyond comparison and are most sovereign, like those of a king. To speak of him as a whole, he is like the "mountain and ocean.
Only then can one truly be said to have lost the self. Previously, one saw only the waters of the dependent and primary realms as being one and the same.

Regarding the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*: within it, the internal body has not yet been extinguished; only upon encountering the Buddhas of the mountains and seas does one finally attain the extinction of the body.

From this point on, apart from the *nirmita-āśraya* (the dependent retribution), no *sambhoga-sarīra* (the primary retribution) can be found; apart from the *sambhoga-sarīra*, no *nirmita-āśraya* can be found.

The dependent and primary retributions are mutually identical; the internal and external are non-dual. Therefore, it is said that [the Buddha] is equal to the ten directions. Second, in the conclusion of the answer, I, by means of...
"Et cetera" means that all water is of one and the same nature as a single treasury. Regarding "attaining the patience of non-arising" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti):
by this, one realizes that the very essence of all water is unborn; that which appears to arise does so through delusion. Its very essence is unceasing;
that which appears to cease does so through delusion. Thus, there is only the one [reality] that is neither arising nor ceasing.

The principle of arising: from the initial stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) onward, through partial realization and partial entry, up until the ultimate ocean of fruition at the stage of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), there is nothing but non-arising.
Therefore, it is said that one "attains the peerless."
The fourth section, "Contemplating Wind within the Great Element of Water as Lapis Lazuli," is divided into two parts. First, the introductory narrative, concerning meeting the Buddha and so forth.

Second, the concluding response, concerning the Buddha’s questions and so forth. The first part is further divided into three sections. First, meeting the Buddha and receiving his instruction (beginning with "A bodhisattva named Lapis Lazuli"). Second, practicing contemplation according to the instruction (beginning with "I, relying upon the teaching...").

Third, attaining realization through the perfection of contemplation (beginning with "Encountering the Buddha again..."). Regarding the first of these: the name of the bodhisattva is Lapis Lazuli (*vaiḍūrya*). Contemplation...
By taking the wind-element as the great object of realization, he attained wondrous wisdom;
there is no dharma that he does not penetrate clearly, just like lapis lazuli, without any difference. Therefore, he is named Lapis Lazuli Light.

As for the Buddha named Immeasurable Sound, he likewise contemplates the wind-element and realizes its pure, original nature pervading the entire Dharma-realm. Since the wind already pervades the Dharma-realm, the wind is immeasurable; sound, too, pervades it.
Within the Dharma-realm, sounds are infinite; therefore, he is titled "Immeasurable Sound.

Thus, we know that the Bodhisattva is named "Lapis Lazuli Light" based on the wisdom that performs the contemplation, whereas the Tathāgata is titled "Immeasurable Sound" based on the object of that contemplation.

"Revealing and showing" refers to the reception of the teaching below. "Fundamental enlightenment is wondrously luminous" corresponds to the two preceding phrases: "the nature-enlightenment is wondrously luminous. This...

The essence of the wondrously luminous nature is stillness within movement and movement within stillness. By awakening to this wondrously luminous nature, one can thoroughly comprehend all phenomena (*dharmas*).

Therefore, when observing the environmental retribution (*āśraya-vipāka*) of the world and the personal retribution (*vipāka-phala*) of sentient beings, one sees that they are entirely produced by false causes and conditions, being set in motion and transformed by the power of the wind.
Next, regarding the observation of the realms (*dhātu*) and so forth, this is the primary [point].
Contemplate what has been described above as the world, which is the environmental retribution (*niśraya-vipāka*), and sentient beings, which are the personal retribution (*sattva-vipāka*).

When the environmental retribution is analyzed, one speaks of "contemplating the realms" (*dhātu*) and "contemplating the worlds" (*loka*). When the personal retribution is analyzed, one speaks of "contemplating the body" (*kāya*) and "contemplating the mind" (*citta*).

"Contemplating the establishment of the realms" refers to their fixed orientation in the east, west, south, and north. "Contemplating the movement of the worlds" refers to the past, present, and future.
This is because of transformation and change. To observe the movement and stillness of the body means that walking, standing, sitting, and lying down are not uniform.
To observe the movement and thoughts of the mind means that birth, abiding, change, and extinction are a continuous flow.

Although there are differences between the world, the body, and the mind, when one observes the reason for their movement, it is solely due to the power of delusory wind. Therefore, it says, "I, in [this state]," and so forth. Some people, by means of these...

The two phrases concerning "movement" explain the true nature (*tathatā*). Not only do they not accord with the preceding phrase "all are," but furthermore, how would one interpret the subsequent two phrases, "coming from nowhere"?
In the section beginning with "At that time," the various manifestations of movement are precisely brought forth;
though they differ, their nature is the single *tathāgatagarbha*. Within this *garbha*-nature, what could there be that comes? As for that which comes, it is...
They come from falsehood; therefore it is said that they "come from nowhere. Within the nature of the treasury, what departure could there be?
Their departure is likewise a departure through falsehood; therefore it is said that they "depart to nowhere. Since it is said that there is no coming, and again that there is no departing—
Thus, one knows that although it is moved and turned by the winds of delusion, the entirety of delusion is itself the True. Therefore, it says, "At that time," and so forth.

The section beginning with "The ten directions" specifically clarifies the delusory appearance of movement. The phrase "The ten directions," etc., comprehensively summarizes that the world, body, and mind are all equally delusory.
"Just as one... is a simile; "one vessel" is a metaphor for the storehouse nature (*ālaya-vijñāna*), while "storing a hundred mosquitoes and gnats" is a metaphor for...
"All sentient beings" refers to all living creatures. Their "chirping and clamorous cries" are a metaphor for inverted views and false delusions.
"In a mere fraction of an inch" and so forth is a metaphor for all sentient beings transmigrating through the three realms of existence and cycling through the six destinies within the trichiliocosm.
Although a hundred mosquitoes may buzz and clamor wildly within the vessel, it remains entirely unmoved;

thus one knows that the world, the body, and the mind are illusory, driven by the power of the wind element, yet the nature of the storehouse (ālaya) has never been moved. This is why it was said previously, "At that time, I became awakened... (and so forth).
All of this arises from the perfection of contemplation through the great element of wind; therefore, one is able to realize things in this way. Among these three [elements], when encountering...

The Buddha’s two phrases signify the perfection of contemplation. From this point on, not long after meeting the Buddha, one realizes that which is movement is stillness and that which is stillness is movement.
Although the appearances of movement and stillness exist, movement and stillness themselves are ultimately unattainable.

Thus, one knows that although all phenomena are said to arise, they have never truly arisen; and although all phenomena are said to cease, they have never truly ceased. Therefore, it is called "meeting the Buddha."

...and so forth. From "At that time" onwards, this correctly clarifies the signs following the attainment of the stage of abiding after awakening to the patience of non-arising (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
At the head of all movement in the eastern direction lies the Land of Immovability; it is movement that is stillness.

Furthermore, the Land of Immovability being at the head of all movement signifies stillness that is movement. Since this has already been partially realized, it is said that "the mind opens" and "one sees. That which is meant is:
The three wisdoms are known within a single moment of mind, and the five eyes are seen within a single eye.
It is not merely that one sees that land; one also sees one’s own body as the son of that Dharma King. It is not merely that one is the son of that Dharma King;

one also sees oneself serving the Buddhas of the ten directions. From this, whether in body or mind, the light of wisdom immediately arises, penetrating and illuminating everything with clarity. One fully understands.
Because there is no obstruction, it is said, "At that time," and so forth. In the second part, the conclusion and response, the phrase "I [perceive]...

refers to contemplating the entire substance of the wind as the *tathāgatagarbha* (store-nature), wherein the power of false and deluded movement has nothing upon which to rely. The phrase "causing the ten directions...

should be understood as follows: one must know that all Buddhas are ultimately the wondrous original enlightenment (*mūlapratyavekṣaṇājñāna*), in which movement is quiescence and quiescence is movement.
As for "clarifying this": the ultimate realization of all Buddhas is not distinct from the ultimate; it is precisely the partial realization of Bodhisattvas.

The partial realization of Bodhisattvas is not distinct from the partial realization; it is precisely the ultimate realization of all Buddhas. Although they are called cause and effect, cause and effect are non-dual.
Although they are called one and many, one and many are mutually identical. Therefore, it is said: "Joining the palms," and so forth.

Furthermore, the "Contemplation of the Great Emptiness of the Treasury of Space" (Ākāśagarbha-śūnyatā-mahā-dharmadhātu) is divided into two parts: first, the causal origination, beginning with "The space... and so forth; second, the concluding response, beginning with "The Buddha asked...

and so forth. The first part is further divided into three sections: first, from "The space... downward, clarifying that which is attained; second, from "At that time... downward, revealing that which is manifested...

[The section on] "Clarifying. Third, this section below explains the source [of the name]. Regarding the first part: as for the Bodhisattva named Ākāśagarbha (Space-Treasury), through the perfection of the contemplation of the great element of space, he has realized the nature-awakening of true emptiness and the true awakening of the nature of emptiness—pure and fundamental from the beginning, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.
This is what is called space. Yet this space merely abides as such; within it there is nothing contained, for it is all-pervading emptiness.
This space is indeed true emptiness (*śūnyatā*). True emptiness is not a void;
it can contain all phenomena and can also give birth to all merits, just as a treasury is replete with various riches and pours them forth.
That which is born is the Treasury of Space (*ākāśagarbha*). "I am equal" means that through the perfection of clear contemplation, there is that which is attained.

When the Tathāgata refers to Śākyamuni’s time of practicing the causal stages, *Dīpaṃkara* (Light-Maker) is none other than Dīpaṃkara Buddha himself. Because he shared the same teacher as Śākyamuni—namely, Dīpaṃkara—it is said, "I am equal.
Through the contemplation of emptiness, one realizes that while the great root of causes and conditions is subject to arising and ceasing, its essential nature is neither arising nor ceasing.
Extending this analysis to the four great elements and all phenomena, they are all characterized by arising and ceasing, yet fundamentally neither arise nor cease.

The true emptiness thus attained pervades the entire Dharma-realm; taking the Dharma-realm itself as one's body, and because the Dharma-realm is boundless, it is said that one attains a "boundless body."

Next, within this [section], it describes how the Great Function arises from the Dharmakāya. First, "At that time," and so forth, reveals the non-duality of object and wisdom (*ālambana-jñāna-eka-rasa*).

Second, "Furthermore, at... and so forth, manifests the non-duality of the arising of Buddhas. Third, "The various banners," and so forth, shows the mutual identity of the environment and the inhabitants (*āśraya-adhiṣṭhāna*).
Within the context of the non-duality of object and wisdom, the "four great jewels" are mentioned; these jewels are capable of containing all things and can also produce them.
It gives rise to all things. What are now called the four great precious jewels manifest the four wisdoms of inconceivable true emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
When this Dharmakāya issues forth to illuminate existence, it is the wisdom of wondrous existence;
when it issues forth to illuminate emptiness, it is the wisdom of true emptiness; and when it issues forth to negate both simultaneously, it is the wisdom of neither.
The wisdom that arises when [the two aspects] are simultaneously illuminated is the wisdom of simultaneous identity. Thus, the four great precious jewels manifest the four inconceivable wisdoms.
These four wisdoms all arise from the realization of the True Emptiness Dharma-body, giving rise to the wisdom capable of contemplating the four great elements;
hence it is said, "At that time," and so forth. Furthermore, by means of the four great precious jewels...
"Shining upon Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust" means that these Buddha-fields as numerous as motes of dust are the objective realm of the four great elements being contemplated.

Because the *dharmakāya* is boundless, the Buddha-fields of the ten directions are likewise the *dharmakāya*. Thus, by means of the *dharmakāya*, the wisdom of the four great elements arises to illuminate the Buddha-fields of the ten directions;
therefore, this is manifested through "illumination" and so forth. Although there is the contemplation that acts as the subject of observation, [the object is...]
This is the Dharmakāya. Although there is an object of contemplation, that object is also the Dharmakāya. Object and wisdom are of one suchness; subject and object are non-dual.
There is nothing that is not true emptiness, pervading the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is manifested through the transformation of all things into empty space.
One should know that empty space has always been pervasive. Now, since the object and wisdom have been transformed into empty space, the object and wisdom themselves remain unmoving.
Thus it is. Arising from the *dharmakāya* of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*), object and wisdom are as one; in this way, there is no duality between the [sentient] beings and the Buddha.

This may further be divided into two parts. Furthermore, in the section below, "the non-duality of the Buddha and sentient beings within one's own mind" refers to the phrase on the "flowing and pouring.
"The manifestation of the Great Perfect Mirror within one's own mind" is the essential principle of the self-nature of true emptiness. True emptiness...
Within the nature itself, the ten dharma-realms (dharmadhātu) can be fully contained. It is like a great round mirror upon its stand, wherein nothing fails to appear as a reflection.

Therefore, one’s own mind and so forth are used to manifest this. Since the essence of self-nature already possesses the ten realms, it in turn gives rise to ten kinds of wondrous wisdom to illuminate those ten realms.
Although the wisdoms themselves are not ten in number, because the realms are ten, [the wisdoms correspond accordingly].
Wisdom is likewise tenfold; therefore, it is manifested through the internal liberation and so forth. Within these ten realms, both sentient beings and Buddhas are fully present.
Since they are possessed by their very nature (*svabhāva*) and arise from that same nature, they are called "Buddhas born of self-nature."
Since it is said that the self-nature gives rise to wisdom which illuminates the ten realms, the wisdom of each of those ten realms likewise illuminates the ten realms.
Therefore, this is manifested through the metaphor of flowing and pouring. This reveals that within both the sentient beings and the Buddhas, there are respectively sentient beings and Buddhas;
thus they are called the "Buddhas and sentient beings of others. Although there are these two kinds—self and other—both are equally the true emptiness from which all things arise.
For this reason, the ten realms of one’s own mind pervade the Dharma-realm, and the ten realms of others’ minds likewise pervade the Dharma-realm;

thus, they are manifested as extending to the very limits of empty space. Since it is said that they are one and the same True Emptiness Dharma-realm, although there is "self" and "other," self and other are non-dual.
Even the mutual identity of the environment and its inhabitants (*śāśraya*) is not dual. Below the various banners, the environment interfuses with the inhabitants, and the body...

It can descend. Because it correctly engages with the basis, it is said that "all banners and so forth" are contained within it; for the self-nature of true emptiness (*śūnyatā*) does not fail to encompass anything.
Thus, all Buddha-fields of the ten directions appear therein. True emptiness is precisely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).
Having appeared as true emptiness, it returns to engage with the Dharma-body. Although there is a multiplicity of banners and a singularity of the body, they are one and the same true emptiness.

The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is like space, wherein the two do not obstruct one another; therefore, it is manifested by means of various banners and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the body is able [to do so]":

since the true emptiness of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) is already capable of encompassing all things and can further respond universally to all things, even though the body may be small and the land may be large, it is solely through this intrinsic nature of true emptiness that it can respond universally. Thus, it is said that "the body is able [to do so]."
This is made manifest. Thus one knows that while the body remains as one, the various *dhvajendra* (banner-king) lands are exceedingly numerous.

By means of the many, one enters into the one, identical to space in its lack of obstruction. It is like a thousand pearls entering into a single pearl, or a single pearl entering into a thousand pearls;
in these layered reflections, the one and the many are unimpeded. Furthermore, one knows that the lands within a single atom are vast.
It is but a single body; how small it is! Yet, by means of its smallness, it accords with the great.

It enters skillfully without effort, like a single jewel reflecting a thousand jewels, and those thousand jewels reflecting back upon the single jewel; they illuminate one another, and the large and the small mutually contain one another.
...and so forth. "Extensively practicing," etc., is the summary. By means of such banners, he enters into all bodies; furthermore, with a single body, he universally reflects throughout all lands.
This is not a state of non-action (*asaṃskṛta*). He extensively expounds the Dharma to deliver sentient beings and performs the Buddha-work:

sometimes teaching the sudden (*tun*), sometimes teaching the gradual (*jian*), and sometimes first revealing the three vehicles (*triyāna*) before finally converging them into the one vehicle (*ekayāna*). There is not one...
Yet these are not non-Buddhist activities (*buddhakārya*). For some, with the capacity for joy, he speaks of the world; for some, with the capacity to generate goodness, he speaks of human conduct;
for some, with the capacity to destroy evil, he speaks of antidotes; and for some, with the capacity to enter into principle, he speaks of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Furthermore, there is not a single one that is not a Buddhist activity. Thus, he speaks of the sudden, the gradual, the opening of the three, the convergence into the one, and the mundane.

Whether speaking of the realms (*dhātu*), of persons, of antidotes, or of the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*), all are adapted to the specific capacities of beings; thus, there are few who encounter contradiction.
Therefore, it is said that they "extensively practice" and so forth. Such is the mutual identity of the environment and the inhabitants (*niśraya-vastu*).

Furthermore, within this identity of environment and inhabitants, the body is identical to empty space, clearly manifesting that both the environment and the inhabitants are one with the true void *dharmadhātu*. This is the realization of the Great Emptiness through contemplation alone.

One attains the body of the true emptiness and boundless *dharmadhātu*. Thus, object and wisdom are of one suchness, self and other are non-dual, and the environment and its inhabitants are mutually identical;
all ultimately converge within the nature of the *ākāśagarbha*. Within the third section, "Explaining the Source," there are also two parts:

from "This great" (*cǐ dà*) onwards is the actual explanation, while from "In the same" (*yú tóng*) onwards describes the realization. The single phrase "This great" refers back to the aforementioned object and wisdom.
This is one such instance, up to the point where the environment and its inhabitants are non-dual.
However, this spiritual power arises from realizing the wondrous wisdom of the four great elements through contemplation of them. Therefore it is said: "By me... (and so forth).

That the four great elements have no basis means that one has realized that the four great elements within one's own body are entirely without anything upon which they can rely. How is it known that they have no basis? It is because of their arising.
They arise from false conditions and perish through the separation of those conditions. Since they both arise and perish in falsehood, how could there be any basis for them?

To fully realize that at the time of arising, there is never actually any arising, and at the time of ceasing, there is never actually any ceasing, is to see that their entire substance is the self-nature of true emptiness, neither arising nor ceasing; thus it is said, "the four great elements," and so forth—not only these four.
Great delusion arises and ceases; empty space is entirely like this, and the Buddha-land is likewise so.

Since empty space and the world are analogous to the four great elements within, they are the very substance of the arising and ceasing of delusion, which is the non-arising and non-ceasing of the self-nature of true emptiness.
Therefore, it is said that empty space is "non-dual" and the Buddha-land is "originally identical. Chenwu (Chen Wuzhen) spoke of them as being "equal."

This means that having observed the four great elements within and the empty space of the Buddha-land, one awakens to the clarity that their arising is non-arising in its very essence, and their ceasing is non-ceasing in its very essence. There is only the principle-body (li-ti) of non-arising and non-ceasing;

once this principle-body is realized, it manifests as wondrous function (miao-yong), and for this reason, there is great spiritual power. Second, the conclusion of the answer: "Wondrous power is perfect."

"Clarification" means that this wondrous and subtle power of wisdom shines forth perfectly and is fully revealed. In the sixth section, "Maitreya’s Contemplation on the Greatness of Consciousness," there are two parts: first, the causal origin (the passage beginning with "Maitreya, etc."); second, the concluding response (the passage beginning with "The Buddha asked, etc."). The first part has three sub-sections: first, Maitreya and others meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching; second, [the passage beginning with] "Throughout kalpas... [which describes] relying upon the teaching...; third, [the passage beginning with] "At that time... [which describes] the transformation of the body. Regarding the first sub-section, it is further divided into two: first, Maitreya and others meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching; second, [the passage beginning with] "Then the World-Honored One... [which describes] the Buddha bestowing predictions upon them. Regarding the second sub-section, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Throughout kalpas... [which describes] relying upon the teaching to cultivate practice; second, [the passage beginning with] "After cultivating for many kalpas... [which describes] attaining the fruit of the prediction. Regarding the third sub-section, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "At that time... [which describes] the transformation of the body; second, [the passage beginning with] "Then the Buddha... [which describes] the Buddha praising their merits. Regarding the second main part, the concluding response, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha asked... [which describes] the Buddha posing questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya providing the answers. Regarding the first sub-section of the concluding response, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha asked... [which describes] the Buddha posing questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions.
