Regarding the second sub-section of the concluding response, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha said... [which describes] the Buddha praising his merit. Regarding the first sub-section of the second part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha asked... [which describes] the Buddha posing questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions. Regarding the second sub-section of the second part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha said... [which describes] the Buddha praising his merit. Regarding the first sub-section of the first part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya and others... [which describes] Maitreya and others meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching; second, [the passage beginning with] "Then the World-Honored One... [which describes] the Buddha bestowing predictions upon them. Regarding the second sub-section of the first part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Then the World-Honored One... [which describes] the Buddha bestowing predictions upon them; second, [the passage beginning with] "Then the Buddha... [which describes] the Buddha praising their merits. Regarding the second sub-section of the second part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha said... [which describes] the Buddha praising his merit. [which describes] the Buddha posing questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions. Regarding the second sub-section of the second part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya said... [which describes] Maitreya answering the questions; second, [the passage beginning with] "The Buddha said... [which describes] the Buddha praising his merit. Regarding the first sub-section of the first part, it is further divided into two: first, [the passage beginning with] "Maitreya and others... [which describes] Maitreya and others meeting the Buddha and receiving his teaching; second, [the passage beginning with] "Then the World-Honored One... The second section, "Cultivating Contemplation Based on the Teachings," is divided into three parts. First, the brief introduction: "At first, regarding... and so forth. Second, the detailed explanation: "That which is entered... and so forth.

Third, the concluding clarification: "Arising and ceasing... and so forth. Regarding the first part, "At first, regarding... means that at the initial stage, upon hearing the teachings, one immediately practices according to those teachings.
As for "its external," it excludes the sensory objects (*viṣaya*) of movement and stillness; as for "its internal," it excludes...
It is not a consciousness of discursive discrimination; it exists solely within the faculty of hearing. Therefore, it is called "within hearing.
This fundamental hearing is originally perfect and without deficiency; its entire substance is the characteristic of non-arising and non-ceasing.

For this reason, the text below states, "If drums are struck simultaneously in the ten directions, one hears them all at once," and so forth. Previously, [the faculty] followed along with the objects of sound due to conditions, but now it is reversed and made perfect.
Fullness constitutes a deficiency; even turning permanence into transience is entirely the mark of arising and ceasing.

This is what is called following along and emerging [from it] to form the flow of birth-and-death and desire. Now, by means of the wondrous contemplation of non-arising and non-ceasing, one contemplates back toward the wondrous realm of non-arising and non-ceasing.
Thus, the three states such as "deficiency" and so forth are, in their entirety, the three states such as "fullness" and so forth.
What is meant is that one enters [the stream] in reverse to realize the flowing nature of nirvāṇa; hence it is called "entering the stream" (*rūpa-pravāha*).

Since this is the dharma-nature (*dharmatā*), all marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are entirely absent; hence it is called "losing the object. To combine these points, it is said, "first, regarding equality," and so forth.
Within this very heading, the four characters "entering the stream and losing the object" encompass everything from the beginning of the first fascicle without exception. Therefore...
The Tathāgata questioned thus, and the Bodhisattva spoke thus. How is it known that this encompasses everything without exception?
Since the single character "flow" (*liú*) is itself the *dharmatā*, it has already been used previously to reveal to Ānanda the eternally abiding true mind within the true mind.
In manifesting true vision, it reveals the quiescent and eternal true vision; this is "one truth, all truths," encompassing everything without exception.
Furthermore, from the five aggregates (*skandha*) up to the eighteen realms (*dhātu*), they are in their entirety the wondrous true suchness-nature of the Tathāgatagarbha;
this is "one existence, all existences," encompassing everything without exception. Moreover, beginning with the element of earth and ending with the element of consciousness...
The essence is pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. This is "one within all" and "all within one," encompassing everything without exception.
Furthermore, for Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra, it was taught that the empty Tathāgatagarbha is not any of the ten realms;
that the non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is precisely the ten realms; and that the empty-and-non-empty Tathāgatagarbha is both the negation of the two [extremes] and yet the ten realms.
Both are the "neither-nor. Through their mutual identity, the ten realms are all mutually identical.

This is the inconceivable threefold truth—entirely empty, entirely provisional, and entirely middle—which encompasses everything without exception. Furthermore, regarding the sequence of practice since its inception:

the first determination is established based on the nature of perfect stillness, which is neither-arising-nor-ceasing; within the second determination, those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified.
It is pure. Furthermore, it encompasses all things without exception. This is how the character "flow" (liú) encompasses all without exception.

Moreover, the single character "entry" (rù) is the wondrous practice of the inconceivable: such as the true emptiness of *śamatha*, the wondrous provisionality of *samādhi*, and the perfect centrality of *dhyāna*;
as well as Pūrṇa’s statement that "resting is itself bodhi," where truth is not obtained from without; and the request for its practice.
In the first sense, it refers to the revolving of the profound stillness within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
In the second sense, it refers to the person who enters into oneness, encompassing all without exception. Thus, even by means of the single character "entry" (*ru*), everything is fully subsumed.

Furthermore, the two characters "without object" (*wusu*) serve to destroy delusion, just as in *śamatha* one destroys the deluded mind; this is the state of having no basis for reliance in the seven locations.

In these three locations, there is no substantial entity that can serve as a basis; this destroys false views. Having already destroyed the discrimination of objects and conditions, one further destroys the vision of the second moon within the essence of the faculty.
One also departs from such characteristics as right and wrong, large and small, expansion and contraction, harmony and disharmony.

Within *samādhi*, the five aggregates (*skandhas*) and the three categories (*dhātus*) are all freed from the characteristics of false arising and ceasing. Within *dhyāna*, the seven stages beginning with earth...

The four great elements are all characterized by neither causes-and-conditions nor spontaneity; they arise from the delusions of Pūrṇa Maitrāyaṇīputra. The characteristics of the four elements mutually oppress one another, yet the root of delusion is fundamentally without cause.

If the狂心 (mad mind) were to cease, these characteristics would vanish. Furthermore, within the first definitive decision regarding the practice requested, the fundamental root of the five aggregates and birth-and-death was resolved;
within the second definitive decision, the six sense organs and the root of afflictions were minutely examined.

Fundamentally, all are subsumed without exception. This principle—that the two characters "lost" (*wang*) and "place" (*suo*) subsume everything without exception—is likewise so when explained according to the specific text.
First, upon entering the flow of the nature of hearing, the object-field of sound (*śabda-dhātu*) is lost.
Second, upon entering the flow of contemplative wisdom, the nature of hearing is lost. Third, upon entering the flow of the contemplative wisdom that can empty [all], contemplation...
That which is lost to wisdom: once one enters the stream of profound emptiness, that which can empty the contemplative wisdom is itself lost.
Thus, the four characters "entering the stream" and "losing the locus" encompass everything without exception—whether subsequent or prior, distant or near, false or true, principle or practice.
If it is not what the Tathāgata has realized, it is precisely what the Bodhisattva cultivates.

Furthermore, that which is not cultivated by Bodhisattvas is precisely what the Tathāgata has realized. How could it be that this initial skillful means and wondrous gate of perfect penetration is otherwise?
Within the second section, "Explanation and Establishment," there may also be four parts. First, "That Which Is Entered" and so forth:

entering the flow of the nature of hearing causes the auditory object (*śabda*) to perish. Second, "In This Way" and so forth: entering the flow of contemplative wisdom causes the hearing itself to perish.

The first is the sphere of the nature [of phenomena]. The second consists of the exhaustion of hearing and so forth; it is the sphere where the flow of the principle of the Truths enters and the wisdom of contemplation is lost. The third is the realization of emptiness;

it is the sphere where the flow of profound emptiness enters and the principle of the Truths is lost. However, within each of these four texts, there are two characters that constitute the essential core, while all others merely serve to clarify them.
Among the first, it is "already tranquil" (既寂); among the second, it is "gradually increasing" (漸增); among the third, it is...

It does not abide; it is this which is the ultimate perfection among the four. As for the initial phrase "that which is entered," some claim it refers to the "entry into the stream" from the aforementioned "non-abiding in objects.
This is also incorrect. "Object" (*suō*) here is a redundant particle; "that which is entered" (*suǒ rù*) likely refers to the stream of the *dharmatā* (dharma-nature) that is revealed.
This state of quiescence should correspond to the two characters "quiescent-extinction" (*jīmíè*) found in the subsequent text.
"Appropriate. As for the phrase "already tranquil," the meaning is that previously the nature of hearing followed after deluded objects;

now that it is perfectly illuminating, it naturally manifests its own perfection and no longer undergoes the arising and ceasing as before. It is, in this very moment, true tranquility; hence it is said, "already tranquil.

Thus one knows that with these two characters, "already tranquil," the Perfect Penetration has already been grasped. What follows below is nothing more than an explanation of this "already tranquil" state and...

It is simply that there is no longer anything [to be lost]. As for the statement that "movement and stillness are equal": previously, the sense organs and their objects confronted one another and were mutually entangled;
now, having already entered the flow of the Dharma-nature, the two characteristics of sound—the object of hearing—namely movement and stillness, do not arise of themselves.
Therefore, it is said that "movement and stillness are equal. In the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna), one only speaks of "hearing" when there is movement and sound; in stillness, [it is not so].

If there is no sound, one might say that hearing does not exist; however, in the Mahāyāna, hearing is certainly present when sound vibrates, and it is also present when sound is still, because its nature is constant.
This is what is meant by "entering the nature of hearing while the flow of the auditory object (śabda-dhātu) ceases.
Next, the phrase "thus" refers to the nature of hearing that has been entered. At this stage, the practice advances further than before, and the wisdom capable of observation gradually...
The object of contemplation becomes increasingly manifest; hence it is said, "thus gradually increasing.

Reaching this point, not only is the sound-object that is heard no longer found, but the hearing-nature that hears is also unobtainable; hence it is said, "hearing and the object of hearing are exhausted.

This constitutes entering the flow of contemplative wisdom where the hearing-nature has vanished. Regarding the third phrase, "exhausting hearing," etc., it means that although the aforementioned hearing-nature...

The [subjective] mind perishes, yet the wisdom capable of emptying it remains. Now, although the nature of hearing has already been exhausted, one still does not abide within that state of the exhausted nature of hearing.

Advancing from this, even the awakening that performs the observation perishes, leaving only the ultimate truth revealed. Therefore, it is said: "The awakened subject and the object of awakening are both empty.
This constitutes the entry into the stream of ultimate truth, where the observing wisdom has perished. The fourth line says: "The emptying of awakening, etc."
In this state, the contemplative wisdom of the previous stage has already vanished, and the principle of truth revealed therein is free from even the slightest defect;

hence it is said that "the realization of emptiness is perfectly complete. However, to rest here alone is not yet extraordinary or sublime. One must proceed further and repeatedly negate even this principle of truth itself;
hence it is said that "that which empties and the emptiness itself are extinguished. This constitutes entering the stream of profound emptiness, wherein the principles of truth have utterly perished.
In this way, there is no flow that does not enter, and nothing that does not perish. This is merely to explain and establish the four characters:
"cease" (zhǐ), "enter the flow" (rùliú), and "perish the object" (wágsuō). If these four are combined with the five fascicles of text on "untying the knots," they constitute the first two sections.
That very [textual passage] states: "This root is first understood and first attained as the emptiness of persons"—this is the third passage.
"That very emptiness is perfectly luminous, becoming the liberation of dharmas"—this is the fourth passage. "That very liberation and dharmas are both empty, resulting in non-arising.
As for the two phrases "tranquil extinction" (*śānta-nirvāṇa*) below, they correspond to the passage "this is called a bodhisattva," and so forth. (3)
In the concluding summary, regarding the two characters "quiescence" (ji) and "extinction" (mie): speaking generally, the absence of the afflictions of the five abodes within is called quiescence;

the absence of the two kinds of birth-and-death without is called extinction. What is now referred to as "the extinction of birth-and-death" means that from the moment one enters [the state where] the nature of hearing has extinguished the object of sound, one repeatedly dispels [delusions] and progressively advances until birth-and-death itself has been extinguished.
Rather, it is simply that the quiescence of neither-arising-nor-ceasing manifests before one. Nevertheless, one should proceed through the four preceding stages in their proper sequence.
Regarding arising and ceasing: entering the nature of hearing is "arising," while the vanishing of the auditory object is "ceasing.

This continues until entering the profound emptiness is "arising" and the vanishing of the principle of truth is "ceasing. To speak further: although the auditory object has vanished, the nature of hearing...

It still remains; it is still subject to arising and ceasing, and has not yet attained quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*). It is like when the nature of hearing has perished but the wisdom of contemplation still remains—it is still subject to arising and ceasing, and has not yet attained quiescent extinction.
It is like when the wisdom of contemplation has perished but the principle of truth still remains—it is still subject to arising and ceasing, and has not yet attained quiescent extinction.
Only when one reaches this point and repeatedly eliminates everything until it is utterly exhausted is it truly quiescent extinction, not arising and ceasing.
Therefore, it is said that they are merely arising and ceasing. One must examine the two characters "manifest" (*xiànqián*) with care.

This does not mean that what was previously absent has only now been acquired, which is called "manifesting before one. Rather, it means that these are inherently possessed; though they were previously hidden due to delusion, they are now revealed through awakening and clarity.

Regarding the phrase "suddenly," etc., within the context of entering realization through the perfection of the three contemplations: since it is said that "when birth-and-death has ceased," there is no delusion that is not destroyed;
and since it is further said that "quiescent extinction manifests before one," there is no virtue that is not revealed.

Thus, the mundane world of the six realms and the supramundane world of the four types of noble ones are utterly unobtainable, and one transcends them. To designate this as the destruction of delusion and the manifestation of principle, one does not cling to it.
If one does not cling to existence, one transcends the six realms of existence. If one does not cling to emptiness, one transcends the two vehicles.
If one does not cling to the Middle Way, one transcends even Bodhisattvas and Buddhas. What is called "non-being" means that all ten realms are equally non-existent.

Therefore, it is said that they appear "suddenly," and so forth. Furthermore, this does not obstruct the ten realms, which remain perfectly present. This is because when delusion is shattered, principle is revealed;

thus, all six realms are the wondrous existence of the six realms, all two vehicles are the wondrous existence of the two vehicles, and all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are the wondrous existence of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
That is to say, the ten realms are simultaneously identical [to the ultimate]. Therefore, it is said:

The ten directions are perfectly luminous. Regarding the phrase "first, the supreme cloud harmonizes with the above" and so forth: the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment is that which all Buddhas have realized and attained;
it is precisely what Avalokiteśvara possesses. Now that quiescent extinction has manifested before him, he who possesses it has likewise realized and attained it.
Thus, that which all Buddhas realize is a realization wherein there is nothing to be realized; it is the realization of Avalokiteśvara.

Realization. That which Avalokiteśvara realizes is also realization. There is nothing realized, yet he realizes that which all Buddhas realize. Although cause and effect differ, that which is realized is non-dual;
therefore, it is said that "above, he accords with [the Buddhas]," and so forth. Since the principle and essence are identical, his power of compassion is likewise so.

All Buddhas possess great unconditioned compassion (*nirālambana-mahāmaitrī*) that universally takes as its object all sentient beings within the *dharmadhātu*; Avalokiteśvara of the present is likewise able to do so.

Therefore, it is said that they are equal to the Buddha. Second, regarding the phrase "sentient beings of superior excellence," there should also be the clause "the fundamental, wondrously enlightened mind.
That this is not mentioned now is because, although sentient beings possess it in its entirety, it remains within delusion and has not yet been realized.
Question: Since there are ten realms, why do you speak only of the six paths? Answer: When viewed as a whole, there must be a middle between the upper and lower harmonizations;

the middle refers to the Bodhisattvas, while the upper refers to the Buddhas. However, the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) are omitted because these practitioners have already severed the afflictions of views and thoughts and have realized the limited truth (*paricchinna-satya*). Believing themselves to have reached the ultimate, they no longer recognize the existence of the Buddha’s [realm].

One may look up to one's own state of misery; thus, it is treated briefly. Regarding "with those who are equal": "compassion" (bi) refers to compassionate resentment, while "looking up" (yang) refers to yearning admiration.
Those sentient beings wander through the ocean of birth and death, undergoing the greatest suffering;

those Buddhas transcend far above the mountain peak of nirvana, abiding in supreme peace and bliss. One feels compassionate resentment for one's own birth and death, and yearns with admiration for the Buddhas.
Regarding this elevation: when Avalokiteśvara seeks to uproot their suffering, he likewise shares the sentient beings' sorrow, resentment, and yearning;

thus it is said that he is "equal to them. Some say that compassion (*karuṇā*) belongs to the sentient beings, while yearning belongs to Avalokiteśvara. If that were so, they would be different rather than identical.
Thus we know that Avalokiteśvara has not only realized the wondrous clarity of original enlightenment, but that both loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and compassion are also [realized].
This is the realization.
Fourth, the section on the arising of function through realization is divided into three parts: first, the thirty-two marks of a Great Man; second, the twenty-four fearlessnesses;
and third, the four inconceivable qualities. Regarding the first [the marks], there are again three sub-sections, the first of which concerns the World-Honored One.

The first section provides a general summary; the second, from "World-Honored One" onwards, presents specific details; and the third, "This is called," concludes by returning to the title. Within the initial general summary, regarding "like an illusion" and so forth:
the two characters for "hearing" (*wen*) refer to the nature of hearing, which is neither born nor extinguished. "Perfuming" (*xun*) refers to the process of habitual conditioning.
To cultivate is to refine. To take the nature of hearing—which is neither arising nor ceasing—as the object of perfuming is what constitutes "hearing-perfuming" (*śruta-vāsanā*).
To take the nature of hearing—which is neither arising nor ceasing—as the object of cultivation is what constitutes "hearing-cultivation. This is that which possesses the nature of hearing.
Since it is the nature of hearing that serves as the object of cultivation, one cultivates throughout the day yet finds no cultivation to be attained;

yet this does not hinder the clear manifestation of cultivation—this is called "like an illusion. Furthermore, regarding the sense-object of sound up to the principles of the Truths (*tattva*), if one does not direct the mind toward them, they remain;
if one directs the mind toward them, they vanish—this is called "vajra. To discipline and straighten sentient beings by means of these dharmas is called...

Samādhi. This Dharma consists of hearing and cultivating through hearing; "illusion" and "vajra" are the metaphors. Because the Dharma and the metaphor are explained in conjunction, it is said to be "like an illusion," and so forth.
Regarding "entering all lands": since Avalokiteśvara resides at the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), he has partially realized the Land of Quiescent Light (śāntaprabhāsa-kṣetra).

This is because he manifests in response to the three types of beings from within that Land of Quiescent Light. Since his thirty-two manifestations do not go beyond the ten realms (daśadhātu), [he appears] within the ten...
Within the realms: if it accords with Bodhisattvas, one enters the Realm of True Reward; if it accords with the Two Vehicles, one enters the Realm of Expedient Means;
if it accords with the Six Paths, one enters the Realm of Shared Dwelling. Therefore, it is said that "one enters all lands. Second, the specific demonstration is divided into two parts:

first, the supramundane body; second, the mundane body. The first [the supramundane body] further has four parts: first, the Buddha-body; second, the Pratyekabuddha; third, the *vidyādhara-pratyekabuddha*; fourth...

This refers to the Śrāvakas. Regarding the phrase "all Bodhisattvas" within the initial Buddha-body: the term "Bodhisattva" encompasses both the Separate (Byō) and Perfect (En) teachings; therefore, the word "all" (sho) is used.

The characters for "entering," "advancing," and "manifesting" all refer to the period when [the path] is about to be accomplished but has not yet been accomplished; this remains the case throughout what follows.

For those of the Separate Teaching, the realization of the "Middle Only" constitutes outflow-free wisdom (anāsrava); for those of the Perfect Teaching, the realization of the "Perfect Middle" constitutes outflow-free wisdom.
The person of separate capacity does not fall into either of the two extremes; therefore, this is the "Middle of the Separate" (*butian zhong*).

The person of perfect capacity does not fall into the sequential three truths; therefore, this is the "Middle of the Perfect" (*yuanzhong*). Thus, taking non-outflow (*anāsrava*) as superior understanding constitutes the manifestation of the perfect.

For the person of separate capacity, the sequential Dharma is taught to cause them to sever the twelve grades of ignorance and thereby attain liberation from the death-and-rebirth of transformation (*nirmāṇa-maraṇa*). For the person of perfect capacity...
He expounds the Dharma of perfect interfusion, causing them to sever the forty grades of ignorance and likewise liberate them from the death and rebirth of transformation.

This is because those of separate capacity take the realization of the Perfect Teaching as their object of superior understanding and manifest it as perfect. As for the Bodhisattva who can manifest the Buddha-body:
although he is currently a bodhisattva, in the past he was already the Tathāgata Dharmaprabhāsa. Thus, he manifests a Buddha by means of a Buddha.

One should not raise such an objection. Furthermore, if one already abiding in the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) can manifest as a Buddha within a hundred worlds, how much more so for one at the profound stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) manifesting a Buddha-body—why then should there be any difficulty?

However, the Bodhisattva in question has not yet entered the stages (*bhūmi*) according to the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-yāna*), nor has he ascended to the [final] rank according to the Perfect Teaching (*yuan-jiao*).

For example, even an ordinary practitioner who is a Dharma teacher can preach the Dharma to an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva (Samyaksambuddha-bodhisattva) to shatter the ignorance of the final birth-phase;
now, when an Equal Enlightenment Bodhisattva manifests as a Buddha-body to preach the Separate and Perfect Teachings and enters the stages (bhūmi), what difficulty could there possibly be?
Thus, it is clear that one need not explain the Manifestation Store (Nikāya) and the Shared Teaching by means of the Separate and Perfect Teachings.
This is because those for whom this is intended are of the Separate and Perfect [vehicles], not the Tripitaka or Shared [vehicles].

Regarding the two types of Pratyekabuddhas, the phrase "quiescent, wondrously luminous" refers to what the *Lotus Sūtra* calls "delighting in solitary, sublime stillness and seeking spontaneous wisdom.

For their sake, the twelve links of dependent origination are taught, so that they may practice forward contemplation of arising and reverse contemplation of cessation to sever the afflictions of views and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa* and *bhāvanā-kleśa*). Although they are pratyekabuddhas, [they are included here].

Since manifesting the body to preach for them is no different from being in the presence of a Buddha in the world, it must be so. If one dwells alone on a solitary peak, contemplating conditions to awaken to the Way, that belongs to the period when no Buddha exists;
there, one attains liberation without waiting for the preaching of the Dharma. The present case is not like this;

therefore, the twelve links of dependent origination (*dvādaśāṅga-pratītyasamutpāda*) were established so that they might contemplate them in both direct and reverse order. Third, among the *pratyekabuddhas*, they sever the twelve...

Regarding "causes and conditions" and so forth: this refers to observing the process of origination in forward order and observing the process of cessation in reverse order. The exposition of the Dharma is the same as before.

Among the four types of śrāvakas, those who have attained the Four Noble Truths and so forth refers to those who, by contemplating the thirty-two aspects of the two sets of Four Noble Truths across the upper and lower realms—and specifically the single aspect of emptiness within the final [truth] of suffering—attain the realization of the Path of Seeing (darśana-mārga). They then enter the Path of Cultivation (bhāvanā-mārga) to attain cessation.

Furthermore, when one attains the Path of Seeing (*darśanamārga*), one should again contemplate the True Reality (*tattva*) and proceed to the stage of the Path of Cultivation (*bhāvanāmārga*) to realize the Truth of Cessation (*nirodhasatya*).

Moreover, from the stages of Heat (*uṣmagata*) and Summits (*mūrdhan*) up to the Arising of Similar Understanding (*kṣānty-anulomika-avabodha*), although understanding has been attained, suffering cannot be suppressed, origination cannot be summoned, the path cannot be traversed, and cessation cannot be realized.
Although a similar understanding has been attained, the True Principle remains unmanifest; thus, [the practitioner] returns...

One must cultivate the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (saptatriṃśad-bodhipākṣika-dharmāḥ), which constitute the Truth of the Path (mārga-satya), in order to realize the Truth of Cessation (nirodha-satya).

Second, the worldly bodies are divided into three: first, the celestial bodies; second, the human bodies; and third, the eight classes [of spirits]. Regarding the first [the celestial bodies], there are again two: first, the sovereign deities (rāja-deva); second, the subordinate deities (pāratantrika-deva).
The first king is Heaven; this refers to the two heavens of form and desire. Within the phrase "the first Brahmā King," there are three instances of the character for "desire" (*yù*).

Some read them all as the "desire-to-intermingle" (*hù-yù*) of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, but this is not correct. The two "desires" of the upper and lower [realms] refer to the "desire-for-enjoyment" (*lè-yù*).
The aspiration for sensory objects is merely the "desire-for-the-five-sensory-objects" (*wǔ-yù-yù*). These five desires are the root of afflictions and the cause of distraction and agitation. Its...

To clarify that the desire for the five objects of sensual pleasure is no small matter and must not lead to transgression—since there is no other way to avoid transgressing the five desires than by ceasing desire so that the sense organs remain pure—it is said that "the mind of desire" and so forth.
This is because one must cultivate revulsion toward the suffering, coarseness, and obstructions of the realm of desire.
For those who aspire to the Brahma heavens, such as the Pure, the Sublime, and the Detached, he preaches the precepts, goodness, and meditative concentration (*dhyāna*).
Regarding the two types of Śakra: for those who aspire to be the Lord of Desire, since Śakra is the sovereign of the desire realm, he is able to govern the six heavens.
If we speak in terms of the primary heavens, there are eight heavens in each of the four directions, totaling thirty-two;
that which resides in the center serves as the sovereign. The Three Maheśvaras are the sixth heaven of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*).
The Four Great Maheśvaras are the summit heaven of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), who has three eyes and eight arms, rides upon a white bull, and holds a white fly-whisk in his hand.
The second category consists of those belonging to the devas. Regarding the four heavenly kings (*cāturmahārājika*): they are also classified as belonging to the devas. Some may ask:

"Since they are themselves 'heavenly kings,' why are they said to be 'belonging to' [the devas]? This is not so; because they are the external ministers of Śakra, they are said to belong to the devas.
The title "King" used here is their original designation as devas, signifying that they are able to protect the world. Second, the human class has three parts. First:
There are three kinds of assemblies: first, the assembly of the laity; second, the assembly of the Dharma; and third, the mixed assembly. Regarding the first, the assembly of the laity:

among the kings of men, those who delight in being kings go forth as kings themselves, and they are able to cause all under heaven to go toward them and take refuge in them. Now, there are four types of kings of men. The great ones are the four, beginning with the Golden Wheel-turning King (*cakravartin*);
down to the smallest, which are called the "scattered like millet" (*kṣudraka*). This is said because they are extremely numerous, like scattered grains of millet.
Among those with great learning, he was one whom the world honored and yielded to, for his years were many and his virtue profound, such that he was esteemed and deferred to by the world.
Among lay practitioners, he was one who delighted in discussing renowned doctrines; this means he desired to discourse on the Way and debate virtue, composing books and establishing teachings.
He did so because he wished to discuss the Way and debate virtue in order to transform and guide those in the present, and because he wished to compose books and establish teachings.
They establish a model for future generations. Because these individuals possess virtue but hold no official rank, they are called *gṛhapati* (lay devotees).

Furthermore, those who purify their minds, minimize their desires, and abide in the Way are also called *gṛhapati*. Among the officials, those who love governing the state are the Three Dukes and the Chief Ministers;
those who adjudicate the administration of districts are the Governors and District Magistrates. Among the *brāhmaṇas*:
Those who love various arts and techniques refer here to those who observe the celestial bodies and calculate the waxing and waning [of the moon] and so forth.
By observing the stars and calculating the waxing and waning, they are able to pursue auspiciousness and avoid calamity; thus it is said that they "maintain themselves through self-protection.
Second are the assembly of the Dharma: among the bhikṣus, those who uphold the various precepts should include both śrāmaṇeras and bodhisattvas. This is because one wishes to achieve...
"O Bhikṣus, you merely maintain the Bhikṣu precepts. Among the Bhikṣuṇīs, those who ride upon the precepts are those who observe the five hundred precepts.
Because women’s sexual passions are difficult to subdue, their precepts are double those of the Bhikṣus. These are the three mixed assemblies."

Regarding the "Mistress of the Household": one who establishes herself through internal governance is said to be thoroughly proficient in the *Xiǎoxué* (Lesser Learning) and other such texts, and to be fully endowed with the duties of a wife and the decorum of the inner quarters.
As for the terms "family" and "state": from the rank of Great Officer (*dàfū*) downward, all are referred to as a "family."
All those from the rank of kings and marquises upward are designated as "states. A "female ruler" (*nǚzhǔ*) refers to the consort of the Son of Heaven.
A "lady" (*fūrén*) is the wife of a lord of a state. A "noble lady by appointment" (*mìngfù*) is one who has attained honor and status through her husband.

As for a "great lady" (*dàjiā*), "jia" should be read as "gu"; she is merely a teacher to the consorts and queens. Among the boys, those whose male organs remain intact do not engage in sexual desire throughout their lives.
As for the phrase "among the maidens, those who do not seek to be violated": these are virgins who do not wish to marry.
Because they do not wish to marry, their fathers, elder brothers, and kinsmen force them to marry; this constitutes an act of violation.
Although they are thus violated, they themselves do not marry, and they do not regard the violation itself as a violation; therefore, it is said that they "do not seek to be violated."
Section Thirty-Eight, Part Two. First, the explicit explanation of the eight classes of beings; second, the emergence of humans and non-humans. Regarding the first:
those who desire to depart from the ranks of devas do not find birth among devas to be true happiness, for it is entirely brought about by the power of merit.

When that merit is exhausted, they must inevitably fall back down. It is just like an arrow shot upward into the sky: when its force is spent, it finally falls. This is what is meant by "even if one is born..."
"Is it not better to go back to the Western Land than to remain in this state of 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception'? Therefore, I joyfully desire to depart from the ranks of the devas.

Regarding the various dragons (*nāgas*), there are many different kinds: there are those who protect the world, those who protect the sun and moon, and those who bring rain, as clarified in the *Liang* [Dynasty] Treatise.
Since there are many other types as well, the term "various" (*zhū*) is used. Among these two [categories], they are those who delight in humans and those who cultivate themselves as humans.
It is also said that preaching the Dharma and upholding the precepts are wholesome. Regarding the phrase "these names, etc. among the three fetters:
although what is manifested consists of thirty-two marks, they do not transcend the ten realms. These ten realms are inherently complete within a single momentary thought;

they manifest in accordance with conditions and respond to stimuli to reveal themselves according to the capacities of beings—this is what constitutes their wondrousness. Although such bodies are manifested, they are not for [the sake of]... [the self].

That which is defiled by them is what constitutes purity. Now, as for this capacity of a single thought-moment to respond within the ten realms, it arises fundamentally from the fact that mindfulness possesses both inherent goodness and inherent evil.
If one wishes to manifest the Buddha-realm, it is the manifestation of inherent goodness; if one wishes to manifest the nine [other] realms, it is the manifestation of inherent evil.
Although there is good and evil, they are all entirely inherent in nature (*xingju*). This is because they are realized through awakening.
Because it is the sublime function of the entire body, it is said that "all [are accomplished] by means of... (and so forth), as well as through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisaṃskāra*).
The fourteen fearlessnesses and the four inconceivables below should all be concluded and clarified according to this same principle.
The twenty-four fearlessnesses are also divided into three parts: first, the general explanation beginning with "The World-Honored One"; second, the specific demonstration beginning with "Firstly";

and third, the concluding summary beginning with "These names. Regarding the initial general explanation, it says "the wondrous power of non-action" because the cultivation arises entirely from the nature and the cultivation returns entirely to the nature;
as it is established in accordance with the nature without depending on artificial fabrication, such functional power exists.

It is said that the wondrous power of non-action causes the bodies of all those of equal rank to undergo "revolving and returning," which refers to the subsequent passages on the revolving and returning of seeing and hearing;
it causes their minds to undergo "revolving and returning," which refers to the subsequent passages on severing delusive thoughts so that the mind is free from killing and harming.
In sum, I have realized perfect penetration and entered samādhi; thus, my entire body and mind are nowhere not pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. Therefore...
It enables those sentient beings to obtain fourteen kinds of merit of fearlessness within their own bodies and minds.
Some say that fearlessness belongs to the sentient beings while the merit belongs to the Bodhisattva; however, these need not be viewed separately.

In essence, it is because the Bodhisattva possesses inconceivable compassion and yearning that they naturally attain the ability to cause sentient beings to leave suffering and obtain happiness; therefore, it is called "fearlessness."

Since causing others to leave suffering and attain happiness must necessarily involve merit, it is called "merit" (*guṇa*). To specifically demonstrate this, it is divided into fourteen sections, the sequence of which can be seen [in the text].

Within these fourteen passages, the phrase "by me" (*mayā*) should appear below each "should" (*yathāpi*), and the phrase "causing all sentient beings" (*sarvasattvān*) should be followed by the sentence "observing their sounds" (*teṣām śabdān vyavalokya*); that these appear only at the beginning and end here is an abbreviated version of the text. However...
The speaker should supplement this.
Regarding the initial section on "Fearlessness Toward Suffering": the phrase "by me" means to ask how this fearlessness comes to be;
it exists solely because I, the Bodhisattva, do not observe the sound with an observing mind. Therefore, it is said, "by me. As for...
The following points should all be understood as follows: "Not observing the ear" means not allowing the faculty of hearing to pursue auditory objects.
"Observing with observation" means using the wisdom of contemplation to observe the nature of hearing itself.

Because one does not observe the ear, the faculty of hearing does not engage with external objects; furthermore, by observing with observation, the nature of hearing returns to its true source. Thus, one should know:
All the various sufferings and afflictions of all sentient beings arise because the sense organs (roots) take objects (dust) as their conditions, and the objects in turn interact with the organs.
As the organs and objects become entangled without ceasing, there consequently arise the sufferings of the three obstacles: afflictions, evil karma, and its karmic retribution.
The Bodhisattva does not merely contemplate sounds; rather, he contemplates the very observer. Not only this...
Distant indeed is suffering and affliction; yet one may also attain perfect penetration. Thus it is said, "It is by means of us.

Such is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s own practice. Therefore, among all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who possess suffering and affliction, those who contemplate the sound of his name do not contemplate through Avalokiteśvara, but rather contemplate the contemplator; they naturally attain the faculty of their own roots.

There is no dependence on sense objects; sense objects do not enter the faculties. When these two characteristics—the faculty and the object—no longer couple with one another, that which was falsely acquired vanishes, and true nature is revealed.
All three obstacles and their associated suffering and afflictions will naturally attain liberation. Therefore, it is said, "causing them [to attain this]. As for "observing their sounds":
if explained in detail, although this is practiced among sentient beings, one must necessarily fully understand the path of observation. If...
To speak briefly: it is precisely because it says "contemplate the sound of its name" that the meaning is contained therein.
By this principle, one should know that contemplating the sound is taught from the perspective of sentient beings, whereas the *Lotus Sūtra* is taught from the perspective of bodhisattvas.

Regarding the phrase "knowing and seeing" within the context of fearlessness toward the two calamities of fire: one should understand that this refers exclusively to the faculty of sight (*cakṣur-indriya*).

The single character "knowing" (*jñāna*) is used here merely as a conventional adjunct. Now, a person's seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing interact with the four great elements internally and externally.
Since seeing belongs to the mind (*citta*), and the mind itself belongs to the element of fire, the seeing of the eye likewise belongs to fire. It is by means of this [fire-like] eye that one sees.
Regarding all forms (*rūpa*): at their inception, they give rise to discrimination; in their culmination, they give rise to craving. Both discrimination and craving are afflictions (*kleśa*).
Once there are afflictions, there is the fire of affliction. With the presence of the fire of affliction, one inevitably creates evil karma (*karma*), whereby there is the fire of evil karma.
Given the existence of afflictions and evil karma, one inevitably undergoes retribution; thus, there is the fire of retribution. As for these...
The fire of afflictions extends to practitioners of the Two Vehicles; the fire of evil karma extends to ordinary beings of the six realms;
and the fire of retributive fruit extends up to the First Dhyāna. This is spoken from the perspective of pursuing delusion.

If, however, the Bodhisattva now knows and perceives the reversal of these [fires], they not only cease pursuing delusion, but also manifest the True. Where the true nature is manifested, the fire of afflictions—
This is precisely Prajñā. The fire of evil karma is itself liberation; the fire of retribution is itself the Dharmakāya.
In its essential nature, it is pure and inherently pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm. How could there be anything to be grasped as either true or false?
Therefore, it is said that "cognition and vision revolve back. Such is the self-cultivation of this Bodhisattva. By means of this, he is able to cause all [sentient beings] within the Dharma-realm...

Sentient beings who are within the fires of the three obstacles, upon hearing the sound of his name and title, shall likewise be able to shatter their deluded minds and manifest their true nature, so that they are no longer burned by the fires of the three obstacles.

Even if they should at times enter [the fire], the Bodhisattva’s power of compassion will protect and sustain them; thus the fire itself will be unable to burn them. Therefore, it is said: "To cause all..."

It is the same. One should understand that regarding fire, it is called "great" because while worldly fire only burns the physical body and the life of retribution (*vipākajīva*), the fire of afflictions (*kleśa*) and the like can burn the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) and the life of wisdom (*prajñājīva*); therefore, it is called great.
The same applies to the great waters below.
Regarding the fearlessness amidst the three fires of destruction: "observing and listening" means observing the nature of hearing itself, rather than pursuing the objects of sound.
"Returning" means that the nature of hearing turns back and returns to the true nature.
Thus, all the waters of afflictions, evil karma, and the retribution of the three obstacles are, in their very substance, identical to the three virtues of *prajñā*, liberation, and the *dharmakāya*.
There is nothing that is not the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha; it is entirely the wondrous nature of True Suchness (Tathatā). Therefore, it is said: "Listening and hearing revolve back.

This is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s own practice. Thus, because his faculty of hearing has been restored, he is able to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who are submerged in the waters of the three obstacles—whoever contemplates the sound of his name—to likewise have their listening and hearing revolve back.
Furthermore, they are not drowned by the waters of the three obstacles. Even if at some time they were to be submerged, the Bodhisattva’s power of compassion would embrace and protect them;
thus, the water itself would be unable to drown them. Therefore, it is said that "he causes all [beings] to be equal."

Regarding "cutting off extinction and so forth" within the fearlessness of the four ghost-king realms: delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is the mechanism of killing, and the deluded mind is the intent to kill.

If the mechanism of killing and the intent to kill do not arise, yet the causes and conditions for killing remain close at hand, one knows that sentient beings are constantly engaged in cycles of enmity and retribution;
this is truly because both the mechanism of killing and the intent to kill have not been severed. Now...
Since ancient times, the Bodhisattva has severed all murderous impulses and has likewise extinguished the very mind of killing;
thus, they shall never again act as an adversary in a cycle of karmic retribution. This is none other than the luminous and pure principle-body of the single Dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is said that they have "severed and extinguished" these tendencies. This is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s own practice. Since this is so—
The luminous and pure essence of reality pervades the entire dharma-realm; all sentient beings are my own essence of reality.
Therefore, it is possible for any sentient being within the dharma-realm who possesses murderous intent or a murderous mind to perceive the names and sounds of others.
Having spontaneously attained the cessation of delusive thoughts, the mind is free from malice; all karmic debts and grievances are completely liberated.

Thus, one does not enter the realm of ghosts. Even if one should happen to enter it, the Bodhisattva’s power of compassion will encompass and protect them, so that the ghosts themselves are unable to cause harm.
Therefore, it is said: "He causes all [sentient beings] to be equal."
Regarding "the hearing-perfuming and so forth" within the context of the five fearslessnesses amidst weapons and blades:

one should know that all sentient beings constantly encounter the infliction of blades, staves, and poisons because they follow after delusory objects due to the root of delusion. As they form attachments everywhere, they cannot abandon them on their own;
thus, they bring about the retributive fruits of various blades and staves. What is now called "perfuming the hearing" and so forth—the word "hearing" (*wen*) above refers to delusory hearing.
The "hearing" mentioned here is true hearing. "Perfuming" means that one perfumes deluded hearing with wondrous wisdom; "accomplishing" means that through deluded hearing, true hearing is perfected.
Therefore, it is said: "perfuming hearing to accomplish hearing. Previously, the six sense organs were entirely deluded in their functioning, each being obstructed and separated from the others.
Now that true hearing has been restored, the six organs are likewise dissolved and eliminated. Therefore, it is said: "the six organs are dissolved and restored."

Although the auditory object (śabda-viṣaya) has coming and going, its entire substance is empty and quiescent; now, the dissolution of the six sense organs is likewise entirely empty and quiescent like the auditory object.

Therefore, it is said that they are "the same as the hearing of sound. This refers to entering into one state without delusion, whereby those six faculties of cognition are simultaneously purified. Such is the accomplishment of this Bodhisattva’s own practice. By means of this, he is able to—
If sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who are being harmed by blades or clubs should hear the sound of his name,
their six sense faculties will likewise be restored and made identical to the hearing of sound, and those blades and clubs will all be shattered into pieces.

Therefore, it is said that they "can cause," and so forth. Even if there were to be an occasion when the calamities of war and weapons inevitably descend upon them, the Bodhisattva’s power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) will provide protection;
even if their body were to be cut, it would be like cutting water—without harm—and like blowing on light—it would remain unmoved.
Since it is like cutting water or blowing on light, although [the violence] is inflicted, it is as if it were not. Therefore, it is said:
To make them equal:
within the darkness and fearlessness of the six ghosts, those who have been permeated by hearing and so forth must know that all sentient beings each possess the original luminous self-nature.

Throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that does not perfectly illuminate; throughout the entire dharma-realm, there is nothing that is not perfectly manifest. To turn this into obscuration is to act in opposition to this truth.
If it is not manifested, it is obscure. For this reason, all sentient beings within the dharma-realm are in a state of obscurity; however, the Bodhisattva is not so.

Within the auditory nature that is neither born nor extinguished, they give rise to the contemplative wisdom that is neither born nor extinguished, which in turn perfumes the self-nature that is neither born nor extinguished.
By practicing and maintaining this for a long time, they enter deeply into their original state.
The singular primordial luminosity (*ekāgra-ādi-prakāśa*) is manifested from this; once this primordial luminosity is manifested, it in turn gives rise to wondrous wisdom (*prajñā*).
The power of this wondrous wisdom pervades the entire *dharmadhātu*, causing all the profound darkness within the *dharmadhātu* to be utterly destroyed so that it may never again be whole.
Therefore, it is said that "it is perfumed by hearing" (*śruta-vāsanā*), and so forth. This is the accomplishment of the Bodhisattva’s own practice, just as [all] darknesses are [dispelled].
"Nature" refers to yakṣas and the like. The wondrous wisdom of the bodhisattva illuminates the entire dharma-realm, yet yakṣas and the like cannot fully perceive it.

Therefore, when sentient beings within the dharma-realm contemplate the sound of his name, they too can hear its subtle resonance clearly and pervasively throughout the dharma-realm; however, those who are obscured in darkness, such as yakṣas, cannot approach it.

Even if there were those who approached [the Buddha] at that time, the Bodhisattva’s power of loving-kindness protected them; let alone not speaking of harm, they would not even have been able to see with their eyes.
Therefore, it is said that he "can cause" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "the nature of sound is equal" within the section on the Fearlessness of the Seven Shackles and Locks: sounds that have been heard since time immemorial were transformed by delusion;
now that the nature of sound is perfectly dissolved, the delusory objects have vanished—this is the aforementioned "vanishing of the objects.

Furthermore, the act of hearing that has existed since time immemorial was also transformed by delusion; now, as hearing is observed to turn back into itself, the true nature is revealed—this is the aforementioned "returning into."
It flows thus. In this way, both faculty and object vanish; subject and object are non-dual.

There is nothing that is not originally pure and fundamentally pervasive throughout the entire Dharma-realm; therefore, it is said that the nature of sound is such. This is how the Bodhisattva’s own practice is accomplished.
Since the faculties and objects are one and the same Dharma-realm, he is thereby able to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to contemplate his name.

Regarding the sounds of names and voices: when the nature of sound is completely dissolved and the faculties of hearing and seeing are turned back into their source, one cannot be bound by any fetters, shackles, or manacles;
therefore, it is said that [this practice] "can cause" such things.
Regarding the phrase "extinguishing sound" within the section on the fearlessness of the eight classes of thieves:
one must understand that the nature of all hearing is identical to the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) and is all-pervasive in its capacity to hear.

Nevertheless, because it has been defiled since beginningless time by the false objects of sound, the nature of hearing itself has also become delusory. Now, the Bodhisattva, through the power of contemplative wisdom, extinguishes that delusion.

The sensory objects (viṣaya) perfect the nature of hearing. Once the nature of hearing is perfected, it pervades the entire Dharma-realm; once the delusive objects are extinguished, they likewise pervade the entire Dharma-realm.
Since neither the faculties nor the objects are anything other than the Dharma-realm, the power of compassion realized therein must also pervade the Dharma-realm.
Therefore, it is said that "the sounds are extinguished," and so forth. Such is the accomplishment of this Bodhisattva’s own practice. Thus it is.
Since the power of compassion already pervades the Dharma-realm, all sentient beings within that realm are encompassed by my compassionate power.
Therefore, it enables all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm who contemplate the sound of his name to likewise extinguish deluded sounds and perfect their faculty of hearing.
The faculties and their objects are none other than the Dharma-realm; even if one travels upon perilous paths, even bandits cannot cause harm.
Therefore, it is said that "it can cause," and so forth.

Regarding the ninth [point], "Fearlessness amidst Greed": as for those who have cultivated their hearing and so forth, they must understand that the true essence of the auditory nature possessed by all sentient beings is perfectly detached from the sensory object of sound.
This is because the internal faculty of hearing acts as a medium, drawing in the external sensory object of sound—a deceptive thief—which plunders the family treasure of the true nature.
From this, the family treasure is lost; yet, only this subtle and wondrous [nature of the Bodhisattva remains].
The wisdom of contemplation perfumes the auditory faculty so that it neither arises nor ceases;

thus, when the auditory faculty is detached from the sensory object of sound, the delusive thieves of sound cannot plunder the true nature, which is the family treasure. Therefore, it is said, "perfuming the hearing," and so forth.
Such is the accomplishment of this Bodhisattva’s own practice. Furthermore, he is able to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm to contemplate his name.
As for sound, it can likewise permeate the faculty of hearing so that it is not carried away by forms, and it completely transcends all craving and desire.
Therefore, it is said that it "can cause" and so forth.

Regarding the "pure sound" among the ten forms of fearlessness concerning anger and resentment: one must understand that the anger and resentment of all sentient beings arise because the sense organs (*indriya*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) are intertwined and neither abandons the other.
If one can cause the sense organs and their objects to mutually vanish, anger and resentment will naturally be left behind.
Furthermore, one should know that all auditory objects (*śabda-viṣaya*) are fundamentally and originally pure; this is solely because the deluded sense organs have run wild.

Consequently, [the former] would likewise be overturned as false and illusory. Now, the Bodhisattvas of today are already able to fully comprehend that these are purely sounds of the fundamental nature (*dharmatā*) and not illusory sense-objects.

Since there are no illusory objects externally, there are likewise no illusory faculties internally. When the faculties and their objects are immediately and perfectly interfused, everything is nothing other than the pure and original state.
Since there is no faculty capable of confronting anything, how could there be an object to be confronted? Therefore, it is said to be "pure sound."
It is equal [to this]. Such is the accomplishment of this Bodhisattva’s own practice.

Furthermore, it enables all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who hear the sound of his name to realize the perfect interfusion of sense organs and objects, such that there is neither subject nor object, and all anger and resentment are completely eliminated.

Eleventh, regarding the fearlessness of light and darkness: as for "dissolving the defilements" and so forth, all sentient beings possess the originally inherent, intrinsically luminous nature of awareness (*prakṛti-bodha*).

This intrinsic luminosity has been obscured and rendered unmanifest due to involvement with delusory objects (*viṣaya*). Now, the Bodhisattva’s three wisdoms are perfectly observed and the three truths (*trisatya*) are perfectly revealed;
thus, all preceding sense-objects (*pūrva-viṣaya*) dissolve and fall away, and the original luminosity is thereby restored. Thus, if...
If body and mind are as one within the single, pure *dharmadhātu*, there is absolutely nothing to be grasped as "this" or "that.
It is like the illumination of lapis lazuli, which is not unpenetrating; it is like the transparency of lapis lazuli, wherein there is not a single obstruction.
Therefore, it is said that "dust is eliminated," and so forth. Such is the accomplishment of this Bodhisattva’s own practice; he is further able to cause the multitudes within the *dharmadhātu*...
Those who give rise to contemplation of the sound of his name and title likewise attain the dissolution of defilements and the revolution of luminosity, no different from lapis lazuli.

All obscurations of ignorance, such as the dullness of grasping at signs and the stupidity of lack of knowledge, as well as the nature of the hindrance of nescience (*avidyā*) and all types of *ātyantika* [obstructions], are forever and completely removed; hence it is said that "it can cause," and so forth. *Ātyantika* here means...
There is no nature of goodness. Furthermore, it is said that one does not delight [in it], because one practices with the lack of a nature of goodness and a lack of delight in *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding "melting the form" (*rongxing*) and so forth among the twelve fears of seeking a son: all the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*) that have existed from the beginning are none other than the pervasive totality of the Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*).
Yet, by pursuing delusive objects (*bhrāntaviṣaya*), the true essence of the faculty of hearing is lost, and the physical form consequently remains as a residue.

Obstructions no longer exist, and all is again harmoniously integrated. The Bodhisattva, by means of the subtle contemplation of the three wisdoms within a single mind, realizes that the nature of hearing is, in its very essence, neither arising nor ceasing. That which was previously lost has now been restored;

the true substance of the nature of hearing is fully recovered, and that which remained obstructed before is likewise harmoniously integrated. Thus it is said, "the form is restored," and so forth. From this point on, it is pure.

Purity is fundamentally such that it pervades the entire Dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). Without exerting effort within the site of practice (*maṇḍala*), one is able to enter into the mundane world without destroying that world.
This is what is meant by "the Dharma-realm uniting with the Dharma-realm. Whether "that" or "this," they are one and the same Dharma-realm;
how, then, could there be movement or destruction? Therefore, it is said to be "immovable," and so forth. Thus, without departing from the present...
Abiding therein, one is able to make offerings to as many Buddhas as there are atoms; without departing from a single thought-moment, one becomes a son of the Kings of Dharma.
This is the merit of making offerings to the Buddhas; this is the wisdom of being a Prince of the Dharma.
Both merit and wisdom are fully perfected, and the functions of this dharma-gate are unsurpassed. Therefore, it is said that "one is able to pervade," and so forth. This Bodhisattva...

Such was his own accomplishment. Furthermore, he is able to cause all sentient beings within the Dharma-realm who seek a male child—whoever hears the sound of his name—to likewise attain the state of a Bodhisattva.
Their physical forms are dissolved, their faculty of hearing is restored, and the worlds of the sites of enlightenment interpenetrate one another.
Thus they make offerings to the Buddhas to cultivate merit for the sake of the Dharma.
The Prince cultivated wisdom. Thus, a son endowed with merit and wisdom was born according to his own wishes; hence it is said, "able to cause," and so forth.

Regarding the thirteenth [section], "Seeking a Daughter Without Fear": as for the phrase "the six faculties" and so on, since the Bodhisattva’s faculty of hearing has already realized perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), the remaining...

The faculties (*indriya*) are likewise perfect. As it is said: "When one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation. Therefore, they are called the "perfect penetration of the six faculties.
Since these six faculties are perfectly penetrating and are all capable of clear illumination without obstruction, they are called "clear illumination without duality.
Because this perfect penetration includes everything without exception, it is said to "contain the worlds of the ten directions. Because this clear illumination—

Second, because there is nothing that is not fully penetrated, it is called the "Great Perfect Mirror. Although it contains the ten realms, it is such that when one speaks of the myriad dharmas, not even a single speck of dust can be established;
this is the True Suchness Tathāgatagarbha, the true emptiness wherein all things are simultaneously empty.

Furthermore, it is established as the "Perfect Mirror," wherein the myriad phenomena of the universe are naturally and simultaneously manifested; this is the non-emptiness wherein all things are simultaneously existent.

This is the *ālayavijñāna*. Taken together, it is called the "empty *tathāgatagarbha*," because the *tathāgatagarbha* of true emptiness can contain the ten realms and is naturally able to receive and accept all the secret Dharma-gates of the Tathāgatas within even a single mote of dust.

Furthermore, by establishing the Great Perfect Mirror based on the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*, one is able to naturally accord with and never lose any of the secret dharma-gates possessed by all Tathāgatas, even those as minute as motes of dust. To synthesize these points, it is said that one "accords with" and so forth.

Alternatively, it may be established as the inconceivable contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) capable of observation, which is the Great Perfect Mirror; this is the inconceivable empty *tathāgatagarbha*.
This is the realm of principle that is observed. It is the state wherein object and wisdom are of one suchness (*yixu*), and subject and object are non-dual.
Because wisdom is like the realm, one is naturally capable of receiving and accepting the dharma-gates of the *rajas*-sized Tathāgatas in accordance with them.

Because the realm is like wisdom, one likewise naturally receives and accords with the dharma-gates of the *rajas*-sized Tathāgatas without error. Regarding the term "receiving and acceding" (*chengshun*): [it refers to] the *rajas*-sized Tathāgatas...
That which is taught and realized is precisely what the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has cultivated and awakened to;
that which the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara has cultivated and awakened to is precisely what the dust-like Tathāgatas have taught and realized.

Since cause and fruit are equal and non-dual, the secret Dharma-gates possessed by those who have attained the fruit should naturally be received by those on the path of the cause without fail. This is...

This is for the sake of compliance. Such is the personal practice of this Bodhisattva. Being able to comply with and not oppose the Tathāgata, he possesses the gentle virtue of the feminine principle (the Earth).
Furthermore, by receiving and retaining the Dharma-gates without losing them, he possesses the capable duties of the wife’s way.
Therefore, he is able to cause those within the Dharma-realm who seek a woman [to find one].
Those who give birth while contemplating the sound of his name and title shall likewise be like Bodhisattvas:

their six sense faculties will be perfectly penetrating and luminous, non-dual, encompassing the ten realms, establishing the perfect mirror, and receiving the Dharma-gates with compliant grace and without error.
Thus, the women who cherish and revere him with form will naturally have their wishes fulfilled upon giving birth; hence it is said that he "is able to cause," and so forth.

Regarding the fourteenth section, "The Fearlessness of Proclaiming Names," it may also be divided into three parts. First, from "These three" downwards, the teachings of the various sages are described.
Second, from "By me" downwards, one's own wondrous efficacy is clarified. Third, from "It can cause" downwards, the equality and non-differentiation are clarified.
As for the teachings of the various sages, it goes without saying that this applies to the world-transcending sages and worthies.
The sages and worthies of the world are none other than manifestations of the teachings of the supramundane sages.
The first is Confucius, who established the models of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, and wisdom for the world; in Buddhism, he is the Bodhisattva Mañjuśrī (Niu-tong).
Thus, the *Acaranga Sutra* states: "The present Mañjuśrī is that very Zhongni. The second is Laozi, who...
Regarding those who established pure and profound models for the world: in Buddhism, this is Kāśyapa Bodhisattva.
Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* (Wuxing jing) states: "The present Kāśyapa is that Laozi. Third is Yanzǐ.
Regarding those who established models for the world through their sagacity and keen intelligence: in Buddhism, this is Jingguang Bodhisattva. Thus, the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:
The present Jingguang is that former Yan Hui. By this, it is clear that the three teachings share a common source yet diverge into different branches.

However, as their gateways and courtyards differ, their pedagogical methods are distinct. Thus, the Buddhist school says: "To expound the dharmas that express [the truth] and transform the mind that clings to objects is called 'Teaching' (jiao).
The Ruist school says: "'Teaching' means emulation; when those above act and those below emulate them, it constitutes Teaching. The Daoist school...
It is said: "Abiding in the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), one acts without speaking of teachings. This is stated in reference to China in contrast to India;

other cases may be understood by analogy. Thus, it is called these "three grades. Regarding the "wondrous function of oneself," it is called "developing the wondrous ear-gate" because the nature of hearing is fundamentally the perfect penetration (*pariśuddha*) of non-arising and non-ceasing; one should always cause this to be realized as the originally possessed state.
Because it is inconceivable, it is said that he "developed the wondrous faculty of the ear. As for the phrase "thereafter," previously he had not attained this Dharma-gate of the ear-faculty;

thus, whenever he made a discrimination, he would immediately become attached to craving. Now that he has realized the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, his entire body and mind naturally cease to discriminate, yet they can pervade the entire Dharma-realm; they naturally cease to crave, yet they can contain all phenomena.

The realms are such that the large and small merge, and the one and the many are without obstruction; they cannot be conceived by the mind nor discussed in words. Therefore, it is said, "and thereafter," and so forth.
Within this state of equality and non-differentiation, one is able to cause the equality of merits to be without difference, and the equality of names and titles such as "I" to be without difference.
This is because of the equality of our correct illumination being without difference. The intent is that which belongs to me—
Regarding the perfect penetration realized through cultivation, although individuals may be one or many, their perfect penetration does not differ.
The essence of perfect penetration is solely the single *tathāgatagarbha* nature; how could there be any distinction of one or many, or any separation between self and other?
Therefore, the merit of upholding my name is equal, equal, non-dual, and non-dual with the merit of upholding the names of all those [other Buddhas].
The comparison in the "Universal Gateway" chapter of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka Sūtra* carries this same meaning. Regarding the three concluding summaries, the phrase "is named, etc.

generally summarizes the fourteen fearlessnesses. Alternatively, it may summarize only the fourteenth [fearlessness], as it can encompass the entire Dharma-gate of universal penetration, which extensively reaches all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm; hence it is said that "blessings are complete for all sentient beings."

The "Three or Four Inconceivable Sections" is divided into two parts. First is the general explanation, beginning with "The World-Honored One, etc. The second part consists of specific indications, beginning with "The Equality, etc.
Within the initial general explanation, "Inconceivable Wondrous Virtue" is like the single moon in the sky whose reflection reaches ten thousand waters;
the water does not rise upward, nor does the moon descend downward, yet they naturally respond and intersect in the Way, beyond the reach of mental calculation.
This is merely a discussion of terminology. Second, the detailed exposition is divided into four parts, the sequence of which can be seen [in the text].
In all four, one first clarifies the realization (*prāpti*) and subsequently clarifies the sublime function (*vṛtti*). Regarding the first, it causes one to attain great mastery;

this is because we have realized it, and thus it is our own sublime function. Within the section on realization, the upper "sublime" character (*miao*) refers to the contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) that performs the observation, while the lower "sublime" character refers to...

Regarding the nature of hearing that is the object of contemplation: because the nature of hearing is itself both arising-and-ceasing and fundamentally non-arising-and-non-ceasing, one takes this very nature of hearing and develops it into the contemplative wisdom of non-arising-and-non-ceasing to serve as the illumination of contemplation.

Thus, the nature of hearing—which is non-arising-and-non-ceasing—manifests in its own essence. Such is the nature of hearing that is the object of contemplation: it is both arising-and-ceasing and non-arising-and-non-ceasing.
That which cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words is the wisdom that is able to contemplate; this is precisely birth-and-death as non-birth-and-death.
Because these things that cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words are integrated, it is called the "wondrously wondrous hearing-mind.

Previously, the nature of hearing was not manifest, for the faculty of hearing depended upon the object of sound. Today, since the nature of hearing has become manifest, the delusive objects—[the false dust]—...

That from which they were lost is the mind-essence; thus it is said that the essence of the mind abandons hearing. In this way, when one faculty returns to its source, all six faculties are liberated;

hence the mention of "seeing, hearing," and so forth. Upon reaching this state, it is natural that the six faculties function interchangeably, being nothing other than the perfectly interfused Dharma-realm.

Therefore it is said that a single perfect fusion is achieved, wherein no delusion remains unshattered and no obstruction remains unremoved, such that there is no wealth of merit and Dharma that is not attained.

Because it is fully endowed [with these qualities], it is called the "Pure Jewel-Awareness. If this passage is combined with the preceding instruction on practicing contemplation according to the teaching:

"First attaining" (*chū-haku*) is the heading corresponding to "initially at the... (*sho-o*); "the essence of mind" (*shin-sei*) and following is the explanation corresponding to "that which is entered" (*sho-nyū*).
The phrase "forming one" (*cheng yixia*) is a summary that clarifies birth, cessation, and so forth. Within the "sublime function" (*miaoyong*), there is thus our "form-teaching" (*xingjiao*).

The "ability to speak" and so forth constitute the "sound-teaching" (*shengjiao*). Although what is clarified below stops at form alone, there has never been a manifestation of form without the preaching of the Dharma;
therefore, both are indicated together. The sublime countenance as well as secret mantras (*guhyamantra*) are all realized through the totality of the whole body. They, in turn...
It is manifested from the inherent nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, it is said that "appearance" refers to the wondrous appearance, and "mantra" refers to the secret divine mantra.
That which is called *śakara* at the beginning means "firm"; it refers to the indestructible firmness of the vajra.
That which is called *mudrā* for the arms means "seal-pattern," because there are seal-patterns upon the arms. That which is called "pure" for the eyes—
As for "Jewel" (Ratna), it is because the five eyes are seen within a single eye. Its head serves as the totality of the six sense organs, manifesting the Dharmakāya.
Its arms possess the power of uplifting and lifting, manifesting liberation (vimukti). Its eyes possess the virtue of illuminating, manifesting prajñā.
As for the mention of eighty-four thousand in each case, this refers to the eighty-four thousand [afflictions] that are to be destroyed.
The entirety of the thousand afflictions, up to the eighty-four thousand cycles of birth and death, is the manifestation of the Great Function of the Three Virtues.
