Since its head is the Dharma-body, it manifests eighty-four thousand heads in order to cause all sentient beings throughout the Dharma-realm who experience karmic retribution to fully realize and enter the wondrous virtue of the supreme Dharma-body. For this reason...

The arms are liberation itself. Therefore, because he wishes to cause all sentient beings of evil karma within the Dharma-realm to realize and enter the wondrous virtue of supreme liberation in their entirety, he manifests arms numbering eighty-four thousand.
Since the eyes are *prajñā* (wisdom), because he wishes to cause all sentient beings of affliction within the Dharma-realm to [realize it] in their entirety...
Because he has realized and entered the sublime virtue of unsurpassed *prajñā*, his manifested eyes are likewise eighty-four thousand.
"Or compassionate" (*ci*) serves as a general conclusion for what follows: if there are sentient beings who are weak and yielding, he manifests a compassionate countenance to gather them in;
hence it says "or compassionate. If there are sentient beings who are violent and aggressive, he manifests a majestic countenance to subdue them; hence it says "or majestic. If...
To sentient beings with distracted minds, he bestows the power of concentration (*samādhi*) to restrain them; hence it is said, "or concentration.
To sentient beings who are dull and obscured, he bestows the power of wisdom (*prajñā*) to illuminate them; hence it is said, "or wisdom.
Such qualities as compassion and majesty, concentration and wisdom, are all inconceivable, wondrous functions for the protection and salvation of sentient beings; hence it is said:

The phrase "rescue and protection" and so forth provides a general explanation. In the middle [section], it is called "Wondrous Virtue of Non-action" (*anabhisaṃskāra-guṇa*), while here it is called "Attaining Great Sovereignty.
Their significance is one and the same. Second, it should be understood as causing fearlessness.

Third, regarding "causing the relinquishing of stinginess and greed," the term "causing all" means causing all sentient beings to relinquish all feelings (*vedanā*). These include painful feelings, pleasant feelings, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feelings.
All perceptions are entirely non-perceptions; even the non-perception of non-perception is itself not perceived. In this way, all stinginess and greed are without exception destroyed.
Therefore, it is said that "all are made equal. Regarding the fourth [point], "fulfilling what is sought," the phrase "I have attained" and so forth refers to this.
Someone may raise this doubt: "If one has already attained the Buddha-mind and realized the ultimate, why should one further make offerings to the various Tathāgatas?

It is simply not understood that Buddhas likewise make offerings to Buddhas for two reasons. First, while sentient beings practice by following the current of saṃsāra, Bodhisattvas have already realized the path by flowing against that current.
Those who flow against the current do so precisely because they wish to further broaden their practice. For...

Therefore, one makes offerings to the Buddha. Second, regarding the ultimate attainment (*niṣṭhā-gata*): although within that ultimate state one has only attained partial realization (*pradeśa-prativedha*), it is not said that one "directly realizes the ultimate," but rather that one "realizes the ultimate.
One must still practice further deeds to advance toward the supreme fruit (*phala-koṭi*). For this reason, one makes offerings to the Buddha;
thus it is said, "I have attained [it]," and so forth.

In the second part, the response to the question: regarding the phrase "I have followed," by reversing the hearing to hear the nature of hearing itself, one takes the nature of hearing as the object of the mind;
once this nature of hearing is revealed, what is called birth and death is extinguished and quiescent extinction manifests. From this, wondrous functions arise.
"One should manifest the thirty-two responses" means that one immediately manifests the thirty-two responses. "One should manifest the fourteen fearlessnesses" means that one immediately manifests...
Regarding the fourteen fearlessnesses (*vaiśāradya*), "that which should be manifested through the four inconceivables" refers to the manifestation of the four inconceivables.

These are established in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) and appear according to the capacities of sentient beings; they do not rely on artificial fabrication nor require strenuous effort. This is what constitutes sovereign mastery (*vaśitā*). Therefore, it says, "I have [attained them]," and so forth.

As for "entering through causes," this means that characteristics are identical to the nature. Since the nature of hearing has already entered into both nature and characteristics, [there is no longer any distinction].
Second, it is called "the mark of entering the stream.

Third, it is called "the emergence of the name. Regarding the passage beginning with "The World-Honored One," etc., it means that because that Buddha, due to my initial entry into the stream within hearing such that the objects were lost, and continuing until birth-and-death were extinguished and quiescent extinction manifested before him, he immediately conferred upon me the prediction [of enlightenment] and named me Avalokiteśvara.

IV. At that time, the World-Honored One departed. This is the text concerning the manifestation of auspicious signs and the seal of approval. It is divided into two parts: first, from "At that time" onwards, prior to the sealing;
second, from "Immediately" onwards, after the sealing. Within the first part: regarding the Master [Guanyin], this is the general seal of the perfect penetration of the twenty-five sages.
How is it known that this is a general seal for all the sages? Because light was emitted from his five limbs, which constitutes the five... [text fragment ends].
Since they are said to be equally liberated, when these are mutually combined, they form twenty-five. This is why it is called the "Universal Seal.

Thus one knows that among the twenty-five kinds of perfect penetration—whether in this land or other lands, whether by those on the path of cause or those who have attained the fruit—all without exception cultivate this and all without exception realize this.
For this reason, the Buddhas of their own lands emit light, which flows down and bathes those others.

The crowns of the Buddhas of that land and the crowns of the various Bodhisattvas are illuminated by the light emitted from the Buddhas of this land, which in turn drenches the crowns of the Buddhas and the Great Beings (Mahāsattvas) of this land.

This precisely symbolizes that the various Dharma-gates of perfect penetration represent the oneness of the Buddha and sentient beings, the non-duality of self and other, the common source of past and present, and the equality between teacher and disciple. Below the forest trees, there is a separate seal for visualization.

The sounds represent the Bodhisattva’s perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*). The forest trees and so forth symbolize that once the faculty of hearing has attained perfect penetration, the entire Dharma-realm is *prajñā*.
This is what is meant by "the nature of sound is true emptiness; the nature of emptiness is true sound. Therefore, it says "forest trees and so forth."
"Intermingling light," and so forth, indicates that having attained the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, the entire dharma-realm is the Dharma-body.
This is what is meant by "the true emptiness of the nature of form, and the true form of the nature of emptiness. Thus it is said, "intermingling light," and so on.

These various terms clarify the benefits obtained by the great assembly. Since the assembly beheld the auspicious sign of the seal, they immediately attained the perfect penetration that is sealed. Therefore...
It is said that these various [attainments] are also called the Vajra Samādhi because the faculty of hearing is perfected and pervasive.

In the latter part of the seal, the phrase "at that very moment" and so forth signifies that from the Heaven of the Ultimate Truth (Paramārtha-dhātu), one initiates inconceivable and wondrous practices to accomplish the dharma-wealth of merit.
That blue, yellow, and white represent the forty stages. That they are interspersed and intermingled represents that at each stage, by means of the faculty of hearing...
"Rooting in wondrous conduct" refers to the process of practice. "The ten directions, etc. signifies advancing from the forty stages to achieve the fruit of the sevenfold eternal abiding;
for the essence of the sevenfold eternal abiding pervades the Dharma-realm. "This Sahā world, etc. signifies that birth and death have been extinguished. "Only seeing, etc.
signifies that quiescent extinction has manifested before one. "Chanting the Brahma hymns, etc. signifies having attained the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty.
This Dharma-gate must always circulate so that, in future generations and in the worlds of gods and humans, each may cultivate and realize the nature-endowed Dharma.
Fifth, "At this, the Tathāgata departed" refers to the passage where Mañjuśrī selects [the disciples]. This is divided into three parts; first, "At this, [he] departed."
First, the issuance of the command; second, Mañjuśrī’s departure and his reception of the mandate; third, the great assembly below attaining benefit. The first [section] further has two parts:
first, the command to testify that there is no superiority or inferiority, as in "In this regard, they are equal"; second, the command to select those who have a specific reason, as in "I now...
In the first of these, the command to Mañjuśrī for the purpose of selection is given because Mañjuśrī clearly perceives the Buddha-nature.
Possessing the wisdom of both the provisional and the ultimate, one will surely be able to penetrate all gateways to perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-dharmamukha*).
To whom does this correspond as the appropriate teaching for Ānanda and for sentient beings of future generations? For this reason, the Tathāgata commanded Mañjuśrī.

Regarding those [who ask] "Who is equal to whom?"—the meaning is that among the practices cultivated by the various sages, there appears to be superiority and inferiority, yet in reality there is no superiority or inferiority; there appears to be distinction, yet in reality there is no distinction. Why is this so?

For this reason, although there are those who enter through the analysis of form (*rūpa*), those who enter through the substance of form, those who enter through the sequential, and those who enter through the perfect fusion (*yuanrong*), that which they enter is the same *tathāgatagarbha*.

For those who enter through perfect fusion, it is the *tathāgatagarbha* within the Perfect [Truth]; for those who enter through the sequential, it is merely the *tathāgatagarbha* within the Middle [Truth]. As for the substance...

Those who enter through form contain the nature of the central treasury within it; those who enter by analyzing form depart from the nature of the central treasury that transcends both annihilation and permanence.
It is like many people ascending together into a single hall: upon that hall, there is fundamentally no distinction between center and periphery;

yet for those who have ascended, there are simply differences such as left, right, front, and back. Thus it is said, "those [who enter] equally. Regarding the second [section], from "Ānanda attained awakening" onwards...

"Corresponding phrase" (*yingju*): "When" (*dang*) here means "in contrast to" (*dui*). The intended meaning is that within the twenty-five methods of practice, one must consider who is capable of corresponding to the faculties of those present and ready for instruction so as to easily attain accomplishment, and who is capable of corresponding to the capacities of sentient beings in future generations so as to easily attain accomplishment;
thus it says, "I now," and so forth. From this, one knows that among the various sages, there is originally no single perfect method of penetration (*yuan-tong*).

Regarding their superiority and inferiority, as well as their distinctions, [the Buddha] merely wishes to guide sentient beings according to their capacities; this is why it is necessary to select and discern them.

This section on Mañjuśrī receiving his mandate is divided into two parts: first, from "Mañjuśrī" downward, the Sūtra’s author describes the scene; second, from "Awakening delusion" downward, Mañjuśrī himself performs the selection.
Within the first part, the description of the scene, the phrase "receiving the Buddha's spiritual power" indicates that while each of the sages has already presented their own practice...
In the realization of the Tathāgata, there is neither superiority nor inferiority; yet Mañjuśrī selected the ear-faculty’s perfect penetration from among twenty-four dharmas.
Had it not been for the majestic power and spiritual authority of the Tathāgata, I fear that the various sages would have been unable to avoid feelings of shame.
Mañjuśrī could not entirely avoid having a sense of pride; for this reason, he spoke these verses by receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power.

This section consists of three parts: first, the statement of intent; second, the selection and exclusion; third, the summary. 1. Statement of Intent: "The ocean of awakening... and so forth. 2. Selection and Exclusion: "The perception of form... and so forth. 3. Summary.
Homage is paid and the text proceeds. This section has two parts: first, the description of the cultivation of perfect penetration;

second, the description of the selection of perfect penetration. The first part has three sub-sections: first, a direct elucidation of the fundamental substance, namely "The ocean of awareness," etc.;

second, the arising of delusion from the truth, namely "The original luminosity," etc.; third, the fact that the substance of delusion is fundamentally non-existent, namely "From emptiness arises," etc. The first of these directly elucidates the fundamental substance.

Regarding the "Essence" (*tǐ*): One should raise the question, "Within the fundamental essence of the awakened nature (*xingjué běntǐ*), how could there be any 'perfect penetration' (*yuántōng*) to be cultivated?
It is only because of a single moment of non-awakening that delusion arises from the Truth; therefore, one must practice cultivation to return to it.

Thus it is said, "The ocean of awakening" (*juéhǎi*), and so forth. The word "ocean" (*hǎi*) is a metaphor. Some take it as a direct explanation of the Dharma, which is incorrect. As the following text states:
Is this not like a single bubble arising from the sea? The meaning is that the nature of the great ocean is not only utterly limpid and clear, but also utterly complete and perfect.

Now, the essence of the awakened nature is likewise as utterly limpid and clear as the great ocean, and as utterly complete and perfect as the great ocean; therefore, it is said that "the nature of the ocean of awakening is limpid."

"Perfectly still. The "clarity and perfection" of the preceding phrase refers to being quiescent yet illuminating; the "perfect stillness" of the following phrase refers to being illuminating yet quiescent.
In essence, wherever there is profound stillness, there is perfect fullness; wherever there is perfect fullness, there is profound stillness.

However, the true nature of the awakened body has from the beginning been both quiescent and capable of illumination, and illuminating and capable of quiescence. These aspects are mutually integrated and mutually transcended, beyond the reach of thought or speech.
To deliberate upon this is to realize that it is the primordial and wondrous source. Thus, what perfect penetration could there be within such a fundamental substance that might be cultivated?

The true luminosity of the fundamental substance is like this. Second, regarding the arising of delusion from truth: the substance of the self-nature of awakened luminosity is inherently and originally luminous;
this is called "primordial luminosity. If one were to give rise to a single luminosity capable of illumination, then there would immediately be a single...
The darkness that is illuminated exists because its capacity to illuminate arises from delusion; thus, that which is illuminated also exists through delusion.
Since both are established as being delusory, once the delusory darkness of the object is established, the delusory brightness of the subject immediately perishes.
Therefore, it is said that "original brightness" and so forth. This is in contrast to the preceding passage concerning the "inherently luminous nature of awareness."

"Original brightness is true," as was previously stated regarding the nature of awakening being inherently luminous. The character "illuminate" (*zhào*) refers to the luminosity of the capacity to illuminate, as was previously stated regarding delusion acting as the luminosity of awakening.
The two characters "that which is produced" (*shēng suǒ*) refer to how awakening is not that which is illuminated, yet because of illumination, an object is established, as was previously stated.

The phrase "the object being established" (*suǒ lì*) refers to how the object has already been falsely established, thereby giving rise to your false subjectivity, as was previously stated. Delusion...

Regarding the phrase "delusively there is empty space and so forth": this means that prior to the establishment of subject and object, the nature that exists is primordial luminosity (*ādi-prakāśa*), and the emptiness that exists is true emptiness (*tathatā-śūnyatā*).

At the very moment delusive subject and object are established, that primordial luminosity is inverted into ignorance (*avidyā*), and that true emptiness is inverted into inert emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). Therefore, it is said: "due to delusive confusion, there is empty space."

Emptiness. Since there is both the ignorance that acts as the perceiving subject and the stubborn emptiness that serves as the perceived object, these one subject and one object become mutually entangled.
Thus, the world of flux and the realms of spatial direction are established upon this very occasion.

Therefore it is said: "Relying on space, worlds are established. These two phrases are like the previous discussion on how there is neither identity nor difference, wherein blazing illumination constitutes difference.
Since there is both empty space and the world, there is the insentient realm, which is what is called the "retributive environment" (*niśraya-vipāka*).
Furthermore, regarding sentient beings, which refers to their primary retribution (*vipāka*), they are established upon a single basis and a single retribution.
This is accomplished at the moment when ignorance and delusive thoughts coagulate and solidify; thus it is said, "when thought solidifies," and so forth.

The "solidification" here does not refer to the clarity of profound stillness, but rather to the coagulation of delusion. It is like the aforementioned state of sentient beings who are neither identical nor different.

Regarding "the three delusions are fundamentally non-existent within the midst" and "emptiness arises, etc.": this refers to the fact that the nature of awareness (*jñāna*) is originally a wondrously pure and luminous essence.
Because of a single moment of non-awakening, there subsequently arise the ignorance that acts as the subject (*ālambaka*) and the empty space that serves as its object (*ālambana*).
This empty space arises from within the great nature of awakening. To illustrate this by means of a metaphor, it is like [waves arising] from within the great ocean.
A single bubble arises. Although the single bubble is small, the entire bubble is the sea; although empty space is illusory, the entirety of the illusion is the Truth.

Therefore, it is said that "space arises," and so forth. Since empty space has arisen, both the primary retribution of sentient beings and the secondary retribution of the lands—all of which are subject to outflows (*sāsrava*)—arise in dependence upon empty space.
Therefore, it is said that "outflows [arise]," and so forth. Since it has already been stated that "space arises,"...

The Great Awakened One is like the ocean, and [the individual self] is like a single bubble. When the bubble ceases, there is not even the slightest mark of cessation to be found, because the bubble is itself the ocean.
As for empty space, it does not await cessation; it was originally and fundamentally non-existent, because the delusion is itself the truth.

Therefore it is said: "When the bubble ceases, the void was originally non-existent. Since even the empty space that can give rise [to phenomena] cannot be found, how could the three realms of sentient beings and lands—which are produced from it—possibly exist?
Thus it is said: "How much more so the various three realms of existence. In this way, one knows that the essence of delusion is fundamentally non-existent from the beginning.
Second, in the section describing the selection of the perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa*), regarding the phrase "returning to the source," etc.:

Having previously explained that delusion arises from the truth and that the nature of delusion is fundamentally non-existent, one who wishes to turn back from delusion and return to their own original nature must realize that this very essence is primordial clarity, lacking even the slightest differentiation. Therefore, it is said: "Returning to the source, the nature is non-dual.
Nevertheless, returning to the source requires expedient means (*upāya*), and these expedients are by no means limited to one or two; hence it is said: "Expedient means have many gates."
The "many gates" refer to the cultivation of the twenty-five sages. They were all sages; regarding this self-nature (*svabhāva*), there was not a single aspect through which they did not penetrate.
Therefore, it is said that the nature of the sages has nothing it does not penetrate. It is precisely because there is nothing they do not penetrate that [this is so].
That which is practiced by the various sages may be compliant, yet contrary to what is practiced by Avalokiteśvara;

or that which is practiced by Avalokiteśvara may be compliant, yet contrary to what is practiced by the various sages. Thus, whether compliant or contrary, there is not a single instance that is not a skillful means.

Therefore, it is said that both the "conforming" and "reversing" [practices] are skillful means (*upāya*). Thus, one should know that the practices cultivated by the twenty-five sages—both conforming and reversing—are all termed skillful means.

As for those such as Ānanda in the present and sentient beings of future generations who are at the stage of the initial resolve (*ādikarmika*), there will inevitably be differences in the speed of their progress depending on how they rely upon these methods;
hence the phrase "the initial resolve, etc. Regarding this slowness and speed, it is as previously explained regarding the attainment of *anupassanā* (contemplation).

The distinction between perfect penetration and non-perfect penetration is said to differ by factors of ten million times a kalpa. Thus, one knows that following [the path] is swift while going against it is slow.

Such being the case, if one wishes to reach those who are suited to the teaching and those in the final age, one must carefully discern and select among these variations of opposition and conformity, slowness and speed.
For this reason, I have first set forth the meaning in this manner.
Second, regarding the selection: one should know that this selection does not mean that sentient beings lack perfect penetration.
For instance, Mañjuśrī clearly perceived the Buddha-nature, yet the Tathāgata further stated, "In their practice, there is truly no superiority or inferiority.
How could one contradict what was seen and oppose what was commanded by claiming that the various sages were not [enlightened]? It was merely for the sake of Ānanda and others in the present...

Now, in this degenerate age, the faculties of sentient beings vary—some are sharp and some dull; their capacities range from great to small—and thus it is impossible to accommodate everyone individually.

This is why there must be a process of selection. One should understand that what is being selected concerns the capacity, not the Sage; it concerns the emotional state, not the Dharma. As it is said: "The Dharma has neither greatness nor smallness;
greatness and smallness reside in the emotional state. The Sage has neither sharpness nor dullness; sharpness and dullness reside in the capacity. This is the general principle.
This consists of three parts: first, the exclusion of what is not; second, the identification of what is; third, the concluding demonstration. The first part has four sections:

first, "Furthermore, as for form-perception," which excludes the contemplation of the six sense objects (*ṣaḍ-viṣaya*); second, "as for seeing-nature," which excludes the contemplation of the five sense faculties (*pañca-indriya*);

third, "as for consciousness-seeing," which excludes the contemplation of the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*); fourth, "If one uses," which excludes the contemplation of the seven elements (*sapta-dhātu*). Regarding the first of these:

This is divided into six parts, the sequence of which may be seen. From the verse on the discernment and contemplation of form (*rūpa*) onwards, up to the verse on the discernment and contemplation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) and so forth, one should in all cases take the perfect and pervasive functioning of the ear-faculty as the basis for such discernment and selection.
The intent is that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha never fails to possess these three; yet, among the twenty-four dharmas, there appear to be instances where one or more are lacking.
2. As for those who are deficient, they may practice; however, only sages are capable of this, while beginners cannot do so themselves.
This is why there are always phrases such as "how" and "what. Within the initial section on the contemplation of form (*rūpa*), one should first raise the point:
"Is it through the *upaniṣad* (proximate cause) of what is contemplated that one attains realization of the Perfect Penetration? This refers to the Sage.
This is why he is able to do so. As for Ānanda and ordinary sentient beings, it is feared they would not be able. Why is this?

It is because of their perceptions of form (*rūpa-saṃjñā*), and so forth. These perceptions of form and the like are entirely formed through the conjunction of the characteristics of ignorance and perception.

The mind that seeks awakening cannot penetrate through to integration; therefore, it is called "perception of form" (*rūpa-saṃjñā*). Since there is no penetration, there is no thoroughgoing understanding.
That which is not thoroughly understood is necessarily non-constant. If these three factors are not fully present, one cannot attain perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna*);
hence the words "how could it be," etc. The twenty-three verses that follow should all be interpreted according to this principle.
[The character] "tián" (怗). Second, examining the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*). This refers to that which Śāriputra examined to realize perfect penetration.

Regarding the phrase "but these names, phrases, and phonemes (*nāma-pada-vyañjana*)," the character "yī" (伊) should be read as "tā" (彼). A name (*nāma*) expresses intrinsic nature; a phrase (*pada*) expresses distinctions;
and a phoneme (*vyañjana*), which is the syllable, serves as the basis for these two. Thus, one knows that a name is not a phrase, and a phrase is not a phoneme; hence it says "one."
This does not include all [of them]. Third, it excludes those who contemplate the sense-object of fragrance, such as the one who realized perfect penetration by contemplating the "Array of Fragrance.
Fourth, it excludes those who contemplate the sense-object of taste, such as the brothers Bhaiṣajyarāja and Bhaiṣajyasamudgata who realized perfect penetration by contemplating it.
Fifth, it excludes those who contemplate the sense-object of touch, such as Bhadrapāla who realized perfect penetration by contemplating it. Sixth, it excludes those who contemplate...

The dharma-object (*dharmāyatana*). This is that which Kāśyapa contemplated and realized as his perfect penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-abhisamaya*). Regarding the term "dharma" and so forth: the dharma-object is the residual shadow of the five sense-objects;
therefore, it is said that the dharma is called the internal object. Nevertheless, the dharma-object serves as the basis for the mental faculty (*manas-indriya*).
Thus, the dharma-object (dharmāyatana) is that which is relied upon. Therefore it is said: "To rely on an object, there must be a locus.

Since there is a dharma-object as the basis relied upon, there must necessarily be the mental faculty (manas-indriya) as the subject that relies. This constitutes the relationship of subject and object. That which belongs to the object cannot be the subject; that which belongs to the subject cannot be the object.

Furthermore, among those that serve as the basis, there are three types: wholesome, unwholesome, and neutral. There are cases where [a basis] pertains to the wholesome but cannot pertain to the unwholesome or the neutral;
likewise, there are cases where it pertains to the neutral but cannot pertain to the wholesome or the unwholesome.

Thus, the basis and that which is based upon it do not pervade one another; therefore, it is said that "the basis and the based do not pervade each other. Second, the five faculties are distinguished as five. Next...
First, the observation of the eye faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) is excluded; this was the faculty observed by Aniruddha through which he realized perfect penetration.
Second, the observation of the nose faculty (*ghrāṇa-indriya*) is excluded; this was the faculty observed by Cūḍapanthaka through which he realized perfect penetration.
Third, the examination of the tongue-faculty (*jihvā-indriya*), which is that by which Kūṭadanta attained realization of perfect penetration.
"The tongue is not a sense-field without a source" is a textual corruption; it should read, "The tongue-faculty is not without a source.

Fourth, the examination of the body-faculty (*kāya-indriya*), which is that by which Pilindavatsa attained realization of perfect penetration. "The body and [the objects] are equal" means that "equal" (*tong*) implies union (*he*). "Each" implies...
"Separated. This means that the body which perceives and the touch which is perceived must be in contact for cognition to occur;
if separated, there is no cognition. Between contact and separation, cognition cannot be all-pervasive; hence it is said, "the body and [the object] are equal [in their limitations].

Since the body and touch each have their own boundaries and limits, how could they be mysteriously and perfectly interfused? Therefore, it is said, "their boundaries do not merge in mystery. (The fifth clarification.)

Regarding the contemplation of the mind-faculty (*manas-indriya*), it refers to those who have realized perfect penetration through the object of their contemplation. As for the phrase "the faculties of cognition, etc.":

because the mind-faculty arises in a state of confusion and disorder, its originally tranquil and luminous essence is, conversely, unable to manifest; hence the mention of "the faculties of cognition, etc.
The selection of the six consciousnesses as the next six [faculties] follows a sequence that is evident. First, the contemplation of the eye is selected.

"Consciousness (*vijñāna*). This is that which Śāriputra contemplated and realized as perfect penetration. Regarding "the consciousness and the seeing, etc.," one should speak of the "two-fold conjunction.
That the three are mentioned here refers to the two—root and object—which are the producers, and the single nature of consciousness, which is the produced.
Taken together, they are called "the consciousness and seeing mingled in the threefold conjunction. The "basis" refers to the producing root and object; both are empty.

It is false; this constitutes a non-characteristic (*alakṣaṇa*). Since the fundamental source from which it arises is already illusory and lacks characteristics, how could the sensory faculty (*indriya*) produced by it possess a real essence?

Therefore, it is said, "interrogating the root," and so forth. Second, the discernment of the ear-consciousness (*śrotra-vijñāna*), which is that which Samantabhadra contemplated to realize perfect penetration.
Regarding "mental hearing" (*citta-śravaṇa*): mental hearing is precisely the ear-consciousness. This refers to the ear-consciousness...
It penetrates the ten directions; this arises through the power of Samantabhadra’s practice based on the principle of the Dharma-realm, and is not the power of your auditory consciousness.
Therefore, it says "the mind hears," and so forth. Since one must arise from the principle of the Dharma-realm to perform Samantabhadra’s practice, a beginner cannot enter it on their own;
hence it says "a beginner cannot enter. Third, it distinguishes the contemplation of nose-consciousness, as in the case of Śundara.

This refers to what Nanda contemplated to realize perfect penetration. Fourth is the contemplation of the tongue-consciousness, which refers to what Pūrṇamaitrāyaṇīputra contemplated to realize perfect penetration.

Regarding "preaching the Dharma" and so forth, this means that while they assist in turning the wheel of the Buddhas' Dharma, it is entirely through sounds and written characters acting as a skillful introduction;
these can only bring about awakening for those who have already attained realization. Therefore, it says "preaching the Dharma" and so forth.

Furthermore, the names, phrases, and sentences that are spoken therein are all subject to arising and ceasing and are of a tainted (sāsrava) nature; therefore, it is said that "names and phrases are not untainted.
Fifth, this excludes the contemplation of the body-consciousness (*kāyavijñāna*), which was the object of Upāli’s contemplation for realizing perfect penetration.
Regarding "observance and violation" and so forth, this refers to what should be maintained and what should not be violated within the precepts; it merely serves to restrain the faculty of the body.
That is all. Apart from the body itself, there is nothing else that can be bound. Therefore, it is said that this pertains to the observance and violation [of precepts] and so forth.
Sixth, the examination of the mental consciousness: This refers to what Maudgalyāyana observed to realize perfect penetration. Regarding "supernatural powers" and so forth:

this means that supernatural powers are fundamentally brought about by past causes and have no connection with the mental consciousness’s discrimination of dharma-objects (*dharmadhātu*). Why is this? Because...
The object of its mental focus does not depart from the substance of dharmas (dharma-viṣaya). Therefore, supernatural powers (abhijñā) are not concerned with discrimination;

hence it is said that "supernatural powers are equal," and so forth. Fourth, the discernment of the contemplation of the seven great elements is divided into seven parts, the sequence of which can be seen clearly.

The seven characters for "nature" (*dhātu*)—from the nature of earth up to the nature of mindfulness—are the natures of false and illusory differentiation; they are not the true nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. First...
First, the contemplation of the earth element: this is that which the Bodhisattva Earth-Holder contemplated and realized as perfect penetration.
Second, the contemplation of the water element: this is that which the youth Moonlight contemplated and realized as perfect penetration. Suchness is neither conceptualization nor discernment.

This means that its hidden nature is suchness (*tathatā*), immovable; it cannot be made into suchness and immovability through conceptual thought, recollection, or mental observation (*vitarka-vicāra*).
Third, this distinguishes the contemplation of the fire element, which was practiced and realized as the perfect penetration by Ucchuṣma.
"If one [uses] equality," etc., means that while he loathed the existence of the fire of desire and sought liberation from it, he was unable to fully comprehend lust.
Because one should realize that desire is fundamentally pure, it is said, "If by [the element of]... and so forth.

Fourth, this excludes the contemplation of the wind-element, which was the object of contemplation through which the Dharma Prince Vairocana attained perfect penetration. "If by... and so forth refers to movement, which is the wind-element.
Stillness is the nature of the treasury. Once there is movement and stillness, they form a pair of opposites; how could this be the unsurpassed essence of enlightenment? As it is said:

"If a dharma is established through dependence, that dharma itself remains dependent. Therefore, it says, "if by means of equality," and so forth. Fifth, the exclusion of the contemplation of emptiness:
this refers to that which was contemplated and realized as perfect penetration by the Bodhisattva Ākāśagarbha. Regarding the phrase "if by means of": by...

That space originally arises from a single thought of non-awakening (*abodha*). Since it is non-awakening, it is not without difference from the awakened essence (*bodhi*) sought as the object of realization;

thus it is said, "if one [uses] equality," and so forth. Sixth, this excludes the contemplation of the element of consciousness (*vijñāna-dhātu*), which was the object of Maitreya’s contemplation through which he realized perfect penetration.
Seventh, this excludes the contemplation of the element of sight (*darśana-dhātu*), which was the object of Mahāsthāmaprāpta’s contemplation.

This refers to those who have realized perfect penetration. Regarding the phrase "cause and effect now differ in their responses," it means that while the nature of thought fundamentally belongs to the realm of birth and extinction, perfect penetration is inherently neither born nor extinguished.
To seek the fruit of non-birth and non-extinction through the cause of birth and extinction is what is meant by the statement that the names of cause and fruit do not correspond to one another;
hence it is said, "Cause and effect now differ in their responses."

The second selection consists of five parts. First, directly taking up the faculty of hearing, namely "I now," and so forth. Second, clearly elucidating the person and the Dharma, namely "departing from suffering," and so forth.
Third, definitively distinguishing merit and fault, namely "this present," and so forth. Fourth, instructing and rebuking Ānanda, namely "Ānanda," and so forth.
Fifth, exhorting practice and offering praise, namely "the great assembly," and so forth. Within the first section, "directly taking up the faculty of hearing," it begins with "I now," and so forth.

This means that [the Master] considered that, from the time he began practicing the discernment of form (*rūpa*) onward, none of those methods were suitable for the present recipient, Ānanda, nor for future sentient beings.
Yet both the present recipient and these sentient beings are inhabitants of this Sahā world.
That which benefits them depends solely upon the faculty of hearing. That which they require must be the teaching through sound.

Since the Tathāgata has appeared in this Sahā world, he naturally accords with these specific capacities; thus [he says], "I now... (and so forth). This "Vaipulya" (Equanimous/Universal) is not the same as names, words, or phrases;
it is the true teaching. It does not exist by means of conceptualization or discriminative cognition; this is what constitutes...

It is pure. While in other regions other faculties may be sharp and acute such that all five sense objects can serve as the substance of the teaching, in this Sahā world it is only the faculty of hearing that is acute;
therefore, to accommodate this faculty of hearing, one must follow the teaching of sound. Thus it is said: "In this region, [the Dharma] is equal."
Regarding "desiring to attain [the state of] equality" and so forth: this clarifies the cultivation of perfect penetration through the faculty of hearing;

it corresponds to the previous section on "first, regarding hearing," and so on. Second, the detailed explanation of the person and the dharma is divided into two parts: first, "departing from suffering" and so forth, which praises the person by means of the dharma;

second, "I now" and so forth, which reveals the dharma by means of the person. The first part is further divided into two: first, regarding hearing, which is "departing from suffering" and so forth; second, regarding the mind, which is "wondrous" and so forth.

Regarding "sound" and so forth: first, as for "being free from suffering" and so on—being free from suffering means that what previously arose and ceased has already been extinguished, yet because that which was non-existent does not perish, one attains liberation;
this is precisely the manifestation of the aforementioned quiescence (*śānti*), because there is no flow into which one does not enter.
Therefore, it is said: "being free from suffering, one attains liberation. Such matters pertain only to my Avalokiteśvara.
He is able; thus it is said, "How excellent is Avalokiteśvara! This refers to entering realization through contemplation. The phrase "at all times" clarifies the arising of function from realization.
The phrase "at all times" indicates that the duration is extremely long. The phrase "entering the subtle" indicates that the lands to which he responds are extremely numerous.
The phrase "attaining the great," etc., indicates that his power and function are extremely vast. Thus it is said, "he attains the great."

Regarding the term "etcetera": for an exceedingly long time and across an exceedingly vast number of lands, the Bodhisattva manifests forms according to the various types of beings and divides his body to preach the Dharma.

Whether through the thirty-two marks of response, the fourteen fearlessnesses, or the four inconceivables, these are established in accordance with the nature of reality (*dharmatā*) without relying on artificial fabrication.
It is like the single moon in the sky whose reflection appears upon ten thousand waters; the moon does not descend, nor do the waters rise up.
It ascends. That the Way of resonance and response intersects is naturally so. Among these two, as for "wondrous sound": sound is originally the nature of sound, which is true emptiness;
true emptiness is the nature of true sound. It is simply because sentient beings, through moment-to-moment discrimination, transform it into something coarse and heavy.

It is not that [the sound] is inherently wondrous; rather, it is because the Bodhisattva does not give rise to discrimination, but through wondrous contemplation realizes that the very essence of sound is inconceivable.
Therefore, it is called "Wondrous Sound" (Miaoyin) and "Avalokiteśvara" (Guanshiyin). This is precisely the practice of "turning the hearing back to hear one's own nature.
As for "Brahmic Sound" (Fanyin), this refers to the fact that sound has always been pure and fundamental, pervading the entire Dharma-realm. This is truly due to sentient beings...
When mind after mind gives rise to craving and attachment, it becomes defiled and is not pure.

Only when a Bodhisattva does not give rise to craving and attachment, and through wondrous contemplation realizes that the very substance [of phenomena] is pure and free from defilement, is he called "Brahma-sound.

As for "the sound of the ocean tide," the tides of the sea arise in accordance with their proper seasons without the slightest error; so too does the Bodhisattva’s preaching of the Dharma accord with [the needs of beings].

The teaching according to the capacity [of beings] is likewise so. Therefore, it is called the "Ocean Tide Sound. Regarding the two phrases concerning "saving the world": the beings saved by the Bodhisattva do not exceed the ten realms.

By saving the six paths of existence, they cause them to leave behind the causes and effects of *dṛṣṭi-heya* (delusions to be abandoned through insight) and *bhava-heya* (delusions to be abandoned through cultivation), as well as the *paricchinna-bheda* (segmented) nature of causality;

hence, it is said, "Saving the world, all are brought to peace and security. By saving those of the three vehicles, they cause them to realize the eternal nature of the secret treasury of the three virtues; hence, it is said, "Transcending the world."

To attain the eternal abiding (*nitya-sthiti*). If one proceeds according to the Dharma taught through the thirty-two manifestations, causing each member of the world to achieve fulfillment, this is "saving the world" so that all may find peace.
Causing those who transcend the world to each attain liberation, this is "transcending the world" to attain the eternal abiding.

Second, the section on revealing the Dharma by way of persons is divided into three parts. First, from "I now... onwards, it reveals the perfect virtues (*pūrṇa-guṇa*). Second, [the section on] the eyes... [etc.]

The passage on "not inferior" reveals the quality of pervasiveness (*vibhutva*). The three passages on "sound" reveal the quality of permanence (*nityatā*). The passage on "perfection" should likewise be understood by way of the five faculties;

it reveals the perfection of the ear-faculty by contrast with the non-perfection of the others. This analogy can be seen throughout. As for the passage on "permanence," since the other five faculties are not permanent, that [quality] must pertain to the ear-faculty at the end.

This can be seen from the beginning and the middle. Regarding the two phrases concerning the mouth and nose, they appear to be misplaced, as they concern three faculties [when only two are mentioned].
Because they are known simultaneously. Otherwise, what commonality would there be between the mouth, nose, and eyes?
Regarding these three, even if they were equal—as previously explained—even if one were in a dream, the nature of hearing would not be obscured. One should conclude by stating:

it is not said that the nature of my hearing is not complete because there is no sound of drums from the ten directions, nor is the nature of my hearing obstructed because there is no sound from behind a wall.
Pervading and penetrating, it is free from the dust of sound and the coming and going of objects; yet my nature of hearing does not remain permanently fixed.

It is what is called "luminous throughout the space between heaven and earth" and "vast within the sphere of seeing and hearing. In this way, it is perfectly complete, thoroughly pervasive, and eternally abiding.
Up to the point of being eternally abiding and fully perfected in thorough penetration: to mention one is to include the three; to speak of the three is to mean the one.

Although the one and the three differ, the nature of hearing is not distinct. From the emergence of perfect virtue, it becomes *dhyāna*; up to the emergence of the virtue of permanence, it becomes *samādhi*.
The subject of contemplation and the object of contemplation are one and the same within the nature of hearing. This is why it is called the "Secret and Sublime Gate of the Primary Expedient Means.
Regarding the third section, which analyzes merits and faults: the first two phrases refer to the merits.

The intent is that, having been selected from among all things, it is discussed solely in terms of the teaching of sound; thus, it is most clearly expounded for the Sahā world, as was previously stated regarding its purity.

"Sound" (*śabda*) refers to what is heard. Some claim that the *Śabdavidyā* (Science of Phonology) attained here is the same as the *Vyākaraṇa* (Grammar) among the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*) of the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra*.

This is not so. That *Vyākaraṇa* pertains to the interpretation of glosses and etymologies; if it were the case [here], it would still merely belong to the analysis of words and phrases (*padavyañjanavibhāga*).

How could this be considered the true essence of the teaching? It is the fault of sentient beings. Sentient beings do not awaken to and are deluded regarding the essence of their fundamental faculty of hearing;
they pursue the objects of sound, whether through craving and attachment or through discrimination, thereby causing them to wander through the cycle of birth and death.
Therefore, it is said that sentient beings are equal. All ordinary worldlings are like this.

As for you, Ānanda, although you differ from those ordinary worldlings in that you have attained much learning within the Buddha-dharma, yet your extensive learning merely serves to increase your capacity for rote memorization.
Therefore it is said: "Even though Ānanda possesses a powerful memory, and although your own strong memory was originally intended for liberation, you have instead been captured by Dhanagā;
thus you cannot escape falling into the heterodox. Hence it is said: "One cannot avoid falling into heterodox thoughts.
Is such a state not precisely like an ordinary celestial being who, following the dust of sound, sinks into delusion? Therefore it is said: "Is this not following [the senses]?"

Regarding the "returning of the flow" (*xuanliu*): if one is to achieve liberation, one must attain the "revolving of the flow" as practiced by Avalokiteśvara. If the flow can be made to revolve, then the Dharma-nature will enter;
one will naturally obtain the non-delusion in which birth and death have been extinguished and quiescent extinction (*nirvāṇa*) manifests before one.

Therefore it is said: "By revolving the flow, one attains non-delusion. The fourth instruction to Ānanda is divided into two parts. First, concerning a single faculty: Ānanda, depart... [text continues].

Second, regarding the six sense faculties, [the text] moves on from seeing and hearing. First, concerning the initial section: the phrase "Ānanda" is an exhortation to listen. The phrase "I, having received...
refers to the selection of the ear-faculty among all the holy ones, which is due entirely to the majestic power and spiritual authority of the Tathāgata, and is not my own intention as Mañjuśrī.
The two phrases beginning with "proclaiming" specifically praise the three dharmas, such as śamatha. Regarding the "Vajra King," this is the emptiness of śamatha.
Both are empty; like an illusion, they are both provisional within the samādhi of the provisional. They are inconceivable. Within dhyāna, they are both the middle.
These are the phrases of the Buddha-Mother, summarily praising the three dharmas of śamatha: namely, "The Buddhas of the ten directions all enter the single path to nirvāṇa.
Therefore, it is called the True Samādhi of the Buddha-Mother. Your hearing of these two lines praises the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.
This is the secret gate of all Buddhas, for all take this as their primary expedient means.
The two phrases beginning with "desires" refer to Ānanda’s accumulation of learning having become a fault, such that his power of the Way was not yet complete.

The two phrases beginning with "about to hear" refer to Ānanda using the faculty of hearing to uphold the Dharma spoken by all Buddhas; why does he not turn back from hearing to hear his own nature? Hearing is not—
The two lines refer to the manifestation of the faculty of hearing in relation to its object. The phrase "the hearing turns back" refers to the aforementioned "entering the stream.
"Sound detaches" refers to the aforementioned "losing the locus. "Who can name that which is able to detach?

refers to the meaning of the principle of the essence of contemplative wisdom being a profound emptiness, as previously stated. Second, regarding the six faculties, there are three parts: first, the dharma of the single faculty; second... [text ends]

These are like the analogies of "the world" and so forth. Third, the convergence of the six sense organs and so on. Within this teaching, the first two lines concerning the single organ provide a general clarification that can be understood.
From "seeing and hearing" onwards, there is a specific clarification. The line on "seeing and hearing" refers to the illusory delusion of the six sense organs, which is like a film over the eye.
The line on the "three realms" refers to the insubstantiality of the six sense objects, which is like flowers in the sky. From "hearing again" onwards...

The six faculties are viewed as a unity. "Hearing is restored" means that one immediately enters the stream [of the Dharma]. When the cataract-afflicted faculty is removed, the nature of hearing is restored, and all deluded faculties are instantly eliminated.
"Dusts are extinguished" means that the objects of perception have perished. "Awakening is perfect and pure" refers to the profound emptiness of both contemplative wisdom and the ultimate principle.
"Purity reaches its limit" means that birth and death have been extinguished. "Light penetrates everywhere" means that quiescent extinction is manifest before one.
The above constitutes practicing contemplation in accordance with the teachings. The phrase "quiescent illumination" refers to entering realization through contemplation.

Furthermore, "quiescence" (jing) signifies the ultimate stillness; "light" (guang) signifies pervasive penetration and illumination. When quiescence reaches its ultimate limit, there is light that penetrates and reaches everywhere—this is "illumination within stillness.

Because penetration arises from the ultimate limit of stillness, it is "stillness within illumination. In this way, stillness and illumination are non-dual, and object and wisdom are of one suchness. All that exists...
There is no void that it does not encompass. Thus it is said: "Quiescent illumination encompasses the void. The phrase "returns" and so forth refers to the arising of function from realization.
If one were to be deluded by false thoughts, one would engage in moment-to-moment discrimination regarding all worldly phenomena, with mind after mind clinging in greed and love.
Now, having attained the reversal of falsehood and the return to truth, one looks back upon the world as if it were a matter within a dream. As for what is called "the time of dreaming":
It is not that they do not exist; rather, even until one reaches full awakening, they cannot be found. Now that you have realized the truth, you observe that illusory objects are likewise so.
Thus it is said, "Returning... and so forth. While the world is in a dream, even the courtesan Dhanagā is in a dream.
Since she is in a dream and you are already awake, you ought to urgently awaken from that dream. Who could possibly detain you further?
...the form [of the ear]. Therefore, it is called "Māṭaṅga" and so forth. Thus, it is not only the faculty of hearing that is like this;
all six faculties are likewise so. Regarding the second analogy, one should first state: "Since one faculty has already returned to its source," and so on.
If explained by means of the analogy, it is like the magical arts of a magician. Therefore, it says, "As in the world," and so forth. Some say that "illusion" (māyā)...
To create men, women, and so forth is merely the art of a worldly puppeteer; this is not so.
This is the illusory art of a great master of illusion, who conjures forth various men, women, and others with spirits and movements that are truly alive.

Thus, one knows that the two characters "illusory creation" (huàn zuò) correspond in meaning to the three characters "a single stroke of the mechanism" (yī jī chōu). Furthermore, it is said: "The illusory person is a metaphor for the *tathāgatagarbha*. Illusion...

The preceding analogies were used to illustrate how delusion arises from the Truth; however, this particular analogy of a single puppet emerging from the ear-organ serves to show the return from delusion back to the Truth.
If it were otherwise, then the subsequent method would not correspond with what precedes it. Now, the skillful illusionist is a metaphor for sentient beings.
The single word "illusion" (*māyā*) is a metaphor for the clarity and brilliance of consciousness (*vijñāna*). "Creating various men and women" is a metaphor for the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*).

"Though they are seen," and so forth, is a metaphor for how, although the six harmonious combinations are formed, their origin is but a single brilliant clarity. The two lines beginning with "ceasing the mechanism" are a metaphor for achieving rest and restoration in a single location.
If you view it in this way, it will then correspond to the principle of the teaching. Among the three combinations, the six sense organs and so forth...

This can be seen through analogies. "In one place," etc., means that when one ceases [the outward flow], one no longer follows the stream to exit; instead, one immediately returns to hearing the self-nature and enters it.
"Dust and grime," etc., refers to the passage at the end of the fourth fascicle: "Conceptual marks are dust, and cognitive consciousness is grime; when both are left far behind," and so forth.

The two lines beginning with "The remaining dust" distinguish the stages of realization; this means that there are still slight remnants of the dust-like marks of ignorance that have not yet been eliminated.

"Exhausted" refers to the stage still remaining at the final moment of the Vajra-like Samādhi, which is termed "with-learning" (śaikṣa). Only when ultimate exhaustion is attained is one at the summit of the mountain of Nirvāṇa.
Thus it is said: "When residual dust remains, one is still among those with-learning. Upon reaching the essence of the fruit of Subtle Enlightenment, there is no delusion that is not exhausted.

There are no obstructions that are not eliminated, no principles that are not revealed, and no wisdom that is not perfected; thus it is said that when clarity reaches its ultimate limit, one is a Tathāgata.

The fifth section, "Exhortation to Practice and Praise," is divided into two parts: first, the exhortation to practice, which begins with "The great assembly departed"; second, the praise, which begins with "This is the departure.
Within the first part, the six groups of disciples and others primarily exhort Ānanda and the rest to cultivate the perfect penetration of the ear faculty. Immediately following...
It is a turning. Regarding "those who hear the stimulus in a perverted way": ordinary beings have hitherto made perversion their business; their faculty of hearing pursues the objects of sound.
Now, they turn back the faculty of hearing to hear their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). If this intrinsic nature is revealed, one spontaneously attains unsurpassed *bodhi*.
Because the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty possesses such power, it says, "Turn back your [hearing]," and so forth. This is the middle section.
"This is [the case for] all such [beings]" correctly praises the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*).

There are no *tathāgatas* as numerous as motes of dust who have not attained realization through these three methods of perfect penetration of the ear-faculty, namely *śamatha* and so forth. "Path" (*mārga*) and "gate" (*dvāra*) are different;

"path" refers to the three dharmas of *śamatha* and so forth, while "gate" refers to the initial expedient means of the ear-faculty. From "In the past... onwards, it clarifies this in terms of the three periods of time.
This is the reason why all Tathāgatas follow the single path to the gate of nirvāṇa. Following the explanation of the text, one should then select [the following]:
"It is not only Avalokiteśvara who is thus; I, Mañjuśrī, am likewise. It is not only I, Mañjuśrī, who am thus;
future practitioners are likewise. It is not only future practitioners who are thus; the bodhisattvas of the present are likewise."
It is not only that the bodhisattvas of the present are thus; the Tathāgatas of the past were likewise so.
From this one may know that the bodhisattvas of the present and those who will study in the future shall all become Tathāgatas by means of this. Therefore it is said:
"This is the single path to nirvāṇa for the buddhas as numerous as motes of dust."
The section on the three fetters is divided into two parts. First, showing the intent of the selection, beginning with "Truly as... and so forth.

Second, showing the intent of the exclusion, beginning with "As for the rest... and so forth. Regarding the first part, "Truly as... and so forth may be understood as follows. One who has accomplished the mind of *nirvāṇa*:
what was previously called the "gate of *nirvāṇa*" is here called the "mind of *nirvāṇa*"; their meaning is identical. *Nirvāṇa* possesses the three virtues, such as the *dharmakāya*.
Regarding the essence of this principle, the faculty of hearing likewise possesses the nature of hearing characterized by the three qualities of perfection, penetration, and sameness.

Although one resides in the fruit and the other in the cause, the three qualities of the faculty of hearing serve as the means to realize the three virtues of *nirvāṇa*, while the three virtues of *nirvāṇa* in turn provide the support for the three qualities of the faculty of hearing.
Thus, the reason why the cause is the cause is that there is no separate cause apart from this.
One takes the three virtues of the fruit as the cause; that which constitutes the fruit does not exist apart from being the fruit itself, for it takes the three dharmas of the cause as the fruit.
This means that by means of the mind of the causal stage—which is neither arising nor ceasing—one achieves the awakening of the resultant stage, which is likewise neither arising nor ceasing.
Such a principle can only be realized through the Perfect Penetration of the Ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva.
Therefore, it is said that Avalokiteśvara is supreme. Regarding the phrase "the rest," this refers to the twenty-four skillful means;
although all have attained perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*), this is entirely due to the majestic spiritual power of the Tathāgata.
As for "attaining liberation from worldly toil through phenomenal forms" (*shi-xiang she-chen-lao*): examples include Lūdrāyaṇa losing his sight and Pilindavatsa emitting poison.
And because of [the presence of] Nanda, Upāli, and others, it says "and the rest. This is not merely two phrases;

rather, it is because the twenty-four sages—who were not long-term practitioners—share the same level of shallow and deep cultivation, thereby manifesting that the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara is indeed shared by those who have long cultivated both shallow and deep levels of practice.
Thus, although Nanda, Upāli, and the others are said to have attained the Perfect [Enlightenment], [their realization differs from that of Avalokiteśvara].

It is pervasive; however, it may be made suitable for a beginner to study, yet it is not as convenient for subsequent stages of the mind as the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara, which can be studied by both beginners and those at later stages.

It can only be explained in relation to deep stages and is not as convenient for explaining in relation to shallow stages as the ear-faculty of Avalokiteśvara, which can be explained for both shallow and deep levels. Therefore, it is said that "it is not equal [to that]."
The third section, the summary, has two parts. First, the request for empowerment, prostrations, and so forth; second, the actual conclusion of the skillful means and so forth. Regarding the first:

as for the phrase of prostration, it refers to the Three Jewels in their essential unity, because the *tathāgatagarbha* possesses three aspects. The empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the Jewel of the Saṅgha;
the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the Jewel of the Dharma; and the empty-and-non-empty *tathāgatagarbha* is the Jewel of the Buddha.
This is precisely the Buddha-treasure. The "outflow-free phrase" (anāsrava-pada) refers to the three treasures as a single essence, which constitute the perfect fusion of the three truths.
Regarding their emptiness: it is the emptiness of all things in one; it does not fall into the partiality of the conventional or the middle. The same applies to the conventional and the middle.
Because it cannot be conceived by the mind or discussed in words, it is called "outflow-free and inconceivable. If one looks directly at the text, this is...
I shall summarize the principles to praise this person. I pray you will add two phrases:
namely, that in the present, there is the Tathāgata’s command to me, Mañjuśrī, the selection of Avalokiteśvara as witness, and Ānanda’s personal hearing.
As for the future, once the Tathāgata has entered parinirvāṇa, when I, Mañjuśrī, am no longer present, Avalokiteśvara no longer appears, and Ānanda is no longer involved—only...

Fearing that doubts might arise regarding this life, I have requested [the Buddha] to add [this clarification]. As for the "expedient means" (*upāya*) and so forth in the middle section, the intent is as follows:
the Tathāgata commanded me to select from among the twenty-five dharmas those who are capable of being the appropriate recipients—namely, Ānanda and future sentient beings.

This faculty of the ear alone is the skillful means (*upāya*) that directly corresponds to Ānanda and to sentient beings of the final age who are submerged in saṃsāra; hence it says, "the skillful means," and so forth.

By means of this alone, one attains cultivation; the wondrous gate of perfect penetration (*pariniṣpanna-avavādaka*) will spontaneously be accomplished, and the ocean of the fruit of Nirvāṇa will certainly be realized and entered.
It is able to transcend the twenty-four dharmas; hence it says, "but by means of this," and so forth. Truly.
As for my sincere intention being thus: speaking in the first instance, that which I have sifted and selected is true and without falsehood, real and without delusion.
As for the meaning of the second instance, it means that I have received the majestic power of the Tathāgata to perform this sifting and selection.
In the twenty-four holy ones there is truly no sense of shame; in me, Mañjuśrī, there is likewise no pride.
Thus it is said: "The true mind is thus.
Thirdly, this is the passage concerning how Ānanda and the great assembly obtained benefit. Regarding the phrase "body and mind became clearly manifest," since—

If one attains the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*) and practices accordingly, the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) can be produced and the life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*) can be prolonged.
"It is like, for example," and so forth, is a metaphor for how a single thought of non-awakening causes one to transmigrate through the three realms; this refers to "there being people" and so on.

Although the metaphor does not yet explicitly reveal the Truth, it illustrates that by hearing the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty as a means of entry into the methods of *śamatha* and so forth, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha can be spontaneously realized.

"Manifesting" means for the sake of clarity and so forth. "All attain their original mind" means that all have attained a thorough penetration of the wondrous luminosity of original enlightenment (*mūla-bodhi*).
"Distant from dust and free from defilement" is also as stated at the end of the fourth fascicle: "conceptual appearances are the dust, and cognitive consciousness is the defilement," and so on.

This "purity of the Dharma-eye" corresponds to the perfection of the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*). As for the Bhikṣuṇī Śrī and others, since they attained this through the power of the Perfect and Sudden Sutras, it is not the four fruits of the Lesser Vehicle, but rather the seventh stage of faith within the Perfect Teaching.

Third, from "Ānanda adjusted his robes" onwards, there is the further presentation of the textual passage concerning the rules for formal standing. This consists of two parts: first, the request based on doubt;
second, the response and instruction. The first part [the request] also has two sub-sections: first, from "Ānanda," the scribe of the sutra describes the ritual protocol;
second, from "Great Compassion," Ānanda presents his words. Within the first of these, the description of the ritual protocol by the scribe, the mind and its traces are perfected.

"Clarification" means that previously one had only understood the principle-nature (*li-xing*) but had not yet attained its practice; thus it could only be called "the mind being perfected," while the traces [of realization] were not yet clear.

Now, with the opening of this Dharma-gate of perfect penetration, there is a path for progressive cultivation; it is no longer merely a matter of the mind being perfected, but the traces are also made clear.
Regarding "a mixture of sorrow and joy," there are two meanings. First, speaking from the perspective of one's own practice: "joy" refers to rejoicing...
Whether in principle or in practice, there is nothing within one’s own mind that is not clearly understood.

As for compassion, one pities oneself for the fact that although both principle and practice are inherently complete (*xingju*), why was this unknown in the past and only now realized? Second, speaking from the perspective of transforming others:
as for rejoicing, one rejoices that the great assembly present now has each attained the purity of the Dharma-eye, up to and including the arousal of the bodhi-mind.
Focus the mind. As for those who feel compassion, they grieve that sentient beings of future generations have not yet obtained such benefits of the Dharma;
how can their eyes become pure, and how can they give rise to the awakened mind? Thus, this single feeling of compassion and this single feeling of joy intersect with one another;

this is called "the intersection of compassion and joy. Second, Ānanda’s statement is divided into three parts: first, he recounts what he previously realized, namely the Great Compassion and so forth; second, he presents...
Regarding the current aspiration, "Now I pray... and so forth, these three lines formally state the request. Regarding the initial section, "I now... and so forth:
since one has heard that the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing serves as the primary expedient means, the fruit-stage of the Buddha can naturally be attained.
Therefore, it says, "I now... and so forth. It has already been clarified that by practicing according to this Dharma-gate, Nirvana is first realized.
Because they have understood the path to which they must return, it is said that "they are among these. Next, regarding the phrase "having not yet [crossed over] themselves," etc.:
because their afflictions (*kleśa*) have not yet been destroyed and birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) has not yet been severed, it is said "they have not yet crossed over themselves.

Furthermore, because they subdue their delusions while practicing the causal conduct of transforming sentient beings, it is said "first crossing over others," etc. Regarding "self-awakening already perfected": this refers to the ten bodies being fully endowed with the three wisdoms (*trijñāna*).
It is also complete. As for "being able to awaken others," it means manifesting in accordance with the various types of beings throughout the *dharmadhātu*.
Regarding the phrase "responding to the world" and below, one should conclude by saying: "In the manner spoken by the Tathāgata, such as this; in the manner heard by me, Ānanda, such as this.

Although I have not yet destroyed my afflictions (*kleśa*) nor severed birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), I shall likewise subdue my delusions, cultivate the causes, and vow to deliver the beings of the final age."

Therefore, it says, "Although I... and so forth. Among the three [categories], regarding the World-Honored One, one should supplement the text above by saying: "How can one vow to deliver sentient beings of the末 (mo) age?

There is no other [way] than precisely these very sentient beings... and so on. As for those who preach the Dharma as false teachers (*mithyā-śāstṛ*), this does not refer to non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) being called false teachers;
rather, it refers to those within the Buddha's teaching who destroy the Dharma. This is what is meant by the "lion's body... and so forth.
The internal worms merely consume the lion’s own flesh. As the Great Master Zhiyi stated in the *Contemplation of the Mind Treatise* (*Guanxin lun*):

"There are three kinds of false teachers: namely, Dharma masters, Vinaya masters, and Chan masters. Though they are called Dharma masters, their conduct is entirely inconsistent with the characteristics of the various dharmas.
Though they are called Vinaya masters, they frequently transgress and violate the precepts, having no true connection with the discipline."
Although they are called Chan masters, they do not understand the reason for Chan; they merely act with reckless simplicity through a single blow or a single shout.

Regarding those who wish to gather [the assembly] equally: when the Buddha appeared in the world, the Dharma-preacher was the Tathāgata, whose physical form and mind were both supreme, and the audience who heard the Dharma possessed such sharp and keen faculties.
In the末代 (final age), the Dharma-preacher is not the Tathāgata, and thus his physical form...
The minds of both [teacher and listener] are inferior. The listeners are a great assembly whose faculties are dull and rigid.

Therefore, it is necessary to rely upon the provisional establishment of a *maṇḍala* (place of practice) to gather their minds and keep them far from demons. Thus, one may personally attain the cause of non-arising and non-ceasing, and realize the fruit of non-arising and non-ceasing.
However, how exactly is this *maṇḍala* to be established? Hence, it is said: "Desiring to gather," and so forth.

The second part, the Response and Demonstration, is divided into four sections: first, the praise and permission from "At that time" onwards; second, the admonition and permission from "You now" onwards;

third, the reception of the mandate from "Ānanda" onwards; and fourth, the exposition from "The Buddha said" onwards. Within the first section, the praise and permission, the phrase "Excellent, excellent!
praises him not only for benefiting the great assembly of the present, but for his further desire to benefit the sentient beings of the末代 (final age).

The first two or three [sections] can be understood [from the context]. The fourth, the Section on Expounding, consists of four parts: first, the observance of prohibitive precepts, beginning from where it says "The Buddha addressed Ānanda";
second, the recitation of divine mantras, beginning from where it says "Ānanda, you have heard"; third, the establishment of the *maṇḍala*, beginning from where it says "If there is a final age";
and fourth, the repeated request to expound the mantras, beginning from where it says "Ānanda prostrated himself. The second, third, and fourth [parts] all appear in the [eighth] fascicle.
This constitutes the seventh fascicle. It is further divided into two parts. First, the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" generally elucidates the three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*).

Second, the passage beginning with "Ānanda" specifically opens up the four grave offenses (*catur-guru-dharma*). Within the first section, which generally elucidates the three trainings, the *Vinaya-piṭaka* is presented.

Regarding the term "definitive" (*niyata*), it carries two meanings: first, that these were personally expounded and resolved by the Tathāgata’s own mouth, being fixed and never to be altered; this is called...
Certainty. Second, the certainty that sentient beings receive from the Tathāgata shall never be destroyed; this is called "certainty. As for what is meant by "equality":

the precepts serve to cease evil and prevent wrongdoing. Having heard this Dharma-door of Perfect Penetration, one should immediately turn back the hearing to hear the nature of hearing (*śravaṇa-svabhāva*) as a means of gathering the mind.
Employing inconceivable wondrous contemplation, one contemplates the inconceivable nature of hearing. Not...
One can only contemplate the wondrous; that which is contemplated is likewise wondrous—namely, the mind of hearing that is both wondrous and sublime.
All evils cease, and all transgressions are prevented; thus it is said that "restraining the mind constitutes precept.

Consequently, the nature of hearing is in its very essence true stillness, which is termed "concentration. Therefore, it is said that "from precept arises concentration. Furthermore, because the nature of hearing is inherently such...
Perfect illumination is what constitutes wisdom; hence it is said that "wisdom is generated from concentration.

Although the three [trainings] beginning with precepts are all subsumed within the single act of collecting the mind, this section opens up the three trainings, while the subsequent sections clarify the four types of discipline (*vinaya*).
In this way, one is naturally freed from the causes of the five abodes (*pañca-vihāra*) and the fruits of the two deaths (*dvividha-mṛtyu*); thus it says, "This then," and so forth.
Second, the four grave offenses are distinguished individually. These four kinds of restraint are neither the same as those of a bodhisattva nor the same as those of a bhikṣu.

Why is this? A bhikṣu is merely said to restrain his body and refrain from [unwholesome acts]; here, however, it is stated that his mind does not engage in sexual misconduct, up to and including his mind not engaging in false speech.
Thus, one knows they are not the same as those of a bhikṣu. Furthermore, the precept against killing comes first for a bodhisattva; now...

By placing the precept against sexual misconduct at the forefront, it is clear that this differs from the Bodhisattva path. Nevertheless, what is the intent behind these four types? There is no other reason:
for those who uphold the Bodhisattva vows, there is the Brahma Net Sūtra; for those practicing as Bhikṣus, there is the Dharmaguptaka Vinaya.
However, we are currently cultivating this perfect penetration of the ear organ. Should we be disturbed or harmed by demonic activities, then regarding those four...
The various precepts must not be lacking. All meditative concentrations (*dhyāna*) and samādhis ultimately resolve back into the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.

This is divided into four parts, the sequence of which may be seen [in the text]. Each contains clear instructions on maintaining and violating the precepts, intended to facilitate the transmission of the teaching by distinguishing between the heterodox and the orthodox.
