First, regarding the precept against sexual misconduct, the clarification of maintaining and violating it is further divided into two: first, maintaining it leads to the severance of birth and death (as in the passage beginning "If all..."); second, violating it leads to falling into the realm of Māra.
"Way. This refers to your cultivation of equanimity. Regarding the initial maintenance [of the precepts], it cuts off birth and death within the cycle of existence.
If one were to raise the point regarding those above [the ordinary level], it would say: "All sentient beings transmigrate through the six realms and are submerged in the four modes of birth;

all this is brought about by a lustful mind. Therefore it is said: 'If [the various... (and so forth). As for 'their minds are not lustful,' etc.: lust is the cause of birth and death. Since the cause no longer exists..."
How could a fruit arise? Therefore, it is said that "his mind was equanimous. The meaning of the three subsequent types follows this same principle.

Second, regarding the transgression that leads to falling into the path of Māra, there are two parts: first, "You have practiced... and so forth, which clarifies the mistaken fall; second, "After my extinction...

and so forth, which provides an admonition for the period after [the Buddha's] passing. Within the first part, the phrase "You have practiced... implies that you, Ānanda, originally intended to practice this samādhi.
Because one seeks to emerge from worldly afflictions (*kleśa*), it is said, "You practice," and so forth. If the lustful mind is not severed, how can one emerge from these worldly afflictions?
Therefore, it is said, "The lustful mind," and so forth. If sentient beings in the final age wish to cultivate *samādhi* but do not eliminate the lustful mind, how can their wisdom arise?
How can meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) manifest before them? Even if they rely upon cultivation...
Through the power of practice, wisdom is able to manifest before one. However, because lust is not severed, one will inevitably fall into the path of Māra;
thus it is said, "Even if one possesses [virtue]," and so forth. The three subsequent types are to be understood in the same manner. Regarding "inevitably falling into the path of Māra":

although the original aim of practicing samādhi is to ascend, there is no choice but to fall into the path of Māra when the mind of lust acts as an obstacle. This is because Māra is most fond of lust. Therefore...
The lustful mind is moved by this; it is what is called "seeking to ascend, yet falling instead. Now that one has fallen into the path of Māra, how many kinds of Māras are there?

It is as described above regarding the "superior grade" and so forth. However, while lust should lead to a fall into hell, the reason one falls into the realm of Māra is to repay the causes of one's wisdom and meditative concentration (*samādhi*).
Once those causes of concentration and wisdom are exhausted, one will inevitably fall into hell. As for each person’s own claim [to superiority], it is merely... others.
Originally, these people were practicing the wisdom-concentration (jñāna-samādhi), but because they did not sever their lustful minds, they fell into the path of Māra.

Consequently, they claimed for themselves that they had attained the Unsurpassed Way, unaware that they had actually fallen into the path of Māra. This is the second admonition regarding the period after [the Buddha’s] parinirvāṇa.

Regarding the "Dharma of the Final Age" (*mofa*): it should be explained by correlating the teaching, practice, principle, and fruit with the periods of the True Dharma (*saddharma*) and the Semblance Dharma (*saddharmapratirūpaka*).

Because their lustful minds are not severed, they engage extensively in greedy lust. Because they cultivate *samādhi*, they act as "good spiritual friends" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Since they possess much greed and desire, they inevitably give rise to attachment;
furthermore, because they act as spiritual friends, they inevitably give rise to false views (*mithyādṛṣṭi*). In this way, they cause one another to follow along [into error].

Such sentient beings have lost the path to Bodhi; therefore, it is said, "to cause all [beings] to be equal," and so forth. The second section, the division on the transmission of the teaching, has three parts:

first, from "You shall teach" downward, is the instruction on severing [delusions]; second, from "For this reason" downward, is the statement of the intent; third, from "You must certainly" downward, is the actual severance.
Within the instruction on severance, "Tathāgata" refers to Śākyamuni, and "former Buddhas" refers to the ancient Buddhas. As it is said:

"The sages of antiquity and the sages of later times share the same standard. Since the *vinaya* was spoken personally by the Buddha alone—just as ritual, music, and military expeditions must issue from the Son of Heaven—it is said, "This is called," and so forth.
The three subsequent categories should also be understood by this analogy. The explanation of the underlying intent is divided into three parts:

first, the principle (*dharma*), which begins with "Therefore," and so forth; second, the metaphor (*upamāna*), beginning with "Like steaming," and so forth; third, the application (*upanaya*), beginning with "You, by means of," and so forth.

All of these can be seen within the section on "Right Abandonment" (*samyak-prahāṇa*). Regarding the phrase "one must eliminate the trigger for lust": the "trigger" (*ji*) refers to the mechanism of a crossbow, that is, the bolt.

Once released, it possesses the power to topple its target. For this reason, even if one is able to restrain the body from acting and control the mind so that it does not arise, if the trigger remains, it may still discharge again.
Therefore, one must cause the very nature of that [lust] to be severed, leaving no further possibility [for it to recur].
Therefore, it is said that they must be equal. The three points regarding the subduing of the heterodox and the orthodox can be understood as being like us.

Second, regarding the third precept on killing, there are two parts: first, clarifying observance and violation, which also has two sections. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, it clarifies that through observance one cuts off birth and death; this can be understood.

Second, from "You practice" onwards, it clarifies that through violation one falls from supernormal powers. This also has two parts: first, "You practice," etc., clarifies falling into error. Second...
Regarding the first admonition concerning my extinction: after my passing, those who fall into error at the outset will all become ghosts upon death;
those who remain upright will become spirits. Regarding the second admonition concerning my extinction, there are again three parts: first, the specific designation, "After my extinction";
second, the removal of obstacles, "Ānanda, depart"; and third, the reprimand, "How can you... In the first part, the specific designation, he himself says, "I eat meat."

Regarding the term "etcetera": how could ghosts speak? They do so either by possessing others or by manifesting transformed bodies. Within the resolution of these two objections, regarding the phrase "I have permitted," etc.:
a doubt arises as to why the Tathāgata, having already stated that he does not permit bhikṣus to eat meat, previously permitted the eating of the five kinds of pure meat.
Therefore, it is explained: "That which I permitted you to eat previously as the five kinds of pure meat was merely..."
"It was permitted that a sick bhikṣu might eat [meat]. Now, does the bhikṣu who eats meat actually have an illness? Is what he eats truly one of the five 'pure' meats?
Thus it says, "I have commanded," etc. This section on "Meat" below correctly sets forth the five pure meats.
Within the threefold censure, regarding the phrase "even if one should obtain," it means that one is also able to know the good or bad fortune of the future and the causal conditions of the past.

However, this is not the ultimate truth; therefore, it is said to be "semblance-like. Second, regarding the instruction to turn [the teaching] over: "Furthermore," and so forth. Third, regarding the initial instruction for severing [delusions]:

"Your teaching," and so forth. Second, the explanation of the underlying intent: "For this reason," and so forth. Third, the actual severing: "You must ensure," and so forth. The first [section] is readily understood.
Next, it is further divided into three parts: the lower dharma, the lower analogy, and the lower application; thus, the dharma, the analogy, and their correspondence are to be understood.

Within the application, there are again two sections: first, the direct correspondence regarding "purity" and so forth; second, the explanation establishing [the point] with "if all... and so forth. The first is understandable.
Regarding the middle section, as for the phrase "not wandering in the three realms," some say it should be placed below the word "bhikṣu. This is also [correct].
It is not necessary. In short, it is simply that by not repaying past debts, one does not wander through the three realms. Regarding the phrase "like ordinary people":
at the beginning of the kalpa, when the beings of the Ābhāsvara Heaven first descended, they did not touch the "earth-flavor" (pṛthivī-rasa) and were naturally able to fly back and forth.
Once they ate the five grains, they became attached to conditions and could no longer fly; thus it is said, "like ordinary people. Among the three types of right abandonment (*samyak-prahāṇa*):

It must be as stated above: "If one eats the five grains, one's feet shall not leave the ground. Now, by wearing silk, cotton, boots, shoes, and the like, one creates a karmic connection with sentient beings;
thus, one will naturally have to repay this debt within the three realms. Only by abstaining from such things—neither wearing them nor eating them—can one truly escape this.
Therefore, it says, "it must be made so," and so forth. As for "the parts of the body," the body refers to the consumption of its head, eyes, and bones.
[This refers to] the marrow and so forth. As for "the parts of the body," it means wearing their silk, cotton, furs, and wool.
Third, regarding "as with me" and below, the conclusion of the heterodox [views] is clear.
Third, the precept against stealing. First, the explanation of observance and violation also has two parts. First, as for observance, it severs birth and death; Ānanda departs. Second...

If one commits [an offense], one falls into the heterodox paths; you must cultivate [the path] to leave them behind. The first part is clear. Regarding "if one commits [an offense], one falls into the heterodox paths," there are two sections:

first, from "you must cultivate" onwards, it clarifies falling into error; second, from "when I have passed away" onwards, it provides an admonition for after my extinction. Within the first section clarifying falling into error:

Those who fall into the wrong path do so because they have not eliminated their thieving mind; since they fail to avoid the various ways of self-concealment, they belong to the category of the heterodox, and thus encounter such karmic results.
The second section, "The Admonition for After My Extinction," is divided into two parts: first, the specification [of the teaching], beginning with "After my extinction...

and so forth; second, the instruction on repudiation, beginning with "My teaching... and so forth. Within the first part, regarding the phrase "deceiving and deluding," those who possess wisdom will naturally not engage in such things.

Those who are deluded by this will find it difficult to escape, especially those lacking in discernment. Sometimes [the Buddha] speaks of terrifying matters, or matters of sin and merit, to cause them alarm and agitation;
hence the terms "deceiving" and "deluding," and so forth. Second, the teaching on rebuking also has three parts:
first, from "I teach" below, the teaching to abandon greed; second, from "How can" below, the rebuke of doubt and error; third, from "If I" below, the teaching on retribution. First:
In the middle [section]: "Those who beg for food according to the directions" refers to those who beg for food in accordance with the prescribed rules and regulations.

"Those whose lives are exhausted" means that after this single lifetime, they will never again return to the triple world; this is what constitutes having an exhausted life. Next, in the middle [section], "those who rely upon us."
When the Buddha was in the world, there were many non-Buddhists who sought to harm the Tathāgata but could never find an opportunity.
They then made a vow, saying: "While the Buddha is currently present, we are unable to harm him. We swear that in the future age, we shall don his robes and preach his teachings;
furthermore, we shall perform various acts of heterodox conduct to destroy his doctrine. Now, that time has arrived. This is it.
Because there are various instances of destroying the Dharma and the Sangha by setting out on such journeys, it is said [in the scriptures] "and so forth.
Among these three types of acts, regarding the burning of one lamp or the burning of a finger joint and so on: this is not merely a matter of a single lamp or a single finger;
rather, that person has already completely relinquished all their *pariṇāmanā* (dependent retribution), and they further offer even their *upapatti* (primary retribution) as a gift. As for...
Regarding the act of lighting a single lamp with one's own body or burning a finger-joint and so forth: furthermore, one employs wondrous contemplation to enter into this state.
Within, there is no sentient being who can offer; without, there is no Tathāgata to whom an offering is made.

In between, there is furthermore neither a body nor a finger to be burned or ignited—there is only the essence of the principle of true reality (*bhūtatathatā*). For this reason, such a person is able to repay [their debt] all at once.
To repay former debts and to attain certainty within the Dharma—those such as ourselves are cited as examples.
When the Buddha was in the world as an ordinary person, he saw five hundred bhikṣus all consuming exquisite delicacies, and he rebuked them, saying:
"You people who ought to eat the fodder of horses, how can you consume such exquisite delicacies? For this reason, even when [he attained]...

Even after attaining Buddhahood, he was still subject to the retribution of eating horse-grams for ninety days. Since it was thus even for the Tathāgata, how can those who are bhikṣus today not be cautious?
How can they not be cautious? Part Two: Causing Others to Teach, which has three sections. First, the instruction on severance: "You must teach [others] to... and so forth.
Second, the statement of the underlying intention: "For this reason... and so forth. Third, the actual severance: "You must certainly cause... and so forth.

The first [point] is clear. The second, the exposition of the intention, also has three parts: namely, the principle (*dharma*), the analogy (*upamāna*), and the synthesis (*yoga*). The principle and the analogy are clear. Regarding the synthesis:

as for "body, flesh, and so forth," first, it is identical to the bodies of sentient beings in being composed of the four great elements; second, it is identical to the bodies of sentient beings in sharing the same *tathāgatagarbha* nature.
Thus one knows that whether from the perspective of phenomena or principle, there is nothing to be discarded internally and nothing to be sought externally.

There is no one capable of receiving it; hence the mention of "body, flesh, and so forth. Furthermore, because this body is intended to be relinquished at every moment, it is shared with all sentient beings.
Regarding the phrase "not taking [anything] equally," it refers to the teaching that, beyond the three robes, one may possess the "one hundred and one" monastic requisites.
The Buddha’s intention was fundamentally not to grant permission, because [the teaching] was of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*); hence it is said, "not bringing," and so forth.

The three right abandonments (*samyakprahāṇa*) may be understood accordingly. Regarding the section beginning with "Three, as I... and below, the conclusion concerning the false and the correct may likewise be understood.

The fourth is the precept against false speech. Regarding the initial clarification of its observance and violation, there are also two parts. First, the section beginning with "Ānanda and others" refers to what was previously maintained;

this is self-evident. Second, the section beginning with "If Mahā-... clarifies what is now being maintained. This also has two parts: first, the clarification of reckless speech, which begins with "If Mahā-..."; second, the admonition for after my extinction, which begins with "After my extinction...".

The first of these [the clarification of reckless speech] further has three parts: first, the heading indicated by "If Mahā-..."; second, the explanation beginning with "That is to say..."; [and third, the conclusion].
The characteristics [of the offense]. Third is the summary of the transgression; the first is easily understood. Regarding the second, the explanation of the characteristics:

"seeking that person’s prostrations, repentance, and so forth" means desiring that person to perform prostrations, repentance, and expressions of gratitude toward oneself, and to make offerings to oneself.

One says to the person before one: "I have now attained the fruit of Srotāpanna," and so on. The third [point] is easily understood. Second, the admonition to extinguish [the offense] after [it has occurred] is divided into two parts.
First, the section beginning with "At first, when I was about to pass away" provides a discernment; second, the section beginning with "How could it be... delivers a reprimand. Regarding the first:

"Acting as śramaṇas and so forth" refers to manifesting their outward forms; "committing adultery, theft, and so forth" refers to engaging in the same activities. This is precisely the "common purpose" (samānārthatā) among the four means of integration (saṃgrahavastu).

That is to say, transforming those of a similar kind through those of a similar kind, and integrating those who share a common purpose through a common purpose. [They] leaked the Buddha’s secret causes.

Regarding the word "etcetera": it refers to the Tathāgata’s command for various bodhisattvas and arhats to manifest their forms. This is for two reasons: first, to rescue sentient beings from suffering;
second, to fulfill the practices of a bodhisattva. Therefore, there is no leakage of the Tathāgata’s secrets.
This is the domain of those bodhisattvas and arhats who have already attained accomplishment; it is not something that beginners can yet anticipate or know. Hence, it is said:
In the end, they never spoke of it themselves, nor did they lightly mention that they were unlearned. The sole exception was when their lives were ending;

this was not to publicly delude the masses, but merely to provide a private indication. This is like the words of Nanyue regarding the Iron Wheel, the words of Tiantai regarding the armor of the five grades of merit, the verses on the "True Contemplation" (Zhenguan) Master’s counting of his fingers, and even the cases of Yongming and Dingguang—all of which are instances of this.

...as well. Second, the reprimand can be understood. Second, the section on causing [others] to turn toward the teaching is divided into three parts: first, "Your teaching... and below, which teaches cessation; second, "Therefore...

and below, which reveals the underlying intention; third, "If there are... and below, which is the actual cessation. Within the first part, regarding the teaching of cessation, the phrase "furthermore, after...
means that following acts of sexual misconduct, killing, and stealing, one must further sever these [afflictions]; hence it says "furthermore, after... and so forth. Second, revealing...
The "intention" (*manas*) is also threefold: namely, the dharma, the analogy, and the synthesis. The dharma and the analogy are self-evident. The synthesis is further divided into three parts.
First, the "my teaching" section is the primary synthesis; second, the "how much more so" section is the secondary synthesis. Within the first [section], there are again three parts.

First, the dharma is applied to the dharma, as in "my teaching," etc. Second, the analogy is applied to the analogy, as in "for example," etc. Regarding the first of these: "direct mind" (*ṛju-citta*) refers to its essential nature (*tattva*).
"Being without deviousness or falsehood" means that one's conduct and demeanor are free from circuitousness and delusion;

this can be understood next. There are two further points of transition, each consisting of two parts: first, the application to the lower dharma; second, the analogy beginning with "like biting," etc. The dharma is understandable.
Regarding the analogy of "like biting," etc., these words originate from the *Zuozhuan*. It says therein: "Now if..."
If one does not take [the scent], there will be no time for regret; this is what is meant by "regretting when it is too late.
It refers to how, once the musk from within the navel has been taken by another, even if one regrets it, it is already beyond remedy. For now, I am merely borrowing its phrasing, but not its intent.

Therefore, it does not say "deer and humans" alone; the intention is that one who wishes to seek bodhi through false speech is like a person trying to bite their own navel with their mouth—how could they succeed?
Thus, it says "like biting," and so forth. The third [section], "Right Abandonment," can be understood. The third [section], "As I...
and below, which concludes the discussion on the heterodox and the orthodox, can likewise be understood.
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Six;
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Seven.
Expounded by the Great Master Yisong of Tiantai.
Recorded by Lingshu, Disciple of the Yuxi Gate. Part Two:
From "Ānanda, as you have asked" onwards, this is the text concerning the recitation of the divine mantra. It is divided into two sections: first, the summary of what preceded;

second, the elucidation of the present subject. Within the first section, the summary of what preceded, [it describes] the three types of bodily and four types of verbal actions that give rise to [rebirth].

Regarding the claim that there are "no causes," some raise the following doubts: "The three mental [actions] are greed and so forth; the three now mentioned—sexual misconduct and so forth—are the three bodily [actions].
Why, then, do you instead take the body as the root and the mind as the branches? This is not the only issue.

Furthermore, regarding the four verbal [actions], since false speech was already included among the four [mental actions], how can there still be four [verbal actions]? These arguments are all incorrect.

If we discuss the causes that give rise to rebirth, regarding the karma created by the three types of bodily and four types of verbal actions following greed and other afflictions, those of the body are considered primary, while those of the mind are secondary.
Therefore, when observing the precepts, it is sufficient if internal thoughts such as lust do not arise.
If this were to arise, then one would destroy everything; how could the three actions of the body and four of the mouth not be established?
Now, although false speech is included within the preceding four [categories of verbal action], when we speak of the "four of the mouth," it must be mentioned in conjunction with them.

If one were to mention only the "three of the body," it would be inconvenient. Regarding all demonic activities, one should state above that: "If the mind does not hang upon sensory objects such as forms and fragrances..."
Since the inner mind is tranquil, external objects are naturally empty; from where, then, could any class of māras arise? Therefore, it is said that "all are equal," and so forth.

Second, the clarification of the present section is divided into two parts: first, the exhortation to maintain [the practice] beginning with "If there should be... and second, the experimental test beginning with "Furthermore, you... and so on.

The first [section] also has two parts. The first is the direct exhortation, namely "If there be... and so forth. The second is the concluding exhortation, namely "This is... and so forth. Within the first, the direct exhortation: regarding "If there be...
and so forth, the previous four types are present karma, which one can naturally subdue; that which is within this [mantra] is past habituation (*vāsanā*).
If it were not for divine spells (*vidyā-mantra*), how could it be extinguished? Therefore it says, "You should teach... and so forth. Recite this with single-minded devotion.
Regarding this single mind, it shall be explained through two aspects: the phenomenal and the principle.

As for "the radiance from the Buddha’s crown," it refers to the light emitted from the Buddha’s crown, within which emanated Buddhas appear, and these emanated Buddhas preach the mantra; thus it is called "the Buddha’s crown" and so forth.
"Mahā" and so on is a Sanskrit term; in this language, it means "Great White Parasol. "Great" (Mahā) is named according to its essential nature, as it pervades all things.
Because it is the Dharma, "White" (śukla) is a designation for purity, as it is free from defilement. "Canopy" (vitāna) has the meaning of universal coverage, as it encompasses all dharmas.
Therefore, "Great" (mahā) is the Dharmakāya; "White" is Prajñā; and "Canopy" is Vimukti.
As for the "unsurpassed divine mantra," it possesses the essential substance of these three virtues; it is most honored and beyond addition, most supreme and beyond comparison.

Therefore, it is called "unsurpassed. Furthermore, because it cannot be fathomed or conjectured, it is called a "divine mantra" (*śrīmantra*). As for the mark of the invisible crown (*anavalokitamūrdhatā*), this refers to the summit of the Buddha’s *uṣṇīṣa*.
Bodhisattvas such as Avalokiteśvara and those up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) serve as the nurses for the Buddha.
Even if one seeks to see it, one cannot see it; this is the essence of the inconceivable fruit-virtue.
Only a Buddha and a Buddha can fully exhaust its depth; therefore, it is called the "Crown Protuberance Invisible to All.

Regarding the "unconditioned mind-Buddha," although the Tathāgata possesses the cultivation of causal practices, that cultivation arises from the nature such that there is no cultivation to be cultivated. Although the Tathāgata possesses the fruit-virtues...

This is the realization that, having extinguished cultivation and returned to the nature, there is nothing to be realized. Therefore, although all treasuries of the Dharma are taught, they are also intrinsically possessed by the nature;
thus, it is a teaching of non-teaching. Although all sentient beings are transformed, they are also intrinsically possessed by the nature.

This transformation is a transformation without anything being transformed; it does not depend upon fabrication or conceptual designation. Therefore, it is called the "unconditioned Buddha of the mind.
Regarding the phrase "from the crown [of the head]," this specifically clarifies that the transformation-Buddha is the one who speaks the mantra.

Since the aforementioned Buddha is the Buddha of the mind, although the current mantra is spoken by the transformation-Buddha, from where does this transformation arise? It flows forth from the single essence of nature; thus, the mantra is also said to be the mind.
Mantra. However, how can reciting and upholding it cure past habitual tendencies? One must understand the essence of the mantra.
Since it is called *mahā-sattva-trātṛ*, it is entirely the inconceivable threefold virtue (*tri-guṇa*).

As the essence of the upheld mantra is the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) pervading all places, the nature of the mind that upholds it is likewise the Dharma-body pervading all places. Thus, [the capacity to uphold it]...
There is nothing that is not the Dharma-body among both the grasper and the grasped; how then could the Dharma-body possess residual habits (*vāsanā*)?
Indeed, these very residual habits, in their essential nature, are themselves the Dharma-body. This can be seen by analogy with *prajñā* and liberation (*vimukti*).

Thus, all such residual habits are in fact the three virtues (*triguṇa*). These residual habits are self-governed without being deliberately treated; this is what is meant by "breaking without breaking."
There is nothing that it cannot destroy. It is for this reason that I teach people to recite mantras to cure their habitual tendencies.

Part Two: Describing the Manifestations of Efficacy is divided into two sections. First, "You should first... and so forth, which clarifies the manifestation of efficacy; second, "That person should then... and so forth, which provides a comparative analysis.

Regarding the first section, as for the phrase "I also proclaim," when Caṇḍālī heard the ultimate, firm principle, she had already attained the three fruits [of the śrāvaka], as well as the river of craving.

It has become withered and dry. Since she chose the Perfect Penetration (*pariśuddha-āyatana*), she has further attained the four fruits of arhatship; hence the phrase "the heart of craving," and so forth.
However, that the four fruits were achieved and the heart of craving was liberated both resulted from the power of the transformation Buddha’s recitation of the mantra;
hence the phrase "I too proclaim," and so forth. Even a courtesan who had accumulated [karma] over many kalpas was able to swiftly liberate her heart of craving and swiftly attain [the fruits].
Having realized the fruit of the Way, how great indeed must the power of that mantra be! Second, the comparison has two parts. First, the actual comparison: "He was still equal [to her]," etc.
Second, providing an analogy: "It is like," etc. Regarding the first part, there are three points of difference in the comparison between Ānanda and Ḍākinī:
the difference between a worldly courtesan and a world-transcending Śrāvaka, which is the distinction between defilement and purity. There is no... [text ends].
In practicing with the mind to seek the supreme path, there are differences in being slow or swift;
in realizing cessation and attaining the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) to become definitively a Buddha, there are differences in being superior or inferior.

If even those who are defiled, slow, or inferior can suddenly eliminate long-standing habits and realize the fruit of the Way, how much more so for those who are pure, swift, and superior, who will quickly eliminate outflows (*āsrava*) and attain the Buddha-way themselves.
It is not difficult; therefore, it is said that "they are still [like this]," and so forth. Regarding the second point, the phrase "for example," etc., has two meanings.
First, speaking from the perspective of attaining the Buddha-way: when a śrāvaka seeks the Buddha-way, it is like scattering fine dust.

By means of the empowerment of divine mantras, seeking [the Way] is like scattering fine dust in a following wind; it will naturally be carried along by the current without any hardship or perilous obstacles.
Second, this is explained from the perspective of counteracting past habitual tendencies. Counteracting past habitual tendencies is like winnowing fine dust;
when one applies empowered mantras to counteract them, it is like winnowing fine dust with a favorable wind. They will naturally and spontaneously dissolve away without difficulty or obstacle.
Therefore, it says, "For example," and so forth.

Third, regarding the passage on "if there be those in the final age" concerning the establishment of the *maṇḍala*: this is divided into two main parts. First, a brief clarification, beginning with "If there be those in the final age," etc.

Second, a detailed exposition, beginning with "Ānanda addressed the Buddha," etc. Within the first part, there are further two sections: first, the preliminary preparations (*upāya*), beginning with "If there be... and so forth;
second, the actual cultivation (*bhāvanā*), beginning with "Thereafter," and so forth. Regarding the preliminary preparations, the phrase "If there be... refers to...
Regarding those who, in this degenerate age, seek the path of the unsurpassed Bodhi at the site of true enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa): this is the field for attaining the Way.
If one says they wish to sit [in meditation], they are merely at the stage of the cause; this is the field for cultivating the Way. For one who seeks to realize the Way must first cultivate the Way;
since both aspects are present here, it is said, "If there be... and so forth. As for "first maintaining [the precepts]," this refers to the bhikṣu.
One should maintain [the precepts]. It is not merely a matter of restraining the body so as not to act, nor is it simply a matter of restraining the mind so that it does not arise;
one must also restrain the mind such that it is ungraspable, for only then does one possess pure precepts. As for the requirement of equanimity:

if one receives the prohibitive precepts, unless one is oneself a teacher of pure, true precepts, how could one possibly clarify every detail—whether great or small, light or heavy, maintained or violated, permitted or prohibited?

Because it is accomplished by persons, it is said that one "must [practice] equally," and so forth. Reciting and maintaining [the mantra] one hundred and eight times serves as the antidote to the one hundred and eight afflictions (*kleśa*).
Furthermore, this single passage clearly elucidates five conditions: first, "maintaining [the precepts]" and so forth refers to the purity of ethical discipline (*śīla-viśuddhi*).
One must first cultivate the fifth [practice]: associating with virtuous friends. Second is the fulfillment of the precepts and the necessities of life, such as food and clothing.
Third is dwelling in seclusion and quietude, such as by burning incense. Fourth is reciting these [mantras], which brings all distracting affairs to rest.
When these five conditions are fulfilled, the five desires may be censured, the five hindrances may be abandoned, the five matters may be regulated, and the five dharmas may be practiced.
Thus, by encompassing the "one five," the remaining four are fully included. Within this single phrase, the meaning of the preparatory practices for the twenty-five [days] is entirely contained.
Second, the section on formal cultivation is divided into three parts, namely the three periods of seven days. First, thereafter, etc.
This refers to the first seven days; second, Ānanda and others for the second seven days; third, those such as these for the third seven days.
Regarding the beginning, the phrase "then afterwards" and so forth indicates that the ritual for delimiting the boundary (*sīmā-bandha*) is not fixed:
some use a blade to draw a line on the ground as the limit, some use white mustard seeds scattered and thrown as the limit, and some use five-colored threads passed through the four outer sides.
Regarding the establishment of limits: some take the reach of the mind’s visualization as the limit, while others take the sprinkling of pure water as the limit;
all of these are permitted by the Buddha’s regulations. "Seeking throughout the ten directions" means seeking for the Buddhas to come and respond.

During the second seven-day period, bhikṣuṇīs may perform repentance rituals on the same altar as others; however, they must avoid being objects of derision, for this is the natural course of the Dharma.

In these present degenerate times, such practices are no longer appropriate. As for laypeople who wish to join the ritual on the same altar, they must receive the precepts, don the monastic robes, and prepare the full ceremonial regalia of a Buddha;
once they exit the altar area, these requirements are no longer necessary. Those who have made the Bodhisattva vows are as follows: [text continues below].
In the extensive exposition, there is first the teaching on the original vow. Regarding the phrase "I myself," etc., within the three-week period, this refers to the Buddha manifesting his body.

Since he has already sought out the Buddhas of the ten directions during the first week, they now come to respond to him; this is what is meant by the mutual resonance of cause and response. It is like the moon being reflected when water is clear:
once the water of the sentient beings' minds is clear, the moon of the Buddha naturally manifests its appearance. This is the skillful means.
Regarding the phrase "reciting and upholding," it goes without saying that this refers to the actual practice of recitation and upholding.

Furthermore, although on the first seven days there was the seeking of the Buddhas of the ten directions, on the second seven days there was the making of vows, bathing, and performing the path-practice during the six periods, and on the third seven days there was the practice of not sleeping.
These are all merely provisional explanations. To speak fully, this applies to all three periods of seven days. This is why the summary within the section on the three weeks states:
"In this way, for three weeks he did not sleep," and so forth.
The second part, the extensive demonstration, is divided into two sections: first, the request made by Ānanda and others; second, the response and instruction given by the Buddha.

Regarding the initial request, the phrase "I have received," etc., refers to the aforementioned four types of discipline (*vinaya*) and the practice of recitation and cultivation as the unsurpassed compassionate instruction.
Since the request for the establishment of the ritual site (*maṇḍala*) has already been made, one now further hears of the discipline and the practice of cultivation.
If explained briefly, its great significance has already been grasped; thus it is said that "the mind is already awakened.

From this point forward, the practice one cultivates is the practice of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), and the principle one realizes is the principle of definitive meaning. It is spontaneously accomplished at the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*);
hence the phrase "knowing for oneself" and so forth. This concludes the preceding section. Below, under the heading "The Age of Dharma-Decline," follows the formal request for the present teaching.
This means that I previously asked the Tathāgata how sentient beings in the final age might collect their minds and establish a site for the Way (bodhimaṇḍa).
Now that I have heard the method for collecting the mind, I still do not know how to establish a site for the Way so as to accord with the Tathāgata’s pure regulations;
hence the words "in the final age," and so forth. Pure Regulations.
As for the principle: whatever the Tathāgata has established is by no means in vain. In its inception, it must rely on principle to establish phenomena;
in its continuation, it must rely on phenomena to manifest principle. Only then can phenomena and principle be mutually integrated, and cultivation and nature operate in tandem.
Thus, it causes practitioners of later generations to realize the principle whenever they encounter a phenomenon. If they do so realize...
Its principle is itself fused with its phenomena; whether phenomenon or principle, whether contemplation or object, all are nothing other than pure and original, pervading the entire Dharma-realm.

This is what is meant by the saying: "A single flower or a single incense offering brings merit equal to the sands of the Ganges; a single gaze or a single prostration extends its efficacy throughout the Dharma-realm. This constitutes the rule of purity.
Therefore, from the subsequent establishment of the altar down to the practice of seated meditation, [all must accord with this principle].
The five chapters all clarify the meaning by means of the rules for purity.
In the second response, there are generally five sections: first, from "If, in the age of the末 (mò) [degenerate] world, people depart," it clarifies the rules for establishing purity;
second, from "Taking the milk of a white cow," it clarifies the rules for providing offerings with purity; third, from "In the space of the altar,"...
The first clarifies the rules for the purity of image installation; the second clarifies the rules for the purity of walking meditation (caṅkrama) during the first seven days;
and from the third seven-day period onwards, it clarifies the rules for the purity of seated meditation (dhyāna). These matters can be seen within these five chapters.

However, since these practices are established based on principle, one must likewise manifest that principle through the very acts themselves. This is evident throughout the middle section of each instance.
A single prostration and a single circumambulation are nothing other than using phenomena to manifest principle.

The first section, "The Ritual Procedures for Establishing the Altar and Purifying [the Site]," is divided into two parts. First, the manifestation of selecting the root-capacity (of the practitioner), such as "if it is the end [of the age]" and so forth.

Second, the manifestation of practicing the causal conduct, such as "square" and "round" and so forth. The first part is further divided into three. First, selecting those of the perfect capacity from among the inferior, such as "if it is the end... and so forth. Second, if it is not... [and so on].
The following section distinguishes between the *Zang* (Tripitaka) and *Tong* (Shared) teachings. Thirdly, it specifically selects the *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching from below.

Within the initial selection of those with the capacity for the Perfect (*Yuan*) Teaching, the phrase "if at the end [of the age]" etc., precisely reveals that sentient beings of the final age cultivate the Dharma-gate of perfect penetration.

First, the mention of the Snowy Mountains symbolizes the adoption of the Perfect Teaching's Dharma; the Snowy Mountains stand loftily above all other mountains, just as the Perfect Teaching transcends all other teachings.
Therefore, the Snowy Mountains are used first to represent this. As for the "powerful white ox" that is able to move all things:
the faculties of the Perfect Teaching (Yuanjiao) do not merely transport one out of the three miserable realms, the triple world, and the three voids;
they further enable one to enter into the three virtues. Thus, the great white ox is used to represent this. The white ox eats only the fragrant herbs of the Snowy Mountains. The Perfect...
The wisdom possessed by the vehicle is exclusively the three subtle wisdoms; therefore, it is symbolized by feeding on fragrant herbs that are rich and succulent.
The white ox drinks only the pure water of the Snowy Mountains; likewise, the teachings possessed by those of perfect capacity are exclusively the wondrous samādhi of the true aspect (dharmatā).
Therefore, this is symbolized by drinking only pure water. The dung of the white ox is most subtle. Perfect...

Because the specific measure and number of the phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing of ignorance within the faculties of those with the Perfect Capacity (yuan-ji) are subtle, they are represented by cow dung.
The dung produced from a cow that has eaten fragrant herbs and pure water is both stained and pure; it is fit to be blended with incense.

Likewise, although those with the Perfect Capacity possess ignorance, because they possess perfect understanding, they realize that the three delusions, when stained, are in their very essence the Three Virtues.
Intrinsic nature (*dhātu*) is such that delusion is entirely identical to truth, and hindrances are entirely identical to virtue. Therefore, it is symbolized by mixing excrement with incense.

Regarding the earth, one takes this excrement and mixes it with sandalwood paste. Since those of perfect capacity realize that the defilement of the three delusions is entirely the nature of the three virtues, there is not a single thing that is not the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the intrinsic nature, and the principle.
Taking this as the object of contemplation, the surface of the earth is thus smeared with the paste.

Second, regarding the selection between the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings: "If it were not the Snowy Mountain" means that since the Snowy Mountain above represents the Dharma of the Perfect Teaching, the present statement "if it were not the Snowy Mountain" refers to the Tripiṭaka and the Shared Teachings; therefore, it uses "if it were not the Snowy Mountain" as a metaphor for them.
The teachings of the *Tripiṭaka* and *Shared* vehicles stop at the destruction of the two delusions of views and thought; therefore, they are symbolized by the foul odor of the ox.

The wisdom of these two vehicles merely analyzes and negates the substance [of phenomena], and their principle is merely the partial truth (*prādeśika-satya*); they cannot reveal the ground of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) which is one's own nature.

Therefore, they are symbolized as being unfit for anointing the ground. Third, regarding the distinction within the *Distinct Teaching*: that which distinguishes it from the [other] equals is the Perfect Teaching (*yāna*), though it may not yet be fully realized.

It is easy to understand. As for the *Zhàng* (Shared) and *Tōng* (Penetrating) teachings, these must be further discerned; one should therefore seek the *Bie* (Distinct) Teaching. Thus, it is distinguished by means of this designation.

For those of the distinct capacity to cultivate contemplation: they enter from the conventional into emptiness, emerge from emptiness into the conventional, and subsequently return from both emptiness and the conventional into the Middle Way.
At the beginning, the conventional and emptiness are equal; in the subsequent stage, emptiness and the conventional [are likewise equal].
These aspects are equal. Subsequently, although there is the provisional emptiness that enters into the Middle Way, these aspects remain equal.
Because they advance according to a sequential order, it is called "Equal Contemplation" (*samadarśana*). Therefore, it is symbolized by the "Level Plain.

Those of distinct capacities do not realize that total delusion is itself truth and that total obscuration is itself virtue; they insist on abandoning delusion to reveal truth and destroying obscuration to achieve virtue. For this reason—
By piercing through and removing the surface layer of the earth, one uses a separate implement to shatter the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*).

This reveals the pure *tathatā* (suchness), which is the principle of the *but-madhyamaka-satya* (the middle truth of "only"). Therefore, the five feet represent the five stages of dwelling. Yellow is among the five colors, and earth is among the five elements;
thus, yellow soil represents the principle of the *but-madhyamaka-satya*. One further understands that this principle extends throughout the ten categories.
The gates of liberation are constituted by the sequential combination and division of the ten fragrances; thus, these are taken as equal to serve as their representation.
Since one knows that these involve the ten perfections (pāramitās), one further knows that the ten perfections traverse eighty-four thousand subtle dharma-gates;
therefore, a sieve of the ten fragrances is used as powder to represent them. Having known the principle of the Middle Truth alone, one again traverses the subtle dharma-gates.
Because one will eventually attain the single realization of practice and principle, it is symbolized by the blending of the soil.

Because principle and practice are darkly unified and the understanding is likewise profound, it is symbolized by the formation of clay. One should know that this Middle Truth alone can serve as the object of contemplation.

Therefore, the ground and surface are smeared with [powder] to represent them. From the "Perfectly Round Mechanism" (yuan ji) up to this point, the exposition has clarified what is known solely in accordance with the capacities of the faculties (gen ji);
it has not yet explained what is practiced. As for the causal practices that follow, they clarify what is practiced. These two representations of causal practice are further divided into two:
first, practicing the perfect cause, such as the "Square and Round"; second, practicing the distinct causes, such as the "Mirror Outside" and so forth.
Regarding the phrase "square and round" in the context of the initial fulfillment of the causal stage: this refers to those who construct a platform by piling up earth;

it does not refer to those who construct a platform by clearing away earth, for clearing away earth constitutes a mere site (*āyatana*). As for the measurements of sixteen feet (one *zhang* and six *chi*) for both the square and the round:

these do not mean that each dimension is individually sixteen feet. The circular shape of the platform symbolizes the self-nature of perfect luminosity; the eight corners symbolize the essence of the eight consciousnesses; and the sixteen feet symbolize the sixteen modes of perception. If one were to depart from this...
The sixteen modes of perception and the essence of the eight consciousnesses have no self-nature of perfect luminosity that can be apprehended.
Apart from this self-nature of perfect luminosity, neither the sixteen modes of perception nor the essence of the eight consciousnesses can be found.
It is just as one cannot find a ritual altar apart from its sixteen corners and eight-sided shape, nor can one find the sixteen corners and eight-sided shape apart from the altar itself.
It is so. To further extend this reasoning: apart from the sixteen modes of perception, the essence of the eight consciousnesses cannot be found;

and apart from the essence of the eight consciousnesses, the sixteen modes of perception cannot be found. It is just as there can be no eight corners apart from the sixteen-foot [Buddha-body], nor a sixteen-foot body apart from the eight corners.
This is precisely the essence of the eight consciousnesses, which are perfectly integrated such that they arise and perish simultaneously.
The entire body is the unborn and undying, perfectly luminous self-nature; thus, a square altar sixteen feet on each side is used as a representation of the eight-cornered altar.
That the mind reaches the lotus flower represents the wondrous practice of the perfect penetration of the ear-organ arising from the self-nature of ignorance.
Although there are four kinds of lotuses, such as the golden and others, only one kind is used, according to the resources offered.
One should simply adjust the abundance or scarcity [of offerings] as appropriate. Having cultivated the sublime practice of the ear-faculty, one must uphold the prohibitive precepts;

thus, one takes the nature of hearing itself as the means of restraint. This is symbolized by placing a bowl within the flower, representing what was previously called "taking the collected mind as the precept.
Once the precepts are upheld, concentration naturally arises; this is symbolized by filling the bowl with water. For...

"In the midst of autumn in the eighth month" refers to the intense dew of the eighth month symbolizing the stabilization of the Middle Way; this is as previously stated: that concentration arises from ethical discipline (*śīla*).

Once both discipline and concentration are complete, sublime wisdom (*prajñā*) will necessarily be produced; thus, it is symbolized by water settling upon the petals of a flower. This is as previously stated: that wisdom arises because of concentration.
Although there are these three trainings (*tri-śikṣā*), they are all fully contained within the wondrous practice of the faculty of hearing. Therefore...
The "cloud-flowers" represent the middle [stage]. Taking eight round mirrors symbolizes the eightfold right wisdom (*aṣṭāṅga-samyagjñāna*).

Placing them equally [around] means that the flowers represent sublime conduct (*sucarita*) and the bowls represent the precepts (*śīla*). Surrounding the flowers and bowls with the eight round mirrors signifies that for a person of perfection, there is no separate conduct;
their conduct is solely wisdom. For a person of perfection, there is no separate precept; their precept is solely...

Taking wisdom as the precept, it is therefore said that one "takes up the eight [precepts]," and so forth. Second, regarding the specific causes: as for "outside the mirror" and so on, such is the nature of universal practice (*paryāptacaryā*).
How, then, can distinct practice (*viśeṣacaryā*) be manifested? Therefore, "outside the mirror" and so forth are used as its manifestation.

Establishing a lotus flower outside the mirror symbolizes the path-practice of the Distinct Teaching (*bhedavyavahāra-śāsana*). Establishing an incense burner symbolizes the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*) of the Distinct Teaching.

This refers to wisdom (*prajñā*). Although there are both the practices of the path (*mārga-caryā*) and the wisdom of contemplation (*vipaśyanā-prajñā*), these are collectively categorized as sequential; therefore, they are symbolized by an arrangement of alternating flowers.
Furthermore, the reason both are said to be "sixteen" is that the practices of the path and the wisdom of contemplation all correspond to and shatter the sixteen types of false views from past lives.
As for the adornment of the incense burner, it symbolizes the sequential contemplation of the Distinct Teaching (*prativedha-śāsana*). Once this sequential contemplation is perfected, however—
The central principle ought to be made manifest; therefore, it is symbolized by pure burning agarwood. Since the principle is thus revealed, the twelve grades of ignorance should be severed;

therefore, this is symbolized by the fire that causes one not to see [the wood]. The two preceding sections, which symbolize the faculties and the causal practices, clarifying the ritual rules for purifying the altar, are hereby concluded.
Second, the section clarifying the ritual procedures for making offerings is divided into two parts. First, taking white [substances] and so forth represents one's own practice (*sva-caryā*).

Second, causing others to take [them] and so forth represents transforming others (*parārtha*). The first part is further divided into two. First, taking white [substances] and so forth represents the perfect cause (*pariniṣpanna-hetu*) actualizing the perfect fruit (*pariniṣpanna-phala*).

Second, each instance of "taking" (*ādāna*) represents a specific cause (*viśeṣa-hetu*) actualizing a specific fruit (*viśeṣa-phala*). The first of these is further divided into two. First, it clarifies the cause: taking white [substances] and so forth. Second, it reveals...
The fruit. "To offer," etc. This section has two parts: first, the primary practice, from "taking" down to "white"; second, the auxiliary practices, from "together with all" down to "practice.
Within the primary practice, "taking the milk of a white cow" symbolizes the emergence of the three subtle wisdoms from the nature of hearing.
Using a white cow as the basis for the five colors and walking swiftly represents wisdom being the precursor to the myriad practices, its contemplative illumination being perfect and complete.
Furthermore, milk can nourish the physical body (*rūpakāya*), while wisdom can increase the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*); thus, white cow’s milk is used to symbolize this.
By means of these three subtle wisdoms, one contemplates the sixteen modes of perception as the entirety of the wondrous realm; therefore, they are placed in sixteen vessels to symbolize this.
Moreover, when milk is placed within a vessel, the vessel becomes milk, symbolizing that the entire realm is identical to wisdom. When the vessel is placed [within the milk]...
Since milk is itself the vessel, it symbolizes that complete wisdom is identical with the objective realm. Realm and wisdom are one; subject and object are non-dual.
Therefore, taking white cow’s milk and placing it in sixteen vessels serves as its representation. As for the milk being used for fried cakes, the cake is circular.
This serves to symbolize the wondrous realm of the sixteen insights, which are perfectly observed and perfectly illumined by sublime wisdom.
Accordingly, if they arise as empty, they are all empty; even so, if they arise as the Middle Way, they are all the Middle Way. Therefore, it is represented by using milk to make fried cakes.

Such is the primary practice (*samyak-pratipatti*). Next, regarding the auxiliary practices (*upāya-pratipatti*), the phrase "together with all" (*bing zhu*) is used in contrast to the primary practice.
Furthermore, the granulated sugar symbolizes the four foundations of mindfulness; the oil cakes symbolize the four right efforts; the milk gruel symbolizes the four bases of psychic power;

the *sugandha* (sandalwood) symbolizes the five faculties; the honey ginger symbolizes the five powers; the pure ghee symbolizes the seven factors of enlightenment; and the pure honey symbolizes the eightfold noble path.
Taken together, these represent all thirty-seven factors of enlightenment without exception. Such are the auxiliary practices.

All the sublime wisdom of the primary practice (*maula-pratipatti*) of cow’s milk, as well as the auxiliary practices (*anuloma-pratipatti*) such as the path-factors of sugar and so forth, are entirely perfected within the sublime practice of the ear-organ (*śrotra-indriya*).

Therefore, they are represented on the exterior of the lotus. Since both the primary and auxiliary practices correspond to the sixteen modes of cognition (*ṣoḍaśākāra-jñāna*), each is represented by sixteen [petals].
Furthermore, there is nothing in these primary and auxiliary practices that does not penetrate thoroughly into the ear-organ.
Because it represents sublime conduct (*sucarita*), it is surrounded by flowers on its exterior. This lotus is the principal great lotus among them;

it is not the same as the sixteen [lotuses] established outside the mirror. One represents the totality (*pariṇata*), while the sixteen represent the particulars (*viśeṣa*), for their characteristics differ.
Second, regarding the manifestation within the fruit: "with offerings," etc., refers to the aforementioned sixteen vessels of cow's milk and...

The sixteen vessels of sugar and so forth should each be offered to the Buddha to symbolize that when the primary and auxiliary causes are perfected, it is the natural law that one shall attain the unsurpassed fruit of Buddhahood.

Having already made offerings to all Buddhas, they are now offered to the Bodhisattvas to symbolize that all Great Bodhisattvas likewise attain the fruit of Buddhahood through these sublime practices.
Furthermore, this reveals that what the practitioner performs is precisely what the Buddhas have realized.

That which is cultivated by Bodhisattvas refers to that which the Tathāgatas of the past have already accomplished through this gateway, and that which the Bodhisattvas of the present are now each entering with perfect clarity (*pariniṣpanna*).
Therefore, it is represented by "to offer" (*feng*) and so forth. Second, representing the distinct cause as yielding a distinct result also has two parts.
First, clarifying the cause: this is indicated by the word "each" (*mei yi deng ye*). Second, manifesting the result: this is the phrase "enjoying the Buddha" (*xiang fo ju ye*). First [part].

Furthermore, there are two parts: first, each instance begins with a general summary; second, from "In the *Tuṣita* heaven" onwards, it provides a specific explanation. Regarding the first, "each instance," etc.:
the Tathāgata’s meals invariably take place at midday, which is the midpoint of the yang, capable of symbolizing the inconceivable Middle Way.
Now, when it says "midnight," this is the midpoint of the yin, precisely symbolizing the "but-middling" truth (*butongdi*) of pure *tathatā* as revealed by the Separate Teaching (*biejiao*).

This refers to the principle; hence it is said, "always [using] equal [measures]," and so forth. Since one wishes to manifest the principle, it is necessary to destroy the afflictions of the five abodes;
therefore, taking half a *liang* of honey symbolizes this. Since one wishes to destroy delusions, one should practice the three successive contemplations (*san guan*);

therefore, using three *he* of clarified butter symbolizes this. Once the contemplations have dissolved the delusions, they can be destroyed; once the delusions are destroyed, the principle can be manifested. From this point on, it refers to the fruit of the teaching.
The head may be struck; therefore, a small brazier is separately placed before the altar to serve as its symbol. This is the general summary.

Next, regarding the middle [section], the two phrases beginning with "With the *dōu*" symbolize the contemplation of entering emptiness from the conventional (*prajñapti*). By means of incense, it is transformed into water.
There is only its fragrance, yet entirely lacking its substance. When entering from the provisional into emptiness, one perceives only the ultimate truth, with no provisional marks at all;
it is like the water infused with *turuṣka* incense. Therefore, this is used as a metaphor for the phrase "bathing."
This symbolizes entering the provisional from emptiness. Since the charcoal has already been bathed with fragrant water, only the charcoal remains and there is no water at all.
When one enters the provisional from emptiness, one perceives only the conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) and there is no ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya) whatsoever;
it is just like bathing that charcoal. Therefore, this is used as a symbol. Furthermore, this single phrase symbolizes entering the Middle Way from both emptiness and the provisional.
This is the contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). Having washed the charcoal with water and then ignited it with the charcoal, one sees only the fire, with no trace of either water or charcoal remaining.

When entering the Middle Way Contemplation (*madhyamaka-vipaśyanā*) from the perspectives of the Empty and the Provisional, one negates the two extremes (*anta-dvaya*) and manifests only the Middle Principle (*madhya-tattva*);

this is like making the fire blaze fiercely. Therefore, this is used as a metaphor for it. The above illustrates the three contemplations in this manner. "Throwing [the fire] down" below illustrates...
Both the negator and the object of negation are unattainable. Previously, there was the negator of the three contemplations, which is like clarified butter (*sarpis*);

there was the object of negation, the five abodes (*pañcavihāra*), which is like honey (*madhu*). Reaching this point, although there is a negator and an object of negation, as well as a contemplator and an object of contemplation, all are unattainable;
there is only the principle of the Middle Way (*madhyamaka*). It is like casting the clarified butter and honey into a blazing furnace and burning them away.

It is exhausted; therefore, it is used to represent this. From this point on, the principle of the three virtues across the twelve divisions will be nearly perfected, and the delusions of ignorance across the twelve grades will be nearly eliminated.
The distinct cause is thus established, and one should attain the fruit of Buddhahood according to the teaching; therefore, it is represented by the offering to the Buddha.

Above, the perfect cause has produced the perfect fruit, and the distinct cause has produced the distinct fruit; thus, one's own practice is already accomplished. Since one's own practice is already accomplished, one should in turn transform others;
therefore, below there is the passage beginning with "causing them to... and so forth. Second, regarding the transformation of others, the phrase "causing them to...

refers to the previous offerings, which were confined only within the altar. Therein, the phenomenon was entirely the principle, and the nature gave rise entirely to cultivation, thereby manifesting...

The practice is spontaneously accomplished. Nevertheless, all sentient beings have not yet realized this. For this reason, banners and flowers are suspended everywhere throughout the four directions so that they may likewise perceive it;
this is to manifest that the entirety of phenomena is itself principle, and that the entirety of cultivation is itself nature.
Because sentient beings have hitherto functioned solely through the consciousness-mind, when they reach this state, they perceive those very phenomena and thereby realize their underlying principle.
The five, six, seven, eight, and so forth of the consciousnesses each transform individually into wisdom; thus, there are four wisdoms, which are represented by the four [wisdom-wheels].
Furthermore, the banner possesses the quality of movement and transformation;

anyone who beholds it can transform afflictions into bodhi and transform birth-and-death into nirvana, and thus the hanging banner represents this. The flower represents the sublime practice of the faculty of hearing.
All who behold this shall thoroughly comprehend it; they will likewise be able to turn the hearing back toward the nature of hearing and accomplish the sublime practice of the ear-faculty.

Therefore, a suspended flower is used to signify this. Thus, having perfected one's own practice, the work of transforming others is also accomplished. This concludes the clear exposition of the ritual rules for making offerings.
The section on the ritual procedures for arranging the images in the Threefold Hall has three parts: first, arranging the images of the four walls beneath the altar;

second, one should arrange the principal image facing forward below [the central area]; third, arranging the images of the external protectors beneath Śakra. Regarding the arrangement of images in these three locations:

This is intended to cause the practitioner to give rise to reverence upon beholding the image, and through that reverence, to attain awakening. First, the altar chamber represents the self-nature (*svabhāva*).
The four walls represent, within that self-nature, the cultivation of the *śrotra-indriya-samādhi* (the samādhi of the ear faculty) through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.

They may also represent the wisdom that illumines existence, the wisdom that illumines emptiness, the wisdom that illumines both existence and emptiness, and the wisdom that illumines neither existence nor [emptiness].
It is the wisdom of emptiness. The Tathāgata is the ultimate, final fruit; the Bodhisattva is the true cause for cultivation.
The establishment of the ritual chamber likewise symbolizes the ultimate fruit and the true cause of one’s own nature.

Furthermore, when the practitioner cultivates this samādhi as an offering, they should act as if realizing the ultimate fruit as the Tathāgata has realized it, and they should act as if being a Bodhisattva.

The cultivation of the causal conditions for realizing the truth is precisely this seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, which can thus be manifested as what is called "peaceful bliss, wondrous permanence"—namely, the six sense faculties.
Among these two [aspects], that which faces forward symbolizes the Middle Way principle realized by the Tathāgata;
it is the Reward Body Buddha (Sambhogakāya) Vairocana. This is translated as "Pure Fulfillment" (*Jingman*). It is because all delusions are shattered without exception.
"Purity" means that there is no virtue that is not manifested as complete. One cultivates this samādhi as an act of offering.
This signifies that the practitioner, like Śākyamuni Tathāgata, shall likewise destroy all delusions and manifest all principles to become a Sambhogakāya Buddha.
Śākyamuni is the Nirmāṇakāya Buddha who is the teacher of the Sahā world; he is called "Capable Benevolence" (Nengren). He dwells neither in saṃsāra nor in... [nirvāṇa].
Nirvāṇa. Returning to the Sahā world to teach and transform sentient beings, one cultivates this samādhi as an act of offering.

This signifies that the practitioner should likewise, like Śākyamuni Tathāgata, dwell neither in saṃsāra nor in nirvāṇa, but return to the Sahā world to teach and transform sentient beings, becoming a Nirmāṇakāya Buddha. Maitreya is none other than Śākyamuni’s successor in the future.
He is a Buddha, here called Maitreya. It is said that his benevolence flourishes in this world and his compassion reaches the future kalpas;

he bestows happiness upon all sentient beings and uproots suffering for all sentient beings. One cultivates this samādhi as an act of offering to manifest that the practitioner, too, should be like Tathāgata Maitreya, flourishing in benevolence in this world and reaching in compassion in future lives, [bestowing] all [happiness].
To bring joy to sentient beings, to uproot the suffering of all sentient beings, and to serve as a successor for the future—this is Akṣobhya, the Buddha of the East.
"Akṣobhya" translates here as "Immovable. While the East is the source of all movement, there resides the Tathāgata Immovable.
This refers to the realization of the non-duality of movement and stillness—that which is still within movement and movement within stillness. To cultivate this samādhi is...

One should make offerings to him. This represents that the practice of entry should also be like the realization attained by Tathāgata Akṣobhya: movement is itself stillness, and stillness is itself movement;
movement and stillness are non-dual. Amitābha is the Buddha of the Western Quarter; here [in Chinese] he is called "Immeasurable Light."
He is also called Amitāyus. He possesses forty-eight great vows and sixteen sublime contemplations (*vipaśyanā*) for gathering in sentient beings so that they may be reborn in his land.
To practice this samādhi as an offering, one should likewise embody the forty-eight great vows and sixteen sublime contemplations of Tathāgata Amitābha.
This refers to the gathering of sentient beings to be reborn in the Pure Land. Those mentioned above are all Tathāgatas who have attained the fruit of Buddhahood;

the various Great Bodhisattvas below are those still on the path of cause. Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva is called the "Great Master of Transformations" because he can manifest the thirty-two forms of response, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables, and further manifests eighty-four thousand śakaras.
This is because [Avalokiteśvara] possesses eighty-four thousand arms like *mudrā*s and eighty-four thousand pure jewel-eyes.

Avalokiteśvara is the master of the perfect penetration of the ear-faculty (*śrotra-indriya*). From the point where one enters the stream within hearing and loses the external objects, up until the cessation of birth and death and the manifestation of quiescent extinction—this samādhi is cultivated as an offering. It signifies that the practitioner, too, should likewise...

Just as Avalokiteśvara, beginning from entering the stream within hearing and losing the objects of perception, until birth-and-death had ceased and quiescent extinction was manifested before him, gave rise to the thirty-two manifestations, the fourteen fearlessnesses, and the four inconceivables;
and with eighty-four thousand *śakara* heads, *mudrā* arms, and pure jewel-eyes, he became the sovereign of perfect penetration. Thus it is said in the *Golden* [Sutra].
Vajragarbha, because that which destroys has nothing to be destroyed, yet there is nothing it does not destroy, it is called "Vajra" (Diamond).
Because it possesses nothing, yet there is nothing it does not possess, it is called "Garbha" (Womb/Treasury). To cultivate this samādhi is to perform an offering.
The practitioner who manifests [this state] should likewise be called Vajragarbha, having shattered all delusions and perfected all virtues, just like Vajragarbha himself.
Because these two classes of Bodhisattvas are positioned to the left and right of the five Buddhas, it is said that they are "established on the left and right.
Thus far, we have discussed the Tathāgata’s ultimate fruition and the Bodhisattva’s cultivation of the true cause; now, we shall address the manifestation [of this state].

The arrangement is as follows. Among these three, Śakra is the lord of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*). Those who fully cultivate the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions are protected externally by him while practicing this samādhi;
this signifies that the practitioner’s observance of the precepts is complete and that wholesome qualities are not failing to arise.
Brahmā is the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*). Those who are able to distance themselves from the six desires and give rise to meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) practice this...
Maitreya acts as its external protector; this signifies that the practitioner’s aspirations will not fail to be fulfilled and that meditative concentration (*samādhi*) will inevitably arise.
Ucchuṣma is precisely the one who achieves success through the contemplation of the great fire for the purpose of subduing sensual desire;

practicing this *samādhi* likewise serves as an external protection, signifying that the practitioner shall also attain freedom from desire and achieve the Fire-Light *Samādhi*. From Śakra downward...
As for the "external protector" (*bāhya-rakṣaka*), this generally signifies that the practitioner has achieved perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*).
In the future, anyone who constructs an altar to cultivate perfect penetration shall likewise receive external protection; thus, one knows that the external protector possesses great majestic power.
The placement of the altar wall facing the sun signifies the presence of great compassion (*mahā-karuṇā*). Relying upon this compassion, it enables the practitioner’s cultivation.
One attains mastery of this samādhi through self-realization and enters into its realization.
By virtue of its majestic power, it causes the samādhis practiced by the practitioner to remain free from the interference of celestial māras, heterodox deities, and externalists.

Having completed the clear exposition of the ritual rules for the purification of the image, the fourth section—the ritual rules for the purification of the practice of the Way—is divided into three parts. First, hanging the mirror (and taking equal measures). Second, the time limit.

Regarding the initial section and so forth, the three practices are established. That is, within that same section, the passage concerning "hanging a mirror" has traditionally been categorized under the "Arrangement of Images.
Now, it is divided and placed within the "Procession" because later on there is the passage where mirrors reflect each other's light and the Buddha strokes [the crown of the head].
Furthermore, since the preceding section concerns the arrangement of images, what relevance would a mirror have there? Therefore, it is divided and included within the Procession.
The taking up of the eight mirrors symbolizes the eightfold correct wisdom of the person who has attained the fruit.

Their suspension in empty space symbolizes the eightfold correct wisdom contemplating the wondrous realm of the ultimate emptiness (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*). The mirror within the altar represents the wisdom of the person on the path (*pratipannaka*).
That now the empty space, the mirrors, and the face all face one another perfectly symbolizes that the wisdom of the person on the path penetrates through to the person who has attained the fruit.
The wisdom of the fruit [attainment] thoroughly penetrates the wisdom of the causal stage. Although cause and effect differ, their wisdom is non-dual.
The forms and shadows that interact are the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and the external protectors who are sages; those who practice the cultivation of samādhi are ordinary persons.
Thus, through the interaction of the forms and shadows of the Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and external protectors, they engage with the person practicing samādhi.
Form and shadow: the form and shadow of the practitioner of samādhi enter into the form and shadow of the external protection of Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.

Although form and shadow are distinct, the holy and the ordinary are one and the same limit. This precisely reveals that the essence of the perfectly luminous self-nature is such that cause and effect, as well as the holy and the ordinary, are entirely equal.
As it is said: "The environment and inhabitants of Avīci hell are entirely within the self-mind of the ultimate Sage. Vi...
The body and land of Lu do not depart from the single thought of an ordinary person below. Second, the division of time limits has two parts: first, the initial seven days;
second, the second seven days; third, the third seven days. Now, I shall explain them collectively.
"Constantly practicing at one time" refers to the Samādhi of Constant Practice. Furthermore, as for "sitting upright" mentioned in the text below:
This refers to the Samādhi of Constant Sitting. One hundred and eight recitations correspond to the counteracting of the one hundred and eight afflictions.

"My Vinaya," and so forth, refers to the ten great vows within the Brahma Net Sūtra. It means that one should constantly practice the Way during the six periods of the day and single-mindedly make vows and maintain mantras;
this covers the full seven days of practicing the Way, seven days of making vows, and seven days [of maintaining mantras].
This refers specifically to the recitation of mantras. However, speaking in general terms, throughout the twenty-one days, one should practice walking meditation, make vows, and recite mantras.

By thus practicing walking meditation, making vows, and reciting mantras, one fully realizes the principle that phenomena are identical to reality and that cultivation arises entirely from the nature.
This is why the Buddha came to touch one’s head with his hand. Regarding the phrase "mirrors reflecting light" and so forth, it means...

Within the mutual reflection of the light from the mirror of emptiness before one and the mirror of the [Buddha’s] countenance, the Buddha manifests his body to rub the crown of the practitioner’s head.
Through this rubbing of the crown, hindrances may be destroyed and virtues may be manifested. This is similar to the previous brief explanation of the three-week period;
though the texts differ in length, their meaning is essentially the same. The three practices are divided into two parts. First, the main section...

"Accomplished" (*cheng*) refers to Ānanda and others. "Not accomplished" (*bùchéng*) refers to [others] such as Ānanda. Regarding the first part, the two characters "ji" (that) and "yú" (in/at) follow upon the previous mention of the "touching of the head" (*módǐng*).
This means that if a practitioner diligently practices for twenty-one days, they will experience the Buddha touching their head;
