at that very site of practice (*dōuchǎng*), they shall immediately attain clarity and purity of body and mind. As for "clarity and purity of body and mind," it is because of their cultivation...
When this ear-faculty samādhi attains the realization of perfect penetration, once a single faculty returns to its source, all six faculties achieve liberation;

this is what is meant by the clarity and purity of the body. Furthermore, from "entering the flow and losing the objects" until "quiescence manifests before one," there is only the single essence of pure luminosity;
this is what is meant by the clarity and purity of the mind. Taken together, it is therefore said that both body and mind are clear and pure.
If explained by means of a metaphor, it is like the transparent clarity seen through both the interior and exterior of lapis lazuli.
Regarding the second point, although the text emphasizes the preceptor (*śikṣācārya*), all ten individuals are equally emphasized. This is what is meant by:
"if one is pure, all become pure; if one achieves success, all achieve success; should there be even one who is impure, all become impure."
Purity: if one is not accomplished, all are unaccomplished; the relationship between them is by no means trivial.
Were it otherwise, such ritual arrangements would be merely laborious and ultimately devoid of benefit. The Tathāgata’s golden mouth has exhorted us with such earnestness.
Those who today establish altars and practice samādhi—should they not be cautious? Should they not be cautious? Clearly practice the path of purity.
The rules for the procedure are concluded.
Within the rules for the purification of the fivefold practice of seated meditation (*dhyāna*), regarding the phrase "sitting upright," etc.:

it means that after previously practicing walking meditation, making vows, or reciting mantras, one arrives at this single flavor. Through the subtle and secret contemplation of *śamatha* and so forth, one accomplishes the wondrous third [stage].

This is obscure. Regarding those of sharp faculties and so forth: [Question] If such a teaching of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) is practiced only by those of sharp faculties, why is it that what they realize stops at the first fruit (*srotāpanna*)?
[Answer] There are two points of view. First, speaking from the perspective of the profound depths:
*Srotāpanna* means "one who has entered the stream. Now, having practiced this samādhi, one has already attained entry into the stream and has forgotten...

Therefore, one borrows the "entry into the stream" (*srotāpanna*) of the Śrāvaka vehicle merely to name the "entry into the stream" that is realized here. Second, this is spoken from the perspective of the shallowest level:

although it is called *srotāpanna*, it refers to the initial stage of faith (*śraddhā*). This is because one borrows the first fruit of the *Hīnayāna* (the *Āgama* teachings) to clarify the initial stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching (*Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra*);
it is not actually the first fruit of the *Hīnayāna* teachings. If it were not the initial stage of faith in the Perfect Teaching, how could it be...?
Why is it that above there is the statement regarding the clarity and purity of body and mind, while below there is the phrase concerning the infallibility of attaining Buddhahood?

"Infallibility in attaining Buddhahood" means that one has already reached the stage of non-retrogression (*avaivartika*). This is simply because ignorance is about to be shattered and the Middle Way is about to be revealed.
The explanation of the pure rules for sitting in meditation (*dhyāna*) above is now complete. Your question below is general; its intent is to address you, Ānanda.
The previous question asked me: "How does one establish the ritual for purifying the site of the path where the Buddha is invoked?
Such is the ritual for purifying the consecrated altar (*maṇḍala*), up to and including such is the ritual for purifying seated meditation (*dhyāna*).

Only then can it be called 'establishing the ritual for purifying the site of the path where the Buddha is invoked. Therefore, it says, 'As you have asked,' and so forth. This concludes the third section: Establishing the Site of the Path.
[End. Fourth, Ānanda prostrated at [the Buddha’s] feet and departed; this is the re-request for the text of the mantra. It is divided into three parts: first, the re-request by Ānanda and others;

second, the actual exposition beginning with "At that time" (*atha khalu*); third, the protection and maintenance beginning with "When this was said" (*idam avocad bhagavān*). The first part is further divided into three.
First, from "Ānanda" onwards, the narrative of the power of the mantra may be understood. Second, from "I only pray" onwards, this is the formal request;
as for the phrase "not yet having heard it personally," when the Tathāgata was in the city of Śrāvastī preaching the mantra, Ānanda was in the brothel of the courtesan Ḍombī;

therefore, it is said that he had not yet heard it personally. Third, from "At that time" onwards, the assembly’s prostration may also be understood. Part Two: The Section on the Actual Exposition, which has four subsections.

First, regarding the section "At that time" and below, within the manifestation of the Tathāgata: "The World-Honored One, etc. refers to transformation upon further transformation, which is what is meant by the supernormal power of unconditioned transformation (*avyākṛta-nirmāṇa-abhijñā*).

Second, regarding the section "The great assembly," the observation and listening of the assembly can be understood accordingly. Third, regarding "Namo" and below, it concerns the preaching of the authentic *dhāraṇī*.
A *dhāraṇī* is a secret term and is not translated; although it is not translated, there are instances where it is translated—specifically, only its characters are translated.

The meaning is not translated. Since it is said that they are not translated, it is not necessarily the case that one must specify which part is the term for taking refuge, which part is the title of the King of Ghosts, or even which part is the name of a faction.

Rather, the sūtra text is the manifest; this manifest expression is the *tathāgatagarbha*. The dhāraṇī is the secret; this secret expression is also the *tathāgatagarbha*. Although the manifest and the secret...

Since the nature of the sublime treasury is one, it is known that what is manifest has nothing to be manifested, for the manifest is entirely the secret; and what is secret has nothing to be secreted, for the secret is entirely the manifest.
Section Four: Exhortation to Uphold by Enumerating Benefits, divided into two parts. First, Ānanda and others concerning the merit of the fruit;
second, Ānanda and others concerning the practice of the cause. The first part is further divided into three. First, a general explanation of the benefits, concerning Ānanda and others.
Second, the specific presentation of the five pairs; third, the general conclusion and summary. Regarding the first section, the general clarification of the benefits:

as for the statement that "this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa and so forth give birth to all Buddhas," it is like the aforementioned "Single Path to Nirvāṇa" of the Bhagavāns of the ten directions, which is an explicit exposition (*nītārtha*). Now, this Buddha-uṣṇīṣa mantra gives birth to the Buddhas of the ten directions.
This is a secret exposition. Thus, one knows that both the Exoteric and Esoteric teachings are equally capable of giving birth to all Buddhas.

Now, the mantra is the principle of the three virtues (triguṇa) of the Great White Parasol; what the Buddhas realize is precisely the essential body of these three virtues, and it is for this reason that they are the Buddhas who are born [therefrom].
Because this divine mantra is able to give birth to the Buddhas of the ten directions, there is a further distinction below.
This demonstrates the five pairs. First, they are presented individually, divided into five sections: first, the pair of attaining enlightenment and subduing Māra;
second, the pair of the response-body preaching the Dharma; third, the pair of bestowing predictions and uprooting suffering; fourth, the pair of seeking the higher and transforming those below.

The fifth entry concerns the entrustment of the Dharma in pairs. Within the first pair: "The Perfectly All-Knowing One" (Samyaksambuddha) refers to being "correct" by not leaning toward either emptiness or existence—the three [natures].
It refers to "perfect knowledge" regarding the entirety of emptiness, the entirety of the provisional, and the entirety of the middle.

This is the realization of the three knowledges within a single moment of mind, as well as the perfection of the three types of awakening. By upholding this mantra-heart, one subdues [afflictions] and so forth.
This dharma is like the Vajra King: it cannot be broken by insentient things, nor can it be destroyed by grasping. Therefore, all māras are subdued and all non-Buddhists are restrained.
Regarding the three pairs, as for the various "great" and "small" calamities: there are nine great calamities, while small calamities are beyond counting.
Regarding the five pairs, as for those such as the strict purification of the precepts, it is as in the present Nirvana of the Tathāgata.

Within this assembly, the rules of discipline are upheld while the eternal truth is discussed; hence it is said that "all have attained purity. This section on the summary and conclusion is divided into three parts:

first, from "If I... onwards, it refers back to the detailed exposition; second, from "If one speaks... onwards, it provides specific names; third, from "You all... onwards, it exhorts the preservation [of the teaching].

Regarding the first of these three points: the reason that [the teaching] is not exhausted even after kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges is that what it elucidates is the *tathāgatagarbha*.

This permeates past and present without beginning or end, and pervades the *dharmadhātu* without coming or going; therefore, it cannot be fully expounded even throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Regarding the second point, the specific explanation is clear. Regarding the third point, the phrase "you all" and so forth is intended precisely to use the small to illustrate the great.

This uses the shallow to illustrate the profound. It means that even the fruits of the Hīnayāna cannot be attained without this mantra, let alone those of the Mahāyāna who wish to sit at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa).
There is no possibility that one could distance oneself from the works of Māra while abandoning this mantra;
therefore, it says, "You all... Second, regarding the causal practices, there are two parts. First: Ānanda, if any [who have] departed...

The first part, "I shall now explain the transcription," clarifies that this encourages the practice of upholding [the text]. It can be understood. The second part, "Ānanda, I am now departing; I shall now explain the recitation," likewise encourages the practice of upholding.

This is divided into three sections: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, there is a general explanation; second, from "You should know" onwards, there is a detailed demonstration; third, from "For this reason" onwards, there is a concluding summary. The first section can be understood.
Regarding the second, the detailed demonstration, there are ten points. The first is that it can eliminate all calamities. "You should know," etc.
1. It can generate all virtues; such as Ānanda and others. 2. It is not produced in other places; from the [first] stage and so forth. 3. It gathers all merits;
these various [practices] and so forth. 4. All practices are accomplished; therefore, it is equal. 5.
It can extinguish karmic obstacles; such as Ānanda and others. 6. It fulfills one's aspirations; furthermore, it is equal. 7. It can bring peace to the state.

Ānanda and the others [attained this]. For nine years, the obstacles of famine were removed; Ānanda and the others [attained this]. The malevolent stars of the ten evils did not enter; Ānanda and the others [attained this].
Regarding the initial statement, "cannot burn," etc.: one who is able to uphold this mantra possesses nothing other than the single reality-body of the Dharma-realm.
How could they further be harmed by water, fire, and so forth? Regarding the three [categories]:

from the first *kalpa* to the final body—the initial mind is called the first *kalpa*, and the final mind of the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*) is called the final body. Regarding the four [categories]:
Regarding the statement that "all these sentient beings shall be given to this person": if this were so, then samādhi would likewise be wisdom. This is not the case;
although it is said that these merits are bestowed, the merit obtained by the upholder is of the same single *dharmatā* (store-nature) as that realized by all Buddhas.
While it appears as though they are being given, in reality, they are not obtained without cause. Among the six [precepts], even if one should violate the prohibitions...
"Regarding the time before receiving [the mantra]" refers to the period prior to having received and upheld the mantra. "Even if one transgresses" specifically points to the aforementioned offenses.
"Should one be defiled by impurities, etc. again refers to the period after receiving the mantra. "Even if one does not construct a mandala"—
The term "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to manifest the power and function of the mantra; it does not mean that one may practice *samādhi* without constructing a ritual altar (*maṇḍala*).

Regarding the eight [deities], *daśa* means "banner" (*dhvaja*). Regarding the ten [categories], as for the twenty-eight great malevolent stars (*mahā-graha*), some say there are twenty other malevolent stars separately, but this is not so; these very twenty-eight stars may also serve [as the basis].
"Good. It may also be made evil. If a person practices good, even evil becomes good; if a person practices evil, even good becomes evil.
As for one into whom no evils or calamities can ever enter, why would auspiciousness not enter either? Since calamities do not arise, there is nothing that is not auspicious;
what need is there to wait for something to enter to be considered auspicious? If one were to wait for it to enter..."
Because there may be that which appears auspicious yet is actually inauspicious, it is said that "calamities and blessings can never enter.
The third section is the conclusion, which is easily understood. Regarding the third part, the Section on Protection and Sustenance (*parigraha*), there are six subsections:

first, from "At that time" onwards, the Vajras; second, from "Then" onwards, the Heavenly Kings; third, from "Furthermore there were" onwards, the spirits and deities (*yakṣas*); fourth, from "Furthermore there were" onwards, the celestial deities (*devas*); fifth... [text truncated].
Furthermore, there are those of lower spiritual power. Sixth, "At that time" refers to Vajragarbha. The first five [points] are understandable.

Regarding the sixth, as for "wandering at ease with a distracted mind," this is not the same as the distraction of ordinary beings; it merely means that he does not observe the formal retreat boundaries (*sīmā-bandha*).
Regarding my statement that "I have crushed his head with a precious vajra," one might ask: "Vajragarbha Bodhisattva is one of great compassion;
how can he perform such an act of non-compassion? The answer is that one must understand that Vajragarbha also possesses both the gates of subduing (*damana*) and gathering (*saṃgraha*).
Since he is dealing with evil, he should subdue it through majestic power; therefore, he employs the precious vajra. As for the good...
One gathers them in through the power of loving-kindness (*maitrī*). This is why one constantly causes this person’s actions to accord with their wishes;
it is simply because this single [quality] possesses both compassion and majestic authority.
After Ānanda had risen from his seat and departed, this third section reveals the text on the stage of ultimate firmness.
Initially, Ānanda requested the supreme skillful means of śamatha by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attain bodhi;
thus, there is cause and fruit, as well as the primary task within the cause. The Tathāgata answered in general that there are three.

The *Mahā-mati* is the Great Buddha-Crown *Śūraṅgama* King, which fully embodies the myriad practices and serves as the wondrously adorned path through which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions transcend all at once.

It is because all sentient beings do not know the eternally abiding true mind—the essence of pure nature and luminosity—and instead employ various false thoughts, that they undergo the cycle of rebirth.
This applies from the beginning to the end of the stages of practice, including all those in between.
Thereafter, there will be no further indirect or evasive aspects. This single round of question and answer exhausts the great purport of the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*.

Thereafter, [the Bodhisattva] did not weary of repeated entreaties, requesting instruction one by one; the Tathāgata, based on the opening and closing of form and mind, answered in detail for each point.

From the "Investigation of the Mind in Seven Places" up to the passage in the fourth fascicle which asks, "How can you still deceive yourself by retaining visual and auditory faculties?"—this section as a whole elucidates the ultimate truth.

This is the principle of firmness, as described in the *Yuantong shu* (Commentary on the Perfect Penetration), which states that the three inconceivable truths are employed to respond to the request for the three types of cessation (*śamatha*).
Having already established a comprehensive and perfect understanding, [Śāriputra] requested entry through the door of the jeweled mansion.

The Tathāgata, based on the two definitive meanings, then had the twenty-five sages each present their method of perfect penetration, until Mañjuśrī selected among them and specifically pointed to the faculty of hearing.

From the initial expedient of the faculties up to the rules for concentrating the mind, establishing the *maṇḍala*, and the dual cultivation of Exoteric and Esoteric teachings—none of these are not matters of the gates of practice (*caryā-mukha*).
This is what is meant by: "Based on the ultimate, adamantine principle, one gives rise to the ultimate, adamantine practice.

As stated in the *Yuan-tong-shu* (Commentary on Perfect Penetration): "Relying on understanding to give rise to practice in order to clarify the inconceivable cultivation. This leads us to the principle herein.
Since the practices have now been fully set forth, one must extensively expound upon the stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*) to demonstrate the signs of realizing the fruit; thus, this passage arises.

However, with reference to the proximate context, it is stated within the section on the gate of practice (*caryā-mukha*) regarding the benefits: "One contemplates the Buddha, bodhi, and great nirvāṇa."
One clearly understands the path by which the family returns; since there must be various stages on the road back home, one requests [instruction].
If one bows from afar, at the beginning it is said: "Thus, from start to finish, the stages of realization are forever free from all deviousness.
Now, because it is necessary to clarify this auspiciously, one requests [it]. This precisely corresponds with the initial general request to attain Bodhi. The text is divided into two parts.

First is the request, made by Ānanda and others. Second is the response and instruction, beginning with "At that time," and so forth. The first section [the request] is further divided into two parts.

First, from "Ānanda" onwards, the narrative style (*jīngjiā*) describes the circumstances, which may be understood as they stand. Second, from "We" onwards, the interlocutors (*dāngjī*) present their words, which is divided into three sections:

first, the simultaneous presentation of delusion and enlightenment, namely "We," and so forth; second, the formal application for the stages of realization, namely "World-Honored One," and so forth; third, the assembly performs a prostration.

They immediately acted accordingly. Regarding the opening phrase, "We who are such as these": those who are foolish will inevitably rely on their own [limited] views, and thus they crave much learning;

those who are dull-witted will inevitably find it difficult to enter, and thus they do not seek liberation. The above describes delusion. From "Receiving the Buddha’s [instruction]" below, the realization is set forth.

This refers back to the Ear-organ Perfect Penetration (*śrotra-viṣaya-samanta-prativedha*) and the rules for concentrating the mind and establishing the ritual site (*maṇḍala*), which were His compassionate teachings. [Thus] one attains...

Regarding the phrase "correctly practicing through perfuming" (*samyag-vāsanā-bhāvanā*), this refers to the previously mentioned "hearing the illusory-like, hearing-perfuming, and hearing-practicing Vajra-samādhi.

This cultivation is not something distinct from itself; it is entirely the self-nature of the faculty of hearing that constitutes the cultivation. Likewise, this perfuming is not something distinct from itself;

it is entirely the self-nature of the faculty of hearing that constitutes the perfuming. This is what is meant by "correctly practicing through perfuming. Thus, one should know that [it is] not possible...
To initiate cultivation based on the totality of nature is a confused practice and not the correct cultivation. Previously, there was only the body of birth and death;
now, having attained the method of correct cultivation through the faculty of hearing, one shall transform this body of birth and death into an indestructible vajra-body.
Previously, there was only the mind of birth and death; now, having attained the correct cultivation through the faculty of hearing—
Dharma: one should turn away from the discriminating mind and realize the mind of the eternally abiding true mind.

Therefore, both body and mind become joyful, and one attains such abundant benefits. Within the second [section], there are two meanings regarding those who thus cultivate and realize the Buddha’s samādhi:
first, all that the Tathāgata cultivates takes the nature as the cultivation; in cultivation, there is nothing to be cultivated.

All that the Tathāgata has realized is realized through the nature; there is realization, yet nothing is realized. Now, it is not said that one cultivates the entire nature or realizes the entire nature;
rather, the single character "Buddha" encompasses both. Therefore, it is called "Buddha-samādhi.
Second, this method of the ear-faculty’s perfect penetration within samādhi was expounded from the golden mouth of the Buddha; now, by means of that which can speak [it], [it is transmitted].
This person clarifies the Dharma that has been taught. Therefore, it is called the Buddha’s samādhi.

As for those who have not yet reached nirvāṇa, because the initial mind is contrasted with the subsequent mind, there are many intermediate stages; hence it is said they have "not yet reached nirvāṇa.

Within the section on the formal request, one should divide the text into four categories: "How," "To what extent," "Where to go," and "What is it? This corresponds to the first part of the following passage.
The first pair of opposites is fully explained below. Now, some take the first [of the three] as a general request and the latter three as specific requests.
As for the beginning—where one reaches and through what gradual stages this practice is initiated; as for the continuation—where one proceeds to and deeply enters the stages of realization;
and finally, where one reaches the ultimate limit of the cause—it is certain that these three gradual stages must occur prior to the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*).

Thus, the three gradual stages constitute one category; the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) constitutes one; the ten faiths through the four stages of added practice (*catur-āvasthā-prayoga*) constitute forty-four positions;
the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*) constitute ten; and the stages of Equality (*samatā*) and Subtlety (*sūkṣma*) constitute two.

As for the subsequent statement that there are "fifty-five positions on the true path to Bodhi," this is because the stage of Subtle Enlightenment (*sūkṣma-abhisambodhi*) is not a "path," and the stage of Dry Wisdom is not "true. Furthermore, these three gradual stages are that which brings about accomplishment.
This is that which is accomplished. Therefore, it is later stated that "pure cultivation and realization gradually penetrate deeper," and again that "all are due to the three kinds of progress.

Because one is thus able to accomplish the fifty-five stages, only fifty-five are mentioned. Nevertheless, there are differences in the depth of realization and the relative height or lowliness of the stages:
first, those who cling to principle while being deluded regarding phenomena; second, those who cling to the partial while being deluded regarding the perfect.

If it is said that principle is fundamentally without cultivation, how could there be further realization? Since the Tathāgata’s nature and virtues are naturally possessed, what is called "cultivation and realization" merely refers to the manifestation of these phenomena.
Furthermore, it is said that in the practice of the Perfect and Sudden, one directly arrives at the goal;
how could there be so many stages to be traversed? If, despite practicing, one cannot enter directly, one must necessarily rely upon provisional stages to attain it.

As for those who have realized it, they do so only through partial and gradual means rather than through the perfect and sudden; yet this is not the case. If we discuss the principle (*li*), then the principle is sudden awakening;

if we discuss its practical application (*shi-yong*), the sequence must be fully exhausted. To claim that the principle alone is sufficient and to disregard cultivation—how could one realize and enter [the truth] in such a manner?
It is like a family member who has wandered abroad: if they wish to return home, they must necessarily follow the path.
There is no lack of temporal limits and sequential order. Discussing the principle of sudden enlightenment is like one who already knows their way home;
discussing the causal sequence of events is like returning home by following a path. If one discusses its perfection, this refers to those of sharp faculties;
if one discusses its partiality, this refers to those of dull faculties. Since there is a distinction between sharp and dull, there is inevitably a difference in speed. Nevertheless, its...
Both cultivation and realization are indispensable. How could there be a perfect [attainment] devoid of stages, with partialities of high and low?
It is like two people traveling together to another land and returning; one who is clever finds a shortcut, while one who is dull finds a circuitous route.
Although there are shortcuts and detours, the path is the same; it is only that upon reaching home, there is a difference in timing.

The latter is merely the ear. Now, those of the Perfect and Sudden [Vehicle] are like those who are sharp and intelligent, finding the direct path; those of the Partial and Gradual [Vehicle] are like those who are dull and slow, taking the circuitous route.
There is only a difference in the speed with which they realize the fruit. How could the stages of cultivation and realization possibly be discarded?

It is because people of later generations cling to principle while being deluded about phenomena, and cling to the partial while being deluded about the perfect—these are the two types of people. For this reason, Ānanda made his request.

The Tathāgata taught that if one claims there are no stages of cultivation or realization regarding principle and perfection, these are all instances of violating the sacred scriptures and misleading sentient beings; this can be understood from the third [section].

The second part, the response, is divided into three sections. First, from "At that time" onwards, the praise and permission; second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the reception of the teaching; third, from "The Buddha said" onwards, the actual exposition.
Within the first section on praise and permission, the phrase "Excellent, excellent" is used twice: the first praises his cultivation of perfect practice based upon perfect understanding;
the second praises his request for perfect realization based upon perfect practice. Regarding the term "provisional indication" (*xuánshì*), it refers to... from [the following].

This is the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*). By practicing it, one spontaneously breaks through ignorance and partially manifests the three virtues (*tri-guṇa*), reaching the summit of the mountain of nirvāṇa and sitting at the site of awakening (*bodhimaṇḍa*). It is free from any sign of deviousness or any matter of retreat;
this is the path of correct cultivation. Regarding the second, "receiving the teaching," "carving out the heart" refers to what the *I Ching* calls "carving out the wood for a boat."
Now, "taking up" means to set aside deluded thoughts and empty the mind of its impurities. The third section, "The Correct Exposition," is divided into two parts:

first, the general clarification, beginning with the words "The Buddha said," etc.; second, the specific demonstration, beginning with the words "Ānanda," etc. Within the first part, regarding the passage beginning with "You should know," one should first state:
"The Tathāgata, wishing to reveal the stages and positions of the various sages, first clarifies the two causes of inversion regarding the world and sentient beings."

It is precisely because the wondrous nature is profoundly still and perfect, transcending all names and marks. Within this, there are not even the provisional designations of "support" (the environment) and "supported" (the beings);

how, then, could there be any signs of the realization of wisdom or severance? It is only because of delusion regarding the truth and the arising of false, inverted natures that enlightenment is transformed into afflictions, thereby forming the twelve classes of sentient beings.
If one can reverse the false and return to the true nature so that it is no longer inverted, birth is transformed.
Taking death as *nirvāṇa* thus establishes the sixty stages of the sages; this source of delusion and awakening is something that must be known.
Thus, the world and sentient beings exist because of delusive ignorance, and even *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa* are established in contrast to such delusive ignorance.
Nevertheless, within the essence of the wondrous nature, not a single characteristic can be found. Therefore, one must first demonstrate the state of inversion.
These are taken as that which is destroyed. Furthermore, the stages and positions are clarified as that which is realized. Regarding "the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous":
it is called "perfect" (*yuan*) because it is complete and pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm; it is called "luminous" (*ming*) because its clarity and purity illuminate all things.
Within this wondrous nature, the world, sentient beings, bodhi, and nirvana are all merely names and signs. They have been perfectly detached from the beginning;
thus it is said, "One should know," and so forth. That there are currently worlds and sentient beings is due to their existence through the delusion of arising and ceasing.
The reason such delusion arises is entirely because of a single moment of non-awakening; from this, causes come into being.
It refers to the false arising through the conjunction of conditions and the false cessation through the separation of causes and conditions. Furthermore, it arises because of delusion;
thus, due to ignorance there is the world and sentient beings. It ceases because of birth; thus, this sequential flux proceeds from end to beginning once again.
Therefore, it is said that "it is due to delusion," etc. Moreover, there are Bodhi and Nirvana that can be cultivated and realized.
This means that since one has already arisen from the True to produce the delusory, by returning from the delusory to revert to the True, there arise both Bodhi and Nirvana;

thus it is said that "delusion is extinguished," and so forth. Regarding the second designation, "transformation of the basis" (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*): while in delusion, one gives rise to the delusory, turning away from the Real and relying upon the illusory;
thus there exist the world and sentient beings—this is the first transformation of the basis. When one returns from the delusory to...
True. When one transforms birth-and-death to rely upon the ultimate reality (*tattva*), there arise bodhi and nirvāṇa; this is yet another transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
Thus we know that the world and sentient beings do not exist due to anything else, but simply arise from delusion regarding the truth and giving rise to the false.
Likewise, bodhi and nirvāṇa do not exist due to anything else, but simply consist in the return of the false to the truth. Yet, within the essence of self-nature, both are—
It is not so. These are the two designations for the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*). This passage precisely clarifies the reason for [the existence of] both bodhi and nirvāṇa.

Its intent is to reveal that the single principle is originally devoid of names and characteristics; it is only because one must now speak of stages and positions—due to the cessation of delusion—that one is compelled to provisionally establish these names and characteristics.

The second part, the detailed exposition, is divided into two sections. First, from "Ānanda, you now depart" onwards, it explains the arising of delusion from the truth (*tattva*) to clarify inversion.

Second, from "Ānanda, thus departing" onwards, it explains the return from delusion to the truth to clarify the stages and positions (*bhūmi*). The first section is further divided into two: first, from "Ānanda" downwards, the intent is stated;
second, from "Ānanda" downwards, the characteristics are shown. Within the initial statement of intent, regarding the phrase "first, one should," etc.:

The meaning is this: since the two designations for the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti) are named "True" precisely because they result from the cessation of delusion, one must not fail to know the cause of that false and inverted [delusion].
If one knows its cause, then delusion can be extinguished and inversion will not arise; if it does not arise, then there is no arising at all.
Therefore, it is said that this is the true samādhi. It is like seeking out a rebel: one must first know the rebel’s...

This is the location [of the discussion]. Second, the demonstration of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) also has three parts: first, the combined clarification concerning Ānanda and others; second, the analytical explanation concerning delusion regarding the source and so forth;

third, the mutual involvement of the three periods of time and so forth. Regarding the first, the combined clarification, this is the combined clarification of the characteristics of the arising of worlds and sentient beings.

Some say that it clarifies only sentient beings and not the worlds, because the initial passage merely says: [...]* *Note: The ellipsis indicates the portion of the original text provided in the prompt.*
It is merely because of sentient beings. This is not so; it is simply that the introductory heading refers exclusively to sentient beings, whereas what is actually established possesses both aspects.
By means of the two phrases concerning "nature," it first clarifies that while the reality exists, there is delusion.

The first phrase points to the aforementioned wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity (*miao-xing yuan-ming*), which is the wondrous luminosity of the nature-awakening (*xing-jue miao-ming*) and the fundamental awakening’s luminous wondrousness (*ben-jue ming-miao*), as well as the original luminosity of the self-nature of the mind.
The "pure and luminous essence" (*śuddha-prabhāsvara-svabhāva*) merely changes the phrasing [of the previous section]. The second line concludes the preceding and introduces the following:

it means that this true nature (*tathatā*) is originally luminous and wondrous, devoid of darkness; this is called "luminous nature. It is originally perfect and complete, devoid of deficiency; this is called "perfect nature.
Within such luminous and perfect nature, delusion was originally non-existent; yet because of a single moment of non-awakening, delusion arises.

Therefore it is said, "Based on illumination" (and so forth). These two phrases concerning "based on illumination" precisely give rise to delusion. For the nature is fundamentally perfect and luminous;
yet, if one intends to take a single illusory illumination as the "activator," then that true nature is inverted and becomes the "activated.
However, since the true nature is inherently and originally luminous, what need is there for it to be activated? If one posits a single "activator," then there must be a corresponding "activated."
...the nature [of the mind]. Thus it is said that "through illumination, the nature is manifested. Once the duality of subject and object is established, deluded perception arises from this;
hence it is said that "from the nature, deluded perception arises. This is as previously stated: "The awakened nature must be luminous, yet it falsely becomes the awareness of luminosity.
Within the perfectly luminous mind-nature, even the real does not exist—how then could there be delusion? Now, once deluded perception has arisen, then [it is finished]...

Ultimately, through non-existence, one achieves ultimate existence; thus it is said, "from the end," and so forth. This is like how, within the aforementioned state where there is neither identity nor difference, a vivid differentiation is established.
Regarding the phrase "this existence" (*yǒu*): the upper character refers to the "existence" of ultimate existence, which takes ignorance as its essence.
The lower character points to the root-body (*mūla-kāya*) and the physical world (*bhājana-loka*). Since [it] arises from non-existence...
To say that "it exists" while being [based on] ignorance is to take the cause of delusion as its cause; therefore, it is not truly its cause. Thus, it is said:

"This existence," and so forth. Since the productive cause is itself ignorance—entirely illusory and thus a non-cause—then the characteristics of both that which is produced and abides (the sentient beings) and that which is produced and inhabited (the world-system) are likewise [illusory].
They are all likewise empty and false, and no fundamental basis can be found; therefore, it is said that they "dwell in non-abiding," and so forth.
Since the ignorance that gives rise [to them] is empty and false, the worlds and sentient beings that arise from it are also all empty and false.
From within this non-abiding emptiness and falsity, worlds and sentient beings emerge in profusion; therefore, it is said that they are "rooted in these," and so forth. (Combined)
This clarifies that sentient beings in the world are thus.

The explanation is divided into two parts. First, from "The initial delusion regarding the source" downward, it explains the inversion of sentient beings. Second, from "Ānanda" downward, it explains the inversion of the world.
While the opening statement does not mention "sentient beings," the concluding text refers to them as "sentient beings. This is what is meant by "concluding where one began."
This refers to the "introduction" (提). In this context, the term "world" (*loka*) is used to introduce the subject; however, the concluding passage does not mention "world.

This is what is meant by an introduction without a formal conclusion. Regarding the first part: the four lines on "delusion regarding the fundamental" provide a general demonstration of the perversion of sentient beings.
The following three lines are intended to specifically clarify the perversions of sentient beings within the partial and gradual [teachings]. The two lines beginning with "not true" specifically...
This clarifies the inversion of sentient beings of the Two Vehicles. The six successive phrases specifically clarify the inversions of sentient beings in the Six Realms.
By means of these, the inversions of all sentient beings in their entirety are clarified. Within the initial general explanation, regarding "delusion regarding the source" and so forth:
from what do all sentient beings arise? They all arise from deluding their own original, perfectly luminous self-nature.
The nature [of sentient beings] arises from the false delusion of a single thought-moment of ignorance; hence it is said that they are "deluded regarding their original [nature]," and so forth.

Since they arise from the false delusion of ignorance, how could there be a substantial essence of true nature to be found? If that which gives rise to delusion has no substance, upon what could the sentient beings produced thereby rely?
Hence it is said that "the nature of delusion," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "within the partial and gradual [teachings], about to... and so on: this refers to the partial and gradual...

Ordinary people are unable to realize that the delusory is itself the true; they must necessarily destroy the delusory to manifest the true. [However,] one must know that within the self-nature, both the true and the delusory are unobtainable.
If you wish to discard the delusory and restore the true, then even that "true" which you seek to restore is itself delusory.
Since the true does not even arise, how could there be a discarding of the delusory? Therefore, it is said, "If you intend to... and so forth.
Thus we know that those who follow the partial and gradual [teachings] are merely in a state of inversion. Regarding the statement that within the Lesser Vehicle (Hīnayāna) there is no true equality:

practitioners of the Two Vehicles necessarily seek to depart from existence in order to manifest emptiness; they do not realize that to abandon the view of existence and fixate upon emptiness is already delusion.
Therefore, it is said that they are "not real. To further seek the true nature by departing from the view of existence and seeking within emptiness is even more delusory.
Thus, it is collectively stated that they are "not real," and so forth. "Non-characteristics" refers to delusory characteristics; they are merely delusions within delusion.

The section beginning with "non-existence" (非生) correctly demonstrates that delusion cannot be found. The four instances of the character "non-" (非) here should not be viewed as identical to the preceding "non-"; they all serve to eliminate [delusion].
This is an explanatory gloss. "Neither arising nor abiding" means that arising, abiding, change, and cessation are the characteristics of ignorance;

if one examines them within the perfectly luminous nature of the mind, they are utterly unfindable. Here, the two characteristics of change and cessation are omitted for brevity; hence it is said, "neither arising nor abiding.
"Neither mind nor phenomena" means that the body, sensations, mind, and phenomena are the substance of ignorance; if one examines them within...
The perfectly luminous nature of the mind is likewise unattainable. It merely sets aside the two dharmas of body and sensation; therefore, it is said to be "neither mind nor dharma.

If one wishes to contemplate the four [dharmas] of body, sensation, and so forth, in order to destroy the four [characteristics] of arising, abiding, and so on, thereby manifesting the partial truth and seeking to restore the true, one will instead produce delusion upon delusion.
Furthermore, the four characters "non-" (fei) may be developed from the preceding "non-characteristic" (feixiang).

This refers specifically to delusion (*moha*), though it does not yet mention karma or sentient beings. "Arising" (*utpāda*) and "abiding" (*sthiti*) describe its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); "mental phenomena" (*caitta-dharma*) describe its substance (*svabhāva*).
This directly points to the root from which delusion arises as being grounded in mental phenomena; the characteristics of the arising of karmic response reside in arising and abiding.
The meaning is that since seeking to restore the fundamental is not genuine and is already delusory, all mental states whatsoever are delusion upon delusion;
hence it is said that they are "neither arising nor abiding," and so forth. Thus we know that the beings of the two vehicles are merely inverted. This clarifies [the nature of] the six realms.
"Successively revolving," and so forth, refers to ordinary sentient beings who, from a single moment of non-awakening, have the six sense objects incite the six sense faculties;
these six faculties, in turn, take the six sense objects as their objects, mutually inducing one another and arising again and again.

This is what is referred to below as "the six confused and delusive appearances. Therefore, it is said that they "arise successively"; arising without ceasing, they consist purely of false afflictions.
Because it is seen [to arise], it is said that "the power of birth brings forth illumination. Since afflictions have already been established, one will naturally create karma;

therefore, it is said that "they are perfumed so as to form karma. Once karma has been formed, one will naturally experience its retribution; therefore, it is said that "those with identical karma respond to one another. Regarding those with identical karma:

among the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*), this refers specifically to the womb-born and egg-born. That which is common to the three karmas of the parents and oneself constitutes [this identity]. This is what is meant.

They share the same karma. Once its retribution has been summoned, there must necessarily arise the signs of extinguishing through the repayment of killing, stealing, and lust, as well as the signs of being bound by the entanglements of killing, stealing, and lust;
hence it is said, "because there is [karma]," and so forth. Thus we know that the sentient beings of the six realms are merely inverted.
If one discusses their partiality or gradualness—whether they belong to the Two Vehicles or the six realms—not a single one is not inverted. All are...

It exists because of a single moment of ignorance; thus, it is said at the outset that "one is deluded regarding the fundamental," and the conclusion likewise states, "it is due to this," and so forth.

Second, in the explanation of the world and sentient beings' inversions, the phrase "there is existence" (*asti*) explains the meaning of *loka* (world), while "not caused by" (*na hetu-*) explains the meaning of *loka* (time/age).
"There is existence, there is what belongs to it, not what is caused by it," etc., reiterates the preceding point that "this existence and what belongs to it..."
Causes and conditions, etc., serve as the causes of the world. This means that because "this exists," all things come to be; thus, the four directions and their divisions arise falsely.

Once these segmented boundaries have been established, there arises the capacity to speak of "that which can" (the cause) as referring to delusion and karma, and "that which has" (the effect) as referring to sentient beings.

Therefore, it is said that "this exists," and so forth. This means that fundamentally there is no true cause, yet delusion acts as the cause; fundamentally there is no abode, yet [delusion] establishes it.
Delusion constitutes that which is "dwelled upon. Because of this, there is transformation and flux, whereby the three periods of time are established.
"That which is caused" refers to afflictions and karma; "that which is dwelled upon" refers to the sense-faculties and bodies of sentient beings.

Since non-abiding ignorance perfumes that which is dwelled upon moment by moment, it is said that they are not causes, and so forth. Thus, one knows that the perversion of the world also arises from ignorance.

It is that which exists through clarity. There are two parts to the three aspects involved: first, the three periods of time are presented as headings; second, from "For this reason" onwards, they are explained and clarified.

Within the initial presentation, regarding the "three periods of time" and so forth: it is not like the previous case where one first traverses the periods and then traverses the directions. Rather, it means:
The environment as retribution and sentient beings as primary retribution mutually interpenetrate, giving rise to the six types of delusory appearances.
From this mutual interpenetration, there is no cessation; thus, one naturally brings about the twelve classes of transformed sentient beings.

The second part, the clarification of the explanation, also has two sections. First is the explanation of the formation of causes, which begins with "Therefore," and so forth. Second is the explanation of the attainment of results, which begins with "Riding upon this," and so forth.
Within the first section, the explanation of the formation of causes, the phrase "due to movement" refers to the mutual interpenetration of phenomena mentioned in the preceding text.
Because of this ignorance and lack of awakening, the sense organs and their objects arise in mutual production; this constitutes the state where, due to movement, there is sound and so forth.
This is identical in meaning to the previous principle of how the clarity of awareness and the dullness of emptiness interact to produce agitation.

The phrase "due to movement there is sound" governs the five subsequent phrases, while the phrase "due to flavor one knows phenomena" reaches back through the five preceding phrases. Thus, there is both a vertical penetration and a horizontal pervasion, reaching both above and below.

Below. By means of the faculty (indriya) one conditions the object (viṣaya), and by means of the object one draws forth the faculty; the characteristics of their mutual production are fully exhausted herein.

If one wishes to clarify this with explicit precision, it begins with the phrase "because of movement there is sound," transmitted down through successive stages until it says, "because of movement there is dharma.
Subsequently, it proceeds through successive transmissions from the single phrase "knowing dharma through taste" [until the conclusion].
And above. It says: "From the cognition based on phenomena (*dharma*) up to the seeing based on form (*rūpa*)," the intermediate stages can be inferred accordingly.

Regarding the six signs of distracted delusion: the mind may take sound as its object and suddenly again take form as its object; or it may take fragrance as its object and suddenly again take flavor as its object.
Within the six sense objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*), there is no fixed essence whatsoever. These constitute the six signs of distracted delusion. Because of this—
Within the midst of chaotic thoughts, one habitually cultivates the nature of evil karma.
This takes the twelve inversions, such as desire and so forth, as its basis, thereby creating the ten non-virtuous actions such as killing; this constitutes the formation of the nature of karma.
Because this formed karmic nature eventually results in the fruit of suffering, the twelve divisions revolve without ceasing by means of this. (10)

Second, regarding the distinctions: each is spoken of in terms of its own category. As for the twelve wheels revolving and mutually serving as causes and effects, it refers to the exhaustion of the twelve transformations and so forth;
for example, sound exists dependent on form, fragrance exists dependent on form, and so on, up to existence itself existing dependent on form.
Dharma. Furthermore, fragrance arises because of sound, taste arises because of sound, and so on, up to form arising because of sound.

In this way, the six sense objects arise mutually in six permutations. Moreover, hearing arises because of seeing, smelling arises because of seeing, and so on, up to cognition arising because of seeing;
furthermore, smelling arises because of hearing, tasting arises because of hearing, and so on, up to seeing arising because of hearing. Thus it is.
The six sense organs act as one another, each also possessing six aspects. Taken together, this constitutes the exhaustion of the twelve transformations and their single return to the source.

Second, the explanation of the attainment of fruition has three parts: first, "Riding upon this... and so forth establishes the name; second, "Ānanda... and so forth reveals the characteristics; third, this is... [the conclusion].

This concludes the summary of names. Regarding the initial listing of names, the phrase "riding upon these" refers to how, due to the world's inversion, each of the six sense-objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) manifests within the others;
these objects then entice the arising of beings. Within the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍindriya*), sentient beings undergo six types of deluded and chaotic appearances.
When these false thoughts grasp and cling to the six sense-objects, they may sometimes take them as empty.
Deluded transmigration moves through inversions, even unto the inversion of killing; thus it is called retribution.
There are those born from wombs and those born from eggs, which undergo mutual transformations; these are also the six types of confusion, lacking a fixed destination.

Regarding the twelve classes of beings, such as those born from eggs, according to treatises such as the *Yogācārabhūmi-śāstra* and the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya*, those that emerge from a shell are called egg-born (*aṇḍaja*), and those that emerge from an amnion are called womb-born (*jarāyuja*).
Emerging from moisture is called "moisture-born" (*saṃsvedaja*). Departing from the old to move toward the new is called "transformation-born" (*upapāduka*).

Since there is no substantial essence and it exists solely due to luminous color-form, it is called "possessing form" (*rūpin*). Being empty and devoid of the characteristics of form is called "formless" (*arūpin*). Achieving a substance solely through the mind of perception is called "possessing perception" (*saṃjñin*).

Being inert and lacking any cognition is called "without perception" (*asaṃjñin*). Although [the latter] exists, its own substance is not real, as it is established by relying upon that [other]; therefore, it is so designated.

If [it] does not exist, [one asks]: "If it were not possessed of form (*rūpin*), one would originally have no perception (*saṃjñā*); yet by means of that perception, the mind establishes the substance of the self. If [it] were not possessed of perception, [one says]:

"I have the perception that 'this is my child,' whereas he has no perception of 'these are my parents'; although he lacks that perception, it currently manifests as my perception that 'this is my child.
If [it] were not without perception, some say: "That which possesses form is the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*); that which lacks form is the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*)."
The realms—the realm of perception and non-perception up to the realm of neither-perception-nor-non-perception—as well as the four heavens of the formless realm, such as the sphere of infinite space:
if one were to speak thus, it would be incorrect in every respect. First, because cause and effect would be inconsistent; second, because name and meaning would be inconsistent. Why is this?
These twelve classes of beings are, in their essence, those whose six faculties are deluded by false conceptions. If...
Now, as for the realms of form and formlessness, those who practice meditative concentration are born in those heavens.

If one who is currently in a state of distracted thought were also born in those heavens, then by what cause would it be inferior while the fruit would be superior? Therefore, if such a claim is made, the cause and effect do not correspond.
The following passage states: "There are *kalala* of form that transmigrate through the realms; there are *kalala* without form that transmigrate through the realms;
and so on, up to *kalala* that are neither with nor without perception which transmigrate through the realms.

What is meant by these "kalala of form" and "kalala without form"? Their meaning refers to the realms of form (*rūpadhātu*) and formlessness (*ārūpyadhātu*). Therefore, if one were to [interpret it] in this way...
This is said to mean that name and form are not yet conjoined. It should be understood that these twelve categories are discussed solely within the context of the Desire Realm (kāmadhātu);

for this reason, they are all termed *kalala*. As for those above the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven—namely, the devas who possess meditative concentration—it is not necessarily the case that they, like the sentient beings of the lower realms, are subject to the six types of confusion and lack of order.
This can likewise be known regarding the two upper realms; it is simply not known [in those higher states].

This is merely a brief indication based on what can be verified among the manifest and the obscure in the present. To claim that it extends throughout the two upper realms would be a profound violation of the Buddha’s intent.
Within the second section, "Manifesting Signs," there are twelve divisions whose sequence may be seen; these twelve types all arise from the six disturbances.

Deluded conceptualization acts as the cause for the arising of the twelve categories of inversion; furthermore, with these twelve inversions acting as conditions, one creates the karma of the ten unwholesome actions and so forth.
Thus, one pursues delusion to distinguish between ascent and descent, and follows karma to differentiate between lightness and gravity.
This is the reason for the classification into these twelve categories. However, within each individual category, there are eighty-four thousand types of distracted thoughts (*vikalpa*).

This is because these afflictions and distracted thoughts each exist in their own right; they merely transform according to the specific category, whereby the afflictions manifest predominantly according to that category.
Thus, for categories such as fish and birds, flight and submersion manifest predominantly, and so forth. All [afflictions]...

The afflictions (*kleśa*) all belong to the categories of "flying" and "sinking. Consequently, there arise eighty-four thousand deluded thoughts of flying and sinking, which will be clarified by the following examples.
Furthermore, it should be understood that these are the deluded thoughts occurring upon the fruition of the corresponding classes of beings;

they are not the six types of deluded false thoughts, such as the initial movement, which occur within the causal stage. Regarding the phrase "caused by the world," etc., within the first category of initial movement, these refer to the six types of deluded false thoughts.
Regarding "perception": when one gives rise to false movement and inversion amidst the six sense objects, that perception has both rising and sinking;
thus, through the combination of these energies, it is formed. Consequently, there are eighty-four thousand [beings] who fly as winged creatures and sink as turtles and snakes.

This, too, is the inevitable consequence of the underlying principle. Other cases may be inferred by analogy. They are called "false" because they arise from perception; they are "movement" because...
As for those who are inverted, it is also because of their perceptions (*saṃjñā*). As for those formed by vital energy (*śukra*), it is because the egg is produced through the mingling of energies.
As for those that fly or sink, it is because their perceptions have varying degrees of weight: if the perception is light, one ascends and flies; if the perception is heavy, one sinks and falls.

Thus, we know that fish are characterized by heavy perception, while birds are characterized by light perception. Within this, there is falsity (*mṛṣā*), as well as the subsequent defilements (*saṃkleśa*) down to enmity (*vaira*).
Harm and so forth; furthermore, these disturbances of inversion, as well as the inversions of lower desires down to the inversion of killing, all belong to the afflictive hindrance (*kleśāvaraṇa*).
These vital energies forming flight or sinking, and so forth, down to the anomalies forming the parents and so on, collectively belong to the evil hindrances.
These include the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) and the *kalala* stage, such as fish and birds, down to the non-ideation beings mentioned later in the text.
The "southern lands," the "owls," and so forth, all belong to the category of obstacles resulting from karmic retribution. This is detailed in the *Jiaoguanzhimiao*.

Within the category of desire, there are horizontal and vertical deluded thoughts; these arise precisely from the delusive imaginings of the six sense faculties when one gives rise to defiled desires and inverted views.

At such times, there is both the perverse and the correct. If correct, one is reborn vertically as a human or an immortal; if perverse, one is reborn horizontally as an animal. Thus, the perverse and the correct interact with one another.
Half belong to the category of *nāgas*. When *nāgas* are in the sky, they are vertical; when in the water, they are horizontal.

The mention of "defilement" (*saṃkleśa*) and "desire-inversion" (*kāma-viparyāsa*) is because they are born as sentient beings. Regarding "nourishing and completing," it is because the womb is formed through the union of semen.

Among the various destinies (*gati*), "upside-down and chaotic conceptions" refers to the time when one gives rise to attachment and the inversion of the destinies due to the six types of deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). At that time, one pursues [the object].
The mind turns its back on faith and, being fickle and arbitrary, brings about its own form. Whether overturning or turning over, whether flying or running, it has no fixed destination.
To speak of "attachment" and "inverted destinations" is because these are produced through the convergence of conditions.

Within the category of provisional phenomena, when new and old chaotic thoughts arise and undergo transformation during the time of provisional inversion, the mental impressions diverge, and the new and the old [are separated].
There is further transformation. Thus, at the time of taking birth, some transform from crawling to flying, or shed their skin to fly and then become submerged;

they form according to their kind, borrowing and passing on one another's forms. To speak of "transformation" and "borrowed inversion" is because these beings manifest through the response of detachment.

Within the category of obstructions (*āvaraṇa*), attachment is what is manifested; the rest may be understood accordingly. Within the category of afflictions (*kleśa*), this refers to one who, out of a genuine weariness with existence, clings to emptiness, extinguishes the body, and returns to non-existence.
By dissolving and dispersing [the mind] in this way, one eventually forms hidden and chaotic thoughts, such as those of Śūnyatāmanas (the "Empty-Body" spirit).

Among the categories of the "shadow-like," this refers to those who follow in the footsteps of others and attach themselves to their shadows; appearing as if they exist and yet as if they do not, they construct [their existence] through memory.
Thus, they secretly form disordered thoughts (*vikalpa*), which induce rebirth among the classes of spirits, ghosts, and elemental essences.

Among the categories of the "deluded," those with "withered and disordered thoughts" are precisely those who, at the time they give rise to ignorance and inversion, possess minds like earth or wood and bodies like metal or stone.
This is merely a plan for long life and eternal dwelling; thus, it results only in withered and chaotic conceptualizations.

Among the categories of beings, there are those that do not possess physical form yet constitute a *kalala* (embryonic stage) of form: this refers to that which is not substantial in its own essence, but arises by depending upon another, occurring through mutual reliance due to false and inverted causes.
An example is the *śiśumāra* (water-jelly). Among the categories of nature, there are those that are neither form, nor perception, nor the *kalala* of the formless realm.

The physical substance itself is originally non-existent; it is only through reliance upon curses and incantations that it takes on form and substance. This occurs precisely because perverse karma draws forth one another and the nature is inverted;

it does not arise from the principle of natural physiology. Among the classes of beings, those who are "without thought yet conceive the notion of thought" (kalala) are originally without thought, yet they give rise to the notion of self based upon that substance.
This is precisely due to deluded and false conceptualization, whereby they falsely apprehend others and take them in as their own.

It already exists; thus, it becomes the *pulu* (digger wasp) and other such creatures. Indeed, the *pulu* and others were originally silkworms; it is not that they possessed the perception of a bee and thereby became bees.

Therefore, it is said that "different substances mutually transform. Among the categories of killing, there are those who are not without the characteristic of perception, such as the *kalala* and *arbuda*.

This is because [the mother] has the perception of "this is my child," and thus it is said they are "not without the characteristic of perception. However, the clod of earth and the poisonous fruit originally have no father.
Because they harbor the thought of their mother, they are called "thoughtless" (asaṃjñin). This is precisely because they repay enmity with harm and respond to injury with killing.

It truly arises from having nurtured all beings during the causal stage: beginning with the care of a parent, it ends in slaughter and injury; thus, kindness turns into enmity, resulting in the birth of creatures such as the *tittira* (the earth-owl).
At first, they are clearly father and son, yet in the end, they must devour him. Such is the nature of these species following one another in accordance with their karma.
The retribution is unfailing; it is simply that it occurs not by design, but spontaneously. The "shattered mirror" (pòjìng) is actually a beast that devours its mother, not a bird.
If one must speak of it as a bird, one should say it is like the "equal-to-the-earth" (děng-rú-shàng-tǔ) owl and other such creatures.
The three fetters can be understood as explained above. This concludes the section on how, by means of birth and extinction, the twelve classes of beings are established.
In general, this is intended to reveal that because of delusion regarding the Truth, there arise the various differences of the world and sentient beings, their manifold inversions.
If one were to shatter these delusions, there would then be Bodhi and Nirvana, with slight variations in the stages of realization and entry; thus, delusion and awakening are mutually inverted.
The intent lies in awakening. Based on awakening, the stages are explained, serving as a response to Ānanda’s previous [inquiries].
*The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama*, Fascicle Seven;
*The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama*, Fascicle Eight.
Tiantai Master Yisong spoke; recorded by his disciple Lingshu of Yuxi. Part Two:
From Ānanda’s departure in this manner, [the text] returns from delusion to truth, clarifying the passages concerning the other stages. These are the stages herein.
Next, opinions among the assembly were diverse and conflicting. Some took the three gradual stages (*san jianci*) as being horizontally pervasive across all positions.
Others held that the stage of dry wisdom (*ganhui*), the three gradual stages, and the five ranks and ten faiths of the Perfect Teaching (*yuanjia*) are entirely subsumed within them.

Still others maintained that the seven [stages] consist of the twelve [positions]—both single and combined—up to the stage of Sublime Enlightenment (*miaojue*). Yet others argued that the sutra text merely mentions fifty-five positions, and so forth.
Regarding those who allow for sixty stages of the sages, or who separately open up the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) by means of the Vajra-mind:

I shall now attempt to resolve this through the questions posed by the interlocutor and the six levels of "attainment" (*ji*) established by our own school; thereafter, there will naturally be no further room for debate.
There are four parts to the interlocutor’s questions. First, the general request states: "Before reaching Nirvana, what is the ground of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*)? (40)
Regarding the four minds, the subsequent specific request asks: "By what gradual sequence does one attain the eye of cultivation?
To what place must one go to enter the stages (*bhūmi*)? What is meant by the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambuddha*)?

In the Tathāgata’s response, he first clarifies the gradual sequence, next clarifies the forty-four minds of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*), then clarifies the ten stages, and finally clarifies Equal Enlightenment; therefore, he concludes by saying:

In this manner, through these successive layers of single and double stages totaling twelve, one finally reaches the culmination of wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*). The sequence is so orderly that there is no need for further elaboration; it is like the six levels of "equivalence" (*liu-ji*) in our own school.

The ordinary person’s inherent possession of the saintly positions constitutes the stage of principle-equivalence (*li-ji*). From this point, hearing [the teaching] constitutes name-equivalence (*ming-zi-ji*).

Dry wisdom (*gan-hui*) constitutes the stage of contemplative practice-equivalence (*guan-xing-ji*). The ten levels of faith constitute semblance-equivalence (*xiang-si-ji*). From the ten abidings up to the [ten practices, ten transferences, and ten grounds]...

Awakening is the "partial realization" (prativedha) stage of identity, while wondrous awakening is the "ultimate" stage of identity. Thus, one should know that these three gradual stages herein refer precisely to the positions of advancement through names and titles;
for they do not merely involve understanding the terminology, but also enable the cultivation of contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), though one has not yet entered the [bodhisattva] ranks (*bhūmi*).

This is not the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). If one cultivates this without ceasing, in the near term it can subdue the five abodes [of ignorance] and lead one to the Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*);

in the distant term it can shatter the three delusions and allow one to ascend to partial realization. Thus the Sūtra says: "Because the faculties do not flow outward, they revolve back to their source.
This continues until the six functions no longer operate, at which point the person attains the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*. All of these are the Tathāgata’s prophetic indications.
The merit of the subsequent stages depends upon this; it is not through the practices of the three gradual stages themselves that such a result can be achieved.

This is the essential point, which one must deeply understand. Yuan Tongliu said: "This Dharma begins its cultivation at the stage of names and letters, and its perfection is reached upon entering the stage of contemplative practice (kuan-hsing).
How profound these words are! Within the Stage of Dry Wisdom (*ganhui-di*), one employs inconceivable contemplation (*bùsīyì guān*).
Contemplating the inconceivable realm, one realizes that the aggregates, sense bases, and elements are fundamentally the Tathāgata-garbha.
Since the two attachments to self and phenomena are understood to be devoid of any inherent reality, it is said that the grasping mind is empty and luminous, consisting purely of wisdom.

Furthermore, since the Tathāgata-garbha is solely wondrous, awakened clarity, it is said that the wondrous nature is perfectly luminous, illuminating the ten directions. However, while the initial moisture of desire is drying up, one has not yet connected with the flow of the Dharma.

It is judged that this undoubtedly belongs to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*). Within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*), one is able to destroy the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) within the realm of desire and form, as well as the "dust-like" afflictions (*rajas*) both within and beyond those realms, thereby subduing the delusions of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-ālaya-vāsana*).

Thus, it is said that in the first faith, all deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) are extinguished without remainder; since each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding, the nature of these ten faiths can be understood. This is called the "non-characteristic" (*alakṣaṇa*).

Is it not so? Within these stages—the ten abodes, ten practices, ten transferences, four preparatory stages, ten grounds, equal enlightenment, and wondrous enlightenment—although there are differences in depth, each stage involves both partial breaking and partial realization, and thus possesses all merits.

Consequently, these are collectively categorized as partial realization; only the final wondrous enlightenment is termed "ultimate identity. Furthermore, the concluding text states that they are "repeatedly single and manifold."
When the twelve [stages] reach their ultimate end in wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*), then the twelve function as that which brings about this ending; they reside in the cause.
Wondrous enlightenment is that which is brought to its end; it resides in the fruit. How could one possibly combine wondrous enlightenment with these to make seven?

One should know that the three gradual stages, the stage of dry wisdom (*gan-hui*), the four stages of application (*jia-xing*), and the stage of equal enlightenment (*deng-jue*) are called "single" [stages]. The ten faiths (*xin*), ten abidings (*zhu*), ten practices (*xing*), ten transferences (*xiang*), and ten grounds (*di*) are called...
Furthermore, not only does this avoid contradiction in terminology, but its meaning is also well-founded; thus, the sixty stages of the sages can also be understood from it.

As for the scripture’s mention of the "fifty-five positions on the true path of Bodhi," this is, for example, like the *jianci* (gradual) *qianhui* (dry wisdom) of Wuxing—it is neither true wondrous enlightenment nor the path itself.
Let those who understand examine this in detail. The text is divided into two parts: first, the direct answer.
Ānanda, it is thus that one departs. The two knots are manifested; this is the departure through various stages.
The first section is further divided into ten parts, beginning with the three gradual steps and concluding with Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*); the sequence may be seen therein.
The first three sections are further divided into two parts: first, Ānanda and others summarize the preceding; second, "You now," etc., clarifies the present.

Within the first summary of the preceding, the phrase "such dharmas as these" refers to how each of the twelve classes of sentient beings previously mentioned possesses all twelve classes within itself.
Those twelve classes arose due to the causes of the twelve perversions, resulting in the experience of the twelve perversions.
As for the fruits: now, each individual fruit returns to support its respective cause.

Just as the category of "womb-born" produces the remaining eleven types, so it is likewise for all categories up to and including those who are not non-percipient. Thus, it says "such as these. This is like the following analogy:
within the essence of wondrous, pure luminosity, a single moment of non-awakening immediately gives rise to the twelve classes of beings, each possessing ten [aspects].
Second: It is like pressing upon empty space to cause flowers to appear. Pressing the eyes is a metaphor for the inversion of a single moment of non-awakening.
The chaotic flowers are a metaphor for the six types of disordered deluded thoughts, each of which further possesses twelve categories.
"Inversion" refers to the downward correspondence. Regarding "inversion" and so forth: the essence of nature-purity and luminosity is fundamentally subtle, wondrous, and perfect.
Regarding "fulfillment": because of perversion, that which is perfect and complete is inverted into twelve categories of deficiency.
Regarding the nature of pure luminosity, which is originally subtle, wondrous, and real: because of perversion, that which is real is inverted into twelve categories of falsehood.
Regarding the nature of pure luminosity, which is originally subtle, wondrous, and pure: because of perversion, that which is pure... [is inverted].

The twelve categories of defilement arise from purity. That which is by nature pure, luminous, and fundamentally subtle and wondrous becomes, due to inversion, the twelve categories of darkness and obscurity that obscure its clarity. It is like a clear, pure eye seeing the bright sky;
yet because of a single squeeze of the eyes, wild flowers proliferate chaotically within the void. These flowers in the sky exist only because of the squeezing of the eyes.
Yet they exist. The twelve inversions arise from a single moment of non-awakening; hence it is said that "inversions," and so forth.
This is because the true nature (*dharmatā*) is inconceivable, yet these inherent qualities of that nature are overturned to produce disordered thoughts. The power of karma is likewise inconceivable.
Second, the clarification of the present [state] is further divided into three parts. First, the heading: "You now," and so forth. Second, the inquiry and enumeration.
What is meant by "how"? This clarifies the three [aspects of] explanation. What is meant by "how"?

In the initial section where the topic is raised, the phrase "you now," etc., although it restates the previous request, actually encompasses the two preceding gates of understanding and practice. For indeed, there is nothing to be cultivated in cultivation.

Taking non-arising and non-extinction as the fundamental basis for cultivation, one turns back the hearing within the faculty of the ear to reflect upon one's own nature, thereby revolving the inverted mechanism of hearing;
this constitutes the essential method of cultivation. Realizing that there is nothing to be realized, one fully realizes what is originally possessed by all sentient beings;
thus, within the eternally abiding true mind, one flows inwardly toward the ultimate subtlety. Therefore, it is said: "You now cultivate..."
This is the realization. As for what is called "the Buddha’s samādhi," it distinguishes this from the cultivation and realization of the partial or gradual paths.
