It refers to the fundamental cause of the originally disordered thoughts—those which are mutually inherent within each of the aforementioned categories.

Furthermore, it refers to how sound arises because of movement, and so on, up to how one knows dharmas because of flavor. To eliminate these thoughts, one must establish a gradual sequence; therefore, it says, "establishing the three."
"Gradually," and so forth, refers to this. "As pure" below establishes a metaphor. This metaphor illustrates the causal mind entering into practice.

The two characters "remove" (qu) and "discard" (ju) specifically illustrate the meritorious practices of the three gradual stages (*san jianci*). The poison and honey metaphorize the twelve inversions (*dvādaśa-viparyāsa*);

just as poison and honey can destroy the physical body and its life-span, these inversions can destroy the *dharmakāya* and the life of wisdom. Therefore, they are likened to poison and honey. The hot water metaphorizes the faculty of hearing (*śrotra-indriya*).

The correct practice of the Dharma-gate is likened to ashes; the auxiliary practices of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are likened to incense; and that which is realized is likened to nectar.

This means first purifying the causal mind and subsequently realizing the merit of the fruit. Furthermore, the two characters "remove" (qu) and "discard" (ji) collectively symbolize the three gradual stages (*san-jian-ci*).
Purifying the vessel and the poison-honey are the same as before; the hot water and so forth specifically symbolize the three gradual stages. To oppose their manifestation...
Karma is likened to hot water; its innate nature (*prakṛti*) is likened to various fragrances; and its auxiliary causes are likened to various ashes.

Because one cultivates the samādhi of the ear-faculty through these three gradual stages, the subsequent storage of nectar represents the fifty-five positions and the state of wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therefore, the concluding summary below demonstrates that because of these three progressive advancements, one is well able to achieve perfection.
Regarding the fifty-five stages, one should know that the three gradual sequences are the means by which one progresses and achieves,
while the fifty-five stages are that which is progressed toward and achieved.

Regarding the two parts—the inquiry and the enumeration—the first two lines constitute the inquiry, while the following six lines constitute the enumeration. The inquiry is self-evident. Within the enumeration, each section consists of two lines:

the upper line refers to cultivation (*bhāvanā*), and the lower line refers to cessation (*prahāṇa*). As for "cultivation," it means that from the very beginning, one does not allow the faculty of hearing to follow after sounds, but repeatedly turns the hearing back toward its own nature.
"Eliminating its auxiliary causes" refers to [abandoning] the five pungent herbs, which serve as its sustenance.
This assists the cause for the correct nature (*samyaktva*). However, this is merely one aspect among food and drink;

by analogy, one may extend this principle to eliminate all causes that give rise to afflictions (*kleśa*) through the engagement of the five sense faculties. This serves as the initial gateway for entering realization.

As for "true cultivation," it refers to turning the hearing back toward one's own nature (*svabhāva*), diligently applying oneself to the gradual refinement of true samādhi. To "excavate the correct nature" means to kill [the delusions].
Adultery is the true nature of all sentient beings, for it causes them to enter into various sufferings. The *Sūtra of Perfect Enlightenment* states:
"All sentient beings take sexual desire as their very life-force. If one now excises and removes this, the cycle of birth and death can be brought to rest.
As for "further advancement," it refers to advancing one's practice through this method of "listening to the internal" (*pratyāśravaṇa*), thereby opposing its present manifestation.
"Karma" refers to the continuous, moment-to-moment creation of new karma within the six sense-faculties as they manifest before one.

To "contravene" it means to prevent the internal six faculties from again flowing out toward the six sense-objects, until they flow back and become unified, so that the six functions no longer operate.
In this way, there is no such thing as karma manifesting before one that is not contravened. Furthermore, one contravenes present karma and eliminates its auxiliary causes from the past.
It carves away their inherent nature. What is discussed in any given scripture does not go beyond these three phrases. Why is this?

If one indeed contravenes their manifest karma and eliminates their auxiliary causes and so forth—these three—then perfect understanding opens up from this, and perfect practice is accomplished from this.
From this point, one may realize the stage of perfection; thus, one may request the title of the *Perfect Sūtra*.
Consequently, the seven realms of existence will naturally be understood through diligent study, and the five aggregates will naturally be understood through detailed discernment.

Therefore, it is said that all that is discussed in this sūtra does not transcend these three phrases. Although the three practices such as cultivation are listed herein, they exclude the auxiliary causes and so forth.
"Those abandoned by the three. This explains below that which is abandoned during the middle stage of the Path of Seeing; it does not mention those cultivated therein.
This is because that which is cultivated constitutes the means of abandonment; thus, by citing that which is abandoned, the means of abandonment—the vision—is also implied.
Furthermore, since everything previously cultivated is nothing other than the cultivation of practice and so forth, only abandonment is mentioned here, and not cultivation.

The third section, the "Explanation of the Section on Clarification," is divided into three parts: namely, "Eliminating Auxiliary Causes" and so forth. The sequence is evident. Within the first part, "Eliminating Auxiliary Causes," there are again three sections:

first, the interrogative phrase "How is it? which poses the question; second, the explanation beginning with "Ānanda"; and third, the conclusion beginning with "Ānanda. The first, the interrogation, is self-evident.

The second, the explanation, is further divided into three: first, clarifying the reasons, starting from "Ānanda"; second, exhorting the abandonment of pungent foods, starting from "Ānanda"; [and third, the conclusion]. The second [section], "Exhorting the Abandonment of Pungent Foods," begins with "Ānanda."
Furthermore, there are three points regarding the departure from faults. Thus it departs. The first section is established as the causal basis:
because one wishes to sever the auxiliary causes of the five pungent vegetables (*pañca-garaka*), these four types of food are used here to describe their origin.

Therefore, the phrase "eating sweets" concludes the discussion of the four foods, while the phrase "eating poison" refers to the five pungent vegetables. As for the expression "unable to sustain themselves," it means that each possesses a physical form.

Life cannot exist without nutriment; therefore, it necessarily subsists by depending upon nutriment. Regarding the four types of nutriment, such as edible food (*kavaḍīkāra-āhāra*) and so forth, the explanations provided in the sūtras and śāstras vary.

However, since these twelve classes of sentient beings reside solely within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), one should know that the four nutriments must also be explained in relation to the desire realm.
First, regarding edible food: "edible" (*kavaḍa*) means "lump" (*piṇḍa*). Both the sūtras and śāstras refer to this as "lump-food" (*piṇḍa-bhakṣa*).

To grasp with the hand is called "lump" (*kavaḍa*). What is now termed "portion" (*kavaḍīkāra*) refers to a divided portion. Food has the sense of providing nourishment; it takes the three—odor, flavor, and tangibility—as its substance.
Upon entering the stomach, it undergoes transformation and deterioration, thereby nourishing the sense faculties. Therefore, it is called "nutriment by mouthfuls" (*kavaḍīkārāhāra*).

Regarding the second, the nutriment of contact (*sparśāhāra*): "contact" (*sparśa*) is equivalent to "encounter. This refers to the six objects, such as form and so forth, which are encountered by the six sense faculties.
When encounters with qualities such as softness, smoothness, cold, or warmth give rise to joy and pleasure, they are all capable of sustaining and benefiting the sense faculties;

therefore, it is called the nutriment of contact. Thus, the *Fanyi mingyi ji* (Collection of Translated Terms and Meanings) states: "That which loves upon seeing a form is called 'nutriment. Is this not the meaning of contact? Even if it were not contact, [it would still be so].
Regarding eating: why is it that when one observes theatrical performances and the like, one does not eat all day yet remains free from hunger?

Third, as for "reflecting on food": "reflection" refers to mental volition (*manas*), which is the sixth consciousness. This means that when one reflects upon a desirable object, a sense of longing arises, which is able to nourish the sense faculties.
It is like a person suffering from hunger who reaches a place where food is available; by looking toward the food they hope to obtain, their body does not perish. Therefore—

It is called the nutriment of thought. Regarding the fourth, the nutriment of consciousness (*vijñānāhāra*): "consciousness" has the meaning of grasping and maintaining; it refers to the eighth consciousness.

Because it is sustained by the power of the preceding three nutriments, this consciousness is able to increase its capacity for grasping and maintaining the sense faculties (*indriya*). Therefore, it is named the nutriment of consciousness.

In the second section, "Exhortation to Abstain from Strong-smelling Vegetables," it is clearly explained that consuming pungent plants is unsuitable for a practitioner. The two lines concerning "eating sweets" clarify that there are both benefits and harms to what one eats;

this refers to the five pungent plants (*pañca-gandhaka*) as being of the nature of poisons. Although they do not cause death, they incite lust and increase anger—how can these be anything other than poison?
Therefore, those who seek *samādhi* should sever these [addictions]. The details regarding the five pungent plants are as explained elsewhere.
Commentary: To say that the arousal of lust and the increase of anger are both "aiding the fire" is because they are among the three types of faults and calamities.

Furthermore, within these, there are two parts: first, from "In this way" onwards, it clarifies the person who preaches the Dharma; second, from "As for food" onwards, it clarifies the person who practices seated meditation.

The first part is easily understood. Regarding the middle section, as for "the powerful Māra king" and so forth: the Māra king only fears that the practitioner will achieve success, and thus he desires to destroy them at that time.
Now, since you have cultivated dhyāna yet consume the five pungent roots, celestial beings and sages will not come to protect you, and the Māra King may take advantage of this opening to enter.
Therefore, it is said that "those of great power" and so forth [will appear]. "Manifesting as... refers to manifesting their own bodies. "Slandering and reviling" refers to preaching the Dharma.
Regarding "at the end of life" and so forth: having heard such teachings, after one's life ends, one becomes a member of his retinue and receives the blessings of Māra.
They will all fall back into hell. Those who revile and destroy the prohibitions and precepts cannot save themselves; instead, they go on to revile those who uphold the precepts, saying:
"Why must one be so meticulous and fastidious, holding strictly to the precepts? To speak thus is to preach what is not the Dharma as being the Dharma.
As for those who praise lust, anger, and delusion, it is because a Mahāyāna sūtra states: "Lustful desire is itself the Way; greed and delusion are likewise."
This is likewise so. One might then claim that lust, anger, ignorance, and the like do not obstruct the Path;

yet one fails to realize that these are words for attaining the nature through the realization that total delusion is itself the truth. To interpret them otherwise would be what is called "teaching non-Dharma as Dharma. The three fetters may be understood accordingly.

Second, the excision of the correct nature (*samyaktva*). This also consists of three parts: the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion. The first, the inquiry, may be understood as it stands. The second, the explanation, also has three parts:
first, a direct demonstration of the practice, such as "Ānanda and others"; second, the actual presentation of the method, such as "one should contemplate" and so forth;

third, a preliminary clarification of the efficacy, such as "the prohibitions and precepts" and so forth. Within the first section, the direct demonstration of the practice, the initial phrase provides a general clarification of the adornment.
"Holding" refers to the specific explanation of maintaining strict observance following the section on severing [the defilements]. This means ensuring that lust and killing do not arise.
Regarding lust, it must be ceased from the mind; one does not merely refrain from physical action, but also ensures that the thought does not arise.

When one reaches this state where even the mind of non-action and non-arising cannot be apprehended, it is said that "lustful thoughts are forever severed. Alcohol can lead to disorder and serves to incite the nature of desire.
Therefore, meat can harm compassion because it gives rise to the intent to kill. To assist one's meals with fire while refraining from eating raw flesh is the ultimate prevention of killing.
Alcohol fundamentally clouds the nature; if a practitioner drinks it, that which is luminous becomes, conversely, obscure.
That which was once alert and lucid now becomes dull and obscured; thus, the loss of one’s wisdom-life (prajñājīvitendriya) is evident. Meat inherently destroys compassion.

Although there is a distinction between humans and animals in form, their substance is fundamentally the same in possessing Buddha-nature (buddhadhātu). If one eats their flesh, [one commits a grave offense].
This immediately severs the seeds of Buddha-nature; thus, the loss of one’s Dharmakāya can also be known.
This is why one should not consume alcohol or meat. That this is directed at practitioners and the like serves as an implicit exhortation to maintain [the precepts].

This should be understood. Second, regarding the actual presentation of the method: "One should contemplate," etc., correctly demonstrates the method for severing desire. "Just as," etc., refers to the world.
A venomous snake merely kills the physical body and takes one’s life as retribution; however, lust can destroy both the Dharma-body and the life of wisdom.
In the world, those called "enemies" or "robbers" are termed "robbers" for plundering wealth and "enemies" for taking one's life.
Now, lust not only plunders the wealth of merit and the Dharma, but also robs the life of wisdom; therefore, it is likened to a venomous snake and an enemy-robber. This is what is most grave.

Everything depends on the two characters "contemplate" (*guan*). The subsequent points regarding maintaining the body without movement and maintaining the mind without arising derive their power entirely from this.
The phrase "first maintain," etc., further clarifies that there is a sequence in observing the precepts and they must not be bypassed. "First maintain" refers to the *bhikṣu* precepts;

"subsequently practice," etc., refers to the Bodhisattva precepts. Recently, there have been those who claim that the *bhikṣu* precepts are difficult to maintain while the Bodhisattva precepts are easy.

It is easy to maintain. However, while it may still be possible for a bhikṣu to grasp and hold [the body] by keeping the body motionless, if a bodhisattva fails to grasp the mind and lacks such sustained holding, it is truly lamentable that this [bodhisattva practice] becomes easier [to neglect] than that [monastic discipline]. Third, regarding the "preliminary clarification of the efficacy":

"prohibitions and precepts," etc., refers to the preliminary enumeration of its effects. These pertain to the proximate stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) and the remote stage of semblance-realization (*sādṛśya*).

Therefore, the prohibitions and precepts serve to eliminate discursive thoughts and cultivate contemplative practice. This "purity" eliminates that which resembles [true realization]. The subsequent section on the violation of manifest karma and its preliminary explanation of efficacy is likewise so.

Regarding what is called "the accomplishment of the precepts": it means that regarding the two types of [transgressions], sexual misconduct and killing, one maintains the body so it does not move and maintains the mind so it does not arise;
thus the precepts shall be accomplished. Because sexual desire is severed forever, they will never again give rise to one another. Forever...

There is no killing through signs, for killing has been severed. Since there are no causes for the karma of killing or giving birth, how could there be the karmic retribution of killing or giving birth?
"Stealing" refers to taking by stealth; "robbery" refers to taking by force. "One who is without burden" means one who is free from the karmic burden of debt.
Regarding "not returning past debts": for example, if one had previously coveted offerings through great false speech, one would have to repay that debt;
since there is now no falsehood, there is no need to repay. In short, as lust, killing, stealing, and lying are all purified, it is said that the prohibitive precepts are accomplished.
This is a preliminary description of the efficacy of attaining the practice of contemplation in the future. Thus it is said, "This purity," and so forth. This is the preliminary [explanation].

To describe the corresponding effects and verifications, they are precisely the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). Not requiring the divine eye (*divyacakṣus*) is the purification of the eye faculty. Hearing the Dharma is the purification of the ear faculty.
Personally receiving the holy instructions is the purification of the tongue faculty. Attaining supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) is the purification of the body faculty.
Purification of past lives (*pūrvanivāsa*) is the purification of the mind faculty. Although the nose faculty is omitted here, it may be understood by extension from the ear. If one requires...
To explain this, it can also be understood as being presented in contrast to the "purity of the six sense organs" (*ṣaḍindriyaviśuddhi*) in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra*.
This is because it describes the effects that are similar [to those of the sūtra]. The three conclusions may be seen accordingly.

The third section concerns the contradiction with present karma; it also consists of three parts: the inquiry, the explanation, and the conclusion. The initial inquiry is self-evident. The explanation likewise has three parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the actual cultivation of meritorious practice is presented;
second, from "the ten directions" onwards, the preliminary manifestation of efficacy is clarified; third, from "from this" onwards, the establishment of practice according to its course is shown.

Within the first part, the actual presentation of meritorious practice, [it states] "by means of non-attachment to lust," etc.; if one does not rely on the previous [teachings], it would not stop there.
There is no lust, and so on, up to and including the absence of false speech, which is likewise complete. Furthermore, according to the text, it is not only that there is no covetous lust;
rather, regarding all objects encountered by the six sense faculties, there is no greed at all. This is why it says "regarding external [objects]," and so forth.

If the six external sense-objects do not cause much wandering and dissipation, then covetous lust will be absent. For such wandering and dissipation toward external objects gives rise to manifest karma; now, since there is no covetous lust...
When [the mind] does not stray outward, the revolving flow of desire naturally returns to the fundamental awakening. Thus, when the sense objects are no longer conditioned, this realm is stilled;
when the faculties have nothing to pair with, these objects are empty. When both faculty and object vanish, one enters the "one extinction" which extinguishes the six.

Therefore, it is said that one "reverses the flow," and so forth. Alternatively, the phrase "returning" means entering the flow; the phrase "extinguishing the six functions" means the disappearance of the objective field. This is...

This is the ultimate form of contravention. Nevertheless, regarding the contravention of manifest karma, if one wishes to understand it in detail, it is fully explained in the "Ten Modes of Contemplation" (*Daśa-yāna-vidhi*) within the *Xuanyi* (Profound Meaning), where its meaning is exhausted.

This is precisely how merit and practice are manifested. Second, within the preliminary explanation of the efficacy and verification: the section beginning with "The ten directions" clarifies contemplative practice (*guanxing*).

The section beginning with "Body and mind" clarifies the stage of semblance (*xiangsi*). The section beginning with "This person" clarifies partial realization (*fenzheng*). This is because of the contravention...

Regarding the meritorious practices of manifested karma that have already passed: in the near term, one may attain a semblance [of realization]; in the distant term, one may attain partial realization (*praveśa*).
As for contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*), it is even more proximate than this. Within contemplative practice, the "ten directions" and so forth constitute the objects of observation.
That these are luminously pure is entirely due to the wisdom of the observing subject. It is by means of the wisdom of the observing subject that the objects of observation are illumined.
The objective realm is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli; if the observed realm gives rise to the observing wisdom, it is like a bright moon suspended within lapis lazuli.

Because the realm and wisdom are identical as one, and the subject and object are non-dual, it may also be said that the bright moon is the single, total mind, while the lapis lazuli is the six sense-objects and the lands. Thus, their characteristics—
The phrase "resembling the middle" and the single phrase "body and mind" together provide a general heading for the purification of the six sense faculties.
"Wondrously perfect and equal"—it is called equality not because it is non-dual or non-distinct, but because upon reaching this state, the principle of wondrous clarity corresponds and resembles it;
it is like comparing a melon to a gourd or brass to gold. Thus, it is said to be "wondrously perfect and equal," which precisely manifests its purity. This also accords with the Dharma.

This is explained here in contrast to the "Purity of the Six Faculties" (ṣaḍindriya-viśuddhi). Because the ten realms are all perfectly seen, perfectly heard, and even perfectly known, it says "all," and so forth.
Furthermore, it may also mean that the phrases regarding body and mind have no [external] counterparts for the faculties.
The "wondrously perfect phrase" is so called because it does not give rise to discrimination. The "phrase of great attainment" is so called because one is not turned by external conditions.

"All things are equal" refers to the manifestation of the principle of the Dharmakāya, wherein the inherent nature and virtues are perfectly luminous. This is what is meant by "partial realization" within the stage of entering the realization of non-arising.
From the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), one may know that there is progressive advancement at each step.

Regarding the third section, "Establishment According to Practice" (*anuvartana-vyavasthāna*): the phrase "from these [stages] onwards" intends to clarify in advance that all fifty-seven stages are fully present within the preceding effects.
Whatever practice you initiate is the level of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), which is established as the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) and the noble stages (*ārya-bhūmi*).
The practices that are initiated constitute the "identity of semblance" (*sādharmya-tathatā*), which is established within the stage of the ten faiths (*daśa-śraddhā*).

The practices that are initiated constitute the "identity of partial realization" (*pradeśa-prativedha-tathatā*), which is established within the forty-six sublime stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*), namely the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*), the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*), the ten transferences (*daśa-pariṇāmana*), the four preparatory stages (*catur-prayoga*), and the ten grounds (*daśa-bhūmi*).
As for what follows below, it begins with "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) and culminates in the "sublime" (*māyopama*).
Awakening and all that intervenes are stages established through the development of the three gradual sequences;
therefore, these three gradual sequences constitute the primary foundation. The three fetters (saṃyojana) may be understood accordingly. Question:

Since the three kinds of gradual sequences were previously determined to belong to the stage of progress within the "name-and-character" (nāmamātra), why does the commentary sometimes refer to them as "practice-observation" (kriyā-caryā) and sometimes as "characteristics" (lakṣaṇa)?

[Objection: It seems [the stages] refer to those from the first abode (prathamā bhūmiḥ) onwards. Not only would this contradict your own words, but would it not further mean that what was previously stated has no basis in the sūtras?
[Response: Did we not say before that these three gradual stages are cultivated within the phase of "names" (nāma)?

They approximate the stage of contemplative practice (vipaśyanā-caryā), while ultimately they extend to the true and semblance stages. Therefore, regarding the statement that "in the world there is forever no mutual killing or giving birth," this—

When one correctly subdues the five abodes (*pañca-vāsa*), the proclivities (*anuśaya*) of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct no longer arise; this pertains to the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).

When one perceives the ten directions within the physical bodies of one's parents, this refers to the correct purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*), wherein the views and afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have first fallen away;
this pertains to the stage of semblance (*sādṛśya-bhūmi*). The above constitutes the second gradual sequence. Within the third gradual sequence, "the ten directions," and so forth, are the same.
The preceding refers to the stage of preparatory practice (*prayoga*). "Body, mind, and so forth" refers to the stage of similarity (*sādṛśya*) as previously described.

"This person" and so forth refers to the stage of partial realization (*bhūta-avasthā*), wherein one correctly analyzes and partially realizes the three virtues by breaking through ignorance. The Tathāgata skillfully provides these preliminary indications in advance.
To cause sentient beings to practice directly and immediately as the foundation for realization, the subsequent text concludes:

"In this way, all these three stages of gradual progress accomplish the fifty-five positions of the true path to Bodhi. This is like the principle of not forgetting the single basket of earth that completed a tower nine fathoms high.
Now, as to why they are called both "three gradual stages" (sān jiàn cì) and "three stages of progress" (sān zēng jìn):

Thus, the first gradual stage clarifies only the faults and afflictions; the second gradual stage not only clarifies the meritorious practices, but also anticipates the semblance effects of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*);

as for the third gradual stage, it not only clarifies the semblance effects of contemplative practice, but further clarifies the effects of partial realization (*bhūta-avasthā*). Thus one knows that each subsequent stage is superior to the preceding one. This is...
The "three gradual stages" are also called the "three progressive advancements.
The passage beginning with "Second, from the point where Ānanda says 'this good man... clarifies the text on the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

This directly follows the preceding section on establishing the noble stages according to the practices undertaken, thereby elucidating the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*). From this point onward, [the text] generally responds to the immediate occasion (*pratyarha*).
"What is meant by the 'ground of dry wisdom' and the request regarding the forty-four minds? Good son, this refers to those who practice the three gradual stages.
Because they have hollowed out their fundamental nature, the craving of desire has withered and dried up. Because they have severed present karma, the faculties and their objects no longer meet.
If there were craving as the cause and the faculties and objects as the conditions, there would still be a residual physical body."
Regarding the phenomena that have arisen: since they have now given rise to non-attachment such that the six faculties no longer function, both causes and conditions are severed.
From what, then, could the remaining physical form continue to manifest before us? This refers back to the preceding discussion concerning the evil that has been extinguished.
The section beginning with "the mind that clings" correctly clarifies the present state by means of the good that has arisen. This is because one does not engage in discursive thought...
Contemplating the inconceivable realm, one realizes that the aggregates, sense bases, elements, and spheres are fundamentally the Tathāgatagarbha;

thus, the two attachments to self and phenomena are seen to have no real nature, which is why it says "the mind of attachment," and so forth. Yet, the Tathāgatagarbha possesses subtle, wondrous, awakened clarity that perfectly illumines the Dharma-realm;
this is why it says "the nature of wisdom," and so forth. The golden color shining outward is called *yan* (polishing/adornment); here, the light of wisdom shines outward as its adornment.
It is also like this. "Qian has the lower" concludes by clarifying the meaning of the name. As for the "flowing water of the Dharma," it specifically refers to the Buddha-nature of the Middle Way.

The two characters "flowing water" are spoken of as a metaphor; that is, the principle of the Middle Way Truth is a source far-reaching and a stream long-lasting, surging on without exhaustion, and is thus likened to flowing water.
The phrase "not yet meeting with [the next]" means that the habit-energy of desire is precisely at the initial stage of drying up.

The complete subduing of the five stages of dwelling constitutes the initial "drying. Although this involves complete clarity, complete illumination, and the complete subduing of the five stages of dwelling, when compared with subsequent stages, the habitual tendencies of desire (*kāma-vāsanā*) have not yet been fully exhausted at this stage; therefore, it has not yet connected with the "water of principle" of the middle [stages].

Within the six stages of "attainment" (*liù jí*) in our school, this is precisely the stage where the contemplation of the five abodes (*wǔ zhù*) is first established during the practice of the path of cultivation (*guān xíng*).

The third section, "Self-Attainment," begins with the words "With this mind one departs," which directly follows the preceding passage on establishing the noble stages according to the practices undertaken;

it serves to clarify the text concerning the stage of semblance within the ten faiths (*shí xìn*). Regarding the term "faith" (*xìn*) mentioned within the first stage of faith: it refers to faith in the Buddha of the Middle Way.

This refers to a nature of profound patience and resolute aspiration that is unshakable. There are ten such states of mind, which are collectively termed "faith" because faith is their primary characteristic.

This very mind refers back to the previously mentioned state of the Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-vipaśyanā*). By relying on the perfect and universal application of the ear-faculty through the wondrous *śamatha* and other practices, one perfectly subdues the five abodes of delusion, and the contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā*) manifests before one. Thus, one flows into the Middle Way from the center. This is because...
This mind takes the eternally abiding Middle Way as its essence; now it flows into that Middle Way from within the Middle Way.
Alternatively, one may contemplate the Middle Way by means of the contemplation of the Middle Way and thereby flow into it; thus it is said, "by means of this," and so forth.
Because of this flowing-in, the delusions of views fall away first, and the eternally abiding, perfectly wondrous principle unfolds like a blooming lotus flower.
It unfolds and manifests itself. Therefore, it is said that "the perfect and wondrous [mind] unfolds. The above clarifies the preceding stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*).

From "from the True" onwards, it clarifies the fundamental position. That is to say, from the fundamentally wondrous and perfect mind of Dry Wisdom, one again brings forth and clarifies the semblance-of-true, wondrous mind of faith.

Therefore, it is said that "from the True [Nature]," and so forth. When the mind and the principle are in profound accord and resemble one another, the eternally abiding true mind is revealed, which can certainly be trusted;
hence, it is said that "wondrous faith abides eternally. Because the eighty-eight afflictions (*kleśas*) are all completely purified, it is said that "all," and so forth.
The two phrases concerning the Middle Way refer to receiving the name of the first stage of faith (*śraddhā*). This is because the ability to believe is the cause for the practitioner.

The mind is that which believes in the principle of the Middle Way Truth (*madhyamā-pratītyasamutpāda*). Since all admixture with delusion has been exhausted, the pure and true intention is manifested;
for the capacity to achieve [enlightenment] is entirely the principle itself, and thus this principle is faith. Now, "abiding" (*vihāra*) is precisely faith.

Some say that the ten levels of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*) are derived from the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*), and therefore the term "abiding" is frequently used. This is not so. If it were the case, then each successive stage should be described as follows:
Regarding "faith": why is it that the preceding and succeeding [passages] speak of abiding in the middle, yet also speak of the mind?
One must realize that this refers to the stage of semblance in the Perfect Teaching; it is merely the stage of abiding.

Within the mind of two moments of thought, as for "true faith," the previous statement—“from the truly wondrous and perfect, one again gives rise to the truly wondrous”—refers precisely to the first stage of faith. As for "clarity," at this stage one advances to sever [delusions].
Regarding the delusions of thought: all the elements of faith are perfectly luminous, eternally abiding, and even more clearly manifest.

Precisely because they are clear and manifest, all things are universally penetrating (*yuan-tong*), and mindfulness and wisdom appear before one. This phrase serves as the heading; the subsequent section on the "aggregates" (*skandha*) and "bases" (*āyatana*) demonstrates the characteristics of this universal penetration.

When the aggregates and bases do not constitute obstructions, there is horizontal penetration through all phenomena; when the three periods of time are clearly evident, there is vertical penetration across many kalpas.

"Discarding this body and receiving another body" refers to birth-and-death in discrete segments (*paricchinna-jarāmaraṇa*). "All habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) refers to both the active afflictions (*kleśa*) and their residual impressions (*anuśaya*).

That "they all appear before one" is due to the fact that mindfulness and wisdom are perfectly clear and lucid, such that one remembers without forgetting; for this reason, the name of the meditative stage is established as "Abiding of the Mind in Mindfulness.
Generally, the former [stage] is deep faith in the inherently existing Buddha-nature (*tathāgatagarbha*), whereas this [stage] is the recollection of the seeds of recent cultivation.

Regarding "nature": among the five faculties, it refers to the faculty of mindfulness (*smṛtīndriya*). Regarding "three minds of vigor": "wondrously perfect" (*miaoyuan*) refers to the first mind of faith;

"pure and true" (*chunzhen*) refers to the second mind of faith. It means that what was previously wondrously perfect and pure and true now, reaching this stage, has its true essence (*zhenjing*) manifest through transformation.

Hence, it is called "wondrously perfect," and so forth. "Transformation" (*hua*) means change. This signifies that all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been completely transformed into true luminosity (*bhūtaprajñā*).
Therefore, it is said, "beginningless," and so forth; this expresses its purity and lack of admixture.

By means of this pure and refined faith, one advances toward the true, pure, and wondrous principle of the Middle Way; hence it is said, "exclusively by," and so forth; this expresses its progress without regression.

For this reason, it is called the mind of diligence (*vīrya*). Within the four minds of wisdom, the phrase "the mind of purity" (*citta-śuddhi*) points back to the aforementioned mind of diligence, indicating that its principle is further clarified.
The phrase "pure" (*viśuddha*) elucidates its fundamental state, indicating that its wisdom is further perfected.
Thus, the contemplative wisdom that is able to illuminate and the essence of the mind that is illuminated are such that principle and wisdom are one; subject and object are not [dual].
Second, this is called "the dwelling of the mind in wisdom. Regarding the phrase "maintaining the clarity of knowledge" within the five states of meditative concentration (*pañca-samādhi-citta*):
previously, one had relied solely on wisdom, such that wisdom was predominant and concentration was scarce. Upon reaching this stage, concentration and wisdom are balanced.
All intellectual practices as well as the fundamental principle (*tattva*) are maintained without loss; this is what is meant by "maintaining the clarity of knowledge. Thus it is said.
Thus, one is able to be tranquil yet luminous, and luminous yet tranquil; tranquility and luminosity are non-dual. Therefore, it is said that they are "all-pervasive, tranquil, and profound.

Furthermore, the object is like the wisdom, and the wisdom is like the object; object and wisdom are identical as one. Therefore, it is said that they are "tranquil, wondrous, and eternally凝 (congealed/still).

This is a profound realization of the *Śūraṅgama-samādhi*, and is thus called "abiding in the mind of concentration. Regarding the six stages of non-retrogression, "the light of concentration illuminates and clarifies" means:

This refers to the simultaneous application of both meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*). At this stage, the delusions of thought (*vitarka-kleśa*) are about to be severed or have already been exhausted;
the nature of clarity (*vidyā-svabhāva*) penetrates even deeper, and there is only progress forward without any regression. Therefore, it is called the "Non-regressing Mind" (*avinivartana-citta*).

Furthermore, these five stages of mind are identical to the five faculties (*pañcendriya*); once the five faculties are established, they become the five powers (*pañcabala*), whereby the five hindrances can be dispelled forever.
There is no regression; thus, because the nature of clarity penetrates deeply, one merely receives the name "non-regressive. Seventh, within the mind that protects the Dharma:
the phrase "advancing the mind" indicates the simultaneous application of the aforementioned concentration and wisdom. The phrase "maintaining and abiding" clarifies the present:

it means that through profound contemplation of non-duality, one is able to protect, preserve, and sustain [the Dharma]. From this, one becomes of the same spiritual lineage as the Tathāgatas of the ten directions regarding the Middle Way.

This "connection" (jiajie) is what is called the dwelling that protects the Dharma (*dharmapālaka-vihāra*). Previously, while the five stages of delusion were completely subdued and one possessed their dry wisdom, one had not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma-water.
Now, as both view-delusions and afflictions are exhausted, one perceives the principle of the Middle Way that accords with [the Buddha's] vision; therefore, it is called "connection.

Within the eighth stage, the Mind of Dedication (*pariṇāmanā-citta*), "awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) refers to the dharmas obtained during the seventh stage of faith (*śraddhā-bhūmi*); this is what is maintained.
"The mind capable of maintaining" refers collectively to the aforementioned mind that protects the Dharma.
Regarding "is able to," although the principle of the Middle Way Truth and the spatial dimensions of the ten directions have previously intersected, it was simply the Buddhas who came to receive me.

I have not yet been able to respond to the Buddhas. Now that the afflictions of view and thought (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) have been completely severed, and the "dust-sand" [afflictions] (*rajas-aṇu*) have further been destroyed, one can turn back what was previously received and return to it;
this is what is called "reverting the fruit to the cause" (*phala-pratyāhāra-hetu*), whereby one proceeds from the cause toward the fruit.

As for "the light of compassion," this refers to the Bodhisattva at the eighth stage of faith who cultivates the wisdom of emerging into the conventional (*niryūha-jñāna*), which possesses the meaning of bestowing happiness. It may also be directed toward...

Those who previously came to cultivate initial enlightenment (shijue) by means of fundamental enlightenment (benjue) now turn the cultivation of initial enlightenment toward the nature of fundamental enlightenment and abide therein.
To illustrate this through a metaphor, it is like the reflection of light between two mirrors facing each other:
the two aspects of fundamental and initial enlightenment merge and both vanish, while the two dharmas of cause and effect mutually revert. Thus, one attains [enlightenment].

The wondrous reflections interpenetrate one another infinitely; this refers to the principle inherent within both cultivation and nature. It is neither quiescence nor illumination, yet it is both quiescent and illuminating.
Having transcended subject and object, it is absolute and free from all relativity; it is only through self-correspondence and cannot be demonstrated through words, and is thus called "wondrous.
Because it turns the light back toward faith, it is termed the "mind of dedication. Among the nine minds of precept-holding:
The phrase "the light of the mind" (*citta-prabhā*) refers back to the preceding [stage of] faith. "Obtaining the Buddha... and below clarifies the fundamental station (*mūla-pada*).
Because the light of the mind of prior initial awakening (*ādi-bodhi*) operates secretly and stably, one attains the eternally stable fundamental awakening (*mūla-bodhi*) of the Buddha.

This fundamental awakening is precisely the Middle Way, the Ultimate Truth (*paramārtha-satya*), which is free from the defilements of the two extremes; it is the unsurpassed, wondrous purity. Now, one abides therein.
The unconditioned Dharma does not permit even the slightest loss, while the evils of ignorance naturally find themselves restrained; therefore, it is called the "mind of precepts" (*śīla-citta*).
Within the ten vows, the phrase "abiding in the precepts" refers back to the preceding stage of faith, while the phrase "able to roam" clarifies the fundamental station.
Since one can thus cease the evils of ignorance, within the essence of the precepts there is nowhere that one does not possess mastery.
Therefore, it is said that one dwells in the sovereignty of the precepts. Ignorance can be analytically dismantled, and the Middle Way can be analytically revealed.

Upon entering the first stage (*bhūmi*), one may immediately manifest the eight phases of attaining Buddhahood within the hundred realms. Hence, it is said that one can travel throughout the ten directions.

Because the Bodhisattva of the Ten Good Deeds has resolved upon the Great Mind, they have forever departed from the ocean of suffering in the triple world; this is called the mind of aspiration (*praṇidhāna-citta*).

Furthermore, regarding the passage concerning the four [stages] of the noble son Ānanda departing, it follows what was previously established according to his practice and attainment of the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*).

This clarifies the text on the ten abodes (*daśavihāra*) within the stage of partial realization (*praveśa-sākṣātkriyā*). As for what is called "abiding," the *Renwang jing* (Benevolent Kings Sutra) states: "The prajñā that enters into principle is named..."
This constitutes "abiding. By means of the dharma of non-abiding, one abides in the three virtues of a Buddha and all Buddha-dharmas, progressing from the shallow to the deep.
From within this, contemplation manifests before one, opening the Buddha-eye and accomplishing the knowledge of all modes (*sarvākārajñatā*).

From the first to the tenth [stage], one respectively severs one grade of ignorance and realizes a portion of the Middle Way. Regarding the "good son" in the first stage, it refers to the fulfillment of the ten stages of abiding (*daśa-vihāra*).
"Regarding 'the person': 'with true equality' refers back to the preceding ten stages of faith. 'The mind's essence' and so forth correctly clarify the fundamental position.
As for 'true skillful means,' there are two meanings: first, that which arises from nature is called 'true,' while that which reveals nature through cultivation is called 'skillful means.
Second, being able to penetrate the delusions of inversion—that is, the very nature of ignorance—is what gives rise to [skillful means]."
Through the single mind and threefold contemplation, one cultivates the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing.
Prior to entering the stream, this may only be called the "semblance skillful means. Once one has entered the stream, it may then be called the "true skillful means.

Thus, we know that the ten stages of faith mentioned above all arise from cultivating the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing based entirely upon the intrinsic nature; hence it is said, "by means of the true," and so forth.
Thus it is. Once these ten minds have arisen, one further advances to break through one grade of ignorance; the preceding ten minds become refined and pure, surging forth with radiance.
Therefore, it is said that "the essence of mind emits radiance. Each and every mind interpenetrates one another like the jewels of Indra’s net, layer upon layer.
Taking each individual mind as possessing all ten minds, they transform from semblance-wisdom into true-wisdom, becoming perfectly round.

Because one achieves the single-mindedness of the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), it is said that "the ten functions," and so forth. Thus, these ten minds constitute the state of semblance (*sādṛśya*).
Here, the first stage is designated as "partial realization" (*vibhāga-satya*) in contrast to the state of semblance; conversely, the first stage is what constitutes partial realization.

Now, the ten minds are similar yet differentiated as the stage of "partial realization" (vibhāga-satya). From this point, the so-called three causes unfold and the three virtues are perfectly realized;
this is called the Stage of Resolving the Mind (Cittotpāda-vihāra). The phrase "within the mind" (*citta-madhye*) refers to the two subsequent stages.

"Within the mind" points back to the preceding first stage, using the former to clarify the present fundamental position. The phrase "within the mind" refers precisely to this Perfectly Accomplished One Mind (*pariniṣpanna-ekacitta*).

In this context, wisdom (*jñāna*) is that which brings forth illumination, while principle (*tattva*) is that which is illuminated. The phrase "pure state" (*śuddha-pada*) is a metaphor for the radiance of the mind’s essence;
the phrase "manifesting within" (*antaḥ-prakāśa-pada*) is a metaphor for the mutual interpenetration of the ten functions (*daśa-kārya*), and so forth. Regarding the phrase "by means of the former":

this refers to employing the mind of the first stage (*prathama-bhūmi*), which was formed through the aforementioned ten functions, as the wisdom of middle observation (*madhyama-vipaśyanā-jñāna*), and applying diligent effort to its subtle cultivation.

To cause them to enter into a dark resonance with principle (*li*), giving rise to immeasurable virtuous functions—this is "treading upon it to form the ground," which is named the Dwelling of Cultivating the Ground (*Caryā-bhūmi*).
This is the third dwelling among the four stages of the mind-ground (*citta-bhūmi*). The first two phrases point to the preceding stage;

"wandering and treading" clarifies the current stage. Regarding the phrase "mind-ground" and so forth: "mind" refers to the wisdom of initial enlightenment (*ādi-bodhi*) produced in the first dwelling; "ground" refers to...

The second is the realm of the original enlightenment (honkaku) that arises from the dwelling-place. Here, the beginning and the origin are unified, and wisdom and the realm are identical as one; thus it is called the "ground of the mind" and so forth.
Having attained this identity of wisdom and realm, and the non-duality of the beginning and the origin, at this point wisdom becomes increasingly profound and principle becomes increasingly manifest.
From these six perfections and myriad practices, one travels freely throughout the ten realms; mind and objects are perfectly interfused like milk and water, without any obstruction or hindrance.
Thus it is said that one "travels and treads" [upon them]. Consequently, the capacity for transformation and guidance is further expanded.
The sentient beings to be delivered are even more universal; therefore, it is called "abiding in practice" (*caryā-vihāra*). "Practice" (*caryā*) refers here to the four preceding abidings.
The phrase "receiving from the Buddha" clarifies its fundamental position. This is the wondrous practice of the Tathāgata, for he traverses the ten directions without obstruction or hindrance.
Since the Bodhisattva is thus able to be non-dual with the Buddha, it is called "practice."
They are the same as the Buddha. Since their practice is identical, they fully receive every portion of the Middle Way without exception;
thus it is said that they "receive the Buddha’s portion. This is illustrated by the example of the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) mentioned below:

when an ordinary person’s prior existence has ceased and the subsequent existence has not yet arisen, the body of the intermediate state seeks out those of similar karma to serve as its parents; hence it is said, "as in the case of the intermediate state," and so forth.
Thus, through the conjunction of the three conditions, one grasps the residual body to take rebirth. This intermediate state (*antarābhava*) is invisible to ordinary beings.

Now, for a Bodhisattva at the fourth stage of dwelling, whose practice and principle are identical to those of the Buddhas, there is a profound resonance between the Father of Expedient Wisdom and the Mother of Real Wisdom.
Therefore, it is said that "at the stage of the aggregates, there is dark communion. For this reason:
Receiving the Buddha’s practice and principle, one enters the lineage of the Tathāgata to entrust oneself to the holy embryo; hence it is said, "entering the lineage of the Tathāgata.
For in the mundane world, the royal lineage is esteemed as noble, while in the supramundane, the Buddha-lineage is esteemed as noble; this is called the Dwelling of Birth in Nobility.
Since one has already traversed the five lower dwellings, the first two phrases point back to the preceding dwelling, clarifying the fundamental position through metaphors such as the embryo.

Regarding the phrase "having already entered" (*jiyou*): since one has begun by attaining dark resonance with the fundamental source and entering the lineage of the Tathāgata, the embryo of the Way (*daotai*) is now fully formed, and one becomes a direct descendant of the Buddha;
hence it is said, "having already entered," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "like an embryo" (*ru tai*):

from the moment one enters this stage, the provisional manifests the real, and through the real, the provisional is revealed. One is fully capable of resembling the Buddha without any deficiency, just as a person who perfectly resembles his father.

"Mother. Thus it is said, "like a fetus," and so forth. Because this perfect, penetrating, and wondrous equipment is fully endowed with all skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), it is named the "Abode of Full Endowment of Skillful Means.
Regarding the phrase "countenance and appearance," this refers to the sixth abode. The first sentence points back to the preceding abode;

the phrase "mental characteristics and so forth" clarifies its own position. Since it was previously stated that "the human marks are not deficient," this [phrase] here specifically indicates "countenance and appearance."

"Like the Buddha": "appearance like the Buddha" means that his meritorious practice is identical to that of the Buddha; "mental characteristics also identical" means that the principle-nature (*li-ti*) is likewise not different.
Since both essence (*ti*) and function (*yong*) are identical to those of the Buddha, he naturally attains the rectitude of his mind;
this is called the "Abiding in Rectified Mind. This refers to the seventh stage among the seven stages of body and mind. The first phrase also points back to what preceded.

"Day by day, equal and right clarity increases. This means that since its essence and function are identical to those of the Buddha, all mental objects and the mind-intelligence themselves naturally merge into one, no longer divisible.
Therefore, it is said that "body and mind merge into a single unity. From this, the principle-essence becomes increasingly manifest and the function of wisdom becomes increasingly expansive;
hence, it is said that "it increases day by day," and within this, there is naturally no regression.
Because [the practitioner] bends [toward the goal], it is called the "Abode of Non-retrogression. This refers to the eight abodes following the tenth body. There are two types of the ten bodies:
first, the body of the śrāvaka, the body of the pratyekabuddha, the body of the Tathāgata, the dharma-body, the wisdom-body, the space-body, and the karma-faculty-body.
The body of sentient beings and the body of the land—within these two, the body of the Tathāgata itself contains ten bodies, namely:
the bodhisattva body, the vow body, the transformation body, the sustaining power body, the adorned body, the majestic power body, the mind-born body, and the merit body.
The Dharma-body and the Wisdom-body—these two kinds are fully possessed by the Tathāgata of the ten bodies.

Upon entering this stage, because the preceding mental wisdom regarding the objects of the body increases day by day, one personally realizes and attains them; therefore, it is said that "the ten bodies, etc. are attained.
As for what is called "at one time," it means that when one is perfected, all are perfected. It is simply that from the very beginning, the essence and its source are conjoined;

though the form is complete, it is subtle. For this reason, it is named the "Abode of Youthful Truth" (*kumārabhūmi*). The formation of the body refers to the subsequent nine abodes. The first two characters point to the prior fulfillment of the ten bodies.
As for "emerging from the womb" and so forth, these refer to the fundamental station. From the essence, function arises, thereby continuing and upholding [the lineage].

The noble lineages (āryavaṃśa) constitute the true sons of the Buddha. Because one directly inherits the family estate of this Dharma-king from them, it is designated as the "Abode of the Dharma Prince" (*dharmarājaputrabhūmi*).
This indicates that the following ten abodes follow from it. To represent the attainment of adulthood:
although one has previously emerged from the womb as a Dharma prince, one is still immature in years and thus not yet considered an adult; now, however, one’s age is at its prime, and one ought to...

This serves to manifest that the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakṣa-dharmas) have been perfected, making one capable of responding to and transforming beings within the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu). The following passage from the *Rāṣṭrapālaparipṛcchā-sūtra* provides an analogy:

when a worldly king sees his crown prince reach maturity, he assembles his ministers and officials, takes water from the four oceans, pours it into a golden vessel, and sprinkles it upon the prince’s head to signify his attainment of adulthood.
He then commands him to leave the inner palace and entrusts him with the governance of the state, dividing the responsibilities of instruction and administration.
The edict states: "Now, the Bodhisattvas of the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*) are likewise so. They are consecrated with the water of the Buddhas' wisdom;

they are capable of performing the Buddha-deeds and receiving the office of great wisdom. Therefore, it is said they are 'equal to the kingdom,' and this is called the Stage of Consecration (*abhiṣeka-vihāra*).

As for the fact that the Cloud of Dharma Stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*) is also called the Bodhisattva of Consecration, one should know that while the names are the same, the meanings differ. This is because they share a partial similarity."

The only difference lies in the depth of their attainment. As for the terms "Heir Apparent" (shìzǐ) and "Crown Prince" (tàizǐ): the son of a feudal lord is called the Heir Apparent, while the son of the Son of Heaven is called the Crown Prince.
Here, however, I am speaking in general terms for the sake of common usage, rather than distinguishing between these specific titles in my text.
Fifth, from the passage "Ānanda, these good men having departed... onwards, it follows what was previously established regarding their practice and the stages of the sages (*ārya-bhūmi*).

This clarifies the textual section on the ten practices (*daśa-caryā*) within the stage of partial realization (*pratyakṣa-sākṣātkriyā*). As for what is called "practice," it refers precisely to the period following the ten abidings (*daśa-vihāra*);

through the inconceivable true illumination of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā*), one further undergoes ten cycles of wisdom and severance (*jñāna-prahāṇa*), progressively shattering the ten grades of ignorance (*avidyā*). This is what is meant by that.

Regarding practice, there are two meanings: vertical and horizontal. To discuss the vertical: the first practice is not equal to the second, and so on, up to the ninth practice being not equal to the tenth.
To discuss the horizontal: within each individual practice, all ten practices—and even immeasurable practices—are fully present; this is what is meant by "one practice is all practices.
In every thought-moment, one advances and enters spontaneously into the *sāmbhāra-pāramitā*, which arises through the very nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*).
"Extensive. Because all merits from both self-cultivation and the transformation of others are equal to empty space, it is called the stage of the Ten Practices (*daśa-pratipatti*).
Within the first practice, the phrase "good son" also refers to one who has achieved the Ten Abidings (*daśa-vihāra*).

"Attaining Buddhahood," and so forth, refers to those at the Ten Abidings who manifest as human beings and become Dharma Princes; they thus possess the immeasurable, wondrous virtues of a Tathāgata. These are the wondrous virtues.

This refers to the ten bodies and so forth. The phrase "the ten directions" clarifies the fundamental station. By relying on these sublime virtues, one accords with the ten directions. As the *Lotus Sūtra* says:

"Profoundly penetrating the characteristics of sin and merit, he shines universally throughout the ten directions. Because one possesses the superior [virtues] and accords with the inferior [realms], attaining great Dharma-joy, it is called the "Practice of Joy.
The following two practices are "skillful" [in their application]. This is the first practice of the upper [section].
Because he accords with both his own practice and the transformation of others, he gives rise to joy.

Now, having skillfully promoted wondrous virtue so that there are no sentient beings who do not receive benefit, it is said that he is "skillfully able," and so forth. Since sentient beings have thus obtained abundant benefit, [he rejoices].
This is precisely what is called the "practice of benefiting others. While it primarily belongs to the category of altruism, one's own practice is never lacking therein.

These refer to the three lower practices of self-awakening (*svasaṃbodha*). Regarding "self-awakening" and so forth: since it is called "self-awakening," one must necessarily seek upward toward the Buddhas;
regarding the Buddha’s teachings, one attains them oneself without the slightest contradiction. Since it is called "awakening others," one must necessarily transform the multitudes.

[He] is born [with this quality]. Furthermore, regarding the capacities and dispositions of sentient beings, he is able to avoid even the slightest refusal. Therefore, they are raised together as "self-awakening" and so forth.
If there were even a slight contradiction or refusal regarding the capacities for the teachings, resentment would inevitably arise in the mind;
since there is now no contradiction or refusal, there is naturally no resentment, and thus it is called "non-resentment. The following four lines concern its categories. Category...
"Kindred" (*jāti*) refers to the fact that within the aforementioned self-awakening and awakening of others, all wisdom and principle are nothing other than a single principle-body (*tattva*).

From this principle-body, power and function spontaneously arise, vertically penetrating the three periods of time and horizontally encompassing the ten directions; hence it is said that "they give rise to," and so forth.
Since they vertically penetrate the three periods of time, the three periods are equal, being devoid of coming or going. Thus, their transformation—

It leads from the inexhaustible. Furthermore, it extends horizontally throughout the ten directions; as these ten directions are universally penetrated without distance or proximity, its transformative guidance is likewise inexhaustible.
Therefore, it is named the "Inexhaustible Practice. The five lines below [the phrase] "all" refer to the practice itself.
All things arise from the same category as the finger-tip; they exhaust the three periods of time and pervade the ten directions.

Having attained equality, they are without coming or going; having attained penetration, they are without distance or proximity. All are harmoniously integrated into a single rational essence; therefore, it is said that "all are equal.
Although they constitute a single rational essence, there is no absence of differentiation, which leads to discrepancies and errors. Therefore...
It is said that there is no error. Since there is no error, one naturally avoids delusion and confusion; therefore, it is called the practice of being free from delusion and confusion.

Regarding the phrase "as for the following six practices," and so forth: while the preceding practice of inexhaustibility may be described as manifesting difference within sameness, it was not yet able to manifest sameness.
However, the practice of being free from delusion and confusion may be described as each distinct characteristic individually revealing sameness.
However, that which manifests as identical does not necessarily manifest as distinct; yet now, within identity, distinction is manifested—hence it is said, "then within equality.

Furthermore, within distinction, identity is manifested—hence it is said, "each and every one, etc. From this, phenomena and principle are mutually fused, and the ultimate and the conventional are simultaneously revealed.

That is to say, sequential progression (saṃbhāra) does not obstruct perfect integration (yuganaddha), and perfect integration does not obstruct sequential progression. Therefore, it is called "skillfully manifesting" (sukha-prakāśana).
...so it is. These seven lines below follow this pattern. The two characters "thus" (*rúshì*) inherit the preceding discussion on identity and difference.

Because the preceding principles of phenomena and noumenon are mutually fused and the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously revealed, herein the objects and realms are manifested such that every single thing is unimpeded.

The ten directions of empty space are fully contained within a single mote of dust; this is the manifestation of objects. Within each and every mote of dust, the realms of the ten directions are manifested; this is the manifestation of...
This is the realm (*dhātu*). Although it is said that the small manifests as large and the large manifests as small, the large and small are mutually inclusive without one encroaching upon the other;

therefore, it is collectively described as "manifesting as dust and so forth. Thus we know that when a world is contained within a minute atom, the world does not become small, and when a world enters into a minute atom, the atom does not become large.
They are all-pervasive, mutually inclusive, and harmoniously fused—beyond the reach of thought.

Because those who deliberate upon this are thus called "those who practice non-attachment," it is named the Practice of Non-Attachment. The "various" [practices] refer to the eight practices mentioned below.

Regarding "various" and so forth, this collectively summarizes what has preceded: either manifesting difference within sameness, or manifesting sameness within difference, or [manifesting] both sameness and difference as one.
The realms and the dust-particles are non-dual; there is not one that is not the empty truth of *prajñā*. Therefore, it says "various kinds" and so forth.
Since all are the inherent virtue of *prajñā*, they are entirely those things spontaneously accomplished through the wondrous power of non-action (*anabhisamskāra*).

Hence, they are called the "venerable practices. The phrase "such as these" refers to the nine subsequent practices. The term "such as these" points back to the four aforementioned modes of manifestation: identity, difference, and so on.

This refers to what was previously stated. If there were even one thing that were not Prajñā, it would not be perfect fusion (*yuanrong*). Now, since all are Prajñā, it is said to be "perfectly fused in this way.
Reaching this point, there is not a single thing that is not the track of the Buddhas; therefore, it is said that "it can accomplish [the state of] equality," and so forth.

Thus, all these are wholesome dharmas (*kuśala-dharma*) arising from cultivation based on the complete nature; therefore, they are designated as "wholesome dharmas. Each of the ten [categories] follows this pattern.
The two characters "one by one" (*yi yi*) also refer back to what precedes. Regarding the phrase "all are pure," there are two interpretations.

If considered according to their essential substance: the untainted (*anāsrava*) is *prajñā* (wisdom); the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) is *vimukti* (liberation); and the primordial state is *dharma* (the reality).
It is the body itself. If one acts as a cause and condition, it is pure and untainted—meaning it is not defiled by the ignorance of ordinary beings or outsiders regarding desire and existence;

it is the single true unconditioned—meaning it is not the result of the strenuous, partial cultivation and realization of the provisional vehicles of the Two Vehicles. This is because its nature is inherently so.
The intent behind composing these two lines is to clarify that cultivation arises from the nature; thus, the full practice of cultivation does not obstruct its presence within the nature.

Consequently, it is pure and does not belong to the outflows (*āsrava*); it is primordial and does not fall into the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Being thus true and not false, real and not empty, it is called "the Real" (*bhūtatathatā*).
This summarizes the preceding eight, nine, and ten lines, and continues the sequence from the previous four, five, and six lines.

This is made manifest. Generally speaking, the preceding four lines concern the cultivation of the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*), while these current three lines clarify their accomplishment.
This, however, is merely stated from a general perspective.
Sixth, from the passage "Ānanda, when these good sons depart" onwards, it follows what they have previously practiced to establish them in the noble stages (*āryabhūmi*).

This clarifies the text concerning the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*) within the stage of partial realization (*pratyakṣa-bhāga*). As for "dedication" (*pariṇāmanā*): "dedication" (*pari*) has the meaning of turning;

"direction" (*ṇāmanā*) has the meaning of tending toward. It means turning one's myriad practices toward three destinations. For example, once one's own practice is complete, one should then deliver sentient beings. Thus:
It is the turning of oneself toward others. It is the crossing over of the mark of "no-crossing-over," which is the turning of phenomena toward principle.

It is the turning of the unconditioned mind toward the path of Nirvana, which is the turning of the cause toward the fruit. This is also the turning toward sentient beings, toward the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and toward Bodhi;
it is also the mind of great compassion, the profound mind, and the true mind. These are present as examples in all subsequent stages below. This is so.
This constitutes the ten dedications (*pariṇāmanā*). Within the first dedication, the phrase "good son" likewise refers to one who has perfected the ten practices.
The statement "fulfilling the supernormal powers" summarizes the first through the eighth practices; the phrase "having accomplished the task of becoming a Buddha" summarizes the ninth practice.

"Pure, clean, and genuine" refers to the tenth stage mentioned above. "Far removed from all lingering afflictions" means that when the practice of the ten stages is perfected, self and others are equalized and emptiness and existence are harmoniously integrated;
thus, no afflictions can remain or create obstacles, and they are all completely transcended.

This summarizes and concludes the ten practices. "When one should deliver" (*dang du*) clarifies the fundamental position. The word "should" (*dang*) has two meanings. First, it has the sense of exhortation;

that is, since one's own practice is already perfected, one "should" deliver sentient beings, "should" bring about their extinction and liberation (*nirvāṇa*), "should" turn toward the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), and "should" head toward *nirvāṇa*, and so forth.
Second, it has the sense of the actual state; that is, when one is truly delivering sentient beings, that is itself their extinction and liberation.
The mark indicates that there is no sequence of before and after. This is identical in intent to the *Vajracchedikā*. For the practice of dedication involves the deepest compassion and vows;
therefore, one must deliver sentient beings. If there were a "one who delivers" and a "those delivered," it would be termed conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and not the path to Nirvāṇa.
The reason for practicing dedication (*pariṇāmanā*) is that one should rescue and protect all sentient beings while simultaneously remaining free from the conceptual mark of "sentient beings.

Furthermore, the phrase "should deliver" refers to dedicating oneself toward others; the phrase "extinguishing and eliminating" refers to dedicating phenomena toward principle; and "dedicating the peerless" refers to the ultimate dedication.
This is the turning of the cause toward the fruit. Thus, while blazingly delivering sentient beings, there are no sentient beings to be delivered;

and while there are no sentient beings to be delivered, one still blazes forth in delivering them. Therefore, this is called "rescue and protection," and so forth. Among the two vehicles, that which is destructible is destroyed.

If there were a characteristic of birth in the deliverance of sentient beings, this characteristic would be subject to destruction. Now, although one delivers sentient beings, there is no birth to be delivered;

thus, that which is subject to destruction is destroyed. Therefore, it is said: "destroying that which is subject to destruction. Although above one has destroyed that which is subject to destruction, the mind capable of destroying is not empty and is likewise subject to destruction.
Now, one further destroys that which is capable of destroying; thus, one is far removed from all forms of detachment.
Upon reaching this state, there is only the single True Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), which is forever indestructible; hence it is called "indestructible. This is because there are two meanings:
first, that it does not hinder the constant saving of sentient beings throughout the day; second, that once deluded attachments are dispelled, the principle naturally manifests itself.

Among the three directions, regarding the phrase "original enlightenment" (*mūla-avabodha*): when that which is superior—the destructible and the destroyer, the separable and the separator—is transcended, then the principle of original enlightenment manifests of itself, and the wisdom of primordial luminosity (*ādi-prakāśa*) reveals itself. Therefore, it is said that "original enlightenment is profoundly still.

Thus, the essence of my own awakening is equal to that of the Buddha, non-dual and undivided; hence it is said that "awakening is equal to the Buddha's awakening. That by which all Buddhas are Buddhas is solely...
Regarding this essence of awakening: since the Bodhisattva’s awakening is equal to that of the Buddha, they are therefore said to be equal to all Buddhas.
Among the four directions, the phrase "diligence" refers to the aforementioned fundamental awakening being profoundly still.

The phrase "the ground is like [the Buddha]" means that the aforementioned wisdom is like the Buddha's wisdom; now, the principle realized is likewise like that of the Buddha, and thus the ground is the Buddha-ground. It is thus.
Because the ground of practice (*bhūmi*) and the ground of fruition are inconceivably one, it is called "all places. This refers to Vairocana pervading all places.
Within the five orientations, the mention of "worlds" and so forth indicates the mutual fusion of the two preceding positions.
For "worlds" are the places reached, while the "Tathāgata" is the Buddha who is equalized with them; furthermore, the world...
The very ground is like the ground of the Buddhas. When the Tathāgata’s awakening is equal to the awakening of the Buddhas, then wisdom illuminates the object and the object illuminates wisdom.
Object and wisdom are mutually fused without mutual obstruction; subject and object are non-dual. Therefore, it is said that they are "mutually equal.
In this way, within a single pore there are immeasurable jewel-adorned lands, or within a single atom there are immeasurable [Buddhas].
Come! Its wondrous function is inconceivable, and its merit is inexhaustible; therefore, it is called the "Inexhaustible Treasury. Regarding the six directions:
as for the direction of equality, within the ground of the actual reality of original enlightenment (*mūlabodhi*), one gives rise to the mind that acts as the pure and wondrous cause.

By means of this pure and wondrous cause, one in turn realizes unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*. Thus, one knows that the former [direction] is the arising of the cause from the fruit, while this [direction] is...
Because this vehicle attains the fruit through its causes, it is said to be "simultaneous" and so forth. All such roots of goodness are without exception compliant and without exception equal;
therefore, it is called "compliant and equal. Within the seventh stage, the phrase "true roots and so forth" refers back to what preceded.
This means that when the roots of goodness of equanimity can thus accord with reality, the true root is established. When one is true, all are true;
the Buddha-mind will soon be seen, and the entire body of sentient beings will manifest before one. Therefore, the sentient beings of the ten directions are all my own original nature.
It is accomplished by its original nature; once accomplished, all are accomplished. That is to say, when one awakens, all awaken together.
Thus, the three thousand realms within the fruition are collectively termed "Eternal Bliss. Therefore, it is said that "the nature is perfect," and so forth.

In this way, one contemplates the mind, the Buddha, and sentient beings as all being in accord with equality. Hence, it is called "accordance with equality. Among the eight directions, "all are equal" refers back to the preceding two.
The former [aspect] is the manifestation based upon causes to attain the path to *nirvāṇa*, which is the departure from all marks; this is emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The latter is the perfect fulfillment of nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) that does not abandon sentient beings, which is all phenomena (*sarvadharma*);

this is the provisional (*prajñapti*). Only through "immediacy" (*ji*) is there the Middle Way (*madhyamā-pratipad*) of dual negation; this is what is advanced toward and revealed by the fundamental position. Thus, it is by means of "only immediacy" and "only departure."

Being entirely without attachment is what constitutes the "True" and the "As-it-is. Therefore, it is called the characteristic of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Ninth, regarding the section on "Truly Attaining":

this restates the preceding point that by being free from both [identity and difference], one is entirely without attachment and personally realizes True Suchness; hence it says, "truly attaining that which is as-it-is.
