Although one is free from both identity and difference, this does not preclude being simultaneously both identical and different; therefore, it says, "unimpeded throughout the ten directions. This is precisely the dual [aspect].

Illumination reveals the Middle Way; therefore, it is called "unbound liberation. In the tenth stage, the "Inherently Virtuous" phrase reiterates that the three truths are fully present as described above.

The "Dharma-realm" phrase correctly clarifies the present point: the Dharma-realm is precisely the three truths simultaneously negated and merged into a traceless state, yet without hindering the simultaneous illumination of the three truths, wherein the cultivated and the inherent are perfectly distinct. Negation and illumination occur at once. Contemplate this.
It is beyond the reach of deliberation; therefore, it is called "the extinction of measure. Only when measure is extinguished is there no measure. Thus, it is named the "Infinite Dharma Realm.
To summarize the ten kinds of dedication mentioned above, they are divided into three general categories: the first two and the seventh are directed toward sentient beings.
The third, fourth, fifth, and sixth stages are directed toward Bodhi; the eighth and ninth are directed toward True Suchness (Tathatā);

and the tenth stage is that which universally encompasses the Dharma-realm (Dharmadhātu). If one proceeds further, each of these stages possesses three meanings: turning oneself toward others, turning causes toward the fruit, and turning phenomena toward principle.
Seventh: "Ānanda, after these sons of good family have departed, they will follow their previous practices as they were undertaken and establish themselves in the noble stages.

This clarifies the text concerning the four stages of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) within the partial realization (*praveśa*). It is divided into two parts. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, it concludes the preceding section and introduces the subsequent one.
The second [section] below correctly clarifies the preparatory practice (*prayoga*). Within this, the initial portion—“All these...

and so forth—concludes the preceding [topic], while the subsequent portion—“...accomplishes... and so forth—introduces what follows. The phrase “this good son” refers to one who has accomplished the ten stages of dedication (*daśa-pratipatti*).

As for the expression “all these,” it concludes that the stage of dry wisdom (*śuklavidarśana-bhūmi*) constitutes one [unit], and the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and dedication constitute forty; when combined, they form [the total].
This is the forty-first mind. Regarding "purity": it means that because one has fully realized the nature while giving rise to cultivation, there is no longer any delusive defilement;
furthermore, through the power of subduing and severing, one eliminates the ignorance of the various stages—this constitutes purity. Regarding "added practice" (*prayoga*):

the term "added practice" applies generally to both the Great and Small Vehicles, as well as to the partial and the perfect; therefore, the term "wondrously perfect" is specifically used to distinguish it. This refers to the ten stages (*bhūmi*).
Because it is difficult to arouse [the aspiration], one further cultivates the four practices prior to the stages (*bhūmi*).

Since the principles to be realized are profound and their application is increasingly subtle, one must engage in further investigation and study before being fit to ascend to the stage of the sages; therefore, they are all designated by the name of the *bhūmis*.

Regarding the phrase "In the initial stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one uses 'equality'": this means that one takes the enlightened essence (*bodhi-tattva*) of the Buddha of the first stage (*prathamā-bhūmi*) as the causal mind for oneself.

Because one subsequently realizes the enlightened essence of the Buddha of the first stage by means of this very cause, it is called "equality. Regarding the phrase "if [the stage] has emerged or has not yet emerged":
this refers to the fact that the principle of the first stage is about to manifest, hence it is said "if emerged"; however, the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the first stage have not yet been eliminated.
Although it has been broken through, it has not yet become manifest; therefore, it is said that "it has not emerged. This is like the following analogy:

for one who drills wood to produce fire, although they have not yet obtained the fire, they perceive the sign of warmth. Although they perceive the sign of warmth, it is in reality not yet fire. It is the same with the Bodhisattva:
while the principle of the first stage (*bhūmi*) has not yet become manifest, it appears as if it were already manifest. That is to say...
Although one has already broken the delusions of the first stage (*bhūmi*), in reality they have not been broken; therefore, it is said, "it is like," etc.
It is from this metaphor that the name "Stage of Warmth" (*uṣmagata*) is derived. Regarding the second, the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdhan*):

the phrase "again by means of equality" means that previously one took the Buddha’s awakening of the first stage as the causal mind for oneself, whereas now one brings about the awakening-body of the Buddha of the first stage through one's own causal mind. Hence, it is said, "again."
This is because they are equal. As for "if it relies" or "if it does not rely," this refers to the fact that the essential substance (li-ti) of the first stage (*bhūmi*) appears as if manifest;
hence, it is said "if it relies. However, since the delusions of the first stage have not yet been destroyed, it still does not truly rely [on that substance];

hence, it is said "it does not rely. This is like the analogy of ascending a height: just as one who climbs a high mountain, although not yet having entered the void, already has their body at the mountain peak.

This is what it means for the body to enter empty space. If one says that one has already entered empty space, yet still has not left the mountain peak, this is because there remains a subtle obstruction below.
It is the same with the Bodhisattva: it is said that they have not yet manifested the principle of the first stage (bhūmi).

It appears as though it has already been manifested, meaning that the delusions of the first stage (*bhūmi*) have supposedly been shattered; however, since they have not actually been shattered, it is said to be "like ascending," etc.

Furthermore, this is merely a metaphorical designation for the "Summit Stage" (*mūrdha-bhūmi*). Regarding the phrase "the mind and the Buddha are equal" within the three stages of patience (*kṣānti*), this refers to the initial position:
taking the Buddha’s awakening of the first stage as one's own causal mind. In the subsequent position, one takes one's own causal mind as the [Buddha of] the first stage.

The Buddha awakens to the ground. Upon reaching this stage, the mind and the Buddha are mutually identical and devoid of dualistic characteristics; thus, they are certainly neither identical to the Buddha nor separate from the mind.
This may be called skillfully attaining the Middle Way. Therefore, it is said that "the mind and the Buddha are equal. The following analogy regarding patience illustrates this:
a person who practices patience toward an event, though the event exists, has no form to be grasped. This is what is meant by "non-attachment. Although it is so called...
To have patience regarding the reality of formless phenomena is not to transcend them; it is the same for the Bodhisattva.

To maintain in one’s mind that there is an initial stage of the ground of patience is the middle way; it should be understood as non-arising, just as patience toward phenomena is not a state of harboring attachment.
To maintain in one’s mind that there is no initial stage of the ground of patience is the middle way; it should be understood as...

The essence does not perish; it is like enduring that an event has not arisen. Therefore, it is said to be "equal to endurance" (*kṣānti*). It is also called the "Stage of Endurance" (*kṣānti-bhūmi*) by way of its metaphorical designation.

Within the fourth stage, the "Supreme Mundane Dharma" (*laukikāgra-dharma*), there are numerical phrases: namely, in the Stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), one takes the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind;
in the Stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), one takes one's own mind as the Buddha’s awakening; and upon reaching the Stage of Endurance, the minds and the Buddha are mutually identical.
The same applies to both; they all possess numerical figures and finite limits. As for this stage, it is not only non-mind—it is neither Buddha nor mind.
Since mind and Buddha are identical, there are no longer numbers or measures; how could there be finite limits? Therefore, it is said that "numbers and quantities are extinguished.

The phrase "delusion and awakening are equal" explains the reason why numbers and quantities vanish. In the stages of *uṣmagata* (Warmth) and *mūrdhan* (Summit), one regards the Buddha’s awakening as one's own mind. One...
To take one’s own mind as the Buddha’s awakening is to be deluded regarding the Middle Way. In the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*), the mind and the Buddha are identical and lack dual characteristics;
this is to have awakened to the Middle Way. This is precisely that which has number and measure, yet is not extinguished by number and measure;
hence it is said that one is deluded regarding the Middle Way of awakening. Only in this stage can it truly not be said that [there is] "mind" and "Buddha."
"Identity" (*ji*) and "separation" (*li*) are likewise not to be called the dual separation of mind and Buddha; between identity and separation, there are no names or designations.
Therefore, it is said that "the two have nothing to be designated. Being thus, it is the most honored and most noble; hence, it is named the "Supreme of the World" (*lokāgra*).

Regarding the "Supreme Worldly Dharma" (*laukikāgradharma*): in the *Āgama* teachings, it is that which is about to destroy the delusions of views (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) and is about to reveal the partial truth (*pratyeka-satya*).

This is the Supreme Worldly Dharma. Herein, that which is about to ascend to the First Ground (*bhūmi*) is considered supramundane (*lokottara*), while that prior to the Grounds is merely mundane (*laukika*).

These four stages are distinguished by means of the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*): on the stage of Heat (*uṣmagata*), it is "the Buddha is the mind"; on the stage of Summits (*mūrdhan*), it is "the mind is the Buddha"; on the stage of Patience (*kṣānti*)...

"Mind itself is Buddha. "The Stage of Supreme Worldly Dharma (laukikāgra-dharma) is neither mind nor Buddha. Some say that this refers to the ordinary person within the teachings of the Four Preparatory Practices (catvāraḥ prayogāḥ).

However, since this sutra is of the Perfect and Sudden (yuan-dun) teaching and furthermore occurs after the Ten Stages of Dedication (daśa-pratipatti), how could there be a name for an ordinary person within the Tripitaka?
What they fail to realize is that although this sutra is indeed Perfect and Sudden, all its terminology is entirely borrowed from the Three [Vehicles].

The Teaching [Vehicle]. The four kinds of preparatory practice (*prayoga*) constitute the stages of the *pitaka* teaching. Now, the preparatory practices involving effort prior to the [first] stage (*bhūmi*) are also listed as four stages;

this is to clarify the meaning of the Perfect [Teaching] by borrowing from the *pitaka*. For example, the aforementioned Stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi*) is a stage of the Shared Teaching (*sādhāraṇa-śāsana*).

It is now opened up and listed prior to the [first] stage, meaning that one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s stream of Dharma, and the habit-energy of desire is beginning to dry up; this is to clarify the Perfect [Teaching] by borrowing from the Shared [Teaching].

This is the intended meaning. Regarding the stages of faith, abiding, practice, and direction (*śraddhā-vihāra-pratipatti-mukha*), there is both sequential arrangement (*pratipatti*) and perfect interpenetration (*pariniṣpanna-yoga*), and within this perfect interpenetration and sequential arrangement, although the beginning and end are non-dual, one advances vertically through each stage. This appears no different from the Separate Teaching (*pratyeka-śāsana*).

Thus, the intent here is to clarify the Perfect Teaching (*pariniṣpanna-śāsana*) by borrowing from the Separate Teaching. For this reason, the stages and positions herein differ from those in scriptures such as the *Ratnaketu-paripṛcchā* (Renwang jing) and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*.
Recently, I have seen those who claim that one is immediately a Buddha at this very moment, with no further distinctions of stages or positions, yet still say that each stage is different.

How can this be considered the Perfect and Complete Teaching? Alas! When discussing various principles, beginning and end are equal; when speaking of the various teachings, cause and effect are clearly distinct.
Who would say that the Perfect Teaching has no stages or degrees of depth? It is simply that while the names are borrowed for the sake of manifestation...

The meaning is perfectly complete. This refers to what is called "borrowing names without employing their meanings. Generally speaking, this concludes the answer to the question, "What is meant by the forty-four minds of dry wisdom?
From the passage beginning with "Ānanda, these good sons... onwards, it also follows the previous discussion on the stages established according to the practices they undertake.

This is the passage concerning the ten stages (*bhūmi*) within the section on partial realization through clarity. As for what is called a "stage" (*bhūmi*): a stage takes solidity as its essence and production as its function.
From the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuṣka-prajñā*) onward, the various practices and dharmas cultivated are all in accord with the fundamental nature.

There is nothing that is not ultimately firm and solid until it reaches the state of perfected reality (*bhūtatā*). All Buddha-dharmas and all merits arise from this; therefore, it is called a "ground" (*bhūmi*).

If discussed in a general sense, the first ground is the cause and wondrous enlightenment is the fruit. However, if one investigates further, each ground serves as both the cause for the subsequent grounds and the fruit of the preceding grounds.
Moreover, this is not limited to this alone; from the initial stage of abiding (*prathamavihāra*) onwards, every position functions in this manner.
Regarding the stages of cause and fruit: the beginning is the cause, the culmination is the fruit, and the intermediate successive stages are both cause and fruit.
Within the first stage (*bhūmi*), "good son" refers to a bodhisattva who, following the ten stages of dedication (*pariṇāmanā*), is capable of practicing the four preparatory conducts (*prayoga*).
Regarding the phrase "in the great," etc.: Bodhi is the essence of the merit of wisdom; it is the three truths, inconceivable, which only Buddhas and Buddhas can realize.
Upon reaching this stage, one is also able to penetrate without obstruction and reach through without hindrance;
thus it is said, "in the great," etc. As for the term "well-attained": by adding four practices to the ten dedications, one proceeds from this point with ease.
This is because they flow into the ocean of *sarvajñā* (all-knowledge). Thus, their wisdom is identical to the Buddha’s wisdom;

therefore, it is said that "their awakening penetrates that of the Tathāgata," because they have thoroughly realized the wisdom of the fruit of Great Bodhi. Their principle is identical to the Buddha’s principle;

therefore, it is said that "they exhaust the realm and fruit of the Buddha," because they have thoroughly realized the essential substance of the principle of Great Bodhi. As for the term "exhaust" (*jin*), it means that by means of the One, one attains [it all].
This is because of all [the stages]. That which was expected by the initial resolve—this principle of wisdom—is now finally entered, and one’s joy is inexhaustible;
therefore, it is named "Joy" (Pramuditā). Because one is able to personally bear the burden of all sentient beings and accomplish all wholesome dharmas, it is called a "ground" (bhūmi).

The meaning of "ground" for the subsequent stages can be understood by analogy with this. Within the second ground, the phrase "different nature" refers to the preceding ground, while "same nature" [refers to the current one].

The phrase "clarifying the present" means this. Regarding what is called "different nature": as previously stated, regarding one's own mind and the Buddha’s awakening, they are termed "different nature.

That mind and Buddha are non-dual is termed "same nature. When the distinctions between mind, Buddha, and their non-duality have dissolved, and duality has no further referent—such that awakening penetrates the Tathāgata and reaches the ultimate fruit of the Buddha-realm—this is termed "entering sameness. It is by arriving at this state that one comes here.

When both the mind of oneself and the mind of the Buddha do not establish as two distinct fruits, and even that "non-duality" has nothing by which it can be designated, one reaches the first stage (*bhūmi*).
At this point, awakening, its essence, and even the state of joy (*pramuditā*) are all unattainable; therefore, it is said that "even the common nature is extinguished."
Thus, within the ground of the principle of the *tathatā* (suchness), difference is inherently a defilement; sameness is also a defilement;
and the absence of any designation for both sameness and difference is likewise a defilement. Precisely because there is still the presence of joy (*prāmodya*), it remains a defilement.
Now, since even this sameness has been extinguished and completely eliminated, it is called the "Stainless Ground" (*vimalā-bhūmi*). Within the third ground, [there is] tranquility...
Regarding "the arising of extreme clarity": previously, one has merely departed from defilement, but has not yet reached the departure from that departure.

Now, even this departure from defilement is further transcended; this constitutes the ultimate stillness. From this true awakening, clarity becomes increasingly manifest; this is the "arising of clarity.

It is like an ancient mirror which, after being freed from dust, is further polished until it is still and clarity arises. This is what is meant by "when stillness reaches its ultimate, light penetrates through."
Therefore, it is named the Ground of Radiant Light (*prabhākari-bhūmi*). Regarding "the light is supreme" within the fourth ground, this refers back to the arising of light mentioned previously.

That is to say, in the preceding stage, it was like a fire that has just begun to burn, its radiance not yet full; here, however, it is like a fire blazing intensely, becoming a great and fierce mass of light.

It accords with the nature of awakening; therefore, it is called "fulfillment of awakening. What is meant is that its quiescent illumination encompasses empty space; hence it is named the Ground of Blazing Wisdom (*Arciṣmatī-bhūmi*).

"Blazing Wisdom" is spoken of by combining both the dharma and its metaphor. Among the five grounds, "all things being equal" refers to the Joyous Ground (*Pramuditā*), which is free from heterogeneity;

the Stainless Ground (*Vimalā*), which is free from homogeneity; the Radiant Ground (*Prabhākārī*), which advances from stillness toward clarity; and the Blazing Wisdom Ground, which proceeds from clarity [toward radiance].
[It is] fulfilled. When one reaches this stage, the aforementioned similarities and differences have long since been distanced and are utterly beyond reach;
hence it is said that "all are equal. Since nothing can reach it, it transcends all, and nothing can transcend it;
therefore, it is named the "Difficult-to-Conquer" (Sudurjayā) bhūmi. Regarding "equality with the unconditioned" (asaṃskṛta-samatā): as for all [the preceding stages], since they... [are not so].
One is able to reach it. Only the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) essence of true suchness (*tathatā*) is revealed in its absolute solitude; hence it is called "unconditioned," and so forth.
Because this true suchness is revealed in its solitude, it is named the Ground of Manifestation (*Abhimukhī-bhūmi*).

Regarding the seventh ground, "reaching the limit of the extent of true suchness": previously, true suchness had already manifested; now, wisdom pervades according to the object, and practice encompasses the entirety of the essence, reaching its very boundaries.

Therefore, it is said that one reaches the limit of true suchness (*tathatā*). Since this practice accords with the essence and pervades the entire limit of true suchness, it is called the Ground of Far-Going (*dūramgamā-bhūmi*).

Regarding the "one mind of true suchness" within the eighth ground: after the nature of true suchness has been revealed, one further exhausts it through the practice of far-going until, upon reaching this stage, there remains only the wondrous mind of true suchness—namely, the fundamental body and the vessel-world.

Throughout the realms, within a single body, and even in a single hair-pore, all are *tathatā* (Suchness). Because they penetrate to the very source of all phenomena, it is called the "one mind of *tathatā*.
Since all functional activities arising from this are entirely unmoving and indestructible, it is named the "Immovable Ground" (*acalā-bhūmi*).

Within the ninth ground, the manifestation of true [enlightenment] clarifies the fundamental stage. Ānanda and others summarize the preceding and reveal the subsequent. Regarding the beginning, there is the manifestation of *tathatā*.
Regarding "function" (*yòng*): it is the essence of the true, immovable principle; that very essence of the principle gives rise to the function of wisdom.

Because this entire wisdom illuminates objects and this entire object gives rise to wisdom, every point is transparently clear and free from obstruction; hence it is called the Stage of Excellent Wisdom (*Sādhumatī-bhūmi*).

Regarding the phrase "these various [stages]" in the middle section: there are differing opinions. Some maintain that it should be placed below the Stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samalaṃkāra-bhūmi*). However...

Regarding the citation of the five stages of Vijñaptimātratā as proof: in the system of Vijñaptimātratā, the thirty minds prior to the [ten] bhūmis are called the stage of equipment (sambhāra-avasthā).

The four preparatory practices are called the stage of application (prayoga-avasthā). Ascending to the first bhūmi is called the stage of penetration (prativedha-avasthā). From the second bhūmi upward is called the stage of cultivation (bhāvanā-avasthā).

Only the state of wondrous enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) is called the ultimate stage (niṣṭhā-avasthā). Alternatively, it may refer only to the four preparatory practices up to the ninth bhūmi; that is to say, the former...
This concludes the forty-one minds in total. This [text] merely uses the four [stages] to manifest the stage of cultivation (*bhāvanā-avasthā*) as a concluding summary.
Alternatively, some take the word "these" (*śeṣa* or *ete*) to mean that it does not only refer to those from the nine stages downward, but extends to refer to the higher stages as well.

All of these [interpretations] fail to recognize that this is a conclusion of what preceded and a manifestation of what follows. The intended meaning is: "These aforementioned Bodhisattvas, from this point onward..."
Because there is no further cultivation, it is said that "cultivation has reached its completion. Because the merit thus obtained is ultimately accomplished, it is said that "merit is perfected.
This reveals what follows. It is not only what preceded it that constitutes cultivation; this ninth stage (*bhūmi*) is also cultivation.
Therefore, it says, "and also refers to," which concludes what has gone before. For "cultivation" (*bhāvanā*) means the act of learning and practicing. As [for example...]
When a person studies an art and has not yet mastered it, they practice until it is perfected. Once perfected, they employ the art directly without further practice or study.

This is also like that: from the stage of an ordinary person practicing to enter the stage of Dry Wisdom (śuklavidarśana), through practicing faith, understanding, conduct, vows, and the stages of effortful and effortless cultivation up to this ground, one proceeds from essence to function; this is what is meant by "having completed the cultivation."

[The stage of] fulfillment. Thereafter, one merely severs hindrances and benefits sentient beings, extensively performing the Buddha-activities; though it is called "cultivation," it is not [ordinary] cultivation.

Within the ten stages, the phrase "the cloud-shade of compassion" (*maitrī-chāyā*) manifests both the dharma and its metaphor. For "compassion" refers to the great pity (*mahākaruṇā*) of the Bodhisattva, and "cloud-shade" is used to capture its characteristic of vast moisture.
"Subtlety" (*miao*) refers to the great wisdom (*mahājñāna*) of the Bodhisattva, and is like a cloud... [is used to capture its characteristic].
Regarding the meaning of its universal pervasiveness: this serves as the covering, while the ocean of *nirvāṇa* is that which is covered—the innate, fundamental nature and virtue of sentient beings.
That is to say, it is primordially quiescent and does not undergo further extinction.

Now, having completed their cultivation and perfected both compassion and wisdom, Bodhisattvas exist solely for the benefit of others; thus, with the canopy of great kindness and the clouds of wondrous wisdom, they universally...
It covers the originally existing nirvāṇa of sentient beings, uprooting inherent suffering and revealing inherent bliss. As for the title "Dharmamegha" (Cloud of Dharma):
the single character "Dharma" encompasses both compassion and wisdom; "Cloud" refers to the inclusion of the aggregates (*skandhas*).
Within each and every moment, each and every mark, each and every excellence, and each and every pore, it rains down immeasurable and boundless dharma-rain, sufficing all as if like [the ocean].
The *skandhas* are like clouds. Regarding *nirvāṇa* as an ocean, it is intended to convey the sense of its encompassing the hundred rivers and reflecting them infinitely.
Taken together, this answers the question of where one must go to be said to have "entered the stages" (*bhūmi*). Thus concludes [the section on] entering the stages.

The ninth section, "The Tathāgatas Return Against the Stream," also follows the preceding [section] on establishing the stages of the noble ones according to their respective practices; it is the passage clarifying the partial realization of Middle Enlightenment (*madhyama-abhisambodhi*). It consists of two parts:

first, the clarification of the fundamental stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*), beginning with the words "The Tathāgatas, etc. *Note: The term "Middle Enlightenment" (中等覺) refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*Samyaksambodhi*) within the ten stages of Bodhisattvahood, specifically the tenth stage, where one is equal to a Buddha in all respects except for the final, ultimate transformation.*
Second, explaining the Vajra Dry Wisdom (*vajra-śuṣka-prajñā*). This refers to Ānanda and the others. Regarding the beginning:

the term "flow" (*liú*) in the phrase "the Tathāgata flows against the current" (*rúlái nǐliú*) specifically points to the ocean of the fruit of wondrous enlightenment (*mìojiào guǒhǎi*), namely, the flow of *nirvāṇa*.

Since the Tathāgata has already realized wondrous enlightenment, yet does not abandon sentient beings, he steers the compassionate vessel in reverse and emerges by flowing against the current; hence it is said, "the Tathāgata flows against the current. As for the Bodhisattvas...
One proceeds toward the ocean of fruition, correctly grasping it to flow along with the current; thus it is said, "and so forth.

When the Tathāgata has just entered and is about to emerge, and the Bodhisattva is about to enter but has not yet entered—at this precise point of intersection between emergence and entry—the two awakenings, the initial and the fundamental, are equal and non-dual.
Therefore, it is said that because the limits of awakening intersect, it is named Equal Awakening (*samyaksambodhi*).

Next, within this section, from the stage of "dry wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) onwards, there is a summary of all the preceding stages. This "Awakened One" (*buddha*) refers to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samya-saṃbodhi*).

"First attaining the diamond-mind" (*vajra-citta*) refers to the final mind following Equal Enlightenment. It severs the last remaining grade of the ignorance of the "mark of arising" (*utpatti-nimitta-avidyā*).
This ignorance is the most difficult to sever; it is like a substance in the world that is so hard and solid that only gold [can cut it].

Only that which is adamantine can destroy it. As for the characteristic of arising—ignorance—it is only the final mind (*paścima-citta*) that can sever it. Because both the dharma and the metaphor are presented together, it is called the "Adamantine Mind" (*vajra-citta*).
Whenever one enters a stage, there must necessarily be three minds: the initial mind at the moment of entry, the central mind once entered, and the final mind as one is about to exit.
This [final mind] is when one is about to exit Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) and enter Sublime Enlightenment (*tathāgata-bhūmi*); it is therefore called the "final" [mind].
"Mind-Ear. Regarding the "initial Dry Wisdom within the Vajra Mind": it refers to the initial drying up of the ignorance of the marks of arising (*utpatti-nimitta-avidyā*).
Because it has not yet connected with the ultimate flow of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-water, it receives the name "Dry Wisdom. Wēnlíng separately establishes this as a distinct stage;

however, according to the text which states, "this is what is first attained through awakening," we know that this Vajra Dry Wisdom is attained within the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
This is clear. Furthermore, the *Sūtra of the Necklace* states that within the nature of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*) there is a wisdom named Vajradhvaja.
How could one then claim that this is something distinct from it? Since it says "only now attained," we know that upon reaching Equal Enlightenment, one again gives rise to the Vajra-mind.

Having again traversed the various stages and shattered the shadows of conditioned objects, one has already entered wondrous enlightenment (*miao-jue*); therefore, it is undoubtedly the final mind of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-sambodhi*).
Thus, the fact that both the preceding and the present [stages] are called "Dry Wisdom" (*gāndhī*) and "the First" each carries two meanings.

Regarding why both the preceding and the subsequent are named Dry Wisdom: as for the Dry Wisdom of the preceding stage, it refers to the complete subduing of the afflictions of the five abodes; because they are subdued...
It does not arise; therefore, it is called "dry" (*khan*). Because it has not yet encountered the water of principle within the stage of semblance, it is called "Dry Wisdom.
Furthermore, as for this Dry Wisdom herein, it completely severs the afflictions of the five abodes; because they are severed and do not arise, it is called Dry Wisdom.
Moreover, because it has not yet encountered the water of principle within the ultimate stage, it is also called Dry Wisdom. This is because the former [stage] was already... [complete].
"Subduing without anything to be subdued" refers to subduing the five stages of dwelling (*pañca-vihāra*) that are to be severed.

This is the "perfect severance," wherein there is nothing to be severed, yet one severs the five stages of dwelling that were previously subdued. Thus, although the preceding and succeeding stages differ in their depth, both are identical in terms of subduing and severing.
Therefore, all are given the name "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*). Regarding the fact that both the preceding and subsequent instances of Dry Wisdom are called "the first":

the former refers to the initial drying up of the habit-energies of desire once the five abodes have been completely suppressed through Perfect [Contemplation]; the latter refers to the initial drying up of the phase of birth once the five abodes have been completely severed through Perfect [Contemplation].
Thus, one should know that the "first" of the former is spoken in relation to the Ten Faiths, whereas the "first" of the latter is spoken in relation to Sublime Enlightenment (*miao-jue*).

He said: "Furthermore, the ultimate state and the initial mind are non-dual in their sequence. For example, when Sudhana first received the inspiration of faith through Mañjuśrī, he saw Mañjuśrī again upon reaching the stage of Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), being exhorted by him to give rise to faith once more. This reveals that the single mind of the beginning and the end has its cause and effect mutually penetrating.

In this way, the relationship between the final mind of the Vajra [stage] and the initial Stage of Dry Wisdom (śuṣka-prajñā-bhūmi) becomes even clearer. What further use is there [for other teachings]?"

Is this not establishing a separate stage? Question: It can be understood that the "Dry Wisdom" (*śuṣka-prajñā*) mentioned previously refers to when the habitual tendencies of desire are completely subdued and their seeds are first dried up, yet one has not yet connected with the Tathāgata’s flow of Dharma. Now, however, one completely cuts off the ignorance of the *saja* (birth) phase;
how could one still be called "Dry Wisdom" if one has not yet connected with the Ocean of Wondrous Adornment? Answer: The "Vajra Dry Wisdom" simply exhausts the ignorance of the *saja* phase.
This is merely the initial stage. However, as one has not yet attained the rank of Wondrous Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi), it may also be said that [the ultimate goal] has not yet been reached.
The above concludes the response to the question: "What is meant by the Bodhisattva of Equal Enlightenment (samanvāgata-bodhisattva)?"

The ten [stages] proceed thus in successive layers. This also follows the preceding section on establishing the stages of sagehood according to the practices undertaken, serving as the text that clarifies the ultimate identity with wondrous enlightenment (*miàojué*).
"Successive layers" refers to the various preceding stages. Regarding the "twelve single and double":

this is based on the names of the single [stages], which are eleven, and the names of the ten [stages], which are twelve. There are seven single [stages]: the stage of dry wisdom (*gānhuì*) and the four stages of applied practice (*jiāxíng*).

This refers to Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Furthermore, there are the ten faiths, ten abidings, ten practices, ten transferences, and ten stages (*bhūmi*); taken together, these constitute twelve.
Regarding the phrase "repeatedly single and multiple," it refers to the "single" stage of the three gradual sequences and the stage of dry wisdom (*śuṣka-jñāna*).
Furthermore, the complex of faith, abiding, practice, and orientation is advanced to the simple of the four preparatory practices (*prayoga*).

Again, the simple of the four preparatory practices is advanced to the complex of the ten stages (*bhūmi*). And again, the complex of the ten stages is advanced to the simple of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*).
Therefore, it is said that there are twelve instances of "repeatedly alternating between the simple and the complex. Thus is it explained.

Commentary: The twelve [stages] naturally possess their own twelve; the simple and the complex naturally possess their own simplicity and complexity; the layers upon layers naturally possess their own layering. There is no need for forced effort.
Why trouble various schools by each putting forth their own views? Some combine *kandhī* (dry wisdom) through to *samyaksambodhi* (equal enlightenment) to constitute the twelve.
Others take faith, practice, abiding, and the stages (*bhūmi*) as the "simple," and the ten transferences as the "complex. Still others take *kandhī*, *uṣmagata* (warmth), and *mūrdhan* (summit)...

The "Patience" (kṣānti) stage, the "World-First Dharma" (laukikāgradharma), and the "Equal and Sublime" (samyaktva-saṃkalana) constitute the "single seven. Faith, abiding, practice, direction, and the stages (bhūmi) constitute the "double ten.

Let us examine this by means of the text. Regarding the ten faiths, the ten abidings, and so forth: if they are single, they are all single; if they are double, they are all double. How could some be single and others double? Furthermore, the text states:
"In this way, through the successive layers of the single and the double—twelve in total—one finally exhausts the wondrous enlightenment (miao-jue). Thus...

The twelve [links of dependent origination] constitute the cause, and wondrous enlightenment constitutes the fruit. Furthermore, how could one take the fruit as the cause and thereby erroneously establish the doctrine of the "single seven"?
If this were so, then the three gradual stages would be taken as a horizontal encompassing of all positions, with the "vajra-like mind" (*vajropamasamādhi*) subsequently opened up separately;
this would be a near-perfect progression. This is precisely the summit of the Mountain of Nirvāṇa, where one forever parts from the parents of ignorance.

All dharmas are unarisen; Prajñā is unarisen; non-arising is itself unarisen. Taking emptiness as one’s seat, one accomplishes the fruit-stage of the most honored, most supreme, and wondrously awakened pure Dharma-body.

Therefore, it is said that they are "equal. This concludes the preceding section, which, by means of returning to the true from the delusive, clarifies the attainment of the fruit of the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) across the sixty stages of the sages.

The second section concludes from this point with the passage beginning "From these various stages. This is the text that summarizes and clarifies [the preceding]. It is divided into three parts: first, the summary of the cultivation of contemplation, beginning with "These various...

and so forth; second, the summary of the gradual progression, beginning with "Ānanda... and so forth; third, the summary of the heterodox and the orthodox, beginning with "Acting thus... and so forth. Regarding the first part: as for "These various...
and so forth, it is a general conclusion stating that the merit of all the stages arises from the three contemplations. Indeed, all the stages are the objects...

The "passing through" (li) refers to the three contemplations acting as the means of passage. Furthermore, this concluding clarification ensures that those who enter the practice do not skip over stages;
these various grounds collectively encompass all positions. Regarding the "Vajra" and so forth:

because the practitioner requested the sublime *śamatha* and the other three contemplations, the Tathāgata first employed the mind, the six sense-bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), and the seven elements (*mahābhūta*) to open up understanding for the practitioner. Next, then...

Based on the two meanings of definitive determination and the perfect penetration of the faculty of hearing, the practice suited to the capacities of the audience is initiated; this leads us to the present section.
Based on the mutual reversal of delusion and awakening, the fifty-five stages are extensively set forth so that the audience may know what is to be realized and entered.

Although the three factors of understanding, practice, and realization differ, they are collectively not apart from the three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*). For "understanding" consists in awakening to these three.

It is contemplation (*vipaśyanā*). The practitioner cultivates these three contemplations, and their realization likewise occurs through these three contemplations; thus it is said that "all are by means of [these].
Because not even a single speck of dust can be established before one's eyes amidst the myriad dharmas, it is called "Vajra Contemplation.
Because not even a single speck of dust is established while the myriad dharmas stand forth in full array, it is called the "Ten Profound Similes of Illusion. These ten profound...
Regarding the metaphors: as another sutra states, they are like an illusion, a mirage, flowers in the sky, the moon in water, and so forth—ten in total.
These are elucidated in the Mahayana; therefore, they are called "profound metaphors. Śamatha is cessation (zhi), and vipaśyanā is contemplation (guan).
To speak of "śamatha and so forth" means that within cessation there is contemplation, and within contemplation there is cessation; it excludes [the notion of them being separate].
Illuminating non-duality, where emptiness and existence are one as they have always been, is thus called *śamatha* and so forth.
As for "employing all Tathāgatas," it is because this is the bodhi attained through the practice of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.

Thus, one knows that the adamantine observation (*vajra-vipaśyanā*) is the inconceivable true emptiness of *śamatha*. The ten kinds of profound metaphors, such as the illusion-like, are the inconceivable *samādhi*.
This is the wondrous provisional [aspect]. Śamatha and so forth are the inconceivable perfect middle of dhyāna.
As previously stated, this is called the "Wondrous Lotus, Vajra-King, Jewel-Awakening, Illusion-like Samādhi.
It is also proclaimed as the "Vajra-King, Illusion-like, Inconceivable Buddha-Mother True Samādhi. This is applied at each stage.
One practices in such a way that there is nothing to be practiced; practice arises entirely from the fundamental nature (*xing*), and this is the perfected meaning of practice.

One employs this at every stage to realize it, yet there is nothing to be realized; practice is dissolved back into the nature, and this is the perfected meaning of realization. This constitutes pure cultivation and realization.

From this point, proceeding from the beginning to the end and from the lower to the higher, one practices circular contemplation and circular illumination, breaking through and revealing [the stages] until they are fully exhausted.

This constitutes the gradual and profound entry. One should know that all of these are directly penetrated by the two characters [of the Pure Phrase], meaning that all fifty-five stages are cultivated and realized through the three contemplations. Regarding these two [contemplations], as it says:

These [concluding remarks] likewise serve as a general summary of the beginning and end, attributing all merit to the initial stage of the three gradual processes. This is what is meant by the saying:

"In building a mountain nine fathoms high, one must not forget the first basket of earth. It means that although a practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching has reached the ultimate fruit through the causes, their setting out and advancement must revere the original resolve.
Therefore, it is reiterated with solemnity to show that all fifty-five stages arise from this.
This is the power of the three gradual advancements. Therefore, as it was previously stated: "From this, one gradually practices;

according to what is enacted, one establishes the stages of the sages," we know that the three gradual advancements are the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) that enable advancement, while the fifty-five [stages] are that which is advanced and accomplished.
Within these three, the phrase "acting in such a manner" and so forth simultaneously indicates both the false and the correct, so that one may understand them.
Discrimination: This distinguishes improper and deviant cultivation that results in the states of external paths, celestial Māras, or the partial and small vehicles.
Beginning from the gradual stages and culminating in Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), at every level one employs the three—such as adamantine observation—as the means of progression.
Thus, delusions are severed from this, and principle is realized from this; this is called "right contemplation. To act contrary to this is "deviant contemplation. Furthermore, there is...
There are two points of intent. First, it means that the fifty-five stages of the true path to Bodhi are all entered through three progressive increases;
this constitutes correct contemplation (*samyag-darśana*). Anything outside of this is erroneous contemplation. Second, one should know that Bodhi is not attained through gradual succession.
One gradually attains bodhi. This is like space, which has no measurement; yet one measures space with a ruler.
In this way, bodhi is itself gradual, and the gradual is itself bodhi. Furthermore, there are six kinds of conceit regarding non-arising.

Those at the sixth stage do not give rise to despondency; yet, if one negates the stages and grounds and adheres exclusively to abstract principle, this is what Yongjia meant by saying that practicing without relying on the stages belongs entirely to the realm of Māra and external paths.
Thus, it is said, "to act in such a manner," which is precisely the intent behind the critiques found in the Vaipulya sutras.
From the time Mañjuśrī departed until this point, the fourth section concludes with the text titled "Ultimate Solidity.

Previously, for the sake of Ānanda and the others, the ultimate principle of solidity was clarified to open the way for perfect contemplation; the practice of ultimate solidity was demonstrated to initiate perfect cultivation;
and the realization of ultimate solidity was revealed to enter into perfect verification. Thus, the Tathāgata has explained each point in exhaustive detail.
This is a detailed explanation. The function of this single scripture is thus complete and exhaustive. However, these three [aspects] are what are explained by it;
therefore, this single scripture is that which explains those three. Since that which is explained is preeminent, that which explains it is likewise honored.
Furthermore, names are the guests of reality, while reality is the host of names. Now that there exists the reality of this ten-fascicle distinct text, [the name is established].
It is fitting that there be no general title for this entire scripture; hence the question as to what it should be called.

Nevertheless, the reason the names of the sutras must necessarily rely upon Mañjuśrī is truly because, in principle, the three truths are fully contained within a single mind; in practice, the three contemplations are cultivated within a single mind;
and in realization, the three virtues are attained within a single mind. This is what is meant by "subtle, wondrous, perfectly interfused, ultimate, and firm."

Truly, were it not for one of great wisdom and great virtue, there would ultimately be no means by which to define names and summon the essence to serve as the guiding framework for doctrine and practice.
Therefore, Mañjuśrī presided over these matters from beginning to end: first, he led the assembly to receive offerings; next, he went to provide protection with mantras;
thereafter, he requested an inquiry into the nature of the realization of reality; and subsequently, he selected the faculty of the ear as the most perfect path. Now...
Furthermore, he requested that the title of the sutra be finalized, for it is said that "only through wisdom can one enter the great ocean of the Buddha-dharma.

According to the subsequent detailed investigation of the seven destinies and the thorough analysis of the five aggregates, the main body of the teaching (the *zhengzong*) therein was not yet concluded. Why, then, was the title finalized at this point?

It is because the initial revelation of the secret cause (*miyin*), followed by the opening of the path of cultivation and realization (*xiuzheng*), culminating finally in the ultimate fruit (*jiuguo*), completes the correct course of the sutra. Therefore...

This question is titled "Establishing the Previous Section of the Teaching. Although there are various elucidations in the subsequent text, they all generally fall between the two pillars of practice and realization, being merely their residual traces. Therefore, what follows serves as an aid to the Path.

The text is divided into two parts: first, from "At that time" onwards, is the question; second, from "The Buddha said" onwards, is the answer. The initial question is further divided into two: first, the question regarding the Sūtra.
Title: Two Questions on Upholding the Dharma. In the first question, the phrase "what should it be? implies that for every specific text there must be a general title for that scripture.

This means that the specific has nothing to distinguish itself apart from the general, which serves as its specific; and the general has nothing to encompass apart from the specific, which serves as its general.
It is the process of branching the general into the specific and gathering the specific to form the general. Furthermore, the meaning of a title is distinct [from the text].
There are many [explanations], yet if we cite the most essential, they do not exceed five layers of profound meaning (*xuan-yi*).

Only when one can name it can one know what its essence (*ti*) is, what its principle (*zong*) is, what its function (*yong*) is, and furthermore, what its doctrinal characteristics (*jiao-xiang*) are.
Therefore, it is asked: "What should this sutra be named? Yet, it is not yet known how to receive and uphold this sutra.
As for the method, he asks: "I and others as well. In the response, the Buddha tells him the name of the sūtra: "You should uphold this sūtra by its title.
This response contains five aspects, which are explained in sequence. First, regarding the phrase "this sūtra" and so forth:
this derives its name entirely from the divine mantra, and its meaning encompasses the essence, the doctrine, and the function. *Siddha...* [The text continues with the mantra.]
"Many *tālaras*": this is the general designation for divine mantras. Because they are spoken from within the Great Buddha-Crown (*uṣṇīṣa*), they are called "Unsurpassed.

Because they can distinguish between demons and outsiders, they are called the "Precious Seal. Because all Buddhas of the three periods of time have, without exception, relied upon these to shatter all deluded thoughts and penetrate the illumination of all phenomena, they are called the "Pure Sea-Eye. This is because Ānanda was listening to the Dharma with his conditioned mind.
When one arouses the mind based on perceived appearances, one has not yet escaped being turned by sounds and forms. Within the light of the Tathāgata, transformation-buddhas appear;

these transformation-buddhas preach mantras to rescue and protect them. When they return to the presence of the Buddha, they immediately request from the Tathāgatas of the ten directions the sublime *śamatha* for attaining bodhi, and so forth.
The Tathāgata replies that there is a samādhi called the Great Buddha-Crown, which [pervades] the ten directions.

The Tathāgata’s path of wondrous adornment transcends all other gates. From this point on, it explains cultivation and realization, shatters the false to reveal the true, beginning with the causal mind and culminating in the ultimate fruit.
It involves the dual cultivation of the Exoteric and Esoteric, wherein both the essence and the doctrine are fully revealed. Therefore, it concludes as follows:
This sutra is titled *The Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa, the Supreme Jewel Seal*. This indicates that the esoteric is manifest.

"The Pure Ocean-Eye of the Tathāgatas of the Ten Directions" indicates that the esoteric is the manifest. Within this single title alone, the great purport of the entire scripture is fully and exhaustively expressed.
Furthermore, as for the title "Saving and Protecting One’s Kinsmen and Causes," it is named by employing the seal to accord with the essence of the principle.
The first phrase provides a general heading. Ānanda was the Buddha’s younger cousin and his attendant, and thus [the relationship] was intimate;

the bhikṣuṇī Śīlabhadrikā initiated the teaching through the use of erotic arts, and thus it served as the cause. Regarding the word "protect": this refers to the command for Mañjuśrī to take the dhāraṇī and go to protect them, and so forth.
The section beginning with "deliverance" clarifies the intimacy and the cause. What is meant by "deliverance"? It is that which causes Ānanda and Aṅgā to attain...
This refers to the bodhicitta that enters the ocean of universal knowledge (*sarvajñatā*). Bodhicitta is the true cause that is neither born nor extinguished;

the ocean of universal knowledge is the ocean of the fruit of perfect, universal awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Ānanda previously sought the fruit of permanence with a mind subject to birth and extinction;
now the Buddha reveals this so that the name and designation of the causal-ground mind may accord with the awakening of the fruition-ground.

This is because they are mutually consistent. Now, "deliverance" (tāraka) refers to the extinction of evil; "attaining the bodhicitta and entering the ocean of universal knowledge" refers to the generation of good.
Since the functional power (*vṛtti*) is thus manifested, the essence (*tattva*) and the fundamental principle (*mūla*) are thereby established.

Regarding the third point, that it is also called "Tathāgata," etc., this is a designation derived from its essence, fundamental principle, functional power, and the characteristics of the teaching (*śāsana-lakṣaṇa*). "Causes" refers to the two causes of the Exoteric and Esoteric [teachings]. "Divine mantra" (*mantra*)...

Taking the secret as the cause: the Great Samādhi takes the subtle and wondrous as its secret. By relying on this for practice, one enters the flow of the Dharma-nature through the three contemplations within a single mind.
By relying on this to realize the fruit, one attains sudden enlightenment in *dhyāna*, advances through the stages of sainthood, and reaches the perfection of Bodhi in non-attainment.
Thus, the cultivation of nature, cause, and effect are each perfectly complete. One who can expound this must investigate it thoroughly.
This concludes the explanation of the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*). Fourth, as for the statement that it is also called "Great Vaipulya" (*Mahāvaipulya*):

this name is derived by combining its essence (*svabhāva*), doctrine (*artha*), and function (*prayojana*). "Great, Square, and Vast" (*Mahā-vai-pu-lya*) refers to the Dharma. "Great" signifies permanence and omnipresence; "Square" signifies the capacity to guide and sustain;
and "Vast" signifies being all-encompassing and extensive. Thus, these correspond respectively to the three virtues (*triguṇa*). "The King of the Wondrous Lotus" is a metaphor based on the cause.
That the fruits are equally manifest signifies the meaning of "encompassing and vast. That defilement and purity are non-dual signifies the meaning of "guiding and sustaining.
Being supremely sovereign, like a king, signifies the meaning of "eternal and pervasive. The above dharmas and metaphors all reveal the essence of the Buddha-mother’s *dhāraṇī*;
that is to say, the ten kinds of mantra-hearts mentioned in the preceding text are based upon this guiding and sustaining power.
It is called the "Mother of All Buddhas" because it enables one to attain perfect omniscience (*samyak-saṃbodhi*) and subdue all Māras and externalists.
Regarding its being called the "Consecration" (*abhiṣeka*) and so forth among the five [aspects], this name is established by employing both the essence (*tattva*) and the doctrine (*siddhānta*).
As for the term "consecration," in India, all profound Vaipulya sūtras containing esoteric language are generally subsumed under this category. If we consider the present sūtra specifically:
Thus, the Buddhas emit light that pours over their crowns in mutual interpenetration, clarifying the Bodhisattvas' reception of office through the consecration of the water of wisdom;
it is for this reason that it is so stated. Regarding "the various Bodhisattvas," the Sūtra says:

"The Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, within their own abiding samādhi, realize and perceive that both the seeing and the objects of seeing are fundamentally the wondrously pure essence of bodhi—namely, the three categories."
The seven elements are all the Tathāgatagarbha, the wondrous nature of True Suchness; therefore, it is called Śūraṃgama. Śūraṃgama is ultimate firmness.
That is to say, the three—principle, practice, and realization—are all ultimately firm;
thus it is termed Śūraṃgama. Regarding "ten thousand practices": within this samādhi, all other samādhis are entirely contained. [This is] the Buddha-bodhi...

"Satsu" (薩) means it is not shared with the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). As the Sūtra says: "There is samādhi... and so forth; therefore, it is called "the myriad practices of all Bodhisattvas.
Second, the answer regarding upholding: "How should one receive and uphold [this]? This is because Mañjuśrī requested that the name of the sūtra be finalized for the sake of its dissemination.
Now, among these five names, each is established according to the three aspects of essence (*tattva*), doctrine (*siddhānta*), and function (*prayojana*), as well as the teaching (*dharma*).
Regarding the mutual explanation of these points: in our school, the interpretation of the title consists of five successive layers, beginning with "name" (*nāman*) as listed in the sutra.

"Essence" (*tattva*) refers to the eternally abiding true mind; "principle" (*siddhānta*) refers to subtle and secret contemplative illumination; and "function" (*karman*) refers to the shattering of delusion to reveal the truth.
As for the characteristics of the teaching, they constitute the "fresh butter" (*piṇḍa*) of the Mahāyāna.
When Mañjuśrī answered the names and meanings, his intent necessarily encompassed the five chapters; thus, when he said "I shall uphold them," he was in fact decisively upholding all five chapters.

However, the ancients explained the essence, the doctrine, and the function individually beneath each of the five names. They failed to realize that by citing any single name, one can exhaustively encompass the whole.
Therefore, I shall now provide a detailed explanation for each of the five chapters, as there is a specific purpose behind them.
Although the title is composed of five parts, why does the compiler of the sutra establish the heading by retaining only two? First, within the first title, there is a general inquiry;

because the particulars are subsumed within the general, only "Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa" is taken. Second, within the second title, obtaining the Bodhicitta is simply the secret cause for entering the pervasive [reality].
The "Ocean of Knowledge" (*Jñānasāgara*) is merely a stage of cultivation and realization; because it is subsumed within the third [title], it is entirely omitted.
In the fourth title, the specific is subsumed into the general, and furthermore, by using that general name to enter the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa, it is likewise entirely omitted.

In the fifth title, the "Mantra of Consecration" (*Abhiṣekamantra-pada*) is subsumed into the definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) of the third [title]; therefore, it is named the "Great Buddha-Usnīṣa" (and so forth). This is the principle of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa.

Principle (*li*) is the essence (*ti*). The Esoteric Cause and the Teachings of Definitive Meaning (*liao-yi-jiao*) constitute the doctrine (*zong*). The myriad practices of the Bodhisattva constitute the function (*yong*).
Thus, it is said that "raising one is [simultaneously] three," for they are inconceivable. By opening with this title, immeasurable merit is obtained.
Having understood these five chapters in this manner, one should take them as the method; therefore, it says: "You should..."
Receiving and upholding [this].
From the point where these words were spoken onward, this constitutes the second major chapter, the text on the Aids to the Path (*bodhipakṣa*).

Generally speaking, throughout the Tathāgata’s single period of transformative teaching—preaching the Dharma for forty-nine years across more than three hundred assemblies of sutras—it can all be summarized as follows: [it does not go beyond...]
Regarding the two practices of the primary and the auxiliary: when one practices, there must be both the primary and the auxiliary, just as a bird has two wings or a carriage has two wheels.
If that bird had but a single wing, how could it soar aloft? If that carriage had but a single wheel, how could it bear a heavy load?
Only when both wings are fully equipped does the bird naturally rise up on the whirlwind; only when both wheels are present can the carriage proceed.

Complete. One who possesses both weight and distance will surely be able to travel swiftly and at ease. Thus, when these two are viewed in conjunction, it becomes clear that the two practices—the primary and the auxiliary—must not be neglected one-sidedly.
This is what is meant by "the eyes and feet supporting each other so that the Pond of Coolness may be reached.
For this reason, from the first fascicle onwards, one first relies on the ultimate, steadfast mind to open the perfect understanding, and subsequently relies on...
First, one gives rise to perfect practice by relying on the ultimately firm mind. Second, one realizes the perfect stage by relying on the ultimately firm mind.
Third, one attains the perfect position by relying on the ultimately firm mind. Fourth, one concludes the perfect scripture by relying on the ultimately firm mind.
These four constitute the complete primary practices. Should the auxiliary practices be omitted or left unexplained, it would cause the practitioner to cultivate samādhi; however, if...

A difference of a single moment, or even the loss of a single thought, leads either to falling into the suffering of the seven realms of existence or being turned by the demons of the five aggregates.

Thus, at the outset, Ānanda posed questions to investigate the gravity of the emotional thoughts that lead to the karmic retributions of ascent and descent, so as to provide advance warning to practitioners and prevent them from falling.

In this regard, as a secondary matter, the Tathāgata again provides a detailed analysis of the methods for breaking and destroying the five aggregates (*skandha*), lest the karma of Māra become rampant;
he offers a premonition to practitioners so that they do not fail in this. Now, first, we shall analyze the seven realms of existence (*gati*) in detail.
To investigate the underlying intent: since the previous section on Perfect Penetration has concluded, Ānanda poses a question, saying:
How does one establish the site of enlightenment (*maṇḍala*) and remain far removed from the works of Māra? The Tathāgata has shown that taking the mind into restraint is the precept;
the fourfold discipline is as bright as ice and frost. Thus, the sentient beings of the six realms will not themselves follow the continuity of birth and death.
Yet, although one maintains the precepts, if one errs in even a single practice or errs in a single view, one eventually comes to destroy both view and precept, like a jewel [lost].
As for those like Lianxiang, who held that both sin and merit are empty—just as Shanxing and others did—they all fell into hell in their very physical bodies.
Following this path to seek liberation, they pass through the realms of ghosts, animals, and humans, and even reach the ranks of celestial immortals or asuras;
none of these states fail to arise from a single moment of biased or deviant thought. Therefore, those who follow the Perfect and Sudden Teaching must be most careful.
Therefore, the formal request concludes by saying: "I only pray that you will enlighten the ignorant, so that all sentient beings who uphold the precepts may hear this definitive meaning.
This leads to the Tathāgata’s concluding response: "It is entirely due to following along with killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct that one undergoes this cycle of saṃsāra;
because these habitual tendencies are not extinguished, one falls into the paths of Māra. The Tathāgata says such people are truly to be pitied. Thus, it must be explained in detail in this manner.

As for "discrimination": it is precisely because what was previously explained regarding the twelve classes of beings merely demonstrated the characteristics of cause and effect within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), yet the realms (*dhātu*) and destinies (*gati*) were not fully expounded.
Therefore, at the conclusion of the sutra, [the interlocutor] summarizes the aforementioned wondrous nature to pose a question.

The subsequent text’s elucidation of the ten causes of habitual practice (*daśa-śīla-hetu*) and the sixfold mutual retribution (*ṣaḍ-vyavahāra-vipāka*) all concern the causes and effects of the six types of deluded discrimination.

This is consistent with [the preceding]. It is divided into two main parts: first, the request through doubt, which includes the passage beginning "The Buddha spoke these words"; second, the response and instruction, which includes the passage beginning "The Buddha told [them]...

The first part is further divided into two: first, the description of the scene by the scribe of the sutra, beginning from "The Buddha spoke these words" onwards; second, Ānanda’s formal address, beginning from "Of great majesty... onwards.
Regarding the opening exposition of the secret seals (*mudrā*) and so forth within the initial narrative of the scripture’s compiler: this sutra contains both manifest and secret seals.

The three *tathāgatagarbhas* constitute the manifest seal, while the Great White Parasol (*śvetachattra*) constitutes the secret seal. Thus far, the account has described the construction of the altar and the hearing of the mantra.

To reveal the secret mudrās, it is further heard that their formation is also called "perfect" (*yuan*), which likewise serves to manifest the seals; hence the phrase "heard concurrently," and so forth.

In total, what is discussed in this sutra does not transcend these two modes of expression: the exoteric and the esoteric. Regarding "sudden enlightenment" and so on, this refers to the perfect cultivation of the three contemplations (*trivipassanā*);
by citing *dhyāna* (the middle contemplation), the other two are implied. It does not mean that from this point onward only *dhyāna* is being discussed. This refers to...
The "vajra-contemplation" and so forth previously mentioned during the cultivation of the preparatory stages (*prayoga*) are all perceived simultaneously; these constitute the "ability to advance.

As for the various noble stages (*āryabhūmi*), they are the "objects of advancement," which are also mentioned here by implication; hence the phrase "sudden awakening" and so forth. Regarding the "superior and wondrous principle":
as delusions are destroyed bit by bit, the principle is revealed bit by bit. According with the text, one attains realization, and the wondrous concentration manifests.

Therefore, it is said that "the mind and its deliberations are voidly concentrated"; this constitutes the subject that cuts off, while the cultivation of the mind within the three realms and so forth constitutes the objects to be cut off.
As for the use of terms such as "cutting off and removing," it is because each of the nine stages (*bhūmi*) within the three realms has nine grades.
Now, rather than saying "six grades of the desire realm," it says "six grades of the three realms"; and rather than saying "afflictions" (*kleśa*), it says "subtle afflictions. This is because...
This is precisely what Wēnlíng meant by "superior sudden severance," like cutting a handful [of hair]: when one is severed, all are severed.
It is not merely that the first six grades of the desire realm are severed; rather, the first six grades of each of the two upper realms are simultaneously severed at once.

If one were to claim that because the realization is shallow despite hearing the profound, one can only attain the second fruit, this would still not be the case. Since this is a horizontal severance of the nine grades across the three realms...
The first six grades of the [Ten] Grounds do not stop at two fruits; they should be three fruits.

Since these three fruits result from the power of the Perfect and Sudden Sūtras, they should correspond to the period after the initial stage of faith and before the seventh stage of faith within the Perfect Teaching—constituting the three fruits—and not merely refer to the three fruits of the Tripitaka (Śrāvaka) teaching. Interpreting it in this way alone accords with the Perfect Sūtras.

Ānanda’s presentation of his words is divided into three parts: first, the praise and description, beginning with "Great majesty" (*mahātejas*); second, the statement of doubt, beginning with "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*);

and third, the formal request, beginning with "May you deign to... Regarding "great majesty" (*mahātejas*): it is called "great majesty" because it is capable of causing the subtle afflictions (*kleśa*) of the triple world to be severed and eliminated.
It is called "great virtue" (*mahāguṇa*) because it is capable of causing the mind and mental factors to become increasingly refined, sublime, and serenely concentrated upon the wondrous principle.

Furthermore, if one refers to the original text, it is because [the Buddha] opens up the sunken delusions of sentient beings that they are called "Great Power," and because he enables them to obtain great benefit that he is called "Great Virtue.
Regarding "the compassionate voice being without obstruction": if one preaches the Dharma, one must depart from the false to manifest the true;
thus, the true obstructs the false. Moreover, one must depart from defilement to manifest purity; thus, purity obstructs defilement. Now...
That which the Tathāgata has taught is such that the false is itself the true, and the defiled is itself the pure; this is the unobstructed nature of his compassionate voice.
It may also be said: as it is for one person, so it is for many; he never abandons the distant for the sake of the intimate, nor the evil for the sake of the good.
O Śubhākara and others, just as we abide within the Tathāgata’s great majestic power, so too do we partake in the Tathāgata’s great virtue of compassion.

This is the section on the locus. Therein, the presentation of doubts is twofold, and each of these is further divided into two parts. First, "If this [world] departs" is a general inquiry based on principle; second, "As for the jewel... is a specific inquiry based on phenomena.
Within the first part, the general inquiry based on principle: first, "If this... refers to the True (the *tathatā*) as the object of the question; second, "The Buddha-body...
refers to the delusory (the *māyā*) as the object of the question; third, "World-Honored One... concludes the question. Regarding the first point, "If this... and so forth: it is, in fact, ...

This refers to what was previously stated by the Tathāgata: that the three categories and seven elements are, in their entirety, the nature of the Tathāgata-garbha, none of which fail to pervade the Dharma-realm;
furthermore, these natures are both pervasive and mutually inclusive without one eclipsing the other. For this reason, these points are cited as the opening of the inquiry.
The underlying intention is: if this wondrous mind is fundamentally all-pervasive, perfect in all things, then [the states of] birth and Buddhahood—

They share the same source; the environment and its inhabitants are equal. Inferring it in this way, whether it be the insentient—such as the great earth, grasses, and trees—or the sentient—such as wriggling creatures and all living beings—not a single thing is not the true nature of the original source. Therefore, it is said, "if such as these.
This True Suchness is the ultimate true essence realized by the Tathāgata; therefore, it is said, "is precisely" and so forth.

This single phrase precisely cites the ultimate fruition as a verification. Next, regarding "the Buddha-body and so forth," the intended meaning is that since the Buddha-body is truly real, it stands to reason that each and every thing should be true and every phenomenon should be real.

Why, then, do the six realms of existence, such as the hells, still exist? Therefore, it says, "the Buddha-body and so forth. Within the third [section], regarding "the World-Honored One and so forth," the intended meaning is...
This means that within the essence of wondrous purity and clarity realized by the Tathāgata, these [six realms] should not exist.

Now that these six paths of rebirth do indeed exist, are they inherently present within the true essence from the beginning, or do they arise from the habitual delusions of sentient beings? Thus it says, "World-Honored One," and so forth.
Such is the general inquiry according to principle. Second, regarding the specific inquiries based on phenomena, the passage beginning with "World-Honored One" intends to clarify...

Although these are collectively categorized as the same class, they are presented as three distinct matters for the purpose of inquiry; namely, killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying—these four are the definitive and clear instructions of the Tathāgata.
Should one, due to a single moment of deviance, violate even one of these precepts of discipline, [the consequences are grave].
This leads to suffering for many kalpas; not only can one fail to transcend birth and death or escape worldly toil, but it is precisely through this that one falls into the Avīci Hell.
Therefore, I have inquired in advance to clarify these matters so that you may know how to maintain your vigilance and avoid such errors.

For example, those such as Bao and others, though they upheld the Bodhisattva precepts, secretly engaged in sexual misconduct—this constitutes a violation of the precepts. To falsely claim that one engages in sexual desire [without restraint] is likewise a transgression.

There is no retribution for sin; this refutes [the view of] karma. The intention [of the opponent] is that killing must necessarily result in the repayment of one's own life, and stealing must likewise require the restitution of one's property.
Now, sexual desire is certainly not the repayment of one's life as in the case of killing, nor is it the compensation for property as in the case of stealing.
Thus, there would be neither karma nor retribution; hence the statement regarding "false speech" and so forth. Since this [view] has been refuted...
The transgression of violating the precepts is already grave; furthermore, to destroy one's right view makes the offense even more severe.

For this reason, one undergoes the retributive fruit of being born amidst the great, fierce-flaming lotuses, and the karmic fruition of falling into the Avīci Hell. Although these are distinguished as the "flower" (causal) and "fruit" (resultant) stages, they both constitute falling into hell while still in one's living body.
King Virūḍhaka, harboring an old grudge, slaughtered the clan of the Gautamas; this constitutes the offense of killing. Śunakṣatra claimed that all offenses...

If one claims that "all merit is empty; by performing merit one gains no merit, and by committing evil there is no retribution of suffering," this is likewise a false view and constitutes a great lie.
For this reason, when Rāvaṇa slaughtered the Gautamas, he was destined for hell; and because Sunakṣatra possessed such false speech, he too was destined to fall into hell.
Thus, both were cast alive into the Avīci hell. This concludes the inquiry regarding these various [views]. The meaning is as follows:
This refers to the aforementioned three types of persons who fall into hell; their locations are not uniform. Is there a fixed common locus (*sabhāgatā*) where they reside?

Do those who have committed offenses enter this place together as a collective? Or do they naturally each undergo their retribution privately, according to the specific karma they have individually created and according to their respective places?
Therefore, it says, "these various [beings]," etc. This is based on the answer below which clarifies the assembly.

Regarding "private commonality" (*sabhāgatā*): although individuals act and experience their own karma separately—such that one person does not experience what another has done—they nevertheless share a commonality by experiencing the same hell together.
This does not mean they lack fixed locations; it refers to what the Master of Wuxing called "separate karmas with a shared retribution."
Regarding the third petition: "I only pray that you will... and so forth, concludes the request by expressing the intention to seek instruction. As for the words "Now, these various...

and so forth, it is because the precepts have the meaning of restraining the mind; if one does not know that the retributions of the six realms of existence do not deviate by even a hair's breadth, [the precepts cannot be maintained].

How can one fear the fruit [of karma] while severing its causes? Since body and mind are both severed, one desires that the Tathāgata clarify this so that one will never again commit offenses such as killing, stealing, or sexual misconduct, thereby falling [into evil realms].
The second part, the response and demonstration, is divided into two sections: first, the Buddha’s praise and permission; second, Ānanda’s exposition.
Within the first section on praise and permission, "Excellent and virtuous" constitutes the praise, while "You now... constitutes the permission. Regarding the praise, the phrase "causing all...
indicates that Buddhas and sentient beings are fundamentally of one essence. This essence is *tathatā* (suchness), for Buddhas have already realized that this essence is solely reality.

The essence of sentient beings in the six realms is not real; they even reach a state of nihilistic emptiness that denies cause and effect, claiming that the nature of the offenses of killing, stealing, sexual misconduct, and lying is fundamentally void.
Thus, they remain immersed in the three realms, ignorant of karmic retribution. Such individuals are all called people of false views.
Now, because of your request, I have clarified the causes and effects of ascent and descent within the seven destinies without error; thus, all sentient beings...
Birth arises entirely from the production of deluded habits; yet the wondrous, pure, and luminous mind is originally perfect and pervasive, sharing the same essence as the Buddhas.
Why, then, enter into the nihilistic view of "vast emptiness" that negates cause and effect? Therefore, it is said, "How joyous!
and so forth, which serves as a praise. The subsequent permission can be understood accordingly.
