Second, regarding the exposition, there are likewise two types of responses: general and specific. This does not mean that the general response answers the general question and the specific response answers the specific question;
rather, within the general [response] one also answers both the general and specific questions, and within the specific [response] one also answers both the general and specific questions.
First, the general: "All sentient beings," and so forth. Second, the specific: "All these," and so forth. This has two parts. First, from "all" downwards...

The direct answer consists of two parts: the sequential analysis and the concluding summary. The first part further divides into two: first, the division of internal and external, which refers to "all sentient beings" and so forth;
second, the distinction between destinies and births, which refers to "all worlds" and so forth. The first of these [the internal/external division] also has two parts:

first, the brief enumeration beginning with "all sentient beings," and second, the detailed explanation beginning with "the internal division. Within the brief enumeration, the phrase "all sentient beings" and so forth refers to what was previously...

Question: If the essence of the Buddha is truly such that there are no further six realms of existence, and it is now said that the reality is fundamentally pure—such that the wondrously perfect, wondrously pure, and luminous mind is originally complete—then it can be known that the sentient and the Buddha are of one substance and all phenomena are equally true.

As for the previous question regarding whether [the afflictions] are inherently existent or produced by deluded habituation, it is now stated that they arise from deluded habituation due to that deluded perception.
Thus, it can be known that the whole is entirely illusory and not inherently existent. "Seeing" is precisely delusion (*kleśa*), and "habitual tendencies" (*vāsanā*) are precisely karma.
Based on this, they are divided into two parts: internal and external. This is the general heading; what follows below provides the detailed explanation.

Now, these internal and external divisions do not go beyond the two categories of emotion (*qing*) and thought (*xiang*). To speak of the "internal" is to speak of emotion; emotion is concentrated within. As will be shown below...
When the mind is directed toward delicacies and the like, it rushes outward; thus, this emotion never fails to take external objects as its condition (*ālambana*).

However, those objects which serve as conditions are all merely things enjoyed by the bodies of sentient beings. Therefore, both the emotion and the perception are "emotional," and both the internal and the external are "internal.
This is what is meant by "arousing craving conditioned by the body. Thus, they are called "internal. The "external" is spoken of in terms of "perception" (*saṃjñā*); [this is] perception.
To "roam externally" as listed below—such as focusing the mind on the Buddha-lands—is to manifest a conceptual visualization;
yet this visualization is actually a quiet dwelling within. Nevertheless, what is being dwelled upon consists entirely of objects that sentient beings long for outside of themselves.

Therefore, when both feeling and perception are perceived as external, both the internal and external become external; this refers to what is called "rejoicing in those superior realms. Hence, they are termed "external.
Because the internal and external parts differ in their ascent or descent, the three realms and six paths all arise from deluded habitual tendencies.

The second section, "Explanation of the Manifested Divisions," is divided into two parts: first, the section beginning with "The internal part" explains the internal division; second, the section beginning with "The external part" [explains the external division].

The explanation of the external divisions consists of two parts. First, the formal explanation; this includes the internal divisions and so forth. Second, the conclusion; this includes "all cravings" and so forth.
Within the first part, the formal explanation, the two phrases defining the names are clear.

Regarding the fourfold analysis of the meaning of the causes: the initial attachment toward an object constitutes craving and defilement; the persistent clinging and refusal to let go constitutes deluded sentiment. As for "the habituation of sentiment not ceasing":
Deep-seated habits secretly nourish the karma of greed. That which can produce the water of craving ensures that once the karma of falling has been formed, downward descent cannot be avoided.
Now, water is a material thing belonging to form (*rūpa*); emotion is an immaterial phenomenon belonging to mind (*citta*).
That emotions accumulate to produce water is precisely because the deluded mind can dissolve form, as is described below in terms of "interpenetration."

It is conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Therefore, the meaning of the parallel phrases can be understood as explaining its characteristics. Second, regarding the formation of the middle [category], "outflows" (*āsrava*) and "fetters" (*saṃyojana*):

"outflows" refers to flowing forth and wandering; "fetters" refers to binding and constraining. It is through the fettering of emotional attachment that one flows forth. Regarding the two phrases on "moistening":
The formal conclusion states that craving gives rise to water, thereby revealing the cause of one's downfall. Second, the explanation of the external factors also has two parts:

first, the formal explanation, beginning with "the external factors" and so forth; second, the conclusion, beginning with "all perceptions" and so forth. Within the first part, the formal explanation:

The external [explanation] consists of two phrases for defining the name, which can be understood. Regarding the "various thirsts" and so forth used to explain the meaning through the various fourfold sets (*catuṣkoṭi*):

when first hearing of the sublime realm, one gives rise to a mind of aspiration and longing, like one who is thirsty and longs for a drink. One’s perceptions (*saṃjñā*) are intensely driven, and the mind constantly transcends [the ordinary]. Thus it is said, "due to the various [thirsts]," and so on.
Regarding "the accumulation of perceptions" and so forth: breath necessarily moves from below upward; now, as perceptions accumulate without ceasing, they will certainly...

It forms the cause for transcendent elevation; thus it is said, "the accumulation of thought," and so forth. Therefore, the meaning of the phrase "and so forth" can be understood as explaining "thought.

The second part, "forming the conclusion," can likewise be understood. Second, regarding the distinctions among the realms of rebirth: this directly follows the preceding terms "sentiment" (*qing*) and "thought" (*xiang*) to clarify the process of ascending and sinking.
This section also has two parts: first, "all... and so forth, which clarifies the reason for the cessation of the preceding aggregates (*skandhas*); second, "pure thought... and so forth.

The first part clarifies the reason for the cessation of the preceding aggregate (pūrvānta-skandha), while the latter clarifies the reason for the arising of the subsequent aggregate (aparānta-skandha).

In the middle, "all worlds" refers collectively to the seven destinies (sapta-gati). Regarding the two phrases on birth: generally, all beings love life and hate death; this is the nature of all things.

Therefore, when born, one follows one's habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), which is what is meant by the desire of knowledge and views to remain in the world. When dying, one goes against those habits, which is what is meant by... [the text continues].
The karmic destiny of a nation shifts constantly; thus it is said that "birth follows [the conditions]," and so forth.

Regarding "at the moment of death," a person receives consciousness (*vijñāna*), breath (*āśvāsa-praśvāsa*), and warmth (*uṣman*) as the three constituents of life. At birth, consciousness first enters the womb, taking up the father’s semen and the mother’s blood as the seed;
next comes breath, and subsequently warmth. At death, one first abandons warmth, then breath, and finally [consciousness].
The consciousness has been relinquished; yet it is now said that "warmth and tactile sensation have not yet departed," which refers precisely to the moment between being about to die and having died.

At this point, all actions—whether good or evil—have their karma completed and are ready to induce their fruits. As the previous retribution has ended and the subsequent retribution is about to continue, all various karmas compete to gather;
the strongest first draws one forward, manifesting all at once. Therefore, it is said, "in a single lifetime," and so forth. Regarding "death-contrariety" (*shi-ni*) and the like:
The desire to live is a habituation to conformity; the fear of death is a habituation to opposition.
When this life is about to end and the desire for death approaches, these two habits intersect within the heart; hence it is said that death is an opposing force, and so forth.
Those who die cannot devise a plan for themselves; they are distinguished by their ascent or descent according to the gravity of their mental inclinations and conceptions. (2)
The reason why five stages arise from the subsequent state of darkness following clarity is as follows: First, when pure thought is devoid of emotion, the pure thought departs.

Second, when emotion is predominant and thought is slight, the slight thought departs. Third, when emotion and thought are equal, the emotion departs. Fourth, when emotion is predominant and thought is slight... [the emotion departs].

Sentimentality mostly departs. The five are pure sentimentality without thought; these are equal in their pure sentimentality. Within the first stage, "pure thought without sentiment," this clarifies the destiny of the heavens.
If the deceased’s consciousness was characterized by pure thought without sentiment during life, then at the moment of death, it will immediately fly upward and be reborn in the heavens.
These heavens should be understood as referring to those from the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven upward. Observe.
It can be understood that those with inferior conceptions and much passion but little [virtue] reside only below the Four Heavens;

these are precisely those whose karma consists of the ten wholesome acts of the superior grade, yet who lack merit, wisdom, and pure vows. As for those who "fly" and so forth, this refers to the Dharma-gate of the Pure Land, which must take faith, practice, and vows as its three primary pillars.
Since they possess pure conceptions and, moreover, are endowed with merit, wisdom, and practice, it is appropriate [for them to attain rebirth].

Their minds open and they see the Buddha, thereby attaining rebirth there. This is one specific path discussed separately within the context of the "two thoughts" (erxiang). All subsequent sections are treated in this same manner.

The second [category] consists of "two thoughts and many emotions" (erxiang duoqing), which clarifies the destinies of immortals, ghosts, and so forth. The phrase "many emotions" is used as a general heading, which is then specifically detailed below.
Specifically, one emotion and nine thoughts constitute the state of a flying immortal (feixian); two emotions and eight thoughts constitute a powerful ghost (daligui).

O King, those with three feelings and seven perceptions are the flying yakṣas; those with four feelings and six perceptions are the earth-walking rākṣasas. This concludes the summary of their wandering.
These beings, vertically, do not transcend the four heavens; horizontally, they do not go beyond saṃsāra.

Although it is said that because their perceptions are many they can leap lightly, they cannot travel far. They are unimpeded only in coming and going within the four heavens; thus one knows that their previous births were as follows.
Those in the heavens constantly dwell within the celestial realms, just as an emperor resides permanently in his palace while his ministers merely visit for a time.
These beings practice only the lower grade of the ten wholesome actions, lacking both virtuous vows and a virtuous mind.

Among them, those at the lower level have a predominance of conceptual thought (*saṃjñā*) and little meditative concentration (*samādhi*). Nevertheless, because they possess virtuous vows and a virtuous mind, they are able to protect the Dharma, protect the precepts, and protect mantras;

they likewise protect the upholding of the precepts, the recitation of mantras, and meditative absorption (*dhyāna-samādhi*). These are individuals for whom the vehicle is urgent but the precepts are lax;
therefore, they sit in the lower seats to hear the Great Dharma. These are none other than the eight classes of beings (*aṣṭau gaṇāḥ*). This, too, is based on the predominance of conceptual thought.
This briefly opens up a separate path. When the three—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), and volition (*cetanā*)—are equal, it clarifies the human realm.

If, during one's life, feeling, perception, and volition are equal, then at the time of death one neither flies upward nor falls downward. This is because perception is fundamentally based on flying; since it is now balanced by feeling, one is unable to fly, and thus it is said one "does not fly.

Feeling is fundamentally based on falling; since it is now [balanced... [Note: The provided source text appears to be incomplete. The translation above reflects the full logical structure as presented in the extant portion.]
Because the perceptions (*saṃjñā*) and other factors are balanced, one does not fall; hence it is said "not falling. Thus, neither flying nor falling, where is one born?

It is simply that the head’s roundness symbolizes Heaven and the feet’s squareness symbolize Earth—one who stands as a third constituent alongside Heaven and Earth to form the "Three Powers" (*trikaṭuka*).
Therefore, it is said that one is "born among humans. As for "the perceptions being clear," etc., it is because perception belongs to...

The luminous belongs to the realm of clarity (*āloka*), while the emotional belongs to the realm of obscurity (*tamas*). The luminous is characterized by acuity; the obscure is characterized by dullness.

Although ideation (*saṃjñā*) is equal to the emotional in nature, when the luminosity of ideation possesses power, it prevails as luminous and acute. Although the emotional is equal to ideation in nature, when the obscurity of the emotional possesses power, it prevails as obscure and dull.

Thus, one knows that ideation and the emotional constitute the karma of general retribution (*sāmānya-vipāka*), whereas the obscure and the luminous constitute the karma of specific retribution (*viśeṣa-vipāka*). This is based on...

The equality of emotion (*citta*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) opens a distinct path [for humans]. When emotion is fourfold and perception is manifold, it clarifies the destinies of animals and the like.

To speak of emotion being manifold and perception being few refers to the "horizontal births" (*tiryag-yoni*). Within these horizontal births, further distinctions of gravity and lightness are made to differentiate between those with fur and those with feathers.
This is because those that travel on the ground and do not fly are considered grave, while the feathered species that fly [are considered lighter].
To cite this as "light" is also to distinguish one specific path within the six sense-faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and four types of perception (*saṃjñā*).

Regarding the seven afflictions (*kleśa*), the section below clarifies the realm of hungry ghosts (*preta*). As for "sinking beneath the water-wheel": the Sūtra states that this earth is forty-eight thousand *yojana* thick and rests upon the water-wheel.
The water is sixty thousand *yojana* thick. Since the hungry ghosts now dwell even further below this, it is so stated.
"Sinking beneath the water-wheel" means that water can harm oneself. Water is a substance that extinguishes fire;

however, because hungry ghosts receive the retribution of the fire-wheel, even if there is water present, it transforms into fire. Therefore, it is said that "water can harm oneself. Ninth, the section below clarifies the realm of hell.
"Sinking down through the fire-wheel": *dong* (洞) means to penetrate clearly; it refers to sinking so as to pass beyond the fire.
Below, it meets the wind-circle (*vāyu-maṇḍala*). Since fire abides supported by wind, the bodies of those in this hell enter the region where wind and fire intersect.
However, because a single thought has not yet been exhausted, they do not fall to the very bottom. One explanation states that the wheel of fire refers to the eight hot hells;
thus, when the body enters the region where wind and fire intersect, one transcends the cold and enters the heat. The eight emotions and two thoughts are omitted here for brevity.
It is said: Speaking in terms of "nine feelings and one perception" (*navāśaya-ekasaṃjñā*), rebirth in the Avīci hell is precisely nine feelings and one perception.
Rebirth in the intermediate hells (*sāntara*) due to lighter offenses consists of two perceptions and eight feelings; therefore, it is not described as eight feelings and two perceptions.

Rather, the distinction between light and heavy is made within the categories of nine feelings and one perception alone. Furthermore, this is distinguished separately from within the states of nine feelings and one perception, and eight feelings and two perceptions.
This is the path. "Purely emotional and thoughtless" clarifies the most grievous hells. Generally, there are three grades of the Avīci Hell:

first, light; second, heavy; and third, most grievous. If the consciousness of a deceased person was purely emotional and thoughtless during their lifetime, then at the moment of death, they will immediately sink and fall into the most grievous Avīci Hell. This is due to the ten non-virtuous actions of the highest grade.

Because of their karma, it is said that they are "purely emotional" and so forth. Thus, one should know that those with nine thoughts and one perception constitute the heavy *ānantarya* (immediate) offenses, while those with eight thoughts and two perceptions constitute the light *ānantarya* offenses. Those who do not slander the Mahāyāna and so forth will attain liberation even when the kalpa is destroyed;
however, if they harbor such [afflictions] within their minds while also slandering the Mahāyāna and so forth, then even though this kalpa is destroyed, they will enter again into the ten directions.
In hell, there is no end to one’s period of suffering; this is discussed as a specific path within the category of those dominated by emotion (*qing*). Alas!

The ascent and descent through the six realms of existence are entirely due to the differences between thought (*xiang*) and emotion; this is as clear as looking at the palm of one's hand—how can one not feel regret?

Furthermore, the state where emotion and thought are equal is possible only for human beings; thus, those who clarify their thoughts will become wise, thereby liberating themselves from birth and death and severing the cycle of rebirth.
[If one] turns back and cultivates samādhi, aspiring for unsurpassed bodhi, it would be as easy as turning over one’s palm. How unfortunate [it would be]!

If one abandons this and does not cultivate it, there will be no use for one’s efforts. This second point follows the text that concludes the response regarding the commission of evil karma and so forth;
it is the formal answer to the previous question. Previously, Ānanda asked: "Do these various hells have fixed locations?"

This refers to individual private retribution. Although this answer establishes that while each person’s private retribution has a fixed location, it constitutes "individual karma with collective retribution" (*bieye tongbao*), following this principle of "conformity" (*suiyi*)—meaning that one invites retribution according to the specific evil karma one has created—it does not mean that the results induced by shared karma lack a fixed location.
Furthermore, because the original individual karma created by each person cannot fail to be extinguished or exhausted, it is said that [the two types of retribution] exist concurrently.
The original ground. This concludes the general response above.

Second, the specific response begins by clarifying the ten habitual causes and six intersecting retributions of the hells, continuing through to the seventh, the asuras, where causes and effects are distinct and not at all confused.
For the practitioner of the Perfect and Sudden Teaching, who understands these are not [the ultimate] through the teachings, then this which is presently before them—

A single thought is emotion, it is conceptualization, it is light, or it is heavy. Since one does not even cling to the realms of humans and devas, how could one lose one’s footing in the three miserable paths?
This is also divided into two parts: first, "All these" and so forth, which provides the direct answer; second, "Thus, the hells," which concludes and clarifies the point.
The first part has seven sections, namely the seven destinies (*gati*), which can be seen in their proper sequence. First, the hells.

This is divided into three parts: first, the enumeration beginning with "these and so forth"; second, the explanation beginning with "what are these?"; and third, the conclusion and indication beginning with "these names.

Regarding the first, the enumeration: the phrase "these and so forth" refers to the fact that while the preceding treatise discussed the transition from superior to inferior states of *saṃjñā* (perception) and *kāma* (desire), the present section clarifies the transition from inferior to superior states of karmic retribution (*vipāka*). These are linked together for the sake of rhetorical convenience; thus it says, "these and so forth."
[The phrase] "Thus it is said" refers back to what preceded. "To create the ten [karmas]" and so forth marks what follows. "Cultivation" (*xi*) refers to perfuming (*vāsanā*);
that is, when the ten afflictions (*kleśa*) give rise to consciousness at the gates of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍindriya*) and create karma, one is born into the evil destinies (*durgati*).

This serves as the cause for inducing future retribution. Regarding the "six intersections": for example, when creating the cause of karma through the eye, the other five [organs] act as auxiliaries; therefore, at the time of receiving retribution, [the result manifests].
It pervades all. This is also brought about by these six types of deluded false thoughts. The second section, "Explanation of the Clarification," is divided into two parts.
First, the explanation of the ten habitual causes: "What are the ten habits... and so forth. Second, the explanation of the six mutual retributions: "What are the six mutual... and so forth.

The first part [the ten habitual causes] is further divided into two. First, the general inquiry: "What are... and so forth. Second, the specific explanation beginning with "Ānanda... and so forth. The first, the general inquiry, may be understood as follows.

Understood. There are ten further specific explanations, the sequence of which can be seen [in the text]. However, although all ten are called "causes" (*hetu*), they differ so subtly that it is difficult to distinguish between them.

Therefore, the retribution experienced within the state of suffering is used as a means of differentiation. Although the sixfold mutual retribution is said to discuss the "fruits" (*phala*), it is likewise difficult to argue over their duration;
thus, one relies on what was created during the causal stage to make the discussion. This is why, among the ten causes, there is the element of earth (*pṛthivī*).
Regarding the various implements of the hells and other such items, within the six retributions there are matters such as retribution through vision and the induction [of future states].
As for those who subsequently emerge from hell to become hungry ghosts, from hungry ghosts to become animals, and from animals to emerge as human beings—
though these are said to be manifold and each distinct— they all arise collectively from the invocation of the ten causes.
For this reason, each [category] has ten [subdivisions], corresponding to the ten causes. This means that cause and effect are orderly and naturally do not become confused.

First, regarding the habit of lust: attachment and defilement are called "lust" (*yín*); frequency and repetition are called "habit" (*xí*). "Intercourse" refers to the mutual union of mind and object.
Indeed, a solitary mind does not arise, nor does a solitary object manifest; therefore, whenever the habit of karma arises...

They necessarily take turns regarding one another as objects of defiled union; hence it is called "intercourse" (*jiaojie*). Terms such as "mutual calculation" (*jiaoji*) and even "mutual clamor" (*jiaoxuan*) all use the character *jiao* (to intersect/interact).
That which "arises from mutual friction" refers to what is known as "you love my heart, and I cherish your beauty.
From this point on, neither can let go; hence it is said they "grind and rub without ceasing. One should know that this single phrase precisely clarifies the habit of sexual desire (*yinxixiao*).
This refers to the characteristic of "receiving" (*jiejie*). It is likewise to infer the cause from the effect.

Since the effect consists of the mutual retribution of the various sense organs, we know by verification that in the present state of receiving and so forth, one organ acts as the primary agent while the other organs mutually construct [the experience];

thus it is called "receiving" and so on. This is the creation of the cause. As for what follows, it is the resulting of the fruit. Now, when they intersect and arise through mutual friction, they manifest...
Because the causes have already been established, if one does not cease or stop, then through accumulated perfuming, seeds are formed.

Thus, at the time of death, one immediately perceives a great, fierce fire erupting within. This, too, is the true emptiness of the nature-fire within the Tathāgatagarbha, manifesting according to karma.
This can be understood by means of the analogy of the person descending. Second, regarding "the two habits," these are what are experienced within the primary fruit. Part Two.
Regarding "the habitual tendency to ignite": by means of one's own mind habituated to lust, one takes the perception of the fierce fires within that hell as an object of pleasure.
With the whole body rushing toward and clinging to it, the habitual tendency of lust ignites the environment, and the fire burns the mind.
This refers to the iron beds and so forth; this is the nature of the primary retribution. Thus, one should know that all the retributions experienced within the hells arise from their causes.

Because the habituation to sexual misconduct within the intermediate state is predominant, these instruments of suffering appear as objects of immediate pleasure. If one becomes attached to them for even a single moment, they instantly become instruments of suffering;
thus it is said, "therefore there are," and so forth. Furthermore, "therefore there are great, fierce fires" refers to the habitual results (*vāsanā-phala*).

"Therefore there are iron beds and the like" refers to the retributive results (*vipāka-phala*). For this reason, the following section clarifies that these are reviled and abandoned by the sages and worthies, thereby causing [beings] to...
Sentient beings who uphold the precepts shall not fall into transgression. "Color-indicators" (se-muk) refers to names or designations. The Tathāgata is the Master of the Teaching;
he identifies this habit of sexual indulgence as the fire of desire. Bodhisattvas are those who follow the teaching;

hearing what the Buddha has spoken, they remain pure and refrain from transgression, just as one avoids a pit of fire. Since the Tathāgata and the Bodhisattvas have thus instructed and admonished us, how could we not be cautious? Ten.

The general purport of this chapter should be understood in this manner throughout; subsequent sections may be inferred accordingly. I shall provide a brief explanation here and will not elaborate further.

Regarding the second [type], the habituation of greed (*lobha*): to take and grasp without satiety is called "greed. As for the term "intercourse" (*saṃsarga*), it refers to mutual plotting between self and other.
"Arising from mutual attraction" means that this greed of plotting is triggered by the act of grasping and drawing in through the mouth.

Drawing the breath inward is called "inhaling" (*āśvāsa*); this refers to craving external objects, just as one draws air into the mouth. The accumulation of cold, the solidification of ice, and so forth, are because craving and attachment belong to the element of water.

Therefore, at the moment of death, these [sensations] arise immediately to serve as the conditions that draw forth the fruit [of rebirth]. The sounds "ṭa-ṭa" and so on are the cries of enduring the cold;
the colors "blue," "red," and so on are the sensations of the cold. Regarding the craving for water: in the western direction, there exists a "craving-water" (*tṛṣṇā-udaka*). People...
To drink from it is to become greedy; it is like the "Greedy Spring" (Tanquán) of this region. The "Water of Delusion" (Chishuǐ) below is likewise.

Among the three habitual tendencies of pride (*māna*), to rely on oneself and look down upon others is called pride. Regarding the phrase "relying on one another," it refers to relying on bandits, relying on power, and so forth.

The sentiment of pride fundamentally belongs to water, yet its nature is loftily exalted, like water rushing upward against the current; therefore, it is said to "flow and surge without ceasing. As for "beating" (*gǔ*):
Like the wind blowing upon things, all these carry the sense of surging upward and rushing against. "Seeing arrogance" refers to seeing the arrogance within the mind;

it does not mean that the act of seeing itself constitutes arrogance. All subsequent instances should be understood in this manner. Regarding the fourth habit of anger (*krodha*), the state of the mind being enraged is called anger.
"Mutual collision" means that they alternately give rise to fury toward one another. "Mutual opposition" refers to the objective conditions of mutual resentment.

Furthermore, as for "the mind heating up and emitting fire": when one encounters adverse conditions that disturb the mind, one cannot find relief; it is because of this that there is heat. From this heat, fire is emitted.
By means of this mental fire, one smelts the vital energy (*qi*) to make it rigid, enabling even a coward to possess strength.

Among the five practices of deception, "fraud" refers to being deceitful and untrue. "Mutual enticement" refers to the mutual practice of deceiving and luring one another. As for "mutually... [the text continues].
"Chao" (調) refers to mutual flattery, harm, and instigation. "Shengmu jiaojiao" (繩木交校) is as explained by Gu Shan; it is like water below.
This means that one who practices flattery and deceit must soak [the victim] for a long time before they can bind them so that they cannot escape.
It is like water soaking a field where weeds and grasses spread and entangle. To ensnare another with words is called slander (*chán*); to act secretly and treacherously is *jiān*.
Deceit is like a thief. It is like one who fears wolves and jackals; it greatly resembles a dog. It possesses a preponderance of deceitful intent.
Whenever it encounters a person, it pursues its prey as if for death; waiting for the person to be unguarded, it springs forward and bites them. Those who fall victim to it are not few.
Therefore, when observing its deceptive habits, one remains as wary of it as one would be of wolves and jackals. Among the six habitual tendencies of deception, the "deceiver" acts with madness.
To deceive others: "entangle" (罔) refers to false accusation, such as falsely representing the unreal as real or the non-existent as existent.
To "fabricate evil with a soaring mind" means to employ empty pretenses to ensnare others while they remain unaware of falling into their schemes.
Therefore, at the moment of death, one sees dust and dirt; this arises from the resonance of a soaring mind. Excrement and urine, etc., arise from... [text continues].
Deceit is the cause of being ensnared. Because deception can harm others, one undergoes drowning. Because deception can cause the mind to soar and stir, one undergoes leaping and tossing.
Drowning and leaping refer to sinking while submerged and soaring while aloft. Flying and falling, drifting and sinking, refer to soaring while aloft and sinking while submerged.
Among the seven habits of resentment, the habit of grievance harbors hatred and secretly inflicts injury; thus, it evokes the experience of being hidden and obscured.
Regarding the matter of those who harm by contravening [the truth]: these are the most evil of ghosts, who act against correct principle and secretly injure others.
Among the eight types of views (*dṛṣṭi*), "view" refers to understanding; "mutually illuminating" means that each, by means of their own views, engages in false conceptualization.
*Satkāya* refers to the view of a self-identity (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*). *Dṛṣṭiparāmarśa* and *śīlavrataparāmarśa*: the term "parāmarśa" (taking as supreme) carries the meaning of clinging.

Erroneous understandings and various karmas collectively encompass all views. In total, they do not go beyond clinging to annihilation, clinging to permanence, both [annihilation and permanence], or neither [annihilation nor permanence].

Therefore, it is said that they "mutually clarify" and "give rise to opposition. Regarding "giving birth to opposites," the four views of annihilation and permanence are mutually opposed to one another.
"Shattered. This is like water poured from one vessel into another. "Like travelers on a road," etc., is a metaphor for those with divergent views each pursuing their own way.

Among the nine types of crooked habits (*ku-āśaya*), that which is perverse and not upright is called "crooked" (*wang*). This refers to worldly expressions such as "wrongful suffering" (*kuang-yang*).
The "converging mountains" and so forth all represent mutual entrapment and harm, leaving no sense of escape for the person. This is measured by the scale of balance (*heng*).
"Dù" (measure) corresponds to "dù" (to cross over). To claim that it refers to the sound of a bell is incorrect.

It is likely that "héng" (balance) refers to the scale used to distinguish between lightness and heaviness, while "dù" (measure) refers to the fathoms and cubits used to compare length and shortness. Among the ten types of litigation, the former involves falsely accusing someone of what they do not possess;

this, however, involves interrogating someone regarding what they actually possess. Whereas previously the matter was concealed, it is now exposed—what is called "uncovering the hidden faults of others."
"I" refers to oneself. Whether one petitions the king or his ministers, or proclaims [one's grievances] within one's village or clan, these are all categories of litigation;
hence the phrase "the habit of litigation (*sòng-xí*) and so forth. The term "concealment (*fùcáng*)" differs from the preceding text.

The preceding text all concerned fundamental habits, whereas this concerns the secret concealment of what has been exposed. This is because such a habit of litigation exists precisely due to that secret concealment; therefore, it is designated as such. Thus, the term...
This constitutes a hidden malice; it is likened to walking upon the sea while carrying a mountain upon one's head.
Second, "What are the six retributions? This explains the text concerning the sixfold mutual retributions. Previously, the ten causes were practiced, and the fruit was contained within the cause;

this was intended to manifest the specific causes. Now, the sixfold mutual retributions are the fruit, and the cause is contained within the fruit; this is required to reveal that which follows from the cause.

The fruit and its two meanings require one another; thus, the manifestations of hell appear vividly before one’s eyes. How can one not fear the fruit and sever its cause? This is divided into two parts:
first, the inquiry as to what is being investigated; second, the explanation as to how it is explained. Within the inquiry, the first sentence provides a general inquiry.

This can be seen. All four propositions collectively clarify that consciousness (*vijñāna*) permeates the three natures and is thus able to create karma; whereas the sense faculties (*indriya*) are exclusively indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) and serve merely as conditions for consciousness.
When consciousness perceives an object, the object depends upon the faculty to be apprehended; therefore, the retribution experienced now also issues from the faculty.
The explanation is divided into two parts. First, "What are they? is the general inquiry. Second, from "First" onwards, is the detailed explanation. The general inquiry is self-evident.

The detailed explanation consists of six parts, the sequence of which is clear. However, since the first three and the last one refer to the faculties (*indriya*), they are called "retribution of seeing" through to "retribution of thinking.
The middle two refer to the objects (*viṣaya*), thus they are called "retribution of taste" and "retribution of touch. This correctly shows that the six consciousnesses perform [these functions].
The karma, the faculties, and the objects necessarily coexist as causes. Within each of the six passages, two parts can be distinguished: first, a general heading;

second, an explanation beginning with "This seeing," and so forth. This explanation has three sections: first, from "This seeing" downward, the intersection of cause and effect; second, from "Manifesting the light" downward, the intersection of the faculties and their objects;
third, from "In this way" downward, the mutual interaction of the six faculties. The first section concerns the reception [of results] through the ripening of karma.

First, because the causes and effects of retribution are linked in succession. Second, because at the time of performing karma the faculties and objects correspond, the faculties that receive the retribution likewise correspond to their objects.

Third, because at the time of performing karma one faculty acts as the primary agent while the remaining faculties assist in its completion—what is called "exhausting the twelve transformations into a single revolution"—therefore, at the time of receiving retribution, they likewise intersect with one another. First.
Regarding the "root of seeing" (*darśana-indriya*): the character "retribution" (*vipāka*) should be read as "karma" (*karman*).

This refers to the fact that it is on the causal ground that one invites evil fruits; only then is it truly "fruit. Therefore, the commentary states, "the karma of seeing. To say "inviting evil fruits" is precisely the retribution of seeing.
It is no different from the previous passage: "The habit of lust arises from mutual friction. Here, the four [elements] intersect through the karma of seeing.
The phrase "the primary cause and its fruit intersect" means that because the eye-faculty belongs to the element of fire, it perceives fire; this is the sign of the moment of death.
When the deceased descends to receive rebirth according to their karma through the Right Vehicle, they ride upon smoke to enter hell; this is the sign of entering hell.

The phrase "the manifestation of the two signs" refers to the intersection of the primary faculty and its object. What the eye-faculty perceives is nothing other than light and darkness. Such is the vision.
Fire and the others refer to the actual mutual interaction of the sense faculties. Burning and hearing: hearing belongs to water. Burning and smelling: smelling is primarily governed by air.
Burning and tasting: the tongue belongs to metal. Burning and touching: the body belongs to earth. Burning and the mind: the mind belongs to fire.
All these are said to be "seeing fire burn," because the five faculties assist in accomplishing the faculty of seeing; therefore, it is through seeing that one perceives.

The retribution of fire causes the remaining faculties to experience their respective retributions. Furthermore, one may consider that what follows here constitutes the primary retribution of the fundamental faculty (the eye), while what follows below constitutes the secondary retribution of the remaining faculties.
This is because at the time when karma is created by the visual faculty, the six types of deluded conceptualization arise:

movement causes the seeing of forms; because of forms, there is fragrance; and so on, up to because of forms, there are mental objects (dharmas). Therefore, the fundamental faculty first perceives them with intensity.
Regarding fire and so forth: because movement has form as its cause, one sees fire burning;
because sound has form as its cause, one hears it. This principle may be seen applied to the following five examples. Second, within the faculty of hearing:
Previously, one saw waves and heard them as belonging to water; thus, that which is confronted by the faculty of hearing consists only of the two objects of movement and stillness.

The present mention of "opening and closing" is merely a variation in the phrasing. Various forms of clamor—such as chopping, burning, pounding, grinding, flaying, and tearing—cause the spirit and mind to become bewildered and disordered.
When there is silence and nothing is heard, it is like walking through a vast wilderness, solitary and without refuge; hence, the vital spirits sink into oblivion. This is what is being questioned.
"Rebuking" (*ze-wen*) means to interrogate or cross-examine; it belongs to the category of the auditory object (*śabda-viṣaya*). All such things are the result of the karmic response to hearing.

Regarding the commentary stating "seeing as thunder, etc.": hearing belongs to water and seeing belongs to fire. When water pours upon fire, it creates an interaction between yin and yang, resulting in thunder.
Among the three olfactory faculties, one first perceives poisonous vapors, for the nose governs the vital breath (*prāṇa*). [The phrase] "surging forth from the earth," etc., follows.
To speak briefly: some may have previously been in hell and now emerge once more;
others may first emerge from the soles of their feet and enter hell. However, this ground from which they emerge is not actually the ground of hell.
Because the nose possesses inhalation and exhalation—inhaling, it enters downward; exhaling, it exits upward—the consciousness likewise emerges from the ground.
Furthermore, from the heights above, one falls downward into the Avīci Hell. "Substance" (*zhì*) has the meaning of obstruction; "treading" (*lǚ*) has the meaning of passage.
That fish is spoiled is called "rottenness" (*nèi*); that soup is spoiled is called "off-flavor" (*shuǎng*). That meat tears apart is called a "gash" (*zhàn*).

Among the four flavors, iron nets appear first because the tongue belongs to the element of metal; it is also because of greed for flavor that one sees iron nets, for [greed] is like using nets to capture birds and beasts.

Regarding the characteristics of the net and so forth: inhalation arises from taking what is favorable within the causal conditions, while exhalation arises from relinquishing what is adverse within the causal conditions;
it is for this reason that there is the retribution of inhalation and exhalation. As for "bearing" and "enduring": bearing refers to taking responsibility, and enduring refers to patience.
At the time of killing within the causal conditions, sentient beings bear your suffering and endure your suffering; such is the resulting retribution.
At that time, it is likewise so. Among the five faculties of touch, one first sees a great mountain; because the body belongs to the earth element, this is also a matter of touch through contact.
"Stabbing" refers to piercing the flesh with a blade. Among the six faculties of mind, one first sees an evil wind.
Because the mind is active and further associated with wind, those that are "square" or "located" are all places for the punishment of offenses.

The threefold demonstration of the divisions is divided into three parts: first, from "This is called... downwards, it directly reveals the falsity; second, from "If various... downwards, it further clarifies the degrees of lightness and heaviness.
Third, this concludes the response to the question. Regarding the first part:
"This is called," and so forth, means that what is termed delusion arises falsely from one's own originally perfect luminosity. Thus, such evil causes invite such evil effects;
yet, if one traces them back to their origin, they are merely manifestations within the Tathāgatagarbha according to karma. Regarding the second part: "Those who collectively create evil karma."
The six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) create [the world] by being fully endowed with the ten causes. As for "each creates," this means that each of the six organs also fully creates the ten causes;

however, because they occur at different times—successively rather than simultaneously—it is said that they act "individually. This refers to the fact that one [organ] does not function concurrently with the others. Regarding the "conjunction of organs and objects":

In some cases, they involve both their respective objects (*viṣaya*), whether two, three, or even five; or they involve both their respective faculties (*indriya*), likewise two, three, or even five. Body, speech, and mind constitute three among the six faculties.

Killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct constitute three among the ten unwholesome actions (*daśākuśala*). When the three types of action (*trikarma*) are not combined, there are only two faculties involved.
When one instance of killing and one instance of stealing are combined, there are only two unwholesome actions involved. Or, [there may be] just one instance of killing...

First is theft; or one instance of sexual misconduct and one of theft; or one instance of sexual misconduct and one of killing. Regarding "seeing with a single faculty": this refers to the eye seeing a single object.
Furthermore, the "seeing" above can be understood as the faculty that sees, while the "seeing" below is the object seen—what is meant by a single faculty and a single object.
This constitutes the commission of a single karma, which is one of the ten non-virtuous actions (*daśākuśala*). Within this context:

These are categorized into five levels. First, those like the "various lower" [beings] commit the ten unwholesome deeds through all six sense faculties; as this is the most grave, it results in the most severe Avīci hell.

Second, those "lower than the six faculties" commit the ten unwholesome deeds with each of the six faculties individually; compared to the former, this is lighter, yet compared to what follows, it is more grave, and thus it results in the next level of Avīci hell.
Third, those "lower than body and speech" commit only three unwholesome deeds through the three [faculties of] body, speech, and mind; compared to the preceding...

In the first case, [the karma] is light; compared to the latter, it is still heavy, and thus one experiences the eighteen hells. In the second case, the three karmas are inferior, and two faculties stop at committing two evils;
compared to the former, this is even lighter, yet compared to the latter, it is still heavy, and thus one experiences the thirty-six hells.
In the fifth case, the views are inferior, and a single faculty commits only one type of karma; being only light and not heavy, one experiences the one hundred and eight hells. Although there are...
Regarding the distinction between light and heavy: all that is created is a cause for hell, and thus all brings about the fruit of hell.
Generally speaking, if the number of root karmas is small, the offense is light; if the number of hells is many, the suffering is light.

This is why, as the root karmas gradually decrease, the number of hells gradually increases. Thus, even though they are equally hells, the distinctions of lightness and heaviness are made in this way. (3)

"By these [means]" refers to the formal conclusion answering the previous questions regarding whether [the afflictions] exist from the beginning, or arise from delusive habituation, or are shared experiences (*sabhāga*), and so forth.
"Distinct actions and distinct experiences" means that although the karma one creates is distinct, the experience of its retribution is the same;
for example, in the world, there are various differences such as killing a person or plundering wealth.

Even when they sit together in the same prison for their crimes, this demonstrates that the various private states of shared existence all arise from deluded habituation and have no connection to what is originally present.
Second, regarding the passage beginning with "Furthermore, Ānanda, having departed," which clarifies that one emerges from hell and becomes a hungry ghost (*preta*), it is divided into three parts:

first, the general explanation, which begins with "Furthermore" and so forth; second, the specific demonstration, which begins with "If, however" and so forth; and third, the concluding summary, which begins with "Ānanda" and so forth.
Within the first section, the general explanation, the phrase "Furthermore" and so forth means that one merely emerges from hell and becomes a hungry ghost; this should be understood.
Originally human beings, they fell because of their pure passions, slandering the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha, and committing the ten evil deeds. Thus they descended;
only when their retribution here is exhausted do they become ghosts. This is why it is specifically stated in each section that "this person's retribution is exhausted.
Second, the specific exposition is divided into ten parts, the sequence of which can be seen. These ten correspond to the ten causes mentioned previously. First:
The preceding section was similar to the current one; if one examines it further, there are slight discrepancies in the sequence, which will become clear as one proceeds downward.

Regarding the first category of ghosts, those who were originally guilty of greed for material things: because in their causal state they committed all manner of evils due to craving for various objects, they invited the suffering of hell;
thus it is said, "originally caused by [greed]," and so forth. That all ten categories mention "greed" is because without greed, none of them could have come into being.
This is incorrect. One should know that all ten characters ought to include the four characters "if at the original cause" (若於本因).

This is because, although the retribution for hellish offenses has been exhausted, the habit-energies of greed have not yet been forgotten; thus, upon encountering objects, one immediately becomes attached to them, thereby forming their physical shape.
This is precisely what is formed through the habituation of greed. Among the two types of *pó-guǐ* (drought-demons), the *pó* is a female ghost. Regarding those who commit the sin of craving beauty:
they receive the retribution of hell due to their habituation to sexual desire. Although their specific punishment has ended, the habit of lust has not been forgotten;
therefore, upon encountering wind, they assume form—the wind being the "wind of lust. Among the three types of *mèi-guǐ* (possessing ghosts), [those who] crave...
Delusion and deceit have habitual tendencies as their cause; greed is the cause, and the ghost is the effect. By means of this cause, the effect is verified as clearly as the sun and stars.
Other cases may be understood by analogy. Among the ghosts of the four poisons, greed, resentment, and hatred have habitual tendencies as their cause.

Among the five types of *lei-gui* (malevolent ghosts), those who take the habit of greedily recollecting resentment as their cause; among the six types of *yao-gui* (hungry ghosts), those who take the habit of greedily harboring arrogance as their cause;
and among the seven types of *yan-gui* (suffocating ghosts), those who take the habit of greedily practicing deception as their cause.

Among the eight classes of *māṅ-liǎng* ghosts, those who take the habit of greedily seeking illumination as their cause do so because they follow the false principles of the four views, such as eternalism and nihilism.
Among the nine classes of *yì-shǐ* (servant) ghosts, those who take the habit of greedily fabricating falsehoods as their cause do so because they skillfully manipulate and concoct deceptions.
Among the ten classes of *chéng-sòng* (messenger) ghosts, those who take the habit of greedily joining factions and litigating as their cause do so [because they engage in partisan disputes].

Because they take their private mental states as a faction, these three fetters are formed therein. As for "these people" and so forth, this is precisely the formation of the realm of hungry ghosts, which is likewise a construction of delusion;
it is not that the essence of True Suchness (tathatā) inherently possesses such things from the beginning.
Third, "Furthermore, Ānanda, having departed... This is the passage concerning how one emerges from the class of ghosts (*preta*) and becomes an animal (*tiryagyoni*).

It is divided into three parts: first, the general explanation, beginning with "Furthermore"; second, the specific illustration, beginning with "Strange objects" (*wùguài*); and third, the conclusion, beginning with "Ānanda.
Within the first section, the general explanation, the phrase "the karma of ghosts" refers to those who possess nine *manas* and one *vijñāna*, as well as those with eight *manas*.

Those with both [false] conceptions enter hell. When their karmic retribution in hell is exhausted, they emerge as ghosts; when their karmic retribution as ghosts is again exhausted, they emerge as animals.
Thus, both emotion and conception have already become empty. Therefore, it is said that the karma of ghosts and so forth is equal.

One should know that while in hell and as ghosts, one was truly undergoing the retribution for one's offenses; now, as an animal, one is merely repaying the original debt. Hence, it is said: "Now, regarding..."
[They are] equal. Second, the ten [categories] are shown individually; their sequence can be seen [therein].

While the previous ten ghosts had an uneven correspondence with the ten causes, the current correspondence with the ten ghosts is without discrepancy. Within the first category, the owls (*khyāyasa*), regarding "strange things" and so forth:
This refers to those who previously encountered objects that took form to constitute their ghostly state; when those objects dissolve, the retribution of the ghost likewise ends.

They then become a species of owl among the beasts of the world; hence they are called "strange objects" and the like. Second, regarding the category of "ominous portents," as for those whose retribution ends with the dissipation of wind:
this is because their previous ghosts took form by encountering wind; once that wind has dissipated, the retribution of the ghost [ends].

These too shall come to an end. Yet, how could the winds of the world ever come to an end? When one encounters the "wind of lust," once that wind of lust is exhausted, its retribution likewise comes to an end.

The subsequent cases may be understood by analogy with this. As for those belonging to the category of "ominous portents" (*jǐuzhēng*), they include such things as flocks of sparrows, swarms of rats, the dancing *shāngyáng* bird, and cranes.
Those belonging to the category of "many in three" are the foxes and their kin, who act with seductive charm toward people.
Fourth, those who mostly become members of the poisonous class are the vipers, snakes, adders, scorpions, and so forth.

Fifth, those who mostly become members of the parasitic class are the *kāṭa* and *krimi* worms within the body. Sixth, those who mostly become members of the food class are those killed by humans to serve as sustenance for their bellies.
Seventh, those who mostly become members of the laboring class are those driven by humans to carry loads.
Eighth, those that mostly belong to the category of "corresponding types" (yìnglèi), such as the swallow in spring and the wild goose in autumn.

Ninth, those that mostly belong to the category of "auspicious omens" (xiūzhēnglèi), such as the qilin and the phoenix. Tenth, those that mostly belong to the category of "conforming types" (xúnlèi); "conforming" means following along, such as the cock presiding over dawn and the dog presiding over night.
The third section, "Concluding the Composition," is divided into two parts. First, from "Ānanda" onwards, there is a direct demonstration of their falsity.
The second [point], "As you have [said] below," restates the facts to reach a conclusion and reveal the truth. In sum, all these are created by delusion;
they do not exist within the wondrous, luminous nature from the very beginning.
Fourth, "Furthermore, Ānanda, having departed... This is the passage concerning how one emerges from the animal realm and returns to the human realm.

It is divided into three parts: first, a general explanation from "Furthermore" onwards; second, a specific demonstration from "You now" onwards; and third, a conclusion from "Ānanda" onwards. The first part [the general explanation] is further divided into two:
first, a counter-interrogation regarding the surplus, which begins with "Furthermore"; second, the difficulty of exhausting karmic retribution, which begins with "Ānanda."
Regarding the beginning and middle [of the section]: "From these [cases]... means that one should know that the retribution for fruits is such that not even a hair’s breadth can be mistaken.
In the world, those who rely on their strength often fail to repay what they owe; indeed, many rely on their strength to take more than their share.

Can their hearts be free from shame? Regarding the middle and subsequent sections: "If one uses the lower [method]," it clarifies that when money and goods have been taken, the debt must be fully repaid.
Stop. As explained below, the retribution for killing one’s own body and life continues without rest.

Unless one possesses the power of the subtle and wondrous three contemplations (*trividha-vipaśyanā*) or encounters a Buddha appearing in the world who teaches the Dharma to enable one to repent, this [retribution] cannot be brought to an end.

Within the second section, "Specific Indication," there are also ten points, the sequence of which can be seen. These do not differ from the ten points previously presented regarding animals; each and every one says:

Regarding "repaying the debt and regaining human form": because among humans there were those whose causes consisted purely of emotion, or where emotion was predominant and reason was slight, they fell into hell;

upon emerging, they became ghosts, and as ghosts, they further became animals. When all their karmic offenses have been fully repaid, they return to a human body—this is what is meant by "repaying the debt and regaining human form.
As for "convergence" (*sancha*), there are two meanings. First, it refers to the fact that humans must...

One must observe the precepts and cultivate goodness before one can enter; this constitutes "intermingling" (*cancheng*). This first category consists of those who, having emerged from hell, have again received human form;
they were originally not part of the primary class, but exist as an intermingled group. Therefore, it is called "intermingling.

Within the first category, the "obstinate class" (*wanglei*) refers to those who, due to their habits of greed, are reborn as beasts such as owls or as ghosts such as *guai*. The rest may be inferred accordingly.

"Know that those of the 'corresponding to the category' type are such as the *shèyàn* (local swallows) and the autumn geese; because they take habitual perceptions as their cause, they are able to grasp at the four [perversions] such as permanence and thereby calculate false principles.
For this reason, these humans likewise participate in this literary tradition. Those of the 'auspicious omen' type are such as the *línpíng* (unicorn) and the phoenix;
because they take deceptive habits as their cause, they are able to fabricate and concoct falsehoods. For this reason, these humans likewise participate in..."
This is "High and Clear. Regarding "following the categories," this refers to such things as the morning cock and the night dog;

because their habituation to litigation serves as the cause, they are able to bring forth the hidden secrets of people. Therefore, they are considered to participate in the faculty of intelligence. "The three knots are formed" and so forth:
this properly concludes that all [these phenomena] arise from false delusion. "If one does not encounter them" and below further clarifies what it is like if one does not see them.
If one hears the Dharma, this cycle of saṃsāra will never come to rest. Therefore, it was stated previously in general terms:
"Except for śamatha and the Buddha, there is nothing in the world that can bring a cessation.

If one must see the Buddha and hear the Dharma for the cycle of saṃsāra to cease, then that Buddha must not be unseen and that Dharma must not be unheard. Yet, is it not difficult to see the Buddha and hear the Dharma? As for...
This means: "While the Buddha was in the world, I remained mired in samsara; now that I have obtained a human body, the Buddha has entered parinirvāṇa.
For this reason, he is to be pitied.
Fifth, from Ānanda there is again a departure, which clarifies the passage concerning returning from among humans to the realm of the immortals (*ṛṣi*); such is not heard in other sutras.
Regarding the class of immortals (*ṛṣi*), it is simply called the "six realms" (*ṣadgati*), as they are subsumed under the category of humans. "Immortal" (*xian*) means to transcend or to transform;
it refers to transcending a short lifespan to attain a long one, and transforming a coarse physical substance into a subtle one. This too is divided into three parts; first, a general explanation.

[This refers to] Ānanda and others. Second, the specific indication [refers to] Ānanda and others. Third, the conclusion [refers to] Ānanda and others. Within the initial general explanation, "furthermore, etc.
means that their cause does not rely on the Buddha-dharma to cultivate the three contemplations. "Specifically cultivating, etc.
means that they furthermore do not cultivate the causes of precepts, goodness, and meditative concentration, but instead cultivate the causes of humans and devas; hence it says "specifically."
Regarding the cultivation of deluded thoughts: those who "preserve their thoughts to solidify the form" do so because human life is long, yet rarely reaches a hundred years.
Now, wishing to refine the essence to solidify the body and pray for longevity, they employ the method of preserving thoughts to solidify the form.

The rest may be understood accordingly. Second, the specific demonstration consists of ten categories. Within the first, the "Earth-Walking Immortals," those who "ingest substances" refer to those who take medicinal drugs. These drugs are of two kinds: those produced by nature...
This is the distinction of "mastery" (*shu*). This is precisely what is meant by "mastering" (*fu-er*); thus it is called "ingesting and taking.

If one considers the plants and trees of the world, these are all "raw" medicines—such as *bai zi* (pine seeds) and *huang jing* (yellow essence). When the path of nourishing the body is perfected, it refers to gaining efficacy through such ingestion.

The "practice of moving upon the earth" does not refer to physical locomotion, but rather to the practice of the gate of cultivation (*xing-men*). Below this, there is the practice of flying, up to and including the ultimate state.

Their practices are all identical. Second, the flying immortals (*khecarī-ṛṣi*) may be understood as such. Third, among the wandering immortals (*vicarī-ṛṣi*), their transformative arts are perfected;
this refers to their ability to transmute stone into gold and refine cinnabar into silver, all of which they accomplish. Fourth, among the space-walking immortals (*antarikṣacarī-ṛṣi*).

Regarding "the perfection of the essence of vital energy" (*qi-jing yuancheng*): this refers to first refining the vital energy so that it enters the essence, and subsequently refining the essence so that it enters the spirit;

all these attain accomplishment. Among the "heavenly-flying immortals" (*xingxian*) of the Five Indias, "solidifying the fluids and such" refers to the accomplishment of solidifying the celestial pond, the throat-essence, the fluids, and their like.
Among the "universally-transcending immortals" (*tongxing xian*), "solidifying the color of the essence and such" refers to...
They gather the refined essence of the sun and moon and grasp the exquisite beauty of mountains and rivers; there is nothing they cannot accomplish.
Among the Sevenfold Path of Practice Immortals (*saptavidha-caryā-siddha*), those who have perfected their arts and methods are able to transform and guide others through this dharma.

Among the Eightfold Illumination Practice Immortals (*aṣṭavidha-avabhāsa-caryā-siddha*), those such as those with firm and steadfast contemplation may focus their thoughts on the navel center (*nābhi-cakra*) or fix their mindfulness upon the crown of the head (*uṣṇīṣa*).

There is no [attainment] that is not accomplished through these gates. Regarding the "firmness of sexual union" (*saṃyoga*) among the nine classes of *siddha* practitioners, some claim this refers to the practice of "harvesting and battling" (*cai-zhan*).

This is not the case. Looking at what precedes it—beginning with the firmness of ingesting elixirs, followed by the firmness of herbs and plants, and culminating in the firmness of contemplation (*bhāvanā*)—how could one engage in such defiled acts at this stage? It is simply...
Within the inner mind, by means of the union of the male and female principles (*puruṣa* and *prakṛti*), there is nothing that cannot be accomplished through the integration of yin and yang.

Regarding the "firm transformations" among the ten types of *siddhas* who have transcended worldly action: this refers to their ability to transform at will, such as remaining as still as a river or transforming themselves into sheep;
there is nothing they cannot accomplish. Regarding the "distinct attainment of the principle of birth" within the three stages of formation: it is like [the case of] the celestial beings.
The myriad things are generated and transformed by the Yin and Yang and the Five Elements. Qi forms their bodies, which last for no more than a hundred years.
Now, those who cultivate the Way have already attained longevity; thus it is said that they have separately acquired the principle of life and live for ten million years.
This is a general statement. If one were to further investigate, even immortals possess a lifespan of eighty-four thousand kalpas. This, too, is within the cycle of saṃsāra.
The term "and so forth" indicates that although they may be superior compared to other human beings, they cannot avoid falling once their merit is exhausted.
As it is said: "Even after passing through ten million years, one cannot escape becoming a single skull. This is because they are all deluded and do not cultivate the true samādhi.
From "Sixth, from Ānanda" at the beginning of the ninth fascicle, up to the start of the section on the heavenly realms, is the text concerning the celestial destinies (*deva-gati*).

It is divided into three major sections, which correspond to the three realms (*tridhātu*). First, regarding the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*): it is defined as the desire realm because it possesses the five desires, namely wealth, form, fame, pleasure, and sleep.
This is further divided into two parts: first, the formal explanation starting from "Ānanda"; second, the conclusion starting from "Ānanda. The first part is the formal explanation.
This is divided into six parts; these are the six heavens of the desire realm (*ṣaḍ-kāmadhātu-deva*). Their sequence can be seen [in the scriptures].

From the sixth heaven upward, through all four levels of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*), it is all described in terms of causal practice—that is, which specific practice leads to rebirth in a particular heaven.

Regarding the six heavens of the desire realm, they all take the thinning of the flavor of sexual desire among human beings as the cause for attaining birth in those heavens. To explain this passage, one should contemplate it within the context of the causes.
[The Master] acknowledged: "If one were to explain this by dividing it according to the acts of mutual embracing and so forth among the six heavens of the desire realm, it would not be so.

Regarding the first, the Heaven of the Four Great Kings (*Cāturmahārājakāyika*), 'not yet being able to equal [the gods]' means that while they have not yet escaped from sexual misconduct (*abrahmacarya*) itself, they do not at all engage in sexual misconduct with others' spouses.
As for 'clarifying and polishing to produce luminosity,' it is because, by virtue of not committing sexual misconduct, their minds naturally become clear and luminous."
...and at the end of their lives, etc. By taking the cause of this life’s clarity, they induce the fruit of being adjacent to the sun and moon;
by returning clarity to obtain clarity, what is called "the correspondence between cause and effect" is not faltered.

Second, regarding the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven, "in the Pure Abodes," etc., means that they have not yet cultivated the meditative concentrations of the desire realm. Third, regarding the Yāma Heaven, "directing desire," etc., means encountering...

Even when encountering objects, one cannot avoid being moved by them; yet, having briefly engaged in such activity, one does not remain attached. Thus it is said that "desire is mobilized," and so forth.
The section on "regarding people" below correctly explains the preceding section above: because desire is mobilized for a brief encounter, it is said that "movement is slight";

because there is no lingering thought or recollection upon departure, it is said that "stillness is predominant. The fourth [heaven], Tuṣita, is the Heaven of Contentment (*Santuṣita*). At all times...

"Quiescence and so forth" refers to the moment of correctly practicing the *anāgamya-samādhi* (the preparatory concentration). "Ascending to the subtle and refined" refers to being born in the Heaven of Contentment (*tuṣita*).
Regarding the phrase "not descending to the lower realms," this heaven is divided into two enclosures: the outer and the inner. If it is the outer enclosure, it is where the various devas reside;
there are celestial maidens and other objects of desire, yet even these are not exempt from the three calamities. As for the inner enclosure:

It is the dwelling place where the Bodhisattva of the Successive Stage (Upapadya-bodhisattva) resides. Not only is there no sexual desire there, but it is also beyond the reach of the three calamities;
for this reason, the various heavens from Yāma downward are all unable to provide assistance or response.

Consequently, those among people today who admire the Inner Court and wish to seek rebirth in that heaven do not realize that even if a beginner were able to renounce [the world], [they would still be unable to attain it].
The world is magnificent; yet, if one passes through the realm of the celestial maidens in the outer court even once, one cannot avoid being turned by them.
How could one then be born in the inner court because of you? If one remains in the outer court, when one's merit is exhausted, one will inevitably fall back down.
It would be better to cultivate the Pure Land: it may be that one is not born there at all, but if one is born, one is certain to attain rebirth. Therefore—
An ancient worthy said: "Even if one were born as high as the Heaven of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception, it would not be as good as returning to the Western Land.
Regarding the phrase "amidst the horizontal [pleasures] of the Five Heavens of Enjoyment of Emanation":

although objects of desire are presented before one in a crisscrossing array, I remain without mind, because their flavor is like chewing wax; thus it is said, "amidst the horizontal," etc. This does not mean that one has accomplished the task.
At the moment of union, the sensation is like chewing wax. Thus, it was said at the outset: "I have no desire; you should perform the act.
As for those who delight in transformations (*nirmāṇarati*), they can themselves transform whatever objects they find pleasurable.

Within the sixth heaven, the Heaven of Controlling Others' Transformations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), there are those who transcend both the realm of transformation and the realm of non-transformation. "Transformation" refers to the Heaven of Delighting in Transformations, while "non-transformation" refers to the four heavens preceding it.
Because they are able to transcend the five lower heavens, they are able to be born in the sixth heaven.

As for the Heaven of Mastery over Others' Emanations (*paranirmita-vaśavartin*), whatever objects of enjoyment they desire are emanated by others to serve as their pleasure; they do not need to emanate them themselves.
This is what is called the King of Māras. Among gods and humans, those who cultivate *samādhi* will inevitably be disturbed and harmed by him within the five lower aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

This refers to what is known as the celestial Māra (*devaputra-māra*). This is simply because he had not yet received the Buddhist teachings. The formation of the three fetters can be understood accordingly.
*The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama*, Volume Eight;
*The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Usnīṣa Śūraṅgama*, Volume Nine.
Recorded by Lingshu, disciple of the Yuxi Gate, based on the teachings of Great Master Yisong of Tiantai. II.
From the time Ānanda departed from the world, this is the passage clarifying the heavens of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*). As for why they are called the "Form Realm," it is because...

Although their meditative concentration (samādhi) surpasses that of the six lower desire realms, they are still ensnared by form; therefore, it is called the Form Realm (rūpadhātu). It is divided into two parts:
first, the specific explanation, beginning with "Ānanda, as for the world... and so forth; second, the summary, beginning with "Ānanda, these ten... and so forth.
The first part is further divided into four, which are the four dhyānas (*dhyāna*). Their sequence may be seen [in the text].

The first dhyāna is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the actual explanation; second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the conclusion. Within the first part, the actual explanation, there are three heavens:
first, the Brahma-pārṣadya (Assembly of Brahmā), like the subjects of a king; second, the Brahma-purohita (Ministers of Brahmā), like the ministers and aides of a king;
third, the Mahābrahmā (Great Brahmā), like the sovereign monarch of a kingdom. If [one asks] about the second and third...
The same applies to dhyāna. "Among the Brahma-multitude [devas], they do not rely on dhyāna" means that those who cultivate celestial practices do not cultivate the Great Samādhi of Śūraṅgama.
"They possess no wisdom" means that those who cultivate celestial practices do not cultivate the subtle contemplation of śamatha.
These two phrases should apply to all the subsequent heavens; their omission here is for the sake of brevity.
This sutra clarifies that the only perfect penetration is that of the ear-faculty; it is the Great Śūraṅgama Samādhi, the sublime contemplation of śamatha and so forth.
Since the practice of celestial beings (deva-yoga) is not what is being cultivated here, it says "without depending on," etc. Furthermore, at every conclusion, it states:
"Although this is not the true cultivation of samādhi. It merely means that one can refrain from sexual desire by restraining the body.
This is merely a matter of fact. "If his practice descends" means that although he maintains this resolve, no lustful thoughts arise.

"This person" refers to one who, before reaching the lower stages of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*), is reborn in the Heaven of the Brahma-multitude (*Brahmakāyika*) as an attendant of the Brahmā King. "In this way," and so forth.
The names of the [ten] fetters can be understood. Second, regarding the Heaven of Brahma’s Ministers (*Brahmapurohita*): the phrase "habituation to desire" refers to their freedom from carnal lust;

the phrase "freedom from desire" refers to the manifestation of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). Regarding the various phrases, it means that within the four modes of deportment—walking, standing, sitting, and lying down—they are constantly in accord with the five precepts and meditative concentration.
As for the phrase "such persons," it refers to those whose spiritual practice has already been perfected.
Below, he should be reborn as a Brahmā king’s assistant. Thus ends the section on the names; this may be understood. Among the three types of Brahmā kings, regarding the phrases on body and mind:
"clinging to the body" means not engaging in sexual acts; "clinging to the mind" means not giving rise to lustful thoughts; "clinging" here also implies detachment.

The phrase on "dignified deportment" refers to the fact that among the four modes of deportment, he possesses only meditative concentration (*dhyāna*). The phrase on "purity" means that he maintains the five precepts with such brilliance as ice and frost.
The phrase on "addition" clarifies that sexual desire is the cause of distraction and awakens one to the fact that sexual desire is the root of affliction and delusion.
Regarding the passage "this person," he should have been reborn in this life as a Great Brahma King (*Mahābrahmā*). Thus it is said.

The lower section concludes with the names [of the heavens], which may be understood. Regarding the second section, "The Formation of the Middle [Heavens]," these three phrases mean that because they have already abandoned the coarse and obstructive suffering of the six desire realms and have already attained the pure, wondrous, and detached state of the first dhyāna, these three heavens are superior to the lower six desire realms; therefore, they are called "Superior Flow" (*viśeṣa-gati*). The phrase "All [beings]...
and so forth correctly clarifies that they have already abandoned the coarse and obstructive suffering of the six desire realms. The phrase "Pure... and so forth correctly...
