This clarifies that one has already attained pure, wondrous detachment. Although it is not equal [to the ultimate], this sutra elucidates only the *śrotra-indriya-samādhi* (ear-faculty samādhi), which is a supramundane, most superior concentration.
Since this is not what is currently being cultivated, it says, "although it is not equal. The subsequent sections should be understood accordingly.
The second dhyāna is also divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the actual explanation; second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the conclusion.

The first part, the actual explanation, consists of three sections, which correspond to the three heavens. Regarding the first, the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*), the subsequent two sentences state that although Mahābrahmā is the lord of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*), because he possesses speech, if one considers meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), he is not equal to those in the second dhyāna.

"Departing" means that, just as the second dhyāna is superior to the first dhyāna, it is called "next" and so forth. The phrase "perfection" refers to his ability to cultivate the fundamental dhyānas and the four immeasurable minds (*catur-apramāṇa*).
The phrase "clarifying the mind" refers to the arising of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). The phrase "tranquil and profound" refers to the arising of wisdom (*prajñā*) from concentration.
The section beginning with "Thus" concludes the names. As for why he is called "Limited Light" (*Parīttābha*), it is in contrast to the subsequent "Immeasurable" [lights].
The Master Guang said: "The character 'shǎo' (few) should be read with the third tone; it refers to 'a little. The same applies to the 'shǎo' in 'shǎojìng' (slightly pure).

Regarding 'the two immeasurable lights,' 'light upon light' means that these rays of light further produce light. 'Illuminating the ten [directions]' refers specifically to illuminating its own realm;
it does not mean illuminating other worlds to constitute the ten directions. This reveals that the benefits of dhyāna increase and the benefits of light become more abundant."
Thus, it is named "Immeasurable Light" (*Amitābha*). Regarding the phrase "sucking in and holding" within the context of the three types of light and sound, it appears to be a textual corruption;

it should rather read "holding the perfection and sucking in the light. This likely refers to holding the perfected *brahmacarya* of the Heaven of Limited Light (*Parīttābha*) and sucking in the light of the Heaven of Immeasurable Light.
Beyond this heaven, one no longer employs verbal language for expression; instead, light itself constitutes the essence of the teaching.

Therefore, it is said that they "inhale and sustain" [the light], and so forth. Regarding "emanating transformation," etc.: since light is taken as the essence of the teaching, one uses light itself to proclaim and transform others.
This transmission is inexhaustible and excels the coarseness of spoken language; hence it is said that they "emanate transformation," and so forth.

For this reason, the name is concluded as "Light-Sound" (Ābhāsvara). In the second section on the formation [of the world], regarding the character "xuán" (suspension/anxiety) in the phrase "all anxieties and suspensions," some say:
It should be viewed as the character for "sorrow" (chōu). This is not so; rather, it refers to the mind being in a state of anxious longing.
Since the second dhyāna is characterized by the joy and bliss born of concentration, it is said that "all are equal.

As for "pure and equal," this means that one has already attained the pure, wondrous, and detached state of the second dhyāna, and has already suppressed the coarse and obstructive afflictions of the first dhyāna and the six realms of desire.
The third dhyāna is also divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" downwards, the actual clarification; second, from "Ānanda" downwards, the conclusion.
The first part, the actual clarification, consists of three sections, which correspond to the three heavens. Regarding the first, the Heaven of Limited Purity (*Parīttaśubha*):

the phrase "such as these" refers back to the light accomplished by the Heaven of Utmost Light and Sound (*Ābhāsvara*). The phrase "discarding the sound," etc., means that upon reaching this stage, one further advances in cultivation and discards the teaching [of light].

The "light-sound of the essence" (*tī-ābhāsvara*) reveals the wondrous concentration of its fundamental station. Regarding the phrase "arising and accomplishing," it refers to the further advancement of that concentration.
Since the third dhyāna is the stage of joy and bliss born of seclusion (*vivekaja-prītisukha*), and this [stage] now constitutes its beginning, it is said to "pervade the bliss of cessation.
Thus, as one advances—if the second becomes the bliss of cessation, and the third returns to the bliss of cessation—it is thereby given this name.

This refers to the "Limited Purity" (*paritta-śubha*). Within the two [levels of] "Immeasurable Purity" (*apramāṇa-śubha*), such as the "Purity of Infinite Space," it is said that the benefit of their meditative concentration (*samādhi*) advances further than the former.
The rest may be understood accordingly. This is why they are named "Immeasurable Purity.

Within the "Universal Purity" (*śubha-kṛtsna*), such as the "Universal World," it is also said that their meditative concentration advances even further than the former. This is why they are named "Universal Purity."

In the second section, the conclusion, the phrase "endowed with great [qualities]" and so forth indicates that this meditative absorption has arisen. The phrase "attaining the state beyond words" indicates its joy and bliss.
The phrase "the state of peace and security" clearly demonstrates the excellence of the bliss of the third dhyāna.
Regarding the four dhyānas of the fourth [dhyāna]: if one follows the previous three [dhyānas], then there should likewise be only three heavens, ending with the Bṛhatphala (Vast Fruit).

However, because the Puṇyaprasava (Merit-Love) has already advanced, there are now two divergent paths. If one follows the level path, one attains the Bṛhatphala; if one follows the winding and deviant path, one becomes an Āsaṃjñika (Non-Perceiving Being).
Thus, we know that the single heaven of the Āsaṃjñika arises from this divergent path. Below these are the five types of Anāgāmin (Non-returners).
The heavens. The noble ones who have attained the three fruits of the path take up residence here; for this reason, the fourth dhyāna contains ordinary (pṛthagjana) devas.
If one were to distinguish them: those in the Vihāra-bṛhatphala heaven are still ordinary devas, as they belong to the fundamental dhyānas.

The single heaven of the Asaṃjñisattvas belongs to non-Buddhists (tīrthika), for they falsely reckon the state of non-perception to be nirvāṇa. The five heavens of the Anāgāmins are where the noble ones who have attained the third fruit reside.
Furthermore, within the same dhyāna, there are three types of "going. For now, we shall divide them into two. First, the four heavens of ordinary beings; next, the going of devas.
Second, the five heavens of the *anāgāmin*; within these, there is also "going. The first [of the four heavens] is further divided into two:
first, the actual explanation below; second, the conclusion beginning with "these four," etc. Regarding the first, the actual explanation, there are four, which are the four heavens. The first...

Regarding "the birth of merit" (*puṇyaprasava*), "freedom from oppression," and so forth: this means that one has already departed from the coarse suffering and obstacles of the two dhyānas below it, as well as those of the six lower desire realms.
Regarding "pleasure is not [eternal]," and so forth: this means that one understands that even the pleasure of the third dhyāna is likewise not long-lasting.

In this way, one not only departs from suffering but also relinquishes pleasure; therefore, it is said that "suffering and pleasure are equal. Suffering and pleasure are the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness (*dauṣṭhulya*).

As long as suffering has not been relinquished, pure and wondrous merit does not arise. Now that both suffering and pleasure are suddenly abandoned, the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are likewise extinguished.
When the characteristics of coarseness and heaviness are relinquished, pure and wondrous merit is spontaneously attained; hence, it is called "coarseness and heaviness."

...and so forth. The fourth dhyāna is the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness (*upekṣā-smṛti-pariśuddhi*). Now, at its very beginning, one is already able to attain such a state; it goes without saying that as one progresses further, it becomes even more excellent.

Thus, the concluding title [of this section] may be understood accordingly. Regarding the second [stage], the Heaven of Joy in Merit (*Puṇyaprasava-deva*), as for "equanimity of mind" (*upekṣā-citta*) and so on:
although one has previously abandoned the two objects of suffering and pleasure, they were not yet fully perfected. Upon reaching this [stage], suffering and pleasure are further...
Because it cannot be apprehended, it is said that the "mind of relinquishment is perfectly integrated. Because this understanding is superior, its merit increases further;
hence, it is said "superior understanding" and so forth. When liberation is pure and merit is unobstructed, one attains inconceivable efficacy that extends throughout all future ages;
hence, it is said "attaining the wondrous" and so forth. The conclusion of the names may be understood accordingly. Third, within the "Extensive Fruit":
"From this heaven and so forth" refers to the fact that from the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*), there are two diverging paths.

"If, regarding 'and so forth'" means that starting from the third heaven of the Third Dhyāna, one passes through the Heaven of Merit-Born (*Puṇyaprasava*) and reaches the Heaven of Merit-Love (*Puṇyaprasava*); its merit becomes increasingly perfected.

Their understanding becomes increasingly clear. This refers precisely to those who cultivate and realize the path through the level way; thus it says, "If one [attains] equality," and so forth. The title of the section can be understood accordingly.
The *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the "Great Sovereign" (*Mahāvaśavartin*), which is the present-day *Bṛhatphala* (Vast Fruit).
Now, if the fourth dhyāna also consists of three heavens, then the *Bṛhatphala* would be the highest heaven. Therefore, the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* speaks of the Form Realm (*Rūpadhātu*).

[The text continues with] "the Peak of Existence" (*bhavāgra*). By this, it is clearly known that the "residing" [of consciousness] in the state of non-perception (*asaṃjñin*) and so forth is evident.

Regarding the four states of non-perception, as for the phrase "if one is equal": this means that previously one did not merely feel weary of suffering, but was weary of pleasure as well; hence it says, "if one is equal.

Nevertheless, although the previous [states of] suffering and pleasure have been relinquished, the mind capable of relinquishing them still persists. Upon this mind of relinquishment, one further applies intensive examination and...

Because there is no interruption, it is said, "thoroughly investigating," and so forth. From this state of equanimity, since the mind has already been relinquished, the body likewise cannot be perceived;

hence it is said, "perfectly exhausting," and so forth. Since both body and mind have ceased, all mental concerns are like extinguished ashes, remaining motionless and still for as long as five hundred kalpas; therefore it is said, "mental concerns," and so forth. As for "such a person," it is as follows:
This refers to the judgmental words [of the sūtra]. It means that from the time one has come to loathe both suffering and pleasure, this is the cause of arising and ceasing.
That the mind’s deliberations become ashen and solidified for five hundred kalpas is the fruit of arising and ceasing.

Thus, while such a cause of arising and ceasing may only yield the fruit of arising and ceasing, it cannot by itself manifest the self-nature of perfect luminosity, which is neither born nor extinguished. Therefore, it says, "Such a person," and so forth.
Furthermore, regarding the "first half-kalpa" and so forth, this again extends to the false conceptualization of the fruits of birth and extinction as being *nirvāṇa*.

This is discussed in terms of the beginning and end of five hundred kalpas. When first arriving in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), the power of meditative concentration has not yet been perfected;

it takes half a kalpa for the cessation of the mind to be attained. Therefore, it is said that "extinction occurs during the first half-kalpa. Once one has passed through four hundred and ninety-nine and a half kalpas...
Because the power of meditative concentration (*samādhi*) has declined and cannot restrain [the mind], the intention to attain cessation arises once again;
hence it is said that one is born after the latter half of a kalpa. Based on this, one remains as motionless as ash for only four hundred and ninety-nine kalpas.

This is merely the power of worldly concentration that renders one thoughtless; it is by no means the manifestation of the power of subtle and wondrous insight (*vipaśyanā*). Thus one calculates [it as such].
Nirvana is neither arising nor ceasing; thus, the state of non-conception is categorized as that of the non-Buddhist heavens. The two [sections] forming the conclusion may be understood accordingly.

Regarding the five heavens of the *anāgāmin* (non-returner), they are divided into three parts: first, the indication of the lower grade within this section; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "suffering and pleasure";
and third, the conclusion beginning with "this is not. Within the headings, there are two parts: the primary exposition and the formation of the conclusion. This constitutes the primary exposition.
It was previously divided into two parts; now it is directly divided into three, which is also convenient. In the first part, the "indication" (*biao*), this [text] serves as the general indication.

This can be understood. In the subsequent part, the "demonstration" (*shi*), it means that because one has exhausted the nine grades of afflictions of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*) through the path of abandonment, it says "in the lower [realms]" and so forth.
From this, the partial truth (*pratisaṃvid*) is further revealed: that the suffering of the desire realm and the bliss of the dhyāna heavens are both unattainable [in their ultimate sense].

It is attained; therefore, it is said that "suffering and pleasure are both extinguished. Since the nine grades of afflictions of desire (*kāmānuśaya*) have been exhausted, one no longer takes birth in the lower Desire Realm;

hence it is said that "there is no dwelling place below. However, because the afflictions of the higher stages have not yet been exhausted, there is no impediment to establishing [this state] as a dwelling place within the homogeneous class (*sabhāgatā*) of the fourth *dhyāna*, which is pure in equanimity and mindfulness; hence it is said: "Therefore..."
This is equal [to the previous]. It correctly demonstrates the reason why the noble ones of the three fruits dwell in reliance [upon these stages].
Within the first [section], "No Affliction" (*Avīta*), the phrase regarding suffering and pleasure inherits from what precedes it. As for "the fighting mind does not engage":

if the two objects of suffering and pleasure have not yet been extinguished, then the extinguished object and the extinguishing mind appear to be in mutual conflict and contention. Once suffering and pleasure have both been extinguished, the [extinguishing] mind...
The cessation and that which is to be ceased do not mutually condition one another; this is called the non-interaction of the combative mind.

From this point onward, all belongs to the stage of profound reflection (*bhāvanā-mārga*) wherein one contemplates the truth and progressively abandons the afflictions of the higher stages. Their names are derived either from that which is destroyed or from that which is revealed.

All of these can be seen. Second, regarding "the trigger and the catch moving alone": this refers to the mind capable of extinguishing [objects]. That which can give rise to all things is the "trigger" (*jī*);
that which can contain and encompass all things is the "catch" (*kuò*). Since the preceding objects have already been extinguished, only the capacity to extinguish remains;
this is what is meant by "moving alone. Taken together, they are called "the trigger and the catch moving alone," wherein their intersection is found to have no ground.

If there were a place where the mind and its objects could meet and intersect, then once those objects have ceased and the cognitive mechanism functions alone, this would constitute "investigating the intersection until no ground remains.
Regarding the phrase "the ten directions are equal" within the third [category], "clear vision": if the objects have not yet vanished, that which is manifested is not yet sublime;
once those objects have vanished, the principle is revealed even more clearly. Therefore, it is said that "the ten directions are equal. This—
The "ten directions" in this context refer only to one's own realm, because Arhats have not yet perceived what lies beyond their realm.
Since it is a pure and singular truth, it is said that "there is nothing else," and so forth. Among the four types of *sudarśana* (clear vision), regarding "precise vision" (*jingjian*) and so on:

previously, this was discussed in terms of the subject who sees, thus it was called "wondrous vision, perfectly clear"; now, it is discussed in terms of the object seen, thus it is called "precise vision appearing before one. [The first is] the subject.
In this one place, its principle becomes even more manifest. It is like the casting and forging of metal, wherein its radiance is free from any obstruction;
hence it is said that "casting and forging are unimpeded. This is why the former is named Sudarśana (Good Vision) and this is named Sudarśanā (Good Manifestation).
Regarding the ultimate within the five colors, "ultimately equal" means that since both the seer and the seen have been cast and forged without impediment, all dharmas [are likewise so].

There is not a single subtle potential (*jī*) that is not thoroughly investigated; thus it is said, "to exhaustively investigate all potentials. To "exhaust form and so forth" precisely clarifies this exhaustive investigation of all potentials.

By means of the contemplation of the analysis of emptiness (*prabheda-śūnyatā-vipaśyanā*), one analyzes and analyzes further until one reaches the very nature of the nature of form, thereby manifesting the principle of partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*).
Therefore, it is said, "to exhaust form and so forth"; this refers simply to departing from form and entering into emptiness. For this reason, these five...
These three fruits are the abodes of the noble ones (*ārya*). Regarding the formation of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), this is not uniform.

This clearly demonstrates that although the five heavens are provisionally situated within the four dhyānas, the celestial kings of those four dhyānas merely hear their names and look up to them with reverence;
they are unable to perceive or see their actual forms. Therefore, it is said that "this is not uniform. There is no other reason: the *anāgāmin* is a noble one, whereas the original heaven is not.
"Ordinary people. This means that ordinary beings and sages are naturally and utterly distinct. "As in the present day" and so forth serves as an illustration.
For example, five hundred arhats dwell on Mount Tiantai, and there are also five hundred *devaputra* bodhisattvas dwelling on Mount Zhiti, as described in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*.
Instances such as these cannot be seen by worldly people; therefore, it says "as in the present day" and so forth. From "Second, Ānanda" onwards, this is the general [conclusion].

This is the passage clarifying the realm of form (*rūpadhātu*). "These ten," etc., refers to the fact that they exclusively cultivate meditative concentration (*dhyāna*); hence it is said they "move alone without association.
"Have not yet exhausted," etc., refers to the fact that they are still ensnared by form; hence it is said they "have not yet exhausted the burden of the physical body.
Therefore, from the ultimate [heaven] down to the common eighteen heavens, all are named the realm of form.

Third, "Furthermore, Ānanda... and so forth; this is the passage that clarifies the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). It is called "formless" because it lacks the form that is the fruit of karma (*karmaphalarūpa*); thus, it is said to be "formless.
If the form that is the fruit of meditative concentration (*samādhiphalarūpa*) were still present, it would not be so designated.

This section is divided into two parts: first, the actual clarification, which begins with "Furthermore, Ānanda... and so forth; second, the conclusion, which begins with "Ānanda is [the foremost among] all... and so forth. The first part is further divided into two, the first of which is as follows:

Furthermore, the following section first indicates the categories and secondly explains their characteristics. Within the initial indication of the categories, the phrase "from these" refers specifically to the Akaniṣṭha Heaven.

There are further two types of divergent paths, which correctly indicate the two classes of persons—those who turn their minds [toward awakening] and those who do not, as well as those who are sharp-witted and those who are dull-witted.
Second, the explanation of the characteristics also has two parts. The first clarifies the turning of the mind by those who are sharp-witted, beginning with the words "if one, etc."

...also. Second, it clarifies that those of dull faculties do not turn their minds [toward the Mahāyāna]. If they are "equal," it is as previously stated. First, regarding those of sharp faculties turning their minds:

if, at the lower level, one clarifies the attainment of the "beyond-boundary" (lokottara) state, it establishes the entry from the Small Vehicle into the Great Vehicle. Regarding the initial phrase "if, at... and so forth:
because their faculties are sharp, within the stage of "purity through the abandonment of mindfulness" (*smṛti-pariśuddhi*) in the aforementioned Akaniṣṭha Heaven, they immediately...

When the eight patiences (*kṣānti*), the eight knowledges (*jñāna*), the nine unimpeded knowledges (*anantarya-jñāna*), and the nine liberations (*vimukti*) arise, manifesting as thirty-four moments of mind, one suddenly cuts off all afflictions of the realm of thought (*bhāvanā-heya-kleśa*) to their end.
Thereby, one exits the triple world and attains the fruit of an Arhat of the fourth stage; thus it is said, "If, at the time of... and so forth.

Furthermore, because of the sharpness of their faculties, they do not merely realize the fruits of the Hīnayāna, but are further able to turn their minds toward the Mahāyāna and sever ignorance (*avidyā*).
By seeing the Middle Way, one becomes a Great Arhat. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* states, "One should universally receive offerings therein.
Therefore, it says "becoming an Arhat," and so forth. Second, the section clarifying that those of dull faculties do not turn back is divided into three parts.

First, "If they are below" correctly demonstrates this. Second, "These [people]" and so forth concludes and returns to the main point. Within the first part, the correct demonstration, there are four sections, which correspond to the four formless absorptions (*ārūpya*).

Regarding "if one is in the state of equality" within the initial sphere of infinite space (*ākāśānantyāyatana*): this refers to having already attained the Heaven of Ultimate Form (*akaniṣṭha*) within the stage of purity of equanimity and mindfulness;
hence, it says "if one is in the state of equality. It is difficult to achieve the perfection of the mind of equanimity because that form has not yet been abandoned;
thus, it says "one perceives the body as an obstruction. Now, by dissolving the obstruction of form, one transcends into space. Furthermore, there are three kinds of form.
The same applies here. There is visible and resistant form, invisible and resistant form, and invisible and non-resistant form.
Since these three types are all completely eliminated, it is said that "obstructions are dissolved and one enters emptiness. This is designated as the stage of "visible" [form].

Regarding the second station of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*): the various phrases concerning "obstruction" (*pratigha*) refer to the dissolution of all obstructions into emptiness based on what precedes them.

The phrases concerning "non-obstruction" (*apratigha*) mean that not only are those obstructions dissolved, but even the non-existence of obstruction cannot be apprehended. The phrase "within which... serves to distinguish what remains.

The meaning is this: once all obstructions have been dissolved, even non-obstruction no longer exists. What remains is solely the eight consciousnesses of the *ālayavijñāna*. "All" (*quan*) refers to the retention [of the basis].

The "subsequent" (*mo*) refers to the seventh consciousness, the *manas-vijñāna*. This seventh consciousness merely conceives of the eighth consciousness as its internal self, and it is also able to externally engage the six consciousnesses.
Since the six sense-objects have been dissolved, the six consciousnesses do not function; with nothing external to serve as an object of perception, then—
It is half-absent. Nevertheless, because the substance of the eight consciousnesses is unmoving and their objects of perception still remain, half a portion is retained.
If one views it as a "whole," it may also be understood as half of the whole portion of that manas.
As for "subtle," it is because the eight consciousnesses that serve as its objects are the most subtle of all ignorance; its subject, which perceives them, is likewise [subtle].
It is subtle. Furthermore, it may be understood that the *manas* is entirely present, as are the seven consciousnesses; the six consciousnesses are partially subtle.
This is because what was previously severed were the afflictions (*kleśa*) of the desire and form realms, which constitute the coarse portion.
Those not yet severed are the afflictions of the formless realm; therefore, they are called "partially subtle. As for the subsequent sphere of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [it is even more so].

In the formless realm, when even the residual [form] is about to be exhausted, it is said that the consciousness-mind largely ceases. For this reason, one may regard even this subtle half-portion as the six consciousnesses.
When its obstructions are dissolved and only emptiness remains, and upon reaching this state, even emptiness cannot be apprehended, leaving only the essence of consciousness;
therefore, it is called the Sphere of Infinite Consciousness (*vijñānānantyāyatana*). Within the three [higher stages], such as the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), [emptiness is absent].
The phrase "form" (rūpa) means that both the preceding emptiness and form have perished together. Nevertheless, the substance of consciousness (vijñāna) still remains;

reaching this point, even the substance of consciousness is extinguished, hence it is said that "emptiness and form, etc. This precisely refers to the thought that formlessness (ārūpya) is about to be exhausted. Regarding the phrase "the ten directions, etc.":

"Yǒu" (攸) is equivalent to "suǒ" (所). It is not only that form and emptiness vanish, but furthermore, consciousness and mind are extinguished. There remains only the quiescent True Principle, with nowhere to go;
for this reason, it is called the Sphere of Nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*). Fourth is the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*).

Regarding the phrase "the nature of consciousness, etc.": followers of the Two Vehicles know only the six consciousnesses and do not further know that there are eight consciousnesses, nor do they understand...

The six consciousnesses can be extinguished, but the nature of the six consciousnesses cannot be extinguished, because the nature of the six consciousnesses is the very substance of the eight consciousnesses.
Now, regarding these eight consciousnesses: from the perspective of delusion, they are called the "essence of consciousness"; from the perspective of truth, their substance is fundamentally luminous.

Because you do not know that the six consciousnesses are the substance of the eight consciousnesses, you wish to move them and extinguish them. How could you succeed in moving them? It is for your sake [that I speak thus].

Because it is that which is extinguished, it is called "the nature of consciousness, etc. Since it has been inexhaustible from the beginning, how could its proclamation for your sake ever come to an end?
Therefore, it is called "in the peerless. As for "the source of the arising of consciousness is fundamentally unmoving":

you wish to extinguish it, yet that which you seek to make non-existent actually remains; thus it is said, "as if existing, yet not existing. The nature of consciousness is fundamentally inexhaustible.
"You wish to extinguish it, as if you wished to exhaust that which is inexhaustible; yet in reality, it is inexhaustible. Therefore it is said:

'If it were exhausted, it would not be exhausted. This is called 'equality' (samatā). If we speak according to the main text, 'neither-perception-nor-non-perception' (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) refers to that which exists yet does not exist.
'Neither-non-perception-nor-non-non-perception' refers to that which is 'if exhausted, not exhausted. If we refer to the preceding text, it means they are not the same."

Because it is prior to the station of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*), it is called "neither-perception" (*na-saṃjñā*). Because it is not the same as the preceding station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*), it is called "neither-non-perception" (*na-vi-saṃjñā*).
To summarize these two points: these four heavens consist of two types of beings, namely, noble ones (*ārya*) and ordinary worldlings (*pṛthagjana*).
If one comes from the Akaniṣṭha heaven, one cannot—as the great Arhats have long since done—turn the mind [toward liberation] again and again in successive layers.

Reaching this stage of the Sphere of Neither-Perception-Nor-Non-Perception (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) constitutes the point at which the two delusions of views and thought (dṛṣṭi- and bhāva-āsrava) are completely severed by the Noble Ones (ārya).

If one remains solely in the fundamental heaven [of that sphere], practicing only the fundamental meditative concentration (mauladhyāna), the two delusions of views and thought are merely suppressed but not severed;

they are like grass pressed down by a stone, which sprouts again once the stone is removed, or like fish trapped in ice, which swim away once the ice melts. This is because such mundane dhyāna (sāsravadhyāna) cannot give rise to the outflow-free state (anāsrava).

[The phrase] "and so forth" (*ca*) serves as the formal conclusion regarding ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*). This means that they are only able to exhaust the characteristics of emptiness (*śūnyatā-lakṣaṇa*), but cannot manifest the principle of emptiness (*śūnyatā-tattva*);
hence it says "and so forth. From "not equal" (*asama*) onwards, it formally concludes the section on noble ones (*ārya*).

This means that they are unable—like an Arhat—to turn back from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*) toward the Great Vehicle (*mahāyāna*); rather, they proceed only from the Akaniṣṭha Heaven (*Akaniṣṭha-bhavana*) down through the various stages until they reach here.
Having severed the afflictions of views and thought, they are merely dull *arhats*; therefore, it is said that they "do not proceed from equality.

If one were to proceed from equality, taking the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*) as an analogy, although they do not turn their minds toward enlightenment, they ultimately do not fall away. This is because the Heaven of No-Thought is fundamentally not ultimate;

they falsely reckon it to be *nirvāṇa*, unable to exhaustively penetrate emptiness or investigate the principle, and thus become deluded regarding this tainted heaven, mistaking it for the unconditioned.
An explanation is provided for this: if one does not hear the True Dharma of the Tathāgata and the mind arises again, one immediately falls.

As for Arhats, they differ from those in the state of non-conception (asaṃjñi-samāpatti) in that they do not re-enter saṃsāra; thus it says, "if [the mind] follows," and so forth. The second section, the conclusion, is divided into three parts:

first, a general conclusion regarding the three realms, beginning with "Ānanda" and so forth; second, a specific conclusion regarding the four formless heavens (ārūpya-dhātu), beginning with "Ānanda" and so forth; and third...
The fingers belong to the realm of falsehood; these are all equal. This first section summarizes the heavens, humans, and commoners within the three realms.

The "commoners" are those who practice as ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*); thus, when their merit is exhausted, they return to the cycle of rebirth (*saṃsāra*). This is what is meant by the metaphor of an upward-pointing arrow shot into the sky:
when its force is spent, it falls back down. The various heavenly kings are the "kings"; the kings are those who practice as bodhisattvas through skillful means (*upāya*).
This is why he demonstrates the gradual stages and so forth. Thus one should know that within the three realms, it is not only the five [heavens] of the form realm that are not [the case];
rather, the noble ones of the three fruits, as well as those of sharp and dull faculties in the formless realm, are indeed Arhats and Bodhisattvas.
All the kings of the various heavens within the three realms are manifestations of great sages. Second, the separate conclusion regarding the four emptinesses (*ākāśānantyāyatana*, etc.).

"Among these, 'the four equalities' refers to the four formless heavens, such as the sphere of infinite space, where both form and matter are simultaneously extinguished and the consciousness-mind is entirely ceased, even to the point where the nature of consciousness is unmoving.
This merely concludes the description of the four formless heavens from the perspective of ordinary beings; the rest may be understood accordingly.
Third, regarding 'belonging to the midst of delusion,' this 'all that is equal' refers to the various heavens of the triple world, as well as those mentioned previously."

The four realms beginning with the hells, and the latter one of the asuras, all arise from the false manifestation that occurs when the wondrously luminous nature of mind fails to realize itself for even a single moment of non-awakening.
*Pudgala*— which is translated here as "one who undergoes repeated rebirth"— is also simply the intermediate state (*antarābhava*).
Seventh, next, "Ānanda departs" marks the beginning of the text concerning the asuras. *Asura* here means "no heaven.
This is because they possess celestial fortune but lack celestial virtue; it is also said to mean "no wine. Their nature is such that they are extremely fond of wine.

They gather flowers from the four continents and ferment them in the great ocean, intending to brew wine. However, due to the karmic power of the fish and dragons, the wine cannot be completed, and they consequently give rise to anger.

By nature, they have vowed to abstain from alcohol; thus, if one were to discuss their merit, it could rival that of the heavens, yet if one discusses their virtue, they remain below the level of humans.
They are now listed here in full because they are still encompassed within the four realms of existence (*catur-gati*). How is it that one class of beings is encompassed by the four realms?
It is because, due to their past causes, they are able to uphold the teachings of the supramundane sages by observing the five precepts and the ten wholesome actions.

This is superior-grade goodness; one should be reborn among the devas and is also able to uphold the teachings of the sages of the world, practicing the five constant virtues of benevolence, righteousness, propriety, wisdom, and trustworthiness.
This is medium-grade goodness; one should be reborn among human beings. These descriptions are made from the perspective of what is upheld.
However, if considered from the perspective of their fundamental nature, although they may possess the goodness of precepts and even the five constant virtues, [they lack] mindfulness...
To desire to surpass others and only fear that others might surpass oneself constitutes a middling grade of evil; such a person should be reborn among the hungry ghosts (*preta*).
Not only is there the thought of surpassing others, but there is also the mind of envy (*īrṣyā*):

upon hearing that another person performs virtuous deeds, one feels jealousy in one's heart, thinking, "How can this person perform such a deed? and wishing forever to prevent that other person from being able to practice virtue.

This constitutes a lower grade of evil, for which one ought to be reborn among the animals. Since they possess both this goodness and this evil, they do not abandon their original category but are instead subsumed within the four destinies (*catur-yoni*).
Furthermore, there are those who are subsumed under the four modes of birth (*catur-yoni*):

because ghosts (*preta*) are born from eggs, humans are born from wombs, deities (*deva*) are born by transformation, and animals (*tiryagyoni*) include those born from moisture; thus, some are born in the ocean.

[The section on] "Bottom" (Di) is similar to the moisture-born (*saṃsvedaja*) category of fish and dragons. It is divided into two parts: first, from "Furthermore" (*fù*) onwards, there is the general heading;

second, from "If one" (*ruò yú*) onwards, there is the specific explanation. The specific explanation is further divided into four sections; the general meaning is as before, and the sequence may be seen accordingly.

Within the first section, concerning those included among the egg-born (*aṇḍaja*) class of ghosts, it says: "Those who protect the power of the Dharma" (*hù fǎ lì zhě*). This refers to those who, due to their past causes, were able to revere the supramundane sages.
Because they follow this teaching, they are able to protect the Dharma. Regarding those who "ride the vehicle to enter emptiness": asuras do not possess the five supernatural powers (*pañcābhijñā*);
since they are categorized among the class of ghosts (*preta*), and ghosts possess the five supernatural powers, asuras likewise possess them. The rest may be understood accordingly.

The second section, "From Ānanda, it is thus," is the text that concludes by manifesting the seven destinies (*gati*). This text is divided into two parts: first, how delusion and falsehood give rise to existence;

second, how illumination of the truth results in non-existence. Regarding the first part, there are further two sections: first, from "Ānanda" downwards, the causes of delusion are shown to be false and illusory;
second, from "Ānanda" downwards, it is shown that one subsequently transmigrates due to evil karma. Within the first of these, it says: "the essence... (or *jing*).
Regarding the "thorough investigation of the seven destinies": "thorough" (*jing*) means meticulous; "investigation" (*yan*) means critical examination.
As previously stated, the general response proceeds from the superior to the inferior, while the specific response proceeds from the inferior to the superior.

Through this one-to-one correspondence and back-and-forth progression, one conducts a meticulous examination in such a detailed manner that the causes and effects of the seven destinies become entirely clear. This constitutes the thorough investigation of the seven destinies.

Thus, one knows that the seven destinies all take the various delusive marks of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) as their cause, and consequently result in the sinking and drowning within those same conditioned marks; hence it is said, "all are equal," and so forth.

Their taking birth is due to false conceptualization (*abhūtaparikalpa*); their following after karma is likewise due to this false conceptualization; hence it is said, "false conceptualization," and so forth.

Thus, such false and delusory rebirths follow from karma; they all arise fundamentally from the True Nature giving rise to the delusive, turning away from awakening and uniting with the sensory objects.
Yet, within the wondrously luminous nature of the mind, these are like flowers in the sky—how could they have a root or even a beginning?
Therefore, it is said, "In the wondrous [nature], etc. Next, in the passage "these... etc.," the word "these" again refers to all these sentient beings who are utterly unaware [of this].

They are deluded regarding their fundamental wondrous mind; therefore, although many kalpas have passed, they have not yet returned to true purity and wondrous clarity. Thus it is said, "These [beings]," and so forth.
That they do not know the truth and instead take refuge in what is merely pure is due to nothing other than the three [transgressions] of killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct.
Thus it is said, "All are due to," and so forth. If one can thus turn back from these three, not only will there be none...
It is simply three. Furthermore, it can give rise to the three [virtues] of non-killing, non-stealing, and non-sexual misconduct. Therefore, it is said that one "reverses these.
From this perspective, one should understand that when these three exist, they are called the three evil realms, such as the realm of ghosts;
when these three do not exist, they are called the three good realms, such as the realm of devas. Thus, it is said that there are names such as these. Regarding good and—
Evil. Non-existence and existence mutually undermine and seize one another; from this they revolve and circulate without rest. Therefore, it is said that "existence, non-existence, and so forth.
All of these are established as existence through delusion and falsehood. Second, illuminating the truth, there is no division into four.

First, "If one attains... and below clarifies the wondrous contemplation. Second, "Ānanda... and below provides the words of response. Third, "You must exhort yourself... and below offers encouragement.

[The text] eliminates [these errors]. Fourth, this section below distinguishes between the heterodox and the orthodox. Within the initial explanation of wondrous contemplation (*vipaśyanā*), the phrase "if one attains...
and so forth correctly clarifies the subtle and wondrous three contemplations (*trivipaśyanā*). Although it is called *samādhi*, it also fully encompasses *śamatha* and *dhyāna*.

Because these three dharmas arise entirely from their inherent nature (*dharmatā*), this constitutes the wondrous arousal of *samādhi*. Thus, the phrase "then wondrous... and so forth correctly clarifies the wondrous [contemplation].
This refers to contemplating the wondrous Truth that is revealed. When practicing *śamatha*, the inconceivable method of emptiness-vision naturally manifests before one;
by illuminating it with total clarity, all phenomena are present yet not a single atom is established. This is the state of the principle of true emptiness, the very essence of reality.
This is quiescence (*śānti*). When practicing samādhi, the inconceivable provisional contemplation of phenomena naturally manifests before one;

when one illuminates them perfectly, the myriad phenomena appear in their full clarity. This is the wondrous principle of the reality-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in its very essence—this is permanence (*nitya*).

When practicing dhyāna, if the inconceivable Middle Way (*madhyamaka*) naturally manifests and one contemplates it with total illumination, then within the very substance of emptiness and stillness, the myriad dharmas are vividly present;

and within the vivid presence of the myriad dharmas, their very substance is empty and still. Thus, negation and illumination are equal, and the ultimate and conventional truths are simultaneously revealed.
This is solely the principle and object of the Middle Way; this is what is called "wondrous. Therefore, it is said: "Then it is wondrous."

It is eternally quiescent. Thus, when all phenomena are present before one yet not a single speck of dust is established, and the essence itself is true emptiness, then even good and evil are likewise true emptiness;
how could there be any good, evil, devas, ghosts, or the like to be found?
Furthermore, when the myriad phenomena of the universe are all perfectly manifest and their essence itself is wondrous existence, then even good and evil are likewise wondrous existence.

Furthermore, how could there be any good or evil devas, ghosts, and so forth to be found? Moreover, when one abides in the Middle Way itself—where both negation and affirmation, both identity and difference, and both detachment and non-detachment are simultaneous—even good and evil and the like are themselves the Middle Way. How, then, could there be any good or evil devas, ghosts, and so forth to be found?

Therefore, it is said that both existence and non-existence are non-existent. Upon reaching this point, not only are existence and non-existence the objects to be dispensed with, [but all dualities are likewise].
They cannot be apprehended; even the contemplation that can dispel them cannot be apprehended. Therefore, it is said that "the two do not exist and are both extinguished.
Thus one knows that even the three virtues, such as non-killing, are unapprehendable; how much less could the three evils, such as killing, be apprehended?
Therefore, it is said that "even non-existence is absent," and so forth. When one contemplates in this manner, the suffering of saṃsāra shall be stilled in the present moment.
Thus, the sublime contemplation is clarified in order to illuminate the Truth. Second, regarding the response to the questions:

the phrase "not severed" and so forth directly answers the inquiries as to whether [the afflictions] are inherent to the fundamental nature, whether they arise from deluded habituation, and whether they have a fixed location shared by all individuals.
The first two phrases constitute the heading; "because each" and so forth provide the explanation. Regarding "because each" and so forth:

it means that while the karma created is the private business of each individual, the retribution experienced is the commonality of their shared portion. Thus, there is a fixed location; it is not that there is no fixed location.
Therefore, it says "because each" and so forth. From "from delusion" onwards, it correctly clarifies that all [retribution] is caused by a single moment of non-awakening.
They exist through delusion, like flowers in the sky for which one cannot trace a root or origin; thus it is said, "by one's own delusion," and so forth.
Previously, Ānanda posed his question in this manner, and now the Tathāgata provides his concluding answer in this manner; one question and one answer are perfectly clear.
Regarding the three points for severing [delusion], the phrase "you must exert yourself" (*rǔ xù*)—*xù* carries the meaning of exhortation and encouragement—specifically exhorts him...

This is the cultivation of the Dharma-gate of Perfect Penetration (*pariṣphuṭa-yoga*). Since the preceding sections have already clarified the subtle contemplation (*sūkṣma-vipaśyanā*) and provided answers to the questions, Ānanda should naturally employ this subtle contemplation to sever his delusions and return to the truth;
therefore, he is exhorted to eliminate them. [The text refers to] the three delusions (*trividha-kleśa*).

"It is not [the afflictions of] view or thought" refers specifically to killing and so forth. Since the three karmas of killing and the like arise from the three delusions of greed and so forth, one must first sever their root causes;
thus it says, "You must exert yourself," and so on. The phrase "even if you obtain" below serves as a reductio ad absurdum to clarify this point.

This can be understood. Regarding the fourfold discernment of the heterodox and the orthodox, one should understand that such [passages] are to be applied accordingly. At the conclusion, one should state:
"In this way, it is known that the cause of hell immediately gives rise to the fruit of hell, and so on, up to the cause of humans and devas immediately giving rise to the fruit of humans and devas.

If one can speak thus and cultivate this contemplation, the delusory will be illuminated and destroyed, and the real will be illuminated and revealed; what concern could there be for the Unsurpassed [Enlightenment]?
Thus, Bodhi is not achieved. Having completed the thorough investigation of the seven destinies, the second [section] follows immediately after the departure of the Tathāgata;
it is the passage that provides a detailed analysis of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) within the context of the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣa-dharma*).

When the practitioner is at the juncture where the contemplative practice is about to be perfected but not yet perfected, and when the five aggregates are about to be shattered but not yet shattered, the subject and object...

When you and the adversary stand as enemies, if you can contemplate them with total perfection and illuminate them with total perfection, there is nothing that is not the perfect fusion of the three truths (*triratna*).

In this way, without needing to destroy the māra, the māra will destroy itself. Furthermore, if you can realize that the realm of māra is identical to the realm of the Buddha—as one suchness and not two suchnesses—then again, without needing to destroy the māra, the māra will destroy itself. Should you be unable to contemplate and penetrate in this manner, [the māra will prevail].
If for even a single thought one falls into error or a single view becomes mistaken, then the faction of Māra will seize the opportunity to enter.
Not only will one’s contemplative practice fail to be accomplished, but one will further invite a fall into the evil realms. This is the most critical and urgent juncture.

Yet, Ānanda and the others did not anticipate asking about this; therefore, the Tathāgata, out of his unconditioned compassion (*nirālamba-karuṇā*), returned to speak as he was about to conclude his session. As for "Māra":

In the Sanskrit language, it is fully called *māra*; here it is translated as "the slayer" (*śatru*) or also as "the plunderer. It is able to kill the practitioner's *dharmakāya* and plunder the practitioner's life of wisdom (*prajñājīvita*).
Furthermore, there are the celestial demon (*devamāra*), the death demon (*mṛtyumāra*), the affliction demon (*kleśamāra*), and the aggregate demon (*skandhamāra*).
Although the five māras are all present here, they are broadly divided into two parts: first, the narrative by the sūtra compiler, beginning with "At that time" (*iti*) and so forth;
second, the words of the Tathāgata, beginning with "You all" (*yūyam*) and so forth. Within the compiler’s narrative, regarding the phrase "at that time" and so on:

following the previous section on the three stages of understanding, practice, and realization within the primary cultivation, as well as the concluding titles, [the compiler] further investigates the seven destinies within the auxiliary practices. First...
What the sutras discuss has reached its ultimate point; nothing more can be added. Thus it is said that he was about to conclude his discourse from the Dharma seat.
However, the demon of the five aggregates had not yet been thoroughly examined. For this reason, he turned back toward Mount Purple Gold to speak once again.

Although these are the most critical points for those such as Ānanda, how could they have anticipated this clarification of the turbidity without the Tathāgata’s Buddha-knowledge and Buddha-vision? Therefore—
He universally addressed the great assembly as well as Ānanda. At that time, they surely already knew it;

however, the present assembly and sentient beings of the future age are still unable to know it. For this reason, he formally addresses the great assembly while incidentally mentioning Ānanda, for Ānanda is the one who is the appropriate recipient of the teaching.

The Tathāgata’s discourse is divided into two parts, which are further subdivided into three. First, from "You disciples who are still in training" (*śaikṣa*) onwards, he speaks according to their intentions regarding what to adopt and what to reject.

Second, from "The Buddha said to Ānanda" onwards, he provides an exposition based on the underlying meaning. Third, from "Ānanda immediately rose" onwards, he further resolves remaining doubts. Within the first of these [three], there are again two sections:

first, pointing back to what preceded, namely "You [disciples] etc."; second, clarifying the present context, namely "You still etc. Within the first of these [two], [the section] pointing back to what preceded...

"Turning the mind toward the Great [Vehicle] and so forth" distinguishes this from the Lesser Vehicle (*hīnayāna*). "The true cultivation has already been explained" refers to what was previously stated:

that the Dharma-gate of the ear-faculty, wherein cultivation arises entirely from the nature (*dharmatā*), constitutes true cultivation; this also distinguishes it from those who do not realize that cultivation arises entirely from the nature.
Second, the clarification of the present subject has two parts: first, "You still... and so forth, which fully enumerates what is yet unknown; second...
You should first provide a formal admonition and permission to receive the teaching. Regarding the initial comprehensive enumeration within the section on "not yet knowing":

first is the general enumeration, which refers to "you" and so forth; second is the specific enumeration, which refers to "some of you" and so forth. Within the first [of these], *śamatha* is cessation and *vipaśyanā* is contemplation.
Since both cessation and contemplation are complete, it can be understood that the *dhyāna* of the non-duality of cessation and contemplation is also present. This...

"Raising what has been cultivated" refers to that which has been practiced. "Subtle and minute phrases" refers to that which is not yet known. "Demonic realms and so forth" refers to that which causes one not to know.

When demonic realms appear before one, they are as fully detailed in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā* (Calming and Contemplation), where ten realms are enumerated, ranging from the realm of the aggregates (*skandha*) to the realm of the bodhisattva;
the demonic realm is the fifth among them. For a beginner, one contemplates only the aggregates; the remaining nine are contemplated only once they arise. Thus...

Knowing that the manifestations of Māra appear before one is as described in detail in the *Śamatha-vipaśyanā*. Purifying the mind (*kṣālayati citta*) is not [merely] formal; it has many meanings. To speak briefly:
if the internal mind does not take external objects as its condition, the purified mind becomes naturally correct, and Māra cannot enter.

Furthermore, realizing that the realm of Māra and the realm of the Buddha are a single suchness (*tathatā*) without duality is also for the purified mind to become naturally correct, so that Māra cannot enter. To speak extensively: first...

First, in practicing meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*), one must necessarily purify the prior mind. All past erroneous views and attachments must be entirely repented, severed, and cleansed until nothing remains.

Just as a previously defiled vessel is emptied of its poison and honey and then thoroughly rinsed with ash and incense so that it may hold the nectar of immortality, even the slightest impurity becomes a cause for the arrival of Māra. Second, in general...
The cultivation of the three types of cessation (*śamatha*) are all the water of wisdom that washes the mind.

Just as the cessation of realizing the true nature (*tattva-śamatha*) washes away the afflictions of views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), the cessation of skillful means (*upāya-śamatha*) washes away the dust-like afflictions (*rajas-kleśa*), and the cessation of non-duality (*advaya-śamatha*) washes away ignorance (*avidyā*). Once all three delusions have been washed away, the mind naturally attains correctness.

Should there be even the slightest impurity remaining, one will immediately be possessed by Māra. Within the second section, "Specifically Citing," it says: "Or perhaps you... [This is] an anticipatory statement.
The latter forty-eight kinds are the *skandha-māras*. As will be explained later, the devas, māras, spirits, and *chi-mei* (goblins) are all manifestations within the realm of the *skandha-māras*.
Following the mention of *chi-mei*, one should conclude by saying: "This is a thief; it is certainly not your son.
If you cannot discern this, you will instead mistake the thief for your son. Therefore, it says, "In the mind," and so forth.
If one is a true son [of the Buddha], they alone can inherit the family estate of the Dharma-king;

if one is a thief, not only will they fail to inherit the family estate of the Dharma-king, but their very life-force of the Dharma-body (dharmakāya) and wisdom will instead be lost. How can one not be cautious?

Furthermore, the following section pre-emptively cites the two types—Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas—who appear later within the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate). As for "the first," etc., it is an introduction.
This is an example. That bhikṣu had previously heard what the Tathāgata taught: that one who has realized arhatship does not fall into further existence.
Yet, failing to attain the four dhyānas, he falsely claimed to be an arhat. When his merit was exhausted and he was about to fall, he slandered the Buddha, saying:
"The Buddha said that an arhat does not fall into further existence; I have realized arhatship, yet now I am falling. Thus...
They know that what the Buddha has taught is not [what they have attained]. Thus, to claim realization when one has not yet realized it is a great falsehood;
furthermore, to slander the Tathāgata is another great falsehood. For this reason, one falls directly into the Avīci Hell, as described in detail in the *Fuxing* (Sub-commentary).

The present mention of the "four dhyānas" refers to regarding the attainment of the first dhyāna as the realization of the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), and so on up to regarding the fourth dhyāna as the realization of the fourth fruit (*arhat*).
This constitutes false speech regarding the realization of sainthood (*āryatva*). Since that is so, it is likewise for one who practices samādhi and considers a minor attainment to be sufficient;
hence the phrase "as in the case of the first [disciple]," and so forth. Second, regarding the admonition and permission to receive the teaching:
"You should... below is the admonition and permission, while "Ānanda... below is the reception of the teaching; both are easily understood.
Second, the exposition according to the meaning is further divided into three parts: first, the general clarification, which is the Buddha’s address to Ānanda and others;
second, the specific manifestation, which begins with "Ānanda, you should know"; and third, the summary, which begins with "This is the past.

The first [section] also has three parts: first, the reason for the Buddha’s departure; second, the manifestation of Māra’s agitation regarding "you all"; and third, the exhortation and admonition directed toward them.

The first section also has three parts. First, the single true self-nature; this refers to the passage beginning with "The Buddha said," and so forth. Second, delusion of the true and the arising of the false; this refers to the passage beginning with "Because of you," and so forth.
Third, the original non-existence of the essence of the false; this refers to the passage beginning with "You should know," and so forth.

Within the first of these, the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" correctly clarifies that the single true self-nature is the equality and non-duality of ordinary beings and Buddhas. Within the second, the delusion of the true and the arising of the false, it clarifies its...
The fundamental nature and the arising of Buddhahood are non-dual. It is only because you failed to awaken for a single moment that you became deluded regarding the True and gave rise to the False.

This is like the previous instance where the false was taken as luminous awareness; it is also like the primordial luminosity shining forth. The occurrence of ignorance and craving is like the previous establishment of an object based on luminosity;

it is also like the production of an object from the shining light. The pervasive delusion that arises is like the previous state where the object, being already false, [gave rise to further delusion].

The capacity for your deluded establishment [of phenomena] arises; it is also like the nature of illumination being lost when that which is established [is analyzed]. Thus, there is the nature of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), and so forth.

As previously stated in the section on "Lack of Identity and Difference," difference is vigorously established: because the prior identity is taken as empty space and the difference is taken as the world.

It is also like how, due to delusion, there is empty space, and upon that space, worlds are established. What has been explained above all arises from the characteristics of the unreal, produced by a single thought of non-awakening;
this section below clarifies the meaning of how everything exists through the unreal state of a single thought of non-awakening.
When it says "the lands of the ten directions are not untainted," this specifically points to and distinguishes them from the Land of Tranquil Light (Jigō).
This refers to the land. Generally speaking, in contrast to the three lower lands, it distinguishes [this land] from the Land of Tranquil Light (*śāntaprabhāsa*);

in contrast to the two lower lands, it distinguishes it from the Land of True Reward (*vipākaphala*) within the Land of Tranquil Light; and in contrast to the Land of Common Residence (*sahāloka*), it distinguishes it from the three upper lands.

Regarding the phrase "the essence of the three delusions is originally non-existent" and "one should know," etc.: this means that the world exists because of empty space, and empty space, in turn, exists because of ignorance (*avidyā*). Thus...
Know that ignorance is the producer of space, and space, in turn, is the producer of the world.
However, since ignorance is in its very essence false and illusory, how could there be the space produced by it, nor the world produced by that space?
Therefore, it is said, "One should know," and so forth. The phrase "like a fragment of cloud" uses a fragment of cloud as a metaphor for space.
Because it is easily dissipated, the "Great Clarity" (Taìqīng) is used as a metaphor for true nature (*tathatā*), for it is devoid of movement or change.

A small speck of a fragmentary cloud cannot be found within the vastness of the Great Clarity; this is like the previous analogy of empty space arising from within great awakening, like a single bubble surfacing upon the ocean.
Therefore, it is said, "it is just like," and so forth. Thus, even the production of empty space from true nature is still [like this].
A single speck of cloud appearing in the great void has no point of origin for its arising or ceasing; how much less can there be any "attainment" regarding the worlds produced therein?

Just as the previously mentioned dust-mote lands of the outflows are all produced in dependence upon space—yet when the bubble vanishes, the space itself was originally non-existent—how much more so is this true for the various realms of the threefold existence (*tridhātu*)?
Thus, they are produced through delusion upon delusion. When one investigates the reason for this, it is entirely due to the delusion of a single thought of ignorance (*avidyā*).
It arises from the Real. If one shatters the delusion of ignorance, one awakens that true nature and returns to its original luminosity.
Once the capacity to produce ignorance is shattered, the empty space produced by it naturally dissolves and perishes.

If even empty space is thus, how much more so the worlds and lands, which by their very nature tremble and shatter. Thus, how could there be any substance of delusion to be found? Therefore, it is said: "You all..."
...and so forth. Regarding "developing the truth and returning to the source": "Truth" (*zhen*) refers to the one true self-nature (*svabhāva*), which is inherently possessed from the beginning.

Because one was deluded by falsehoods, that truth was obscured; now that delusion has been shattered, the truth manifests before one—hence it is called "developing the truth. "Source" (*yuan*) refers to primordial luminosity (*prakṛti-prabhāsvara*), which is fundamentally indestructible.

Because one was pursued by falsehoods, that primordial luminosity was lost; now that falsehoods have been extinguished, primordial luminosity naturally returns—hence it is called "returning to the source. Thus, one should know the Buddha...
It is taught that the one true self-nature and the arising of Buddhas and sentient beings are non-dual;

it is taught that through delusion of the truth, falsehood arises, yet within total falsehood there is no truth. You should know that this teaching clarifies that if one shatters that falsehood, falsehood cannot be found.

The explanation of the causes [of the movement of Māra] is concluded. Second, regarding the clarification of the movement of Māra: "You all" refers to the causes for Māra’s movement; "all things" refers to the characteristics of Māra’s movement;
"ordinary beings" refers to whether they understand or do not understand; "clinging to this" refers to what Māra clings to; and "therefore" refers to Māra coming to cause affliction.
As for the phrase "you all," the meaning is this: if you cultivate *samādhi*, you shall awaken to the truth and return to the source.
Those bodhisattvas and great arhats also cultivate *samādhi* and likewise awaken to the truth and return to the source.
There is no principle revealed by one that is not understood by the other, and no essence of realized wisdom that is not mastered by the other. It is like using water—[to wash away defilements].
Merging the water with the light, they enter into the light; both are of the same essence of the single true self-nature, profoundly still. Therefore, it says, "you all are equal.

Such is the cause of the demons' agitation. As for the phrase "all are equal": once one has awakened to the truth and returned to the source, the void shall naturally dissolve and vanish, and the lands shall shake and split asunder.
Thus, the palaces collapse and crack, the great earth trembles and breaks apart, and the waters...
This refers to Lu Feiteng (陸飛騰). In essence, the three items beginning with the palaces are the objects perceived, while the three items beginning with the Māra kings are the perceivers.
There is no one who does not feel awe and trepidation; this means that upon seeing these signs, one is struck with awe and trepidation.

Within the category of "objects perceived," the two characters "without cause" (wúgù) appear in all three instances beginning with the palaces. As for the phrase "without cause," it also applies to the three instances beginning with the Māra kings.

All [phenomena] possess the capacity for supernatural penetration (*abhijñā*), such that they can cause palaces to collapse, the great earth to tremble, and creatures of water and land to leap upward.

Now, since those [spirits] do not employ such penetration yet this phenomenon occurs, it is said to be "without cause" (*nirhetuka*). If something moves without cause, one ought naturally to be struck with awe and trepidation;

thus, we know that the phrase "water and land" also belongs to the category of the perceived object. Since ancient times, all have viewed this as the perceiving subject; it is for this reason that there is no doubt regarding this meaning.

Such are the signs of Māra’s agitation. Regarding "ordinary persons and others": this refers to those such as the Māra kings who, though seeing no cause for it, are moved and thereby give rise to alarm and trepidation.

Among them, those ordinary persons who cannot penetrate [the truth] do not know that this is merely the shifting and vacuous delusion arising when one who cultivates *samādhi* awakens to the truth and returns to the source. This selection [of them] is based on their lack of knowledge, because they have not yet attained [realization].
This is because of the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*). They have departed; they are those of clear knowledge. It should be understood that such is the nature of knowing and not knowing.

However, even if you were to cultivate samādhi and destroy that empty space, how could one who clings to the dust and toil of false delusions allow you to rend it asunder and annihilate it? Therefore, it says, "clinging to these," and so forth. Such is the clinging of Māra. Because of this—

It is for the sake of allowing you to crush and tear them apart. Māras and their like all come to disturb you, the practitioner of *samādhi*, so as not to allow your practice to reach fulfillment or to cause its destruction at that place;
thus it is said, "Therefore," and so forth. Such is the manner in which the Māras come to disturb you.
Thus one knows that the arrival of Māra is fundamentally caused by spiritual cultivation. Should not those who practice be cautious? Therefore, there follows a passage of admonition.
Although it is said that when one awakens to the truth and returns to the source, the empty space, lands, and worlds are destroyed, there still remain classes of Māras upon whom one might rely.
Why then do they so persistently harass the practitioner? It is only because they fear the moment of his attaining Buddhahood.

The radiance of his light shines so brightly that none among the demonic hordes can survive it; thus, they come to cause disturbance at the very moment when [the Bodhisattva’s] attainment is about to be realized but not yet fully accomplished.
Question: When one person develops the true mind and returns to the source, the ten voids are all dissolved and the great earth is entirely rent asunder.
Since ancient times, many have attained Buddhahood; why then do the void and the world remain as they were?
"Is it so? He replied, "When the Buddhas attain Buddhahood and give rise to the True Return to the Source, they only shatter their own ignorance and cease the destruction of their own empty space.
The ignorance of sentient beings is not shattered, and thus emptiness and earth remain as they were.
He asked again, "If it is the case that the Buddhas are precisely destroying their own empty space and great earth, why do celestial Māras and others all see their palaces [as before]?"

"Did the palace collapse, the great earth split open, and all creatures on land and in water leap up in terror? He replied, "According to the teachings of the *lakṣaṇa* school, ignorance has both specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) aspects that differ.
If one destroys specific ignorance, the empty space and the great earth are destroyed, yet those various māras do not even know it themselves.
If one destroys general ignorance, the empty space and the great earth are destroyed, and those various māras [likewise do not know it]."

This should be understood by oneself. Nevertheless, although Buddhas and sentient beings differ in their states of delusion and enlightenment, these sentient beings likewise abide within the world of empty space;
therefore, it is logically necessary to know that they perish when [the world] dissolves. Furthermore, they all belong to the category of the heterodox.
When the Buddha attained enlightenment, he intended precisely to overturn their depravity and restore them to the correct path.
Regarding those beings, it is the natural law (*dharmatā*) that they are interconnected; therefore, there is nothing he does not know. If one were to further investigate this in its ultimate reality:

when the Buddhas achieve Buddhahood, the void is dissolved and the lands are rent asunder, yet the void and the earth remain as they were. There is no other reason for this than that the Buddhas of the ten directions are inherently without [duality].

Measurements are infinite, and sentient beings of the ten directions are likewise infinite; they are all infinite. Precisely when the Buddhas attain enlightenment, it is exactly the time when sentient beings are born.

Thus one knows that when the Buddhas achieve Buddhahood, they shall destroy the lands of empty space, and when sentient beings are born, they shall form the lands of empty space. One destroys and one forms; the two coincide in that very place.
Therefore, in destruction one does not see destruction; in formation one does not see formation; yet they remain ever-present.
This is what is meant by the inexhaustibility of empty space, the inexhaustibility of worlds, the inexhaustibility of sentient beings, and the inexhaustibility of all Buddhas.

The third part is the section on exhortation and admonition, which has two sub-sections. First, the exhortation by means of awakening: "Now, as for those [demons]... Second, the exhortation by means of non-awakening: "If they are not equal...
Regarding the first, the exhortation by means of awakening: "Now, as for those [demons]... This refers to the preceding account of the various māras coming to cause affliction;
therefore, it says "greatly enraged. The two lines concerning "those dusts" contrast the real with the false. Although they are greatly enraged, however...
Within the midst of false and delusive afflictions, since you have already cultivated wondrous contemplation, you abide within the subtle and marvelous awareness of the true nature.
"Like the wind below" is a metaphor for how the false cannot destroy the true. "As you below" is a metaphor for how the true can shatter that falsehood.
"In vain relying on below" means that if you can cultivate with firm resolve, even if others gain strength from you, they remain merely guests.

They cannot destroy your master. [The phrase] "accomplishing the lower" means that if you wish to achieve samādhi and destroy the afflictions and disturbances of others, there is no other method than through your own five aggregates as your master.
The master of the five aggregates is precisely the eternally abiding true mind.
If the master is able to remain alert and aware, the guest-demons will find no opportunity; should the master, however—
In a state of profound darkness, the guest-demons seize the opportunity to enter; hence it is said that they "achieve" [their ends] and so forth. Regarding the phrase "at that very place":
if one wishes for the master of the five aggregates to become alert and aware, one must observe them solely through the three inconceivable and wondrous contemplations of *dhyāna*.
"There is nothing that can be done about you. Regarding "the obscurations dissolve" (*yin xiao*): those demons are darkness, while wondrous observation (*miao guan*) is light.

When wondrous observation awakens and illuminates, the demonic darkness dissolves and falls away at that very thought; how could it further cause disturbance? Therefore, it is said that "the obscurations dissolve," and so forth. This is an exhortation.
Thus, one knows that whether the demons come or not depends solely on whether one cultivates wondrous observation or not. As for that observation:
How could this be tolerated? Second, the middle section uses "non-awakening" as a warning. If one does not apply the correct admonition, it is clarified by the example of Māra at the end;

this then serves as the conclusion and demonstration. The initial statement, "If you are not equal," means that if you do not awaken even once, not only will you be unable to refute others, but you yourself will instead be refuted, becoming a child of Māra and a partisan of Māra.
Therefore, it is said that they are not equal. Regarding the second point, the phrase "such as Ma" and so forth cites that minor instance as an example for this case of intense power.

This means that although Dengga was merely a single courtesan, and she merely used a mantra to curse you—intending only to destroy your single precept against sexual misconduct—your precept-body remained pure;
even when subjected to such influence, it was not destroyed, nor did it fall into ruin or sink away.

It is submerged; thus it is said, "like Ma" and so forth. Regarding the three [types of destruction], this "equal" refers to the intention that even when that single courtesan, Taṅga, violated one of your precepts, you were still unable to overcome her;

now, however, the demonic activities are rampant, and all your inherent merit and wealth, as well as your subtle and wondrous Dharma-body, are utterly destroyed. Therefore, it is said, "it ruins your treasure."

Awaken your entire body. Furthermore, you may treasure this awakened entire body as being entirely the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This is because Ānanda previously stated that one does not attain the Dharma-body without passing through countless *asaṃkhyeya-kalpas*;
therefore, it is said that [this practice] "destroys your Dharma-body. If the Dharma-body is destroyed, the seed of Buddhahood is severed.

As for the nature of this harm, it is as described below. This is further clarified through a metaphor. The intent is that, as previously mentioned, the *ḍākinī* mantra’s harming you is very slight—merely like the plundering of a commoner’s household.
However, when demonic classes cause the ruin of your Dharma-body, it is like a high minister’s family being subjected to confiscation;
thus, it is said to be "like a high minister," and so forth. It is in this way that [it harms].

Admonition: You originally intended to destroy Māra through your practice, yet you have instead been turned by Māra to become his son and his partisan, like a high minister’s family undergoing confiscation of its property.
Investigate the reason for this: it arises from your failure to realize that which is realization.
How can you not exert yourself? This concludes the general clarification.

The second part, the detailed exposition of the divisions, consists of five sections. The first reveals the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*), and so on, up to the fifth, which reveals the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
