To "shatter the five aggregates" does not mean to destroy those five aggregates. Rather, it means that because one has never previously cultivated this Dharma-gate of perfect penetration, this wondrous wisdom has not manifested before one, and one has failed to realize that the very substance of the five aggregates is the *tathāgatagarbha*. Now, having attained this contemplation...
As one gradually advances and enters [the path], one is able to thoroughly comprehend that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are, in their very substance, the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.

This means that while there is nothing to be destroyed when destroying [delusion], delusion is entirely true; while there is nothing to be revealed when revealing [the truth], delusion and truth are non-dual. Furthermore, within the five aggregates, there are horizontal and vertical distinctions of position.

If discussed vertically, the destruction of the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) constitutes the stage of contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*), and the destruction of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is...

The first two of the similar [stages] correspond to the second faith; breaking through the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) corresponds to the third and fourth of the similar stages, which are the second faith;

breaking through the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha) corresponds to the fifth and sixth of the similar stages, which are the second faith; and breaking through the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) corresponds to the seventh of the similar stages, which is the second faith. If discussed horizontally:

If one were able to sever [the afflictions] in a single thought-moment, one would immediately destroy ignorance, manifest the Middle Way, enter the first stage (*prathamabhūmi*), and become a Buddha within the hundred realms.
However, this discussion now proceeds from the perspective of the vertical progression.

First, the aggregate of visible form (*rūpa-skandha*) is divided into three major sections: first, "Ānanda, you should know," etc., which is the heading; second, "Ānanda, you should remain," etc., which is the explanation;

third, "Ānanda, it is thus," etc., which is the concluding exhortation. The first section [the heading] further has two parts: first, the accomplishment of contemplation, namely, from "Ānanda" onwards;
second, the manifestation of the object, namely, from "you should abide" onwards. Within the first part, the accomplishment of contemplation, [it begins with] "You are seated," etc.

Regarding the second, the characteristics of the exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), there are two parts: first, the direct clarification; second, the causal basis. Within the first part, regarding "if movement, etc.": this refers to perception (*saṃjñā*).
To take the characteristics of ideation as its object is what constitutes the movement of thought. Once the movement of thought is exhausted, floating ideations naturally vanish;

thus it is said, "if one moves," and so forth. Regarding "at awakening" and so on, this means that when the aggregate of ideation (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is exhausted, contemplation advances further and the objective realm becomes increasingly manifest.

"One category" and so on refers to the moment the aggregate of ideation is exhausted and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) stands before one. The aggregate of formations flows and shifts from moment to moment; it begins with birth and continues onward.
The "tail" refers to death and its conclusion. When such signs are perceived without exception, it is said that "one category [of phenomena] is thus.
Since practice has already been brought before one, the exhaustion of thought can be known; therefore, it is called the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of perception).

As long as the *saṃskāra-skandha* is not exhausted, one cannot yet escape the marks of perception regarding all phenomena, and thus gives rise to the private attachments of craving and love. Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* is exhausted, one naturally attains transcendence.
It transcends afflictions (*kleśa*). This is why it was stated previously that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) constitutes the essence of the turbidity of afflictions.
Regarding the second cause, "observing its equality": once the principle of reality (*tattva*) is manifested, the origin of delusion naturally becomes visible.

Because one penetrates and thoroughly understands illusory perceptions through this integration, the existence of this aggregate of perception serves as the root of the turbidity of views (*dṛṣṭi-kāṣāya*); hence, it says, "observing its equality."

Second, the explanation of the fulfillment [of the practice] is also divided into ten parts, the sequence of which can be seen [in the text]. Each contains three sections: first, from "Good son" downward, the section on meritorious practice;

second, from "Samādhi" downward, the section on the manifestation of the objective realm; third, from "You now" downward, the section on admonition and exhortation. The beginning and end of each are identical.

There are no separate sections for the preceding or following parts; there are only two present states, which are further divided into two. First, internally generating greed and attachment, such as "the samādhi... and so forth.

Second, externally inviting demonic interference, such as "at that time... and so forth. The external invitation of demonic interference is further divided into two: first, from "at that time" onwards, the demons come to cause disturbance;
second, from "disturbance" onwards, the demons depart and calamities are summoned. Regarding the first, the demons coming to cause disturbance, it is further divided into...

Four points: First, "At that time" and so forth, refers to the arrival of Māra; second, "Its form" and so forth, refers to the manifestation of his appearance; third, "Within the mouth" and so forth, refers to the preaching of the Dharma; fourth, "This name" and so forth, refers to the naming of him.
These ten passages are all like this, though their beginnings and endings differ slightly; I shall briefly indicate these as they appear in the text.
Regarding the first section on the practice of seeking skillful means, the phrase "the skandha of sensation is empty and subtle" refers to that sensation.

Since the *skandha* of form (*rūpa*) has been destroyed, there is only the single Truth. "Not encountering perverse considerations" and so forth: perverse consideration is the *skandha* of perception (*saṃjñā*).

This means that as one is about to destroy the *skandha* of perception, the contemplation advances further; hence it is said, "not encountering," and so on. The same applies to the nine subsequent passages; their meaning is likewise the same.

Within the first section on "internally generating craving and attachment," there is the wisdom accomplished through perfect clarity (*pariśuddha-prabhāsvara*), and the [wisdom] emitted by skillful means (*kauśalya*).
This is its application. To discuss it based on its actual substance: the two "stoppings" are one and the same. Thus, the mind cherishes luminous perfection and seeks skillful means;
even to the point where the mind cherishes longevity and seeks eternal years. Characters such as "sharpened," "soaring," and so forth, all collectively describe the urgency of greedy seeking.

Nevertheless, these two matters are certainly not to be delayed by the practitioner. If the *saṃjñā-skandha* (perception aggregate) is shattered, [the next stage] will naturally manifest before them. Now...
Desiring to shatter the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), his mind delights in perfect clarity and his thoughts greedily seek out skillful means;

this is the very beginning of inviting Māra, which is why external demonic affairs subsequently arise. The subsequent passages—such as "his mind loves to wander" and "greedily seeking experience"—should be understood by analogy with this.
Regarding Māra’s arrival, as for those whose spirits fly and attach themselves to people, they are compared to the "forms" mentioned previously.
Regarding the two aggregates of feeling (*vedanā-skandha*) and perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*), there are two different mental states.

First, when there is externally an object of perception (*ālambana-rūpa*) and internally a feeling that experiences it, the internal and external are intertwined such that form and feeling stand together; at this juncture, Māra enters one’s innermost organs.
However, in this aggregate of perception, there is only a single thought-moment existing within, and no external object can come near before it. He...
The Māra has no means of entry. It is simply that his essence flies forth, attaches itself to an external person, and thus the Māra arrives.

Second, when the preceding form and sensation are in mutual relation, there is an objective sphere that can be seen. Therefore, that Māra no longer manifests as an object, but enters directly into the mind.
At this point, the mental conception and the external object do not meet one another; precisely at the moment of harboring such a thought, it attaches itself to another.

The person appears before the practitioner's field of perception, causing that practitioner to believe and accept it; for this reason, a flying spirit (*fei-jing*) attaches itself to the person. Question:
Since the *māra* does not attach itself to the practitioner, how is it that another person can be possessed by it? Answer: The person who is possessed is also a practitioner; it is not without cause.
It is simply that they have broken through the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) but have not yet broken through the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). For this reason, the flying...
And as for "attachment": how many instances of the character "person" (ren) are there? If one understands each of their meanings individually, they will naturally become clear.
When a flying spirit attaches itself to a person, that person does not realize it; the "person" who has departed from that body is the spirit that has attached itself.
That person who causes the other to see [the spirit] is deluded, confused, and distressed—the "person" who is the third is the one possessed by the demon. As for... [text ends].
What is now being explained is that which is beloved, the perfect clarity, and the sought-after skillful means; the same applies to all subsequent sections.

This is called "ghostly marvels" (preta-vikṛti), referring specifically to the "greedy ghosts" (*rāga-preta*) within the aforementioned realm of hungry ghosts (*preta-gati*). These ten [categories] share many similarities with the ten types mentioned previously.
There are only one or two final points that differ. When the mouth speaks of the sūtras and the Dharma, it merely attaches itself to the sūtras; it is not necessarily the sūtra itself.
What is spoken from the mouth consists only of empty and extravagant words. The same applies to everything that follows; the rest may be understood accordingly.

When the demon departs, calamity beckons. The disciple and the master—the master being the one to whom the demon has attached itself, and the disciple being the one possessed by the demon—both fall into royal peril.

At the time when the demonic activity is at its height, even though the royal law is strict, they may fear that it is indeed genuine and thus dare not move. Once the demon has departed, everything becomes utterly different from before. Thus...
Knowing this to be the work of Māra, one subsequently encounters the king’s law; this is the "flower-retribution" for the difficulty of the king, which is the "fruit-retribution" of hell.

Among the three types of exhortation and admonition: "You should always... and so forth are the exhortations; "being deluded... and so forth are the admonitions. Below these follow the exhortations and admonitions regarding spiritual practice.

Furthermore, when internal greed and attachment arise within the present sensory realm, and external Māras come to disturb and confuse one during their demonic activities, the departure of the Māras brings about calamity.

The middle two [sections] are both the same as the preceding; only the third differs in that it manifests a form—either one's own form or another's form, or causing oneself or another to become small. This can also be seen according to the text, so no further division is made.

Within the second [section], regarding the manifestation of forms resulting from the pursuit of experience, it says: "Heresy secretly arises," and so forth. Heresy and the Right Path cannot coexist. If you...
When the wisdom of contemplation is perfectly clear and illuminates all-encompassingly, erroneous wisdom naturally recedes.
If your mind harbors even the slightest error, then false views will immediately follow; the interval between them is no wider than a hair’s breadth. Therefore, it is called "secret.

Regarding the phrase "dense and tangled" within the internal mind that greedily seeks accord with the principle: this refers to the desire to cause one's practice to accord with the principle of the fruit. [The text then says: "manifesting form."

In the middle [section], it says that there is no external transition or change. This differs from the previous [section], where the listeners were made to become Śakra and so forth, or to sit upon lotus pedestals;
here, one only causes their own nature to open. Therefore, it is said that there is no external transition or change. Within the preaching of the Dharma, there is also the "True Buddha";
this merely distinguishes between the true and the false based on the relative priority of the Mahāyāna and Hīnayāna. [This] washes away the fundamental...
"Mind" refers to the original mind, which denotes the *samādhi* being cultivated. When one is afflicted by demons, one turns true cultivation into perverse practice;
what was previously cultivated no longer remains, much like something that has been washed away.
Among the four types of internal craving for analytical seeking, "craving for the root of the mind" refers to the desire to seek out the primary cause of things.
Therefore, it is simply called "exhaustively surveying" and so forth. Regarding the phrase "manifesting forms, [including] the Buddha and others":

the *nirvāṇa*, liberation, bodhi, prajñā, and dharma-body—specifically the dharma-body—is the manifestation of the secret treasury of the three virtues within one's own internal body. Since this is none other than the non-demonic, how could it be anything else?
Within the five types of craving for a hidden response, amidst the inner mind’s greedy attachment, the mind’s longing elicits a responsive resonance.
This refers to those who desire to precede all Buddhas in their manifestation; thus it is said they "greedily seek a response from the unseen. The rest may be understood.

Sixth, regarding the inner mind that greedily seeks tranquility within the midst of craving: when the mind's attachment penetrates deeply, it means that the more refined one becomes, the more one seeks refinement;
the more profound one becomes, the more one seeks profundity. Thus it is said they "greedily seek tranquility. Within the manifestations of form, each knows [their own state].

The "original practitioner" (mūlakarmika) causes those who previously listened to him to also attain the supernormal power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-jñāna*). Within this, he possesses all five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*);
one should know that even Māra attains these five supernormal powers. The rest is understandable. Regarding the seventh [category], "inner craving for the pursuit of past lives":

among the cravings of the mind, "craving for knowledge and vision" refers to the desire to obtain the three types of knowledge (*trividya*) within a single moment of mind, and to see with the five eyes (*pañcacakṣus*) within a single eye.
"Ear" refers to the name within the list. "Or there are those who proclaim lewdness" means that they announce matters of lust to one another. The rest may be understood accordingly.

Eighth, regarding the inner mind’s greedy seeking of supernormal powers (*ṛddhi*) among the various forms of internal craving: as for "the mind loving supernormal powers," such powers differ in their magnitude. There are small and great types;

the small are attained through cultivation (*bhāvanā*), while the great are attained through realization (*sākṣātkriyā*). That which is attained through realization is the unobstructed power of transformation (*nirmāṇa-ṛddhi*).
Those who attain through cultivation possess nothing more than supernormal powers produced by mental attention (*manasikāra*).

Yet, even these are unattainable in the Lesser Vehicle (*Hīnayāna*), let alone within this Mahāyāna. Regarding the manifestation of forms, the only reason one lacks mastery over weapons is that those [beings] follow false teachings and thus cannot remain unimpeded by them.
As for Bodhisattva Dharanimdhara, who has realized the nature-inherent [wisdom], he is as follows:
Even those weapons do not cause contact. As for those who slander meditation (*dhyāna*) and discipline (*vinaya*): meditation is the nature of clarity, and discipline is the restraint of the body.
If one slanders them, how could such things exist unless it were due to the confusion of Māra? The rest may be understood. Ninth, regarding the internal mind that craves profound emptiness:
among the cravings of the mind, "the mind loving entry into extinction" seeks the true stillness of the very essence itself; therefore, it is...
It is said that they greedily seek the profound emptiness. Within their manifested forms, they possess the mastery of appearing; they likewise possess the mastery of vanishing.

Therefore, it concludes by stating they have "mastery over appearance and disappearance. Regarding their preaching of the Dharma, the phrase "no cause and no effect" means they fail to understand that sentient beings take afflictions as the cause to produce the fruit of birth and death, whereas Bodhisattvas take contemplative wisdom as the cause to evoke [the fruit].
Regarding the fruit of *nirvāṇa*, how could one deny both cause and effect? The rest can be understood accordingly.

Regarding the phrase "those who laboriously investigate the subtle within the inner mind of craving for transformation": this refers to those who exert themselves with diligent hardship to polish and examine the most minute principles in order to seek longevity.
Regarding the phrase "discarding [theories of] partiality and annihilation," etc.: it is because they desire to attain long years and eternal life.

If one wishes to attain transformation (pariṇāma), one must naturally abandon the body of segmented birth (bhavasaṃdhi). As for "transformation," it means transforming coarse form into subtle substance and changing a short lifespan into long years;
this is a general explanation. If one pursues this further, it refers to transforming the retributive life-span and attaining the Dharma-nature body (dharmatā-kāya).
Within the manifestation of forms, [the mention of] "sometimes" and so forth correctly explains the aforementioned lack of obstruction in coming and going.
In some cases, what is distant appears near; in others, what is near appears distant.

Regarding the teaching that "all sentient beings of the ten directions are my children," one must understand that even the doctrines of heterodox outsiders are merely adaptations of the Buddha's own teachings spoken by them.
I have heard the Buddha say that all sentient beings are his children; for this reason, I also speak thus, desiring only to inspire in people respectful faith.

Regarding the name *Candā*, there are two kinds: those who have awakened the resolve (*bodhicitta*) will surely protect the Buddha-dharma, while those who have not yet awakened the resolve will harass practitioners.
As for "benefiting their empty clarity," it refers to greedily grasping at the emptiness and subtlety of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*).

Furthermore, regarding those who do not rely on a teacher: this does not necessarily mean they see [the truth] through someone they have attached themselves to, but rather that they perceive it for themselves.

As for the phrase "mouths both speaking alone": the word "both" (兼) likely refers back to the aforementioned "manifesting beautiful women. "Speaking alone" means speaking only to oneself. The rest is understandable.

The third section, the exhortation to practice, is divided into two parts: first, from "Ānanda" onwards, the detailed exposition; second, from "Ānanda" onwards, the concise summary. This concludes the detailed exposition.
Furthermore, there are two parts: first, the summary of faults and afflictions, concerning Ānanda and others; second, the exhortation to propagate and proclaim, concerning "you now" and others.
Within this extensive section, the summary of faults and the exhortation to propagate differ in their textual intent from the previous passage on the two aggregates of form and feeling.

In those [previous] passages, both were summarized as ten types of present faults and afflictions, and an exhortation was made to propagate them so that sentient beings of future generations might thereby obtain protection.
"Protecting the attainment of the Way. This refers to the ten types [of obstacles] that delude practitioners during the final age; it is spoken to exhort Ānanda to rescue and deliver them.
As for the abbreviated and intermediate versions, the meaning of the text is the same as before. Regarding the summary of faults and afflictions, it says:
"Those who have left the home life to cultivate the Way within my Dharma" involves different ways of inclusion and exclusion. For instance, regarding the true cultivation of *samādhi*:
Such persons are those who are to be gathered. If there are those who, for instance, attach themselves to others and so forth, these are those who are to be rejected.

Those who are rejected are the aforementioned types such as "peddlers" (*prapañca*) and the like—those who wear the robes and consume the food of the Tathāgata, thereby destroying the Dharma of the Tathāgata.
"Nine births and a hundred births" refers to lifetimes, which is to say, successive worlds; this means that such demonic classes will flourish after my parinirvāṇa. To speak briefly:

If one speaks in terms of the immediate future, it refers to nine generations, which is the end of the *saddharma* (True Dharma) period. If one speaks from a distant perspective, it refers to a hundred generations, which is the time of the *pratirūpakadharma* (Semblance Dharma) following the *asaddharma* (End of Dharma).

Regarding the exhortation to propagate [the teaching] in the intermediate period, you, Ananda and others, must understand that if one does not preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, one will ultimately be unable to repay the Buddha’s kindness.
Within the brief summary, there are also two parts: first, Ananda and those below summarize the faults and afflictions; second, you...
The subsequent conclusion regarding the extensive proclamation should be understood by following the same pattern as the preceding examples for form (*rūpa*) and feeling (*vedanā*).

Since the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has both an extensive and an abbreviated version, the remaining four aggregates should be treated likewise. As it is with the middle [aggregate], so it may be inferred for those before and after; therefore, they are presented only in brief and lack an extensive version.
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Nine;
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama Sūtra, Volume Ten.
Expounded by the Great Master Yisong of Tiantai.
Recorded by Lingshu, a disciple of the Yu-xi Gate.
Since that good man [Vimalakīrti] departed from Ānanda, the two aggregates of perception (*saṃjñā*) and mental formations (*saṃskāra*) have been clarified.

However, this is not the same as the previous three aggregates—form (*rūpa*), feeling (*vedanā*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—where demons arise from one's own mind to produce false interpretations; here, there are those who manifest as spirits possessing people to come and cause affliction.
As for "persons," these present two aggregates (skandhas) are merely their own conjectures, which are identical to the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Section Four: Manifesting the Aggregate of Formations (saṃskāra-skandha), divided into two parts. First, following the previous exhaustion of the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā), [it concerns] Ānanda and others. Second, clarifying the present aggregate of formations.

This concerns arising and ceasing, and so forth. First, regarding the section on the exhaustion of prior perceptions (*pūrvakalpa-kṣaya*): "those who are virtuous" and so on is the thesis (*uddiṣṭa*);

"these people" and so on is the explanation (*nirdeśa*). This explanation has two parts: first, the explanation of the exhaustion of perception, which begins with "these people"; second, the manifestation of what is seen, which begins with "awakened clarity. Within the first part:

This dream-vision is not the same as what is taught in the *Śrīmālādevī-siṃhanāda Sūtra*. That sūtra refers to the stages from the first bhūmi (prathamabhūmi) up to the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyaksaṃbodhi*);

there, one not only partially severs ignorance (*avidyā*), but has also severed it until it is nearly exhausted. In this context, however, we are dealing only with the fourth and fifth levels of faith (*śraddhā*) within the stage of semblance (*tatsādṛśya*).

Regarding the cessation of delusions, this involves the severing of the views and thoughts (*dṛṣṭi-kāma-vidyā*); regarding the cessation of the aggregates (*skandha*), it involves the severing of three of the five aggregates. Recently, some have interpreted it according to that [sūtra].

This may be the same as that of a Bodhisattva; however, there are certainly differences regarding the depth of their stages and the coarseness or subtlety of their delusions, which might be considered inconvenient [to equate].

In the context of the present treatise, it refers to the time before the *saṃjñā-skandha* (aggregate of perception) has been destroyed—what is called "running through perceptions by day and binding dreams by night.
Once the *saṃjñā-skandha* is exhausted, since even perception itself cannot be found, from what could dreams arise? Therefore, it is said that "dreams and thoughts are extinguished."
If those dream-thoughts have not yet been extinguished, there will necessarily be thought upon waking and dreaming while asleep.
Waking and sleeping are inherently not constant or identical; once dream-thoughts have ceased, although waking and sleeping still occur, they are always one and the same.

When thought is thus exhausted, the aggregate of perception (saṃjñā-skandha) is ended, and the principle naturally manifests. The wondrously enlightened, luminous essence is empty yet unimpeded, and tranquil yet...
Because it is immovable, it is called "awakened clarity, empty and still. This is explained through a metaphor, like a clear and bright sky.
Therefore, it is said to be "like a cloudless sky. Within the cloudless sky, there is unobstructed penetration and transparency, with no further illusory obscurations;
hence, it is said "no longer" and so forth. Since the observing mind is like the cloudless sky, free from dust and shadows, one knows that the observed mountains...

The rivers, the great earth, light and darkness, form and emptiness are not unseen; however, when they are seen, it is merely like a bright mirror set upon its stand, illuminating all that comes before it.
Thus it is said, "Observing all things, etc. When objects and images arrive, there is never any sticking or clinging;
when objects and images pass away, there is never any trace left behind. Thus it is said, "Coming, there is no [coming], etc."

This is the convergence of dharmas such as empty reception. Since both sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) have been exhausted, the objects (*viṣaya*) have no basis whatsoever within the sense faculties (*indriya*).
This is what is meant by "gathering conditions, shaking inwardly, and abandoning oneself. Furthermore, the faculties likewise have no place of reliance within the objects;
this is what is meant by "rushing outward and fleeing far away. It is like a bright mirror reflecting objects: it is solely empty and still, illuminating only the void. Therefore, it is said:
This refers to "receiving in vain" and so forth.

Second, the explanation of the present *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) further has three parts. First, "the root-source of birth and death" and so forth is the heading. Second, "Ānanda, you should know" and so forth is the detailed explanation.
Third, "Ānanda, it is thus" and so forth is the concluding exhortation. Within the first heading, there are two further sections; the first begins with "birth and death" and continues below.
The characteristic of the movement not yet being exhausted. Second, the characteristic of this movement having been exhausted.

Within the first, the characteristic of the movement not yet being exhausted, "arising, ceasing, and so forth" refers to the characteristics of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—the subtle, dense shifting and moment-to-moment流转 (transmigration) of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Previously, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) had not been destroyed and the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) had not yet manifested. Now that the aggregate of perception has been exhausted, the aggregate of formations stands before one;
therefore, it is said that "arising and ceasing," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "seeing all," *dān* means "exhaustion. This refers to the reason why the twelve categories of beings arise:
they arise solely because the aggregate of formations arises. The reason why the twelve categories of beings cease: they cease solely because the aggregate of formations ceases.

It is for the sake of cessation. Since the twelve classes of beings throughout the ten directions have already manifested their arising and ceasing within the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), there is nothing that cannot be seen;
hence it says, "seeing all," and so forth. As for the phrase "though not yet equal": all sentient beings take consciousness as their root and starting point.

Not only has the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) not been destroyed, but it has also not yet manifested. Therefore it says, "though not yet equal. [This refers to] the aggregate of consciousness.

It has not yet manifested. However, as for the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) being the arising and ceasing of the twelve classes of beings, it is like the shimmering appearance of a mirage;

there is no one who does not see through its depths. Thus it is said that they are seen as equal. Regarding the "shimmering mirage," some say it refers to a brilliant, flashing light, but this is incorrect.
This is actually a solar illusion (*marīci*) consisting of dust and mist, which merely arises and ceases momentarily.

This merely describes the state of clarity suddenly turning into darkness. As for "floating dust," it refers to the six internal sense faculties (*ṣaḍāyatana*) and the six external objects (*ṣaḍviṣaya*) of sentient beings.
When the internal and external correspond and the faculties and objects become entangled, there is conceptual discrimination in every thought-moment and craving and attachment in every mind.
All of this has the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations) as its pivot, just as a door has a hinge; it is what is called the "obstruction. It is like a hole in a door.

This refers to what is called the "mortar. Therefore, it is said to be for the sake of floating [the pestle] and so forth. This is precisely what is called the world of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
Thus, it concludes with the words, "This is then," and so on. Regarding the second part, the characteristics of the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations, there are two sections.

First, the direct elucidation, beginning with "If this... and so forth. Second, the causal basis, beginning with "Observing its... and so forth. Within the first section, the passage starting with "If this" concerns the phenomena (*dharma*). As for the phrase "If this... and so forth:
This refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations). What is called "original nature" (*yuanxing*) is merely the nature of habitual conditioning (*xixing*).

"Original clarity" (*yuancheng*) refers to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*). The six consciousnesses are not originally the substance of original clarity; they only enter into original clarity after having already departed from the preceding four aggregates.

Thus, one knows that both "original nature" and "original clarity" cannot be equated with the self-nature of "original luminosity" (*yuanyang mingzixing*). The phrase "once clarified" (*yi cheng*) below is a metaphor.
"First, the primordial habituation becomes clarified" refers to entering the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) based on one's fundamental nature.

Because this stage is free from the preceding four aggregates and consists solely of the *vijñāna-skandha*, it is called "the primordial habituation becomes clarified. To illustrate this through a metaphor:

it is like turbulent waves transforming into clear, still water. For the *saṃskāra-skandha* (formative aggregate) is like the waves of water, while the *vijñāna-skandha* is like the clarity and stillness of the water.

Now that the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been exhausted, only the fundamental clarity of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) remains; it is like waves turning into still, limpid water.
Thus it is said to be "like waves" and so forth. Nevertheless, the aggregate of consciousness is like a swift-flowing stream; at first glance, it appears to be a fixed, stable entity.

Observing it again, one finds it flowing densely and continuously with scarcely a moment’s rest. Thus, regarding the six consciousnesses, if one speaks in accordance with them, they are likened to clear water;
yet if one refutes this, they are still subject to arising and ceasing. Reaching this point is precisely the sign of the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Therefore, it is said: "The aggregate of formations is abandoned and exhausted. This refers to the subsequent conclusion. The meaning is that as long as the aggregate of formations is not yet exhausted, there remain the moments of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

One contemplates the flux [of the formations aggregate] and perceives how it gives rise to the turbidity of sentient beings. Once the formations aggregate (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is exhausted, the turbidity of sentient beings naturally transcends.
This is why it was said previously that formations constitute the essence of the turbidity of sentient beings. Second, regarding "observing their commonality" within the causal conditions:
once the essence of the True has been revealed, the source of delusion naturally becomes visible. This source is profound, hidden, and obscurely illusory.
This notion—that there is this aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) which serves as the root of the turbidity of sentient beings—is the second [point].

The explanation of the components has ten parts; their sequence can be seen [as follows]: each has (1) the initial [stage], (2) the cultivation of practice, (3) the arising of conceptualization, and (4) the naming of the fetters (*saṃyojana*).
The "cultivation of practice" is identical in being the samādhi of equality. The "naming of the fetters" is identical in being this very equality. All of these are without seeds.
The sections below can be seen [in the original text] and need not be further divided; they differ only in the arising of conceptual calculations and their respective terminations.

Furthermore, there are sub-sections, which I shall now fully indicate: first, regarding the "perfect" (*yuan*) and so forth; second, regarding the "perfect" and so forth; third, regarding the "self" (*zi*) and so forth; fourth, regarding the "parts" (*fen*) and so forth.

Fifth, regarding "knowing" and so forth; sixth, regarding "non-existence" and so forth; seventh, regarding "light" and so forth; eighth, regarding "conduct" and so forth; ninth, regarding "subsequent" and so forth; tenth, regarding "subsequent" and so forth.
These are the categories of the son [of the teaching]; they shall be further divided according to the specific texts.

Regarding the phrase "in the causal practices of the first two [stages], one attains right knowledge, etc.": this refers to śamatha and so forth, which constitute the cultivation of the inconceivable threefold contemplation arising from the entirety of the nature (*dharmatā*).
This distinguishes it from those who cultivate separately outside of the nature, as is the case with the partial [Hīnayāna] and small [vehicles].

Regarding the phrase "concentrated clarity and rectification of the mind" (*niṅ-ming-cheng-xin*): this means that as long as the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) has not been shattered, internal craving and attachment still arise;
thus, it is difficult to speak of "concentration. Once the aggregate of perception is shattered, the internal mind no longer arises—this is what constitutes "concentration.

Furthermore, as long as the aggregate of perception has not been shattered, contemplative wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*) is not clear, and one cannot discern external malevolent spirits; thus, it is difficult to speak of "clarity. Once the aggregate of perception is shattered...
When [delusions] are destroyed, contemplative wisdom becomes increasingly manifest; this is "clarity. Taken together, these constitute the concentrated clarity of the upright mind.
Thus, when no thoughts arise within the inner mind, awakening-wisdom becomes even more manifest. It is not merely that heterodox views and external influences do not interfere;

naturally, Māras find no opportunity. Therefore, it is said that "the ten classes," and so forth. The phrase "thoroughly investigate" should apply to all ten [categories], but their absence in the following nine is merely an abbreviation.
The fundamental substance of sentient beings is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). This is precisely what was previously referred to as "observing the ten directions" and so forth.

Regarding the phrase "only then one attains," it specifically means that once the three aggregates of form, sensation, and perception have been dismantled, one is finally able to minutely examine and investigate the aggregate of formations; hence the expression "only then one attains.

Regarding the phrase "at its source," it specifically refers to the aggregate of formations being present before one, which is the same as what was previously called "the root-source of birth and death" and so forth.

Regarding the observation of those [phenomena]: by means of this intensive investigation and detailed examination of the characteristics of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one sees for oneself that because this aggregate of formations is subtle and hidden, a false conception unknown to people and unseen by people, it is "profound" (*you*).

Yet, because its phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing each have their own distinct limits, it is "clear" (*qing*). Because it can pervade all twelve classes of living beings, it is "round" (*yuan*). Nevertheless, it shifts and changes in a dense and continuous manner.

The flow never ceases; this constitutes "disturbance" (*rajas*). When these illusory marks are about to be destroyed but have not yet been destroyed, they cause agitation within the fundamental luminosity of the self-nature;
this is what is meant by "the movement of the source. This is that which is observed. The observer is the inconceivable *śamatha* and the other two [meditations].
Therefore, it says, "observe them," whereby one immediately and completely realizes that delusion is itself truth. Thus, the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)... [is exhausted].
[This] refutes [the objection]. Should it not yet have been refuted, one would inevitably give rise to false conceptualization; thus, conceptualization arises immediately.
The meaning and intent of the nine subsequent passages are all the same; they may be understood by analogy. Second, the section on "giving rise to conceptualization" is divided into two parts:

first, the combined heading following the section on "perfection"; second, the detailed explanation beginning with "First. Within the combined heading, the phrase "two types of causelessness" refers to the fundamental and the derivative, which can be seen [in the text].

The detailed explanation is further divided into two parts. First is the root [text], which consists of two sections: first, "the equal" (the thesis); second, "the latter" (the explanation). The first part [of the root] is further divided into three:
first, the thesis marked by "the first... is equal"; second, the explanation beginning with "why... is equal"; third, the conclusion beginning with "by this... is equal.

Within the thesis, the phrase "seeing that the root has no cause" refers to the actual arising of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). Within the explanation, the passage "this person... first clarifies the causal basis; "the arising of the faculty" refers to—

This is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Regarding "completely breaking through": previously, the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) was not yet exhausted; thus, the aggregate of formations was covered by it.

Now that the aggregate of perception is exhausted, the aggregate of formations is revealed; this constitutes "complete breaking through. This refers to the state just prior to breaking through, when one has not yet actually broken through.

As for "riding upon the correct emergence of calculation" and saying "riding upon the eye-faculty (*cakṣur-indriya*) and so forth," if one correlates this with the stages, it corresponds to the fifth stage, the Stage of Similarity (*sādṛśyāvasthā*).

The second hexagram, Xìn (Trust), signifies that one is about to attain the purity of the six sense organs and the perfect illumination of the ten realms across the three periods of time; yet this is not yet its time.
Although one may ride upon its power, one perceives only the eighty thousand kalpas of birth and death within the six paths—whether horizontal or vertical, black or white—and so forth.
Within these eighty thousand kalpas, sentient beings are born and die, die and are born; they pass through cycles of birth, death, and rebirth, endlessly.
[The text] ceases here. Therefore, it says "seeing eighty thousand [kalpas]," and so forth; this refers to what is seen. It is merely seeing that which is not yet seen below.

This immediately gives rise to a conceptual calculation regarding the Equal and Right Enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*). From the phrase "it exists of itself" onwards, one should conclude with a reprimand, saying:

"If, through the perfect illumination of wondrous contemplation, there is a perfect manifestation that penetrates past and present, beginning and end, until the stage of the purity of the six sense faculties where one sees in a semblance manner."

Furthermore, since those who have already attained the initial stage (prathama-bhūmi) perceive this through partial realization, how could they mistake eighty thousand kalpas for a realization of sainthood?

The same principle applies to the subsequent stages. Within the summary: the three subtle contemplations constitute "correct knowledge" (samyag-jñāna), while the perfect illumination of these three contemplations constitutes "universal knowledge" (sarva-jñāna).
Correct knowledge distinguishes itself from false knowledge; universal knowledge distinguishes itself from partial or gradual knowledge. Now, due to delusion...

Because calculation results in the loss of wondrous contemplation, it is said, "for this reason," and so forth. There is a correct knowledge that distinguishes itself from heterodox outsiders, whereby one does not fall into the paths of externalists;
there is a universal knowledge that distinguishes itself from partial and gradual [teachings], whereby one personally realizes Bodhi.
Since it is said that both correct and universal knowledge are lost, it follows that externalists should fall [into error] and Bodhi should be confused. All that follows below is...
Thus it is. The two final sections also consist of three parts: the heading, the explanation, and the conclusion; these may be understood by following the previous example. The heading is clear.

In the explanation, the phrase "having seen its root" refers to what is perceived within eighty thousand kalpas. "Knowing that humans... and so forth refers to calculating that worldly phenomena are without cause.
The phrase "now, they are exhausted and equal," etc., means that humans return to being humans, and even animals return to being animals—such as crows.
It returns to being black, and so on, up to returning to being crosswise. My inferior calculation concerns the absence of causes for supramundane dharmas;
my intention is that if there is no cause for bodhi, how can there be the phenomenon of bodhi? Therefore, it says "my [inferior calculation]," and so forth.

The passage beginning with "One should know" combines the mundane and the supramundane; its meaning is that since all mundane dharmas within eighty thousand kalpas are likewise without [causes], and so on.
Regarding causes: even within eighty thousand kalpas of supramundane dharmas, there are likewise no causes. Thus, one knows that all dharmas and phenomena today are entirely without cause.
Some say that the fundamental should produce the derivative; this is also unnecessary.

For if the fundamental itself has no cause, then by extrapolating from the fundamental to the derivative, the latter likewise has no cause. Nevertheless, these two causes—the fundamental and the derivative—comprise a total of eighty thousand kalpas.

It is merely what is seen within [the present]. Beyond eighty thousand kalpas, there is darkness and nothing appears; thus one knows that there is nothing to be observed before, and the beginningless source cannot be found.
There is nothing to be observed after, and the endless end cannot be found. Therefore, though the source and the end are distinguished, both are without cause and share no difference in meaning.
The conclusion of this analogy can be understood from the preceding. Third, regarding the summary of names: this is then...
The term "and so forth" (*ādi*) correctly concludes the discussion of the non-Buddhist outsiders who hold the view of nihilism.
Within the exposition of the two types of pervasive and eternalist views, there are three parts: first, a combined heading;
second, a detailed explanation; and third, a summary conclusion. In the initial combined heading, "perfectly eternal" (*paripūrṇa-nitya*) refers to perfect and permanent abiding.
This is the true arising of conceptualization; what follows is false conceptualization. Regarding the fourth, "pervasive permanence":
those non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) intend for their view to match the Buddha’s perfect permanence, yet it ultimately does not equal it. It is not originally the self-nature of primordial luminosity.

It is called "pervasive" because it serves as the basis for the twelve classes of beings; it is called "permanent" because the principle of transformation—arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing—is never static.
The objects of the first stage are fourfold: first, the four great elements; second, form, sensation, perception, and so forth; third, arising and ceasing; and fourth, permanence.
Indeed, each preceding category is broader than the one following it, while each succeeding category is narrower than the one preceding it. These four are explained in two parts.

Regarding the first two types of permanence—permanence for twenty thousand kalpas and permanence for forty thousand kalpas—they are as previously understood. Regarding the third, permanence for eighty thousand kalpas, and the fourth, the permanence of neither-arising-nor-ceasing, they are as follows: [text continues].
"Constantly within eighty-four thousand kalpas; this person exhausts [them]" and so forth. The "six faculties" (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) refer to the six consciousnesses (*ṣaḍ-vijñāna*);

the capacity is revealed by means of the object. *Manas* refers to the seventh consciousness. "Appropriation" (*upādāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness; it is called appropriation because it contains and stores [seeds].
"Mind, intellect, and consciousness" (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) collectively refer to the eight, seven, and six consciousnesses. Some ask: "How is this the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*)?"

To say that consciousness is not [included] is incorrect. When a practitioner contemplates objects, there is nothing they do not contemplate; it is simply that at the time of deconstruction, they first take form (*rūpa*) and then feeling (*vedanā*), and so forth.
How could one possibly fail to contemplate consciousness? Furthermore, among the dharmas of the three categories (*triskandha*), there is none that is not an object of contemplation.
This [text] speaks only in terms of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*); how could consciousness be absent from them? The fourth point—that which is unborn and unceasing is eternal—is clear. Three.
In summary, this may also be understood as follows: this is precisely the conclusion regarding the eternalist non-Buddhist paths.

Among the three types of practice—eternalism, non-eternalism, and the Middle Way—those who firmly consolidate their correct minds will not be disturbed by external demons; this constitutes their steadfastness.
The non-arising of internal thoughts is termed "concentration" (*niṣyanda*). The further manifestation of contemplative wisdom is termed "rectifying the mind.

The same applies to all subsequent sections. Within the arising of conceptualization, there are also three parts: first, the combined heading from "At one's own... downwards; second, the detailed explanation from "First, one... downwards; third, the summary from "Due to this... downwards.
Regarding the first, the combined heading, the phrase "among oneself and others" refers to the differentiation made by means of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

Regarding self and other: as with the second [case] concerning the land, the third concerning one’s own mind, and the fourth concerning the stream of formations, these are all termed "arising from the conceptualization of self and other.
By this analogy, it refers to the first case, where all sentient beings are born and die within one's own mind, and so forth.

This refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations). These comprise the twelve classes of living beings, who, within a state devoid of self and other, falsely conceptualize self and other.

How could the originally luminous self-nature possess either permanence or impermanence? This is explained in two parts, which further divide into four: first, the self is permanent while those [others] are impermanent;
second, the kalpa is destroyed while the kalpa is not destroyed; third, the self is the transformation of subtle atoms; fourth, formations are permanent.
The rest regarding impermanence—the beginning and the middle—can be understood from the general meaning. As for "contemplating the wondrously luminous mind":

this refers to using fundamental, wondrous contemplation to thoroughly penetrate the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), realizing that it is precisely the wondrously luminous nature of the mind pervading the ten directions.

However, if one fails to investigate with extreme rigor, a single lapse in thought or a single error in perception will cause one to become identical to the calculations of the externalists. Regarding the second [point], one sees...

Regarding "the locus of destruction during the kalpa" and so forth: if one speaks in terms of verticality within a single world-system, everything from the third dhyāna downward is subject to destruction by the three calamities;
this is the locus of destruction. From the fourth dhyāna upward, the three calamities cannot reach; this is the non-destructible locus.
If one speaks in terms of horizontality across various world-systems, perhaps this world-system is destroyed; this is the locus of destruction. Or...

That world is indestructible; this is what is meant by the "indestructible place. Among the three [types of contemplation], the specific observation of one's own mind and so forth refers to the previous contemplation of wondrous clarity, whereas this observes the mind itself—its essence, subtlety, secrecy, and so on. These, too, are instances of giving rise to delusion based on grasping at the Real.
The four [points] can be understood. Within the three [sections], the summary can likewise be understood. Regarding the names of the three fetters (*saṃyojana*), these are equal;
they correctly identify those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold to both eternalism and annihilationism.
The arising of the four theories concerning finitude is also divided into four parts: first, a combined heading regarding the divisions; second, a detailed explanation beginning with "Firstly";

third, a summary beginning with "Therefore"; and fourth, [the conclusion]. Within the initial combined heading, "in the divisions" (*bhāga*) refers both to temporal divisions (*kāla-bhāga*) and spatial directions (*diś-bhāga*).
Although "temporal division" specifically indicates time and "spatial direction" specifically indicates place, in reality, they are mutually inclusive of both time and space.
The two-part explanation is divided into four sections: first, the three temporal limits; second, hearing and seeing; third, self and other; and fourth, arising and ceasing.
Regarding the first [of these], "the mind calculates the source of birth" refers to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) as the fundamental root of the twelve categories of beings.

"The flow of function does not cease" specifically refers to the uninterrupted nature of the *saṃskāra-skandha*'s phases of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing. "Calculating the past and future," etc., refers to the past...
This refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The preceding three aggregates—form, sensation, and perception—have already been dismantled; this constitutes one limit.
As for the aggregate of formations itself, the subsequent aggregate of consciousness has not yet appeared; this constitutes another limit.

"Continuity" refers to the current aggregate of formations as it subtly shifts and incessantly flows on from moment to moment; this constitutes the absence of a limit. Taken together, what is meant is:
The past has already passed; the future has not yet arrived; both are finite. Only the present does not abide, and thus it is infinite.

Among the four [phases], that which is "half-born and half-extinguished" refers to the aggregates of form, feeling, and perception having already been broken—this is the half-extinction—and the aggregate of formations being manifest before one—this is the half-birth. Regarding the three fetters, these are equal.
The "Correct Conclusion" (Zhengjie) likewise refers to those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold both [extremes] and fall outside of the views of eternalism and nihilism.
Among the five types of evasive equivocation (*amarā-vikṣepa*), there are also three parts: first, the combined heading from "At the beginning, regarding knowledge...

onwards; second, the detailed explanation from "First... onwards; and third, the summary conclusion from "Because of this... onwards. Within the combined heading, the phrase "the four inversions" refers to not knowing.
The eternally abiding true mind is inverted when one mistakenly clings to the views of annihilationism or eternalism as being real;

this is what constitutes an inversion. The second section, the explanation of the two types of calculation, further divides into four parts: first, general calculation; second, calculation of non-existence; third, calculation of existence; and fourth, calculation of both existence and non-existence.

Regarding the first [general calculation], "observing transformation" refers to transforming existence into non-existence and manifesting non-existence as existence; this is the general statement. However, regarding birth...
It abides; having abided, it changes; having changed, it ceases. Within this, there is a subtle and continuous flux, which constitutes "transformation.
Thus it is said that one perceives transformation and so forth. Cessation is followed by arising; abiding is followed by arising; change is followed by abiding; and cessation is followed by change.
Their mutual succession constitutes constancy; thus it is said, "the characteristic of seeing, etc.
Regarding the two characteristics of arising and abiding, that which possesses the seeing of what is visible is their arising; thus it is said, "that which is seen, etc.

Regarding the two characteristics of change and cessation, that which lacks the seeing of what is visible is their cessation; thus it is said, "not seeing, etc. Arising occurs in the succession of cessation, and abiding...
When there is no interruption in a different continuum, this is called "increase"; thus it is said, "continuum, etc.

When arising occurs within cessation and abiding occurs within arising, although they constitute a continuum, there is nonetheless that which is departed; this is called "cessation"; thus it is said, "characteristic of arising, etc.
Arising gives rise to arising, abiding gives rise to arising, abiding gives rise to change, and change gives rise to cessation—each is a distinct arising. This is called "existence."

Therefore, it is said that each and every [characteristic] is so. Arising perishes within cessation; abiding perishes within arising; and so on, until cessation perishes within change. They mutually perish. This is what is meant by "non-existence";
thus it is said that each and every [characteristic] is so. One contemplates those eight—change, permanence, and the rest—without exception.
Thus it is said, "by means of contemplation, one contemplates them all. Although it is called contemplating them all, one sees only the one; thus it is said:
He perceived things differently because he applied his mind in a different way. When someone asked about arising, he would immediately answer, "It also arises.
When someone asked about ceasing, he would immediately answer, "It also ceases. Even when someone asked about ceasing, he would immediately answer, "It also ceases.
In this manner, within a single moment, he might speak of arising or speak of ceasing, and so forth.
Some speak of decrease; there is no fixed view to be found. Therefore, it is said, "among those who are equal. Since the teaching is thus, the hearers likewise have no single certainty.
Therefore, it is said, "causing them to be so. Regarding the second [of the three], "clearly observing their mind" refers to observing the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).
"Mutually having no location" is the same as the previous "mutual disappearance of location. Regarding the third, "clearly observing..."
Their minds likewise contemplate the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). Regarding "each having its own place," this refers to their respective places of birth as previously described.

Among these four, one may understand that they both calculate existence and non-existence together. That which grows from the side of a tree is called a branch. All these are said to be "evasive and confused" (*vibhrama*).
If one says "existence" when there is existence, and says "non-existence" when there is non-existence, this may seem correct; what, then, is meant by "distorted confusion"?
One should know that in the original luminosity of self-nature, both existence and non-existence are unattainable. Since one reckons it as either existent or nonexistent, this is distortion.
Furthermore, to calculate that things are neither existent nor non-existent, both existent and non-existent, or mutually non-existent and individually existent—this is confusion.

Therefore, all such views are termed "evasive equivocation" (*amarāvikkhepa*). "Immortality" (*amara*) carries the meaning of "non-transmigration. Those non-Buddhists, desiring to be born in the Immortal Heaven as their fruit, cling to and calculate immortality.
Moreover, "evasive" (*kiao*) refers to being forced or stubborn, while "equivocation" (*luan*) refers to being disordered and confused. By means of...

Deceitful equivocation is practiced with the desire to attain the fruit of immortality. This is termed "intermediate" (*madhyama*). This, moreover, refers equally to those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold both views—that things are eternal and that they are annihilated—thereby transcending [the extremes of] both permanence and cessation.

The third section, concerning the calculation of the arising of the marks of existence after death, consists of three parts: first, the heading at the beginning of the time-period; second, the explanation starting with "Or, by oneself..."; and third, the conclusion starting with "By this...
Regarding the initial heading, the phrase "the marks of existence after death" refers to the calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). These do not go beyond [the views that]:
the self is identical to form (*rūpa*), the self is distinct from form, the self is larger than form, form is smaller than the self, or form exists within the self, and the self is larger than form.
"The small self is within form. This has two explanations, each with two parts. First, the primary calculation; second, the specific calculation.
Regarding the first, "either as oneself" and so forth means that form itself is the self. "Or as seeing" and so forth means that the self is large and form is small.
As for "the self being round," it means that my self is perfectly complete, such that all lands throughout the ten directions exist within me.
Or, for them, it may be that "I am distinct from form. Regarding "the previously perceived," this refers to the form that was the object of perception;
it falls within the category of "self" and merely functions according to the self's employment. Or again, "equal" and so forth means that the self is large and form is small.

Thus, regarding the sixteen aspects of the cycle, based on the four states such as "already arisen" and so forth of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), one takes up the single aggregate of form to establish the first four; the remainder...
The three aggregates (skandhas) likewise each possess four [aspects]. Thus, there are four sets of four, making sixteen characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

Some say that by excluding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and taking the preceding three aggregates together with the subsequent aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), the sixteen are established; this may well be so. Next, regarding the middle [section]:
Regarding the phrase "ultimately afflictions, etc.": the two characters "ultimate" (*bi-jìng*) mean that [they] exist. However, it is not an error to say that afflictions exist and that bodhi exists;
the error lies in these two natures driving alongside one another without touching. Within the section on "establishing names," it says:
"As for establishing the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), etc. Question: Since the first three aggregates have already been refuted, why are they brought up again?
[Question: What is meant by "reckoning"? [Answer: Although the three aggregates (*skandhas*) have been refuted, one still relies upon them to give rise to reckoning.

This is because, although the pervasive conceptualization (*parikalpita*) of the three aggregates has been destroyed, the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) has not yet ceased. Thus, one relies upon it to give rise to sixteen [types of views] to complete the set.

This is merely taking the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) as the self and the other four aggregates as conditions; this, too, is an externalist (*tīrthika*) view of eternalism (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*).
There are also three parts to the calculation regarding the arising of the signless after death: first, the initial heading; second, the explanation following "seeing that...";
and third, the conclusion following "thereby...". Within the heading, "the signless after death" is as can be seen from what has been explained in the commentary.
The explanation has two parts: first, the primary calculation, which views them as equal; second, the specific calculation, which views them as distinct from this equality.
Regarding the first part: "seeing that their form ceases, etc. means that they hold that when there is form, it merely manifests form; when there is perception, it merely binds the mind.
There is a state where sensation (vedanā) merely serves to maintain the continuity of matter (rūpa) and mind (citta) as one's life-span.

Since the three aggregates (skandhas) of matter and so forth have already been destroyed, it is said that "one sees their equality. The phrase "the nature of the aggregates" refers collectively to the three aggregates of matter and so forth that have been extinguished.

"Even though there is equality" points to the solitary persistence of the aggregate of formations (saṃskāra-skandha). "This substance and so forth" points to the aggregate of matter (rūpa-skandha) which has already been destroyed. Based on this, one precisely gives rise to conceptual construction (parikalpa).

"Examination" (*k'an-chiao*) is merely conceptual calculation (*vikalpa*). Regarding the eight signless states (*animitta*), there are four each for cause and effect, such as the cessation of form (*rūpa-nirodha*) and so forth;

these can be understood through individual analysis. In the summary of their names, the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) are the same as before. These are also non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold views of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

There are also three ways of formulating the calculation regarding the "neither-perception-nor-non-perception" (naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana) after death. First, the heading from "at the end of the subsequent [state]" (*paścāt*) down to the end;

second, the explanation from "form and feeling" (*rūpavedanā*) downward; third, the conclusion from "thereby" (*tataś ca*) downward. Within the heading, regarding the phrase "in formations" (*saṃskāreṣu*), this refers to the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāraskandha*) being present before one. This is combined with the phrase "feeling."

This refers to the cessation of the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Regarding the "dual reckoning" category: the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is considered existent when it is present before one, while the aggregate of sensation is considered non-existent once it has ceased.
Regarding the "self-nature" category: sensation, perception (*saṃjñā*), and formations are all mental factors (*caitta-dharma*), and thus they are termed "self-nature.

By means of the presence of formations, one refutes that sensation and perception have already ceased; conversely, by means of the cessation of sensation and perception, one refutes that formations are present before one. This is what is meant.

This is a refutation. The preceding sixth view held that there is existence after death; the seventh held that there is non-existence after death. Now, [this view] denies both existence and non-existence;
hence it says, "this person," and so forth. The commentary also has two parts: first, the specific enumeration, namely "form, sensation," and so on;

second, the general enumeration, namely "furthermore, he calculates," and so on. Regarding the first part: "form, sensation," etc., refers to the three aggregates (skandhas) of form and so forth as being inherently existent from the beginning.

It has long since been extinguished; thus, there is existence that is not [inherently] existent. Regarding "the shifting of formations" (*saṃskāra*), this refers to the fact that the *saṃskāra-skandha* flows and shifts as if it were non-existent;
now, by saying it is "present before one," it means there is existence that is not non-existent.

As for such cycles and so forth, some say that "aggregates and elements" (*skandha-dhātu*) refers to the five aggregates and eighteen elements; this is incorrect. It merely exhaustively investigates the boundaries of the four aggregates. Below is the conclusion.

Regarding the term "among" (*zhōng*) and the expression "also called the five aggregates" (*wǔ yīn*): it is because four of the aggregates are four out of the five, and thus it is a collective designation. As for the "eightfold neither-characteristic":
this means that form, sensation, and the others all possess the characteristic of being neither existent nor non-existent. Regarding "having characteristics and lacking characteristics":
this does not mean that existence itself is a characteristic or that non-existence itself is a characteristic; rather, it means that having characteristics is precisely what is not non-existent.

Regarding "characteristics": the absence of characteristics (*animitta*) is precisely the non-existence of characteristics. This correctly negates both extremes of conceptualization. Next, as for "further calculating [them] to be equal" within the middle [state]:

this refers to the fact that while the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) appears to be non-existent, it actually possesses the flux of change; thus, it is not the case that it is non-existent.

"Erroneous" (*mo*) simply means that one is speaking of its being non-non-existent. Regarding the phrase "the mind arises": since the aggregate of formations is thus, when one investigates the existence of all phenomena, they are found to be non-existent.
Therefore, it is said that they are "reckoned as equal," and so forth. Regarding "existence and non-existence":

since it cannot be called existent and cannot be called non-existent, it is said that both existence and non-existence are negated. Since it is said to be "not existent," it truly cannot be taken as real;

and since it is said to be "not non-existent," the void cannot be taken as empty. Thus, it is said that "the void and the real lose their footing. In the conclusion, it says: "The future limit is shrouded in darkness."
"Et cetera" (*ādi*) refers precisely to the future state that is dark, vast, obscure, and profound, wherein there is no right view.
Within the summary of names, "is" (*asti*) and "is not" (*nāsti*) refer to the non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) who maintain these dual negations.
There are also three aspects to the speculative view of annihilationism (*ucchedavāda*). First, the initial heading at the end; second, the explanation beginning with "Or one views...";

and third, the conclusion beginning with "By this...". The first, the heading, is clear. In the second, the explanation, there are two phrases: First, the phrase "or one speculates" refers to the speculation that after the death of the two types of physical bodies composed of the four great elements—those of humans and devas in the desire realm—there is ultimate annihilation. Second, the phrase "or one desires" refers to the speculation...
In the first dhyāna, one has already departed from the five desires of the lower realm—wealth, form, fame, flattery, and sleep—and thus considers this to be ultimate cessation.

Or, regarding the phrase "suffering": in the second dhyāna, having given rise to joy and bliss, one departs from the directed thought and evaluation (*vitarka-vicāra*) of the first dhyāna, and thus considers this to be ultimate cessation.
Or, regarding the phrase "extreme": in the fourth dhyāna, equanimity and mindfulness are pure, and both suffering and pleasure have vanished; and...
The four formless attainments (*ārūpya*) constitute ultimate annihilation. All [the sūtras] say "or," meaning that one may adhere to any one of the seven types among them.
The same applies to the five types of *nirvāṇa* below; although there are five phrases in the treatise, there are seven forms of annihilation.

This is because the first phrase includes two types—human and celestial—and the latter phrase includes two types—the four dhyānas and the formless realms. Therefore, they are collectively referred to as "such."

"These [beings]" refers to the seven limits (*sapta-anta*), which denotes their seven kinds of boundaries. Because they are severed from here and will never arise again, it is said "present before [the eyes]," and so forth.
Within the summary of names, "these [beings]" means that these seven forms of annihilationism are also established based upon the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
These, too, are non-Buddhists who hold the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Regarding the fifteen ways in which nirvāṇa arises, there are also three [sections]: first, the heading at the beginning; second, the explanation starting with "Alternatively" (*athavā*);

third, the conclusion starting with "By this. The heading is clear. In the explanation, the phrase "Alternatively" (*athavā*) correctly defines its characteristics. The terms "deluded regarding existence" (*bhava-mūḍha*) and so forth are the words of the Tathāgata’s severance [of delusion].
Phrases such as "thus and so forth" (*evam-ādi*) are further combined statements. Among the five types of nirvāṇa, the first is the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) as the primary turning.

Based on the support (*āśraya*), the vision (*darśana*), and the arising of longing (*anunaya*) and so forth, there must be the absence of further saṃsāra as well as the nature of birth and cessation (*utpāda-nirodha-dharmatā*);
all these should be fully present. If they are complete, it should be stated as with the first dhyāna:

"Either by taking the first dhyāna as the true transformational support (*parāvṛtty-āśraya*), one sees that there is no sorrow and does not undergo the nature of saṃsāric birth and cessation, and thus gives rise to longing. Now, regarding the first dhyāna...

They are mutually complete; the intermediate stages may be inferred accordingly. Thus, while the first and last [stages] are abbreviated and the middle three are entirely omitted, one knows that the first is perfectly luminous, the second is free from sorrow, the third is free from suffering, the fourth is supremely joyful, and the fifth is where both suffering and pleasure have vanished—this is the basis for such a reckoning.
The first reckoning concerns the desire realm as the primary locus of transformation.

This refers to those who falsely reckon that the four great elements of the primary retribution within the desire realm are themselves the basis for the transformation of birth and death, and thus they dwell in nirvana.
Their contemplation of the "perfect clarity" (pariniṣpanna-prabhāsvara) and so forth corresponds exactly to their reckoning;

they claim that the desire-realm concentration (*kāmadhātu-samādhi*) and the threshold concentration (*anāgamya-samādhi*) cultivated within the body constitute the perfect clarity of nirvana, rather than the perfect clarity of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). In the first dhyāna, one has already departed from the coarse and painful obstructions of the desire realm.

Because one has already attained the pure, subtle, and detached state of the higher realms, it is called "without sorrow. In the second dhyāna, there is neither vitarka (applied thought) nor vicāra (sustained thought) as there is in the first;
because joy and bliss are born of meditative concentration, it is called "without suffering. In the third dhyāna, bliss is superior;

because the sublime bliss born of detachment fills the interior and pervades the exterior, it is called "supreme bliss. In the fourth dhyāna, because equanimity and mindfulness are purified, it is called...

The dual extinction of suffering and pleasure is the "unconditioned phrase" (*anupādāya-pada*). This corrects the misconception that takes what is not *nirvāṇa* to be *nirvāṇa*. The rest is understandable.
Regarding the title of the section: this [phrase] is likewise a summary indicating that these are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who hold the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

The threefold exhortation also consists of two parts. First is the binding of faults, concerning Ānanda and others. Second is the exhortation to propagate [the teaching], concerning you and others. Regarding the first:
as for those with "mad liberation" through *dhyāna*, this refers to the previously mentioned form, sensation, and perception;

it speaks of the manifestation of the *dhyāna* realm and thus presents these matters. This is because either a demon arises from one's own mind or an external demon manifests its realm. Now, they are merely the same.
Thus, they give rise to false conceptualizations regarding external paths; hence it is said that "mad interpretations" and "deliberate manifestations" lead to this awakening.

All who speak of *dhyāna* do so because, through the cultivation of the three contemplations, they have completely shattered the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). However, by over-exerting themselves in their investigations, they cause demonic activities and false conceptualizations to arise.
The remaining meanings are the same as before and may be understood accordingly. Next, regarding the "branching off": this refers to the lateral branches of a tree.

That which branches out is called a "branch" (*śākhā*); that which diverges along a path is called a "fork" (*viṣākhā*). Those who point toward purity and clarity do so by using a finger as a signpost, desiring that others see the moon.

When a person sees the moon because of the pointing finger, this serves as a metaphor: the scripture’s capacity for expression (*vyañjana*) is like the pointing finger, while the realization of the expressed principle (*artha*) through that expressive scripture is like seeing the moon because of the finger. Because this expressive capacity is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), it is so described.
The phrase "Pure Cloud" serves as an indicative pointer; the rest is the same as before.

Fifth, the manifestation of the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) also has two parts: first, the conclusion of the preceding practice, referring to Ānanda and others; second, the elucidation of the present aggregate of consciousness.
