This refers to "profoundly penetrating equality" and so forth. Regarding the first part: that "excellent" [passage] below clearly elucidates the characteristics of the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations).
It can be understood as a textual heading that contrasts the preceding section on the *rūpa-skandha* (aggregate of form) with the current section on the exhaustion of the *saṃskāra-skandha*.

As for the phrase "sinking, subtle, and the main cord," the *saṃskāra-skandha* is taken as the root of the twelve classes of birth and death; it is therefore metaphorically likened to a "main cord. Once the *saṃskāra-skandha* is shattered, the twelve categories of existence...
The subtle snares of the cycle of birth and death have sunk and been severed; thus it is said, "sunk and subtle," and so forth.
"Response and stimulus" (ganying) is merely a name for the fruit of karmic retribution within birth and death. In the passage following "Nirvana," the principle revealed therein is further clarified.

"Nirvana-heaven" (*nirvāṇa-deva*) refers to the original luminosity of one's own nature; therefore, it is metaphorically called "heaven. It is constantly shrouded by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), just as heaven is [shrouded by clouds].

The darkness of the fifth watch [of the night] has now been dispelled as the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has been shattered; thus it is said that one is about to awaken to the Great Illumination.

The analogy of the rooster is precisely intended to illustrate this "about-to-awaken-to-the-Great-Illumination. That is to say, once the rooster has crowed three times and the eastern sky has turned white, one is currently at the very moment of the approaching dawn;

therefore, it is said to be "like the rooster," and so forth. The passage beginning with "the six sense faculties" clarifies this point; it specifically refers to the fact that the aggregate of formations has already been shattered.

Because the sense organs and their objects do not encounter one another, it is said that "the six sense organs are equal. Regarding "internal and external are equal": the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) is external, and the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is internal.
Because the delusion is shattered and the truth is revealed, it is said that "internal and external are equal."

Second, the explanation of the present [state] is also divided into three parts. First, "profoundly penetrating the ten directions," etc., which is the heading. Second, "Ānanda, you should know," etc., which is the explanation.

Third, "Ānanda, in this way," etc., which is the concluding exhortation. Within the first part, there are two sections: first, the characteristics of when consciousness has not yet been exhausted, which begins with "profoundly penetrating" below;
second, the characteristics of when consciousness has already been exhausted, which begins with "if, regarding" below. Within the first of these, "profoundly penetrating," etc., [is explained].

This means that all twelve modes of birth take the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) as their fundamental cause. Thus, both the "origin" (*yuan*) and the "source" (*you*) are simply the aggregate of consciousness.

As it was said previously regarding the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*): "Although one has not yet fully understood the individual threads of their destinies, when the nature enters the primordial clarity..."
This is because all [phenomena] refer to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*). "Observation by means of equality," and so forth, means that consciousness stands before one.

"The various categories" refers to how consciousness acts as the cause to summon the fruit of the twelve classes of beings. Since consciousness already stands before one, it will naturally dissolve before long; therefore, it is said that "the various categories do not summon [it].
Regarding the passage "In the ten [realms]," etc., it means that the twelve distinct characteristics exist within this very aggregate of consciousness. Thus...

"Clouds" refers to the ten [stages] and so forth. The phrase "refined color" indicates that the benefit manifested is profound. The phrase "manifestation" means that when the aggregate of consciousness (vijñāna-skandha) stands before one, it is called "manifestation";

because consciousness has not yet been exhausted, it is called "mysterious and secret. This is precisely what is meant by the "world of the aggregate of consciousness. Therefore, it says, "This then," and so forth.
Second, regarding the characteristics of consciousness already being exhausted, there are two parts. First, "If one," and so forth. Correctly...

Illumination. Second, examining their common causes and conditions. Regarding the first part: "If, regarding 'equality,'" this again refers to the twelve classes of beings being together within the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Regarding "melting away" (*xiāomó*) and so forth: "melting" (*xiāo*) means to dissolve or transform; "grinding" (*mó*) means to polish or refine, as in the case of working jade.

One melts away the afflictions of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*) to achieve supreme knowledge and vision (*anuttara-jñāna-darśana*), and grinds away the birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) of the six sense organs.
One realizes unsurpassed *nirvāṇa*; hence it is said that the six gates are "worn away. Regarding "the union and opening leading to accomplishment":
"union" refers to what is called the original single essence of clarity; "opening" refers to what is called the division into the six harmonious combinations.

In ordinary beings, there is only opening into six, which constitutes mutual opposition within their functioning. In those at the first fruit (*srotāpanna*), there is only union into one, which constitutes [unity] within their nature.
[The six faculties] are known [to be distinct], yet none of them can be said to be fully accomplished [in isolation]. Now, we find that the six faculties possess one another;

when their fundamental nature is discussed, it is originally one, and when their functions are discussed, they are six. There is nothing that is not fully accomplished. Therefore, it is said that "opening and closing constitute accomplishment. Regarding seeing, hearing, and so forth:
this means that through seeing, one may also hear sounds, smell fragrances, and even know dharmas; through knowing, one may also see forms, hear sounds, and smell fragrances.
The same applies to the intermediate [senses]. This refers to the true mutual functioning of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya*), which are not defiled by the six sense organs themselves;

hence the mention of "seeing, hearing," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the ten directions" and below: it is as clearly elucidated in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* concerning the purity of the six sense organs.

One perfectly sees the environment and its inhabitants throughout the ten directions, and even perfectly knows the environment and inhabitants of the ten realms, as well as the teachings of all Buddhas of the three periods of time; hence the mention of "the ten directions."

It is equal [to the preceding]. Speaking in terms of their respective stages, once the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is exhausted, one immediately enters the stage of "semblance" at the level of the seven stages of faith;

this is precisely what constitutes the purification of the six sense faculties (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*). Therefore, it is possible to attain such a state. This is not like the previous false reckoning that took eighty-four thousand kalpas as the two types of non-causality (the primary and secondary).
For this reason, it is called the exhaustion of the aggregate of consciousness. This concludes the section on the person below.

This means that as long as the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) has not been exhausted, one gives rise to delusions and creates karma, thereby experiencing the impurity of life (*āyuṣka-kaṣāya*) characterized by being born in the morning and dying in the evening, or by the decay of the physical frame.

Once the *vijñāna-skandha* is exhausted, the impurity of life naturally transcends and surpasses itself. This is why it was stated previously that consciousness constitutes the substance of the impurity of life.
Regarding the second cause, "observing their equality," since the substance of True Suchness (*tathatā*) has already been manifested, its...
Delusion arises from one's own views; through inverted and false conceptions, there exists this aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), which serves as the root of the turbidity of life.
The second explanation divides [the components] into ten, the sequence of which can be seen. Each of these ten has three aspects. First, "good son," down to the end of the passage.

The manifestation of consciousness (*vijñāna*). Second, if one falsely gives rise to erroneous conceptions regarding what is inferior; third, this is called "summarizing and indicating the seeds of birth. Only the eighth and ninth [stages] involve the false arising of erroneous conceptions concerning the beginning of the observation of life and of life itself. For the others, there is no difference. "Exhausting all phrases" refers to the exhaustion of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). "At the phrase of consciousness" means that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) manifests before one.

The very source to which one returns is also the aggregate of consciousness; however, there is a distinction between the true and the false. The true is suchness (*tathatā*); the false is arising and ceasing (*utpāda-nirodha*).

Now, when consciousness returns to its source, it is only its falsity that returns, not its truth; therefore, it is said that "one returns to the source at the level of consciousness. Once consciousness has returned to its source...

The arising and ceasing of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) has already ceased; therefore, it is said that "arising and ceasing have already ceased. Below this, it clarifies that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is on the verge of being destroyed but not yet destroyed;

however, one has merely returned to the source of delusion and has not yet returned to the source of truth. Regarding the phrase "can cause," it refers to the purification of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-āyatana*), which is about to be attained but not yet attained;
thus, it simply says "can cause one's own body's faculties to be separated from opening and closing," which is different from what was previously described as "already [attained]."

This is equivalent to "attaining the same as the melting away" and so forth. Furthermore, although the principle of similarity with what follows below is about to be revealed, it has not yet been fully manifested.

However, because one has merely returned to the source of delusion and has not yet returned to the source of truth, it speaks only of the "various classes throughout the ten directions," rather than the "Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the ten directions.
Thus, we know that the section beginning from "capable of leading to the ultimate perfection and original oneness" extends through the nine characters that follow.
All [the following cases] should be understood in this way; one may see the abbreviated form by taking the first as an example for the subsequent ones.

Among the false conceptualizations that arise, if one forms a conception regarding "that which is equal," it is a type of person who falls into such [delusion]. The same applies to all that follows. As for the phrase "if one regards 'that which is equal,'" the intended meaning is:

if the fundamental source to which one returns is not yet realized as true, one must still contemplate and illuminate until one spontaneously attains the return to truth. Even if one were to consider it as true...
If one constantly takes this to be the realization of the holy, one will surely give rise to false views; therefore, it says, "if one [regards] the equal," and so forth.
All subsequent instances of "if one [regards] the equal" should be viewed in this same way. Regarding the phrase "this person":

because they falsely reckon that which is not a cause of true permanence to be a cause of true permanence, it says, "then one falls into the attachment to causes and what is caused. Since this is already a false cause, it cannot by itself realize the truth.
The fruit of constancy is, conversely, to enter into the company of heterodox outsiders; hence it is said, "Sāpī and so forth.
Originally desiring to seek Bodhi while practicing *samādhi*, one reaches the ultimate state of Bodhi and yet instead gives rise to delusion.

Consequently, the knowledge of the three wisdoms within a single mind and the vision of the five eyes within a single eye are both lost. Hence it is said, "Deluded regarding the Buddha and so forth. Below, this is explained away...
The same principle should be applied to all cases, from "capable" and "incapable" up to "real" and "unreal," merely by substituting "capable" and "incapable" for the other terms.
Regarding the concluding indication within the section on the seeds of birth, the phrase "this is called, etc. means that the true and eternal has fundamentally nothing upon which to depend.

If one were to establish this [the seeds] as a cause, then it would have something upon which to depend; therefore, it is said that one establishes a mind that is attained. By means of this cause of delusion, one returns...

Thus, one produces the fruit of delusion; hence it is called "the fruit of that to which one returns. Originally desiring to cultivate the perfect path, one instead uses false conceptualization as the cause, thereby creating an obstruction to perfect penetration.
Originally desiring to realize entry into nirvana, one instead brings about the fruit of delusion through its causes.

They turn their backs on and distance themselves from *nirvāṇa*. Having violated perfect penetration (*yuan-tong*) and having turned their backs on *nirvāṇa*, they are entirely devoid of true cause and effect;

they are merely of the same category as non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Taken together, these are called the "first class" [of deluded practitioners]. The subsequent sections should also be understood by this analogy.
Within the second category, the false conceptualizations of "the capable" and "the incapable," if one—[at the level of] "equality"—... [text fragment ends]
To trace this back to its origin, it is fundamentally not the true essence of self-nature; therefore, those who interpret it as the true essence of self-nature are mistaken.
For such people, my own substance is inherently incapable of producing anything, yet they falsely reckon it to be capable; hence it is said that "the capable is not capable.
Maheśvara is the Great Sovereign Deva of the Form Realm (*rūpadhātu*); "Greatly Arrogant Deva" is an alternative name for him.

Third, among the false conceptualizations of permanence and impermanence: if that which is the fundamental source of refuge is itself illusory, how could the body and mind it possesses be eternally abiding?
To conceive of them as eternally abiding is an error. The passage beginning with "In birth," etc., is the Tathāgata’s refutation of these views;
for they reckon what is subject to arising and ceasing to be non-arising and non-ceasing, and reckon what is not eternally abiding to be eternally abiding.
Therefore, it is said, "in birth," and so forth. Because birth and cessation are themselves non-birth and non-cessation, it is said, "already deluded," and so forth.

Within the four types of ignorance where false conceptualizations arise, if one regards that which is known as being illusory—originally neither pervasive nor perfect—and yet interprets it as being perfect, this is incorrect.
That sentient beings possess knowledge while insentient things lack it is...

This is the correct principle. Now, to calculate that both the sentient and the insentient are all-knowing and universally pervasive is precisely why one falls into the attachment of grasping at knowledge and non-knowledge.

Question: What is the distinction between what is called "sentient and insentient are of the same essence" in the teachings, and the non-Buddhists' claim that all grasses and trees throughout the ten directions are sentient and possess universal, pervasive knowledge? Answer: In the teachings, when it speaks of the sentient and the insentient...
"Sentient beings being of one body" means that they share the same fundamental nature of original enlightenment.
Those lacking cognition are insentient, such as grasses and trees; those possessing cognition are sentient, such as living beings.
Because these are all objects manifested within the single, wondrously luminous mind, they are said to be of one body. This is not the same as the various [theories] calculated by the non-Buddhists.

Sentient beings inherently possess cognition, and plants likewise possess cognition; those whose cognition is pervasive and perfect are identical [in this regard]. Within the false conceptualizations of the five modes of birth and non-birth, there arises a deluded calculation.

If, regarding the state of equality, one fails to realize that it is fundamentally not the true purity of the six sense organs, but instead recognizes it as such, one says, "I have already attained conformity.
Consequently, within the state of equality, one calculates that the essence of consciousness is capable of giving rise to all phenomena.
Furthermore, if the substance of consciousness (*vijñāna*) is that which gives rise to all phenomena, then that which is produced by it should likewise give rise to all phenomena.

For this reason, within each of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) that are produced, one calculates that they each possess the capacity to give rise to all phenomena, and thus claims that each should be venerated.
This is precisely the view of those non-Buddhist outsiders who maintain that all sentient beings are born from time, from space, or from atoms (*paramāṇu*). That is to say:
These four elements are each venerated and served as being understood to be permanent; yet they are merely reckoned as permanent when they are not actually permanent.
Such people fundamentally do not possess the true understanding of permanence; they cannot be said to give rise [to views], nor can they be said to be without the arising [of views].

Therefore, it is said that they harbor attachments to arising and non-arising. This concludes the demonstration within the category of the seeds of arising: the deluded mind follows external objects, which means it is deluded regarding itself.

This fundamental, luminous nature of the essence follows after the objects of the four great elements. It arises within the false calculations of the "six returning to nothingness," such as "if it were at...
and so forth. This perfect luminosity is not itself the self-nature; yet, one calculates it to be perfect luminosity, which is why it says "if it were at...
and so forth. "Not among those who undergo extinction and transformation" means that one cuts off the non-extinction of the multitude of delusions and returns through transformation to the Truth.

Regarding "Yong" and so forth: they falsely calculate that which is not true cessation to be true cessation. These people take what is not the basis of true cessation and, through their false calculations, regard it as the basis of true cessation;

thus, they fall into the attachment of seeking refuge where there is no refuge. Within the seven types of deluded false calculations arising from craving and non-craving, regarding "ruo yu" and so forth:
that which is perfectly complete and eternally abiding is fundamentally not true eternity, yet they form the understanding of it as eternal abiding.
This is delusion. These people [claim that] the permanent cannot be the object of craving; yet they falsely calculate it to be permanent, and thus crave what should not be craved.
Therefore, they fall into craving; it is not that they lack craving, but rather they hold a false attachment. To show how one is born into the seeds of delusion:

those who cling to the "original life-force" (yuan-ming)—the consciousness-aggregate (vijñāna-skandha) is the original source of the lives of all beings—yet this source is not permanent. To cling to it as such...

Because it is permanent, it is said that one clings to the root of life. Regarding "giving rise to deluded seeds of prolongation": because one takes what is impermanent to be permanent, such seeds are produced.
Within the arising of false calculations regarding the eight true [realities] as being without truth, one contemplates life and so forth.

If one discusses the true essence of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*), it pervades the three periods of time. However, the life-root (*jīvamūla*) of the present aggregate of consciousness is not its true essence;
how then could they be mutually pervasive? Such notions as "abiding through the three periods" or "remaining for kalpas" are precisely the arising of conceptual calculations.

For instance, within the orthodox teachings, there is the mention of "retaining habitual tendencies to moisten rebirth," which involves falsely identifying the life-root as being mutually pervasive. Thus, such calculations arise. These people and others do not [understand] this mutual interpenetration.
"Interpenetration" (tōng) means mutual penetration. One should fall into the attachment of either true or false non-existence.

Among the false conceptualizations arising from the nine classes of śrāvakas of fixed nature, "discrimination" (fēnbié) and so forth refer to the two truths of the Path and Cessation, because they are the supramundane cause and effect.

"Coarse" (cū) refers to the two truths of Suffering and Accumulation, because they are the mundane cause and effect. "Sporadic" (shū) means loose or intermittent. "Decisive" (jué) means definitive. "Emergence" (chū) means to come forth.
The cause and effect of the cessation of worldly paths are true; the cause and effect of the suffering and accumulation of the world are false.
To seek *sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* between these two types of cause and effect constitutes the equality of cause and effect.

This is because those of the Hīnayāna know only that the six consciousnesses can be destroyed, yet do not know the purity of the sudden and perfect teaching, in which cultivation arises entirely from the fundamental nature. Therefore...
It is said that they turn their backs on the path of purity; this refers to the "lower fetters" which they have calculated [as their goal].

Because they believe what they have done is already accomplished, it is said that "having entered cessation, they rest. Because they abide in the partial truth (*ekadeśa-satya*), it is said that "they do not further attain equality.

Such people, because they do not know the cultivation and realization of the Perfect and Sudden (*yuan-dun*), indulge only in the partial truth of the Four Noble Truths; therefore, they fall into the category of the Śrāvakas of fixed nature. All those who...
Regarding the phrase "those who have not heard [the teachings]": on one level, this refers to what are called "unlearned bhikṣus.

To speak further, it refers to those śrāvakas of fixed nature who do not hear that there is ignorance beyond the realm [of the threefold world] which can be destroyed, nor that the transformation-death can be severed, nor that unsurpassed bodhi can be attained or realized.

This concludes the indication within the category of "birth-seeds. As for those who give rise to the seeds of entanglement in emptiness, these are what are called those who sink into emptiness and stagnate in quiescence.

Furthermore, among the false calculations that give rise to the fixed nature of the pratyekabuddhas, if one regards the destruction of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) as not being fundamentally the perfectly integrated enlightened clarity, and if one takes this as a realization of holiness (*ārya*) without making further progress, such a person belongs to the stream of the pratyekabuddhas.
This is because their destruction is limited to the six consciousnesses; now, at the point where the aggregate of consciousness is destroyed, they mistake it for *nirvāṇa* and do not proceed further.

Proceeding further: those who are "equal to others" (pṛthagjana) are the pratyekabuddhas; they appear in an age when a Buddha is present and attain awakening by contemplating the twelve links of dependent origination.

Those who are "solitary" (pratyeka) are the solitary realizers (pratyekabuddhas); they appear in an age when no Buddha is present and attain awakening while dwelling alone on a solitary peak, contemplating the falling petals of a flower or the movement of a bracelet.
They achieve the fruit of profound clarity and realize the partial truth of *parinirvāṇa*. This concludes the demonstration.
Regarding those born among the seeds of birth who do not transform the round seed: this refers to their inability to turn from the Small Vehicle toward the Great Vehicle.
Among these ten types, the first seven are non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*); the eighth is the celestial Māra; and the ninth and tenth are the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Question:

How can it be that the two vehicles are also included within the category of Māras? Answer: One should know that when the Tathāgata appears in the world, his original intent is for all sentient beings to...

To realize the original, luminous self-nature and the ever-abiding true mind is truly because the faculties of sentient beings are shallow and inferior, rendering them incapable of hearing [the ultimate truth].
For this reason, one first employs skillful means to entice and guide them. Those who attain liberation through the Four Noble Truths are called Śrāvakas;
those who attain liberation through the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination are called Pratyekabuddhas. However...
Those two individuals, not knowing the skillful means and clinging to a biased emptiness and nirvana, no longer advance;
they thus suffer a great loss of their original nature regarding the Tathāgata and appear similar to the class of Māras.

Therefore, following the description of the Māra-like class, these two are clarified in succession so that they may turn from the Small toward the Great and abandon the Small to take up the Great—this is precisely the intent behind the criticisms and rebukes found in the Vaipulya (fangděng) teachings.

The threefold exhortation to share [the teaching] is divided into three parts. First, within the section on the faults and afflictions starting from Ānanda, the phrase "those in this position" refers to the aforementioned seven types of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), one class of celestial Māras, and those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). The phrase "those who have previously practiced" refers to the various practices undertaken by each of these non-Buddhists and others.

Second, in the section on the exhortation to propagate and proclaim starting from "you all," the phrase "those who have awakened to and understood this meaning" refers to the ten aforementioned classes.

This refers to the meaning of the middle cause, the caused, the capable, and the incapable, and so forth. Regarding "do not allow the demon of views": previously, the "demon of the mind" was said to arise from craving and attachment;
now, the "demon of views" is said to arise from conceptual discrimination. The remaining meanings are the same as those explained previously regarding form, sensation, and so on.
Third, from "In this way" below, the characteristics of clarity are explained in three parts. First, it cites the commonality with all Buddhas: "In this way..."

[They are] equal. The second stage is the realization of similarity, which is the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) and so forth. The third is the transcending into the Diamond [Samādhi], and so on.

Regarding the initial citation within "identical to all Buddhas," the phrase "and so forth" refers to the fact that such *śamatha* and other dharmas are the practices by which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained Bodhi;
therefore, the ten types of the aggregate of consciousness are likewise the [practices of] past Buddhas.

It is by riding upon this that the mind opens and one attains the Way. Since it is said that "by riding upon this the mind opens," one naturally realizes the shattering of the *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) and the manifestation of the Truth;
this is not a matter of being obstructed from perfect penetration (*pariśuddha*) or of losing one's knowledge and vision. Furthermore, it is said that one "attains the Unsurpassed Way."
One spontaneously flows into the ocean of fruition; this is not to turn one's back on nirvāṇa or to be deluded regarding the Buddha’s bodhi.
This is what is meant by the "one path to the gate of nirvāṇa for the Bhagavans of the ten directions. Regarding the second stage, the realization of similarity:

The "aggregate of consciousness" (*vijñāna-skandha*) and so forth correctly clarify the stage of similarity (*sādṛśya*). From the phrase "mutually," etc., one progresses from the stage of similarity to the stage of reality (*bhūta*).

This refers to the partial realization across the forty-one stages. However, there is a distinction between the true and the similar regarding the purity of the six sense organs (*ṣaḍ-indriya-viśuddhi*).

The "similar" refers to the ten stages of faith (*daśa-śraddhā*), which is what is meant by the "mutual functioning of the various organs. The "true" refers to the first *bhūmi* and beyond, which is what is meant by "from within the mutual functioning," and so on. Below...
The transformation that unfolds within this [state] should also be understood through these two meanings.

Regarding "the perfectly luminous and refined mind," etc., this precisely reveals that what is seen is similar to the original luminosity of the self-nature. "Transformation unfolding within" refers to the purification of the six sense faculties.

"Like pure lapis lazuli" is a metaphor for the principle of what is seen, which resembles the perfectly luminous and refined mind. "Containing a precious moon within" is a metaphor for... [the internal clarity].
The "Middle" refers to the manifestation of the function of the purification of the six sense organs.
Regarding the phrase "the third transcends into the Vajra Middle," some say that the previous stage of Dry Wisdom (khan-hui) progresses to the Vajra Dry Wisdom;

this is a gradual progression and represents the "distinct" within the Perfect [Teaching]. Here, however, transcending the ten stages of faith and so forth constitutes an immediate entry; this is the "perfect within the perfect."
This is merely the assertion of one who has not mastered the characteristics of the teachings (jiaoxiang).

How could there be further distinctions within the Perfect Teaching (yuanjiao) such as "the distinct within the perfect" (bieyuan) and "the perfect within the perfect" (yuanzhongyuan)? One simply fails to realize that within each of the four teachings, there are both sharp and dull capacities.
What was previously explained refers to the dull faculties of those of the Perfect [Vehicle], whereas what is clarified here refers to the sharp faculties of those of the Perfect [Vehicle].

This may also be described as a distinction between the characteristics of the Dharma-practitioner (*dharmānusārin*) and the Faith-practitioner (*śraddhānusārin*). Regarding the so-called "Vajra Ten Stages":

on these stages, ignorance is subtle, difficult to shatter, and difficult to sever. From the four preparatory stages (*prayoga*) onward, upon ascending to the first stage (*bhūmi*), that which is difficult to shatter can be overcome.
It destroys; it can sever that which is difficult to sever, just as a vajra can shatter all things that are firm and sharp.

Therefore, it is called the "Vajra Tenth Ground. Regarding "perfectly luminous equal enlightenment": the previously mentioned "perfectly luminous refined mind" was the perfectly luminous self-nature manifested through resemblance;

now, having attained partial realization, one has reached the ultimate limit of the perfectly luminous self-nature, standing in immediate proximity to what is realized by wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
It is near. Therefore, it is said that "Equal Enlightenment is perfectly luminous. The phrase "entering into equality" precisely clarifies Wondrous Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Because one has cultivated the three types of causes—such as *śamatha* and so forth—one attains these three types of fruits; thus, the ocean of wondrous adornments is fulfilled through practice.

The perfection of bodhi is the fulfillment of wisdom (*jñāna*). Returning to the principle of non-attainment is the fulfillment of reality (*tattva*). The fulfillment of practice manifests the virtue of liberation (*vimukti*);
the fulfillment of wisdom manifests the virtue of prajñā; and the fulfillment of reality manifests the virtue of the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). These are the three, beginning with śamatha.
This refers to the inconceivable, perfectly interfused three dharmas arising from nature through cultivation; therefore, they are all called "wondrous.

These all represent the merging of cultivation back into nature within the secret treasury of the three inconceivable virtues; thus, they are also called the "Ocean of Wondrous Adornments" and so forth.
Because that which is cultivated is entirely cultivation of nature, and that which is realized is entirely realization of nature, it is said: "Perfecting Bodhi, returning to..."
There is nothing to be attained. The above concludes the second section, which provides a detailed exposition.
From here on is the third section, the concluding summary concerning the past and so forth. It is divided into four parts: first, from "This is" onwards, the analysis of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*;
second, from "The realm of Māra" onwards, the cessation of Māra and the accomplishment of the Path; third, from "If there are" onwards, the exhortation to uphold the divine mantra; fourth...
You should now reverently receive and practice the Way. First, regarding the beginning: these are the śamatha and vipaśyanā that are capable of analytical discernment.
"Awakened clarity" (*jue-ming*) and so forth refer to the classes of demons perceived by that awakened clarity. Śamatha is cessation; vipaśyanā is contemplation.
As for dhyāna, it is the non-duality of cessation and contemplation; it is merely omitted here. This cessation and contemplation are...
The Tathāgatas of the ten directions attained the realization of Bodhi; therefore, it is said, "This is [the case]," and so forth.

Since they have realized Bodhi, although the classes of Māras number as many as fifty, there are none that they do not perceive with clear and thorough illumination and analyze; therefore, it is said, "Awakened clarity," and so forth.
Taken together, this refers back to the previous passage where all were enumerated: "You still do not recognize," and so on, within the middle section.

"Regarding 'demonic realms' and so forth: Ānanda, if you cultivate this śamatha and vipaśyanā, just as in the past when demonic realms appeared before the various Buddhas, there were none who did not realize their luminosity and thus prevent them from becoming the various consciousnesses. Therefore, it says 'demonic realms' and so forth.

By naturally cleansing the mind, one attains correctness and does not allow demons or externalists to take advantage. Therefore, it says 'mental defilements' and so forth. The above provides a general explanation."
The "skandha-māras" (aggregates as demons) are explained separately below. These skandha-māras and so forth consist of forty-eight types; hence the phrase "skandha-māras and so forth.
The "zhí zhì" (until/leading up to) refers specifically to the two types of śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas; hence the phrase "until and so forth.

Taken together, these correspond exactly to the "subtle demonic activities" and so on mentioned previously in the comprehensive enumeration. Comparing them one with the other, there is not a single point that differs. However...

Previously it was not known; now it is simply known. Among these three [conditions], one must necessarily rely on divine mantras as a secret aid because the era of the final dharma is different from the era of the Buddha, and foolish, dull-witted people are not like Ānanda.
He does not yet recognize that in *dhyāna* there is no contemplation to be cultivated, nor does he know that in preaching the Dharma there are no teachings to be received.
Within his mind, he merely desires to cultivate the *samādhi* of the ear-organ. Look at this person, Ānanda:
he lives in the final age and is moreover dull-witted; he neither understands how to initiate practice through contemplation, nor knows how to open his understanding through the teachings.
If one wishes to cultivate samādhi within the center of the mind, one need not fear the arrival of māras to cause disturbance; rather, one should only fear becoming like a māra oneself.
At this time, Ānanda, if you wish to bring about his attainment of samādhi, there is no other method than to exhort him to single-mindedly uphold the Buddha-ūṣṇīṣa-dhāraṇī.
Even if he is dull-witted and unable to recite it, he may write it down.

In the place where one dwells in dhyāna, or even while wearing the robes of a practitioner, by the power of the secret assistance of this divine mantra, all subtle *skandha-māras* and the like will be unable to cause disturbance or confusion. Thus, this samādhi will naturally be accomplished.
There is no other way. Regarding this divine mantra, there is not a single Tathāgata throughout the ten directions who has not attained Bodhi because of it.
Having subdued the Māras, there was not one who did not recite this [sūtra] to attain entry into Nirvāṇa and transmit its Dharma.

Furthermore, all Vajrapāṇis, all spirits, as well as devas, nāgas, and the eight classes of beings, there were none who did not protect this divine mantra and those who write it down or uphold it. It is because it possesses such power that it is said:

"If among all those who are equal, you, Ānanda, should be equal to them"—this means that for you and others like you who are currently practicing, there is none who does not rely on this *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā* to eliminate demons and achieve *samādhi*.
Furthermore, even for the dull-witted sentient beings of the final age, there is none who does not rely on these divine mantras to keep distant from demons and attain *samādhi*. Such is its power.

It is not that this is the teaching of my single Buddha, Śākyamuni alone. Rather, regarding the exposition of *śamatha* and *vipaśyanā*, it is the divine mantra cultivated and advanced by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions;
furthermore, it is that which the Tathāgatas of the ten directions have thereby brought to ultimate fulfillment.
This is the final legacy and model left behind by the Tathāgatas of the ten directions and myself, Śākyamuni. It is impossible not to revere and respectfully uphold it.

Therefore, it says, "You should [practice] equally," and so forth. Regarding the phrase "the final instructions left behind": this refers exclusively to the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*, and not to the end of a single period of transformative guidance.
What has preceded consists of: first, a general explanation; second, a detailed exposition; and third, a summary conclusion.
This completes the second section, which provides an instructional revelation based on the meaning.

Ānanda immediately followed him. This third section explains the remaining doubts. Previously, the demons arising within the analysis and refutation of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) were addressed;
now, the five aggregates themselves are being analyzed. This is divided into two parts: first, the request based on doubt, consisting of the passage beginning with "Ānanda" and so forth;

second, the response and explanation, consisting of the passage beginning with "The Buddha said" and so forth. The first part [of the request] is further divided into three: first, the description of the scene by the scribe (the *sūtra-kāra*), beginning with "Ānanda"; second...

As the Buddha spoke below, he addressed the specific needs of his audience. First, within the narrative of the sūtra’s introductory section, "hearing the Buddha’s compassionate instruction" refers to the detailed discernment of the fifty kinds of demonic activities that were heard.
"Retaining them without loss" has two aspects: first, regarding one's own practice, as one is correctly cultivating *yuan-tong* (perfect penetration), one should naturally be free from such loss;
second, regarding the transformation of others, as the Tathāgata provides individual exhortations and admonitions, these too should likewise not be lost.

This is an error. Herein, there are also three types of reverent action (*trikarma*): prostrating is the action of body; showing respect is the action of mind; and addressing the Buddha is the action of speech.
Alternatively, it may be held that "recalling and upholding" constitutes the action of mind, though this does not occur simultaneously with the others.

Second, the appropriate audience presents their words in two parts: first, the expression of doubt (beginning with "Just as the Buddha..."); second, the formal request (beginning with "I only pray..."). This concludes the expression of doubt.
Within this, there are three intended meanings. First, the questions concerning the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) all concern how the five aggregates are merely false conceptualizations.

Second, these questions also concern the sequential exhaustion of the five aggregates. Third, such questions concern the boundaries and limits of the five aggregates as they reach their destination. Within the initial set of questions:

"Those who have not yet received subtle instruction" refers to the fact that previously [the text] merely concluded by stating "solid false conceptualization" up to "inverted false conceptualization," without explaining the specific reasons for each of these conceptualizations; hence the phrase "have not yet received," etc. The rest is understandable.

Regarding the second section, the formal request: "For the sake of these people" refers collectively to those whose minds are not clear and whose eyes are not opened, such that they are unable [to proceed].

To know and see that the five aggregates are but the original thought, and to eliminate them sequentially until they are exhausted, reaching the very boundary of the realms—this is what is meant by "attaining the Tathāgata’s arising of unconditioned compassion.
To illuminate and proclaim each of these reasons is not merely to clarify one's own mind and eyes;
it further serves as the eye for sentient beings of the末代 (final age). Therefore, it is said: "I only pray," and so forth.

The intent of this request is as follows: proximately, it is because sentient beings of the final age who delight in practice are exhorted to uphold the divine mantra so that they may achieve accomplishment;
distantly, it is because within each of the seals (*mudrā*), they are exhorted to propagate and proclaim [the Dharma] in the final age.

This is why the request is made, stating that [this teaching] shall serve as the "eye for the future. For the faculties of sentient beings in the final age are extremely dull and obtuse, and they do not understand the object of contemplation.
Although they have attained understanding through the teachings on the arousal of practice and take delight in cultivating samādhi, they do not realize they are being afflicted by demonic influences;
they are like those who lack eyesight. Nevertheless, if they can point the way for others, enabling them to attain purity of mind and vision, [they will be of great benefit].
This constitutes the creation of an eye for the future.

The second part, the explanation of the answer, is further divided into two sections: first, the Buddha’s instruction to depart as the direct answer; second, the exhortation to depart. The first section is further divided into three parts.

The first response concerns delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*), namely "The Buddha then said," and so forth. The second response concerns the causal realm (*hetu-dhātu*), namely "As for you now," and so forth. The third response concerns their eradication, namely "These five," and so forth.

The first [response] is further divided into two parts: first, the general explanation from "The Buddha then said" onwards; second, the specific explanation from "Your own substance" onwards. The first of these is further divided into two:

first, the arising of delusion from the True [Nature], from "The Buddha then said" onwards; second, the fact that the cause of delusion is fundamentally non-existent, from "Delusion is fundamentally... onwards.

In the section "Initially, delusion of the true gives rise to the false," the passage beginning with "the refined truth" (*jingzhen*) precisely clarifies the arising of delusion. The passage beginning with "this originally" (*siyuan*) explains that delusion exists due to confusion.

Regarding the first part, "the refined truth" and so forth refers to the two phrases "the nature-awareness is wondrously luminous" (*xingjue miaoming*). This is precisely the "original luminosity, the self-nature, the wondrously pure and luminous essence.

It does not mean that there is anything left over; it means that while the True [Nature] originally lacks cause and effect, or the environment and its inhabitants (*yi-zheng*), what exists now arises based upon [that original nature].

This refers to their arising through delusion. Thus, one should know that the two characters "not remaining" (*feiliú*) should be read as penetrating through the phrases "dust and grime" and "empty space.

In the phrase "not remaining," there are no results of suffering from the two types of birth-and-death:分段 (*fen-duàn*, *pariccheda*) and 變易 (*biàn-yì*, *pariṇāma*). In the subsequent phrases, there are no causes of accumulation consisting of the afflictions of the five stages of dwelling (*wǔzhù fánǎo*), namely, the views and thoughts (*jiàn-sī*, *darśana-bhāvanā*) and ignorance (*wúmíng*, *avidyā*).

In sum, the primary retribution (*zhèngbào*) is entirely absent. This extends even to the following phrase: [The text continues with the description of the absence of secondary retribution (*èbào*) and the lack of karmic conditions.]
"And there is nothing of the dependent retribution to be obtained. This means that all things, such as the causes and conditions, are fundamentally non-existent;
their present existence is merely what has arisen from delusion. Next, in the middle [section], "This is originally... refers to the True [Nature]. "Delusion by... refers to Delusion.
The various vessel-worlds consist of the three types: the five aggregates, sentient beings, and the lands. What was previously called the "dependent and the primary" is now referred to as...

These three types differ in name and number, yet their essence is the same. This is like the analogy of the [illusory] head and so forth; it correctly illustrates how delusion arises as the cause of falsehood.

"Deluded head" is a metaphor for being deluded regarding the true nature of the primordial luminosity of self-nature; it refers to the false recognition of shadows and reflections, and the arising of the duality of cause and effect, as well as the environment and its inhabitants.

These two delusions have no basis in the original source and are not divided into two. First, regarding "the initial delusion," the following section is the formal refutation, which demonstrates that they do not exist.

This refers to "causality. Second, from "Ānanda" downward, the underlying intention is revealed; the intention is that there is no cause. Third, from "Therefore" downward, it is concluded and demonstrated; this demonstrates the absence of cause.

Within the first section, the formal refutation: from "The delusion is originally... downward, the conceptualization [of causality] is presented; from "That which is empty... downward, it is criticized and refuted.

Regarding the first of these: "The delusion is originally... and so forth, is the conceptualization of non-causal conditions as causal conditions. "Deluded regarding causes... and so forth, is the conceptualization of non-naturalness as naturalness. Next...

In the middle [of the passage], those "empty phrases" raise up the environment while simultaneously encompassing the sentient beings. Just as with the "real phrases," this means that both the environment and the sentient beings are like a magician conjuring up men, women, oxen, and horses.
Speaking from the perspective of appearances (*lakṣaṇa*), what is called "manifestation according to karma" seems to be based on causes and conditions, yet in reality it is not caused by conditions.
Speaking from the perspective of nature (*dharmatā*), what is called "pure and fundamental" seems to be spontaneous.

In reality, they are not spontaneous; they are all the result of sentient beings' deluded minds calculating and conceptualizing, mistaking them for causes and conditions or mistaking them for spontaneity.
Fundamentally, neither causes and conditions nor spontaneity can be found. Therefore, it is said that "causes and conditions" and so forth.

When [the text] refutes causelessness while simultaneously refuting spontaneity, it does so because there is a fear that one might mistake causelessness for spontaneity; thus, both are refuted together. This is the second point regarding the underlying intent.

"Knowing that [it is] delusion," etc., correctly expresses the meaning of the absence of causes and conditions. "How much more so," etc., further emphasizes the meaning of the absence of spontaneity (*svabhāva*).
Within the section providing a summary, "Therefore," etc., is used because Ānanda harbors doubts regarding the five aggregates as being false imaginings;
thus, while the preceding text has clarified false imaginings, it concludes by stating "Therefore," etc. For this reason, each point is explained individually.

This is merely a demonstration of deluded thought (*vikalpa*). The second part, the "Detailed Explanation," is divided into two sections. First, from "Your body... onwards is the actual explanation; second, from "Ānanda... onwards is the conclusion.
The first section is further divided into five parts, which can be seen in their proper sequence. "Firmness" clarifies the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*).

As for the use of the "sour plum" and "hanging cliff" metaphors for the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñāskandha*), it is because, although this section primarily clarifies the aggregate of form, it provides a secondary response to the question regarding deluded thought. Therefore...
This serves as an illustration, and the same applies to the remaining four coverings (*āvaraṇa*). "Your substance," etc., is the heading; it is explained and clarified by us as follows.
Therefore, "your substance," etc., is the concluding response. Regarding "your substance": "substance" refers to the physical body composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).

This specifically clarifies the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*), and thus it is set forth as the heading. These four great elements arise from the two substances—red and white—of the father and mother.
It is formed by two drops. Furthermore, these two drops arise from the mutual desire and affection between father and mother; thus it is said, "Your body, etc. Regarding "your mind":

it arrives through the conceptualization of one's own mind within the conceptualization of father and mother, thereby transmitting the life-force. This transmission of the life-force is precisely what is meant by taking birth.
That is to say, the body and life are formed through the conjunction of three conditions: the father, the mother, and oneself. Therefore, it is said, "You..."

It is the same as the mind. To explain this within the [section on] "Clarifying the Middle": it is like ourselves; the matter can be understood by citing examples. As for "your substance" and so forth:

if your substance were not of the same category as the sour plum, the precipice, or the false imagination, for what reason would water arise in the mouth upon thinking of the plum, or why would a sense of acidity arise in the soles of the feet upon imagining the precipice? This is precisely false imagination (*vikalpa*).
[This] is brought about [by that]. Thus, one knows that your own substance is likewise within conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Therefore, it says, "your substance," and so forth.

Although this is explained by way of conceptualization, it actually clarifies the reason for the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*). By again citing your own substance to verify it as such, one knows that the aggregate of form is precisely your own false conceptualization.
Therefore, the concluding answer says, "For this reason," and so forth. As for "solidity" (*dṛḍhatā*): form takes material obstruction (*sapratigha*) as its [defining characteristic].
Because it is substantial, it is called "firm and solid. Furthermore, one's own deluded thought of entering the womb is cast into the midst of the parents' deluded thought of sexual union;
these three conditions bind together so that they cannot be discarded. Second is "empty brightness," which refers to the *vedanā-skandha* (the aggregate of sensation).

The section beginning with "That is" below provides the explanation; the section beginning with "Named" below provides the concluding answer. Regarding the first part, the phrase "That is, etc. reiterates the preceding matter.

Although it reiterates the preceding matter, the intent lies in the "reception" (vedanā); therefore, it says "true reception. Furthermore, the two phrases beginning with "And as for the causes and conditions of receiving birth" explain the two phrases beginning with "is able to cause.
The passage beginning with "You now, etc. correctly elucidates the aggregate of reception (vedanā-skandha), which experiences the five sensory objects (*pañca-viṣaya*) mentioned previously.
Regarding objects that accord with one’s wishes and bring benefit, or those that oppose one and cause harm—it is for this reason it says, "You now," and so forth.

Since these opposing and conforming conditions, as well as their benefits and harms, are not of a uniform category, it says, "the two manifest and drive you about. Thus, one should know that the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*) is likewise your own deluded thought;
therefore, the conclusion of the answer states, "it is named," and so forth. As for "empty clarity": sensation is the act of receiving and experiencing.

It functions as follows: either it perceives favorable objects as pleasant sensation (*sukha-vedanā*), or it perceives adverse objects as painful sensation (*duḥkha-vedanā*), or it perceives neutral objects as neither-painful-nor-pleasant sensation (*aduḥkhāsukha-vedanā*);
this is called "empty, pervasive, and clear hearing. The third [point], "interfusion," refers to the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).

The section beginning with "By you" (*yena tvaṃ*) explains this clarity; the section beginning with "Then you" (*tatas tvaṃ*) provides the concluding response. Regarding the first part, "By you" (*yena tvaṃ*) refers to perception (*saṃjñā*).

Thought is not the same as the physical body, and the physical body is not the same as thought. One rejects the physical body and follows after thought and sensation, which is why it is said, "Your body is equal [to thought].
It is not only the body that follows thought; the mind is made to conform to it as well, which is why it is said, "The arising of the mind is equal [to thought].
When awake, they are likewise equal—what is called "binding thoughts by day and racing through dreams at night. This correctly explains the mind.

[This refers to] birth and so forth. Thus, one knows that the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*) is likewise your own false imagination. Therefore, the conclusion states: "It is you yourselves.
Regarding "interfusion" (*yōtsū*): perception takes the grasping of marks as its meaning; the mark is the object-condition (*ālambana*), while perception is the subjective condition (*ālambaka*).

However, the mark does not exist by itself; it exists entirely because of perception. This is what is meant by "interfusion and thorough penetration. Fourth, "the obscure and hidden" refers to mental formations (*saṃskāra*).

The section beginning with "The principle of transformation" (*huàlǐ*) below explains [the nature of] the *skandha* of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*). The section beginning with "Then you... (*zé rǔ*) below provides the concluding answer.

Regarding the first part, the phrase "the principle of transformation," etc., clarifies the subtle and continuous shifting characteristics of the *skandha* of formations. The passage beginning with "Ānanda," etc., demonstrates that the *skandha* of formations is fundamentally illusory, and that its very substance shifts—manifesting as the growth of nails and so forth.
Thus, one knows that the *skandha* of formations is likewise your own deluded thought; therefore, this is the concluding answer.

"Clouds" refers to you all. As for "the obscure and hidden": their movement takes "transmigration" as its meaning; because the principle of transformation is inexhaustible, life after life is endless.
That which people neither see nor know is termed "obscure, profound, and hidden. "The five *wangxiang*" refers to the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*).
Furthermore, when you explain "clarity," it serves as a response to the preceding summary of "stillsness" and so forth. This explanation of clarity is twofold; first—
Furthermore, from "Moreover, you... below, the characteristics of consciousness are clearly elucidated. From "Ānanda, secondly... below, delusive thought is shown again. Regarding the first part:

"Both recollection and mindfulness are absent" means that since a long period of time has passed, it is not only the delusion that is absent, but even the mindfulness that recalls it is likewise absent.
In the middle [of the flow], it is so rapid that it cannot be seen; it seems as if it has suddenly ceased, yet it is not that there is no flow—it simply seems as if there is none.

"If it were not equal" serves to distinguish the true from the false and clarify the delusion. "Middle" refers to the long-term habituation; the character for "thread" (*sūtra*) implies that the meaning is also threaded through.

Thus, you should know that your *vijñāna-skandha* (consciousness aggregate) is likewise your own false imagination. Therefore, the conclusion states: "Then the limpid," and so forth. "Limpid" (*zhan*).
This is a delusory stillness, not the perfect stillness. "Entanglement" (wangxiang) means appearing to exist while appearing not to exist.
"Inversion" (dian-dao) means that because one does not know the truth, one calls it false; this is termed "inversion. Thus, the three knots can be clearly seen.
Regarding the second response within the section on "Answering Concerning the Elements" (*dhātu*), the phrase "You now... and so forth is a restatement of the previous question as a response.

"Element" (*dhātu*) refers here to cause (*hetu*), and also to lineage (*gotra*). This is like the meaning previously explained regarding how that which is produced by the eye takes the eye as its element.

Generally, the followers of the Hīnayāna know only that form (*rūpa*) is an element, but do not know that emptiness (*śūnyatā*) is also an element; even up to knowing only that deluded stillness is an element, they do not know...
The "perfectly still" (*yuan-zhan*) is also a realm (*dhātu*); that, however, is shallow rather than deep. As for what is clarified here, both form and emptiness are realms;
even the two kinds of perfect stillness—the delusory and the true—are all realms. This is deep rather than shallow.
Furthermore, within the five aggregates (*skandha*), one may consider form to be shallow and emptiness to be deep, and so on up to the delusory [stillness].

This distinguishes between the shallow and the profound. Therefore, it is stated: "Depending on the shallowness or depth of the *dhātu*. The phrase "only form" and below correctly clarifies the limit, which is simply the boundary of the *dhātu*.
Regarding "the tranquil entry merges with the tranquil": the former "tranquil" refers to false tranquility, the essence of the six consciousnesses;
the latter "tranquil" refers to perfect tranquility, the true essence of the eight consciousnesses as the primordial luminous self-nature.
The third response, "Eliminating [Ignorance]," is divided into two parts. First, "These five" refers to the phenomena (*dharma*). Second, "I have already" refers to the analogy.

Regarding "In the phenomena, existence arises from consciousness": this means that when the five aggregates first arise, they exist because of consciousness, continuing down to the point where form exists because of sensation (*vedanā*).
Regarding "Cessation proceeds by removing form": this means that when the five aggregates are about to cease, the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) ceases first, and then...
The aggregate of sensation ceases; continuing in this manner until the aggregate of formations ceases, and only then does the aggregate of consciousness cease.

To illustrate this with a metaphor: its arising is like a person putting on clothes, gradually increasing from the inside out; its cessation is like a person taking off clothes, gradually diminishing from the outside in.

First, the arising and ceasing are discussed in terms of both the reverse and the direct order, while the actual process of their elimination is precisely pointed out according to phenomena and principle. First, regarding...

Regarding "eliminating them together through principle": one is able to realize that the substance of the aggregate of form (*rūpaskandha*) is the wondrous *tathatā* nature of the Tathāgata-garbha mind.
There is no insentient thing that is not destroyed, and no phenomenon that is not established. How, then, could there still be the delusive thoughts of the five aggregates to be found?

Therefore, it is said, "In principle, they are equal. Second, regarding "exhausting them according to the sequence of phenomena": because their arising proceeds from a sequential order, their ceasing likewise proceeds [from that same sequence].
They are extinguished in succession. For example, the three delusions, though belonging to the Perfect and Sudden teaching, must necessarily be severed in a sequence of first, middle, and last.

It is also like the process of taking off clothes. Therefore, it is said that "the phenomena are not equal [to the principle]. However, this does not mean that emptiness comes first, followed by the provisional, and finally the Middle, as if they were sequential stages.
Such phenomena are not external to the principle; such a principle is not external to the phenomena. This is the principle...

The phenomena and their underlying reality are identical; thus, the ultimate and the conventional are manifested simultaneously. This is also like the fact that the six [knots] do not obstruct their identity, nor does their identity obstruct the six.
In the analogy, the demonstration of the knots on the *kalpavṛkṣa* cloth refers to what was clarified in the section on "the six being resolved and the one vanishing.

The cloth symbolizes the fundamental luminosity of self-nature (*svabhāva*), while the knots symbolize the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If one considers the substance of the cloth, even "one" cannot be found; how then could there be "five"?
Now that these fetters exist, they must be untied, from the first up to the fifth. Thus, in principle, they are extinguished simultaneously;
in practice, they are exhausted sequentially—the meaning lies therein. Therefore, it is asked, "What are they? and so forth.

In this way, Ānanda asks by means of three points, and the Tathāgata answers by means of three points; there is nothing that is not made clear. Hence, below follows a section of concluding exhortation.
Regarding the second section on exhortation, the phrase "you should" and so forth refers to Ānanda’s prior request: "Clarify your mind and eyes to serve as eyes for the future.
Since each point has been explained above and his mind and eyes have already attained purity, it is said that "his mind has attained opening and penetration.
His own practice is thus perfected, and he ought in turn to transform others; therefore, he is exhorted to transmit this teaching to those who will come after him.

This causes consciousness and the other aggregates to emerge; it correctly sets forth the benefits of propagating [the teaching] in the final age. "Deeply wearying of self-arising" is a textual corruption;
it should read "self-arising deeply wearying. Whether it be the primary practice or the auxiliary path, the section on the orthodox doctrine is hereby concluded.
From "Ānanda, furthermore, there are others who depart" onwards is the third section on the circulation [of the teaching].
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he necessarily desires it to be transmitted forever and ever; it is certainly not intended merely to benefit a single region or a single period.
He intends that all beings in the future—throughout all heavens and human realms, in other directions and this land alike—shall without exception receive his teachings and realize the eternal.
This section on "Abiding in the True Mind" is broadly divided into two parts. First, the Tathāgata’s exhortation for circulation, addressed to Ānanda and others.

Second, the scribe’s conclusion regarding circulation, beginning with "The Buddha spoke," etc. The first part is further divided into two. First, the exhortation to eliminate evil, beginning with "Ānanda," etc.

Second, the exhortation to produce goodness, beginning with "Ānanda," etc. The first of these is further divided into three. First, citing the standard of comparison, which begins with "Ānanda," etc. Second, citing... [text continues]

Regarding the comparison: first, from "The Buddha said" onwards; second, the actual comparison, from "one obtains merit" onwards. The first [section] also has two parts: first, the question by Ānanda and others;
second, the answer by Ānanda and others. Within the first part: "Pervading everywhere," etc., refers to the fact that the objects bestowed were precious and extensive.
"Holding them," etc., refers to the fact that the persons to whom they were offered were venerable and numerous. "With a mind free from... refers to the capacity of the giver.
When the mind is focused and earnest, blessings should naturally be abundant; thus Ānanda replied that it was "equal to empty space.
Second, regarding the comparison presented: the phrase "all Buddhas and Tathāgatas" is used to manifest his extraordinary merit, first demonstrating that the speaker is free from falsehood.
The phrase "transforming those in hell" refers to the fact that he has cultivated the perfect penetration of the ear-organ.

In this Dharma-gate, there is nothing that does not employ the perfect illumination of the three contemplations to reveal the wondrous realm of the three truths. How, then, could any sinful karma exist?
This is what is meant by the dissolution of the six sense-objects, which, upon a single thought, are transformed into supreme knowledge and vision. This is the third correct comparison.

Regarding the phrase "attaining equal merit": because that which is expressed [by these teachings] is such that there is not a single thing that is not the Tathāgatagarbha-nature pervading the Dharma-realm.
Since it is called the "Tathāgatagarbha-nature," what dharma would not be fully endowed with its primordial luminosity?
Furthermore, since it is said to "pervade the Dharma-realm," where would it not be omnipresent? Thus, through this perfect pervasiveness, one knows the Tathāgatagarbha-nature.

Since it is already all-pervasive throughout the dharma-realm, then even if the objects previously offered by others were noble and extensive, and the persons to whom they were offered were honored and numerous, these could not themselves transcend the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha and its pervasiveness throughout the dharma-realm.
Second, regarding the exhortation to cultivate wholesome qualities: because one has realized that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is fundamentally empty yet perfectly complete, if...
If one recites according to this, the merit obtained will likewise be so. Therefore, even if the Tathāgata were to explain it extensively for an entire kalpa, he would not yet have exhausted it.
To rely on my teaching is to rely on the sūtras to open up the perfect understanding (*pariniṣpanna-adhigama*).

To practice the Way according to the teaching is to rely on that understanding to give rise to perfect conduct (*pariniṣpanna-caryā*). To directly realize Bodhi is to rely on that conduct to enter into perfect realization (*pariniṣpanna-sākṣātkriyā*).
Thus, one should know that the *Yijou* (依我) section exhorts the circulation of the sutra of ultimate and steadfast teaching;

the *Rujiao* (如教) section exhorts the circulation of the sutra of ultimate and steadfast practice; and the *Zhicheng* (直成) section exhorts the circulation of the sutra of ultimate and steadfast principle.
This is the Right Path (*samyag-mārga*). There is no further section to exhort its circulation, as it is the essence within the factors conducive to enlightenment (*bodhipakṣya-dharma*).
By investigating the seven destinies, one comprehensively elucidates the sūtras concerning the five aggregates and so forth.

Whether as primary or auxiliary, these serve to circulate [the teaching], and the ultimate, firm name for this whole resides therein. Thus, it is no longer necessary to state that the compiler concludes with the transmission;
the underlying intent is already evident.
The Secret Record of the Great Buddha-Uṣṇīṣa Śūraṅgama, Scroll Ten (End)
